<meta>This page describes a 1488 edition of Isidore of Seville's works, printed by Peter Löslein in Venice. It follows the bibliographic description of the physical volume and provides an overview of the "Etymologies," the most famous medieval encyclopedia.</meta>

# PETER LÖSLEIN VENICE

## ISIDORE. Etymologies. On the Supreme Good. <note>Original Latin: Etymologiae. De summo bono.</note>

->1488.<-

Hain 9279; B.M.C., part V, p. 379. <note>These are standard reference numbers used by librarians to identify specific editions of early printed books.</note>

Printed with gothic type, in two columns. It has 136 leaves, the fifth blank; leaves 6-106 and 109-136 are numbered as 1-101 and 1-28; from the Library’s

<column-break/>

copy the blank leaf is missing. The size of a leaf is 286 by 188 mm., and the text in a column measures 232 by 68 mm. The initials are in red.

<column-break/>

The “Etymologies” is an encyclopedia of all knowledge. It was written between 622–633 A.D., during the last years of the author’s life. As the preface emphasizes, the work was the product of life-long reading. This encyclopedia is, indeed, as comprehensive as any of the similar Roman works; its information, however, is superficial, based on bookish knowledge and never on personal observation.

The title expresses the nature of the work. Isidore believed that by explaining the origins of words he could get nearest to their meaning. His encyclopedia is a dictionary, containing a vast number of derivations, many of which are ingenious while others are amusing. Yet Isidore himself warned against a blind confidence in words. His chapter “On etymology” may best elucidate his view, providing also a good example of his method; here is an excerpt:

> “Etymology is the derivation of words, when the force of a verb or a noun is ascertained through interpretation. This Aristotle called a <term>symbol</term> <note>original Greek: σύμβολον</note>, and Cicero called it a *notation* <note>original Latin: notatio</note>, because it explains the names of things; as, for example, *river* <note>original Latin: flumen</note> is so called from *to flow* <note>original Latin: fluere</note>, because it arose from flowing.
>
> “A knowledge of etymology is often necessary, for, when you see whence a name has come, you grasp its force more quickly. For every consideration of a thing is clearer when its etymology is known. Not all names, however, were given by the ancients in accordance with nature, but certain also according to whim, just as we sometimes give slaves and estates names according to our fancy . . .
>
> “Etymologies are given in accordance with cause, as *kings* <note>original Latin: reges</note> from *to rule* <note>original Latin: regere</note>, that is *to act rightly* <note>original Latin: recte agere</note>; or origin, as *man* <note>original Latin: homo</note>, because he is from the earth <note>original Latin: humus</note>; or from contraries, as *mud* <note>original Latin: lutum</note> from *to wash* <note>original Latin: lavare</note> — since mud is not clean — and *sacred grove* <note>original Latin: lucus</note>, because being shady it has little light <note>original Latin: parvum luceat</note>.
>
> “Certain words also were formed by derivation from other words; as *prudent* from *prudence*. Certain ones also from cries, as *jackdaw* <note>original Latin: graculus</note> from *chattering* <note>original Latin: garrulitas</note>. Certain ones also have sprung from a Greek origin, and have changed over into the Latin, as *forest* <note>original Latin: silva</note>. (Elsewhere Isidore explains that *forest* or *xilva* is derived from <term>wood</term> <note>original Greek: ξύλον, transliterated as xylon</note>.)”

The “Etymologies” is divided into twenty books, treating of grammar (1), rhetoric and logic (2), arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy (3), medicine (4), law and chronology (5), theology (6-8), languages, races, empires (9), human anatomy and physiology (11), zoology (12), cosmography and physical geography (13-14), architecture and surveying (15), mineralogy (16), agriculture (17), military science (18), ships and buildings (19), and of provisions and utensils (20). The tenth book consists of a number of words arranged in an alphabetical order, without any organization of the material according to subject-matter.

Isidore’s indebtedness to the Roman encyclopedists is obvious. Varro and the elder Pliny were his chief sources, though he was acquainted with the writings of many other Roman writers as well as with the works of the Church Fathers. His influence during the Middle Ages was immense; all the later medieval encyclopedias were modelled upon his work. But even in his time he was recognised as the greatest scholar of the age. In his own work “On Illustrious Men,” <note>Original Latin: De viris illustribus</note> Bishop Braulio, his friend, inserted a note after his death: “In him antiquity reasserted itself — or rather our time created in him a picture of the wisdom of antiquity . . .”

The theological writings of Isidore are also numerous. Among these “On the Supreme Good” (often called the “Three Books of Sentences”) <note>Original Latin: Libri tres Sententiae</note> is one of the best known. The work is based on the “Moralia” of Gregory the Great.

<summary>This page describes a 1488 Venetian edition of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, explaining its role as a foundational medieval encyclopedia that sought to understand the world through the linguistic origins of words.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the index of Isidore of Seville’s final book (likely Book 20 of the Etymologies, mentioned on the previous page) into the introductory correspondence between Isidore and his friend and colleague, Braulio of Zaragoza. These letters serve as a preface to the Etymologies, detailing the work's creation and Braulio’s role in encouraging its completion.</meta>

# Here begins the letter of Isidore the Younger, Bishop of Seville, to Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza.
<note>Isidore "the Younger" (c. 560–636 AD) is the famous scholar-bishop of Visigothic Spain; he is called "the younger" to distinguish him from other saints of the same name.</note>

To my lord and man of God, Bishop Braulio. From Isidore. With all my heart I have desired to see your face now, and I wish that God would fulfill my vow at some time before I die. For the present, however, I pray that you would commend me to God in your prayers, so that He may fulfill my hope in this life and grant me a place in your company in the blessedness to come. [Written] by his own hand. Pray for us, most blessed lord and brother.

# Braulio to Isidore.

To my lord, and truly my lord: and to Isidore, the chosen of Christ and the greatest of bishops. From Braulio, the useless servant of God’s saints. O pious lord and most excellent of men, my inquiry is late, and the opportunity to write has been given to me tardily: for, as my sins required, I have been hindered not only by the evil of barrenness or want, but also by the plague of a deadly pestilence and the horrible onslaught of enemies <note>original: "hostilitatis". Braulio is referring to the frequent wars and plagues in 7th-century Spain</note> which prevented me from seeking you. Now, however, even if worn down by a thousand necessities and a thousand cares, after a long time of misery—as if awakened, so to speak, from the heaviness of a wicked sleep—I presume to offer this greeting of health through these words of my suggestion. Prostrate in humility of heart and body, I beseech the most excellent power of your blessedness, that you command that this particular servant—whom you have always accepted under that pious gaze of your sacred worthiness—be commended to your care until the end. For I also, as Christ knows, am shaken by such great grief because for such a long and vast time I have not deserved to see your presence. But I hope in Him who does not forget to show mercy, nor does He reject us in the end, for He will hear the prayer of the poor man and represent my wretched self to your sight.

I truly suggest and ask with every kind of supplication that you command the **Book of Etymologies** <term>Etymologiarum: Isidore's massive 20-volume encyclopedia of all human knowledge, which became the standard reference of the Middle Ages</term> (which we have heard is now finished, by the Lord's favor) to be sent to your servant, mindful of your promise. For as I am aware, you toiled there in great part at your servant’s request. And therefore, show yourself generous to me first, so that you may be held both happy and first among the assemblies of the saints.

I also ask that the record of your **Synod** <note>original: "synodi". Likely referring to one of the Councils of Toledo, where Visigothic laws and church canons were established</note>—in which the situary <note>original: "situarius". A rare term, possibly referring to a local official or a specific legal placement</note> of your examination was found, if not purified, at least refined by fire—be sent to us quickly by your son the Lord King at your urging. For our city has also claimed the glory of this suggestion, because there is much need for the truth to be thoroughly investigated in the council.

For the rest, I entreat the mercy of the most high Creator that He may command the crown of your blessedness to be preserved for a long time, for the integrity of the faith and the state of His church. May the most sacred Trinity, through your prayers, render me protected by the grace of your intercession amidst the various and innumerable dangers of this barking world, and keep me safe from every storm of sin, hidden in the bosom of your memory. [Written] by his own hand. I, Braulio, servant of the Lord, shall enjoy you, Isidore, in the Lord—a lamp that burns and does not fade.

<column-break/>

# Isidore to Braulio.

To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio. From Isidore. Because I have learned that you are well, I have given thanks to Christ. I only wish that I could look upon and see the one whose health I have acknowledged in this body. As for what has happened to me, I shall reveal it because of my sins: since I was not worthy to read your eloquent words, as soon as I received your **writing tablet** <term>pictarium: a small wooden or wax tablet used for brief correspondence or notes</term>, a royal servant came to me. I gave that tablet to my chamberlain, and immediately hurried to the Prince <note>Referring to the Visigothic King</note> so that I might later read and reply to it. Having returned from the King’s palace, I not only failed to find your writings, but also whatever else was in the camp perished. Therefore, the Lord knows: my luxury was my merit, since I did not read your eloquence. But I ask that whenever the opportunity arises, you write back to me. Do not take away the grace of your word, so that what I lost through my own fault, I may receive again through your grace. [Written] by his own hand. Pray for us, most blessed lord.

# Braulio to Isidore.

To my lord, and truly my lord: and to Isidore, the chosen of Christ and the greatest of bishops. From Braulio, the useless servant of God’s saints.

The inner and spiritual man is usually filled with joy when the inquiry of a lover joins itself to him. For this reason, it is my wish, my most reverend one—unless the wall of my sins stands in the way—both to embrace you kindly in my inquiry and to receive the slander of my complaints patiently. For I perform both the duty of inquiry and direct the causes of my needs to you against you. I pray, prostrate at the height of your apostleship at the start of this dictation, that you admit this most kindly to your hearing. Though I waver at the objection of slander where there is the intercession of tears, yet there must be both tearful slanders and slanderous tears, if only by the licentious presumption of love for both, and not by the boldness of arrogance.

From here, I shall now begin my case. If I am not mistaken, seven years have circled through time since I remember asking for the books of the **Origins** <note>original: "originum". Another title for the Etymologies</note> compiled by you; and in various and diverse ways I was frustrated when present, and you wrote nothing back to me while I was away. With the delay of the subject, asserting sometimes that they were not yet finished, sometimes not yet written, sometimes that my letters had been intercepted, and opposing many other things, we have reached this very day, and my mind remains without the effect of its petition.

For this reason, I will turn prayers into a complaint, so that what I could not obtain by supplication, I may be able to achieve by provoking you with a grievance. For often a loud cry is known to benefit a beggar. Therefore, I ask you, lord, why do you not grant what you are asked?

Know one thing: I will not let it go as if you imagine I do not want what is denied. But I will seek, and seek insistently, until I either receive it or draw it out at the command of the most pious Redeemer: "Seek and you shall find," and adding: "Knock and it shall be opened to you." I have sought and I seek, even now I knock. Whence I also cry out that you may open. For the discovery of this argument consoles me: that you who despised the one asking, will perhaps hear the one complaining.

Hence, therefore, I bring to your knowledge things that a fool does not know how to suggest with boasting...

Therefore, receive these cries of reproach. Why, I ask, do you still hold back the distribution of talents and the dispensing of food entrusted to you? Now, release your hand: share with the households, lest they perish from the pangs of hunger. You know what the creditor will demand of you when he returns. Whatever you give to us will not diminish your own store. Remember that a great multitude was satisfied by small loaves, and that the leftover fragments exceeded the original size of the bread. Or do you think the gift conferred upon you was given for you alone? It is both yours and ours; it is common property, not private. And who would be so insane as to presume that you should rejoice in private over that which you know how to enjoy blamelessly as common property? For since God has granted you the management <note>original: "œconomiam"</note> of His treasury and the riches of the salvation of wisdom and knowledge, why do you not pour it out with a generous hand—that which you do not diminish by giving? Or, as in the members of our Heavenly Head <note>The "Body of Christ" metaphor from 1 Corinthians 12.</note>, each person possesses what he has not received in such a way that he knows what he has is to be possessed for the sake of another—do you perhaps exist as a miser toward us because you find nothing in us to take back in return? But if you give what is to be had, you bring back the fruit of reward from Him. If indeed you bestow it upon one who has nothing, you satisfy the evangelical commands, so that He may pay you back in the retribution of the just. 

Therefore, I feel a pang of conscience, because I feel nothing good within me that can be shared. Yet we are commanded through charity to serve one another, and that each one should administer the grace he has received to the other, like good stewards of the manifold grace of God; and just as God has divided to each a measure of faith in the single framework of the body's members, so ought he to communicate those things to the other parts. For one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each as He wills. Hence, I run to the one and peculiar help I have left: namely, to an intrusive persistence, since I am destitute of friendship and decorated by no grace of the honorable members. Therefore, hear my voice across so many intervening lands. Pay, pay back what you owe! For you are a servant—a servant of Christ and of Christians—so that you may be the greatest of us all; do not disdain to impress the grace of the present knowledge conferred upon you for our sake into our thirsty souls and those tortured by the hunger for knowledge. I am not even a foot that I might run to the tasks enjoined upon me, nor can I obey the belly of the Church—that is, the judge of the members—with a running obedience, nor can I please the head by being a helpful participant. Indeed, even if I know myself to be among the less honorable members, let it suffice that because it is established that you have received from the Head, it is worthy to pour it out through me; nor should you say you have no need of me, however small I am, for I have been redeemed by the blood of Christ. For the head does not say to the feet, "You are not necessary to me," since those members of the body which seem to be weaker are more necessary; and those which are thought to be more ignoble members of the body, we clothe with more abundant honor; and our less honest parts have greater honesty. So it is that our Creator and Dispenser distributes all things, so that when the divine gifts which one does not perceive in oneself are given to another to be possessed, charity may be increased. Finally, the manifold grace is then well-distributed when the gift received is also entrusted to those who do not have it, because for his sake

to whom it is bestowed, it is considered given. This chapter of the Apostle <note>Referring again to St. Paul's writings on the body of the Church.</note>, which I have partly cited, your prudent charity knows best applies to this King; and no one is unaware that you, without doubt, know better whatever is rumored concerning the King. Therefore, this alone remains, which I also greatly ask: that you grant what is requested; and if not for my sake, then at least for the sake of that charity bestowed by God. For the sake of this charity we are commanded both to know and to offer all things, and without it, all things are nothing. 

But if I have poured out anything superfluous, or anything negligently, or anything with too little humility, or rather uselessly in what I have said, I ask that you receive it all with kindness; forgive it all; and pray that God may forgive it all. Therefore, I also make this known: I ask from you, my lord, the books of the *Etymologies* <note>Braulio is requesting the *Etymologiae*, Isidore’s massive encyclopedic work which Braulio eventually helped edit and publish after Isidore's death.</note>. Even if they are held by many already in worn or chewed-up condition, I ask that you deign to send them to me transcribed whole, corrected, and well-fitted, lest in my snatched greed I be forced to take up vices in place of virtues. 

As for me, I desire that you lack for nothing, and may those rewards be offered freely; so that the condescension of your kindness may command us in that which we are able and strong, provided only that you use our service—or rather, that you enjoy the charity which is God. For I have many questions concerning the sacred and divine pages, the explanation of which the light of your heart might reveal to me, if you command it to shine upon us and unlock the obscurities of the divine law. Nor, if I receive those things which I seek, will I remain silent about them; you unlock this way of gaining confidence. Since you have not pierced me with the stings of shame in this first encounter, and you have given a place of pardon to my ignorance, do not reject the one you loved, however undeserving; for it seems very shameful and base if one who found charity from him whom he loved should recede from it before being satisfied. 

With the devotion of my service, I offer the rights of greeting, and I ask the piety of your most holy power to deign to pray for me; so that you may win over my soul, which tosses daily in evils, through your intercession, and lead it to the port of eternal tranquility, rescued from miseries and scandals. It has been sweet for me to speak to you for a long time, as if I were seeing your face in person. Therefore I have not guarded against wordiness, and perhaps I have run into rashness; but I had to do this or the other, if only so that what you wished to give through humility, you might at least grant through my noisy persistence. See how much boldness the benevolence of your grace has given me! And therefore, if anything in this has displeased you, let it be imputed to the loving author, so that it may take away fear. For "perfect charity casts out fear" <note>1 John 4:18.</note>. 

Relying also on a special grace, I suggest to my special lord, in whom the strengths of the holy Church consist, that because our Metropolitan Eusebius <note>Eusebius was the Archbishop of Tarragona; his death necessitated the appointment of a successor.</note> has departed, you should have the care of mercy. Suggest this to your "little son," our lord <note>Likely the Visigothic King, whom Braulio refers to as Isidore's spiritual student or protege.</note>, that he may appoint someone to that place whose holiness of doctrine may be a model of life for the rest. I commend this present son <note>The messenger carrying the letter.</note> to your most blessed power in all things, so that we may deserve to be enlightened by your eloquence through him, both concerning these things we have suggested here and those things we asked about above.

# The first book of the Etymologies of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, begins.
## On Discipline and Art. Chapter i.

**D**iscipline <term>Discipina: from the Latin "discere," to learn</term> took its name from "learning." Whence it can also be called "knowledge." For "to know" (*scire*) is named from "learning" (*discere*), because none of us knows except what he has learned. Alternatively, it is called "discipline" because it is "full of learning" (*discit plena*). "Art" (*Ars*), however, is so called because it consists of the precepts and rules of "skill" (*artis*). Others say this word is drawn from the Greek <note>original: "αττὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς" (*apo tēs aretēs*)</note>, that is, "from virtue," which they called knowledge. Plato and Aristotle wished there to be this difference between "art" and "discipline": saying that art is concerned with those things that can be otherwise than they are; whereas discipline is that which deals with those things that cannot happen otherwise. For when something is discussed with true reasoning, it will be a discipline; when something plausible and based on opinion is treated, it shall have the name of an art.

## On the Seven Liberal Arts. Chapter ii.

**T**here are seven disciplines of the liberal arts <note>The "Liberal Arts" were the core curriculum of medieval education, considered "free" (liberal) because they were suitable for a free person's mind.</note>. First is **Grammar**, that is, the skill of speaking. Second is **Rhetoric**, which, because of the brilliance and abundance of its eloquence, is considered especially necessary in civil matters. Third is **Dialectic**, also known as **Logic**, which separates truth from falsehood through most subtle disputes. Fourth is **Arithmetic**, which contains the causes and divisions of numbers. Fifth is **Music**, which consists of poems and songs. Sixth is **Geometry**, which encompasses the measurements and dimensions of the earth. Seventh is **Astronomy**, which contains the law of the stars.

## On Common Letters. Chapter iii.

<column-break/>

**T**he foundations of the art of grammar are "common letters," which scribes and accountants follow. The study of these is like the infancy of the grammatical art, which is why Varro calls it "literation." Letters are signs of things and symbols of words, which have such power that the words of those who are absent speak to us without a voice. For words are introduced through the eyes, not the ears. The use of letters was invented for the sake of the memory of things; for lest they flee into oblivion, they are bound by letters. In such a variety of things, not everything could be learned by hearing, nor could it be held in the memory. Letters (*litterae*) are so called as if they were "road-showers" (*legiterae*), because they provide a path (*iter*) for those reading (*legentibus*), or because they are repeated (*iterentur*) in reading. Latin and Greek letters appear to have arisen from the Hebrews. Among them, it was first called *Aleph*; then, from a similar sound, it was drawn among the Greeks as *Alpha*, and thence among the Latins as *A*. For the founder of the letters created the letter by translating the similar sound from the other language, so that we may know the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages and letters. But the Hebrews use twenty-two elements of letters according to the books of the Old Testament. The Greeks have 24. The Latins, proceeding between both languages, have 23 elements. The letters of the Hebrews began from the Law <margin>Moses, Abraham, Isis</margin> through Moses; those of the Syrians and Chaldeans through Abraham. Whence they agree with the Hebrew in both number and sound, differing only in their character shapes. Isis the queen, daughter of Inachis, coming from Greece into Egypt, discovered the Egyptian letters and handed them over to the Egyptians. Among the Egyptians, however, the priests had one set of letters, and the common people another. <margin>Lucan</margin> The Phoenicians first discovered the use of Greek letters, whence Lucan says: "The Phoenicians first, if fame be believed, dared to signify the enduring voice with unrefined figures." Hence it is that the headings of books are written in Phoenician color <note>original: "phoeniceo colore," referring to red ink or minium</note>, because letters had their beginning from them. Cadmus, son of Agenor, was the first to bring 17 Greek <margin>Cadmus, Palamedes, Simonides, Pythagoras</margin> letters from Phoenicia into Greece: <note>original: alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta, eta, iota, kappa, lambda, mu, nu, omicron, pi, rho, sigma, tau, phi</note>. To these, Palamedes added three during the Trojan War: <note>original: H, chi, omega</note>. After him, Simonides likewise added three others: <note>original: xi, theta, psi</note>. Pythagoras of Samos was the first to form the letter **Y** as an example of human life. Its lower stem signifies the first age of life, which is uncertain and has not yet given itself to either vices or virtues. But the "fork in the road" <note>The "Bivium" or Pythagorean Y, representing the choice between a hard path to virtue and an easy path to ruin.</note> which remains begins from adolescence: its right part is steep, but tending toward a blessed life; the left is easier, but leading to downfall and <margin>Persius</margin> destruction. Concerning this, Persius says: "And to you, the letter which spreads the Samian branches has shown the path rising by the right-hand limit." There are five mystical letters among the Greeks. First is **Y**, which signifies human life, <margin>Significance of Y</margin> about which we have just spoken. Second is **Theta** ($\theta$), which <margin>On $\theta$...</margin> signifies death. For judges used to place this letter against the names of those they sentenced to punishment; and it is called theta <note>original: "απὸ τοῦ θανάτου" (*apo tou thanatou*)</note>, that is, "from death." Whence it also has a "missile" through its middle <note>the horizontal bar in $\theta$</note>, which is the sign of death. Concerning which a certain man said: "O theta, a letter much more unhappy than all others." The third is **Tau** (T), demonstrating the figure of the Lord's <margin><image-desc>A simple cross or T-shape.</image-desc></margin> cross. Whence in Hebrew it is interpreted as a "sign." Concerning which it was said to the angel in Ezekiel: "Go through the midst of Jerusalem and mark a Tau on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan." Christ claims the remaining two for Himself: the first and the last <note>Alpha and Omega.</note>.

# Book I

**Column 1:**

For He himself is the beginning and the end, saying: I am the Alpha and the Omega <note>original: "alpha ⁊ ω"</note>. For as they run toward each other, it rolls from A to Ω and then unfolds again from Ω to A, so that the Lord might show in Himself both the beginning's course to the end, and the end's course back to the beginning. Now, all letters among the Greeks and Hebrews are combined to also form numbers. For among them, the letter *alpha* (α) is called "one" in number. Where *beta* (β) is written, it is called "two"; where *gamma* (γ) is written, it is called "three" in that same number; where *delta* (δ) is written, it is called "four." And thus all letters among them have numerical values. The Latins, however, do not count numbers by their letters; these only compose words—with certain exceptions that demonstrate numbers by their shape: such as **I** for one, **C** for a hundred, **D** for five hundred, **L** for fifty, **M** for a thousand, **V** for five, and **X** for ten. The letter **X**, which in its shape signifies the cross, also demonstrates the number ten. The nymph Carmentis first handed down Latin letters to the Italians. She was called Carmentis because she sang of future things in songs <note>original: "carminibus," a pun on her name</note>. Otherwise, her proper name was Nicostrata.
<margin>1.8</margin>
<margin>nicostrata</margin>
Letters are either common or liberal. They are called "common" because many use them in common, such as for reading and writing. They are called "liberal" <note>term: "liberales," meaning suitable for a free person (liber) or a scholar</note> because only those who compose books know them, having mastered the correct method of speaking and composing. There is a twofold mode for letters. For they are divided principally into two parts: into vowels and consonants. Vowels are those which are emitted with a direct opening of the throat without any collision, and are called "vowels" because they fulfill the voice <note>original: "vocem impleant"</note> on their own and make a syllable by themselves, with no consonant adhering to them. Consonants are those which are produced by the various movements of the tongue or the pressing of the lips; they are called "consonants" because they do not sound on their own, but sound together <note>original: "consonant"</note> with joined vowels. These are divided into two parts: into semivowels and mutes. They are called "semivowels" because they have a certain half-sound <note>original: "semifonum"</note> of the vowels. They begin, indeed, from the vowel 'e' and end in a natural sound, such as **f**, **l**, **m**. They are called "mutes," however, because they never break forth unless vowels are placed after them. For if you take away the final vowel sound from them, only a muffled murmur of the letter will sound, such as **b**, **c**, **d**. Vowels, semivowels, and mutes were called "sounds," "half-sounds," and "non-sounds" <note>original: "sonae, semisonae, ⁊ insonae"</note> by the ancients. Among the vowels, **i** and **u** have various meanings among the grammarians. For sometimes they are vowels, sometimes semivowels, and sometimes they stand in the middle. They are vowels because when placed alone they make syllables and are joined to other consonants. They are considered consonants because sometimes they have vowels placed after them in the same syllables, such as in *Iuno* or *vares*, and they act as consonants. They are called "middle" because naturally, when alone, they have a middle sound, as in *illius* or *unius*. Joined to others, they sound thicker, as in *Ianus* or *vanus*. For they sound one way when placed alone, and another when joined. The letter **Y**, moreover, is sometimes called "double" because whenever it is found in meter between two vowels, it is treated as two consonants, as in *Troia*. For its sound is doubled there. The letter **U**, when following **Q**, is sometimes nothing, because in that position it is neither a vowel nor a consonant, as in *quis*. For it is not a vowel because another vowel follows; it is not a consonant because a consonant precedes. Therefore, since it is neither vowel nor consonant, it is undoubtedly nothing. This same letter is also called a "digamma" <note>original: "digāmon"</note> by the Greeks when it is joined to itself and other vowels.

**Column 2:**

It is called "digamma" because it is double, like the letter **F**, which has a double *gamma*. Grammariams wished for joined vowels to be called "digamma" after this likeness, as in *votum* or *virgo*. Among the semivowels, some are called "liquids" <note>original: "liquidae"</note> for this reason: because sometimes, when placed after other consonants in a single syllable, they fail and are excluded from meter. Two of these are liquid among the Latins: **l** and **r**, as in *fragor* and *flatus*. The remaining ones, **m** and **n**, are liquid among the Greeks, as in *Mnestheus*. Now, the ancient writing of the Latins consisted of seventeen letters. From this, they are also named Latin by that logic, namely because they begin with the vowel 'e' and end in a mute sound (as the semivowels do), or because they begin from their own sound and end in a vowel (as the mutes do). In the beginning there were seventeen: **a b c d e f g i l m n o p r s t v**. The letter **h**, however, was added later only for the sake of aspiration. Hence, it is thought by many to be an aspiration, not a letter, which is why it is called the "mark of aspiration," because it raises the voice. For aspiration is a sound raised more fully, the opposite of which is prosody, a sound evenly bent. Salvius the schoolmaster <note>original: "ludi magister"</note> later added the letter **k** to the Latins, so that he might make a distinction in sound between the two letters **c** and **q**. This letter is called "superfluous" because, except for the *Kalends*, it is judged unnecessary; for we express everything using **c**. The letter **q** is sounded neither by the Greeks nor the Hebrews; for no other language except Latin has this. It did not exist previously, which is why it too was called superfluous, because the ancients wrote everything using **c**. The letter **x** was not yet among the Latins until the time of Augustus, but instead they wrote **c** and **s**. Thus it is called "double" because it stands for **c** and **s**; hence it has its name composed from those same letters. Latinity borrowed two letters from the Greeks, **y** and **z**, specifically for Greek names. These were not written among the Romans until the time of Augustus; instead of **z**, they used two **s**'s, as in *hilarissar* <note>original: likely "hilarissat"</note>, and for **y**, they wrote **i**. Three things happen to every single letter: its **name**, what it is called; its **figure**, by what character it is marked; and its **power**, whether it is held to be a vowel or a consonant. Nature gave the power; will gave the order. By some, **order** is also added—that is, which comes before and which follows—so that **a** is first and **b** follows. Now, **a** is the first of the letters among all nations because it is the first to open the voice of those being born. Nations gave names to the letters from the sound of their own language, having noted and distinguished all sounds. For after they observed them, they imposed names and figures upon them. They formed the figures partly by choice and partly from the sound of the letters: for instance, **l** and **o**. One has a thin sound, and so it is a thin rod; the other has a fuller sound, just as its figure is full. The ancients distinguished between the figures of letters and the "apices" <note>term: "apex," a mark used to indicate vowel length or accent</note>. It is called an *apex* because it is far from the "feet" and is placed at the top <note>original: "cacumine"</note> of letters. For it is a lying line drawn evenly above the letter.

### Chapter IV: On Grammar

Grammar is the science of speaking correctly and the logic of writing; it is the origin and foundation of the liberal arts. In the disciplines, it was invented through common letters, so that those who have already learned their letters may know the logic of correct speech through it. Grammar takes its name from letters, for the Greeks call letters *grammata*. It is called an "art"...
<margin>Grammar</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the origins and classifications of the Latin alphabet, detailing the nature of vowels, consonants, and specific letter histories, before defining Grammar as the foundation of the liberal arts.</summary>
<keywords>alphabet, phonetics, Carmentis, vowels, consonants, semivowels, Roman numerals, Grammar, Isidore of Seville, historical linguistics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the foundations of language, transitioning from the mechanics of letters to the formal definition of grammar, speech, and the classification of nouns. [Grammar] exists because it consists of the precepts and rules of the art. Others say this word is drawn from the Greeks, *apo tes aretes* <note>original: "apo tes aretes," meaning from excellence or virtue</note>, that is, from virtue, which is what they called knowledge. **Speech** (*oratio*) is so named as if it were the "reason of the mouth" <note>original: "oris ratio"; Isidore uses this folk etymology to link the mouth (os) with reason (ratio)</note>. For to plead (*orare*) is to speak and to say. Moreover, speech is the context of words combined with meaning. Otherwise, speech without meaning is not truly speech, because it is not the reason of the mouth. Full speech consists of meaning, voice, and letters. Some count thirty divisions of the grammatical art: the eight parts of speech, the articulated voice, the letter, the syllable, feet, accents, punctuation marks, notes, orthography, analogy, etymology, glosses, differences, barbarisms, solecisms, faults, metaplasms, figures, tropes, prose, meter, fables, and histories.

### Chapter 5: On the parts of speech

<margin>Aristotle and Donatus</margin>
Aristotle first handed down two parts of speech: the noun and the verb. Then Donatus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian whose work became the standard textbook of the Middle Ages</note> defined eight. However, all of these return to those two principal parts: the noun and the verb, which signify the person and the action. The rest are merely appendages and draw their origin from these. For the **pronoun** is born from the noun, whose function it performs, such as "that orator." The **adverb** is born from the noun, such as "learned" from "learnedly" <note>original: "doctus" (adj) and "docte" (adv)</note>. The **participle** comes from the noun and the verb, such as "reading" from "I read" <note>original: "lego" and "legens"</note>. Moreover, the **conjunction**, the **preposition**, and the **interjection** fall within the grouping of these others. Therefore, some define only five parts, as they consider the others to be superfluous.

### Chapter 6: On the Noun

The **Noun** (*nomen*) is so called as if it were a "marking-name" <note>original: "notamen," from "notus" (known)</note>, because by its specific word it makes things known to us. For unless you know the name, the knowledge of things perishes. **Proper names** are so called because they are specific; for they signify only one person. There are four types of proper names: the *praenomen*, the *nomen*, the *cognomen*, and the *agnomen*. The *praenomen* (first name) is so called because it is placed before the name, like **Lucius** or **Quintus**. The *nomen* (name) is so called because it notes the clan, like **Cornelius**; for all the Cornelii were called by that name in their clan. The *cognomen* (surname) is what is joined to the name, like **Scipio**. The *agnomen* (nickname) is as if "added" to the name, like **Metellus Creticus**, who was so named because he subdued Crete. For the agnomen comes from an external reason. The *cognomentum* is commonly called so because it is added to the name for the sake of recognition, or because it exists with the name. **Appellative nouns** (common nouns) are so called because they are common and consist of the significance of many things. These are divided into twenty-eight species, among which are: **Corporal**, which are seen or touched, such as "heaven" or "earth"; **Incorporeal**, which lack a body, whence they can neither be seen nor touched, such as "truth" or "justice"; **General**, which belong to many things, such as "animal," for both human and horse and bird are animals; **Special**, which demonstrate a part, like "human," for "human" is a species of animal; **Principal**, which have the first position and are not born from elsewhere, like "mountain" or "fountain"; **Derivative**, which are drawn from another name, like "mountaineer" from "mountain"; **Diminutive**, which are diminished in sense, like "little Greek" <note>original: "graeculus"</note> or "little scholar" from "scholar." Some are **diminutive in sound** because they sound like diminutives but are principal in meaning, like "table" (*tabula*) or "fable" (*fabula*). **Wholly Greek** names are those declined entirely in the Greek way, like **Callisto** or **Calypso**, for so the Greek and Latin say them. **Wholly Latin** are those turned entirely into Latin: the Greek says **Odysseus**, the Latin **Ulysses**.

<column-break/>

**Mixed** (*Media*) names are so called because they are partly Greek and partly Latin. These are also called "bastard" names (*notha*) because they corrupt the final syllables while the first ones remain, as with the Greek **Alexandros** vs. the Latin **Alexander** or **Menander**. They are called bastard just as a person is called a bastard who is born of unequal stock. **Synonyms** (many-named) are so called because there is one meaning in many names, like "earth," "ground," and "soil" <note>original: "terra, humus, tellus"</note>; for they are all the same. **Homonyms** (single-named) are so called because there are many meanings in one name, like "mound" (*tumulus*), which is sometimes a small mountain, sometimes swelling earth, and sometimes a tomb. Thus there is diverse meaning in one name. **Relative** names are so called because they refer to another person, such as "teacher," "lord," or "father" <note>One cannot be a teacher without a student</note>. Those called **opposites** are named for their contrary significance, like "right"; for one cannot be called "right" unless there is a "left." Furthermore, nouns of **quality** are so called because through them it is shown what kind someone is, such as "wise," "beautiful," or "rich." Nouns of **quantity** are drawn from measurement, like "long" or "short." **Patronymics** are so called because they are drawn from fathers, like "Tydides," the son of Tydeus, or "Aeneius," the son of Aeneas. They are also named after ancestors and mothers. **Possessives** (*ctetica*) come from possession, like the "Evandrian sword." **Epithets**, which in Latin are called "adjectives" or "placed-upon," are so called because they are added to nouns to fulfill their significance, such as "great" or "learned." You add them to persons, like "great philosopher" or "learned man," and the sense is full. **Actual** nouns descend from an action, like "leader," "king," "runner," "nurse," or "orator." **Gentiles** come from a clan (*gens*), like "Greek" or "Roman." **Patrial** nouns descend from a fatherland (*patria*), like "Athenian" or "Theban." **Locals** come from a place, like "suburban." **Verbal** nouns are so named because they are born from a verb, like "reader" (*lector*). **Participials** are those that sound like participles, like "lenient" or "prudent." **Verb-like** nouns are so called from a similarity to a verb, like "observer" (*contemplator*). For it is both a verb in the imperative mood, future tense, and a noun because it accepts comparison. All these species descend from the naming of nouns. The second part of the noun is **comparison**. Comparison is so called because it brings forth one thing from the comparison of another. Its degrees are three: positive, comparative, and superlative. The **positive** is so called because it is placed first in the degree of comparison, like "learned." The **comparative** is that which, being compared to the positive, is brought forth from it, like "more learned"; for the more learned knows more than the learned. The **superlative** is so called because it is carried above the comparative, like "most learned"; for he knows more than the more learned.

**Genders** are so called because they generate, like masculine and feminine. The others are not truly genders, but the reasoning and authority of nouns chose to have them. The **neuter** is so called because it is neither this nor that, that is, neither masculine nor feminine. The **common** is so called because it communicates with two genders of nouns, like "this dog" (masculine or feminine). To this the **epicene** is contrary, because it expresses both sexes under one gender, like "this fish"; for its gender is uncertain, as it is discerned neither by nature nor by eyes, but by experienced sense. The **omnigenus** (all-gendered) is so called because it serves all genders: masculine, feminine, neuter, common, and all. **Number** is so called because they show either singular or plural nouns. **Figure** is so called because they are either simple or...

# Book

...are arranged. **Cases** are called such from "falling" <note>original: *cadendo*</note>, because inflected nouns vary and "fall" from their original form. The **Nominative** case is so named because through it we "name" <note>original: *nominamus*</note> something, such as "this teacher." The **Genitive**, because through it we seek the "kind" <note>original: *genus*</note> of anything, such as "the son of this teacher," or because we signify the possession of this teacher. The **Dative**, because through it we show ourselves "giving" <note>original: *dare*</note> to someone, such as "give to this teacher." The **Accusative**, because through it we "accuse" <note>original: *accusamus*</note> someone, such as "I accuse this teacher." The **Vocative**, because through it we "call" <note>original: *vocamus*</note> someone, such as "O teacher!" The **Ablative**, because through it we signify that we are "taking away" <note>original: *auferre*</note> something from someone, such as "I take away from the teacher." **Heptaptota** nouns are so called because they have variations through six cases <note>Though the prefix implies seven, the text specifies six variations; this may refer to nouns that have distinct forms for all standard Latin cases</note>, such as "one" (*unus*). **Pentaptota** because they vary in only five cases, such as "learned" (*doctus*). **Tetraptota** because they are declined in only four cases, such as "side" (*latus*). **Triptota** because in only three, such as "temple" (*templum*). **Diptota** because in only two, such as "Jupiter." **Monoptota** because they use only one case, such as "frugal" (*frugi*).

->### Chapter 7: On the Pronoun<-

A **pronoun** is so named because it is placed "in the stead of a noun" <note>original: *pro vice nominis*</note>, so that the noun itself does not cause boredom when it is repeated. For when we say "Virgil wrote the *Bucolics*," we add a pronoun, "he himself <note>original: *ipse*</note> also wrote the *Georgics*," and thus the variety of meaning removes boredom and introduces ornament. Pronouns are either **finite** or **infinite**. Finite pronouns are so called because they define a certain person, like "I" <note>original: *ego*</note>; for you understand me immediately. Infinite pronouns are so called because they are not for certain persons, for they are used for those who are absent and uncertain, like "who," "which," "what." They are called "less than finite" because they make a commemoration of a known person, such as "himself" or "that one"; for it is certain about whom one speaks. They are called **possessive** because they show us possessing something. For when I say "mine" or "yours," I define something as being mine or yours. They are called **relative** because they refer back to a question, such as "who is it?"; the answer is "it is he." They are **demonstrative** because they have the meaning of demonstrating. For we demonstrate someone present twice, such as "this" (masculine, feminine, neuter). These three are also called articles. **Articles** are so called because they are "bound" <note>original: *artantur*</note> to nouns, as when we say "this orator." However, the difference between an article and a pronoun is this: it is an article when it is joined to a noun, like "this wise man"; but when it is not joined, it is a demonstrative pronoun, like "this" and "that." Primary pronouns are either **original** <note>original: *primogenia*</note> or **derived**. The original ones are so called because they do not draw their origin from elsewhere. These are three finite: "I," "you," "he"; seven infinite: "who," "what sort," "such," "how great," "so great," "which in order," "the whole"; six less-than-finite: "that," "himself," "this," "he," "the same," "himself"; five possessive: "mine," "yours," "his," "ours," and "yours." The rest are called **derived**, because they exist as things drawn out and composed from those, such as "someone," "anyone," and the rest.

->### Chapter 8: On the Verb<-

The **verb** is so named because it sounds by "striking the air" <note>original: *verberato aere*</note> or because this part is frequently "turned about" <note>original: *versetur*</note> in speech. Verbs are signs of the mind by which humans show their thoughts to one another by speaking. Just as the noun signifies a person, so the verb signifies the action and the saying of the person. In the person of the verb, there is the meaning of the one acting and the one suffering. For "I write" is the action of a person. Likewise, "I am written" indicates the action of a person, namely of him by whom one is acted upon. There are two kinds of verbs: those of gram-

<column-break/>

marians and those of rhetoricians. Those of the grammarian fall into three times: the past, the present, and the future, such as "he did," "he does," "he will do." But for rhetoricians, the entire speech is called "verbs," as in "he took us with good words" or "he had good words." In this case, it is not only verbs that fall into the three times, but the entire speech is [called verbs]. The properties of verbs are: forms, modes, conjugations, and kinds. **Forms** of verbs are named from the fact that they "inform" us about each thing; for through these we show what we are doing. The **Perfect** form is named from "completing" <note>original: *perficiendo*</note>, like "I read" <note>original: *lego*</note>, for it must then be said when we read in the present time. **Meditative** forms are named from the sense of "meditating" <note>i.e., the desiderative form expressing a desire to act</note>, like "I am eager to read" <note>original: *lecturio*</note>, that is, I meditate on reading. **Inchoative** forms are after meditation, from the indication of "beginning" <note>original: *inchoantis*</note>, like "I grow warm" <note>original: *calesco*</note>. **Frequentative** forms are from "doing often," like "I read often" (*lectito*) or "I cry out often" (*clamito*). For forms hold the sense; modes hold the inflection. For you do not know what an inflection is unless you first learn what the sense is. **Modes** are named from "in what manner" <note>original: *quemadmodum*</note> they are in their meanings. For the **Indicative** mode is so called because it has the meaning of one indicating, as "I read." The **Imperative** because it has the sound of commanding, as "read!" The **Optative** because through it we "wish" <note>original: *optamus*</note> to do something, as "would that I might read." The **Conjunctive** [Subjunctive] because something is joined to it so that the speech may be full. For when you say, "since I cry out," the sense is hanging; but if I say, "since I cry out, why do you think I am silent?", the sense is full. The **Infinitive** is so called because, while it defines the time, it does not define the person of the verb, as "to cry out," "to have cried out." To which if you add a person—"I ought," "you ought," "he ought" to cry out—it becomes as if finite. The **Impersonal** is so called because it lacks the person of a noun or pronoun, like "it is read"; you add a person—"by me," "by you," "by him"—and it is fully understood. But the infinitive mode only lacks the person of the verb, whereas the impersonal lacks the person of either a pronoun or a noun.

->**Conjugation** is so called because through it many things are "yoked together" <note>original: *coniunguntur*</note> into one sound.<-

For it teaches in which syllable the future tense should end, lest through ignorance someone should say *legebo* instead of *legam*. For the first and second [conjugations] send the future tense in *-bo* and in *-bor*; the third in *-am* and in *-ar*. The **kinds** <note>original: *genera*</note> of verbs are so called because they "beget" <note>original: *gignunt*</note>; for to the active you add the letter *r* and it begets the passive; conversely, from the passive you take away the *r* and it brings forth the active. These are called **Active** because they act, such as "I beat" <note>original: *verbero*</note>, and **Passive** because they suffer, such as "I am beaten" <note>original: *verberor*</note>. **Neuter** because they neither act nor suffer, such as "I lie down," "I sit." If you add the letter *r* to these, they do not sound like Latin. They are called **Common** because they both act and suffer, such as "I embrace" <note>original: *amplector*</note>. These, similarly, are not Latin if the letter *r* is dropped. **Deponent** verbs are so called because they "put aside" <note>original: *deponunt*</note> the future participle from a passive meaning, which will be in *-dus*, such as "to be boasted of" <note>original: *gloriandus*</note>.

->### Chapter 9: On the Adverb<-

The **adverb** is so called because it "approaches the verb" <note>original: *verbis accedat*</note>, as for instance, "I read well." "Well" is the adverb, "read" is the verb. It is called an adverb because, always joined to a verb, it fulfills [the meaning]. For the verb alone fulfills the sense, such as "I write." But the adverb without the verb does not have full meaning, such as "today." You add a verb to it, "today I write," and with the verb joined, the sense is fulfilled.

->### Chapter 10: On the Participle<-

The **participle** is so called because it "takes parts" <note>original: *partes capiat*</note> of the noun and the verb, as if it were "part-taking." For from the noun it claims for itself gender and cases; from the verb, tenses and meanings; and from both, number and figure.

### On the Conjunction Chapter 11.
The **conjunction** <note>original: *coniunctio*</note> is so named because it joins together senses and sentences. By itself, it has no power, but in the coupling of speech, it acts as a kind of glue. It either joins nouns—such as "Augustine and Jerome"—or verbs—such as "he writes and reads." All have one function, whether they join things together or separate them. **Copulative** <note>joining</note> conjunctions are so called because they join the sense or the persons, as in "I and you go to the market"; here it joins the sense itself. **Disjunctive** <note>separating</note> are so called because they separate things and persons, as in "I or you shall do it." **Subjunctive** <note>subjoining</note> are so called because they follow after, such as "because" <note>original: *quia*</note>. For we say "to the king because," "to the man because," "to God because"; we do not say "because to the king," "because to the man," "because to God." **Expletive** <note>filling out</note> are so called because they fulfill the intended matter, for example: "if you do not want this, at least <note>original: *saltem*</note> do that." **Common** are so named because they are placed before or after as you wish, such as "therefore <note>original: *igitur*</note> I shall do this" or "this therefore I shall do." **Causal** are named from "cause," because they think of a reason for doing something, for example: "I kill him because he has gold." **Rational** <note>reasoning</note> are named from the reason which someone uses in acting, such as "how <note>original: *quomodo*</note> shall I kill him so he is not recognized: by poison or by the blade?"

### On the Preposition Chapter 12.
The **preposition** is so named because it is placed before <note>original: *praeponatur*</note> nouns and verbs. **Accusative** and **ablative** prepositions are named from the cases which they serve. **Speech-related** <note>original: *loquelares*</note> ones always cling to words (verbs); they have no power when placed alone, such as *di-* or *dis-*. When joined to verbs, they create a form, such as "I lead apart" <note>original: *diduco*</note> or "I draw away" <note>original: *distraho*</note>.

### On the Interjection Chapter 13.
The **interjection** is so called because, being thrown between <note>original: *interiecta*</note>—that is, interposed—among words, it expresses the emotion of a moved mind: just as when "va" <note>an exclamation of joy</note> is said by one exulting; "heu" <note>alas</note> by one wishing; "he" by one who is angry; "hei" by one who is afraid. These sounds are specific to their respective languages and are not easily translated into another language.

### On the Voice Chapter 14.
**Voice** is struck air, perceptible to hearing, as much as is in itself. The voice is either articulate or confused. **Articulate** belongs to humans; **confused** belongs to animals. Articulate is that which can be written; confused is that which cannot be written.

### On the Syllable Chapter 15.
**Syllable** in Greek is called "conception" or "complex" in Latin. For a syllable is named from the Greek *syllambanein* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ συλλαμβάνειν*</note>, that is, from the "conception" of letters. For *syllambanein* means "to conceive" <note>or to take together</note>. Whence truly that is a syllable which is born from many letters. For we call a single vowel a syllable loosely <note>original: *abusiue*</note>, not properly, because it should not be called a syllable so much as a measurement of time. Syllables are either short, long, or common. They are called **short** because they can never be lengthened. **Long** because they are always lengthened and can never be shortened. **Common** because, by the judgment of the writer when necessity compels, they are both lengthened and shortened. They are granted this by law. Moreover, syllables are called long and short because, through various delays of the voice, they are seen to hold either double or single spaces of time. **Diphthong** syllables are named by a Greek name because two vowels are joined in them. Among us, we know four of these to be true: *ae*, *oe*, *au*, *eu*. The diphthong *ei* was celebrated among the 

<column-break/>

ancients. Among those who measure meter <note>original: *metricos*</note>, a syllable is named a "half-foot" <note>original: *semipes*</note> because it is half of a "foot." For a foot consists of two syllables. Since a syllable is one, it is like a half-foot. Dionysius created the most fitting individual forms for all syllables, and for this reason, he was honored with a statue.

### On Feet Chapter 16.
**Feet** <note>original: *pedes*</note> are those which stand upon certain timings of syllables and never depart from the legitimate space. They are called feet because through them the meters "walk."

<margin>124 feet</margin>
For just as we walk with feet, so meters proceed as if by feet. There are 124 feet in total: four of two syllables, eight of three syllables, sixteen of four syllables, thirty-two of five syllables, and sixty-four of six syllables. Up to four syllables they are called "feet"; the rest are called **syzygies** <note>original: *siciqię*</note>. These feet have specific reasons for their names.

<margin>
Pyrrhic
Spondee
</margin>
The **Pyrrhic** <note>original: *Pirrichius*</note> is so named because it was frequently used either in contests or in the games of children. The **Spondee** is so named because it sounds drawn out; for a certain "drawn-out" <note>original: *tractus*</note> sound was called a *spondeus*, which was poured out near the ears of those sacrificing. Whence those who played flutes in the sacred rites of the Gentiles were called *spondiales*.

<margin>
Trochee
Iamb
</margin>
The **Trochee** is named from the fact that it makes a swift turn of song; for a wheel <note>original: *trochos* / *τρὀχός*</note> runs swiftly in meters. In Greek, a wheel is called a *trochos*. The **Iamb** is so named because the Greeks used *iambizein* to mean "to disparage." For poets were accustomed to fulfill all invectives or disparagements in this kind of poem. The name was given because it pours out, in a way, the poison of a curse or of malice.

<margin>
Tribrach
Molossus
Anapest
</margin>
The **Tribrach** is so called because it is named for "three shorts" <note>original: *ter co[rreptus]*</note>, as it is made of three short syllables. The **Molossus** is named from the dance of the Molossians, which they performed while armed. The **Anapest** in Greek means "struck back" <note>original: *repcussus*</note>. For the Greeks call an *anapestin* a striking-back. It is called struck back because it is struck back by the dactyl, for it is its opposite.

<margin>
Dactyl
</margin>
The **Dactyl** is named from the finger <note>original: *digitus*</note> because, beginning from a longer joint, it ends in two short ones. So this foot has one long joint and two shorts. Whence the hand spread out is called a "palm," and the hanging fingers are "dactyls."

<margin>
Amphibrach
Amphimacer
Bacchius
Antibacchius
Proceleumatic
Dispondee
Ditrochee
Diamb
Antispast
Choriamb
</margin>
The **Amphibrach** has a short syllable on each part with a long one lying in the middle. For *brachis* means short. The **Amphimacer** has long syllables on this side and that, with a short one enclosed in the middle. For *macros* in Greek means long. The **Bacchius** is so called because the *Bacchia*—that is, the sacred rites of Liber <note>Bacchus</note>—were celebrated with this foot. The **Antibacchius** or *palimbacchius* is so named because it is drawn back from the bacchius. The **Proceleumatic** <note>original: *P[ro]celeumaticus*</note> is so named because it is made fit for the "celeuma" <note>a rhythmic call or song</note> of those singing. The **Dispondee**, **Ditrochee**, and **Diamb** are so named because they consist of twin iambs, spondees, or trochees. The **Antispast** is made of opposing syllables: namely, from a short and a long, and a long and a short. The **Choriamb** is so named because a poem composed from this foot is most fit for choirs. The **Ionics** are named for the unequal sound of their numbers; for they have two long syllables and two short ones.

<margin>
Paeans
Epitrites
Syzygies
</margin>
**Paeans** <note>original: *Peones*</note> are named after their inventor. They consist of one long and three short syllables; the long is placed differently according to their various names. **Epitrites** are so called because they always have three long syllables and one short. **Syzygies** <note>original: *Siciqię*</note> are...

<summary>This page defines the final parts of speech—conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections—before moving into the technical foundations of phonetics and poetic meter, explaining the origins of metrical feet like the dactyl and spondee.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical study of grammar, moving from the basic parts of speech into the mathematical structure of poetry (metrics) and the musicality of language (accents). It explains how words are built from rhythmic "feet" and how the pitch of a voice changes the meaning and flow of a sentence.</meta>

Five-syllable and six-syllable feet, as they are called among the Greeks, are formed as a kind of inflection <note>original: "declinationes"</note>. However, these are not strictly considered "feet" themselves; they are called **five-syllable** and **six-syllable** because they do not exceed five or six syllables. For this reason, it is not proper for a name in a poem to exceed these syllables—for example: *Carthaginians*, *of the inhabitants of Jerusalem*, and *of the inhabitants of Constantinople* <note>original: "carthaginensiū . hierosolymitanozū . ⁊ constantinopolitanozū"</note>. To every foot there belongs an **arsis** and a **thesis** <term>arsis/thesis: from the Greek for "lifting" and "setting down," referring to the beat or pulse of a rhythm</term>—that is, the lifting and the lowering of the voice. For the feet of the voice cannot direct their path unless they are lifted and lowered in alternating turns. For example, in the word *arma* <note>the first word of Virgil's Aeneid</note>, "ar-" is the lifting and "-ma" is the lowering. In these two divisions, the legitimate feet are gathered.

**Equal division** <note>1:1 or 2:2 ratio</note> occurs whenever the lifting and lowering are granted an equal division of time—such as two to two. **Double division** <note>2:1 ratio</note> occurs whenever one of these beats is twice as long as the other. **Sescuple division** <note>original: "sescupla," a 3:2 ratio</note> occurs whenever one part exceeds the other by half the number—such as three to two. In a **simple** division, one part is found to be more; in a double, it has one less. Indeed, "sescuple" is said to be half of the double. **Triple division** <note>3:1 ratio</note> is when the larger part contains the whole smaller part three times—that is, three and one. **Epitrite division** <note>4:3 ratio</note> is when the smaller part is contained within the larger, plus one-third part of it. The members of the feet are categorized by equality, or by double, or by sescuple, or by triple, or by epitrite ratios.

Therefore, we divide these feet into **equal parts**:
*   **Pyrrhic** ⌣ ⌣ . ⌣ ⌣ . as in *fuga* (flight). Equal.
*   **Spondee** - - . - - . as in *aestas* (summer). Equal.
*   **Dactyl** - ⌣ ⌣ . - ⌣ ⌣ . as in *maenalus*. Equal.
*   **Anapest** ⌣ ⌣ - . ⌣ ⌣ - . as in *erato*. Equal.
*   **Dispondee** - - - - . - - - - . as in *oratores* (orators). Equal.
*   **Proceleusmatic** ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . as in *aviculla* (little bird).
*   **Diiamb** ⌣ - ⌣ - . ⌣ - ⌣ - . as in *propinquitas* (proximity). Equal.
*   **Ditrochee** - ⌣ - ⌣ . - ⌣ - ⌣ . as in *cantilena* (sing-song). Equal.
*   **Antispast** ⌣ - - ⌣ . ⌣ - - ⌣ . as in *saloninus*. Equal.
*   **Choriamb** - ⌣ ⌣ - . - ⌣ ⌣ - . as in *armipotens* (powerful in arms). Equal.

Likewise, we divide these feet into **double parts**:
*   **Trochee** - ⌣ . - ⌣ . as in *meta* (goal). Double.
*   **Iamb** ⌣ - . ⌣ - . as in *parens* (parent). Double.
*   **Molossus** - - - . - - - . as in *aeneas*. Double.
*   **Tribrach** ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . as in *macula* (stain). Double.
*   **Ionic major** - - ⌣ ⌣ . - - ⌣ ⌣ . as in *iunonius*. Double.
*   **Ionic minor** ⌣ ⌣ - - . ⌣ ⌣ - - . as in *diomedes*. Double.

There is only one which is divided by a **triple** partition—which is the largest, and therefore is least present in meters:
*   **Amphibrach** ⌣ - ⌣ . ⌣ - ⌣ . as in *carina* (keel). Triple.

These are the **sescuple** <note>3:2 ratio</note> feet:
*   **Amphimacer** - ⌣ - . - ⌣ - . as in *insulae* (islands). Sescuple.
*   **Bacchius** ⌣ - - . ⌣ - - . as in *achates*. Sescuple.
*   **Antibacchius** - - ⌣ . - - ⌣ . as in *natura* (nature). Sescuple.
*   **First Paeon** - ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . - ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ . as in *legitimus* (lawful). Sescuple.
*   **Second Paeon** ⌣ - ⌣ ⌣ . ⌣ - ⌣ ⌣ . as in *colonia* (colony). Sescuple.
*   **Third Paeon** ⌣ ⌣ - ⌣ . ⌣ ⌣ - ⌣ . as in *menedemus*. Sescuple.
*   **Fourth Paeon** ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ - . ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ - . as in *celeritas* (speed). Sescuple.

There remain those which we divide by an **epitrite** partition <note>4:3 ratio</note>:
*   **First Epitrite** ⌣ - - - . ⌣ - - - . as in *sacerdotes* (priests). Epitrite.
*   **Second Epitrite** - ⌣ - - . - ⌣ - - . as in *conditores* (founders). Epitrite.
*   **Third Epitrite** - - ⌣ - . - - ⌣ - . as in *demosthenes*. Epitrite.
*   **Fourth Epitrite** - - - ⌣ . - - - ⌣ . as in *fescenninus*. Epitrite.

There are, therefore: [equal] feet; 6 double feet; 1 triple; 7 sescuple; 4 epitrite. The number of syllables in feet extends from two up to six; it does not

<column-break/>

proceed further because feet only extend up to six syllables. **Times** <note>original: "tempora"</note> in feet are the measures of how much each part contains. **Resolution** occurs in feet when two shorts are placed for one long, or four shorts are placed for two longs; for example: *sectaque interiit abiete costas* <note>original: "the ribs perished, having been cut from fir-wood" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.16</note>. In the word *abiete* <note>fir-wood</note>, there is now a resolution of a spondee into a proceleusmatic, in which resolution Virgil always follows a **synaloepha** <term>synaloepha: the merging or dropping of a vowel at the end of a word when the next word starts with a vowel</term>. From one long, two shorts are made; but from two shorts, a long is never made. For solid things can be divided, but things already cut apart cannot be made solid. **Figure** <note>original: "figura"</note> is the mark by which syllables are recognized. Where I see the lower part of a circle placed twice, it is a **pyrrhic** ⌣ ⌣. Where I see a doubled lying "i", it is a **spondee** - -. For the mark of a **short** syllable is the lower semicircle ⌣. The mark of a **long** syllable is a lying "i" -. Meters happen to feet, such as the trochaic from the trochee, the dactylic from the dactyl, and the iambic from the iamb, about which more must be said shortly.

### On Accents Chapter 17.

The **Accent**, which in Greek is called *prosodia*, also took its name from the Greek. For in Greek *pros* <note>πϱος</note> is "to" in Latin; *oden* <note>οδη</note> in Greek is "song" in Latin. Indeed, this name is expressed word-for-word. Latins also have other names for it: for they are called **accents**, **tones**, and **tenors**, because there the sound grows and ceases. It is called "accent" because it is near the song, just as an "adverb" is so called because it is near the verb. It is called an **acute** accent <term>acute: high-pitched</term> because it sharpens and raises the syllable; it is called **grave** <term>grave: low-pitched</term> because it depresses and lowers it. The **circumflex** is the opposite of the acute, because it consists of both the acute and the grave. For beginning from the acute, it finishes in the grave; and thus while it ascends and descends, it creates a circumflex. The acute and the circumflex are similar, for both lift the syllable. The grave seems contrary to both, for it always depresses syllables while the others lift them—as in: *whence comes the sun* <note>original: "vnde venir titan"</note> - ⌣ *soon where he hides the stars*. Here the "vnde" is grave, for it sounds less than the acute and the circumflex.

A monosyllabic part of speech, if it is naturally short like *vir* (man), or long by position like *ars* (art), will have an **acute accent**. If it is naturally long like *res* (thing), it will have a **circumflex**. A two-syllable part of speech, if it has the first syllable naturally long and the last short, is circumflexed, such as *musa* (muse). Otherwise, it is accented with an acute. A three-syllable part of speech, if it has a short middle syllable like *tibia* (flute), then we sharpen the first syllable. But if it has a naturally long second syllable and a short last syllable, like *metellus*, then we circumflex the middle. Four-syllable and five-syllable words follow the rule of the three-syllable ones. A grave accent can be placed with one other accent in a single word; it is never placed with both, as in *catullus*. In a compound word, there is one accent, such as *armipotens* (powerful in arms) or *omnipotens* (all-powerful). Accents are used as rules either for the sake of **distinction**—as in "he is seen on the green shore, a pig" <note>original: "viridiqʒ i littore cōspiciť sus" — Virgil, Aeneid 3.390</note>, so you do not say "metas"—or for the sake of **pronunciation**, so you do not say "meta" shortly, but "meta" prolonged; or for the sake of **discerning ambiguity**, as in "ergo" (therefore). For when the "-go" is prolonged, it signifies a cause; when it is shortened, it signifies a conjunction.

### On the Figures of Accents Chapter 18.

The **Figures** of accents are ten, which are placed by grammarians for the distinction of words. The **Oxeia**, that is, the acute accent, is a line drawn upwards from the left side to the right side, made thus: /
