### Chapter XIX: On Punctuation

Punctuation <term>positura: the physical placement of points to indicate the structure of a sentence</term> is a shape used to distinguish meanings through *commas*, *cola*, and *periods*. When these are placed in their proper order, they show us the meaning of the reading.
They are called "positurae" either because they are noted by "positioned" points, or because the voice is "laid down" there during a pause in the distinction. The Greeks call these *theseis*, and the Latins call them *positurae*.
The first punctuation is called the **sub-distinction**; this is the same as a **comma** <note>A "comma" here refers to a short phrase or clause</note>. The **middle distinction** follows it; this is the **colon** <note>A "colon" here refers to a larger member of a sentence</note>. The **final distinction**, which closes the entire thought, is the **period** <note>The "period" is the complete circuit of the sentence</note>. As we have said, the *cola* and *commas* precede it. Their differences are demonstrated by points placed in different locations. 
For when, at the beginning of a statement, the part is not yet full in meaning and yet one must breathe, a **comma** is made—that is, a small piece of the sense—and a point is placed at the bottom of one letter. It is called a "sub-distinction" from the fact that it receives the point "below" (at the foot of the letter). 
However, when in the following parts the sentence provides a sense, but something of the fullness of the thought still remains, a **colon** is made; we mark the middle of the letter with a point and call it a "**middle distinction**," because we place the point at the middle of the letter. 
But when we make a full conclusion of the sentence after steps of pronunciation, a **period** is made, and we place the point at the head (top) of the letter; it is called a "**distinction**"—that is, a separation—because it separates an entire thought. 
What is found among orators is also found among poets: where a syllable remains after two feet in usage, it is a **comma**, because a "cutting" of the word was made after the scanning. But where nothing remains of a part of speech after two feet, it is a **colon**. A whole verse, however, is a **period**.

### Chapter XX: On the Marks of Sentences

Furthermore, there were certain marks for writings among the most famous authors, which the ancients placed in poems and histories to distinguish the writings. A **mark** <note>original: "nota"</note> is a specific figure placed in the manner of a letter to demonstrate every logic of letters, meanings, and verses. The marks used in books are twenty-six in number, which are listed with the names written below.

<column-break/>

<margin><image-desc>asterisk symbol</image-desc></margin> The **Asterisk** is placed in those things which have been omitted, so that through that mark, the things that seem to be missing may shine out. For "star" is called ***aster*** in the Greek tongue, from which "asterisk" is derived.
<margin><image-desc>horizontal line (obelus)</image-desc></margin> The **Obelus**, that is, a lying little rod, is placed in words or sentences superfluously repeated, or in those places where the reading is marked by some falsehood; it is as if a spear <note>original: "sagitta"</note> should slaughter the superfluous and pierce the false. For a spear is called ***obelos*** in Greek.
<margin><image-desc>horizontal line with dot above</image-desc></margin> An **Obelus with a point above** is placed in those things about which there is doubt whether they ought to be removed or not.
<margin><image-desc>horizontal line with dots above and below</image-desc></margin> The **Limniscus**, that is, a little rod lying between two points, is placed in those places which the translators of Holy Scripture translated with the same meaning but in different words.
<margin><image-desc>symbol like a 'd' with a dot</image-desc></margin> The **Antigraphus** with a point is placed where a different sense is held in translations.
<margin><image-desc>asterisk combined with an obelus</image-desc></margin> The **Asterisk with an obelus**: Aristarchus <note>A famous scholar and librarian of Alexandria</note> specifically used this in those verses which were not placed in their proper location.
<margin><image-desc>paragraph symbol (reversed C with crossbar)</image-desc></margin> The **Paragraphus** is placed to separate things from things that run together in a continuous flow, just as in a catalog places are separated from places and regions from regions; or in a contest, prizes from prizes and matches from different matches.
<margin><image-desc>reversed paragraph symbol</image-desc></margin> The **Positura** is a figure contrary to the paragraph; it is formed this way because, just as the former marks beginnings, so this one separates the ends from the beginnings.
<margin><image-desc>horizontal bracket with dot underneath</image-desc></margin> The **Ciphia**, the lower part of a circle with a point, is placed in those places where a doubtful and obscure question could not be opened or solved.
<margin><image-desc>symbol like a 'Z' or reversed sigma</image-desc></margin> The **Antisigma** is placed for those verses whose order must be changed, as is also found placed in ancient authors.
<margin><image-desc>Antisigma with a dot</image-desc></margin> The **Antisigma with a point** is placed in those places where there are duplicate verses for the same meaning, and it is doubted which one should preferably be chosen.
<margin><image-desc>arrow-like diple mark</image-desc></margin> The **Diple**: our writers place this in the books of ecclesiastical men to separate or demonstrate the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures.
<margin><image-desc>diple with a dot</image-desc></margin> The **Diple peristichon**: Leogaras of Syracuse first used this in Homeric verses to separate Olympus from the sky.
<margin><image-desc>diple with two dots</image-desc></margin> The **Diple pistigme**, that is, with twin points: the ancients placed this in those things which Zenodotus of Ephesus <note>The first librarian of Alexandria</note> had incorrectly added, or removed, or changed; our writers have also used it in these cases.
<margin><image-desc>diple with a horizontal line</image-desc></margin> The **Diple obelismene** is interposed to separate the "periods" <note>complete units of speech</note> in comedies or tragedies.
<margin><image-desc>reversed diple (avertsa)</image-desc></margin> The **Aversa** is used whenever a *strophe* and *antistrophe* are introduced <note>The alternating parts of a choral song</note>.
<margin><image-desc>reversed diple with horizontal line</image-desc></margin> The **Aversa with an obelus** is placed for those things which refer back to something else, such as: *"Are we trying to overturn the Trojan state from its foundation for you? Was it we who exposed the wretched Trojans to the Greeks?"* <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, used to show rhetorical referencing</note>.
<margin><image-desc>diple with a line above</image-desc></margin> The **Diple with an obelus above** is placed when the conditions of places, times, or persons have changed.
<margin><image-desc>two horizontal lines with marks</image-desc></margin> The **Right and Aversa with an obelus above** is placed when a single unit <note>original: "monade"</note> is finished in its place.

There were also other book marks for recognizing those things explained at the edges of the pages; so that when a reader finds such a sign in the main text, by looking back to the third occurrence of that same word or passage, they might know the explanation is where they find a matching mark placed above.

### On Shorthand Marks, Chapter 21

**Ennius** was the first to invent eleven hundred **shorthand marks** <note>original: "vulgares notas"</note>. The use of these marks was so that scribes could write down whatever was said in a debate or in court. Several scribes would stand together, dividing the parts among themselves—how many words each would take and in what order. In Rome, **Tullius Tiro**, the freedman of Cicero, was the first to devise marks, but these were only for prepositions. After him, Vipsanius <note>OCR reads "pfanni[us]"</note>, Philargyrus, and Aquila, a freedman of Maecenas, added others. Then **Seneca**, by collecting, digesting, and increasing the number of all of them, completed the work, bringing it to five thousand marks. They are called "marks" <note>notae</note> because they "note" words or syllables with prefixed characters and bring them back to the knowledge of the readers. Those who have learned these are now properly called **notaries**.

### On Legal Marks, Chapter 22

Certain letters in law books are marks for their words, so that writing may be made faster and shorter. For instance, they used to write:
- **B.P.F.** for "a good deed" <note>bonum factum</note>
- **S.C.** for "a decree of the Senate" <note>senatus consultum</note>
- **R.P.** for "the Republic" <note>respublica</note>
- **P.R.** for "the Roman People" <note>populus romanus</note>
- **D.T.** for "at least" <note>dumtaxat</note>
- A **U** lying on its back <note>supina u</note> for "woman" <note>mulier</note>
- **P.P.** according to its form for "a male ward" <note>pupillus</note>
- An **inverted V** for "a female ward" <note>pupilla</note>
- A single **K** for "a chapter" <note>caput</note>
- Two **K's** joined together for "the sake of a false accusation" <note>calumniae causa</note>
- **I.E.** for "let him be a judge" <note>iudex esto</note>
- **D.M.** for "malicious fraud" <note>dolum malum</note>

Very many similar marks of this kind are found in ancient books. The recent Emperors <note>likely referring to Theodosius or Justinian</note> decreed that these legal marks must be abolished from the law codes, because many clever people were deceiving the ignorant through them. Thus, they ordered that the letters in the laws be written out fully, so that they bring no errors and no ambiguities, but clearly demonstrate what is to be followed and what is to be avoided.

### On Military Marks, Chapter 23

In the brief rosters which contained the names of soldiers, the ancients had their own mark by which they could see how many of the soldiers remained and how many had fallen in war. The mark **T** <note>the letter Tau</note> designated each survivor at the head of their name. <image-desc>The Greek letter Theta</image-desc> The letter **Theta** <note>the Greek letter associated with 'Thanatos' or death</note> was placed next to the name of each deceased person. From this, it even has a "weapon" through the middle, which is the sign of death. About this, **Persius** says:

<column-break/>

"And he is able to prefix the black **Theta** to a vice." <note>This refers to marking a person or deed as 'dead' or condemned</note> Furthermore, when they wanted to signify childhood, they used the letter **Lambda** <image-desc>The Greek letter Lambda</image-desc>, just as they signified death when they placed a Theta at the head. In the distribution of pay <note>stipendia</note>, there were also specific marks.

### On Secret Letter Marks, Chapter 24

The ancients also made **marks for letters** among themselves, so that they could write to each other whatever they wanted to signify secretly in their writings. **Brutus** is a witness to this, who marked what he was about to do in these letters, while others were ignorant of what those letters meant. **Augustus Caesar** wrote to his son: "Because many things happen constantly that must be written and kept secret, let us have such marks between us, if you wish: when something needs to be written in marks, let us write the following letter for each single letter." That is, **B** for **A**, **C** for **B**, and so on for the rest by the same logic. For the letter **Z**, however, one must return to the double **AA**. Some even write with the words reversed.

### On Finger Marks, Chapter 25

There are also certain marks made with the **fingers**, the face, and the eyes, by which people communicate silently with each other when distant, as is the military custom; so that whenever the army agrees on something that cannot be said by voice, it signals by hand. Others, because they cannot use their voice, greet each other by the movement of their swords. **Ennius** says of a certain shameless woman, as if playing ball in a dance: "She gives herself away, and makes herself common. She holds one, nods to another; her hand is busy elsewhere; she kicks one with her foot; she gives a ring to another to be expected from her lips; she calls to one while she sings with another; yet she gives letters to others with her finger." And **Solomon** says: "He winks with his eye, shuffles with his foot, and speaks with his finger." <note>Proverbs 6:13</note>

### On Orthography, Chapter 26

**Orthography** is translated from Greek into Latin as "correct writing." For *ortho* in Greek is "correct," and *graphia* is "writing." This discipline teaches us how we ought to write. For just as the Art <note>Grammar</note> deals with the inflection of parts of speech, so Orthography deals with the skill of writing. For example:
- ***ad*** takes the letter **d** when it is a preposition.
- ***at*** takes the letter **t** when it is a conjunction.
- ***haud*** <note>"not at all"</note> is an adverb of negation ending in **d** and is aspirated at the beginning (*h*).
- When the pronunciation is a disjunctive (*aut*, meaning "or"), it is written with a **t** and without aspiration.
- ***apud*** <note>"at" or "near"</note> is a preposition written with a **d**, just like *ad*, as in *apud patrem* (with the father), though the ancients often used *apud* instead of *ad* with two letters removed from the middle.

Sometimes, however, some letters are rightly placed in the stead of others. There is a certain kinship between the letters **B** and **P**. For we say *Pyrrhus* instead of *Byrrhus*. **C** and **G** also have a certain kinship. For when we say *certum* (certain) and *trecentos* (three hundred), we later say *quadringentos* (four hundred), placing a **G** instead of a **C**. Furthermore, there is a kinship between **C** and **Q**; for we write *huiuscemodi* with a **C** and *cuiusque* with a **Q**. When it is a preposition <note>likely referring to *cum*</note>, it should be written with a **C**, but if it is an adverb <note>the relative *quum/cum*</note>, it should be with a **Q**. For we say *quum lego* (when I read). Regarding **P** and **E** alone: ***Damnum*** (loss/harm) is noted with the **ae** diphthong. ***Equus*** meaning the animal (horse) should be written with a single **e**; ***aequus*** meaning "just" must be written with the **ae** diphthong. ***Exsul*** (exile) should be written with an added **s**, because an "exul" is one who is outside his soil (*extra solum*). ***Exultat*** (rejoices) is better written without the letter **s**. For since the letter **x** itself consists of **c** and **s**, why should another be added to it when the **s** is already in it? ***Aequor*** <note>OCR reads "equoz"</note> should be written with a diphthong because the name is not made from water (*aqua*), but from equality (*aequalitas*). ***Forsitan*** (perhaps) should be written with an **n** at the end, because the full phrase is "if by chance finally" (*si forte tandem*). ***Foedus*** meaning "ugly" with a single **e**... <note>text cuts off</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of orthography (correct spelling) from the previous page, providing specific rules for Latin words, the usage of Greek letters, and the historical evolution of spelling. It then transitions into two new chapters: Chapter 27 on Analogy (grammatical patterns) and Chapter 28 on Etymology (the origins of words).</meta>

should be written. A treaty <note>original: "foedus"</note>, which is a pact, should be written with a diphthong. *Formosus* <note>meaning "beautiful"</note> is written without an "n" because it is named from *forma* <note>meaning "beauty" or "shape"</note>. *Gnatus* <note>meaning "son" or "born"</note>, which is "son," should be written with a "g" because it is derived from *generatus* <note>meaning "begotten"</note>. The letter "h," which is the mark of aspiration in Latin, is joined only to vowels, as in *honos* (honor), *homo* (man), and *humus* (earth). However, in Greek and Hebrew names, "h" is aspirated with two consonants. The interjections *hau* and *heu* <note>expressions of grief or surprise</note> should be written with an "h." Some believed the letter "i," when placed between two vowels, should be written twice, as in *Troia* or *Maia*; however, logic does not permit this. For three vowels are never written in a single syllable. Instead, the letter "i" placed between two vowels is treated as a double consonant. The pronoun "it" <note>original: "id"</note> in the neuter gender is written with a "d," from the words *is, ea, id*, because it forms *idem*. If it is the third person <note>of the verb "to go"</note>, we mark it with a "t," from the verb *eo, is, it* <note>I go, you go, he goes</note>, which forms *itur* <note>"it is gone," the passive construction</note>. The ancients used to place the letter "k" whenever an "a" followed, such as in *kaput* (head), *kanna* (reed), and *kalamus* (pen). But now, only *Karthago* and *Kalendae* (the Calends) are written with that letter. For Greek names, however, they must be written with "k" regardless of which vowel follows. *Laetus* (joyful) is written with the "ae" diphthong because joy <note>original: "laetitia"</note> is named from "breadth" <note>original: "latitudine"</note>; its opposite is "sadness" <note>original: "tristitia"</note>, which causes "narrowness" <note>original: "angustia"</note>. Sometimes we use the letter "l" instead of the letter "d," such as *latus* <note>wide</note> for *datus*, and *calamitas* <note>disaster</note> for *cadamitas*; for the name "calamity" is taken from "falling" <note>original: "cadendo"</note>. It was once asked whether *maxumus* or *maximus* (and similar words) should be written with a "u" or an "i." Varro handed down the tradition that the ancients used to pronounce and write such words with an "i"; therefore, due to the authority of so great a man, the custom was established that *maximus* (greatest), *optimus* (best), and *pessimus* (worst) are written with an "i." *Malo* (I prefer) should be written with one "l" because it is *magis volo* (I want more). *Malle* (to prefer) should be written with two "l"s because it is *magis velle* (to want more). *Nolo* (I am unwilling) has one "l," but *nolle* (to be unwilling) has two "l"s. For *nolo* is *ne volo* (I do not want), and *nolle* is *ne velle*. *Os*, if it signifies a face or bones, should be written with an "o" alone; if it signifies "those persons" <note>original: "personam", referring to the pronoun "hos"</note>, an "h" should be placed before it. *Ora* (boundaries) is said with an "o," but *hora* (hour) should be written with an "h." *Onus* (burden) comes from *ononere* <note>to load</note> and is written with an "o" alone; if it refers to "honor" <note>original: "honore"</note>, it is written with the aspiration of "h." Prepositions and *praeterea* (furthermore) should be written with a diphthong. *Paene* (almost), which is a conjunction, is written with "ae," while *poena* (punishment), which is a penalty, is written with "oe." The letter "q" is correctly placed only when the letter "u" follows it immediately, joined with one or more other vowels so that they form a single syllable. Other things are written with "c." *Quae* (which), the pronoun, is written with "ae," and *que*, the conjunction, is written with "e." *Quid* is written with the letter "d" when it is a pronoun, but with "t" <note>i.e., *quit*</note> when it is the verb whose first position is *queo, quis, quit* (to be able), and in the compound *nequeo, nequis, nequit* (to be unable). *Quod*, when it is a pronoun, is written with a "d," but when it is a number <note>meaning "how many," *quot*</note> it is written with a "t," because *totidem* (just as many) is also written with a "t." *Quotidie* (daily) should be written with a "q," not a "c," so that it means "on however many days" <note>original: "quot diebus"</note>. The letter "r" has a connection with the letter "s." Thus, among the ancients, it was said *honos, labos, arbos*; now it is *honor, labor, arbor*. *Hat* <note>meaning "but" or "yet," a variant of "at"</note> ought to be written with a "t" because its full form is *satis* (enough). But *sed* (but) ought to be written with a "d"; for among the ancients it was said *sedum*, and we have cut off the last two letters. *Tantus* (so great) and *quantus* (how great) used to have an "m" in the middle. For they come from *quam* and *tam*, from which also come *quantitas* (quantity), *quantus*, and *tantus*. *Vae* (woe), the interjection, should be written with "ae," but *ve* <note>or</note>, the conjunction, with "e." *Christ* <note>original: "Xpus"</note>, because it is Greek, should be written with "ch" <note>Chi-Rho</note>; so also *chrism* <note>original: "chrisma"</note>. The letters "y" and "z" are used only to write Greek names. For although in *iustitia* (justice) the letter "t" expresses the sound of the letter "z," nevertheless, because it is a Latin word, it must be written with a "t." The same applies to *militia* (military service), *malitia* (malice), *nequitia* (wickedness), and other similar words. In doubtful words, it was the custom of the ancients that when the same let-

<column-break/>

-ter had one meaning when shortened and another when lengthened, they would place an **apex** <note>a mark similar to an acute accent</note> over the long syllables. For example, to distinguish whether *supra* <note>above</note> referred to the word itself, or a tree <note>original: "arborem"</note>, or a multitude of cattle <note>original: "boium"</note>, it was distinguished by the apex. Likewise, where consonant letters were doubled, they placed a **sicilicus** <note>a hook-shaped mark</note> above them, as in *sella* (seat), *terra* (earth), or *asseres* (beams). For the ancients did not double letters, but instead placed a sicilicus above, which was a mark warning the reader that the letter was to be doubled.

## ->On Analogy Chapter xxvii.<-

**Analogy** <term>Analogia: a Greek term meaning "comparison of similarities"</term> is the comparison of similar things in Greek, or proportion <note>original: "proportio"</note> in Latin. Its power is this: that what is doubtful may be referred to something known that is not doubtful, so that uncertain things are proven by certain ones. The comparison of analogy is gathered in eight ways: by **quality**, **comparison**, **gender**, **number**, **figure**, **case**, **similar syllable endings**, and **similarity of tenses**. If even one of these is missing, it is no longer an analogy (that is, a similarity), but rather an **anomaly** <term>Anomalia: a Greek term meaning "irregularity" or "extra-regular"</term>, which means it is outside the rule. For example, *lupus* (wolf) and *lepus* (hare) seem to match in everything, but they differ in case; for the genitives are *lupi* and *leporis*. For it is a matter of rule that when you ask whether *trames* (a path) is masculine or feminine, *limes* (a boundary) is similar to it in every declension, and therefore it will be masculine. Likewise, if you believe *funis* (a rope) is of uncertain gender, *panis* (bread) is similar to it in declension, and it will be masculine. Also from the comparison of positives: if you say "learned" <note>original: "doctus"</note> or "great" <note>original: "magnus"</note>, these are positives and similar to each other. It also happens through diminutives; for instance, *funiculus* (a little rope) shows that *funis* is masculine, just as *marmusculum* (a little piece of marble) indicates that *marmor* is of the neuter gender. For whatever the gender is in the principal word, it usually remains the same in the diminutive. However, this is not always the case, such as *pistrinum* (a bakery) and *pistrella*. But we ought to know the declension from the positive (that is, the primitive) form and gather the gender from the diminutive.

## ->On Etymology Chapter xxviii.<-

**Etymology** <term>Etymologia: the study of the "true meaning" or origin of words</term> is the origin of words, when the force of a verb or noun is gathered through interpretation. Aristotle called this a "symbol" <note>original: "symbolon"</note>, and Cicero called it an "annotation" <note>original: "annotationem"</note>, because it makes the names and verbs of things known by an example provided. For instance, *flumen* (a river) is so called because it grew by flowing <note>original: "a fluendo"</note>. Knowledge of this often has a necessary use in interpretation. For when you see where a name originated, you more quickly understand its force. Every inspection of a thing is clearer once its etymology is known. Not all names, however, were imposed by the ancients according to nature, but some were also according to whim; just as we sometimes give names to our servants and possessions according to what pleases our will. Hence it is that the etymologies of all names are not found, because some things received names not according to the quality in which they were created, but according to the judgment of human will. The etymologies of names are given either from a **cause**, such as kings <note>original: "reges"</note> from acting rightly <note>original: "recte agendo"</note>; or from an **origin**, such as man <note>original: "homo"</note> because he is from the earth <note>original: "humo"</note>; or from **contraries**, such as mud <note>original: "lutum"</note> from washing <note>original: "lavando"</note> since mud is not clean, and a grove <note>original: "lucus"</note> because, being dark with shade, it shines very little <note>original: "parum luceat"</note>. Some are also made from the **derivation** of names, such as "prudent" from "prudence." Some also from **sounds**, such as "garrulous" from "garrulity." Some have arisen from **Greek etymology** and were declined into Latin, such as *silva* (woods) or *domus* (house). Others have drawn their names from the names of **places, cities, or rivers** where they originated. Many are also called from the **speech of diverse nations**; hence their origin is scarcely discerned. For many are foreign <note>original: "barbara"</note> names, unknown to the Latins and Greeks.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of grammar and linguistics, moving from the spelling of words (orthography) to their definitions, distinctions, and the various errors that can occur in speech and writing. ### Chapter 29: On Glosses
The word "gloss" <note>original: "glosa"</note> derives its name from the Greek interpretation of the word "tongue." Philosophers call this an "adverb," because it designates that word whose quality is sought with one single word. For it declares what that thing is by placing it into one word: as "to keep silent" <note>original: "conticessere"</note> is simply "to be quiet" <note>original: "tacere"</note>. Likewise, "he draws wide" <note>original: "latus haurit"</note> [means] "he draws openly" <note>original: "apertum haurit"</note> or "he runs through" <note>original: "percurrit"</note>. Similarly, when we call a "limit" <note>original: "terminum"</note> an "end" <note>original: "finem"</note>, or interpret "populated places" <note>original: "populatas"</note> to be "devastated" <note>original: "vastatas"</note>; and in every case where the essence of one word is made manifest by one word.

### Chapter 30: On Differences
A "difference" <note>original: "differentia"</note> is a type of definition which writers of the liberal arts call "the same and the other." For the "difference" separates two things that are somehow joined, confused, or cast together, through which it is known what each is. For instance, when it is asked what the difference is between a "king" and a "tyrant," the added "difference" defines what each is: a king is "modest and temperate," while a tyrant is "cruel." For when a difference is placed between these two, what each is becomes known. So it is with other things.

### Chapter 31: On Barbarism
A "barbarism" <note>original: "barbarismus"</note> is when a word is pronounced with a corrupt letter or sound. It is a corruption of a letter, such as *floriet*, when one ought to say *florere* <note>to bloom</note>. It is a corruption of sound if the first syllable is lengthened instead of the middle one: as in "hiding places" <note>original: "latebrae"</note> or "shadows" <note>original: "tenebrae"</note>. Barbarism is named after the barbarian nations, because they did not know the purity of Latin speech. For every nation made subject to the Romans transmitted its own vices of both words and customs to Rome along with its wealth. There is this difference between "barbarism" and "barbarolexis": a barbarism occurs in a Latin word when it is corrupted; however, when foreign words are inserted into Latin speech, it is called "barbarolexis." Also, when a fault occurs in prose, it is called a "barbarism"; when it occurs in poetic meter, it is called a "metaplasm." A barbarism occurs either in writing or in pronunciation. In writing, it happens in four ways: if a letter or syllable is added, changed, transposed, or removed in a word. In pronunciation, it happens in "times" <term>vowel length or quantity</term>, tones, aspirations, and the rest that follow. Through vowel "times," a barbarism occurs if a short syllable is placed for a long one, or a long one for a short one. Through tones: if the accent is moved to another syllable. Through aspiration: if the letter "h" is added where it ought not be, or removed where it should be. Through hiatus: whenever the flow of pronunciation is broken before it is completed, or whenever a vowel follows a vowel, as in "Aonian Muses" <note>original: "musae aonides"</note>. Barbarism also occurs through "mytacisms," "iotacisms," and "labdacisms." A "mytacism" occurs whenever a vowel follows the letter "m," as in "good gold" <note>original: "bonum aurum"</note> or "just friend" <note>original: "iustum amicum"</note>; we avoid this fault either by suspending the letter "m" or by its removal. An "iotacism" is whenever the pronunciation <note>of "i" between other letters</note> is so thin that it seems to sound like one *iota* <note>the Greek letter 'i'</note> instead of two. A "labdacism" occurs if two "l"s are pronounced for one, or whenever we pronounce one "l" too thinly and two too broadly, which is the reverse of what it should be. For we ought to pronounce one broadly and two thinly. A "collision" <note>original: "collisio"</note> occurs whenever the end of the last syllable is the same as the beginning of the next: as in "mother earth" <note>original: "mater terra"</note>.

### Chapter 32: On Solecism
A "solecism" <note>original: "soloecismus"</note> is an improper arrangement of several words together, just as a barbarism

<column-break/>

is the corruption of a single word. For words joined not by the correct law is a solecism, such as if someone said: "between we" <note>original: "inter nobis"</note> instead of "between us" <note>original: "inter nos"</note>, or "to give pardon of the wicked" <note>original: "dare veniam sceleratorum"; uses the genitive case incorrectly</note> instead of "for the wicked" <note>original: "sceleratis"; uses the dative or ablative</note>. Solecism is named after the citizens of Cilicia who, having set out from the city of Soloae (which is now called Pompeiopolis), while staying among the Italians, corrupted and confused their own language and that of the Italians; they gave the name to "solecism." From this, those who speak similarly are said to commit "solecisms." Among poets, however, a solecism is called a "figure" <note>original: "schema"</note> whenever it is found used out of the necessity of the meter. But when no necessity is found, the fault of the solecism remains. A solecism occurs in two ways: either through parts of speech, or through the "accidents" <term>grammatical properties like gender or case</term> of the parts of speech. Through parts of speech: if we put one part for another, for instance, if we apply prepositions to adverbs. Through accidents: that is, through those things which happen to parts of speech, such as through qualities, genders, numbers, figures, and cases. Through all these, therefore, solecisms occur, as Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian</note> explained. They also occur in many other ways. For Lucilius spoke of a hundred types of solecisms, all of which anyone who strives to hold the rule of correct speaking ought to avoid rather than follow.

### Chapter 33: On Other Faults
Among grammarians, "faults" <note>original: "vitia"</note> are those things which ought to be avoided in speech. These are: barbarism, solecism, "acyrologia," "cacephaton," and the rest. Barbarism is a corruption in a single word, such as if one should lengthen the third syllable in "to forgive" <note>original: "ignoscere"</note>. Solecism is the faulty composition of words, as if someone said "among men" <note>original: "inter hominibus"; uses the ablative</note> instead of "among men" <note>original: "inter homines"; uses the correct accusative</note>. "Acyrologia" is an improper expression, such as "may it be permitted for the fearful to hope." For the proper thing for a fearful person is to dread, not to hope. And "in a grassy field" <note>original: "gramineo in campo"</note>. For it is more proper to say a "grassy" field <note>original: "graminosum"</note>, not "made of grass" <note>original: "gramineum"</note>. "Cacephaton" <note>cacophony or ill-sounding speech</note> is said to be either obscene or sounding unharmoniously. Obscene: as in "here, they were encouraged in mind by the words" <note>original: "hic animum arrecti dictis"; the word 'animum' following 'hic' sounds like a dirty word in Latin</note>. Unharmonious: such as "it is pleasing to go and see the Doric camps." For a bad composition happens by beginning with the same syllable that the previous one ended with. And if an unharmonious expression is uttered in any other way, it is called "cacephaton." "Pleonasmos" <note>pleonasm</note> is the addition of a redundant word, such as "thus far the cultivation of the fields and the stars of heaven." For stars are nowhere else but in heaven. "Perisologia" is the redundant addition of many words, such as "may Reuben live and not die," since living is nothing other than not dying. "Macrologia" is long-windedness encompassing unnecessary things, such as: "the legates, since peace was not obtained, returned back home to where they had come from." "Tautologia" <note>tautology</note> is repetitive speech, such as: "if the fates preserve the man, or if he knows the ethereal air, and is not yet seized by the cruel shadows." For everything that is repeated is one thing, announced by frequent speech. "Eclipsis" <note>ellipsis</note> is a lack in speech where necessary words are missing, such as "to whom a quiver of gold" <note>original: "cui pharetra ex auro"</note>; for "was" <note>original: "erat"</note> is missing. "Tapinofis" is a lowliness of speech weakening the status of a great thing, such as "a few appear swimming in the vast abyss." He used "abyss" <note>original: "gurgitem"</note> instead of "sea." "Cacosyntheton" <note>faulty arrangement</note> is a faulty composition, such as "and we tire the backs of the youth with the reversed spear." "Amphibologia" <note>ambiguity</note> is ambiguous speech which happens either through the accusative case, such as that response of Apollo...

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of linguistic errors and ornaments. While the previous page dealt with barbarisms (errors in words) and solecisms (errors in syntax), this page transitions into how these same "errors" become "figures of speech" when used intentionally by poets for artistic effect.</meta>

To Pyrrhus: "I say to you, son of Aeacus, that the Romans you can defeat." <note>original: "aiō te eacida romanos vincere posse" — This is a famous example of grammatical ambiguity; the Latin word order makes it unclear whether the "son of Aeacus" (Pyrrhus) will defeat the Romans, or the Romans will defeat him.</note> In this case, it is not certain whom the usage shows to be the victor. It results in an uncertain distinction: "that a huge war Italy will wage." <note>original: "bellū ingens geret italia"</note> The distinction is uncertain: is it a "huge war" or a "huge Italy"? It also happens through a shared verb, as in: "Cato pleads/is pleaded against," "Cicero accuses/is accused," "Brutus waits/is waited for," "Antony is indignant/despised." <note>The original Latin uses deponent verbs like "deprecatur" and "calumniatur," which can be ambiguous in their direction.</note> In this ambiguity, it is not shown whether they themselves are the ones pleading or accusing, or if others are doing it to them. It also happens through homonyms, when many things are signified by one name: such as "edge" <note>original: "acies"</note>, unless you add "of iron" (a sword), "of the eyes" (sight), or "of soldiers" (a battle line).

## Chapter 34: On Metaplasms

"Metaplasm" <term>Metaplasm: from the Greek for 'transformation'</term> is called *transformatio* in the Latin language. This occurs in a single word due to the necessity of meter or the license allowed to poets. There are several types:

**Prothesis** is an addition at the beginning of a word: such as *gnato* for *nato* [son].
**Epenthesis** is an addition in the middle: such as *relliquias* for *reliquias* [remains], and "descendants remain in *relligione*" for *religione* [religion].
**Paragoge** is an addition at the end: such as *admittier* for *admitti* [to be admitted], and *potestur* for *potest* [he is able].
**Apheresis** is a cutting away from the beginning: such as *temno* for *contemno* [I despise].
**Syncope** is a cutting away from the middle: such as *forsan* for *forsitan* [perhaps].
**Apocope** is a cutting away from the end: such as *sat* for *satis* [enough].
**Ectasis** is a lengthening against nature: such as *italiām* [Italy] by fate, for a fugitive, and "Diana leads the *chozos*" [dances].
**Systole** is a shortening against nature: such as *aquilŭs* Orion, and the "city of *fidenă*," when the first syllable ought to be lengthened.
**Dieresis** is the splitting of one syllable into two: such as "a garment of *pictai* [embroidered] cloth" for *pictae*, and *albai longai* [of long Alba].
**Epitynaliphe** is the gluing of two syllables into one: such as *pariete* [wall] treated as three syllables instead of four, and *genua* [knees], or *phaeton* for *phaethon*.
**Synalephe** is the collision of vowels where words meet: such as "and those of the gods *penit⁹ oū*" [deep within].
**Ecthlipsis** is the collision of consonants with vowels: such as "much was he *multū ille* tossed on lands and the deep."
**Antithesis** is the substitution of one letter for another: such as *impere* for *imperi*, and *olli* for *illi* [to them].
**Metathesis** is the transposition of a letter: such as *evadre* for *evader* [to escape], or *timbre* for *timber*.

Between a "barbarism" <note>an error</note> and "leather" <note>correct speech</note>—that is, Latin and perfect eloquence—stands the **Metaplasm**: it is something that happens in a single word by the logic of a "fault" <note>it looks like an error but is done for a reason</note>. Likewise, between a "solecism" <note>a syntax error</note> and a "phrase"—that is, a perfect connection of words—stands the **Figure**: it is made from a combination of words by a "faulty" logic. Therefore, metaplasms and schemes are middle grounds; they are distinguished by whether the speaker is skillful or unskillful. They are created for the sake of ornament.

## Chapter 35: On Schemes

"Schemes" <term>Schemata: from the Greek word for 'figures'</term> are interpreted in Latin conversation as "figures," which are created in words or sentences through various forms of distinctions for the sake of ornate eloquence. While there are many of these among the grammarians, the following are found:

**Prolepsis** is "pre-emption," where those things which ought to follow are placed before: such as "meanwhile the kings with a huge mass, Latinus..." He ought to have said it this way: "Meanwhile the kings with a huge mass," and immediately added what follows, "proceed from the camps," then said "Latinus" and the rest. This pre-emption of the matter was done for ornament; the "kings" who should have followed were placed in between seven verses, and afterwards it was added, "they proceed from the camps." And then the pre-emption, where those things which should follow were placed before.

**Zeugma** <term>Zeugma: 'a joining'</term> is a closing where several senses are closed by a single word. This happens in three ways: for that word

<column-break/>

which joins the sentences is placed either at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle. At the beginning: such as "Fear empties <note>the verb</note> wine-cups, it [empties] our opinion of us." In the middle: such as "Greece by sighing was given to fate, Gaul [was given] by the court." At the end: such as "For at this time compliance [produces] friends, truth produces <note>the verb</note> hatred."

**Hypozeuxis** is a figure contrary to the one above, where in each individual sense there is its own closing: such as "He approaches the king, and to the king he relates both the name and the race."

**Syllepsis** <term>Syllepsis: 'a taking together' or 'conception'</term> occurs in differing closings, either where a plural subject is finished with a singular verb: such as "the companions and the king having been received" <note>original: "recepťo" - singular verb for plural subject</note>; or where a singular word is completed by a plural verb: such as "we have <note>plural verb</note> mellow apples, soft chestnuts, and a mountain of pressed milk." Syllepsis happens not only through parts of speech, but also through "accidents" and through numbers. For where one is put for many, or many for one, it is a syllepsis. For "one for many," as in: "they fill the womb with the armed soldier" <note>singular</note>, though it was not one, but many soldiers. Likewise, "many for one," as in the Gospel: "the thieves who were crucified with him mocked him," where both are brought in as having blasphemed, though it was only one.

**Anadiplosis** is when a following usage begins with the same word with which the previous usage ended: such as "The screech-owls terrify even the swans; Tityrus becomes Orpheus. Orpheus in the woods; among the dolphins, Orion."

**Anaphora** is the repetition of the same word at the beginnings of several lines: such as "We followed you, burnt Dardania, and your arms. We [followed] under you the swelling sea with the fleets of horses."

**Epanaphora** is the repetition of the same word at the beginning of phrases within a single line: such as "You the grove of Angitia [mourned], you the Fucine glass-like wave [mourned], you the liquid lakes mourned."

**Epizeuxis** is the doubling of a word within one sense: such as "Thus, thus it pleases to go beneath the shadows."

**Epanalepsis** is the repetition at the end of a line of a word placed at the beginning: such as "The love of money grows as much as the money itself grows."

**Paronomasia** is a word with a nearly identical sound but a different meaning: such as "whether it fits you to *abire* [depart] or *obire* [die]," that is, to become an exile or to perish.

**Scheshisonomaton** is a multitude of nouns joined together in a certain circularity: such as "clouds, snow, hail, storms, lightning, winds."

**Paromoeon** is a multitude of words starting with the same letter: such as that in Ennius: "O Titus, you yourself, Tatius, the tyrant, have endured such great things" <note>original: "O Tite tute tati tibi tanta tyzāne tulisti" — a famous example of heavy alliteration</note>. Virgil tempers this well; he does not use this figure throughout the whole line like Ennius, but now only at the beginning: "The cruel [sedes] sits upon arms" <note>original: "Sęua sedes sup arma"</note>; now in the middle: "wherever the lake broadly [late] the liquid [liquidos]..."; or now at the end: "Cassandra alone sang such [tales] disasters [casus] to me."

**Homoeoptoton** is when many nouns are declared in the same case: such as "Standing headlong on the summit," where one case is held throughout; and "moving the tooth and the hand and the rock in the hand."

**Homoeoteleuton** is when many words end in the same way: such as "he departed, he withdrew, he escaped, he erupted" <note>original: "abijt abscessit. euafit. ezupit"</note>.

**Polyptoton** is when a sentence is varied with different grammatical cases: such as "From nothing, nothing can return into nothing." "You may run back to Adarcida and Mappa, with Marcus promising." Marcus said: "It is so; assign the tablets, Marcus."

**Hyrmos** is a sentence that continues the tenor of its speech all the way to the end: such as "There is a place in a long retreat, an island..." for here the sense goes on at length until "From above, a dark grove with shivering shadow hangs over."

**Polysyntheton** is a phrase concatenated with many conjunctions...

<meta>Catchword: -ton</meta>

Having previously discussed metaplasms (changes to individual words), the text now transitions into figures of speech involving groups of words and the formal definitions of "tropes"—the creative ways poets bend the rules of language for artistic effect.</meta>

...as they sing of the correct hearth and arms and Amyclean <note>original: "amycleumqꝫ" — likely referring to Amyclae, a city in Laconia associated with Apollo and Castor.</note>.

**Dialyton**, or **Asyndeton**, is a figure which, conversely, expresses things loosely and simply without conjunctions. For example: "I came, I saw, I conquered." <note>original: "venim⁹ vidim⁹ placuit" — literally "We came, we saw, it was pleasing."</note> **Antithesis** is where opposites are set against opposites to return a beauty to the sentence. For example: "Cold things fought with hot, moist with dry, soft with hard, things with weight against those without weight." <note>A famous description of Chaos from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note> **Hypallage** is whenever words are understood through their opposite arrangement. For example: "giving the South winds to the fleets," when we actually give the ships to the winds, not the winds to the ships.

### Chapter 36: On Tropes

<image-desc>Decorative red initial letter T</image-desc>
Grammarians use the Greek name **Trope**, which is translated into Latin as "modes of expression." These are formed by moving from a proper meaning to one that is not proper, based on a similarity. It is very difficult to list the names of all of them, but here **Donatus** <note>Aelius Donatus was the most influential Latin grammarian of the 4th century; his work was the standard textbook for over a thousand years.</note> has prescribed thirteen for common use.

**Metaphor** is used when a word is borrowed and transferred. We see this when we say "the crops wave" or "strength buds," though we do not actually find "waves" or "buds" in these things; the words are transferred from elsewhere. However, these and other tropical <note>In this context, 'tropical' refers to 'tropes' or figurative language, not a climate.</note> expressions cover things that are meant to be understood with a figurative cloak, so that they might exercise the mind of the reader and not become cheap by being naked and obvious.

Metaphors are made in four ways:
1.  **From the animate to the animate**: such as "he mounts winged horses." Speaking metaphorically, the poet has mixed the wings of a bird with a four-footed animal; because the horse crossed the wilderness in its run, he mixed the speed of a bird with the run of a quadruped.
2.  **From the inanimate to the inanimate**: such as "the pine plows the sea" or "the deep keel presses a furrow." Here, the poet mixes the language of the land with the waters, since "plowing" and "pressing a furrow" belong to the earth, not the sea.
3.  **From the inanimate to the animate**: such as "flowering youth." Here, inanimate flowers are mixed with youth, which has a soul (is animate).
4.  **From the animate to the inanimate**: such as "You, Father Neptune, whose grey temples resound, washed by the clattering brine; for whom the great ocean flows from his chin, and rivers wander in his hair." For chins, temples, and hair do not belong to the ocean; these belong to men.

In this way, the names of other things are most fittingly transferred from one kind to another for the sake of beauty, so that speech may be adorned.

**Metalepsis** <note>A complex trope of substitution.</note> is either a "prior name," as in "the crops wave" (where you cannot say "the waves crop"), or it is **Antistrophos**, which is reciprocal. For example: "the oarage of wings." For we speak of the "wings of ships" (sails) and the "oarage of wings" (birds' flight).

**Catachresis** <term>Catachresis: the 'misuse' or 'abuse' of a word for something that lacks its own proper name</term> is the application of a name belonging to something else. It differs from metaphor because a metaphor grants a new word to something that already has a name, whereas catachresis uses a foreign word for something that has no proper name of its own. For example: "a face most like a laurel" or "the Centaur's keel through the salty shallows." Since "face" and "brow" belong only to animals and humans, if the poet had not applied these names to the ship, he would have had no proper name to call that part.

**Metalepsis** is a trope indicating what follows from what precedes. For example: "And the knotty reed came into his hand." Here, the hand signifies words, and the reed signifies letters.

**Metonymy** is a "trans-naming," where a name is transferred from its original meaning to another. It happens in many ways. It can show the thing contained through the container: "the theaters applaud" or "the meadows low," whereas the humans applaud in the one, and the oxen low in the other. Or, conversely, the container for the contained: "Now first Ucalegon burns," while it was not the man, but

<column-break/>

his house that was burning. Likewise, the thing found represents the inventor: "without Ceres and Liber [Bacchus], Venus freezes" or "Vulcan sends mixed embers to the stars." He wants us to understand "bread" through **Ceres** (the inventor of grain), "wine" through **Liber** (the inventor of wine), "lust" through **Venus**, and "fire" through **Vulcan**. Conversely, the inventor is shown by the invention: "we pray to wine," using the name of the one who found wine among the Greeks.

Likewise, the effect is shown by the efficient cause: "lazy cold" because it makes men lazy, and "pale fear" because it makes men turn pale. Or conversely, the cause is shown by the effect: "the father joins the horses to the chariot and adds foaming bits to the wild beasts." He said "foaming bits," although the bits do not produce foam; rather, it is the horse carrying them that sprinkles them with foam from its breath.

**Antonomasia** <term>Antonomasia: 'in place of a name'</term> is used in place of a proper name, such as "the son of Maia" for Mercury. This trope is made in three ways:
1.  **From the soul**: such as "the great-souled son of Anchises" [Aeneas].
2.  **From the body**: such as "he himself is towering."
3.  **From external things**: such as "the unhappy boy, an unequal match for Achilles" [Troilus].

**Epithet** <term>Epithet: 'added onto'</term> is placed before a proper name: such as "bounteous Ceres," "foul dogs," or "troublesome birds." The difference between antonomasia and an epithet is that antonomasia is put in place of a name, while an epithet is never used without a name. With these two tropes, we either disparage someone, point them out, or praise them.

**Synecdoche** <term>Synecdoche: 'understanding one thing through another'</term> is a grouping where the whole is understood from a part, or a part from the whole. It shows the genus for the species, and the species for the genus. The species is the part; the genus is the whole. A part is understood from the whole: such as "many birds gather where the cold year drives them across the sea." The "whole year" is not cold, only a part of the year, which is winter. Conversely, the whole from a part: such as "when the royal stern [the rear of a ship] had raised the flames." Here, "stern" means the whole ship; and "ship" means those who are in it; and not everyone, but one person raised the flames.

**Onomatopoeia** is a name made up to imitate the sound of a confused voice: such as the "creaking" of gates, the "neighing" of horses, the "lowing" of oxen, or the "bleating" of sheep.

**Periphrasis** is circumlocution, where one thing is signified by many words: such as "he draws vital air." He signifies one thing through this combination of words, which is: "he lives." This trope has a double nature: it either elegantly draws out the truth or avoids ugliness through a roundabout way. It draws out the truth elegantly, like: "And now the early Aurora [Dawn] was sprinkling the lands with new light, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus." He simply wants to say "it was getting light" or "the day was rising." It avoids ugliness by roundabout ways, like: "he sought the quiet of his spouse, sleep being poured through her limbs into her lap." By this roundabout way, he avoids obscenity and decently describes lying together.

**Hyperbaton** <term>Hyperbaton: 'stepping over'</term> is a transgression where the sentence order is changed. There are five types: **Anastrophe**, **Hysteroprotheron**, **Parenthesis**, **Tmesis**, and **Synchesis**.

**Anastrophe** is a backward order of words: "shores around" <note>original: "littoꝝ circū"</note> for "around the shores."
**Hysteroprotheron** is a sentence with the order changed: "after he touched the deep waves and came to the sea." For first he came to the sea, and then he touched the waves.
**Parenthesis** is where we interpose our own sentence, so that a delay in the middle draws out the sense: "Aeneas (for his fatherly love did not allow his mind to rest) sends swift Achates to the ships." The order is: "Aeneas sends swift Achates."

<summary>This page defines and provides examples for essential rhetorical tropes—such as metaphor, metonymy, and synecdoche—explaining how poets use figurative language to add beauty, clarity, or decorum to their writing.</summary>
<keywords>rhetoric, tropes, metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, grammar, Donatus, Latin literature, figures of speech, periphrasis, Virgil, Ovid</keywords>

# I

For that which is placed in the middle is a **Parenthesis**. **Tmesis** <note>original: "Temesis"; from the Greek for "cutting."</note> is the splitting of a single name [or noun] by the insertion of words, such as: "much cloud around the goddess poured a cloak" <note>original: "multu nebule circu dea fudit amictu"</note> instead of "poured-around" <note>original: "circufudit"</note>. **Synecdoche** <note>original: "Syndoche"</note> is where words are gathered together from every part, as in that passage: "Youths, bravest hearts, in vain, if you have a certain desire to follow me in daring the extreme; you see what fortune has befallen our state. All have departed, leaving the sanctuaries and altars by which this empire stood: help us." <note>A famous passage from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (2.348-353). The grammarian is explaining how the narrative structure groups these ideas.</note> Where the city is burning, let us die and rush into the midst of arms. The order is such: "Youths, bravest hearts, in vain help comes to the burning city, because all those by whom this empire stood have departed; therefore, if you have a certain desire to follow me in daring extremes, let us rush into the midst of arms and die."

**Hyperbole** is an "excessiveness" that goes beyond belief, further than what should be believed, such as "the wave strikes the stars" <note>original: "sidera v̄berat vnda"</note> or "the earth opens the deep waves." For this does not increase something beyond belief [to deceive], nor does it stray from the path of signifying the truth: because the words which indicate it may exceed the reality so that the will of the speaker appears without deception. By this trope, one not only increases something but also diminishes it: it increases, as in "swifter than the breeze," and diminishes, as in "softer than a feather" or "harder than a rock."

**Allegory** is "other-speaking" <note>original: "alieniloquiu"</note>; for it sounds like one thing and understands another. For example: "he beholds three stags wandering on the shore" <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.184.</note> where the three leaders of the Punic wars, or the three Punic wars themselves, are signified. And in the *Bucolics*: "I have sent ten golden apples" <note>Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.71.</note>, that is, to Augustus, meaning the ten books of the Eclogues of the shepherds. Of this trope there are many species, of which seven are prominent: **Irony**, **Antiphrasis**, **Enigma**, **Charientismos**, **Paremia**, **Sarcasmos**, and **Asteismos**.

**Irony** is an expression having a contrary meaning through its pronunciation. For by this trope, something is said cleverly either as an accusation or as an insult, such as: "Let Aeolus boast in that hall and reign in the closed prison of the winds." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.140-141.</note> And how is it a "hall" if it is a "prison"? For he resolves this by pronunciation. For "prison" is the pronunciation, while "let him boast in the hall" is the irony, and he announces the whole through a contrary pronunciation by means of irony, which mocks by praising.

**Antiphrasis** is speech to be understood from its opposite, such as a "grove" <note>original: "lucus"</note> because it lacks light <note>original: "lucet"; this is a famous false etymology: *lucus a non lucendo*.</note> due to the excessive shadow of the woods; and "spirits" <note>original: "manes"</note>, meaning mild and modest, when they are actually terrible and immense; and the "Fates" <note>original: "parce"</note> and "Eumenides" (Furies), because they spare no one <note>original: "nulli parcāt"</note> nor do good. By this trope, dwarfs are called "Atlases," and the blind are called "seers," and commonly Ethiopians are called "silvery" <note>original: "argentei"</note>. Between irony and antiphrasis, however, there is this distance: irony indicates what it wants to be understood by pronunciation alone, as when we say to a man acting badly: "It is good, what you are doing." Antiphrasis, however, does not signify the contrary by the voice of the speaker, but only by its own words when the origin is contrary.

**Enigma** is an obscure question which is difficult to understand unless it is opened, such as: "Out of the eater came meat, and out of the strong came sweetness" <note>The riddle of Samson from the Book of Judges 14:14.</note>, signifying the honeycomb extracted from the mouth of the lion. Between allegory and enigma there is this interest: allegory is doubly-natured and indicates something else figuratively under real things. Enigma, however, is only obscure and shaded through certain images.

**Charientismos** is a trope by which harsh things are expressed more gracefully, as when someone asks if anyone has looked for us, and we respond "Good fortune," from which it is understood that no one has sought

<column-break/>

us. **Paremia** <note>A proverb.</note> is a proverb adapted to things and times. To things, such as "kicking against the goad" <note>original: "cōtra stimulū calces"; to resist fruitlessly.</note>, by which is signified that one must resist adversity. To times, such as "the wolf in the story" <note>original: "lupus i fabula"; equivalent to "speak of the devil."</note>; for the country-folk say a man loses his voice if a wolf sees him first, whence that proverb is said to one who suddenly becomes silent: "the wolf in the story."

**Sarcasmos** is hostile mockery with bitterness, such as: "You shall go as a messenger and relate these things to my father, the son of Peleus [Achilles]; remember to tell him of my grim deeds and of degenerate Neoptolemus." <note>Pyrrhus mocking the dying King Priam in *Aeneid* 2.547-549.</note> To this, **Asteismos** is the contrary, that is, urbanity [wit] without anger, as: "He who does not hate Bavius, let him love your songs, Maevius; and let him yoke foxes and milk he-goats" <note>Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.90-91.</note>; that is, because he does not hate Bavius, let it befall him as a punishment that he loves Maevius. Now, Maevius and Bavius were very bad poets and enemies of Virgil. He who loves them, let him do things which are against nature, that is, "yoke foxes and milk he-goats."

**Homoiosis** <note>original: "Omocis"; Greek for "likeness."</note> is translated into Latin as "similarity," through which a demonstration unfolds a less known thing through the similarity of something that is better known. Of this there are three species: **Icon**, **Parabola**, and **Paradigma**—that is, image, comparison, and example. **Icon** is an image when we try to express the form of a thing from a similar kind, such as: "in everything like Mercury, both in voice and color, and golden hair, and the graceful limbs of youth." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.558-559.</note> For the similarity of the species is suitable when a person is introduced. **Parabola** is a comparison from dissimilar things, such as: "Just as a lion, seen in the fields of Libya, settles the enemy coming near," where he compared Caesar to a lion, making a similarity not from his own kind but from another. **Paradigma**, however, is an example of some word or deed, fitting to the matter we propose from either a similar or dissimilar kind, thus: "Scipio died as bravely in Spain as Cato did in Utica." Similarity, moreover, is made in three ways: from equals, from the greater, or from the lesser. From equals: "Just as when a sedition has often arisen in a great [populace]." From the greater to the less: "Just as a lightning bolt driven by the winds through the clouds." From the lesser to the greater: "If Orpheus could summon the spirit of his wife, relying on his Thracian lyre and tuneful strings," as if to say, from a small and brief thing—that is, if he relied on a lyre, I [rely] on piety.

### Chapter 37: On Prose

**Prose** is extended speech and freed from the law of meter. For the ancients used to call that which was extended and straight "prosum." Whence **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar of the 1st century BC.</note> says: "In Plautus, 'straight readings' are signified by 'prosis'." Whence also that speech which is not bent by rhythm but is straight is called "prose speech," in a straight extension. Others say prose is so called from that which is "poured out" <note>original: "pfusa" (profusa)</note>, or from that which proceeds and runs forth more spaciously, with no boundary defined for itself. Furthermore, among both the Greeks and the Latins, the care for songs [poetry] was far more ancient than for prose. For all things were first composed in verse. The study of prose, however, flourished late. Among the Greeks, **Pherecydes of Syros** was the first to write in "loosed speech" [prose]; among the Romans, however, **Appius the Blind** first practiced loosed speech against Pyrrhus. From then on, others also contended in the eloquence of prose.

### Chapter 38: On Meters

They are called **Meters** because they are bounded by certain measures and spaces of feet, nor do they proceed beyond the established dimension of times. Measure...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of literary composition. On the previous page, the author finished explaining figures of speech and tropes. He now transitions into the formal structure of poetry: verse, meter, and the various genres of classical and biblical song.</meta>

# Book [I]

The Greeks call it meter. **Verses** are so named because, with their "feet" arranged in their proper order, they are regulated by a fixed boundary through joints called **caesuras** <note>original: "cesurū"; the rhythmic breaks or "cuttings" within a line of poetry</note>. Lest they should wander further than the mind can sustain, reason established a limit at which the line should "turn back"; and from this very act of "turning back" <note>original: "revertit"</note> they say the "verse" <note>original: "versum"</note> is named. Closely linked to this is **rhythm**, which is not regulated by a fixed boundary but nevertheless runs with reasonably ordered feet; in Latin, this is called nothing other than **number** <note>original: "numerus"</note>. Concerning this is that famous line: "I remember the numbers [the tune], if only I could hold the words" <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (9.45)</note>. In Latin, anything contained by "feet" is called a **poem** <note>original: "carmina"</note>. They believe this name was given either because it is pronounced "piece by piece" <note>original: "carptim"</note>—whence today we say "to card wool" <note>original: "carminare"</note> when cleaning and separating it—or because those who sang such things were thought to be "lacking their minds" <note>original: "carere mente"; a play on the word "carmen" (song) and "careo" (to lack)</note>.

**Meters** are named either from their "feet," the subjects they describe, their inventors, the people who frequently used them, or the number of syllables. They are called after feet, such as **dactylic**, **iambic**, or **trochaic**; for from the "trochee" foot the trochaic meter is born, from the "dactyl" the dactylic, and so on for others. They are named from number, such as **hexameter** <note>six-measure</note>, **pentameter** <note>five-measure</note>, or **trimeter** <note>three-measure</note>. For we call verses **senarii** <note>sixes</note> based on the number of feet; the Greeks call these "trimeters" because they count them in pairs. Tradition holds that **Ennius** was the first to create Latin hexameters, and he called them "long" verses.

Meters are named after their inventors, such as **Anacreontic**, **Sapphic**, or **Archilochian**. For **Anacreon** composed Anacreontic meters; the woman **Sappho** published Sapphic verse; a certain **Archilochus** wrote Archilochian; a certain **Colophon** practiced the Colophonian; the **Sotadean** was found by **Sotades**, a Cretan by birth; and the lyric poet **Simonides** composed Simonidian meters. They are named after those who used them frequently, such as **Asclepiadean**; for Asclepius did not invent these, but they are so called because he used them most frequently and elegantly.

They are named after the things they describe, such as **Heroic**, **Elegiac**, or **Bucolic**. It is called a **Heroic** song because the deeds and facts of brave men are narrated in it. For "Heroes" is the name given to men who are, as it were, "airy" <note>original: "aerei"</note> and worthy of heaven on account of their wisdom and bravery. This meter precedes all others in authority; it is the only one suited to the greatest works as well as the smallest, being equally capable of sweetness and charm. Because of these virtues, it alone obtained the name "Heroic," specifically to commemorate the deeds of heroes. Indeed, compared to others, it is the most simple, consisting of two feet: the **dactyl** and the **spondee**—and often consists almost entirely of one or the other, unless the mixture of the two is perfectly balanced. It is considered the first of all meters. **Moses** is proven to have sung this first in the *Song of Deuteronomy* long before **Pherecydes** and **Homer**. From this it appears that the study of songs was more ancient among the Hebrews than among the Gentiles. Indeed, **Job**, who was a contemporary of Moses, is found to have used hexameter with dactyls and spondees. Among the Greeks, the soldier **Achates of Miletus** is said to have composed it first, or as others think, **Pherecydes of Syros**. This meter was called **Pythian** before Homer, and **Heroic** after Homer. It was called Pythian because the oracles of Apollo were issued in this kind of meter; for when he pursued the serpent Python on Mount Parnassus with arrows to avenge his mother, the inhabitants of Delphi...

<column-break/>

...encouraged him with this meter, saying—as **Terentianus** reports. **Elegiac** verse is so named because the melody of this song is suited to the miserable. Terentianus usually calls these "elegies" because such a closing was originally used for sad moods. However, it is entirely uncertain by whom it was invented, except that among us [Latins], **Ennius** used it first. Among the Greeks, the law of the grammarians still hangs in the balance, so that the matter remains "under the judge" <note>A reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*: "adhuc sub iudice lis est"</note>. For some of them want a certain **Colophon**, and others **Archilochus**, to be the author and inventor.

**Bucolic**, that is, "pastoral" song, is thought by many to have been first composed by shepherds at Syracuse; some say at Lacedaemon [Sparta]. For when the King of the Persians was crossing into Thrace, the Spartan virgins—fearing the enemy—did not dare to leave the city nor perform the customary rustic choral procession for Diana. Therefore, a crowd of shepherds celebrated the same rites with unpolished songs so that the religion would not be neglected. It is called "Bucolic" <note>cow-herding</note> from its majority part, although the conversations and songs of shepherds and goat-herds are also inserted in them.

It is manifest that the prophet **David** was the first to compose and sing **hymns** in praise of God. Later, among the Gentiles, **Mnemosyne** <note>or "Mnematime," likely a corruption referring to the Muses</note> first made them for Apollo and the Muses; this was in the time of Ennius, long after David. "Hymns" translated from Greek into Latin means "praises." **Epithalamia** are songs for those marrying, which are sung by students in honor of the groom and bride. **Solomon** first published these in praise of Christ and the Church. From this, the Gentiles claimed the epithalamium for themselves, and this kind of song was adopted. This genre was first celebrated by the Gentiles on stages, but later it remained only for weddings. It is called an "epithalamium" because it is sung in the "chamber" <note>original: "thalamis"</note>.

**Threnoi**, which in Latin we call "laments," were first composed in verse by **Jeremiah** over the city of Jerusalem and the people when they were led into captivity. After him, among the Greeks, came the lyric poet **Simonides**. They were used at funerals and lamentations, just as they are now. **Epitaph** in Greek is "above the tomb" in Latin. It is the title of the dead which is made for those who have died and are in their "sleeping-place." The life, character, and age of the deceased are written there. **Dochis** <note>likely "Doche," a collection</note> is the Greek name for a work of many books; a **Poema** is one; an **Idyll** <note>original: "idillion"</note> is a few verses; a **Distich** is two; a **Monostich** is one. An **Epigram** is a title, which in Latin is interpreted as a "superscription." For *Epi* means "above" and *gramma* means "letter" or "writing."

An **Epode** in a poem is a short closing line. It is called an epode because it is assimilated to the appearance of the elegiac, where the structure is composed with one longer line followed by a shorter one, and in each case, the shorter lines follow the longer ones as if "singing back" a closing. Lyric poets call these "closings" <note>original: "clausulas"</note>, as if they were cut-off verses placed under whole ones, as in **Horace**: "Happy is he who, far from business," then follows the cut-off verse: "like the ancient race of mortals" <note>Quotes from Horace's *Epode* 2</note>. Thus also **Alternating** verses, in which some part is missing, are similar to the preceding ones but shorter.

Grammarians use the term **Centos** for works composed from the songs of **Homer** or **Virgil**, stuffed together into a single body from many parts here and there, after the manner of a "patchwork quilt" <note>original: "centonario"</note>, according to the skill of the subject matter. Finally, **Proba** <note>Faltonia Betitia Proba, a 4th-century poet</note>, the wife of Adelphus, most fully expressed a Cento from Virgil concerning the creation of the world and the Gospels, with the material composed according to the verses and by the verses...
