...the material into a harmonious arrangement. In this same way, a certain Pomponius, among the other leisure-works of his pen, composed the poem *Tityrus* <note>original: "tityrẽ"; a reference to Virgil's first Eclogue</note> in honor of Christ from the same [Virgilian] poem; he did similarly with the *Aeneid*.

## On Fables, Chapter 39

Poets named **fables** from the act of "speaking" <note>original: "a fando"; Isidore links 'fabula' to 'fari', to speak</note>, because they are not deeds that actually happened, but things "fashioned in speaking" <note>original: "fando fictę"</note>. They were introduced so that through the fashioned conversation of mute animals, a certain image of human life might be recognized. **Alcmon of Croton** is said to have been the first to invent these. They are also called **Aesopic** because **Aesop**, a man from Phrygia, was particularly outstanding in this craft. Fables are either Aesopic or Libystic. They are **Aesopic** when mute animals are imagined to be conversing among themselves, or even things that do not have a soul, such as cities, trees, mountains, rocks, and rivers. They are **Libystic**, however, when a conversation is fashioned between humans and beasts, or beasts and humans.

Poets fashioned some fables for the sake of delight; some they interpreted according to the nature of things, and others according to the morals of men. For the sake of delight: such as those commonly told, or the kind that **Plautus** and **Terence** composed. They fashion fables according to the nature of things, such as **Vulcan** being lame, because by nature fire is never upright. Or like that triple-formed beast, the **Chimaera**: "first a lion, last a dragon, in the middle the Chimaera herself"—that is, a she-goat <note>original: "caprea"</note>. By this, they intended to distinguish the ages of man: the first, youth, is fierce and rushing like a lion; the middle of life’s time is most clear-sighted <note>original: "lucidissimũ"</note> like a goat, because it sees most sharply; then comes old age, bent by misfortunes like a dragon. Similarly, the fable of the **Hippocentaur** was fashioned—that is, a man mixed with a horse—to express the speed of human life, because it is well known that a horse is very fast. 

Regarding morals: as in **Horace**, where a mouse speaks to a mouse, and a weasel to a little fox, so that through a fashioned narration, a true significance is applied to the matter at hand. Hence, Aesop's fables are of this kind, directed toward a moral end; or as in the **Book of Judges**, where the trees seek a king for themselves and speak to the olive, the fig, the vine, and the bramble. All of this is fashioned for the sake of morals, so that a true meaning may come through a fashioned narrative to the point intended. 

In this way, the orator **Demosthenes** used a fable against **Philip [of Macedon]**. When Philip demanded that the Athenians give him ten of their orators so that he would depart, Demosthenes told this fable to dissuade them: he said that once the wolves wanted to deceive the diligence of the shepherds and urged them to enter into a friendship, on the condition that the shepherds hand over the dogs (who were the cause of the quarreling). The shepherds agreed and, in the hope of security, gave up the dogs, who were the most vigilant guardians of their sheep. Then the wolves, with all fear removed, tore apart everything in those flocks, not just for hunger but for lust. Thus, he warned, Philip was demanding the leaders of the city so that he could more easily overwhelm the city once it was stripped of its guardians.

## On the Term "History", Chapter 40

**History** is the narration of deeds done, through which those things that happened in the past are discerned. It is called *historia* in Greek from "to see" or "to know" <note>original: "apo tu istozĩ" / ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱστορεῖν</note>. Among the ancients, no one would write a history unless they had been present and had seen

<column-break/>

the things that were to be written. For we grasp the things that happen better with our eyes than those we gather by hearing. For things that are seen are presented without falsehood. This discipline pertains to **Grammar**, because whatever is worthy of memory is committed to letters. Histories are called **monuments** <note>original: "monumẽtra"</note> for the reason that they grant "memory" <note>original: "memoriã"</note> to deeds done. A **series** <note>original: "series"</note> is so named by a metaphor from "wreaths of flowers" <note>original: "sertis flor[um]"</note> woven into one another.

## On the First Authors of History, Chapter 41

Among us [Christians], **Moses** first wrote a history concerning the beginning of the world. Among the Gentiles, however, **Dares the Phrygian** first published a history of the Greeks and Trojans, which they say he wrote on palm leaves. After Dares, **Herodotus** was considered the first historian in Greece; after him, **Pherecydes** became famous, around the time that **Ezra** wrote the Law.

## On the Utility of History, Chapter 42

The histories of the nations do not hinder readers in the useful things they say. Indeed, many wise men have placed the past deeds of men into histories for the instruction of those living now. Furthermore, through history, the total calculation of past times and years is understood; many necessary things are investigated through the succession of consuls and kings.

## On the Types of History, Chapter 43

The genus of history is threefold. For **Ephemeris** <note>original: "Ephemeris"; from Greek for "of the day"</note> is the record of one day's deeds; we call this a **diary** <note>original: "diariũ"</note>. What the Latins call a diary, the Greeks call an *ephemeris*. **Calendars** <note>original: "kalẽdaria"</note> are those that arrange things by individual months. **Annals** <note>original: "Annales"</note> are the events of individual years. For whatever was worthy of memory, done at home or in military service, on sea or on land, and recorded year by year in commentaries, they named "annals" from these annual deeds. **History**, however, covers many years or times, and through its diligence, the annual commentaries are gathered into books. 

There is this difference between history and annals: history concerns those times we have seen, while annals concern those years which our age has not known. Thus **Sallust** is composed of "histories," while **Eusebius** and **Jerome** consist of "annals" and "history." There is also a difference between history, **argument**, and **fable**. Histories are true things that happened; arguments are things that, even if they did not happen, nevertheless *could* have happened; fables, however, are things that neither happened nor can happen, because they are contrary to nature.

---

### Here begins the second book: On Rhetoric and its Name, Chapter 1

**Rhetoric** is the science of speaking well in civil questions, for the purpose of persuading regarding just and good things, in the affairs of both things and persons. It is called "rhetoric" by a Greek name, from the phrase "from the flow of speech" <note>original: "απο̃ του ρητοριζειν" / ἀπὸ τοῦ ῥητορεύειν</note>, that is, from a "copiousness of speaking." For among the Greeks, speech is called *rhetis* <note>original: "Rhetis"; likely referring to *rhesis*</note>, and a speaker is a *rhetor*. Rhetoric is joined to the art of grammar. In the science of grammar, we learn to speak correctly; in rhetoric, we perceive how we should deliver the things we have learned.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Book I (Grammar) into Book II (Rhetoric), following the discussion of fables and history. It introduces the origins, definitions, and primary classifications of rhetorical study, drawing heavily from Cicero and Quintilian.</meta>

### On the Inventors of the Rhetorical Art, Chapter 2

This discipline was invented by the Greeks—specifically by **Gorgias**, **Aristotle**, and **Hermagoras**—and was translated into Latin by **Tully** <note>original: "tullio"; Marcus Tullius Cicero, the most famous Roman orator</note> and **Quintilian**. It was handled with such abundance and variety that it is easy for a reader to admire it, but impossible to fully grasp it. For while the sequence of speech clings to the memory as long as the mind is focused, once the attention is set aside, the entire recollection slips away. A perfect knowledge of this discipline creates an **orator**.

### On the Name of the Orator and the Parts of Rhetoric, Chapter 3

An **orator** is, therefore, a "good man skilled in speaking." <note>This is the famous definition by Cato the Elder, later championed by Quintilian.</note> Being a "good man" consists of his nature, morals, life, and arts. Being "skilled in speaking" consists of skillful eloquence, which is composed of five parts: **invention**, **disposition**, **elocution** <note>style and word choice</note>, **memory**, and **pronunciation** <note>delivery</note>. The end goal of his duty is to persuade someone of something. This very skill in speaking consists of three things: **nature**, **doctrine**, and **use**. Nature requires talent; doctrine requires knowledge; use requires constant practice. These are the qualities expected not only in an orator but in any skilled person so that they may accomplish something.

### On the Three Types of Cases, Chapter 4

There are three types of cases: **deliberative**, **demonstrative**, and **judicial**. 
*   The **deliberative** type is that in which we discuss various utilities of life—what ought or ought not to be done. 
*   The **demonstrative** type is that in which a person is shown to be either praiseworthy or blameworthy. 
*   The **judicial** type is that in which a judgment of punishment or reward is given regarding a person's deed. 

It is called "judicial" because it judges a person and shows by its sentence whether they are praiseworthy and worthy of reward, or indeed a defendant to be condemned or freed from punishment. The **deliberative** type is so named because one deliberates on each matter within it. This type is twofold: **persuasion** and **dissuasion**—that is, concerning what to seek and what to flee, or what to do and what not to do. 

Persuasion is divided into three areas: the **honorable**, the **useful**, and the **possible**. This differs somewhat from deliberation: persuasion requires another person <note>an audience to be convinced</note>, while deliberation is sometimes conducted within oneself. In persuasion, two things carry the most weight: **hope** and **fear**. 

The **demonstrative** type is so named because it "demonstrates" <note>shows or points out</note> each thing by either praising or blaming it. This type has two species: **praise** and **vituperation** <note>reproach</note>. The order of praise is distinguished by three times: before the person, during the person's life, and after the person. 
*   **Before the person:** such as "what happy ages produced such a person?" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, 1.606</note> 
*   **During the person's life:** such as "O you who alone pitied the unspeakable labors of Troy." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, 1.597</note> 
*   **After the person:** such as "While rivers run to the sea, while shadows cross the mountain slopes, while the sky feeds the stars, your honor, name, and praise shall remain." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, 1.607-609</note> 

In the same order, conversely, this form should be observed in the **vituperation** of a man: before the man, during the man, and after the man. A **commonplace** <note>a general argument against a vice</note> belongs to the demonstrative type of vituperation, yet it differs from it in some way. For vituperation, which is the opposite of praise, is applied specifically to a certain and distinct person. A commonplace, however, is set forth generally against the crime of a deed. Hence it is called a "commonplace" because, in the absence of a specific person, it exposes the crime itself rather than just the man. For a vice is found not only in one person but is common to many.

<column-break/>

### On the Double Status of Cases, Chapter 5

Among rhetoricians, **status** <note>the 'standing' or 'issue' of a case</note> refers to the matter in which the case consists; that is, the **constitution**. The Greeks call "status" *stasin* <note>Greek: στάσιν</note> from the idea of a "stand" or "conflict." The Latins call it this not only because of the fight in which the opponent's proposition is attacked, but because both parties "stand" upon it. It arises from the accusation and the defense. 

The statuses of cases are twofold: **rational** and **legal**. From the **rational** status arise:
1.  **Conjecture** <note>did it happen?</note>
2.  **Definition** <note>what is it called?</note>
3.  **Quality** <note>what kind of act was it?</note>
4.  **Transference** <note>is this the right court or law?</note>

From quality arise the **judicial** and **business-like**. From the judicial arise the **absolute** and **assumptive**. From the assumptive arise: **concession**, **removal of the crime**, **relation of the crime**, and **compensation**. From concession arise **purgation** and **deprecation**.

*   The **conjectural status** is when a deed charged against one person is denied by them.
*   The **definitive status** is when one contends that the deed is not what is charged, but defines what it actually is using definitions.
*   **Quality** is when the nature of the thing is questioned; because the controversy concerns the force and type of the business, it is called the "general constitution."
*   **Transference** <note>original: "translatio"</note> is when the case depends on the fact that either the person bringing the action, or the place, time, law, charge, or penalty does not seem to be the correct one. It is a "translative constitution" because the action seems to need a transfer or change.
*   The **judicial status** is that in which the nature of equity and right, or the reason for reward or punishment, is sought.
*   The **business-like status** is that in which what is right according to civil custom and equity is considered.
*   The **assumptive status** is that which provides nothing firm for a refusal on its own, but assumes something from outside for a defense.
*   **Concession** is when the defendant does not defend the deed that was done, but asks to be forgiven. We prove that this pertains to **penitents**.
*   **Removal of the crime** is when the defendant tries to move the charge brought against them—and their own fault—onto another person or power.
*   **Relation of the crime** is when a deed is said to have been done lawfully because the person was previously provoked by an injury.
*   **Comparison** is when some other honorable or useful deed of another is countered, which it is said was committed so that the other might happen.
*   **Purgation** is when the deed is indeed conceded, but the fault is removed. This has three parts: **imprudence** <note>ignorance</note>, **accident**, and **necessity**.
*   **Deprecation** is when the defendant confesses that they have both sinned and sinned deliberately, yet asks to be forgiven; this type can only happen very rarely.

Likewise, from the **legal status** <note>interpreting written law</note> these arise:
1.  **Letter and Intent** <note>original: "scriptum et voluntas"</note>: when the words themselves seem to disagree with the writer's intention.
2.  **Contrary Laws**: when two or more laws are found to disagree with each other.
3.  **Ambiguity**: when what is written seems to mean two or more things.
4.  **Collection** or **Reasoning**: when from what is written, something else which is not written is also discovered.
5.  **Legal Definition**: when the force of a word is sought, as in the definitive constitution.

Therefore, both rational and legal statuses are counted by some more certainly as **eighteen**; however, according to the rhetorical works of **Cicero**, **nineteen** are found, because he primarily placed "transference" among the rational statuses. Later, Cicero, correcting himself, applied transference to the legal statuses.

It details the various "statuses" or points of contention used in legal defense, such as intent, accident, and legal ambiguity.</summary>

II 10 <note>The page number is likely "10" using a variant of Roman/early modern numbering.</note>

## On the Three-Part Controversy, Chapter 6
According to Cicero, a three-part controversy is either **simple** or **joined**. If it is joined, one must consider whether it is joined from several questions or from some comparison. A **simple controversy** is one that contains a single, absolute question, in this manner: "Shall we declare war on the Corinthians or not?" A **joined controversy** is made of several questions in which many things are sought, in this way: "Should Carthage be destroyed, or returned to the Carthaginians, or should a colony be led there?" It is from **comparison** when it is asked through contention which is better or what is most important, in this manner: "Should an army be sent into Macedonia against Philip to be an aid to our allies, or should it be held in Italy so that there may be the greatest forces against Hannibal?"

## On the Four Parts of an Oration, Chapter 7
The parts of a speech in the rhetorical art are four: the **introduction** <note>original: "exordium"</note>, the **statement of facts** <note>original: "narratio"</note>, the **argumentation**, and the **conclusion**. The first of these rouses the mind of the listener. The second explains the events that occurred. The third creates trust in the assertions. The fourth encompasses the end of the entire speech. Therefore, one must begin in such a way as to make the listener **well-disposed**, **teachable**, or **attentive**: well-disposed by praying <note>or appealing to them</note>, teachable by instructing them, and attentive by exciting them. One must narrate in such a way that we speak briefly and appropriately. One must argue in such a way that we first strengthen our own points, and then shatter the opposing ones. One must conclude in such a way that we stir the mind of the listener to fulfill what we are saying.

## On the Five Modes of Cases, Chapter 8
The species of cases are five: that is, **honorable**, **astonishing**, **humble**, **doubtful**, and **obscure**. The **honorable** <note>original: "honestum"</note> kind of case is one which the mind of the listener favors immediately without our speaking. The **astonishing** <note>original: "admirabile"</note> is one from which the minds of those who are about to listen are alienated. The **humble** is that which is neglected by the listener and does not seem to require great attention. The **doubtful** <note>original: "anceps"</note> is that in which either the judgment is uncertain, or the case is a mixture of honor and disgrace, such that it produces both goodwill and offense. The **obscure** is that in which either the listeners are slow, or the case is seen to be entangled in questions too difficult to understand the business.

## On Syllogisms, Chapter 9
What is called a **syllogism** in Greek is called **argumentation** in Latin. It is called argumentation as if it were a "speech by arguments" <note>original: "argumentis oratio"</note> through which we follow through on a discovered probability. A syllogism, therefore, is the final conclusion of a premise <note>original: "positionis"</note> and an assumption, and of a confirmation, either from the uncertainty of one who doubts or from the confidence of one who proves. For it consists of three parts: the **premise**, the **assumption**, and the **conclusion**. For example, a **proposition** <note>premise</note>: "What is good cannot have a shameful use." The listener agrees. He **assumes** the next part: "Money has a shameful use." He **concludes**: "Therefore, money is not a good." However, not only rhetoricians but especially logicians <note>original: "dialectici"</note> use syllogisms. Indeed, the Apostle <note>likely referring to St. Paul</note> often proposes, assumes, confirms, and concludes, which, as we have said, belong properly to the arts of logic and rhetoric. Among rhetoricians, there are principally two kinds of syllogisms: **induction** and **ratiocination**.

<column-break/>

There are three members of **induction**. First, the **proposition**. Second, the **inference**, which is also called the **assumption**. Third, the **conclusion**. Induction is that which seeks the assent of the person to whom it is directed through things that are not doubtful, whether among philosophers, rhetoricians, or those in conversation. The **proposition of induction** is that which necessarily introduces one or more similarities to the thing to be granted. The **inference of induction** (also called the assumption) is that which introduces the matter under contention and for whose sake the similarities were held. The **conclusion of induction** is that which either confirms the concession of the inference or declares what may be finished by it. **Ratiocination** is the speech by which that which is the subject of the question is proven. 

The **enthymeme**, therefore, is interpreted in Latin as a "conception of the mind" <note>original: "mentis conceptio"</note>, which the writers of the arts are accustomed to call an **imperfect syllogism**. For the form of this argument consists of two parts, since that which pertains to creating trust is done with the law of syllogisms passed over, as in this example: "If a storm is to be avoided, then one must not sail." For it stands as a completed thought from a single proposition alone; for this reason, it is judged to be more suitable for rhetoricians than for logicians. There are two modes of ratiocination. The first is the **enthymeme**, which is an imperfect and rhetorical syllogism. The second is the **epichereina** <note>epicheirema</note>, which is a broader syllogism in rhetorical matters. 

There are five members of the **enthymeme**:
1.  The **convincible**, which convinces by evident reason, just as Cicero did in his speech *For Milo*: "You would not wish the life of this man to be restored through you, if you think you would then be the punishers of the crime of his death." <note>original: "Eius igitur mortis sceleris ultores cuius vitam si putetis per vos restitui posse nolitis"</note>
2.  The **ostentatious** <note>demonstrative</note>, which constrains by a certain demonstration of the matter, as Cicero says *Against Catiline*: "Yet this man lives; indeed, he lives and even comes into the Senate." <note>original: "Hic tamen vivit: immo vivit et iam in senatum venit"</note>
3.  The **sentential**, which adds a general maxim, as in Terence: "Compliance breeds friends; truth breeds hatred." <note>original: "Obsequium amicos: veritas odium parit"</note>
4.  The **exemplary**, which threatens a similar outcome by the comparison of some example, as Cicero says in the *Philippics*: "I marvel, Antony, that you do not fear the ends of those whose examples you imitate." <note>original: "te miror: antoni: quorum exempla imitaris: eorum exitus non pertimescere"</note>
5.  The **collective**, when the arguments are gathered into one, as Cicero says in *For Milo*: "Him whom he did not wish to kill when he could have done so with favor, did he wish to kill with the complaint of others? Him whom he did not dare to kill by right, in that place, or at that time, did he not hesitate to kill with injury, at an unseasonable time, and with the danger of his own head?"

Furthermore, according to **Victorinus** <note>Marius Victorinus, a 4th-century grammarian and rhetorician</note>, there is another definition of the enthymeme from a single proposition, as has already been said, which stands thus: "If a storm is to be avoided, navigation is not to be sought." It can also stand from the assumption alone, such as: "If he is an enemy, he killed him; but he is an enemy." And because the conclusion is missing from it, it is called an enthymeme. Following this is the **epichereina**, descending from ratiocination, which is broader and more executed than rhetorical syllogisms, differing in breadth and the production of speech from the syllogisms of logic. For this reason, it is given to rhetoricians. This consists of three modes. The first mode is **tripartite**. The second is **quadripartite**. The third is **quinquepartite**. The tripartite epichereimatic syllogism is that which consists of three members: that is, the proposition, the assumption, and the conclusion. The quadripartite is that which consists of four members...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of rhetorical logic, moving from the definition of controversies to the structure of the syllogism—a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. It then transitions into definitions of legal and social norms, and various rhetorical exercises used to train students in argumentation and characterization.</meta>

...position: the second is the **assumption** <note>Also known as the minor premise</note>, and one is the conjunction of the proposition or the assumption. The third is the **proof** and the **conclusion**. The **five-part** [syllogism] is that which consists of five members: that is, first, the **proposition**; second, its **proof**; third, its **assumption**; fourth, its **proof**; and fifth, the **conclusion**. Cicero uses this method in the *Art of Rhetoric* <note>Referring to Cicero’s *De Inventione*</note>: "If deliberation and demonstration are types of cases, they cannot rightly be considered parts of any single type of case. For the same thing can be a 'genus' <note>general category</note> to one thing and a 'part' to another; but it cannot be both the genus and the part of the same thing." This continues until the members of this syllogism are concluded.

## On Law, Chapter 10

<margin><image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand) points toward the beginning of this section.</image-desc></margin>

**L**aw <note>original: "Lex"</note> is the ordinance of the people, which the elders <note>the senate or those of higher rank</note> have decreed together with the commoners. For what a king or emperor has proclaimed is called a **constitution** or an **edict**. The establishment of equity is twofold: sometimes in laws, and sometimes in customs. Between law and custom, however, there is this difference: law is written, while **custom** <note>original: "mos"</note> is a practice approved by antiquity—essentially an unwritten law. For law is named from "reading" <note>original: "a legendo," a common medieval etymology</note> because it is written down. Custom, however, is a long-standing practice drawn similarly from "morals" <note>original: "de moribus"</note>. Furthermore, **usage** <note>original: "consuetudo"</note> is a type of right established by morals, which is adopted as law when a written law is lacking. It makes no difference whether it consists of writing or of reason, since reason also commends the law. Furthermore, if law consists of reason, then everything that consists of reason will already be law—provided that it is consistent with religion, compatible with discipline, and profitable for safety. It is called usage because it is in common use. Every law either **permits** something (such as a brave man seeking a reward), **forbids** something (such as no one being allowed to seek marriage with the sacred virgins), or **punishes** (such as one who commits a theft being struck by capital punishment). Laws were made so that human audacity might be restrained by fear of them, and so that innocence might be safe among the wicked, and so that the power to do harm might be reined in among the wicked themselves by the dread of punishment. For human life is governed by the reward or penalty of the law. A law must be honorable, just, possible, according to nature, according to the custom of the country, suitable to the place and time, necessary, useful, and clear—lest it hold anyone in a trap through obscurity—and written for no private benefit, but for the common utility of the citizens.

## On the Maxim, Chapter 11

**A** **maxim** <note>original: "sententia"</note> is an impersonal saying, such as: "Compliance breeds friends, truth breeds hatred." If a specific person is added to this, it becomes a **chria** <note>a Greek rhetorical exercise based on an anecdote</note>, like this: "Achilles offended Agamemnon by speaking the truth," or "Metrophanes earned the favor of Mithridates by being compliant." For this is the difference between a *chria* and a maxim: a maxim is delivered without a person, whereas a *chria* is never spoken without a person. Thus, if a person is added to a maxim, it becomes a *chria*; if the person is removed, it becomes a maxim.

## On Confirmation and Refutation, Chapter 12

**C**onfirmation <note>original Greek: "catasceua"</note> is the corroboration of a proposed matter. **Refutation** <note>original Greek: "anasceua"</note>, however, is the opposite of the former. It proves that what is proposed as having been born, or made, or said, either was not so or is not so: for example, if someone denies that Chryseis existed, or confirms that she did. The difference between these and a **thesis** is that although a thesis may also have a dispute on either side, it is a kind of

<column-break/>

deliberation or exhortation regarding an uncertain matter. Confirmation and Refutation, however, usually deal with things that are not likely but are presented as true. The primary division of Refutation is "the unsuitable" and "the false." The types of the unsuitable are that which is dishonorable and that which is useless. Likewise, the dishonorable is treated in either words or deeds. In words, as if someone should say that the famous Cato the Censor said things that were unbecoming and did not match his authority—for instance, if he were said to have exhorted the youth to wickedness and luxury. In deeds, as if someone should say a person did something abhorrent to their sanctity and name, such as the story of the adultery of Mars and Venus. Falsehood has three types: the **incredible**, such as that a youth saw fleets entering Africa from the Sicilian shore; the **impossible**, as that Clodius set an ambush for Milo; and the **contradictory**, such as that the same man was killed by Milo. For if he set the ambush, he did the killing; if he was killed, he did not set the ambush <note>This refers to the famous legal defense of Milo by Cicero</note>. This distribution, reformed into the opposite, will serve for Confirmation. It will be necessary, however, to arrange the principles so that we say either that the authority of the ancients must be believed, or that no faith should be given to fables. And finally, in Refutation, let us ask whether they intended to signify anything other than what they represented in these figures—such as that Scylla was not a sea-monster, but a seaside woman, and not "girded by dogs" but rather someone rapacious and inhospitable to those who came by.

## On Personification, Chapter 13

**P**ersonification <note>original Greek: "prosopopeia"</note> is when a persona and speech are imagined for animals, things, or people. This is like Cicero in his speech against Catiline: "For if my country, which is much dearer to me than my life, should speak with me, saying..." Thus we also represent mountains and rivers or trees as speaking, imposing a "persona" on a thing that does not have a speaking nature. This is customary in tragedies and is found very frequently in orations.

## On Characterization, Chapter 14

**W**e call that **characterization** <note>original Greek: "ethopeia"</note> in which we imagine the persona of a human being to express their emotion, age, study, fortune, joy, severity, or audacity. For when the persona of a pirate is taken up, the speech will be bold, abrupt, and reckless; when the speech of a woman is simulated, the speech ought to be fitting; and indeed, there is a different style of speaking for a youth, an old man, a soldier, an emperor, a parasite, a rustic, and a philosopher. For one who is moved by joy speaks one way, and one who is wounded speaks another. In this kind of diction, these things are especially to be considered: who speaks, to whom, about what, where, and at what time; what they have done, what they are about to do, or what they might suffer if they neglect these counsels.

## On the Types of Questions, Chapter 15

**T**here are two types of questions: one is **finite**, the other **infinite**. The finite is called *hypothesio* in Greek and "a cause" <note>original: "causa"</note> in Latin, where there is a controversy involving a specific person. The infinite is what is called *thesis* in Greek and "a proposition" in Latin; this does not have a specific person nor is it contained in any specific circumstance—that is, neither place nor time. In a "cause," however, all things are certain, which is why a proposition is, as it were, a part of a cause.

<meta>This page continues the technical instruction on rhetoric. Having previously discussed logic, syllogisms, and the nature of law, the text now transitions to "Elocution" (Style), moving from the internal structure of an argument to the external beauty and correctness of speech.</meta>

### On Style, Chapter 16

<margin>instruction</margin>
Now, in your choice of style <note>original: "elocutionibus"</note>, you must use what the subject matter, the place, the time, and the person listening demand. Do not mix the profane with the religious, the unseemly with the chaste, the light with the heavy, the playful with the serious, or the ridiculous with the sad. One must speak both correctly <note>original: "latine," literally "in Latin," implying proper grammar and purity of language</note> and clearly. He speaks "correctly" who pursues the true and natural words of things and does not deviate from the speech and refinement of the present time. For such a man, it is not enough to see what he says unless he also says it pleasantly and openly; indeed, even that is not enough, unless he also practices what he preaches.

### On the Threefold Style of Speaking, Chapter 17

<margin>differentiation</margin>
Things should be said mildly when they are humble, with gravity when they are stirring, and with moderation when they are in between. For this is that threefold way of speaking: the **low**, the **middle**, and the **grand** <note>original: "humile, medium, grandiloquum"</note>. When we speak of great things, they should be presented grandly; when we speak of small things, with subtlety; when of medium things, with temperance. For in small cases, nothing grand or sublime should be spoken, but one should speak in a mild and "pedestrian" <note>plain or everyday</note> manner. In greater causes, however, where we report on God or the salvation of men, more magnificence and brilliance must be displayed. But in "temperate" causes, where nothing is being done to provoke action, but only to delight the listener, one must speak moderately between the two. However, even if someone speaks of great things, he should not always teach grandly, but rather in a low style when he is teaching, in a temperate style when he is praising or blaming something, and grandly only when he is provoking minds that are turned away toward conversion. The words used should be sufficient in the low style, splendid in the temperate style, and vehement in the grand style.

### On the Phrase, the Clause, and the Period, Chapter 18

<margin>composition</margin>
All speech is composed and constructed from words, the **phrase**, the **clause**, and the **period** <note>original: "comma, colon, periodon"</note>. A phrase <note>comma</note> is a small part of a thought. A clause <note>colon</note> is a member. A period is a circuit or a complete sentence. A phrase is made from a conjunction of words; a clause from phrases; and a period from clauses. A phrase is the end of a joining, such as: "Even if I fear, judges" <note>original: "etsi vereor iudices," quoting Cicero's Pro Milone</note>—behold, one phrase. Another phrase follows: "lest it be shameful to speak for a very brave man." And a clause is made—that is, a "member"—which provides understanding to the sense. Yet the speech still hangs there; and so, through several members, a period is made—that is, the final conclusion of the thought: "Yet the old custom of trials is required." A period should not be longer than what can be delivered in a single breath.

### On Avoiding Faults of Letters, Words, and Sentences, Chapter 19

<margin>precaution</margin>
Furthermore, the pure and honorable eloquence of an orator must be free from all faults, both in letters, in words, and in thoughts. In letters, the joining must be fit and convenient; and thus it must be observed that the final vowel of a preceding word does not clash with the same first vowel of the following word, as in "Egyptian women" <note>original: "feminae aegyptiae," where the 'ae' sounds run together</note>. The structure is better if consonants are joined to vowels. The joining of three consonants which, clashing together, seem to screech and, as it were, "snarl," must be avoided—that is, 'r s r', as in "the art of the studious" <note>original: "ars studiorum"</note>, "king terror" <note>original: "rex terror"</note>, or "the error of Romulus" <note>original: "error romuli"</note>. One should also avoid the consonant 'm' crashing into vowels, as in "truly indeed" <note>original: "verum enim"</note>. Furthermore, speech must lack all those faults which are learned during the first studies of the grammarians.

<column-break/>

### On the Joining of Words, Chapter 20

<margin>instruction</margin>
Regarding words, certain faults must be avoided, such as not using "improper" words, which the Greeks call **acyrologia**. One should love propriety, yet in such a way that one does not occasionally use a "translation" <note>a metaphor</note> for names that are sordid or filthy due to their lowliness. Metaphors should not be far-fetched, but should appear primary and familiar to the truth. One must also avoid over-long **hyperbole**, which cannot be done without confusing other senses. **Ambiguity** <note>original: "ambiguitas"</note> is also a fault to be avoided, as is that vice where some, led by a boastfulness of eloquence, conclude in a long and roundabout circuit what they could have signified in one or two words—a fault called **perissologia** <note>wordiness</note>. The opposite of this fault is a crime: out of a desire for brevity, to "steal" even necessary words. Just as with letters and words, faults of thought must also be avoided, which are learned in the first studies of grammarians. These are **cacemphaton** <note>harsh sound</note>, **tautologia** <note>repetition</note>, **ellipsis** <note>omission</note>, **acyrologia** <note>improper use</note>, **macrologia** <note>long-windedness</note>, **perissologia** <note>superfluity</note>, **pleonasmos** <note>redundancy</note>, and others like them. In contrast, **energy** <note>original: "energia," referring to vividness</note> and **emphasis** <note>deeper meaning</note> extol and adorn speech, making something more understood than what was actually said. For example, if you say: "He shall ascend to the glory of Scipio." Or Virgil: "The fallen ones slipped down" <note>original: "dimissum lapsi per sunt"</note>. For when he says "fallen," he suggests the height of the image. The virtue contrary to this is to diminish with words those things which are great by their nature.

### On Figures of Words and Sentences, Chapter 21

<margin>schemes</margin>
There are also certain "figures" of words in the precepts of eloquence, by which speech is increased and adorned. For because direct and continuous speech creates fatigue and disgust in both the speaker and the listener, it must be bent and turned into other forms, so that it might refresh the speaker, become more ornate, and delight the judge with a different "face" and sound. Most of these were noted above by Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian</note> in the "schemes" of the grammatical art. Therefore, only those which are never or only with difficulty done in poetry, but are done freely in oratory, should be placed here. **Anadiplosis** is the doubling of words, as in: "Yet this man lives. Indeed, he lives and has even come into the Senate." **Klimax** <note>Greek for "ladder"</note> is **gradation**, when the next thought begins from the word with which the previous sense ended, and thereafter the order of speaking is preserved as if by steps. This is the case in the saying of Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus</note>: "From innocence is born dignity; from dignity, honor; from honor, command; from command, liberty." Some call this figure a "chain" <note>original: "catena"</note>, because one thing is linked to another by name, and thus many things are drawn together in a doubling of words. This scheme happens not only with single words but also in the context of words, as in the Greek: "Your childhood was a disgrace to your youth, your youth a disgrace to your old age, your old age a crime against the state." So also in Scipio: "Compelled by force and for nothing, I made a pledge with him. Having made the pledge, I brought him to the judge. Having brought him, I condemned him at the first meeting. Having condemned him, I released him of my own will." **Antitheta**, which in Latin are called "opposites" <note>original: "contraposita"</note>, are most becoming as ornaments of speech when they are placed in opposition, as Cicero says: "On this side modesty fights, on that side impudence; here chastity, there filth; here faith, there [treachery]..."

It also introduces rhetorical figures like anadiplosis, gradation, and antithesis, emphasizing their role in maintaining audience interest and enhancing clarity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical instruction on rhetoric, moving from general style into specific figures of speech (tropes and schemes) and the use of maxims (sententiae). It builds upon the previous discussion of the "threefold style" by demonstrating how specific ornaments of speech create contrast, emotion, and clarity.</meta>

...deception: here, piety. There, crime: here, constancy. There, madness: here, honor. There, baseness: here, restraint. There, lust: here, finally, equity, temperance, courage, and prudence. Indeed, all virtues struggle against injustice, luxury, and laziness; they fight against recklessness and all vices. Finally, abundance conflicts with poverty, sound reason with ruin, a healthy mind with madness, and—lastly—good hope with the desperation of all things. In this kind of struggle and battle, the book of Ecclesiasticus <note>A book of the Bible also known as Sirach; the author is using it here to show that even scripture uses rhetorical contrast.</note> used this kind of ornament of speech, saying: "Good is against evil, and life against death; so is the sinner against the godly. Thus look upon all the works of the Most High; they come in pairs, one against the other."

**Synonyma** <note>Synonymy</note> occurs whenever we signify one thing with several words in a continuous speech, as Cicero says: "You do nothing, you plot nothing, you think nothing." <note>original: "Nihil agis. nihil moliris. nihil cogitas." from Cicero’s Orations against Catiline.</note> Likewise: "I will not bear it, I will not endure it, I will not allow it."

**Epanodos** <note>Regression or repetition</note> is what our writers call "regression." Example: "The dignity of the leaders was nearly equal; perhaps not equal was the dignity of those who followed."

**Antapodosis** <note>Reciprocation</note> is when the middle parts agree with the first and last, as in: "I also blame this deed of yours, Conscript Fathers—not my own, though it was a most beautiful deed; truly, as men, it was not mine, but yours."

**Paradiastole** <note>Distinction</note> occurs whenever we distinguish what is said through interpretation, such as when we call you "wise" instead of "cunning," "brave" instead of "reckless," or "diligent" instead of "stingy."

**Antanaclasis** <note>Punning or Rebound</note> is that which expresses a contrary sense with the same word. Someone asked a son why he was waiting for his father’s death; he responded, "I am not waiting for it [expecting it]; rather, I beg that you 'wait' [remain alive]."

**Antimetabole** <note>Counter-change</note> is a conversion of words which, by changing the order, produces a contrary sense: "I do not live to eat, but I eat to live." And that other example: "If Antony is consul, Brutus is an enemy. If Brutus is the savior of the republic, Antony is the enemy." <note>Referring to the political conflict between Marcus Antonius and Marcus Brutus after Caesar's death.</note> **Erochen**, which Appius called them. Who produced it? Appius.

Now we shall follow with the **Figures of Thought**, which are well worth knowing.

A **Sententia** <note>Maxim or Proverb</note> is an impersonal saying, such as: "Compliance breeds friends, but truth breeds hatred." If a person is added to this, it becomes a **Chria** <note>A short moral anecdote or specific application of a maxim.</note>. For example: "Achilles offended Agamemnon by speaking the truth." Or: "**Metrophanes** earned the favor of Mithridates by being compliant." For this is the difference between a Chria and a Maxim: a Maxim is uttered without a specific person, while a Chria is never spoken without a person. Thus, if a person is added to a Maxim, it becomes a Chria; if the person is removed, it becomes a Maxim.

There are many species of **Maxims**. Some are **Indicative** and others are **Declarative**, such as: "Faith is never safe." Others are **Imperative**, such as: "Go, act, son, call the zephyrs and glide on your wings." <note>A quote from Vergil's Aeneid.</note> Others are **Comparative**, such as: "If I conquer and yet perish, why is it better for me to conquer there?" Others are **Superlative**, expressed with some mental emotion and indignation, as in: "To what do you not drive the hearts of mortals, you accursed hunger for gold?" <note>original: "auri sacra fames," a famous line from Vergil denouncing greed.</note> Others are **Interrogative**, such as: "Young men, what cause compelled you to try unknown paths? What race are you? From what home? Do you bring peace here, or arms?" Others are **Responsive**, such as "from here" or "from there." Others are **Deprecative**, such as: "Rescue me from these evils, unconquered one." Others are **Permissive**, such as: "Fear not, Cytherean; the fate of your people remains unmoved." Others are **Concessive**, which forbid while appearing to urge, as in: "Go, follow Italy with the winds; seek kingdoms across the waves"—though, lest it 

<column-break/>

be misunderstood as actual persuasion, things are mixed in that suggest hidden dangers, like "with the winds" and "across the waves."

Others are **Demonstrative**, such as "Lo!" or "Behold!" Others are **Optative** <note>expressing a wish</note>, such as: "O that Jupiter would bring back my past years to me!" Others are **Derogative**, such as "By no means!" Others are uttered with an **Exclamation**, such as: "What madness, O citizens, has turned peace into arms?" And Cicero says: "O immortal gods! Where in the world are we?" Others are **Exhortative**, when we provoke someone to a sentiment, such as: "Dare, guest, to despise wealth." Others are **Dehortative**, when we draw someone back from a contrary vice or sin. There are also **Affirmative** ones, like "Indeed, why not?" There are **Preceptive** ones, such as: "Plough naked, sow naked, and you will have harvests in the cold." <note>A reference to Hesiod or Vergil’s agricultural advice, implying hard work.</note> There are **Prohibitive** ones, such as: "Do not plant hazel trees among the vines," or "Do not seek the topmost shoots." There are **Negative** ones, like "No" or "Least of all." There are also **Mirative** <note>expressing wonder</note> ones, such as: "Wonderful! To live is not permitted, yet to lust is pleasing." There are those of **Grieving**, such as: "Woe is me, for love is curable by no herbs." There are those of **Knowledge**, like: "As once the Labyrinth in high Crete contained a path." There are those of **Admonishing, Mocking, Groaning, Weeping, Exhorting, Consoling, and Commiserating**—for however many types or figures there are, there are just as many tones in pronunciation.

There are also **Amphidoxae** <note>Ambiguous statements</note>, of which part is honorable and part is dishonorable, such as: "Your will is not your own; you perish greatly for a brother." There are also others: **Procatalepsis** <note>Anticipation</note> is when we anticipate an objection that could be raised against us in order to dilute it, such as: "If any of you, judges, or those who are present, are perhaps wondering..." There are also **Aporiae** <note>Doubt</note>, which is the hesitation of one pretending not to know what he actually knows, or how he should say it.

**Leonensis** <note>Communication</note>, however, is called the communication of counsel with the judges or adversaries, as if you were to say: "I consult you, judges," or "You, adversaries: what would have been proper for me to do, or what would you have done?" **Paradoxon** is when we say that something unexpected has happened, as Cicero says for Flaccus: "He who ought to have been the proclaimer of his praise became the solicitor against his danger."

**Epitrope** is permission, when we leave something to be judged by the judges or adversaries themselves, as Calvus says against Vatinius: "Rub your forehead <note>An idiom for 'cast off shame'.</note> and say that you are more worthy to be made Praetor than Cato."

**Parrhisia** is speech full of liberty and confidence, as in: "I killed not Spurius Maelius," and so on. This figure must be used cautiously; Cicero, for instance, first provided a justification for it.

**Ethopœia** <note>Character-making</note> is when we introduce a speech from another person’s character, as Tully <note>Cicero</note> in his speech for Caelius makes the blind Appius speak with Clodia. **Energia** <note>Vividness</note> is the introduction of deeds done, or as if done, before the eyes, of which we have already spoken. **Metathecis** is that which sends the minds of the judges into past or future things in this manner: "Recall your minds to the spectacle of the conquered, wretched city, and believe that you see the fires, the slaughters, the plunder, the pillaging, the outrages against the bodies of free people, the captivity of matrons, and the butchery of old men."

Regarding the future, however, there is **Anticipation** of those things which the adversary is going to say, as Tully does for Milo, when he sends the minds of the judges into that state of the republic which would exist if Clodius were alive and Milo killed. **Aposiopesis** is when we interrupt what we seemed about to say with silence, often out of anger: "Whom I—! But it is better to calm the troubled waves." <note>The famous line from Neptune in Vergil's Aeneid.</note> **Epanalepsis** is a digression, like so: "The heat of my speaking and the dignity of the matters have carried me a little further than I intended; but I return to the case." **Anamnesis** is the recollection of a matter of which we pretend to have been forgetful. **Apertheis** is when that which...

...I had nearly laid aside the minds of the judges; we reclaim them at the opportune moment. **Aetiology** <note>original: "Etiologia"; the technique of providing a reason for a statement</note> is when we propose something and then provide its cause and reason. **Characterization** <note>original: "Characterismus"</note> is an expressive description of someone's figure, such as: "In all things like Mercury—his voice, his color, his golden hair, and his youthful, graceful limbs." <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid describing the god Mercury.</note> **Epitrochamos** <note>literally "a running over"</note> is when one heaps many briefly expressed thoughts into one place and runs through them with a certain haste, as Cicero does here: "You seek the Republic, the lives of all of you, your goods, your fortunes, your wives, your children, and the rest." **Irony** is when, through simulation, one desires what is said to be understood as its opposite. This happens either when we praise someone we wish to blame, or blame someone we wish to praise. An example of both would be if you called Catiline <note>A Roman conspirator</note> a "lover of the Republic" and Scipio <note>A great Roman hero</note> an "enemy of the Republic." **Diatismos** <note>Distinction or exaggeration</note> either diminishes things that are great or extols the minute. **Epimone** <note>Dwelling</note> is whenever we dwell for a long time on the same sense, like this: "Whom, finally, did he spare? To whose friendship did he keep faith? To what good man was he not an enemy? When did he not either accuse someone, or beat them, or betray them?" **Epangelia** <note>A promise</note> is a promise by which we make the judge attentive, promising that we are about to say something very great or very small. **Prosopopeia** <note>Personification</note> is when both character and speech are imagined for inanimate things. Cicero says of Catiline: "If my fatherland, which is much dearer to me than my life, should speak with me, saying such things..." **Parathesis** <note>A deposit</note> is when we "deposit" something incomplete in the memory of the judges, saying we will return to it when it is opportune. **Pefsis** <note>original: "Pensis"; a questioning</note> is a soliloquy where we respond to our own questions. **Syncresis** <note>Comparison or deferral</note> is when we defer something, perhaps while promising to say something else in the meantime among the figures of thought.

### Chapter XXII: On Dialectic

**D**ialectic is the discipline invented for discerning the causes of things. It is a species of Philosophy called **Logic** <term>Logica: from the Greek 'logos', meaning both 'word' and 'reason'</term>; that is, the rational power of defining, seeking, and discerning. For it teaches, in many types of questions, how the true and the false may be judged through disputation. Indeed, the first philosophers had this in their speeches, yet they did not reduce it to a skillful art. After these, Aristotle brought the arguments of this teaching to certain rules and called it **Dialectic**, because in it one disputes concerning words <note>original: "dictis"; here he links Dialectic to 'dictio'</note>. For a "lection" <note>original: "lectron"</note> is called a speech. Dialectic follows the discipline of Rhetoric because both have many things in common.

### Chapter XXIII: On the Difference Between the Arts of Dialectic and Rhetoric

**V**arro, in his books on the *Nine Disciplines*, defined this Dialectic and Rhetoric with such a simile: Dialectic and Rhetoric are like a man's hand when the fist is closed and when the palm is open. The former contracts words; the latter expands them. Indeed, Dialectic is sharper for discussing things; Rhetoric is more eloquent for teaching those things which require brilliance. The former sometimes comes to the schools; the latter proceeds continuously into the forum <note>The public square where legal and political speeches were held</note>. The former requires very few students; the latter often requires whole crowds. Philosophers are accustomed, before they come to explain the *Isagoge* <note>Porphyry's 'Introduction' to Aristotle’s categories</note>, to show the definition of philosophy, so that they may more easily demonstrate those things which pertain to it.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XXIIII: On the Definition of Philosophy

**P**hilosophy is the knowledge of human and divine things, joined with the study of living well. This appears to consist of two things: **knowledge** and **opinion**. Knowledge is when a thing is perceived by certain reason. Opinion, however, is when a thing remains uncertain and hidden, appearing to be strengthened by no reason—for example: whether the sun is only as large as it seems, or larger than the whole earth; likewise, whether the moon is a globe or hollow; and whether the stars are fixed to the heavens or are carried through the air in a free course; of what size and material the heaven itself consists; whether it is still and immobile or revolves with incredible speed; how thick the earth is, or upon what foundations it remains balanced and suspended. The name itself, translated into Latin, professes the "love of wisdom." For the Greeks call *philon* <gloss>love</gloss> and *sophia* <gloss>wisdom</gloss>. The types of Philosophy are threefold: one is **Natural**, which in Greek is called **Physics**, in which one discusses the investigation of nature. The second is **Moral**, which in Greek is called **Ethics**, in which one deals with morals. The third is **Rational**, which by the Greek word is called **Logic**, in which one disputes how, in the causes of things or the morals of life, truth itself may be sought. Therefore, in Physics the cause of seeking is found; in Ethics the order of living; in Logic the reason for understanding. Among the Greeks, Thales of Miletus was the first to examine Physics; he was one of those Seven Sages. For he, before others, looked upon the causes of heaven and the power of natural things through contemplated reason. Afterward, Plato distributed this into four definitions: that is, **Arithmetic**, **Geometry**, **Music**, and **Astronomy**. Socrates was the first to institute Ethics for correcting and composing morals, and he led his whole study toward the discussion of living well, dividing it into the four virtues of the soul: that is, **Prudence**, **Justice**, **Fortitude**, and **Temperance**. Prudence is that by which evil things are discerned from good; Fortitude is that by which adversities are endured with equanimity; Temperance is that by which lust and the desire for things are restrained; Justice is that by which, through judging rightly, each is given his due. Plato added **Logic**, which is called Rational, through which—having discussed the causes of things and morals—he rationally examined their power, dividing it into Dialectic and Rhetoric. It is called Logic, or "Rational," for *Logos* among the Greeks signifies both "speech" and "reason." Indeed, the divine utterances <note>The Bible</note> are also established in these three types of philosophy. For they usually dispute either about nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes; or about morals, as in Proverbs and scattered throughout all the books; or about logic, for which our writers claim **Theology**, as in the Song of Songs and in the Gospels. Likewise, some doctors have defined philosophy in its name and parts thus:

### Chapter XXV: What Philosophy Is

**P**hilosophy is the probable knowledge of divine and human things, insofar as it is possible for man. Otherwise: Philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines. Again: Philosophy is the **meditation on death**, which is more suitable for Christians, who, having trampled the ambition of the world, live in a conversation...

<meta>This page continues the curriculum of the Liberal Arts, moving from the ornaments of Rhetoric (concluded on the previous page) into the foundational structures of Philosophy and Logic. It introduces the division of knowledge and the classic logical frameworks of Porphyry and Aristotle.</meta>

...they live in a disciplined likeness of the future fatherland. 
Philosophy is divided into two parts: the **speculative** and the **practical**. Others define the system of philosophy as consisting of two parts, of which the first is speculative and the second is practical. The **speculative** <note>original: "inspectiva"; referring to theoretical contemplation</note> is divided into the **natural**, the **doctrinal**, and the **divine**. The **doctrinal** is divided into four parts: **arithmetic**, **music**, **geometry**, and **astronomy**. The **practical** <note>original: "actualis"</note> is divided into the **moral**, the **administrative**, and the **civil**. Speculative philosophy is said to be that by which we transcend visible things and contemplate something of the divine and celestial, which we behold with the mind alone, as these things surpass the gaze of the body. **Natural** philosophy is where the nature of each individual thing is discussed; for nothing is generated in life by confusion, but each thing has its use assigned to it, in which it was defined by the Creator—unless perhaps a miracle is shown to occur by the will of God. **Divine** philosophy <note>original: "diuinalis"; theology or metaphysics</note> is said to be when we discuss either the ineffable nature of God or, to some extent, spiritual creatures of the most profound quality. **Doctrinal** is said to be the science that considers **abstract quantity**. For abstract quantity is that which we separate by intellect from matter or other accidents—such as even and odd, and the like—and treat in reasoning alone. Its species are four: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. **Arithmetic** is the discipline of quantity countable in itself. **Geometry** is the discipline of immovable magnitude and of forms. **Music** is the discipline that speaks of numbers that relate to something: those which are found in sounds. **Astronomy** is the discipline that contemplates the courses of the celestial stars and all their figures, and investigates with searchable reason the habits of the stars toward themselves and toward the earth. Furthermore, **practical** philosophy is said to be that which explains proposed matters through its operations. Its parts are three: **moral**, **administrative**, and **civil**. **Moral** is that through which an honest way of living is sought, and institutes tending toward virtue are prepared. **Administrative** <note>original: "dispensativa"; often referring to domestic management or economics</note> is when the order of domestic affairs is wisely arranged. **Civil** is that through which the utility of the whole city is administered.

### On the Introductions of Porphyry, Chapter 26.

After the definitions of philosophy in which all things are generally contained, let us now explain the **Isagoges** <note>original: "isagogas"; from the Greek for "introductions"</note> of Porphyry. "Isagoge" is indeed said in Greek what "Introduction" is in Latin: specifically for those who are beginning philosophy, containing in itself the demonstration of the primary reasons regarding what any thing is, and declaring it by its certain and substantial definition. For having first established the **genus**, we then join the **species** and other things that may be nearby, and we separate them by distinct commonalities, interposing **differences** until we arrive at the proper expression of that which we seek—as, for example, "Man is a rational, mortal, terrestrial, bipedal animal, capable of laughter." When the genus "**animal**" is said, the substance of man is declared. For "animal" is the genus for man, but because it was broadly open, the species "**terrestrial**" was added, and already that which is either ethereal or aquatic is excluded. Then a difference such as "**bipedal**" is added, which is placed against those animals that rely on many feet. Likewise "**rational**," against those that lack reason. However, "**mortal**" is against

<column-break/>

that which is not an angel. Afterward, through distinction and seclusion, the **property** is added at the final part: "**capable of laughter**" <note>original: "risus capax"; in logic, a 'proprium' is a quality unique to a species but not part of its essence</note>. For it is only the human who laughs. Thus the definition is perfected in every part to declare the human being. Aristotle and Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> considered a full definition of this discipline to consist of genus and differences. Certain later teachers, being more thorough in teaching, divided the view of substantial definition into five parts as if into its members: the first is of **genus**, the second of **species**, the third of **difference**, the fourth of **property**, and the fifth of **accident**. 
**Genus**, such as "animal," is a general term common to all having a soul. 
**Species**, such as "man," is the speciality by which he is separated from other living beings. 
**Difference**, such as "rational" and "mortal." For by these two, man differs from the rest. For when "rational" is said, he is discerned from the irrational and mute creatures that do not have reason. When "mortal" is said, he is discerned from the angels who do not know death. 
**Property**, such as "capable of laughter," for it is the human who laughs, and this belongs to no other animal besides the human. 
**Accident**, such as color in the body or learning in the mind. For these come and change with the variety of time. 
From all these five parts, a sentence of full meaning is made, thus: "Man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter, capable of good and evil." Thus also in every substantial statement, we ought to interpose species and differences for so long until, all things which could be the same being excluded, it arrives at the point where the property is held with certainty. Victorinus the orator translated the *Isagoges* from Greek into Latin, and Boethius published a commentary on it in five books.

### On the Categories of Aristotle, Chapter 27.

The **Categories** <note>original: "cathegoriae"</note> of Aristotle follow, which in Latin are called **Predicaments**; through these, all speech is concluded according to various significations. The instruments of the categories are three: first, **equivocal**; second, **univocal**; third, **denominative**. 
**Equivocal** <note>or "homonymous"</note> are when many things have one name, but not the same definition, such as "lion." For as far as the name pertains, a real lion, a painted lion, and a celestial lion <note>the constellation Leo</note> are all called "lion"; but as far as the definition pertains, the real is defined one way, the painted another, and the celestial another. 
**Univocal** <note>or "synonymous"</note> are when two or more things have one name and definition, such as "garment." For both a cloak and a tunic can receive the name of "garment" and its definition. Therefore, this is understood to be in genera, because they give both name and definition to their forms. 
**Denominative**, that is, **derivative**, are called whatever have their appellation from something else by a change of case alone according to the name, such as "good" from "goodness," or "evil" from "malice." 
Of the categories, however, there are ten species: that is, **substance**, **quantity**, **quality**, **relation**, **position**, **place**, **time**, **state**, **action**, and **passion**. 
**Substance** is that which is said properly and principally: which is neither predicated of a subject nor is in a subject, such as a "certain man" or a "certain horse." **Secondary substances** are said to be those species in which those things first called primary substances are present and enclosed, such as "Cicero" within "man." 
**Quantity** is the measure by which something is shown to be either great or small, such as "long" or "short."

<meta>This page continues the explanation of Aristotle's "Categories" (the ten ways of describing any subject) and transitions into his works on logic: "On Interpretation" (Perihermenias) and the "Syllogisms." It maintains the pedagogical tone of the previous page, categorizing the fundamental building blocks of thought and language.</meta>

**Quality** <note>original: "Qualitas"</note> is what kind of person the orator is: whether he is unrefined, dark-skinned, or fair-skinned. **Relation** <note>original: "Relatio"</note> is that which refers to something else. For when one says "son," a "father" is also indicated. These relative terms begin simultaneously; for "servant" and "master" take the origin of their names at the same time, and one never finds a master existing before a servant, nor a servant before a master. For one cannot precede the other. Furthermore, **Position** <note>original: "situs"</note> is named from "placement," such as whether one stands, sits, or lies down. **Place** <note>original: "Locus"</note> is where one might be: in the forum, or in the street. Now, the movement of Place has six parts: right and left, forward and backward, upward and downward. These six parts also have two aspects: far and near. **Time** <note>original: "Tempus"</note> is as "today" or "yesterday." **State** <note>original: "Habitus"</note> is named from "having" something, such as having knowledge in the mind, virtue in the body, or around the body a garment and other things which are designated by teachers within the category of "having." Now, **Action** and **Passion** <note>original: "agere et pati"; acting and being acted upon</note> consist of the meanings of the agent and the patient. For "I write" has the act of the voice, as it indicates one doing a thing. "I am written" <note>original: "Scribor"</note> belongs to the patient, as it shows itself being acted upon. In these nine categories—of which some examples have been placed—or in the category of substance itself, which is **Being** <note>original: "usia"; from the Greek ousia</note>, innumerable things are found. For even those things which we grasp with the intellect, we publish in speech according to one or another of these ten predicaments. A full sentence containing all of these is as follows: "Augustine <note>Substance</note>, the great <note>Quantity</note> orator <note>Quality</note>, son of that man <note>Relation</note>, standing <note>Position</note> in the temple <note>Place</note>, today <note>Time</note>, wearing a priestly headband <note>original: "infulatus"; State/Habit</note>, is exhausted <note>Passion</note> by debating <note>Action</note>." Being, however, is **Substance**; that is, it is the primary thing which underlies the others; the remaining nine are **Accidents**. It is called "Substance" because every thing exists <note>original: "subsistit"</note> in itself. For a body exists in itself, and therefore it is a substance. Those others, however, are Accidents, which are in the existing thing and the subject, but are not substances themselves because they do not exist independently but are changed, such as color or form. Regarding "of a subject" and "in a subject," it is as if speaking "of the thing itself" and "in the thing itself." Where one speaks "of a subject," it is Substance; as if one were speaking of the essence. But where one speaks "in a subject," these are Accidents; that is, those things which happen to the substance, such as quantity, quality, or figure. Therefore, Genus and Species are "of a subject," while Accidents are "in a subject." Of these nine accidents, three are inside the Being: quantity, quality, and position. For these cannot exist without the Being. Outside the Being are: place, time, and state. Both inside and outside the Being are: relation, action, and passion. It is established that these are called **Categories** <note>original: "cathegorias"</note> because they cannot be recognized except from subjects. For who could recognize what "man" is unless he placed some specific man before his eyes as the subject for the name? This work of Aristotle must be understood because, as has been said, whatever a human speaks falls within these ten predicaments. It will also be beneficial for understanding books that apply to either rhetoricians or logicians.

### On Aristotle’s "On Interpretation" <note>original: "Perihermenias"</note>. Chapter 28.

**N**ext follows the book *On Interpretation* <note>original: "Perihermenias"</note>, which is exceedingly subtle and most cautious through its various forms and repetitions. It is said of this book that when Aristotle was writing it, he "dipped his pen in his mind." The preface of *On Interpretation*: Indeed, every thing that is one, and is signified by one speech, is signified either by a **Noun** or by a **Verb**. These two parts of speech interpret whatever the mind has conceived 

<column-break/>

for the purpose of speaking. For all eloquence is the interpreter of the conceived thing in the mind; Aristotle—a man most skilled in the expression of things and the crafting of speech—calls this *Perihermenias*, which we call **Interpretation**. Specifically, it means that the mind interprets things conceived by it through many words, via **Affirmation** and **Negation** <note>original: "cataphasin et apophasin"</note>. Through affirmation, such as "the man runs"; through negation, such as "the man does not run." In this book *On Interpretation*, the aforementioned philosopher treats seven species: namely Noun, Verb, Speech, Enunciation, Affirmation, Negation, and Contradiction. A **Noun** is a significant sound established by convention, without time, of which no part is significant when separated, such as "Socrates." A **Verb** is that which signifies time, of which no part signifies anything on its own, but is always a sign of those things said of another, such as "he thinks" or "he debates." **Speech** <note>original: "Oratio"</note> is a significant sound of which some part is significant when separated, such as "Socrates debates." **Enunciative Speech** is a significant sound regarding that which is something or is not, such as "Socrates is" or "Socrates is not." **Affirmation** is the enunciation of something regarding something else, such as "Socrates is." **Negation** is the [denial] of something from something else, such as "Socrates is not." **Contradiction** is the opposition of affirmation and negation, such as "Socrates debates" and "Socrates does not debate." The utility of *On Interpretation* is this: that from these interpretations, **Syllogisms** are made, from which logic <note>original: "analectica"</note> is further treated.

### On Dialectical Syllogisms. Chapter 29.

**N**ext follows the **Dialectical Syllogism**, wherein the utility and power of that entire art is shown. Their conclusion greatly helps the reader in investigating the truth, provided that the error of deceiving an adversary through the **sophisms** of false conclusions is absent. There are three formulas of categorical—that is, predicative—syllogisms. There are nine modes of the first formula. The **First Mode** is that which leads to—that is, it collects—a universal affirmative directly from universal affirmatives. For example: "Every just thing is honorable; every honorable thing is good; therefore every just thing is good." The **Second Mode** is that which leads to a universal negative directly from universal affirmatives and negatives. For example: "Every just thing is honorable; no honorable thing is base; therefore no just thing is base." The **Third Mode** is that which leads to a particular affirmative directly from a particular and a universal affirmative. For example: "A certain just thing is honorable; every honorable thing is useful; therefore a certain just thing is useful." The **Fourth Mode** is that which leads to a particular negative <note>Note: text says 'dedicativum particulare' but describes a negative conclusion</note> directly from a particular affirmative and a universal negative. For example: "A certain just thing is honorable; no honorable thing is base; therefore a certain just thing is not base." The **Fifth Mode** is that which leads to a particular affirmative through reflection <note>logical conversion</note> from universal affirmatives. For example: "Every just thing is honorable; every honorable thing is good; therefore a certain good thing is just." The **Sixth Mode** is that which leads to a universal negative through reflection from a universal affirmative and a universal negative. For example: "Every just thing is honorable; no honorable thing is base; therefore no base thing is just." The **Seventh Mode** is that which leads to an affirmative...

The **fourth mode** is that which concludes from a universal affirmative and a universal negative <note>The text says "particular negative," but the example uses a universal negative.</note> to a particular negative directly. For example: some just thing is honorable; no just thing is evil; therefore, some just thing is not evil. The **sixth mode** is that which concludes from a universal affirmative and a particular negative to a particular negative directly. For example: every just thing is honorable; some just thing is not evil; therefore, some honorable thing is not evil.

Those who desire to know these formulas of categorical syllogisms more fully should read the book entitled *On Interpretation* <note>original: "Perihermenias"</note> by Apuleius, and they will learn how these matters are treated even more subtly. For when these things are distinguished and considered, they usefully introduce the reader, by the Lord's favor, to the great paths of understanding. Now let us come to the **hypothetical syllogisms** in the following order. There are seven modes of hypothetical syllogisms which are made with a conclusion. The **first mode** is: if it is day, it is light. But it is day; therefore it is light. The **second mode** is: if it is day, it is light. But it is not light; therefore it is not day. The **third mode** is thus: it is not both

But because it is day; therefore it is not night. The **fifth mode** is thus: it is either day or night. But it is not night; therefore it is day. The **sixth mode** is thus: it is not both day and not light. <note>The OCR reads "no x," likely a misreading of "nox" (night) or a logical symbol.</note> But it is day; therefore it is not night. The **seventh mode** is thus: it is not both day and night. But it is not night; therefore it is day.

If anyone desires to know the modes of hypothetical syllogisms more fully, let him read the book of Marius Victorinus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and rhetorician who converted to Christianity.</note> entitled *On Hypothetical Syllogisms*.
