### On the division of definitions, abbreviated from the book of Marius Victorinus, Chapter XXX.

**D**efinition is a tool of philosophers which, in expressing things, explains what the thing itself is, what it is like, and how it ought to consist of its members. For it is a brief speech, separating the nature of each thing from what is common, and concluding with its own proper meaning. The division of definitions is held to be in fifteen types.

The **first species** of definition is *ousiodes* <note>original Greek: ουσιώδης; "essential" or "substantial"</note>, that is, substantial, which is properly and truly called a definition. For example: "Man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of perception and learning." For this definition, descending through species and differences, comes to the "proper" <note>A logical term for a characteristic belonging only to one species.</note> and designates most fully what a man is.

The **second species** of definition is that which in Greek is called *ennoematike* <note>original Greek: έννοηματική; "conceptual"</note> and in Latin is named "notion." We can call this notion by a common name, not a proper one. It is always formed in this way: "Man is that which by rational conception presides over all animals." For it did not say *what* man is, but *what he does*, as if calling him into notice by a certain sign. For this provides a notice of the thing to others, but does not declare a substantial explanation; and because the former type is substantial, it holds the primacy of all definitions.

The **third species** of definition is that which in Greek is called *poiotes* <note>original Greek: ποιότησ; "quality"</note> and in Latin is called "qualitative." It receives its name from "quality" because it evidently shows of what sort <note>original: "quale"</note> the thing is that is being sought. An example of this is: "Man is he who is strong in talent, excels in arts and the knowledge of things, or chooses what he ought to do, or by mental reflection despises what is useless." For by these qualities, man is expressed and defined.

The **fourth species** of definition is that which in Greek is called *hypographike* <note>original Greek: ὑπογραφική; "descriptive"</note> and in Latin is named "description" by Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>. Using a circumlocution of words and deeds, it declares what a thing is by description. For it asks what a miser is, what a cruel man is, or what a luxurious man is, and the nature of every luxurious, miserly, or cruel person is described. For instance, if we wish to define a luxurious man, we say: "A luxurious man is one who is extravagant and unnecessary in his lifestyle, seeking luxury, overflowing in delights, and prone to lust." These and other things define a luxurious man, but they define him through description. This species of definition is more suited to orators than to logicians because it has a breadth <note>Meaning it is more descriptive and wordy than strict logical definitions.</note> that is placed in both good and bad things in a similar way.

The **fifth species** of definition is that which in Greek is called *kata antilexin* <note>original Greek: κατὰ ἀντίλεξιν; "by synonym" or "word-for-word"</note> and in Latin we call "by synonym." This designates the word for which the thing is being sought in other speech. One and...

Likewise, when we call a "term" an "end," or we interpret "to depopulate" as "to devastate." The **sixth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by difference* <note>original: "cata diaphorā"</note> and we call *through difference*. Writers on these arts name this "about the same and the other," such as when one asks what the difference is between a **king** and a **tyrant**. The difference is added so that each is defined: that is, a king is modest and temperate, while a tyrant is impious and cruel. The **seventh species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by metaphor* <note>original: "cata metaphorā"</note> and the Latins call *through translation*. As Cicero says in his *Topics*: "The shore is where the wave is struck." This can be treated in various ways: sometimes to warn, sometimes to designate, sometimes to praise or to blame. To warn: "Nobility of virtue is a burden of ancestors upon their descendants." To designate: "The boar is the master of the forest." To praise: "Youth is the flower of life." To blame: "Riches are a long travel-provision for a short life." The **eighth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by privation* <note>original: "cata apheresin"</note>, derived from the opposite <note>original: "τοῦ ἐναντίου"</note>. The Latins speak of it as being defined *through the privation of its contrary*. For example: "Good is that which is not evil," "The just is that which is not unjust," and similar things. We ought to use this kind of definition when the contrary is well known; for if "good" is that which profits with honesty, then that which is not such is "evil." The **ninth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by description* <note>original: "cata hypotypōsin"</note> and the Latins call *through a certain imagination*. For example: "Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises." This species always deals with individuals, which the Greeks call *atoms* <note>original: "atoma"</note>. The **tenth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by the omission of the full similar genus* <note>original: "κατὰ ἔκλειψιν ὁλοκλήρου ὁμοίου γένους"</note> and the Latins call *through the lack of the full [description] from the same genus*. For instance, if one asks what an "animal" is, the response might be "like a man." For he has declared the thing through a cited example. This is a property of definition: to declare what that thing is which is being sought. The **eleventh species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by analogy* <note>original: "cata analogian"</note> and the Latins call *according to proportion*. For example, if it is asked what a "thesis" is, it may be answered that it is that which lacks a "foot" <note>A technical term in poetic meter or logic</note> so as to belong to the art. The **twelfth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by praise* <note>original: "cata epenon"</note>. As Tully <note>Cicero</note> says in his speech for Cluentius: "The law is the mind, the counsel, the soul, and the opinion of the city." And elsewhere: "Peace is tranquil liberty." It can also be done through blame, which the Greeks call *psogon*, such as: "Slavery is the lowest of all evils, to be repelled not only by war but even by death." The **thirteenth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *in relation to something* <note>original: "το προς τι"</note> and the Latins call *toward something*. For example: "A father is one who has a son," and "A master is one who has a servant." The **fourteenth species** of definition is *general* <note>original: "cata tonozon"</note>. As Cicero says in his *Rhetoric*: "A genus is that which embraces many parts." Likewise: "A part is that which is subject to a genus." The **fifteenth species** of definition is that which the Greeks call *by etiology* <note>original: "cata ętio-logian"</note> and the Latins call *according to the reason of the thing*. For example: "Day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth." We should know that the aforementioned species of definition are rightly associated with "topics," since they are placed among certain arguments and are mentioned in several places in the *Topics*. But now let us come to the **Topics**, which are the seats of arguments, the fountains of perceptions, and the origins of speech.

<column-break/>

### On Topics, Chapter XXXI.

**Topics** <note>original: "Topica"</note> is the discipline of finding arguments. The division of topics (or "places" from which arguments are drawn) is threefold. For some are inherent in the very thing being discussed; others are called "effects," which are known in a way as being drawn from other things; and others are taken from the outside. Arguments that are inherent in the very thing being discussed are divided into three parts: first, from the **whole**; second, from the **part**; third, from the **mark**. An argument from the **whole** is when a definition is applied to that which is sought, as Cicero says: "Glory is the praise of deeds rightly done, and the reputation of great services to the Republic." An argument is from **parts** when the one defending himself either denies the deed was done or defends that it was done legally. An argument is from the **mark** <note>essentially an etymological argument</note> when some argument is made from the name of the thing itself, as Cicero says: "I was looking for a *consul*, whom I could not find in that *animal*." <note>Cicero is punning on the character of the man versus his title.</note> **Effected arguments** are those which are known to be drawn in some way from other things. They are fourteen in number: first is the argument from **conjugates**, when a word is declined from a noun into a verb, as when Cicero says Verres "swept clean" <note>original: "everrisse," a pun on the name Verres and the verb "to sweep"</note>; or a noun from a verb, as when a "thief" <note>original: "latro"</note> is said to "commit robbery" <note>original: "latrocinari"</note>. Or a noun from a noun, as in Terence: "The beginning of **lovers** <note>original: "amantium"</note> is of the **insane** <note>original: "amantium"</note>," provided that the end of one name differs from another voice formed in a different declension. The **second argument** is from **genus**, when a judgment is spoken about that same genus, as Virgil says: "Woman is ever a fickle and changeable thing." The **third argument** is from **species**, when the species gives credit to a general question, as: "But the Phrygian shepherd <note>Paris</note> did not thus penetrate Lacedaemon." An argument from **similarity** is when things similar to other things are brought forward, as: "To flee the weapons from me, for no right hand shall hurl in vain into the Rutulians; they shall stand as they did in the bodies on the Trojan fields." An argument from **difference** is when things are separated by their differences, as Virgil says: "You see neither the horses of Diomedes nor the chariot of Achilles." An argument is said to be from **contraries** when discrepant things are opposed to one another, as Virgil says: "Is it right for ships made by mortal hand to have immortal hulls, and should Aeneas, certain of himself, traverse uncertain dangers?" An argument is said to be from **consequents** when, something having been established, something else follows inevitably, as Virgil says: "There is not that strength in the soul nor such great pride in the defeated." An argument is from **antecedents** when things are proven from those which were done previously, as Cicero in *Pro Milone*: "Since he did not hesitate to reveal what he thought, can you doubt what he did?" An argument is from **repugnants** <note>contradictions</note> when that which is objected is destroyed by some contrary fact, as Cicero says: "He, therefore, having not only been freed from such danger but enriched with the most ample honor, would have wanted to kill you at home?" An argument is from **conjugates** <note>here meaning related outcomes</note> when it is shown with probability what will come from any matter, as Virgil says: "They believe that if we are driven out, nothing will be lacking to bring all Hesperia under their yoke." An argument is from **causes** when each matter is treated according to common custom, as Terence says: "I was somewhat afraid of you just now, Davus, lest you should do what the common crowd of servants is accustomed to do: delude me with tricks." An argument is from **effects** when something is approved from those things which have been done, as Virgil:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of logical "Topics"—the mental locations where arguments are found. It concludes Book Two of the treatise on rhetoric and logic by categorizing types of evidence and opposites, before introducing the four mathematical sciences (the Quadrivium).</meta>

"Fear reveals degenerate souls" <note>original: *degeneres animos timor arguit*; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>. An argument from comparison is when a line of reasoning is formed through the comparison of persons or causes under an imputation. As Virgil says: "You are able to rescue Aeneas from the hands of the Greeks" <note>original: *tu potes Aenean manibus subducere Graium*</note>. It is an unspeakable thing for us to have helped anyone against the country folk. Likewise, there are arguments drawn from the outside, which in Greek are called <term>atechnoi</term> <note>original: *ατεχνους*; meaning "without art" or "unscientific" because they rely on external evidence rather than the speaker's logical skill</note>. An example of this is testimony. Testimony consists of a fact and is divided into five modes: first, from a person; second, from the authority of nature; third, from the time of the authorities; fourth, from the sayings and deeds of ancestors; fifth, from tortures. The third mode mentioned above, which is from time, is derived into eight species: first, talent; second, wealth; third, age; fourth, fortune; fifth, art; sixth, experience; seventh, necessity; eighth, a coincidence of chance. All testimony is that which is taken from some external thing to create belief. A person is not qualified as testimony unless they have weight to create belief, and they ought to be praiseworthy for the integrity of their character. The authority of nature is that which consists of the greatest virtue. There are many testimonies that bring authority: namely, talent, wealth, age, fortune, art, experience, necessity, and the coincidence of chance events. Credibility is sought from the sayings and deeds of ancestors when the words and actions of men of old are recounted. Credibility is provided by tortures, after which no one believes a person would wish to lie. Those things handled under "time," because they are clear by their own names, do not require definition. It must also be committed to memory that "Topics" provide arguments in common to orators, dialecticians, poets, and lawyers. When they prove something specifically, they belong to rhetoricians, poets, and lawyers; but when they dispute generally, it is manifest that they belong to philosophers. It is a truly admirable kind of work that whatever the mobility and variety of the human mind could find in seeking out meanings through diverse causes could be gathered into one, concluding the free and voluntary intellect. For wherever the mind turns, whatever thoughts it enters into, it must necessarily fall into one of those things which have been mentioned.

## On Opposites. Chapter 32.

There are four kinds of contraries, which Aristotle calls <term>antikeimena</term> <note>original: *αντικειμενα*</note>, that is, "opposites," because they seem to stand against one another as if from an adverse position—such as "contraries." Yet not all things that are opposed to each other are "contraries," though all "contraries" are "opposites." The first kind is of contraries which, according to Cicero <note>original: *Licerone*, likely a scribal variant for *Cicerone*</note>, is called "diverse," because they are only opposed to each other so that they are not the same as those they are opposed to, such as **wisdom** and **folly**. This kind is divided into three species: for there are some of this sort that have a middle ground; some that are without a middle; and some that have a middle ground which nonetheless has no specific name, unless a name is created for both. **White** and **black** have a middle ground, because between them a "pale" or "dark" color is often found. Things are "without a middle" whenever one of two things must happen, such as **health** or **sickness**; there is no middle ground between these. However, those whose middle grounds are without a name are like "unhappy"; the middle ground is "not happy." The second kind is of "relatives," which are so opposed

<column-break/>

to each other that they are compared to one another, such as **double** and **single**. This is the only kind of opposites that refers back to itself. For a thing is not "greater" unless it is referred to something "smaller," and "single" unless referred to "double," or to that which it is opposed. For a relative is opposed to a relative in such a way that the very thing which is opposed either belongs to that which it is opposed, or is referred to it in some way. For the **half** is opposed to the **double**, and it is the half of that double; it is opposed to it in such a way that it belongs to the thing it is opposed to. Likewise, the **small** is opposed to the **large**, so that the small itself is small in relation to the large to which it is opposed. For the former things called "contraries" are opposed in such a way that they do not belong to those they are opposed to, nor are they referred to them in any way. Indeed, **injustice** is so contrary to **justice** that the injustice is not of that same justice, nor is it injustice toward it. The third kind of opposites is **habit** or **deprivation** <note>original: *habit vs orbatio*</note>; Cicero calls this genus "privation," by which he shows that someone had something of which they are now deprived. There are three species of this: the first is in the thing, the second in the place, and the third in the appropriate time. **In the thing**: such as blindness and vision in the eyes. **In the place**: such as the eyes being the place for blindness and vision. **In the appropriate time**: such as saying an infant is "not speaking" or "without teeth," when a young age has denied teeth thus far. For the infant is not "deprived" of teeth which they have not yet had. The fourth kind is opposed by **affirmation** and **negation**, such as "Socrates disputes" and "Socrates does not dispute." These differ from the previous ones because those can be said as single words, but these cannot be said unless they are connected <note>i.e., as a full proposition</note>. This fourth kind has much conflict among dialecticians and is called by them "the strongly opposite," since it does not admit a third option. For some of the others can have a third, as in contraries: **white** and **black**; the third is neither white nor black, but dark or pale. In relatives also, such as **many** and **few**; the third is neither many nor few, but a middling amount. In habit or deprivation, such as **vision** and **blindness**; the third is neither blindness nor vision, but bleary-eyedness <note>original: *lippitudo*</note>. But here, "**he reads**" or "**he does not read**" has no third option.

->Book Two ends<-

### The preface to the four following disciplines begins.

**Mathematics** is called the "doctrinal science" in Latin, which considers "abstract quantity." Abstract quantity is that which we treat in reasoning alone, separating it by the intellect from matter or from other accidents, such as **even**, **odd**, or other things of this sort. There are four species of this: namely, **arithmetic**, **music**, **geometry**, and **astronomy**. **Arithmetic** is the discipline of quantity that can be numbered in itself. **Music** is the discipline that speaks of numbers which are found in sounds. **Geometry** is the discipline of magnitude and forms. **Astronomy** is the discipline that contemplates the courses of the celestial stars and their figures, and all the positions of the stars. We shall describe these disciplines a little more broadly hereafter, so that their causes can be competently understood.

## The third book begins
### On the name of the discipline of arithmetic, Chapter 1.

<margin>What arithmetic is</margin>
**Arithmetic is** the discipline of numbers. For the Greeks call number *rhythmos* <note>original: "rithmon"; the author likely means "arithmos"</note>. The writers of secular literature intended for this to be the first among the mathematical disciplines because it stands alone and needs no other discipline to exist. However, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy, which follow it, require the help of arithmetic in order to exist and subsist.

### On its authors, Chapter 2.

<margin>Authors</margin>
**The discipline of number** among the Greeks is said to have been first written down by Pythagoras, and then more extensively composed by Nicomachus. Among the Latins, Apuleius first translated it, and then Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose work became the standard textbook for arithmetic in the Middle Ages</note>.

### What a number is and from where it is named, Chapter 3.

<margin>Definition of number</margin>
**A number, however,** is a multitude made up of units. For scholars hold that "one" is the seed of number, but is not a number itself. It was given the name "number" (*numerus*) as a term derived from its own frequent repetition. Therefore, "one" (*unus*) draws its name from this; for the Greeks call "one" <term>hena</term> <note>original: "ἕνα"</note>, just as they call "two" and "three" <term>duo</term> <note>original: "δύο"</note> and *tria*. "Four" (*quattuor*), however, receives its name from the square figure <note>the Latin *quadrus*</note>. "Five" (*quinque*) received its name not according to its nature, but according to the whim of the one who gave names to numbers. "Six" and "seven" come from the Greek. For in many names which have an aspiration <note>a "h" sound</note> in Greek, we put an "s" in place of the aspiration. Thus, instead of *hex* we use *sex* <note>original: "her per ser"</note>, and for *hepta* we use *septem* <note>original: "hepra"</note>, just as for the herb *herpyllos* <note>thyme</note> we say *serpillum*. "Eight" (*octo*) comes through direct transfer, just as they say <term>oktō</term> <note>original: "ὀκτώ"</note> and we say *octo*; likewise they say <term>ennea</term> <note>original: "ἐννέα"</note> and we say *novem* (nine); they say <term>deka</term> <note>original: "δέκα"</note> and we say *decem* (ten). These are named from a Greek etymology because they bind and join together the numbers lying below them. For <term>to bind</term> <note>original: "δεσμεύειν"</note> means to join or tie among them. Furthermore, "twenty" (*viginti*) is so named because they are "ten twice born" (*decem bis geniti*), with the letter "u" put in place of "b". "Thirty" (*triginta*) because they are born from a threefold ten, and so on up to ninety. "One hundred" (*centum*) is named from a "circle" <note>original: "canto", perhaps referring to a completion of a cycle</note>. "Two hundred" from "two" and "hundred," and so on for the rest up to a thousand. "A thousand" (*mille*), however, is named from "multitude" (*multitudo*), from which "military service" (*militia*) is also named, as if it were a "multitudinous-ness" (*multiticia*). From this also comes "myriads" (*milia*), which the Greeks call <term>myriadas</term> <note>original: "μυριάδας"</note>, having changed the letter "l" to "r".

### What numbers provide, Chapter 4.

<margin>The utility of numbers</margin>
**The logic of numbers** is not to be despised. For in many places of the Holy Scriptures, it is clear how much mystery they contain. For it was not said in vain in the praises of God: "You have made all things in measure, and number, and weight" <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 11:21</note>. For the number six, which is perfect in its parts, declares the perfection of the world by a certain significance of its number. Similarly, the forty days in which Moses and Elijah and the Lord himself fasted cannot be understood without a knowledge of numbers. So too other numbers appear in the Holy Scriptures, whose metaphorical shapes cannot be explained unless one knows the science of this art. It is also given to us

<column-break/>

on the other hand to exist under the discipline of numbers, since we learn the hours through them, we discuss the course of the months, and we recognize the space of the returning year. Indeed, we are instructed through number so that we might not be confused. Take away number in all things, and all things perish. Take away the calculation of the counting-board from the world, and a blind ignorance embraces everything; nor can man be distinguished from the other animals who do not know the logic of calculation.

### On the first division of even and odd, Chapter 5.

<margin>Even and odd</margin>
**Number is divided** into even and odd. An even number is divided into two: evenly even, evenly odd, oddly even, and oddly odd. An odd number is divided into two: the first and simple, the second and composite, and the third "intermediate," which in one way is first and uncomposed, but in another way is second and composite. An even number is one that can be divided into two equal parts, such as 2, 4, 6, 8. An odd number is one that cannot be divided into equal parts, with one in the middle either missing or remaining over, such as 3, 5, 7, 9, and the rest. An "evenly even" number is one that can be divided equally according to an even number until it reaches the indivisible unit, for example sixty-four: it has 32, 32 has 16, 16 has 8, 8 has 4, 4 has 2, and the number two has one, which is the singular indivisible unit. "Evenly odd" is that which receives a division into equal even parts, but its parts immediately remain indivisible, such as 6, 10, 18, 30, and 50. For as soon as you divide this number, you run into a number that you cannot cut. An "oddly even" number is one whose parts can be divided but do not reach all the way to the unit, such as twenty-four. For these, divided in half, make 12; again in another half, 6; then in another, 3; and that division receives no further cutting, but before the unit is reached, a limit is found which you cannot cut. "Oddly odd" is that which is measured oddly by an odd number, such as 15, 25, 49; because they are odd numbers, they are divided by odd prime numbers, such as seven times seven (forty-nine), and five times five (twenty-five). Among odd numbers, some are simple, some are composite, and some are intermediate. "Simple" are those which have no factors except the unit alone, such as three (only a third), five (only a fifth), and seven (only a seventh). For these have only one part. "Composite" are those which are not only measured by the unit, but are also produced by another number, such as 9, 15, 21. For we say three times three, and seven times three, three times five, and five times five. "Intermediate" numbers are those which in a way seem simple and in another way composite. For example: if 9 is compared to 25, it is "first" and uncomposed, because it has no common factor except the unit. But if it is compared to 15, it is "second" and composite, because there is a common factor in it besides the unit—that is, the number three, which measures nine (three times three) and fifteen (three times five). Likewise, among even numbers, some are "superfluous" <note>also called abundant numbers</note>, some are "diminished" <note>deficient</note>, and some are "perfect." "Superfluous" are those whose factors, when added together, exceed their own total, such as twelve. For it has five parts: a twelfth which is 1, a sixth which is 2, a fourth which is 3, a third which is 4, and a half which is 6. For 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and

So it is with many other similar numbers, such as 18 and many others like it. **Diminished numbers** <note>Also known as deficient numbers.</note> are those which, when compared to the sum of their parts, produce a smaller total. Take for example the number 10, which has three parts: a tenth, which is 1; a fifth, which is 2; and a half, which is 5. For 1, 2, and 5 added together make 8, which is far less than 10. There are perfect numbers: 6 within the tens, 28 within the hundreds, and 496 within the thousands.

# On the second division of the whole number, Chapter 6.

**Every number** is considered either in itself or in relation to something else. This is divided as follows: some are **equal**, others are **unequal**. This [latter] is divided as follows: some are **greater**, others are **lesser**. The greater are divided into five types: 
1. multiples; 
2. <term>superparticulars</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus one part of it, like 3:2.</note>; 
3. <term>superpartients</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus several parts of it, like 5:3.</note>; 
4. multiple superparticulars; 
5. multiple superpartients. 

The lesser are divided similarly: 
1. submultiples; 
2. <term>subsuperparticulars</term>; 
3. <term>subsuperpartients</term>; 
4. submultiple subsuperparticulars; 
5. submultiple subsuperpartients. 

A number **in itself** is one spoken of without any relation, such as 2, 3, 5, 6, and others like them. A number **in relation to something** is a number compared relatively to others; for example, when 4 is compared to 2, it is called double and a **multiple**; 6 to 3, 8 to 4, 10 to 5; and again 3 to 1 is triple, 6 to 2, 9 to 3, and so on. **Equal numbers** are those which are equal according to quantity, for example: 2 to 2, 3 to 3, 10 to 10, 100 to 100. **Unequal numbers** are those which, compared to one another, demonstrate inequality, such as 2 to 1, 3 to 2, 4 to 3, 5 to 6; and universally, whenever a greater is compared to a lesser, or a lesser to a greater, it is called unequal. A **greater number** is one that contains within itself that lesser number to which it is compared, plus something more. For example: the number 5 is "stronger" <note>In this context, *fortior* means numerically greater.</note> than the number 3, because the number 5 has 3 within it, plus two other parts of it <note>i.e., 5 = 3 + (1+1).</note>, and others like it. A **lesser number** is one contained by the greater to which it is compared, along with some part of itself, such as 3 in relation to 5; for it is contained by it along with two of its parts. A **multiple number** is one that contains that lesser number within itself twice, or thrice, or four times, or many times. For example: when 2 is compared to 1, it is double; [3 to 1] triple; 4 quadruple, and so on. Conversely, a **submultiple number** is one contained within a multiple twice, or thrice, or four times, or many times. For example: 1 is contained by 2 twice, by 3 thrice, by 4 four times, by 5 five times, and by others many times. A **superparticular number** is when the greater contains within itself the lower number to which it is compared, and likewise one part of it. For example: when 3 and 2 are compared, they con-

<column-break/>

### Column 2

-tain within themselves two, and one more, which is the half part of two. When 4 and 3 are compared, they contain within themselves 4 <note>The text likely intended to say it contains 3 plus 1.</note> and one more, which is the third part of three. Again, when 5 and 4 are compared, they have within themselves the number four and one more, which is said to be the fourth part of the number four, and others of this sort. A **superpartient number** is one which contains the whole lower number, and beyond this, two, or 3, or 4, or 5, or other parts of it. For example: when 5 and 3 are compared, the number 5 has 3 within it, and beyond that, two other parts of it. When 7 and 4 are compared, they have 4 within them, and three other parts of it; when 9 and 5 are compared, they have 5 within them and four other parts of it. A **subsuperpartient number** is one contained in a superpartient number along with some two, three, or more of its parts. For example: 3 is contained by 5 with two of its other parts; 5 by 9 with four of its parts. A **subsuperparticular number** is the lesser which is contained in the greater number with some one part of itself—either a half, a third, a fourth, or a fifth—such as 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, and the rest. A **multiple superparticular number** is one which, when compared to a number lower than itself, contains the whole lower number multiple times along with one part of it. For example: when 5 and 2 are compared, they contain "twice two" (4) and one part of it <note>i.e., 5 = (2 × 2) + 1, where 1 is half of 2.</note>. When 9 and 4 are compared, they contain "twice four" and one part of it. A **submultiple superparticular** <note>The text here describes what we would call a multiple superpartient ratio.</note> number is one which, when compared to a number lower than itself, contains it multiple times along with other [multiple] parts of it. For example: when 8 and 3 are compared, it contains "twice three" along with two other parts of it <note>8 = (2 × 3) + 2.</note>. When 13 and 6 are compared, they contain "twice six" along with one <note>OCR says "duabus" (two), though 13 = (2 × 6) + 1.</note> other part of it. When 16 and 7 are compared, they contain "twice seven" along with two other parts of it. When 21 and 9 are compared, they contain within themselves "twice nine" with three other parts of it. A **submultiple superpartional** <note>Original: *submultiplex suppartionalis*.</note> number is one which, when compared to a greater, is contained by it multiple times with some of its parts. For example, 3 to 7: [7] contains [3] twice with one <note>OCR says "duabus" (two), though 7 = (2 × 3) + 1.</note> of its parts; 4 to 11 contains [4] twice with three of its parts.

# On the third division of the whole number, Chapter 7.

**Numbers** are either **discrete** or **continuous**. This is divided as follows: 
1. linear; 
2. superficial; 
3. solid. 

A **discrete number** is one contained by distinct units, such as 3, 4, 5, 6, and the rest. A **continuous number** is one contained by joined units; for example, the number 3 is understood in magnitude—that is, it is called a line, or a space, or a solid. **Continuous** is similar, such as the numbers 4 and 5. A **linear number** is one that, beginning from a unit, is described linearly unto infinity. Hence <term>alpha</term> <note>The Greek letter α.</note> is used for the designation of lines, because this letter signifies "one" among the Greeks. A **superficial number** is one contained not only by length, but also by breadth, such as a triangle, a square, a pentagon, or circular numbers...

[Image: Three 'a's representing a line of three units]

### Chapter 8: On the difference between arithmetic, geometry, and music.

**I**t is of interest to note the difference between arithmetic, geometry, and music in how you find the "means" <note>A "mean" is a middle value between two extremes.</note>. In arithmetic, you seek it first like this: you join the extremes and divide the sum to find the middle. For example, let the extremes be 6 and 12. Join them together and they make 18. Divide this in half and you get 9, which is the arithmetic proportion. The middle number exceeds the first by as many units as it is exceeded by the last; for 9 exceeds 6 by three units, and is exceeded by 12 by three units. In geometry, however, you seek it thus: the extremes multiplied together produce as much as the means multiplied together. For example, 6 and 12 multiplied will make seventy-two; the means 8 and 9 multiplied together make the same amount. In music, it is like this: by whatever proportion the middle exceeds the first, by that same proportion the extreme exceeds the middle. For example, given 6, 8, and 12: 8 exceeds 6 by a third part of itself (2), and 12 exceeds 8 by a third part of itself (4).

->**C** The Arithmetic Mean<-
->6. 9. 12.<-
->**C** The Musical Mean<-
->6. 8. 12.<-
->**C** The Geometric Mean<-
->6. 8. 9. 12.<-

### Chapter 9: That numbers are infinite.

**I**t is most certain that numbers are infinite. For at whatever number you think an end must be made, I say that it can be increased—not just by adding one, but it can be doubled or even multiplied by any vast quantity according to the logic and science of numbers. Thus, each number is limited by its own

<column-break/>

properties, such that no one of them can be equal to any other. Therefore, they are unequal among themselves and diverse; each individual one is finite, yet as a whole, they are infinite.

### Chapter 10: What geometry is, and about its inventors and its name.

**T**he discipline of geometry is said to have first been discovered by the Egyptians. Because the Nile flooded and covered everyone's possessions with mud, the need to divide the land by lines and measurements gave the art its name. Later, carried further by the sharp minds of wise men, they began to measure the spaces of the sea, the sky, and the air. For, having been challenged, scholars began to seek out the spaces of the heavens after measuring the earth: how great an interval the moon is from the earth, and how far the sun itself is from the moon, and how great a measure extends to the very summit of heaven. Thus they distinguished the intervals of the heaven and the circuit of the world by a rational system of "stadium" <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> counts. But because this discipline began from measuring the earth, it preserved its name from its origin. For "geometry" is named from "earth" and "measure." For in Greek, "earth" is called *ge* <note>original: "γη"</note> and "measure" is *metron* <note>original: "μετρον"</note>. The art of this discipline contains within itself lines, intervals, magnitudes, and figures; and within figures, dimensions and numbers.

### Chapter 11: On the fourfold division of geometry.

**T**he division of geometry is fourfold: into the plane, into countable magnitude, into rational magnitude, and into solid figures.

Plane figures are those contained by length and width, which according to Plato are five in number. Countable magnitude is that which can be divided by the numbers of arithmetic. Rational magnitudes are those whose measure we can know. Irrational magnitudes, however, are those for which the quantity of measurement is not known.

### Chapter 12: On geometric figures.

**S**olid figures are those contained by length, width, and height, such as the cube and others.

There are five species on the plane. The first of these on the flat plane is the circle. A plane figure is thus called "circumscribed," in the middle of which is a point where all lines converge, which the geometers call the "center" and the Latins call the "point of the circle." The first figure of this art is the **point**, which has no parts. The second is the **line**, which is length without width. A **straight line** is one that lies equally upon its own points. A **surface** is that which possesses only length and width. The boundaries of a surface are lines. The forms of these were not placed among the figures above because they are found within them.

### Chapter 13: On finding numbers according to geometry
You seek numbers according to geometry in this way: the extremes, when multiplied, produce the same amount as the means when they are multiplied together. For example, 6 and 12 multiplied make seventy-two; the means, 8 and 9, when multiplied make the same amount. <note>This describes a geometric proportion (6:8 = 9:12), where the product of the outer numbers (6x12=72) equals the product of the inner numbers (8x9=72).</note>

### Chapter 14: On music and its name
**Music** is the skill of modulation consisting of sound and song. It is called "music" through derivation from the **Muses**. The Muses were named *apo tou mōsai*, that is, "from seeking," because through them—as the ancients intended—the power of songs and the modulation of the voice might be sought. <note>original: "απὸ τοῦ μῶσαι" (apo tou mōsai). This is a classical etymology suggesting the Muses represent the search for knowledge or artistic inspiration.</note> Because sound is a thing of the senses, it flows into the past and is imprinted on the memory. For this reason, the poets imagined that the Muses were the daughters of Jupiter and Memory. Unless sounds are held in the memory by man, they perish, because they cannot be written down. <note>This reflects the era before standardized musical notation, where music lived only in performance and memory.</note>

### Chapter 15: On the inventors of music
Moses says the discoverer of the musical art was **Tubal**, who was of the lineage of Cain before the Flood. The Greeks, however, say that **Pythagoras** found the beginnings of this art from the sound of hammers and the striking of stretched strings. Others report that Linus of Thebes, Zethus, and Amphion were the first to become famous in the musical art. After them, this discipline was gradually organized and increased in many ways. It was once considered as shameful to be ignorant of music as it was to be illiterate. It was employed not only in sacred rites, but in all ceremonies and in all joyful or sad affairs. Just as hymns were used in divine veneration, so were wedding songs used in marriages, and dirges and lamentations were sung to the pipes at funerals. At banquets, the lyre and cithara were passed around, and a convivial type of song was arranged for each of the guests.

### Chapter 16: What music can do
Therefore, no discipline can be perfect without music. For there is nothing without it. Indeed, the world itself is said to be composed of a certain harmony of sounds,

<column-break/>

and the heavens themselves revolve under the modulation of harmony. Music moves the emotions and provokes the senses to different states. In battles, the sounding of the trumpet ignites the fighters; the more vehement the blare, the stronger the spirit becomes for the contest. Likewise, song encourages rowers; music soothes the mind to endure labors, and the modulation of the voice consoles the weariness of every task. Music also calms excited minds, as is read concerning David, who rescued Saul from an unclean spirit by the art of modulation. Music even rouses beasts, and even serpents, birds, and dolphins to listen to its modulation. Furthermore, whatever we speak or whatever is moved by the internal pulsing of our veins is proven to be associated with the virtues of harmony through musical rhythms.

### Chapter 17: On the three parts of music
There are three parts of music: **harmonic**, **rhythmic**, and **metric**. **Harmonic** is that which distinguishes between high and low sounds. **Rhythmic** is that which requires the flow of words to see if the sound fits together well or poorly. **Metric** is that which recognizes the measurement of various meters by a predictable system, such as heroic, iambic, or elegiac meters, and so forth.

### Chapter 18: On the threefold division of music
For every sound that is the material of songs, its nature is established as threefold. First is the **harmonic**, which consists of vocal songs. Second is the **organic**, which consists of breath. Third is the **rhythmic**, which receives its numbers from the impulse of fingers. For sound is produced either by the voice, as through the throat; or by breath, as through a trumpet or pipe; or by impulse, as through a cithara or anything else that produces sound by being struck.

### Chapter 19: On the first division of music, which is called harmonic
The first division of music, called **harmonic**—that is, the modulation of the voice—pertains to cosmic actors, tragedies, or choruses, or to all who sing with their own voice. This produces motion from the soul and body, and from that motion, sound, from which is gathered the music called "voice" in man. **Voice** is air struck by breath, from which words are named. Strictly speaking, voice belongs to humans or irrational animals. For in other things, the word "voice" is used improperly or figuratively for sound, such as: "the voice of the trumpet roared," or "broken voices on the shore." <note>These are literary references, likely to Virgil, illustrating how "voice" is used metaphorically for the sound of waves or instruments.</note> For it is more proper to say that the rocks of the shore "resound," and that the trumpet gives a "terrible sound from its singing brass." **Harmonic** is the modulation of the voice and the concordance or fitting together of many sounds. 

**Symphony** is the tempering of modulation from high and low sounds brought into concord, whether in voice, breath, or striking. Through this, higher and lower voices harmonize so that anyone who is dissonant from it offends the sense of the listener. Its opposite is **diaphonia**, that is, discrepant or dissonant voices. **Euphonia** is sweetness of voice; this is also called *melos* <note>term: melos (the Greek word for song or melody)</note> from its sweetness and from honey (*melle*). **Diastema** is an interval of the voice, made up of two or more sounds. It is named for certain spaces and paths of modulation, verging from one sound into another.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the mathematical principles of geometry into the science of Music, specifically focusing on the definitions of sound and the classification of musical instruments into three categories: organic (wind), rhythmic (strings/percussion), and vocal.</meta>

**Sound** is a sharp utterance of the voice. It is the quantity of harmonic differences which consists in the accent or tone of the voice. Musicians have divided its types into fifteen parts, <note>original: "xv partib'". This refers to the fifteen musical modes or keys in late classical music theory.</note> of which the first is **Hyperlydian**, the newest and sharpest, and the **Hypodorian**, the deepest of all. **Song** is the inflection of the voice; for sound is direct, but sound precedes song. **Arsis** <note>original: "Arsis" (ἄρσις), meaning "lifting."</note> is the elevation of the voice, and it is the beginning. **Thesis** <note>original: "Thesis" (θέσις), meaning "placing."</note> is the setting down of the voice, that is, the end. **Sweet** voices are subtle and thick, clear and sharp. **Perspicuous** voices are those which are drawn out longer so that they fill every place continuously, like the clangor of a trumpet. **Subtle** voices are those in which there is no breath, such as those of infants, or women, or the sick, just as in strings. For the subtlest strings emit subtle and thin voices. **Fat** <note>meaning "rich" or "heavy"</note> voices are those when much breath comes out at once, such as those of men. A **Sharp** voice is thin and high, as we see in strings. A **Hard** voice is one that emits sounds violently, like thunder or the sound of an anvil, whenever the hammer strikes the hard iron. A **Harsh** voice is hoarse and is dispersed through small and dissimilar pulses. A **Loose** voice is one that falls silent as soon as it is emitted, and being stifled, is by no means drawn out longer, as is the case with earthenware. A **Flexible** <note>original: "vinnola"</note> voice is soft and bendable; and "vinnola" is named from *vinnus*, <note>original: "vinnus," meaning a softly curled lock of hair.</note> that is, softly curled. A **Perfect** voice, however, is high, sweet, and clear: high, so that it suffices in the heights; clear, so that it fills the ears; sweet, so that it charms the minds of the listeners. If any of these is lacking, the voice will not be perfect.

### On the second division which is called organic Chapter XX.

The second division is **organic**, consisting of those things which, completed by blowing breath, are animated into the sound of a voice, such as trumpets, reeds, pipes, organs, pandoras, <note>A three-stringed lute-like instrument, though here grouped with wind instruments by Isidore.</note> and instruments similar to these. **Organ** is a general name for all musical vessels. However, that to which bellows are applied, the Greeks call by another name. <note>likely "hydraulis" or "organon pneumaticon".</note> But that it is called an "organ" is rather a common custom of the Greeks. The **Trumpet** was first invented by the Tyrrhenians, <note>The Etruscans.</note> of whom Virgil says: "And the Tyrrhenian trumpet’s clangor bellowed through the air." <note>original: "Tyrrhenusque tubae mugire per aethera clangor." (Aeneid 8.526)</note> It was used not only in battles, but in all festive days for the sake of the clarity of praise or joy. Whence it is said in the Psalter: "Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemnity." For it had been commanded to the Jews that they should sound the trumpet at the beginning of the new moon, which also horns <note>original: "buccinae"</note> do. They say the **Pipes** <note>original: "Tibias"</note> were devised in Phrygia. These were long used only for funerals, and soon also for the sacred rites of the gentiles. They think they were called *tibiae* because they were first made from the shinbones <note>original: "tibijs"</note> of deer and the legs of fawns; then by a misuse of the word, those which were not made from legs and bones began to be called so. Hence also the *tibicen* <note>flute-player</note> is as if the "singer of the shins." **Reed** <note>original: "Calamus"</note> is the proper name of a tree, called from *calendo*, <note>an etymology linking the reed to the pouring out or emitting of voice/heat.</note> that is, from pouring out voices. Some think the **Pipe** <note>original: "Fistulam"</note> was invented by Mercury, others by Faunus, whom the Greeks call Pan. Some say it was by the shepherd Idas the Agrigentine from Sicily. It is called *fistula* because it emits a voice; for in Greek *phos* is "voice" and *staleisa* is "sent." <note>original: "φοσ" and "Σταλεισα". This is a creative medieval etymology.</note> The **Sambuca** among musicians is a type of symphony; <note>The sambuca was a stringed instrument, but Isidore identifies it here as being made of brittle wood, often associated with pipes/flutes in this period.</note> for it is a type of brittle wood from which pipes are also composed. The **Pandora** is named from its inventor, of whom Virgil says: "Pan

<column-break/>

first taught how to join several reeds with wax; Pan cares for the sheep, and for the masters of the sheep." <note>Virgil, Eclogue 2.32-33.</note> For he was among the gentiles a pastoral god, who first fitted unequal reeds for song and composed them with studious art.

### On the third division which is called rhythmic Chapter XXI.

The third division is **rhythmic**, pertaining to strings and percussion, to which are given the species of various **citharas**, the **drum**, the **cymbal**, the **sistrum**, bronze and silver **bowls**, <note>original: "acetabula," literally vinegar-cups used as percussion.</note> or other things which, struck with metallic stiffness, return a tinkling with sweetness, and others of this kind. The use of the cithara and the psalter is forbidden <insert>reproved</insert> as was said before. According to the opinion of the Greeks, the use of the cithara is believed to have been discovered by Apollo. The **form of the cithara** is said to have been similar to the human chest, from which, just as the voice comes from the chest, so the song is issued from the instrument; and it was called by the same name for that reason. For the chest in the Doric tongue is called a *cithara*. Gradually, however, more species of it emerged, such as psalters, lyres, barbits, phoenices, and pectides, and those which are called "indices" and are struck by two at once. Likewise others and still others in a square or triangular form; the number of strings was also multiplied and the type changed. The ancients named the cithara *fidicula* or *fidicen*, because its strings harmonize together so well, just as trust <note>original: "fides," playing on the double meaning of "stringed instrument" and "faith/trust."</note> exists between those who agree well. The **ancient cithara** had seven strings, whence Virgil says: "The seven distinctions of voices." <note>Aeneid 6.646.</note> They are called "distinctions" because no string returns a sound similar to its neighbor. There are seven strings either because they fill the whole voice, or because the sky sounds with seven motions. <note>A reference to the "music of the spheres" and the seven known planets.</note> They are called **strings** <note>original: "chordas"</note> from the **heart**; <note>original: "corde"</note> because just as there is a pulse of the heart in the chest, so is the pulse of the string in the cithara. Mercury first devised these, and he was the first to constrain sound into strings. The **Psalter**, which is commonly called a "canticle," is named from *psallendo* <note>plucking</note> because the choir responds to its voice in harmony. There is a similarity to the barbarian cithara in the shape of the letter **Delta** (Δ). But this is the difference between the psalter and the cithara: the psalter has that hollow wood from which the sound is returned at the top, and the strings are struck downwards and sound from above. The cithara, conversely, has the hollowness of the wood at the bottom. The Hebrews used the **ten-stringed** psalter <note>original: "decachordon"</note> on account of the number of the Ten Commandments of the Law. The **Lyre** is named from *apo tou lyrin*, <note>from "variations".</note> that is, from the variety of voices, because it produces different sounds. They say the lyre was first invented by Mercury in this way: when the Nile, returning to its channels, had left various animals in the fields, a **tortoise** was also left; when it had decayed and its tendons remained stretched within the shell, it gave a sound when struck by Mercury. In the likeness of this, Mercury made the lyre and handed it over to Orpheus, who was most studious of that thing. Whence it is estimated that by the same art he applied the modulation of song not only to wild beasts, but also to rocks and woods. Musicians, for the love of study and the praise of song, even feigned that it was placed among the stars in their fables. The **Drum** <note>original: "Tympanum"</note> is a skin or hide stretched over wood on one side. For it is a middle part of a symphony, in the likeness of a sieve. It is called a *tympanum* because it is half <note>original: "medium"</note>; whence also a half-pearl is called a *margaritum*, and like the symphony, it is struck with a stick.

**Cymbals** are certain hollow bowls <note>original: "acetabula," literally vinegar-cups or small bowls</note> which, when struck against one another, touch and create a sound. They are called cymbals because they are struck together with rhythmic dancing <note>original: "ballematiā," from the Greek for dancing or throwing</note>. For so the Greeks call cymbals *ballematiā*. The **Sistrum** <note>a type of rhythmic rattle</note> is named after its inventor, for it is proven that Isis, the queen of the Egyptians, discovered this kind of instrument. Juvenal says: *Isis and her angry sistrum may strike my eyes.* Hence, women also strike this instrument, because the inventor of this kind was a woman. Whence also among the Amazons, the female army was called to war by the sistrum. The **Tinkling bell** <note>original: "Tintinnabulū"</note> has its name from the sound of its voice, just like the clapping of hands or the creaking of folding doors. The **Symphony** <note>here referring to a type of drum</note> is commonly called a hollow wood with skin stretched on both sides, which musicians strike with small sticks from here and there. In it, from the concord of low and high notes, a most sweet song is made.

### XXII. On musical numbers
You arrange the numbers according to music in a ten-fold way. With the extremes set, for example 6 and 12, the ten-fold proportion is arranged. You see how much 12 exceeds 6 by units <note>original: "monadib'," from monad, a single unit</note>; it is 6 units. You multiply by a square; the series of six makes 36. You join those first extremes, 6 to 12, and they produce 18. You divide the series of thirty-six by eighteen, and a double proportion <note>original: "dipōdi'"</note> is made. You join the result with the sum of the lesser, that is, the series will be 8, and it will be the middle between 6 and 12. Wherefore eight exceeds six by two units, that is, a third of the series; and 8 is exceeded by 12 by four units, a third portion. By the same part it exceeds, it is also exceeded. But just as this ratio exists in the world from the rotation of the circles, so also in the **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmo," the "little world" or the human being</note> it prevails through the voice to such an extent that without its perfection, a man lacks harmonies and does not stand complete. By the perfection of this same music, even poetic meters consist in **arsis** and **thesis**, that is, the elevation and the setting down of the voice.

### XXIII. On astronomy
**Astronomy** is the law of the stars, which tracks the courses of the heavenly bodies, their figures, and the habits of the stars around themselves and around the Earth with untraceable reason.

### XXIV. On its inventors
The Egyptians first discovered astronomy. The Chaldeans were the first to teach **Astrology** and the observation of birth signs. However, the author Josephus asserts that Abraham instructed the Egyptians in astrology. The Greeks, however, say that this art was first devised by Atlas, and therefore he was said to have held up the heavens. Whoever he was, he was moved by the motion of the heaven and excited by the reason of the mind; through the changes of seasons, through the fixed and defined courses of the stars, and through the measured spaces of intervals, he considered certain dimensions and numbers, which, by defining and discerning them into an order, he linked together to discover astrology.

### XXV. On the writers of astronomy
In both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note> indeed, volumes have been written by various people about astronomy; among whom, however, King Ptolemy of Alexandria is held as the chief among the Greeks. He also established the "canons" <note>mathematical tables</note> by which the courses of the stars are found.

### XXVI. On the difference between astronomy and astrology
There is some difference between **astronomy** and **astrology**. For astronomy contains the position of the heaven, the rising, setting, and motion of the stars, or from

<column-break/>

what cause it is so named. **Astrology**, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is **Natural** while it tracks the course of the sun and the moon or the stars and the certain stations of the seasons. But **Superstitious** astrology is that which the "mathematicians" <note>here meaning practitioners of horoscopes or magic</note> follow, who divine by the stars, and who even distribute the twelve signs of heaven through the individual members of the soul or body, and attempt to predict the births and characters of men by the course of the stars.

### XXVII. On the reasoning of astronomy
The reasoning of astronomy consists of many modes. For it defines what the world is, what heaven is, what the site and course of the sphere are, what the axis of heaven and the poles are, what the climates of heaven are, the courses of the sun and moon, and the stars, and the rest.

### XXVIII. On the world and its name
The **World** is that which consists of heaven, earth, and sea, and all the stars. It is called the "world" <note>original: "mundus"</note> because it is always in motion; for no rest is granted to its elements.

### XXIX. On the form of the world
The formation of the world is demonstrated thus: for just as the world rises into the northern region, so it declines into the southern. Its head is, as it were, its face in the eastern region, and its final part is the north.

### XXX. On heaven and its name
Philosophers have said that **Heaven** is round, revolving, and burning. It is called by this name because, like an "engraved vessel" <note>original: "vas cęlatū," a pun on the Latin *caelum* (heaven) and *caelatum* (engraved/embossed)</note>, it has the signs of the stars impressed upon it. For God distinguished it with bright lights and filled it, namely with the sun and the shining orb of the moon, and adorned it with the glittering signs of the sparkling stars. In Greek, however, it is called *ouranos* <note>original: "ουρανοσ"</note> from the word "to see" <note>original: "απο του οραν"</note>, because the air is transparent and purer for looking.

### XXXI. On the position of the celestial sphere
The **Sphere** of heaven is a certain form shaped into a round, the center of which is the Earth, equally enclosed from all parts. They say this sphere has neither beginning nor end, because in a round shape, like a circle, where it begins or where it defines itself is not easily grasped. The philosophers of the world introduced seven heavens, that is, the planets, with a harmonious motion of globes; they record that all things are connected to their orbs, which they believe are bound together and, as if inserted, turn backward and are carried in the opposite direction by their own fixed motions.

### XXXII. On its motion
The motion of the sphere revolves on two axes. One of these is the northern, which never sets, and is called **Boreas**. The other is the southern, which is never seen, and is called **Austronotus**. They say the sphere of heaven moves on these two poles, and with its motion, the stars fixed in it circle from the east all the way to the west, with the northern stars performing shorter circles near the pivot <note>original: "cardinē"</note>.

### XXXIII. On the course of the same sphere
The sphere of heaven turns from the east to the west once in a day and night, in the space of twenty-four hours, in which the sun concludes its course above the lands and under the lands by its own revolution.

III

### 34. On the speed of the heavens

The sphere of heaven is said to run with such great speed that if the stars did not run against its headlong course to delay it, they would cause the ruin of the world <note>Isidore follows the ancient idea that the planets move in the opposite direction to the firmament to provide a "braking" effect</note>.

### 35. On the axis of heaven

The axis is a straight northern line that stretches through the middle of the sphere. It is called an "axis" because the sphere revolves on it like a wheel, or because the Wagon <note>original: "plaustrum," referring to the constellation of the Great Bear or the Big Dipper</note> is located there.

### 36. On the celestial poles

The poles are circles that run through the axis. One of these is the northern pole, which never sets and is called "Boreas" <note>the North Wind</note>. The other is the southern pole, which is never seen and is called "Austronotus" <note>the South Wind</note>. They are called "poles" because they are the cycles of the axes; in the usage of wagons, they are named from "polishing." The northern pole is always visible, while the southern is never seen, because the right side of heaven is higher and the southern part is depressed.

### 37. On the hinges of heaven

The hinges <note>term: "cardines," the pivot points</note> of heaven are the extreme parts of the axis. They are called hinges because the heavens turn upon them, or because they revolve like the heart <note>original: "cor"</note>.

### 38. On the convexities of heaven

The convexities of heaven are its extremities, named for their curvature <note>original: "curvitate"</note>, as in that verse:
> Whenever the moist night closes the convex sky <note>original: "Convexū quotiens claudit nox humida celū," a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>.

For "convex" means curved, as if it were turned or inclining, and in the manner of a circumference.

### 39. On the gates of heaven

The gates of heaven are two: the rising <note>East</note> and the setting <note>West</note>. For through one the sun comes forth, and through the other it retreats.

### 40. On the double face of heaven

The "face" or head of heaven is the eastern region; the lowest part is the northern. Regarding this, Lucan says:
> So the lowest part of the world lies, where the snowy zone and perpetual winters press down <note>original: "Sic mūdi parś ima iacet: quā zona niualis: ppetuuq; pꝛemūt hyemes"</note>.

### 41. On the four parts of heaven

The climates of heaven—that is, the regions—are four. The first part is the eastern, from which some stars rise. The second is the western, where some stars set for us. The third is the northern, where the sun reaches during the longer days. The fourth is the southern, where the sun reaches during the longer nights. The East <note>original: "Oriens"</note> is named from the rising <note>original: "exortu"</note> of the sun. The West <note>original: "Occidens"</note> is so called because it makes the day "fall" <note>original: "occidere"</note> and perish; for it hides the light from the world and brings on the darkness. The North <note>original: "Septentrio"</note> is named after the seven stars <note>original: "septem stellis"</note> of the axis, which revolve and rotate in it. This is properly called "vertex" <note>the summit</note> because it turns. Midday <note>original: "Meridies," South</note> is so called either because the sun makes "mid-day" <note>original: "medidies"</note> there, or because the upper air <note>original: "ether"</note> shines more purely <note>original: "purius"</note> then, for "merum" means pure. There are also seven other climates of heaven, which are like seven lines from east to west, under which different human customs and specifically diverse animals are born. These are named after certain famous places: the first is Meroë, the second Syene, the third Catachoras (which is Africa), the fourth Rhodes, the fifth the Hellespont, the sixth Mesopontus, and the seventh Borysthenes.

### 42. On the hemispheres

A hemisphere is half a part of the sphere. The hemisphere above the earth is that part of heaven which

<column-break/>

is entirely seen by us. The hemisphere below the earth is that which cannot be seen because it has been under the earth for a long time.

### 43. On the five circles of heaven

There are five circles of heaven, by whose distinctions certain parts are inhabited due to their temperate nature, while others remain uninhabitable because of the intensity of cold or heat. These are called zones or circles because they exist in the circumference of the sphere. The first circle is called "Arctic" because the signs of the Bears <note>original: "arcturi signa"</note> are seen enclosed within it. The second is the "Summer" <note>original: "therinos," from the Greek for summer</note> circle, which is also called the "Tropic," because the sun, circling in it, creates summer in the northern regions and does not pass beyond that circle, but immediately returns; hence it is called "Tropic" <note>from the Greek *trepein*, to turn</note>. The third circle is the "Bimerinus," which is called the "Equinoctial" by the Latins because the sun, when it reaches that orbit, makes the day and night equal. For "Bimerinus" in Latin means "day and night" <note>original: "dies atq; nox," derived from the Greek *hemera* (day)</note>; in this circle, half of the sphere is seen to be established. The fourth circle is called "Antarctic," because it is opposite to the circle we named Arctic. The fifth circle is the "Winter Tropic" <note>original: "chimerinꝰ tropicꝰ," from the Greek *cheimerinos* (wintry)</note>, which is called "Hyemalis" or "Brumalis" by the Latins, because when the sun reaches that circle, it creates winter for those in the north and summer for those dwelling in the southern parts.

### 44. On the zodiac circle

The zodiac circle consists of five angles of lines and one single line.

### 45. On the white circle

The Milky Circle <note>original: "Lacteus circulꝰ"</note> is a path seen in the sphere, named for its brightness because it is white. Some say it is the path where the sun travels, and it shines so because of the passage of its own splendor.

### 46. On the magnitude of the sun

The size of the sun is greater than that of the earth. Hence, at the same moment it rises, it appears equally to both the East and the West. As for why it seems only a foot <note>original: "cubitalis," the size of a forearm</note> wide to us, we must consider how far the sun is from the earth; this distance makes it appear small to us.

### 47. On the magnitude of the moon

The size of the moon is said to be smaller than that of the sun. For while the sun is higher than the moon, it still appears larger to us than the moon; if it were as close to us as the moon, it would be seen to be much larger. Just as the sun is greater than the earth, so the earth is greater than the moon by some amount.

### 48. On the nature of the sun

Since the sun is fiery, it becomes hotter due to the great speed of its rotation. Philosophers say its fire is nourished by water, receiving the power of light and heat from the opposite element. Hence we often see it appearing wet and dewy.

### 49. On the course of the sun

They say the sun moves by itself and does not turn with the world. For if it remained fixed in the sky, all days and nights would be equal. And since we see it set in one place tomorrow and in another place yesterday, it is clear that it moves through its own path and does not simply turn with the world. It completes annual orbits in unequal spaces according to the changes of the seasons. Rising, it makes the day; setting, it makes the night.

Isidore blends physical description with etymological explanations to define the medieval cosmological worldview.</summary>

...brings in. For as it goes farther to the south, it creates winter, so that the earth may be enriched by winter moisture and frost. Approaching closer to the north, it brings back summer, so that crops may be ripened by maturity, and those things which are raw in the humidity may be softened by the heat.

### 50. On the setting of the sun <note>original: "De defectu solis," though the chapter describes the sun's general movement and the creation of day and night</note>

The rising sun makes the day; the setting sun brings in the night. For day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth. From the sun, hours are counted; from the sun comes the day when it has ascended; from the sun also the night when it has set. From the sun, months and years are numbered; from the sun, the changes of the seasons occur. When it runs through the south, it is closer to the earth; when it is raised high near the north. For this reason, God established its various courses, places, and times, lest if it always stayed in the same places, its daily heat would consume everything; but as Clement says <note>Likely referring to the "Recognitiones" of Pseudo-Clement, a popular source for medieval cosmology</note>, it receives various courses by which the temperance of the air is dispensed according to the logic of the seasons, and the order of successions and changes is preserved. For while it ascends to the higher parts, it tempers the spring; but when it comes to the height of heaven, it kindles summer heats. Descending again in autumn, it restores temperance; but when it returns to the lower circle, it leaves us the rigor of winter cold from the icy frame of heaven.

### 51. On the journey of the sun

The rising sun has its journey through the south; after it has come to its setting, it enters into the ocean, and travels through unknown paths under the earth, and returns again to the east.

### 52. On the light of the moon

Some philosophers say the moon has its own light, and that one part of its globe is light-bearing, but the other is dark, and by gradually turning it produces various forms. Others, however, say on the contrary that the moon does not have its own light, but is illuminated by the rays of the sun. Hence it also suffers an eclipse if the shadow of the earth comes between it and the sun. For the sun is higher than that place; thus it happens that when it is below the sun, it shines on the upper side, but on the lower side, which it has toward the earth, it is dark.

### 53. On the forms of the moon

The first figure of the moon is two-horned, thus:

The second is "cut," thus:

The third is half, thus:

The fourth is full, thus:
<image-desc>A full moon</image-desc>

The fifth is again half from the larger side, thus:
<image-desc>A half moon (last quarter)</image-desc>

The sixth is again "cut," thus:
<image-desc>A wider waning crescent</image-desc>

The seventh is two-horned, thus:
<image-desc>A thin waning crescent</image-desc>

<column-break/>

But the seventh and a half <note>original: "Septima aut semis"</note> and the twenty-second and a half are in the middle of their orbit. The rest are proportional.

### 54. On the "interlunium" of the moon <note>term: "Interlunium" refers to the period of the new moon when it is invisible</note>

The "interlunium" of the moon is that time between the failing and the birth of the moon. It is, however, thirty days <note>original: "xxx dies" - This is likely a scribal error for "thirty hours," as the moon is only dark for a short period, not a full month</note> that the moon does not shine. It cannot be seen because, being joined to the sun, it is obscured; then, being reborn at that same moment, it is seen as it gradually moves away from the sun.

### 55. On the course of the moon

The moon regulates its monthly spaces in the center by the cycles of being lost and recovered. It moves in an oblique and not a straight course specifically so that it does not fall into the center of the earth and frequently suffer an eclipse. For its circle is near to the earth. When waxing, its horns face the east; when waning, they face the west, rightly so, because it is about to set and lose its light.

### 56. On the proximity of the moon to the earth

The moon is closer to the earth than the sun; therefore, it completes its course more quickly in a shorter circle. For the journey that the sun completes in 365 days, the moon runs through in 30 days. Hence the ancients placed the months in the moon’s cycle, but the years in the sun’s course.

### 57. On the eclipse of the sun

An eclipse of the sun occurs whenever the moon reaches the same line along which the sun is carried, and by placing itself in the way, it obscures the sun. For the sun seems to fail us while the globe of the moon is placed against it.

### 58. On the eclipse of the moon

An eclipse of the moon occurs whenever the moon runs into the shadow of the earth. For it is thought not to have its own light but to be illuminated by the sun; hence it suffers a failure if the shadow of the earth comes between itself and the sun. It suffers this on the fifteenth day of the moon <note>the full moon</note>, until it leaves the center and the shadow of the obstructing earth and can see the sun, or be seen by the sun.

### 59. On the difference between stars, constellations, and heavenly bodies <note>original: "stellarū siderū & astrozū"</note>

Stars, constellations, and heavenly bodies differ among themselves. For a "star" <note>original: "stella"</note> is any single one. "Constellations" <note>original: "sidera"</note> are made of many stars, such as the Hyades or Pleiades. "Heavenly bodies" <note>original: "astra"</note> are large stars, such as Orion or Bootes; but writers confuse these names and use "astra" for stars, and stars for constellations.

### 60. On the light of the stars

The stars are said not to have their own light, but to be illuminated by the sun, just like the moon.

### 61. On the position of the stars

The stars are immobile; being fixed to the heaven, they are carried by perpetual motion. They do not fall during the day, but are obscured by the splendor of the sun.

### 62. On the course of the stars

Constellations are either "carried" or "moved." Those which are fixed to the heaven are "carried" and revolve with the heaven; but certain ones are "moved," such as the <term>planets: wandering stars</term>, which complete their wandering courses within a certain defined limit.
