### On the Various Courses of the Stars, Chapter 63.
Stars are carried through the various spheres of the celestial planets. For some set more quickly and others more slowly; some arrive at their setting later and others sooner; others rise together and yet do not set at the same time. However, all return to their own proper course in their own time.

### On the Distances of the Stars, Chapter 64.
Stars are distant from the Earth at various intervals; therefore, they appear to our eyes with unequal brightness, some more and some less. For many are larger than those we see clearly, but being positioned further away, they appear small to us.

### On the Circular Number of the Stars, Chapter 65.
The "circular number" of the stars is the knowledge of how much time each star takes to complete its circle, whether in length or width. For the Moon is said to complete its circle in eight years <note>referring to the 'octaeteris', an ancient 8-year cycle used to harmonize lunar months with the solar year</note>; Mercury in 20 years; Lucifer <note>the Morning Star, or Venus</note> in 9 years; the Sun in 19 years; Vesper <note>the Evening Star, also Venus</note> in 15 years; Phaethon <note>the planet Jupiter</note> in 12 years; and Saturn in 30 years. By these agreements, they return to the same signs and parts at the completion of their cycles. Certain stars, hindered by the rays of the sun, become anomalous—either retrograde or stationary—just as the poet remembers, saying: "The sun divides the times, who changes day and night, and with powerful rays forbids the stars to go, and delays their wandering courses by reason." <note>A quote from Virgil's Georgics</note>

### On the Planet Stars, Chapter 66.
Certain stars are called "planets," that is, "wanderers," because they travel through the whole world with varying motion. Thus, because they wander, they are called "retrograde" or are made "anomalous"—that is, when they add or subtract portions of their path. Furthermore, when they only subtract, they are called retrograde; however, they make a "station" when they stand still.

### On the Precedence and Advancement of the Stars, Chapter 67.
Precedence or advancement of the stars occurs when a star is seen to perform its usual motion and moves ahead of its custom.

### On Removal or Retrogradation of the Stars, Chapter 68.
Removal or retrogradation of the stars is when a star, while performing its motion, also seems to be moved backward.

### On the Status of the Stars, Chapter 69.
The "status" of stars is that although a star is always moving, it nevertheless seems to stand still in certain places.

### On the Names of Stars and the Reasons they Received their Names, Chapter 70.
->f<- <note>This letter 'f' is a signature mark used by early printers to track the order of the pages during binding.</note>
The Sun is so named because it appears alone <note>original: "solus"</note>, all other stars being obscured by its brightness. The Moon is called "Luna," as if the word were "Lucina" <note>the Roman goddess of childbirth and light</note> with the middle syllable removed; of her Virgil says: "Chaste Lucina, favor us." It took its name by derivation from the light of the sun, because from

<column-break/>

it the moon receives light and returns what it has received. Stars <note>original: "stellae"</note> are named from "standing" <note>original: "stando"</note>, because they always stand fixed in the sky and do not fall. For what we see as stars gliding through the sky are not actually stars, but little fires fallen from the ether. This happens when the wind, seeking higher places, drags the ethereal fire with it, which by its movement imitates falling stars. For stars cannot fall; they are immobile, as was said before, and are carried fixed within the heavens. Constellations <note>original: "sidera"</note> are so named because sailors, by "considering" them, direct their journey and plan their course, lest they be led elsewhere by deceptive waves or winds. Certain stars are called "signs" <note>original: "signa"</note> because sailors observe them in governing their rowing, contemplating their sharpness and brightness, by which things the future state of the sky is shown. But indeed all people look to them to foresee the qualities of the air for summer, winter, and the springtime weather. For by their rising or setting, they signify the qualities of the seasons at certain stations. The first of the signs is the Bear <note>original: "Arcton"</note>, which is situated on the axis and rotates with seven stars revolved within itself. The name is Greek, which in Latin is called "Ursa" <note>the Bear</note>; because it turns in the manner of a wagon <note>plauſtri</note>, our people called it the "Seven Oxen" <note>Septentrionem</note>. For "triones" are properly the oxen of plowmen, so named because they "tread the earth" <note>terant terram</note>, as if they were "teriones." The proximity of the axis prevents the Seven Oxen from setting, because they are fixed in it. The "Bear-Watcher" <note>Arctophylax</note> is so named because he follows the Bear—that is, the "Helice" bear. They also call him "Bootes" <note>the Wagon-driver</note> because he clings to the wagon; it is a sign visible with many stars, among which is Arcturus. Arcturus is a star positioned after the tail of the Greater Bear, in the sign of Bootes; hence it is called Arcturus, as if it were <term>the tail of the bear <note>original: "ἄρκτου οὐρὰ"</note></term>, because it is placed near the heart of Bootes. It rises in the autumn. Orion shines another way before the tracks of the Bull <note>Taurus</note>; and Orion is named from "urina" <note>urine/moisture</note>, that is, from the inundation of waters. For rising in the winter time, he disturbs the sea and lands with waters and storms. The Latins call him "the Cut-throat" <note>iugula</note> because he is armed as if with a sword, and is terrible and most bright with the light of stars. If all these things shine in him, serenity is portended; if his sharpness is obscured, a storm is seen to be imminent. The Hyades are named <term>from raining <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν"</note></term>, that is, from moisture and rains. For rains in Greek are called <term>huetoi <note>original: "ὑετοὶ"</note></term>. Indeed, by their rising they produce rains; hence the Latins also called them "the Little Pigs" <note>original: "succulas," likely a folk etymology confusing 'hyein' (to rain) with 'hys' (pig)</note>, because when they are born, signs of rains are shown; of which Virgil says: "Arcturus and the rainy Hyades." They are seven in the forehead of the Bull and rise in the springtime. The Pleiades are named from plurality, because the Greeks call a multitude <term>pleioteta <note>original: "πλειότητα"</note></term>. They are seven stars before the knees of the Bull, of which six are visible; for one lies hidden. The Latins call these the "Vergiliae" from the significance of the season, because they rise in the Spring <note>original: "Ver"</note>. For by their setting they show winter, and by their rising summer, and the time for early navigation. The Dog Star <note>original: "Canicula"</note>, which is also called Sirius, is in the center of the sky in the summer months; and when the sun ascends to it, being joined with the sun, it doubles the heat and bodies are dissolved and exhausted. From this star, the "Dog Days" <note>dies caniculares</note> are named, when purgations are troublesome. It is called "the Dog" <note>Canis</note> because it affects bodies with disease, or because of the brightness of its flame.

<margin>Commentary 7</margin>
...so that it seems to shine above the rest. Thus, the more they knew it, they called it **Sirion** <note>original: "Syrion." This refers to Sirius, the Dog Star, known for its intense brightness.</note>. A **Comet** is so named because it spreads "hair" of light from itself <note>The word "comet" comes from the Greek *kometes*, meaning "long-haired."</note>. When this kind of star appears, it signifies either pestilence, famine, or war. In Latin, comets are called **crinite** <note>original: "crinitum," meaning "hairy."</note> because they spread flames like locks of hair. The Stoics say there are over thirty types of them, and certain astrologers have written down their names and their effects.

**Lucifer** <note>The "Light-Bringer," or the planet Venus as it appears in the morning.</note> is so named because it carries more light than all the other stars. It is one of the planets. This star is also properly called **Iubar** <note>A Latin term for a beaming light or radiance.</note> because it pours forth a radiance of light; the splendor of the sun, moon, and stars is also called *iubar* because their rays extend like a "jubar" <note>original: "iube." This is a play on words comparing light rays to a horse’s mane (*iuba*).</note>. 

**Vesperus** is the western star, which is said to be named after Vesper, a king of Spain. It is also one of the five wandering stars <note>planets</note>, leading the night and following the sun. It is said that this same star makes **Lucifer** when it rises and **Vesperum** when it sets. It depends on a single status and alternates at its rising.

**Planets** are stars that are not fixed in the sky like the others, but are carried through the air. They are called "planets" from the Greek word *planēs* <note>original: "από τῆσ πλανησ."</note>, which means "from wandering." For they are carried sometimes to the south, sometimes to the north, often against the world's motion, and sometimes with it. Their names are Greek: **Phaeton** <note>Jupiter</note>, **Phenon** <note>Saturn</note>, **Pyroeis** <note>Mars</note>, **Hesperus** <note>Venus</note>, and **Stilbon** <note>Mercury</note>. The Romans consecrated these with the names of their gods: Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. Deceived themselves and wishing to deceive others, they pointed out stars in the sky as a form of flattery to those who had provided them some benefit through love, saying that one star was Jupiter's and another Mercury's. Thus, this hollow opinion was born. The devil confirmed this erroneous opinion, and it spread through time.

Now, regarding those which are called **Signs** by the pagans, in which the images of living creatures are formed from the stars—such as the **Bear** <note>original: "Arcton."</note>, the **Ram**, the **Bull**, the **Scales**, and others of this sort. Those who first observed the stars fashioned the appearance of bodies into the number of stars with superstitious vanity, shaping the images and names based on the stories of their gods. 

For they called the first sign the **Ram** <note>Aries</note>—to which the central line of the world <note>the celestial equator</note> is assigned, as it is to the **Scales**—because of **Ammon**, whom they call Jupiter, because those who make statues fashion the horns of a ram on his head. The pagans established this sign as the first among the signs because they say the sun completes its course in that sign in the month of March, which is the beginning of the year. 

But they also placed the **Bull** <note>Taurus</note> among the stars in honor of Jupiter, because he was fabulously turned into a bull when he carried Europe across the sea. They also established **Castor** and **Pollux** after death among the most famous stars, which they call the sign of the **Twins** <note>Gemini</note>. 

They called the next sign the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note> because when the sun comes to that sign in the month of June, it moves backward in the manner of a crab and makes the days shorter. For this animal has an uncertain leading foot; it directs its step to either side so that its front part is its rear, and its rear is its front. 

**Hercules** killed a huge **Lion** <note>Leo</note> in Greece, and because of his courage, he placed it among the twelve signs. When the sun touches this sign, it gives excessive heat to the world and creates the annual **Etesian winds** <note>Strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow in summer.</note>. 

They also placed the sign of the **Virgin** <note>Virgo</note> among the stars precisely because in those same days when the sun runs through it, the earth, scorched by the sun's heat, bears nothing. For this is the time of the "Dog Days" <note>original: "canicularium dierum." The hottest days of summer.</note>.

<column-break/>

They called the **Scales** <note>Libra</note> such from the equality of the month itself, because on the 8th day before the Kalends of October <note>September 24th, roughly the Autumn Equinox</note>, the sun running through that sign makes the equinox. Hence Lucan says: "At the weights of the just scales." 

They named the **Scorpion** and the **Archer** <note>Sagittarius</note> because of the lightning of that month. The Archer is a man deformed with horse's legs, to whom they add an arrow and a bow, so that the lightning of that month is demonstrated by him. Hence he is called the "Archer." 

They fashioned the figure of **Capricorn** <note>the Goat-Horn</note> among the stars because of the goat that nursed Jupiter; they fashioned the rear part of its body into the likeness of a fish so that they might designate the rains of that month, which usually arrive at the end of the month. 

Furthermore, they named the **Water-Bearer** <note>Aquarius</note> and the **Fish** <note>Pisces</note> after the rainy seasons, because in winter, when the sun turns in these signs, greater rains pour down. 

And truly, the madness of the pagans is marvelous, for they transferred not only fish, but also rams, goats, bulls, bears, dogs, crabs, and scorpions into the sky. For they even placed the **Eagle** and the **Swan** among the stars of heaven for the sake of memory and because of the fables of Jupiter. They believed that **Perseus** and his wife **Andromeda**, after they died, were received into heaven, so they designated their images with stars and were not ashamed to call them by those names. 

They also placed **Erichthonius** the **Charioteer** <note>Auriga</note> among the stars of heaven because they had seen him as the first to yoke a four-horse chariot. For they marveled that his genius approached an imitation of the sun, and because of this, they placed his name among the stars after his death. 

Here **Callisto**, the daughter of King Lycaon, when she had been compressed by Jupiter and fabulously turned into the likeness of a bear by Juno—which is called *arcton* in Greek—after her killing, Jupiter transferred her name with her son into the northern stars; he called her **Arcton** <note>The Great Bear/Ursa Major</note> and called her son **Arctophylax** <note>The Bear-Watcher/Boötes</note>. 

Likewise, the **Lyre** was placed in heaven for Mercury, and the **Centaur Chiron** was numbered among the stars because he had nursed Aesculapius and Achilles. 

However these may be named by men in a superstitious way, they are nonetheless stars which God created at the beginning of the world and ordained to distinguish the times by a certain motion. Therefore, observations of these signs—whether horoscopes or other superstitious things that join themselves to the knowledge of fate and faith—that is, to the notice of our fate and faith—are without doubt contrary to our beliefs. They ought to be so ignored by Christians that they should not even seem to have been written. 

But some, seduced by the beauty and clarity of the stars, have fallen with blinded minds into the "fall of the stars," so that through harmful calculations, which is called **mathesis** <note>A term for astrology or the divination of fate through numbers.</note>, they strive to be able to foreknow the outcome of things. Not only the doctors of the Christian religion, but even the pagans Plato, Aristotle, and others, moved by the truth, condemned this with a concordant opinion, saying that a confusion of things is generated rather than any benefit from such persuasion. For if the human race were pressed by the necessity of birth toward various acts, why should the good deserve praise, or the evil receive the vengeance of the laws? 

And although they themselves were not dedicated to celestial wisdom, they rightly struck down these errors by the testimony of truth. Why then was this [path] of the **seven secular disciplines** <note>The Liberal Arts: Grammar, Rhetoric, Logic, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note> led by philosophers all the way to the stars? Specifically, so that it might lead minds entangled in secular wisdom away from earthly things and place them in heavenly contemplation.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book IV of the *Etymologies*. Having concluded his discussion of the heavens and the stars on the previous page, Isidore of Seville now turns his attention to the "earthly" science of medicine, tracing its origins, its primary schools of thought, and the biological theory of the four humors.</meta>

# Here begins the fourth book
# On Medicine, Chapter 1.

**M**edicine is that which either protects the body or restores health. Its subject matter is concerned with diseases and wounds. To this field, therefore, belong not only those things provided by the art of those properly named physicians, but also food and drink, regime and clothing; in short, every defense and fortification by which our healthy body is preserved against external blows and accidents.

## On its name, Chapter 2.

**T**he name "medicine" is thought to be derived from *modus* <note>original: "modo," meaning moderation or measure</note>, that is, from "temperament," so that it is applied not in excess, but little by little. For nature is distressed by much, but rejoices in a moderate amount. Hence, those who drink pigments and antidotes in excess or constantly are troubled by them. For all lack of moderation brings not health, but danger.

## On its inventors, Chapter 3.

**T**he author and discoverer of the medical art among the Greeks is said to be Apollo. His son, Aesculapius <note>original: "esculapius"</note>, expanded it with praise and help. But after Aesculapius perished by a lightning strike, the practice of healing was forbidden, and the art failed along with its author. It lay hidden for nearly five hundred years until the time of Artaxerxes, the King of the Persians. Then, Hippocrates, born of his father Asclepius on the island of Kos <note>original: "insula coo"</note>, recalled it to the light.

## On the three sects of physicians, Chapter 4.

**T**hese three men discovered as many "heresies" <note>In this context, *hereses* refers to schools of thought or sects rather than religious heresy.</note>. The first, the **Methodic** sect, was discovered by Apollo; it follows remedies and incantations. The second is the **Empiric**, that is, the "most experimental," discovered by Aesculapius; it relies not on signs or indications, but on experiments alone. The third is the **Logical**, that is, the "rational," discovered by Hippocrates. For he, having discussed the qualities of ages, regions, and illnesses, investigated the care of the art through reason. The Empirics follow experience alone; the Logics join reason to experience. The Methodics observe neither the reason of the elements, nor times, nor ages, nor causes; they consider only the substances of diseases.

## On the four humors of the body, Chapter 5.

**H**ealth is the integrity of the body and the temperament of nature consisting of heat and moisture, which is blood <note>original: "sanguis"</note>. From this, health (*sanitas*) is named, as if it were the "state of the blood" <note>original: "sanguinis status." This is a classic medieval folk etymology linking the word for health to the word for blood.</note>. Under the general term "diseases," all sufferings of the body are contained. The ancients did not name it "disease" (*morbus*) lightly, but so that by the very name they might demonstrate the power of death (*mors*) which is born from it. Between health and disease, however, there is "healing" <note>original: "curatio"</note>; unless it agrees with the disease, it does not lead to health. All diseases are born from the four humors: that is, from blood, bile <note>original: "felle," referring to yellow bile or choler</note>, melancholy <note>black bile</note>, and phlegm. For the healthy are ruled by these, and the sick are harmed by them. For when they have grown beyond the course of nature, they cause sickness. Just as there are four elements, so also there are four humors, and each humor imitates its own element: blood imitates air; choler imitates fire; melan-

<column-break/>

-choly imitates earth; phlegm imitates water. And there are four humors, just like the four elements, which preserve our bodies. **Blood** <note>original: "sanguis"</note> took its name from a Greek etymology because it is invigorated and sustained and lives. The Greeks called it **Choler** <note>original: "colera"</note> because it is limited to the space of a single day; hence it is also named *fellicula*, that is, an effusion of bile. For the Greeks call bile *cholen*. It is called **Melancholy** because it is an abundance of bile mixed with the dregs of black blood. For the Greeks call black *melan*, and they call bile *cholen*. In Latin, it is called **Blood** (*sanguis*) because it is "sweet" <note>original: "suauis"</note>; hence men in whom blood dominates are sweet and charming. They said **Phlegm**, however, because it is cold; for the Greeks call cold *phlegmone* <note>Isidore here confuses the Greek *phlegmon* (inflammation/burning) with the quality of phlegm, which he classifies as cold.</note>. From these four humors the healthy are ruled, and from them the sick are harmed. For when they have grown further outside the course of nature, they cause sickness. From blood and choler, "acute" sufferings are born, which the Greeks call *oxias*. From phlegm and melancholy, "old" causes proceed, which the Greeks call *cronia* <note>chronic</note>.

## On acute diseases, Chapter 6.

**O**xia is an acute disease which either passes quickly or kills swiftly, such as pleurisy or frenzy <note>original: "phrenesis"</note>. For *oxu* among the Greeks signifies both "sharp" and "fast." **Chronia** is a prolonged disease of the body, which lingers for many times, such as gout or consumption <note>original: "phthisis"</note>. For *chronon* among the Greeks is called "time." Some sufferings, however, have received their names from their own causes. **Fever** (*febris*) is named from "fervor" <note>heat</note>; for it is an abundance of heat. **Phrenesis** is named either from the impediment of the mind—because the Greeks call the mind *phrenas*—or because they gnash their teeth (*frendant*). For "to gnash" is to strike the teeth together. It is a perturbation with agitation and dementia caused by a choleric force. **Cardiac** <note>original: "cor"</note> took its name from the "heart" when it is affected by some fear or pain. For the Greeks call the heart *cardian*. It is a suffering of the heart with formidable fear. **Lethargy** is named from "sleep"; for it is an oppression of the brain with forgetfulness and constant sleep, like one snoring. **Synanche** <note>Quinsy or severe sore throat</note> is named from the containment of breath and suffocation. For the Greeks call "to contain" *synnechin*. For those who labor with this vice are suffocated by pain in the throat. **Phlegmon** <note>Inflammation</note> is a burning of the stomach with extension and pain. Phlegmon is restlessness with redness, pain, tension, hardness, and vastness. When it begins to happen, restlessness and fever follow; hence it is called *phlegmon* from *apo tu phlegon*, that is, "inflaming"; for so it is felt, and from there it took its name. **Pleurisy** is an acute pain of the side with fever and bloody spit. For the side in Greek is called *pleura*; hence the pleuritic suffering took its name. **Peripleumonia** <note>Pneumonia</note> is a defect of the lungs with vehement pain and sighing. For the Greeks call the lung *pleumon*; hence the sickness is named. **Apoplexy** is a sudden effusion of blood, by which they die suffocated. It is called apoplexy because a sudden fall happens from a lethal stroke. For the Greeks call a stroke *apoplerin*. A **Spasm** in Greek is a sudden "contraction" in Latin, of the parts or nerves with excessive pain. They said this suffering was named from the heart, because it holds the mastery of vigor in us. It happens in two ways: either from fullness...

<meta>This page continues Book IV of the *Etymologies*, moving from the general schools of medicine to the specific classification of diseases. The text follows Isidore’s method of defining ailments through the "etymological" origins of their names, often linking Latin terms to Greek roots to explain the nature of the affliction.</meta>

...or from exhaustion. **Tetanus** <note>original: "Titanus"</note> is a major contraction of the nerves from the neck to the back. **Pleurisy** <note>original: "Pleuris"</note> is a pain in the side. It is called this by physicians because the pain pierces the body as if by a sword <note>The Latin *transuerberet* suggests a striking or piercing through</note>. **Ileus** <note>original: "Ileos"</note> is a pain of the intestines, from which the "ilia" <note>the flanks or entrails</note> are named. In Greek, it is called *eileos* <note>original: ειλεός</note>, meaning "to wrap or twist," because the intestines wrap themselves up due to the pain. These sufferers are also called "torminosi" <note>afflicted with colic</note> because of the torments of the intestines. **Hydrophobia** is the fear of water; for the Greeks call water *hydor* <note>original: "hydor"</note> and they call fear *phobos* <note>original: "phobon"</note>. Hence the Latins also call this disease "lymphatic" <note>original: "lymphaticum," often associated with madness or water-spirits</note> because of the fear of water. It occurs either from the bite of a rabid dog or from the "foam of the air" cast upon the earth; if a person or beast touches this, they are filled with madness or turn to rage. **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus"</note> is so named because in its beginning it is red like fire, and afterwards it becomes black on the outside like coal <note>original: "carbo"</note>. **Pestilence** <note>original: "Pestilentia"</note> is a contagion which, when it catches hold of one, quickly passes to many. It begins from corrupted air and by penetrating into the internal organs. Although this often happens through the power of the air, it nevertheless does not happen at all without the will of Almighty God. It is called "pestilence" as if it were "pastulence" <note>original: "pastulentia"</note>, because it feeds upon <note>original: "depascat"</note> the body like a fire, and the plague descends through the whole body. The same is called a **contagion** <note>original: "contagium"</note> from "touching" <note>original: "contingendo"</note>, because it pollutes whoever it touches. It is also called **inguinaria** <note>buboes</note> from the striking of the groin. The same is called **lues** <note>pestilence/blight</note> from "ruin" <note>original: "labe"</note> and "grief" <note>original: "luctu"</note>; it is so acute that it leaves no space of time for either hope of life or the course of the disease; a sudden faintness comes along with death.

## On chronic diseases, Chapter 7.

**Chronic** <note>original: "Chronia"</note> is a long-lasting disease which lingers for many seasons, such as gout or consumption. For among the Greeks, time is called *chronos* <note>original: "Chronos"</note>. **Cephalea** <note>chronic headache</note> takes its name from its cause, for it is a suffering of the head, and the Greeks call the head *cephale* <note>original: "cephalin"</note>. **Scotothomia** <note>dizziness with darkness</note> takes its name from its symptom, because it brings sudden darkness <note>original: "tenebras"</note> to the eyes along with a turning of the head. **Vertigo** occurs whenever a wind arises and sends the earth into a circuit; likewise, in the crown of a person’s head, the arteries and veins produce a "windiness" and a loosened moisture, and they create a circling in the eyes. From this, it is named "vertigo." **Epilepsy** <note>original: "Epilepsia"</note> took its name because, by seizing the mind, it equally possesses the body. For the Greeks call "seizing" *epilepsis* <note>original: "epilepsin"</note>. It occurs from the melancholic humor whenever it becomes excessive and is turned toward the brain. This suffering is also called the **falling sickness** <note>original: "caduca"</note> because the sick person falls and suffers a spasm. The common people also call these people **lunatics** because the insanity of demons follows the course of the moon. The same is also called **laruatio** <note>haunting by "larvae" or ghosts</note>. It is also the **comitial disease** <note>original: "morbus comitialis"</note>, that is, the "greater and long-lasting" disease by which the "fallen" are held. Its force is so great that a healthy man collapses and foams. It is called **comitial** because among the pagans, whenever it happened to anyone on the day of the assembly <note>original: "comitiorum"</note>, the assemblies were dismissed. Among the Romans, the day of the assembly was a solemn day on the first of January. **Mania** is named from insanity or fury. For the ancient Greeks called fury *mania* <note>original: "manian"</note>, either from iniquity, which the Greeks call *mania*, or from divination, because "to divine" is called *manin* <note>original: "manin"</note> in Greek. **Melancholy** <note>original: "Melancholia"</note> is named from "black bile." For the Greeks call black *melan* <note>original: "melan"</note> and they call bile *chole* <note>original: "colen"</note>. **Epilepsy** occurs in the imagination, Melancholy in the reason, Ma-

<column-break/>

-nia in the memory. **Types** <note>original: "Typi"</note> are cold fevers which by custom were called "etypi" from a herb that grows in the water, which in Latin is called "form and statue" <note>original: "forma atque statuae"</note>. For it is a revolution of attacks and remissions through fixed intervals of time. **Rheum** <note>original: "Reuma"</note> is its Greek name; in Latin, it is called an "eruption" or a "flow." **Catarrh** <note>original: "Catarrus"</note> is a continuous flow of rheum from the nostrils; when it comes to the throat it is called **bronchios**, and when it comes to the chest or the lung it is called **phthisica**. **Coryza** occurs whenever an infusion of the head comes into the bones of the nose and causes a suffocation along with sneezing, from which it received the name *choriza*. **Bronchos** is a suffocation of the throat with cold humor. For the Greeks call the throat *branchos* <note>original: "branchos"</note>, around which are the passages that we corruptly call "branchiae" <note>gills</note>. **Raucedo** <note>hoarseness</note> is a breaking of the voice. This is also called **arteriasis** because it renders the voice hoarse and closed off due to injury of the arteries <note>Isidore often conflates the windpipe with arteries</note>. **Sospirium** <note>sighing/difficulty breathing</note> took its name because it is a difficulty of breathing, which the Greeks call *dyspnoia* <note>original: "dyspnian"</note>, that is, suffocation. **Pneumonia** <note>original: "Peripleumonia"</note> took its name from the lung <note>Greek *pleumon*</note>. For it is a swelling of the lung with an outpouring of bloody foam. **Haemoptysis** <note>original: "Emproicis"</note> is an emission of blood, from which it took its name; for blood is called *haema* <note>original: "hema"</note>. **Phthisis** is an ulceration and swelling in the lungs which tends to happen more easily in young people. **Phthisis** among the Greeks is so named because it becomes a consumption of the whole body. **Cough** <note>original: "Tussis"</note> is named in Greek from "depth" <note>original: "altitudine"</note> because it comes from deep in the chest. Its opposite is that which is higher in the throat where the path trickles down. **Abscess** <note>original: "Apostema"</note> took its name from a "collection." For the Greeks call collections *apostomas*. **Empyema** <note>original: "Empis"</note> is named from an internal abscess, either in the side or in the stomach, with pain, fevers, cough, and abundant bloody and purulent foam. **Hepatic** <note>original: "Eparicus"</note> disease took its name from a suffering of the liver. For the Greeks call the liver *hepar* <note>original: ηπαρ</note>. **Lienosis** <note>spleen disease</note> took its name from the spleen. For the Greeks call the spleen *lien*. **Dropsy** <note>original: "Hydropsis"</note> took its name from the watery humor of the skin. For the Greeks called water *hydor*. For it is a humor under the skin with a swelling inflation and a stinking breath. **Nephritis** <note>original: "Nephresis"</note> took its name from a weakness of the kidneys; for the Greeks call the kidneys *nephros* <note>original: "nephresis"</note>. **Paralysis** is named from a "loosening" of the body caused by much chilling, either in the whole body or in part. **Cachexia** <note>original: "Laceria"</note> took its name from an injury of the body. For the Greeks called a "bad torment" *laceria*. This suffering occurs from the intemperance of the sick person, or bad treatment by medicine, or a slow recovery after illness. **Atrophy** <note>original: "Atrophia"</note> took its name from a wasting of the body. For the Greeks call a cessation of nourishment *atrophia*. For it is a thinness of the body from hidden causes gradually worsening. **Sarcoma** <note>original: "Sarcian"</note> is a superfluous increase of flesh by which they fatten the body beyond measure. For the Greeks call flesh *sarx* <note>original: "sarca"</note>. **Sciatica** <note>original: "Ischiasis"</note> is named from the part of the body that it torments. For the Greeks call the hip bones, the tops of which end at the beginning of the flanks, *ischia*. It occurs from phlegm whenever it descends into the hip bones and creates a "gluing" there. **Gout** <note>original: "Podagra"</note> the Greeks say is named from a "retention of the feet" and from a deadly pain. Indeed, everything that is in the field is loosely called "wild" <note>the text cuts off here, likely beginning a comparison to the pain's ferocity</note>.

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s Book IV of the *Etymologies*, specifically focusing on the naming and nature of various diseases. Having discussed internal ailments on the previous page, he now transitions from digestive and intestinal issues to skin conditions and the general principles of medical treatment.</meta>

we call them. **Arthritis** <note>original: "Artericus morb'"; likely referring to gout or joint pain</note> takes its name from the suffering of the joints. A **Calculus** <note>original: "Calculus"</note> is a stone that forms in the bladder, from which it also received its name. It signifies a condition arising from phlegmatic matter. **Strangury** <note>original: "Stranguria"</note> is so named because it "strains" or restricts the passage of urine. **Satyriasis** <note>original: "Satyriasis"</note> is a constant sexual desire accompanied by the erection of the private parts; this suffering is named after the mythological satyrs. **Diarrhea** <note>original: "Diarria"</note> is a constant flow of the bowels without vomiting. **Dysentery** <note>original: "Dysenteria"</note> is a "division of continuity," which is to say, an ulceration of the intestine. For *dys* means "division" and *entera* means "intestines." It occurs following a flux, which the Greeks call diarrhea. **Lientery** <note>original: "Lyenteria"</note> is so called because it makes food slip through as if along the "line" <note>original: "lineam"</note> of the intestine with nothing obstructing it. **Colic** <note>original: "Colica"</note> takes its name from the intestine which the Greeks call the *colon*. **Rhagades** <note>original: "Ragadię"</note> are so called because they are fissures gathered in the folds around the orifice; these and **hemorrhoids** <note>original: "hemorroide"</note> are named from the flow of blood. For the Greeks call blood *haima* <note>original: "hemą"</note>.

### On diseases which are seen on the surface of the skin. Chapter 8.

**Alopecia** is a shedding of the hair, marked by the thinning of reddish hairs that have a sharp or biting quality; it is called by this name because of its similarity to the animal, the little fox, which the Greeks call *alopex*. **Parotids** <note>original: "Parotidę"</note> are hard swellings or collections that arise from fevers or some other cause in the vicinity of the ears; hence they are named parotids. For in Greek, the ears are called *ota*. **Lentigo** <note>freckles</note> is a trace of small spots formed in a round shape, named after the appearance of a lentil <note>original: "lenticula"</note>. **Erysipelas** <note>original: "Hierisipira"</note> is what the Latins call "sacred fire" <note>original: "sacrum ignem"</note>, which is to say, "accursed," using the figure of speech called antiphrasis <note>a rhetorical device where a word is used to mean its opposite</note>. Indeed, the skin turns red on the surface with a flaming redness. Once this redness is stirred, it invades neighboring areas as if from a fire, so much so that even a fever is excited. **Serpedo** <note>a creeping skin eruption</note> is a redness of the skin with the emergence of pustules, and it took its name from "creeping" <note>original: "serpendo"</note>, because it creeps through the limbs. **Impetigo** is a dry scab, protruding from the body with roughness and a round shape; the common people call this *sarna*. **Prurigo** <note>itching</note> is named from "burning through" <note>original: "perurendo"</note> and glowing. **Nyctalopia** <note>original: "Nyctalmus"</note> is an affliction by which vision is denied during the day while the eyes are open, and returns as the shadows of night rush in; or conversely, as many hold, it returns by day and is denied at night. **Warts** <note>original: "Verrucę"</note> are one thing; **phthiriasis** <note>infestation of lice, or a similar skin condition</note> is another. Warts appear individually, whereas in phthiriasis, one is stronger and many more are found around it. **Scabies** and **leprosy** are both conditions where the skin is rough with itching and scaling. **Scabies** is a thin roughness and scaling; it finally received its name from this: it casts off impurities like "shavings." For *scabies* is as if it were *squamies* <note>from "squama," meaning scale</note>. **Leprosy** is a scaly roughness of the skin similar to the *lepida* herb, from which it took its name. Its color sometimes turns to blackness, sometimes to whiteness, sometimes to redness. In the human body, leprosy is identified if a different color appears variably among healthy parts of the skin, or if it spreads everywhere so as to make everything a single, though corrupted, color. **Elephantiasis** <note>original: "Elephantiac' moꝛb'"</note> is named from its similarity to the elephant, whose skin is naturally hard and rough; the name was given to the disease in humans because it makes the surface of the body similar to the hide of elephants, or because it is a "huge" suffering, just like the animal itself from which the name is derived. The Greeks call **Jaundice** *icterus* <note>original: "Icteris"</note> from the name of a certain animal that is the color of bile. The Latins call this disease

<column-break/>

**the rainbow disease** <note>original: "arcuatũ"</note> from its similarity to the heavenly bow. Varro says it is called *aurigo* because of the color of gold <note>original: "auri"</note>. They think it is called the **Royal Disease** <note>original: "Regiũ moꝛbũ"</note> because it is more easily cured with good wine and royal foods. **Cancer** is a wound named from its similarity to the sea animal; as physicians say, it is curable by no medicines. Therefore, the limb where it is born is usually cut away from the body so that the person may live a little longer, though death will eventually arrive from it, however slowly. A **stye** <note>original: "Hoꝛdeolus"</note> is a very small and pus-filled collection situated among the hairs of the eyelids; it is wide in the middle and tapered at both ends, resembling a grain of barley <note>original: "hoꝛdei"</note>, from which it took its name. A **boil** <note>original: "Furunculus"</note> is a swelling rising to a point, so called because it "glows" <note>original: "ferveat"</note>, as if it were a "little glowing thing" <note>original: "fervunculus"</note>. Hence in Greek it is called *anthrax*, because it is fiery. **Oscedo** is that by which the mouths of infants are ulcerated, named from the weariness of those who yawn <note>original: "oscitantiũ"</note>. **Frenusculi** are ulcers around the opening of the mouth, similar to those that occur in pack animals from the roughness of their bridles <note>original: "frenoꝝ"</note>. An **ulcer** <note>original: "Ulcus"</note> is the rot itself. A **wound** <note>original: "vulnus"</note> is what is made by iron, as if by "force" <note>original: "vi"</note>; and an ulcer is that which hurts <note>original: "dolet"</note> like an ulcer; hence they are called ulcers. A **pustule** is a swelling collection on the surface of the body. A **papule** is a very small elevation of the skin, localized and accompanied by redness; and it is called a papule as if it were a "little nipple" <note>original: "pupula"</note>. **Sanies** <note>discharge or ichor</note> is so called because it is born from blood <note>original: "sanguine"</note>; for when the color of a wound is provoked, the blood turns into discharge. For discharge does not form in any place except where blood has arrived; because everything that rots must be warm and moist—which is what blood is—otherwise it cannot rot. However, *sanies* and *tabes* <note>putrefaction or wasting</note> differ from each other: *sanies* flows from the living, while *tabes* flows from the dead. A **scar** <note>original: "Cicatrix"</note> is the covering of a wound, preserving the natural color in those parts; it is so named because it "covers over" <note>original: "obducat"</note> wounds and "blinds" <note>original: "obcęcat"</note> them.

### On remedies and medications. Chapter 9.

The care of medicine is not to be despised. For we read that the prophet Isaiah sent something medicinal to the ailing Hezekiah, and the apostle Paul said that a little wine was beneficial to Timothy. The cure of diseases consists of three kinds: **Pharmacy** <note>original: "Pharmatia"</note>, which the Latins call "medications"; **Surgery** <note>original: "chirurgia"</note>, which the Latins call "operation of the hands," for among the Greeks the hand is called *cheir*; and **Dietetics** <note>original: "dicta," though usually "dieta"</note>, which the Latins call "regulation," for it is the observation of law and life. There are three types of all healing. The first type is dietetic, the second pharmaceutical, the third surgical. **Diet** is the observation of law and life. **Pharmacy** is the cure by medications. **Surgery** is incision with iron tools. For those things that do not respond to the medicine of drugs are cut out with iron. In ancient times, medicine consisted only of herbs and juices. Such was the practice of healing in the beginning; afterward came iron and other medications. All healing is applied either from **contraries** or from **similars**. From contraries: such as cold for hot, or dry for moist; just as in a man, pride cannot be healed unless it is cured by humility. From similars: just as a bandage <note>original: "ligamentũ"</note> is applied, a round one to a round wound, or an oblong one to an oblong wound. For the binding itself is not the same for all limbs and wounds, but like is fitted to like; these two aids are even signified by their names. For in Greek, an **antidote** <note>original: "antidotũ"</note>...

<meta>This page continues Book IV of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies. On the previous page, Isidore concluded his descriptions of specific skin diseases and physical ailments. Here, he moves into the terminology of pharmacology, medical tools, and the philosophical placement of medicine among the liberal arts.</meta>

...is said in Latin, and the contrary is given. For contraries are cured by the method of medicine with contraries. But on the other hand, also by similars, such as **Picra** <note>original: "picra"; from the Greek for "bitter"</note>, which is interpreted as "bitter," because its taste is bitter. And it received a fitting name, because the bitterness of a disease is usually dissolved by bitterness. But medicines called **Dia-** <note>original: "Dia"; a Greek prefix meaning "through" or "by means of," used to name compound medicines</note> have names from their specific causes. For **Hiera** <note>original: "Hiera"; Greek for "sacred" or "divine"</note> is so called as if divine. **Arteriaca** <note>throat medicines</note> are so called because they are suitable for the passages of the throat, and they soothe swellings of the throat and the windpipes <note>original: "arteriarum"</note>. **Theriac** <note>original: "Tiriaca"; a famous ancient panacea or antidote</note> is a snake-antidote by which poisons are driven out, so that a plague may be dissolved by a plague. **Cathartics** <note>original: "Cathartica"</note> are called in Greek what in Latin are called **purgatives**. **Catapodia** <note>pills</note> are so called because a small amount is drunk or swallowed. **Diamoron** <note>syrup of mulberries</note> took its name from the juice of the mulberry <note>original: "mōre"</note> from which it is made, just as **diacodion** <note>syrup of poppies</note> is so named because it is made from *codia*, that is, from the poppy; just as **diaspsmaton** <note>a medicine made of seeds</note> is so called because it is composed of seeds. It is called an **electuary** <note>original: "Electuariū"; a paste-like medicine</note> because it is swallowed soft. It is called a **trochiscus** <note>a medicinal lozenge or pastille</note> because it is shaped in the manner of a small wheel. For in Greek, a wheel is called *trochos*. **Collyria** <note>eye salves</note> sound in Latin like things that "cleanse the defects of the eyes." **Epithemata** <note>poultices or compresses</note> are so called because they are placed upon other preceding aids. A **cataplasm** <note>original: "Cataplasma"</note> is so called because it is an induction alone. An **emplastrum** <note>plaster</note> because it is "induced" or spread on. A **malagma** <note>emollient</note> is so called because it is softened and kneaded without fire. **Enema** <note>original: "Anema"</note> is called "relaxation" in Greek and Latin. **Pessaries** <note>original: "Pessaria"</note> are so named because they are injected within. A certain Greek named Chiron discovered the medicine for beasts of burden; hence he is depicted as half man, half horse. He is called Chiron from the word for **surgery** <note>original: "apo tēs cheirourgias"</note>, because he was called a surgeon. Doctors call certain days **Critical days**; I believe the name was given to these as a sign of the illness, because they judge the person and by their sentence either punish or liberate them.

### On medical books. Chapter 10.

<margin>a doctor must know the past, know the present, and foresee the future</margin>
An **Aphorism** <note>original: "Aphorismus"</note> is a brief discourse, writing out the complete sense of the proposed matter. **Prognostics** <note>original: "Prognostica"</note> are the foreknowledge of sicknesses, named from "knowing beforehand." For it is necessary for a doctor to recognize the past, know the present, and foresee the future. **Dynamidia** <note>original: "Dynamidia"</note> is the power of herbs, that is, their force and possibility. For in the treatment using herbs, the force itself is called *dynamis* <note>Greek for "power"</note>. From this, the books where their medicines are written are called *dynamidia*. A **Botanical** <note>original: "Botanicum"</note> book is so called because herbs are noted there.

### On medical instruments. Chapter 11.

An **Enchiridion** <note>a handbook or manual of tools</note> is so called because it is grasped by the hand, while it contains very many iron tools. For in Greek, the hand is called *chir*. The **phlebotome** <note>a lancet used for bloodletting</note> is named from "incision." For in Greek, an incision is called *tome*. Similar tools include the **angistrum** <note>a hook</note>, the **spatomele** <note>a probe or spatula</note>, and the **guuia** <note>a lancet or small knife</note> which are called **cupping glasses** <note>original: "cucurbite"; literally "gourds"</note> by the Latins from their similarity to a gourd, or **ventosa** <note>from *ventus*, "wind"</note> from their suction. Finally, animated by spirit through a small fire, and then placed upon the cut body, they draw to the surface everything that seethes between the skin or deeper, whether it be called humor or blood. A **clyster** <note>original: "Clistere"</note> is the instrument through which an enema is injected. A **mortar** <note>original: "Pila"</note> is named from the "pounding" of seeds, that is, their grinding. From this also come **pigments** <note>original: "pigmēta"; here used to mean medicinal drugs or spices</note>, because they are processed in the mortar and pestle, as if they were "pounded pigments." For a mortar is a concave vessel suitable for use by doctors, in which a thing is especially made flat and pigments are usually cut small. But Varro reports that there was a certain **Pilumnus** in Italy who presided over the pounding of fields <note>the grinding of grain</note>, from whom come the names of the "Pilumni" and "Pistores" <note>bakers or pounders</note>.

<column-break/>

From him, therefore, the pestle <note>original: "pilū"</note> and mortar <note>original: "pila"</note> were invented by which grain is pounded, and they are so called from his name. But the **pestle** is that by which whatever is put into the mortar is crushed. A **Mortarium** <note>grinding bowl</note> is so called because there the seeds, already reduced to powder and "dead" <note>original: "mortua"</note>, are seasoned. A **Liticula** <note>a smooth stone or tile</note> is that in which eye-salves are dissolved by being moved around; for it must be smooth. For a rough surface causes the eye-salve to be broken rather than dissolved.

### On odors and ointments. Chapter 12.

**Odor** is named from the air <note>original: "acre"</note>. It is called **Thymiana** in the Greek language because it is fragrant. For **Thyme** <note>original: "Thymio"</note> is a flower which gives off a scent, of which Virgil says: "and the fragrant honey smells of thyme." **Incense** <note>original: "Incensum"</note> is so called because it is consumed by fire while it is offered. **Tetraidos** <note>original: "Tetraidos"</note> are forms of incense stretched out in length, which are made from four pigments. For in Greek, four is *tetra*, and *idos* means form. **Stacte** <note>original: "Stacte"</note> is incense that flows from a pressing, called by the Greeks from the word "to flow" <note>original: "apo tou stazein"</note>, which is to flow or distill. **Myrobalanum** <note>ben nut</note> is so called because it is made from a fragrant nut. Of which Horace says: "and the nut <note>original: "balanus"</note> pressed for your hair." **Oil** <note>original: "Oleum"</note> is pure and mixed with nothing. But an **ointment** <note>original: "Unguentū"</note> is everything that is made from common oil and is enhanced by the mixture of other species, taking on a pleasant scent and smelling from further away. But certain ointments are named after places, such as **Telinum**, which Julius Caesar mentions saying: "And we are anointed in body with sweet Telinum." This was prepared on the island of Telos, which is one of the Cyclades. There are also some named from the name of their inventors, such as **Amaracinum**. For some report that a certain royal boy named **Amaracus**, carrying several kinds of ointments, accidentally slipped and created a greater scent from the mixture; from which now the best ointments are called *amaracina*. They are, however, from the genus of flowers. Likewise, others are named from the quality of their material, such as **rose oil** <note>original: "rosaceum"</note> from the rose, and **cyprinum** from the flower of the cypress, which accordingly represent the scent of their own material. Of these, some are simple ointments which consist of only one species, from which they reflect the scent of their name, such as **dill oil** <note>original: "anetinū"</note>; for it is pure, made from oil and dill alone. But others are **compounds**, which are made from many things mixed in, from which they do not have the scent of their own name; because, with the others that are mixed in prevailing, they produce an uncertain scent, such as *cerotum*, *calcasticum*, and *marciacum*.

### On the beginning of medicine. Chapter 13.

It is asked by some why the art of medicine is not included among the other **liberal disciplines** <note>the seven liberal arts: Grammar, Rhetoric, Logic, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy</note>. This is because those disciplines contain single causes, but this one contains them all. For a doctor is commanded to know **Grammar**, so that he can understand or explain what he reads; likewise **Rhetoric**, so that he may be able to define with true arguments the things he treats; and also **Dialectic** <note>logic</note> for the purpose of scrutinizing and curing the causes of illnesses with reason applied. So too **Arithmetic**, on account of the number of hours in the onset of fevers and the periods of days. No less **Geometry**, on account of the qualities of regions and the locations of places, in which he may teach what each person ought to observe. Furthermore, **Music** will not be unknown to him. For there are many things which are read as having been done for sick men through this discipline, just as it is read concerning David:

...who, by the skill of his music, rescued Saul from an unclean spirit. The physician Asclepiades also restored a certain madman to his former health through a symphony <note>original: "symphonia"; referring to harmonious music</note>. Finally, the physician will also have a knowledge of astronomy, through which he contemplates the calculation of the stars and the changes of the seasons. For as a certain one of the physicians says: our bodies also change according to their qualities. From this it is said that medicine is a "second philosophy." For both disciplines claim the whole man for themselves: just as the soul is cured by the former, so the body is cured by the latter.

### Here begins the fifth book
### On the authors of laws Chapter I.

Moses, of the Hebrew race, was the first of all to explain the divine laws in sacred writings. King Phoroneus was the first to establish laws and judgments for the Greeks. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trimegistus"</note> first delivered laws to the Egyptians. Solon first gave laws to the Athenians. Lycurgus first fashioned the rights of laws for the Spartans <note>original: "lacedęmonijs"</note> by the authority of Apollo. Numa Pompilius, who succeeded Romulus in the kingdom, first issued laws to the Romans. Later, when the people could no longer endure seditious magistrates, they created the **Decemvirs** <note>a commission of ten men</note> to write down the laws; these men translated laws from the books of Solon into the Latin language and set them forth on the **Twelve Tables**. These men were Appius Claudius, L. Genutius, P. Sestius, L. Veturius, C. Julius, A. Manlius, P. Sulpicius, P. Curiatius, T. Romulius, and Sp. Postumius. These ten men were chosen for the drafting of the laws. Furthermore, the consul Pompey first wished to compile the laws into books, but he did not persevere for fear of detractors. Then Caesar began to do it, but he was killed before he finished. Gradually, however, the ancient laws faded away through old age and neglect; although they are no longer in use, a knowledge of them still seems necessary. New laws began with Constantine Caesar and the others who succeeded him, and they were mixed and disordered. Afterward, the younger Augustus Theodosius, following the likeness of the Gregorian and Hermogenian codes, arranged a code of constitutions from the times of Constantine under the specific title of each emperor, which he called "Theodosian" after his own name.

### On divine and human laws Chapter II.

All laws are either divine or human. Divine laws consist of nature, human laws of customs; and therefore these differ, since different things please different nations. **Divine right** <note>original: "Fas"</note> is divine law; **Human right** <note>original: "ius"</note> is human law. To cross through another's field is a divine right, but it is not a human right <note>meaning it may be naturally permissible but legally prohibited by property laws</note>.

### How rights, laws, and customs differ from each other Chapter III.

"Right" <note>original: "Ius"</note> is a general name. "Law" <note>original: "Lex"</note>, however, is a species of right. It is called "Right" <note>ius</note> because it is just <note>original: "iustum"</note>. All right consists of laws and customs. Law is a written constitution. Custom <note>original: "Mos"</note> is usage approved by antiquity, or an unwritten law. For "Law" <note>lex</note> is named from "reading" <note>original: "legendo"</note> because it is written. "Custom" <note>mos</note> is a long-standing usage, drawn only from manners. "Usage" <note>original: "Consuetudo"</note> is a certain right established by manners, which is accepted as law when law is lacking; nor does it matter whether it exists in writing or in reason, since reason also commends law. Furthermore, if law consists of reason, everything that reason has established will be law—provided that it is congruent with religion, convenient for discipline, and beneficial for health. It is called "usage" <note>consuetudo</note> because it is in common use.

<column-break/>

### What natural law is Chapter IIII.

Law is either natural, or civil, or of nations. Natural law <note>original: "Ius naturale"</note> is common to all nations, because it is held everywhere by the instinct of nature rather than by any specific constitution: such as the union of man and woman, the succession and education of children, the common possession of all things, and the one liberty of all; and the acquisition of those things which are taken from the sky, the earth, and the sea. Likewise, the restitution of a thing deposited or money entrusted, and the repelling of violence by force. For this, or anything similar to this, is never considered unjust but natural and equitable.

### What civil law is Chapter V.

Civil law <note>original: "Ius ciuile"</note> is that which each people or each city has established as its own for human and divine reasons.

### What the law of nations is Chapter VI.

The law of nations <note>original: "Ius gentium"</note> involves the occupation of sites, building, fortification, wars, captivities, enslavements, the right of return <note>original: "postliminia"</note>, treaties of peace, truces, the religious obligation not to violate ambassadors, and the prohibition of marriage between foreigners. It is called the "law of nations" because almost all nations use this law.

### What military law is Chapter VII.

Military law <note>original: "Ius militare"</note> involves the solemnity of declaring war, the binding of a treaty, the signal given to join battle against the enemy or to engage; likewise, the signal for retreat; also, military discipline regarding offenses, such as if a post is deserted; also, the measure of pay, the grades of rank, the honor of rewards (such as when a crown or a collar is given); likewise, the determination of booty and its just division according to the quality and labors of the persons, and the portion for the prince.

### What public law is Chapter VIII.

Public law <note>original: "Ius publicum"</note> consists in sacred matters, in priests, and in magistrates.

### What the law of the Quirites is Chapter IX.

The law of the Quirites <note>original: "Ius quiritum"</note> belongs properly to the Romans; no one holds it except the Quirites, that is, the Romans. This concerns matters like legitimate inheritances, formal declarations <note>original: "cretionibus"</note>, guardianships, and acquisition by long use <note>original: "usucapionibus"</note>; these laws are found among no other people, but are property of the Romans and established for them alone. The law of the Quirites consists of statutes, plebiscites, constitutions of princes, and edicts or the responses of the wise.

### What law is Chapter X.

A law <note>original: "Lex"</note> is a constitution of the people, by which the elders, together with the commoners, have sanctioned something.

### What plebiscites are Chapter XI.

Plebiscites <note>original: "Scita plebium"</note> are what the commoners <note>plebs</note> alone establish; they are called "scita" <note>decrees</note> because the common people know <note>sciat</note> them, or because they are decreed <note>sciscitatur</note> and requested to be done.

<meta>This page continues Book V (On Laws and Times), moving from the history of lawgivers to definitions of different types of legal decrees and the specific requirements for wills and witnesses.</meta>

# Book V

#### Column 1

### What a decree of the senate is. Chapter XII.
A decree of the senate <note>original: "Senatus consultum"</note> is that which the senators alone decree for the purpose of consulting the interests of the people.

### What a constitution and an edict are. Chapter XIII.
A constitution or an edict is what a king or an emperor establishes or proclaims.

### What the responses of the wise are. Chapter XIV.
Responses are those things which legal experts are said to answer to those consulting them. From this, the "Responses of Paul" <note>referring to Julius Paulus Prudentissimus, a famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> are named. For there were certain wise men and judges of equity who published composed "civil institutions of law," by which they might soothe the lawsuits and contentions of those in disagreement.

### On consular and tribunitian laws. Chapter XV.
Certain laws are also named after those who established them, such as consular, tribunitian, Julian, or Cornelian laws. For under Octavian Caesar, the replacement <note>original: "suffecti"</note> consuls Papius and Poppaeus <note>OCR reads "pompeius"; historically Papius and Poppaeus</note> passed a law which is called the Papia-Poppaean law after their names; it contains rewards for fathers for raising children. Under the same emperor, Falcidius, a tribune of the plebs, made a law that no one should leave more to strangers in a will than would allow a fourth part to remain for the heirs; from his name, it was called the Falcidian law. Aquilius also established a law which is still called the Aquilian law <note>concerning compensation for damage to property</note>.

### On the "saturate" law. Chapter XVI.
<margin>See Book 2, chapter 3</margin>
A "saturate" law <note>original: "Satyra lex"; a law containing many distinct provisions</note> is one that speaks of many matters at the same time, named for its "fullness" of things and, as it were, from a "satiety" <note>original: "satietate"; being full or satisfied</note>. From this also, "to write satire" is to compose various poems, such as those of Horace, Juvenal, and Persius.

### On the Rhodian laws. Chapter XVII.
Today, the laws of naval commerce are named after the island of Rhodes, in which the practice of merchants existed in ancient times.

### On privileges. Chapter XVIII.
Privileges are the laws of private individuals, as if they were "private laws" <note>original: "privatae leges"</note>. For "privilege" is so named because it is applied to a private person.

### What a law is able to do. Chapter XIX.
Every law either permits something—such as allowing a brave man to seek a reward; or forbids—such as that no one may seek marriage with sacred virgins; or punishes—such as that he who commits a murder should be struck by the capital sentence <note>original: "capite plectat"; beheaded or lose civil status</note>. For human life is moderated by the reward or the punishment of the law.

### Why law was made. Chapter XX.
Laws were made so that human audacity might be restrained by fear of them, and that innocence might be safe among the wicked, and so that the power of doing harm might be bridled in the wicked themselves by the dread of punishment.

### What kind of law should be made. Chapter XXI.
A law shall be honorable, just, possible, according to nature, according to the custom of the country, suitable to the place and time, necessary, useful, and clear, lest it contain anything through obscurity that might lead to a snare; it should be written for no private advantage, but for the common utility of the citizens.

### On causes. Chapter XXII.

<column-break/>

#### Column 2

*Pragma* is Greek for what in Latin is called a "cause" <note>original: "causa"; a legal case or matter</note>. From this, "pragmatic businesses" are named, and a pleader of causes and businesses is called a "pragmatic."

### On witnesses. Chapter XXIII.
Witnesses <note>original: "Testes"</note> are those from whom the truth is sought in a judgment. Every person binds these to himself by agreements before a judgment, so that it is not afterwards free for anyone to either ignore the matter or withdraw themselves; from this they are called "the bound" <note>original: "alligati"</note>. Likewise, they are called witnesses because they are usually present at a will <note>original: "testamento"</note>, just as the signers who seal a will.

### On legal instruments. Chapter XXIV.
"Will" <note>original: "Voluntas"</note> is the general name for all legal instruments; because it proceeds not from force but from the "will," it received such a name. A testament <note>original: "Testamentum"</note> is so called because unless the testator has died, it can neither be confirmed nor can it be known what is written in it, because it is closed and sealed. And "testament" is so called from this: that it is not valid except after the "monument" <note>original: "monumentum"; a pun on "testa-mentum"</note> of the testator. Whence also the Apostle says: "A testament is confirmed among the dead" <note>Hebrews 9:17</note>. Certainly in the Holy Scriptures, "testament" does not only mean this—that which is not valid unless the testators are dead—but they called every pact and agreement a "testament." For Laban and Jacob made a testament, which certainly would also be valid between the living. And it is read in the Psalms: "They have arranged a testament against you" <note>Psalm 83:5</note>, that is, a pact; and there are innumerable such examples. "Tablets of the testament" <note>original: "Tabulae testamenti"</note> are so named because before the use of paper <note>original: "chartae"</note> and parchment, they wrote not only testaments but also correspondence on planed wooden tablets. Whence also the carriers of them were called "tablet-bearers" <note>original: "tabellarii"; messengers</note>. A testament of "civil law" is confirmed by the marks of five witnesses with a subscription. A testament of "praetorian law" is confirmed by the marks of seven witnesses; but the former is done among citizens (hence "civil"), the latter before praetors (hence "praetorian law"). To "seal" a testament is to mark it, that is, so that it may be known what is written. A "holograph" testament is one written entirely by the hand of the author and signed; whence it also received its name. For the Greeks call "whole" *holon* and "writing" *graphin*. An "invalid" <note>original: "Irritum"</note> testament is if he who made the will has suffered a "loss of status" <note>original: "capite diminutus"; loss of liberty, citizenship, or family rights</note>, or if it was not properly made. An "undutiful" <note>original: "Inofficiosum"</note> testament is one in which children are frustrated by being disinherited without the duty of natural piety, and the estate is reduced to outside persons. A "broken" <note>original: "Ruptum"</note> testament is so called because it is broken by the birth of a posthumous child <note>a child born after the father's death</note> who was neither specifically disinherited nor appointed as an heir. A "suppressed" testament is one which is not openly brought forward, in fraud of the heirs, legatees, or freedmen; even if it is not hidden, if it is not produced for the aforementioned persons, it is still seen to be suppressed. A "nuncupation" <note>original: "Nuncupatio"</note> is that which the testator recites from the tablets and wax, saying: "As these things are written in these tablets and wax, so I say, so I bequeath, and so you, Roman citizens, bear witness for me"; and this is called a "nuncupation." For to "nuncupate" is to name and confirm in public. The "right of children" is a mutual alternate writing for the place of a pledge of inheritance between spouses without children. Finally, the ancients say a "codicil" <note>original: "Codicellum"</note> is undoubtedly named after the author who established this type of writing.
