<meta>This page continues Book V, moving from the specific historical laws (like the Falcidian law) to the definitions of legal instruments such as codicils, contracts, and the nature of property rights. Isidore focuses heavily on etymology to explain the "spirit" of the law.</meta>

# V
<sig>c 4</sig>

#### Column 1

A codicil is a writing that requires no solemnity of words; it is held only by the will of the testator, expressed in any form of writing. This benefit was established to assist the wishes of the deceased, either because of the difficulty of legal terminology or the necessity of providing solemn rituals. Thus, the person who writes the title of such a document calls it a codicil. Just as a codicil serves in place of a will, so a letter serves in place of codicils.

<term>Cretio</term> <note>original: "Cretio"</note> is a certain number of days during which an appointed heir either enters upon the inheritance or is excluded once the time for *cretio* has ended; beyond that, he is no longer free to take the inheritance. It is called *cretio* as if it were a <term>decretio</term> <note>original: "decretio"; a deciding or decreeing</note>—that is, to decide or establish. For example: "Let that man be my heir," and he adds, "and let him decide <note>original: "cernito"</note> within so many days." For entering inheritances where no *cretio* was added, a period of one hundred days was established.

A <term>trust</term> <note>original: "Fideicommissum"</note> is so called so that what is committed by the deceased may be carried out. For "faith" <note>original: "fides"</note> is so named because what is said should be done; however, it requests money not through direct words <note>i.e., it was a request based on trust rather than a strict legal command</note>.

An agreement <note>original: "Pactum"</note> is said to be a coming together between parties out of peace, a writing approved by laws and customs; it is called a "pact" as if made out of "peace" <note>original: "pax"</note>, from the word *pango* <note>to fasten or fix</note>, from which "he struck a treaty" <note>original: "pepigit foedus"</note> is derived. A "pleasure" <note>original: "Placitum"; a formal agreement</note> is similarly derived from that which "pleases" <note>original: "placeat"</note>. Others say a pact is what someone does willingly, while a "pleasure" compels even the unwilling—such as when someone is prepared to answer in court, which no one can call a "pact," but rather a "pleasure."

A mandate <note>original: "Mandatum"</note> is so called because formerly, in a business matter committed to another, they would give one another their hand <note>original: "manum dabat"</note>. A "ratified" thing <note>original: "Ratum"</note> is, as it were, reasonable and right; hence, he who promises says, "I profess that I am ratified," which means firm and perpetual. "Rite" <note>original: "rite"</note>, however, means not "rightly" but "according to custom."

A <term>chirograph</term> <note>original: "Chirographum"</note> is a security or a joint-writing like two charts; for in Greek, a security is called "handwritten." Buying and selling is an exchange of things and a contract arising from agreement. "Buying" <note>original: "Emptio"</note>
<margin>1470</margin>
is so called because it passes from me to you. "Selling" <note>original: "venditio"</note> is as if it were "market-selling" <note>original: "venundatio"</note>, that is, from the market-days <note>original: "nundinis"</note>.

A donation is the transfer of any thing. They say it is called a "donation" as if it were the "action of a gift" <note>original: "doni actionem"</note>, and a "dowry" <note>original: "dos"</note> as if "I give likewise" <note>original: "do ite"</note>. For when a donation precedes in marriage, a dowry follows. For the ancient
<margin>th</margin>
rite of marriage was such that the husband and wife bought each other in turn, so that the wife would not seem like a handmaid—as we have it in the law. Thus it is that following the man's donation, the woman's dowry follows.

A "usufructuary donation" is so called because the donor still retains the "use and fruit" <note>the right to use and profit from the property</note> from it, while the right of the person to whom it was given is preserved. A "direct donation" is so named because it passes immediately to the other both in law and in use, and nothing of it is turned back to the right of the donor.

Conditions belong properly to witnesses. They are called "conditions" <note>original: "conditiones"</note> from "proclaiming together" <note>original: "condicendo"</note>, as if they were "joint-proclamations" <note>original: "condictiones"</note>, because not just one witness swears there, but two or more. For "every word stands not in the mouth of one, but of two or three witnesses." Also, they are "conditions" because the speech of the witnesses agrees among themselves, as if they were "joint-sayings."

A stipulation <note>original: "Stipulatio"</note> is a promise or a pledge, from which those who promise are called "stipulators." It is called a "stipulation" from "straw" <note>original: "stipula"</note>. For the ancients, when they promised something to each other, would hold a straw and break it, and by joining it again, they would recognize their pledges; or because they called what was firm "stipulum" according to the proverb.

<column-break/>

#### Column 2

A sacrament is a pledge of a promise; it is called a "sacrament" because it is an act of perfidy <note>faithlessness</note> to violate what anyone promises.

### On Things. Chapter XXV.

An inheritance is a thing which comes to someone by the death of another, either by a legacy in a will or by retained possession. It is called an "inheritance" <note>original: "hereditas"</note> from things "entered upon" <note>original: "aditis"</note>, or from "brass/money" <note>original: "aere"</note>, because he who possesses a field also pays the tax; hence also "things" <note>original: "res"</note>.

"Things" are those which exist within our law. "Rights" <note>original: "jura"</note> are those things which are justly possessed by us and are not another's. A "thing" is named from "having rightly" <note>original: "recte habendo"</note>, and "right" from "possessing justly" <note>original: "juste possidendo"</note>. For that is possessed by "right" which is possessed rightly, and that is "rightly" which is "well." That which is possessed badly belongs to another. He possesses badly who either uses his own things poorly or presumes upon the things of another. He possesses justly who is not ensnared by greed. He who is held by greed is "possessed," not a "possessor."

"Goods" <note>original: "Bona"</note> belong to the honorable or noble; they are called "goods" so that they may not have a shameful use, but rather that men may use them for good things.

<term>Peculium</term> <note>original: "Peculium"</note> belongs properly to minor persons or slaves. For *peculium* is what a father or master permits his son or slave to manage as his own right. It is named from "cattle" <note>original: "pecudibus"</note>, in which all the substance of the ancients consisted.

"Possession of goods" is the right of possession acquired by a certain order and a certain title. An "intestate inheritance" is one which is not written in a will, or if it is written, it has not been issued according to law. "Escheats" <note>original: "Caduca"</note> are so called because the heirs for it have "fallen away" <note>original: "ceciderunt"</note>.

<term>Familiae herciscundae</term> is the division of an inheritance among heirs. For among the ancients, "herciscunda" meant division. "Dividing common property" <note>original: "Communi dividendo"</note> is among those who share a thing; this action orders an arbiter to be given to those requesting it, by whose judgment the things may be divided. An "action for regulating boundaries" <note>original: "Finium regundorum"</note> is so called because they regulate the boundaries for both parties so they are not scattered, provided the controversy is not over a space narrower than five feet.

"Leasing" <note>original: "Locatio"</note> is a thing given for use with a defined payment. "Hiring" <note>original: "Conductio"</note> is a thing received for use with an established payment. A "credited thing" is that which is brought into an obligation such that, from the time it was contracted, it is certain that it must be delivered. "Interest" <note>original: "Usura"</note> is the increase of a loan, named from the "use" <note>original: "usu"</note> of the money credited.

A "loan" <note>original: "Commodum"</note> is that which is of our right and is transferred to others temporarily, with a limit on the time it may be with them; hence it is called *commodum* <note>convenience/measure</note>. A "precarium" <note>a grant by prayer/request</note> is when a creditor, having been asked by "prayer" <note>original: "prece"</note>, permits a debtor to remain in possession of a field pledged to him and to take the fruit from it. It is called *precarium* because it is heard by prayer, as if it were a *precadium*, with the letter 'r' changed for 'c'.

A "loan" <note>original: "Mutuum"</note> is so called because that which is given by me to you becomes "yours from mine" <note>original: "ex meo tuum"</note>. A "deposit" <note>original: "Depositum"</note> is a pledge commended for a time, as if "placed for a long time" <note>original: "diu positum"</note>. Someone is seen to "deposit" something when, out of fear of theft, fire, or shipwreck, he places it with another for the sake of guarding it.

In common speech, there is a difference between a "pledge" <note>original: "pignus"</note> and "earnest money" <note>original: "arra"</note>. For a pledge is what is given for a credited thing, which is taken back as soon as the thing is returned. "Earnest money," however, is that which is first given in part for a thing bought in a good-faith contract and is later completed. For earnest money is to be completed, not taken back. Thus, he who has earnest money does not return it like a pledge.

It covers everything from the etymology of "stipulation" (from breaking a straw) to the moral definition of property rights.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book V of the Etymologies, moving from the definitions of wills and inheritances into the nuances of property law, contracts, and the classification of crimes and punishments. Isidore continues to use etymology—the study of word origins—to explain the legal force of these terms.</meta>

...but it requires completion. <term>Earnest money</term> <note>original: "arra"</note> is named from the thing <note>original: "a re"</note> for which it is handed over. Likewise, there is a difference between a **pledge**, a **trust**, and a **mortgage**. A <term>pledge</term> <note>original: "pignus"</note> is that which is bound because of a thing given, of which the creditor obtains only the possession for a time, while the ownership remains with the debtor. A <term>trust</term> <note>original: "fiducia"</note> is when some thing is either handed over or entrusted in law for the sake of taking a loan. A <term>mortgage</term> <note>original: "hypotheca"</note> is when something is provided as security without the deposit of money or a physical pledge, occurring by a pact or a written guarantee alone.

A <term>moment</term> <note>original: "momentum"</note> is named from the brevity of time, so that a business matter may be restored so quickly as to be immediate, and that which is sought should not be drawn out into any delay; just as there is no space in a moment, the point of time is so brief that it cannot be extended into any delay in any way. 

An <term>instrument</term> <note>original: "instrumentum"</note> is that from which we construct something, such as a knife, a pen, or an axe. <term>Equipment</term> <note>original: "instructum"</note> is what is produced by an instrument, such as a staff, a book, or a tablet. <term>Use</term> <note>original: "usus"</note> is how we employ the equipped thing, such as leaning on a staff, reading in a book, or playing on a tablet; but even the fruit of the fields is called "use" because we use it. These are those three categories. 

<term>Usufruct</term> <note>original: "usufructus"</note> is so called because the fruit of a thing is held by use alone, while the legal right remains with another. <term>Usucaption</term> <note>original: "usucapio"</note> is the acquisition of ownership through the continuation of lawful possession, either for two years or some other length of time. <term>Mancipation</term> <note>original: "mancipatio"</note> is so named because the thing is taken by the hand <note>original: "manu res capit"</note>. Hence it is necessary for the one who receives the <term>mancipium</term> <note>the formal transfer of property</note> to grasp the very thing that is given in mancipation. 

<term>Cession</term> <note>original: "cessio"</note> is the yielding of one’s own property, as in the phrase: "I yield by right of kinship." For we say "to yield" <note>original: "cedere"</note> as if to "concede"—that is, those things which are one’s own. For if we restore the things of another, we do not "yield" them. For "yielding" is properly said when one consents to another against the truth; as <term>Cicero</term> says: "He yielded to the authority of a most distinguished man, or rather, he obeyed." 

An <term>interdict</term> <note>original: "interdictum"</note> is that which is spoken by a judge, not permanently but for the sake of restoring a "moment" for a time, in the interim, without prejudice to the filing of a formal legal action. 

<term>Price</term> <note>original: "precium"</note> is named because we give it "in place of" <note>original: "pro vice"</note> a thing, so that in place of the price we ought to possess the thing we desire. <term>Commerce</term> <note>original: "comertium"</note> is named from "merchandise" <note>original: "merces"</note>, by which name we call things for sale. From this, a "market" <note>original: "mercatus"</note> is also called a gathering of many people who are accustomed to sell or buy things. 

<term>Restoration to the original state</term> <note>original: "integri restitutio"</note> is the repair of a case or a thing. A case is "reintegrated" which has not been fulfilled by the force of authority. A thing is "reintegrated" which has been taken away or extorted by the force of authority.

### Chapter XXVI: On Crimes Established in Law

**C**rime <note>original: "crimen"</note> takes its name from "lacking" <note>original: "carendo"</note>, such as theft, forgery, and other things that do not kill but defame. A <term>wicked deed</term> <note>original: "facinus"</note> is named from "doing" <note>original: "faciendo"</note> an evil that harms another. A <term>shameful act</term> <note>original: "flagitium"</note> is from "burning" <note>original: "flagirando"</note> with the corruption of lust that harms oneself. These are the two types of all sins. 

<term>Force</term> <note>original: "vis"</note> is the power of authority by which either a case or a thing is taken or extorted. **Private force** is if anyone, before a judgment, should eject or drive someone from his own property with armed men. **Public force** is if anyone should kill, torture, beat, or bind a citizen who is appealing before the people, a judge, or a king. 

<term>Deceit</term> <note>original: "dolus"</note> is the craftiness of the mind, from the fact that it deludes; for it does one thing and simulates another. <term>Petronius</term> thinks otherwise, saying: "What is the deceit of a judge? Surely where something is done that grieves <note>original: "dolet"</note> the law."

<column-break/>

...to have deceit. Now hear about "evil." <term>Calumny</term> <note>original: "calunia"</note> is the malicious pursuit of another's lawsuit, named from "deceiving" <note>original: "calvendo"</note>. <term>Falsity</term> <note>original: "falsitas"</note> is named from "speaking" <note>original: "fando"</note> something other than what is true. <term>Injury</term> <note>original: "iniuria"</note> is injustice. Hence is that line of <term>Virgil</term>: "Turnus's injustice warned his mother." It is an injury because it dares something against the order of law. 

<term>Sedition</term> <note>original: "seditio"</note> is called the dissension of citizens, because some go "apart" <note>original: "seorsum"</note> to others. For these people especially rejoice in the disturbance and tumult of a king. <term>Sacrilege</term> <note>original: "sacrilegium"</note> is properly the theft of sacred things; later this name also stuck to the worship of idols. <term>Adultery</term> <note>original: "adulterium"</note> is the violation of another's marriage; because one has defiled the bed of another, it took the name of adultery. 

<term>Shameful intercourse</term> <note>original: "stuprum"</note> or <term>rape</term> is properly illicit sexual union, named from "corrupting." Hence <term>Virgil</term> says: "He gains his spoil," that is, he enjoys his shameful act. The word <term>homicide</term> <note>original: "homicidium"</note> is composed of "man" <note>original: "homo"</note> and "slaughter" <note>original: "caede"</note>. For the ancients called anyone who was found to have committed slaughter upon a man a "homicide." 

The action for <term>parricide</term> <note>original: "parricidium"</note> was given not only against one who had killed a parent—that is, a father or a mother—but also against one who had killed a brother; and it is called "parricide" as if it were the "slaughter of a parent" <note>original: "parentis caedium"</note>. 

The judgment of <term>extermination</term> <note>original: "internecies"</note> was given against one who had made a forged will and because of it had killed a man. The possession of his goods followed his accuser. The meaning of *internecies* is like a certain "killing off" <note>original: "enecatio"</note> of a man. For they used to place the preposition "between" <note>original: "inter"</note> before "kill" <note>original: "necatio"</note>. Thus <term>Ennius</term> <note>The OCR says "Heu" but context suggests Ennius</note>: "To drink the sea dry," and <term>Plautus</term>: "To clear the sea," that is, to drink it up and wash it out. 

<term>Theft</term> <note>original: "furtum"</note> is the secret handling of another's property; it is named from "dark" <note>original: "furvo"</note>, that is, "gloomy," because it happens in the dark. Theft was a capital crime among the ancestors, before the penalty of fourfold restitution. <term>Trespass</term> <note>original: "peruasio"</note> is the manifest seizure of another's property. Theft occurs with those same things that can be moved from place to place, but trespass occurs both with those that are moved and those that are immovable. 

<term>Denial</term> <note>original: "inficiatio"</note> is the negation of a debt when it is demanded by a creditor. The same is <term>abjuration</term> <note>original: "abiuratio"</note>, that is, the denial of a thing entrusted. The judgment for <term>bribery</term> <note>original: "ambitus"</note> is against one who captures and seeks honors by bribery, being destined to lose the dignity which he invaded with a gift. 

The judgment for <term>embezzlement</term> <note>original: "peculatus"</note> is given against those who commit fraud against the treasury and divert public money. For the judgment is named *peculatus* from "money" <note>original: "pecunia"</note>. Theft of public property is not judged in the same way as private property; for the former is judged as sacrilege, since such a person is a "thief of sacred things." 

One is accused of <term>extortion</term> <note>original: "repetundae"</note> who has taken money from allies. In this judgment, if the defendant dies beforehand, the judgment is rendered against his estate. The judgment for <term>incest</term> <note>original: "incestus"</note> is established against sacred virgins or those related by blood; for those who mingle with such people are considered "incestuous," that is, "unchaste" <note>original: "incasti"</note>. 

Those are held on the charge of <term>treason</term> <note>original: "maiestas"</note> who have harmed or violated the royal majesty, or who have betrayed the republic, or who have conspired with enemies. An <term>atonement</term> <note>original: "piaculum"</note> is so called because it can be "expiated"; for those things were committed which had to be expiated in whatever order.

### Chapter XXVII: On Penalties Established in Law

**E**vil is named in two ways: one which a man does, the other which he suffers. That which he does is <term>sin</term>; that which he suffers is <term>punishment</term> <note>original: "pęna"</note>. A punishment is "full" when it is both past and impending, so that there is both pain and fear. It is called "penalty" <note>original: "pęna"</note> because it punishes. It is an epithet, and without an addition it does not have full...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s exploration of legal terminology, moving from the definitions of property and contracts into the classification of crimes and the various forms of legal punishment used in the Roman world. He then transitions to the definition of history and chronicles.</meta>

sensory perception. It applies the **penalty of prison**, the **penalty of exile**, and the **penalty of death**, and thus fulfills the sense of justice. <term>Punishment</term> <note>original: "supplicium"</note> is properly so named not just whenever someone is punished, but when a person is condemned in such a way that their goods are confiscated and reduced to the public treasury. For punishments were once called "supplications" <note>original: "supplicamenta"</note>; a punishment is so called because something is offered to a god from the condemnation of the person, from which we also get the word "to supplicate." Julius <note>Julius Paulus, a famous 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> writes that eight types of penalties are contained in the laws: **loss of property** [fines], **chains**, **flogging**, **retaliation**, **infamy**, **exile**, **slavery**, and **death**. By these penalties, every committed sin is avenged.

**Loss** <note>original: "damnum"</note> is named from the "diminution" of a thing. **Chains** <note>original: "vincula"</note> are named from "binding" <note>original: "vincidiendo"</note>, that is, from narrowing, because they constrain and hold a person back, or because they forcefully bind the necks. **Fetters** <note>original: "compedes"</note> are so called because they contain the "feet" <note>original: "pedes"</note>. **Shackles** <note>original: "pedicae"</note> are snares by which the feet are ensnared, named from "capturing the feet." **Chains** <note>original: "catenae"</note>, however, are named because they hold both steps by "capturing" <note>original: "capiendo"</note> them so that they cannot progress; likewise, they are called chains because they hold themselves together by capturing many knots. **Handcuffs** <note>original: "manicae"</note> are the chains by which the "hands" <note>original: "manus"</note> are captured, though *manicae* is also the word for the sleeves of tunics. A **stock** <note>original: "nervus"</note> is an iron chain by which the feet or even the necks are impeded. A **collar** <note>original: "boia"</note> is the neck-ring of the condemned; it is named from the yoke of "oxen" <note>original: "boas"</note> and is a type of chain.

A **prison** <note>original: "carcer"</note> is where the guilty are guarded; it is called *carcer* because men are "coerced" <note>original: "coerceant"</note> and shut in there, as if it were an "hinderer" <note>original: "arcer"</note> from the act of "hindering" <note>original: "arcendo"</note>. We call the place in which the guilty are kept "prison" only in the singular number. Whence the stalls from which the chariots are released in a race are called *carceres* <note>starting gates</note>, but only in the plural number.

**Lasheings** <note>original: "verbera"</note> are so called because they "beat" <note>original: "verberat"</note> the air when moved. Hence **whips** <note>original: "flagra"</note>, **blows** <note>original: "plagae"</note>, and **scourges** <note>original: "flagella"</note>, because they sound with a blast and a noise on the body. For *plagae* are like "blasts" <note>original: "flage"</note>, although *plagae* and *flagra* are primary words, while *flagella* is the diminutive form. An **eel-whip** <note>original: "anguilla"</note> is that by which boys are disciplined in schools, which is commonly called a *scutica* <note>a leather switch or strap</note>. **Clubs** <note>original: "fustes"</note> are those by which youths are struck for crimes, named because they stand "fixed" <note>original: "praefiri"</note> in ditches, which peasants call "poles" <note>original: "palos"</note>. **Bars** <note>original: "vectes"</note> are so called because they are "carried" <note>original: "vehentur"</note> by hands, used to tear down doors and gates, but these do not pertain to legal penalties. **Rods** <note>original: "virgae"</note> are the tips of the foliage and trees, named because they are "green" <note>original: "virides"</note>, or because they have the "power of reproving" <note>original: "vim arguendi"</note>. If it is smooth, it is a rod; if it is knotty or prickly, it is called by the most correct name, a **scorpion** <note>original: "scorpio"</note>, because it is fixed into the body with a curved wound. **Strikes** <note>original: "ictus"</note> are properly the marks of whips, named from the "agitation" of the air. **Claws** <note>original: "ungulae"</note> are so named because they "dig out" [the flesh]; they are light and ridiculous names for the tools by which the accused are tortured on the rack so that the truth may be found. The **rack** <note>original: "eculeus"</note> is so called because it "extends" the body. **Torments** <note>original: "tormenta"</note>, however, are so named because by "twisting" <note>original: "torquendo"</note> they find what is in the "mind" <note>original: "mentem"</note>. There is also the **Latomia** <note>original: "lautumnium"</note>, a type of punishment fit for flogging, invented by Tarquinius the Proud <note>the legendary last king of Rome</note> for the punishment of criminals. For he first invented these quarry-prisons, torments, clubs, labor in the mines, and exile; and he himself was the first of the kings to deserve exile.

**Retaliation** <note>original: "talio"</note> is the likeness of vengeance, so that someone suffers "in such a way" <note>original: "taliter"</note> as they acted. For this is instituted by both nature and law, that a similar vengeance follows the one who harms. Whence also that saying of the law: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." But *talio* refers not only to returning an injury, but also to returning a benefit. For it is a common term for both injury and beneficence.

**Infamy** <note>original: "ignominia"</note> is so called because he who is caught in some crime ceases to have a name of honesty. It is called *ignominia* as if "without a

<column-break/>

name" <note>original: "sine nomine"</note>, just as the "ignorant" <note>original: "ignarus"</note> is without knowledge, or the "ignoble" <note>original: "ignobilis"</note> is without nobility. This is also called **disgrace** <note>original: "infamium"</note>, as if "without good fame." **Fame** <note>original: "fama"</note>, however, is so called because it is spread by "speaking" <note>original: "fando"</note>, through the conduits of tongues, a serpent for the ears. It is a word used for both good and bad things. For sometimes fame is happiness, as in the phrase "Illustrious fame," which is praise. Or it can be for bad things, as Virgil says: "Fame, an evil than which no other is swifter." But the word "fame" has no certain place, because it is mostly a liar, adding many things or changing the truth; it lives as long as it is not proven. But when you have proven a thing, it ceases to be "fame," and henceforth the thing is called by its name, not by "fame."

**Exile** <note>original: "exilium"</note> is so called as if it were "outside the soil" <note>original: "extra solum"</note>. For he is called an "exile" <note>original: "exul"</note> who is outside his native soil. Whence for those returning by the right of *postliminium*—that is, those to be brought back from exile—who were cast out into injury, they were "outside the threshold" <note>original: "extra limen"</note> of the fatherland. Exile is divided into the **relegated** and the **deported**. A "relegated" person is one whose goods follow them; a "deported" person is one whose goods do not. **Proscription** <note>original: "proscriptio"</note> is exile as a condemnation from "afar" <note>original: "procul"</note>, as if it were a "further writing" <note>original: "porro scriptio"</note>. Likewise, one is "proscribed" because they are "publicly written" <note>original: "palam scriptus"</note>. **The Mine** <note>original: "metallum"</note> is where the crude prisoners are assigned to dig out veins of ore and cut marble into slabs.

**Slavery** <note>original: "servitus"</note> is named from "preserving" <note>original: "servando"</note>; for among the ancients, those who were "preserved" from death in war were called slaves (*servi*). This is the last of all evils, which for free men is heavier than any other punishment. For where liberty has perished, there all things have perished at once.

Of **deaths** <note>original: "mortium"</note>, however, there are diverse cases, such as the **cross** <note>original: "crux"</note> or the **gallows** <note>original: "patibulum"</note> on which men are hung and "tortured" or "suffer" <note>original: "patiuntur"</note>; from which they also take their names. For the *patibulum* is commonly called a "fork" <note>original: "furca"</note>, as if it were "carrying the head" <note>original: "ferens caput"</note>; it kills by hanging and strangling. But the penalty of the *patibulum* is less than that of the cross. For the *patibulum* kills those hung on it instantly, whereas the cross tortures for a long time those fastened to it. Whence also in the Gospel, so that the thieves might die and be taken down from the wood before the Sabbath, their legs were broken, because those hung on wood could not die quickly. 

Death differs also in its very kind. For it is more cruel to have the spirit extinguished by drowning in water, to be burned by fires, to be killed by cold or hunger, or to be exposed to dogs and beasts. To die by the sword is what the "greater age" <note>the ancients</note> desired. For the sword knows how to end life with a "short death" <note>original: "compendiosa morte"</note> without great torture. The **sack** <note>original: "culleus"</note> is a parricidal vessel, named from "hiding" <note>original: "occulendo"</note>, that is, closing. It is a leather bag made from hide in which parricides, along with a monkey, a rooster, and a serpent, are shut in and thrown into the sea. 

The genus of all these deaths is called **animadversion** <note>original: "animadversio"</note>. For *animadversio* is when a judge punishes a criminal; it is called *animadvertere*, that is, to "turn the mind" <note>original: "animum vertere"</note> there, intending to punish the criminal because he is a judge. For this reason, the Romans forbade some condemned people **water and fire**, because air and water are open and given to all; they intended that the condemned should not enjoy what is granted to everyone by nature.

->On the word "Chronicle"<-

<margin>Chapter 28</margin>
**Chronicle** is the Greek name for what is called a **series of times** in Latin, such as the one Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, published among the Greeks, and Jerome the priest converted into the Latin language. For *chronos* in Greek is interpreted as "time" <note>original: "tempus"</note> in Latin.

<meta>This page transitions from Isidore’s discussion of legal terminology and historical records into a scientific and etymological study of time. He moves from the human-made laws of the previous page to the natural laws governing the cosmos, specifically how time is measured and divided.</meta>

### On Moments and Hours, Chapter 29.

**T**ime is divided into moments, hours, days, months, years, five-year periods <note>original: "lustris"</note>, ages, and eras. A **moment** is the smallest and most narrow unit of time, named from the "movement" <note>original: "motu"</note> of the stars. For it is the very edge of an hour in brief intervals, when the sun yields a bit of space to itself and then moves into it. **Hour** is a Greek name <note>Greek: "ὥρα" (hōra)</note>, yet it sounds Latin. For an hour is the "limit" <note>original: "finis"</note> of time, just as "shores" <note>original: "orae"</note> are the limits of the sea, rivers, and garments.

### On Days, Chapter 30.

**D**ay is the presence of the sun: that is, the sun above the earth, just as night is the sun below the earth. For the cause of it being either day or night is the sun being either above or below the earth. A **legal day** is twenty-four hours, until the day and night conclude the space of their course from the rising to another rising sun by the turning of the heavens. Improperly, however, a "day" is considered the space from the rising sun until the setting sun. There are, however, two spaces of the day: the daytime and the nighttime. While a full day is twenty-four hours, the daytime space itself is twelve hours. It is called "day" after its better part. Hence it is in common use that we state the number of days without mentioning the night, just as it is written in the divine law: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day" <note>Genesis 1:5</note>. According to the Egyptians, the day begins at sunset; according to the Persians, from sunrise; according to the Athenians, from the sixth hour of the day <note>noon</note>; according to the Romans, from midnight. Hence that is when **cockcrow** occurs, whose voice announces the coming of day, and when the **midnight breath** <note>original: "mesonictius afflatus"</note> happens. Days are named after the gods whose names the Romans consecrated to certain stars. They called the first day after the **Sun**, which is the leader of all stars, just as that same day is the head of all days. The second after the **Moon**, which is first after the sun in both brightness and size, and from which she borrows her light. The third from the star of **Mars**, which is called the evening star. The fourth from the star of **Mercury**, which some call the "white circle." The fifth from the star of **Jupiter**, which they call Phaethon. The sixth from the star of **Venus**, which they assert is **Lucifer** <note>the light-bringer</note>, which has more light than all the other stars. The seventh from the star of **Saturn**, which, located in the highest heaven, completes its course in nearly thirty years. Furthermore, the pagans gave the days names from these seven stars because they estimated they received something from them: saying they have spirit from the Sun, a body from the Moon, wit and tongue from Mercury, pleasure from Venus, blood from Mars, temperance from Jupiter, and moisture from Saturn. Such was the error of the foolish pagans, who invented such ridiculous fictions for themselves. Among the Hebrews, however, the first day is called "one of the Sabbath," which for us is the **Lord’s Day**, which the pagans dedicated to the Sun. The "second of the Sabbath" is the second <term>weekday</term> <note>original: "feria"</note>, which secular people call the Day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>. The "third of the Sabbath" is the third weekday, which they call the Day of Mars <note>Tuesday</note>. The "fourth of the Sabbath" is the fourth weekday, which is called the Day of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note> by the pagans. The "fifth of the Sabbath" is the fifth weekday—that is, the fifth from the Lord’s Day—which among the pagans is called the Day of Jupiter <note>Thursday</note>. The "sixth of the Sabbath" is the sixth weekday, which among those same pagans is named the Day of Venus <note>Friday</note>. The **Sabbath**, however, is the seventh from the Lord’s Day, which the pagans dedicated to Saturn and named the Day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note>. "Sabbath," moreover, is translated from Hebrew into Latin as "rest," because God rested on it from 

<column-break/>

all His works. It is better, however, that the ecclesiastical custom of speaking from a Christian mouth should take precedence in the names of the days. Yet, if by chance custom drags someone into saying with the mouth what they disprove in the heart, let them understand that all those after whom these days were named were merely men. Because of certain benefits they provided to mortals, or because they were powerful and eminent in this world, divine honors were bestowed upon them by their admirers both in the naming of days and stars; first the stars were named after men, and then the days were named after the stars. **Weekdays** <note>original: "feriae"</note>, however, are named from "speaking" <note>original: "fando"</note>, because on them we have the opportunity for speaking—that is, to speak in divine or human office. Festive days were instituted for the sake of men; weekdays <note>feriae</note> for the sake of divine rites. There are three parts of the day: morning, noon, and the final part. **Morning** <note>original: "mane"</note> is early and full light, and no longer twilight. It is called *mane* from *manum*, for in antiquity "good" was called *manum*. For what is better than light? Others think *mane* is so called after the *Manes* <note>spirits of the dead</note>, whose dwelling is between the moon and the earth. Others think it comes from "air" because it is "thin" <note>original: "manus"</note> and clear. **Noon** <note>original: "meridies"</note> is said as if it were "mid-day" <note>original: "medidies"</note>, or because the day is then "purer" <note>original: "merum"</note>. For in the whole day nothing is clearer than noon, when the sun shines from the middle of the sky and illustrates the whole world with equal clarity. The **final part** <note>original: "suprema"</note> is the last part of the day, when the sun turns its course toward the setting, so named because it "remains" <note>original: "superest"</note> at the last part of the day. **Evening** <note>original: "serum"</note> is named from "closed bars" <note>original: "clausis feris"</note>, when night already comes so that everyone may be safer in sleep. **Today** <note>original: "hodie"</note> is as if "this day" <note>original: "hoc die"</note>; and **daily** <note>original: "quotidie"</note> is formed as "on however many days" <note>original: "quot diebus"</note>. **Tomorrow** <note>original: "cras"</note> means "afterward." **Yesterday** <note>original: "hesternum"</note> is the day before, and is called *hesternum* from the fact that the day itself is now "external" <note>original: "extraneus"</note> to us and has become foreign by passing away. **The day before** <note>original: "pridie"</note> is as if the "prior day." **The day after tomorrow** <note>original: "perendie"</note> means "after the day."

### On Night, Chapter 31.

**N**ight <note>original: "nox"</note> is named from "harming" <note>original: "nocendo"</note>, because it harms the eyes. It possesses the light of the moon and stars so that it would not be unsightly, and to console men working at night, and to be tempered to the needs of certain animals that cannot bear the light of the sun. The alternation of night and day was created for the cycle of sleeping and waking, and so that the rest of night might temper the labor of the day's work. Night happens either because the sun is exhausted by its long journey and faints as it reaches the furthest space of heaven, blowing out its fires, or because it is forced under the earth by the same force that brought it above the earth; and thus the shadow of the earth makes the night. Whence Virgil says:
> Night rushes from the ocean, wrapping the earth and sky in a great shadow. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* II.250</note>
There are seven parts of the night: evening, twilight, the silence of night, the dead of night, cockcrow, early morning, and daybreak. **Evening** <note>original: "vesper"</note> is named from the western star, which follows the setting sun and precedes the following darkness. Of which Virgil says:
> Before the day is closed, Evening settles Olympus. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* IV.434</note>
**Darkness** <note>original: "tenebrae"</note> is so called because it "holds" <note>original: "teneat"</note> shadows. **Twilight** <note>original: "crepusculum"</note> is "doubtful light." For we call a "doubtful thing" *creperum*—that is, between light and darkness. **The silence of night** <note>original: "conticinium"</note> is when all things are silent. For "to be silent" is *conticere*. **The dead of night** <note>original: "intempestum"</note> is the middle and inactive time of night, when action [is not possible...]

Isidore of Seville explains the naming of the days of the week after Roman gods/planets and contrasts this with the Hebrew and Christian ecclesiastical naming systems.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divisions of time. The previous page defined the basic units of hours and days; here, Isidore explores the specific times of night, the structure of the week, the etymological origins of the months, and the celestial mechanics of solstices and seasons. He continues his method of using linguistic roots—often combining Latin and Greek—to explain the natural world.</meta>

...nothing can be done and all things are quiet in sleep. For time is not understood through itself except through human actions. The middle of the night, however, lacks action. Therefore, the "dead of night" <note>original: "intempesta"</note> is inactive, as if it were without time—that is, without the action by which time is distinguished. From this comes the phrase: "You have come at an untimely [intempestive] hour." Therefore, it is called *intempesta* because it lacks time, which is to say, action. **Cock-crow** <note>original: "gallicinium"</note> is named after the roosters, the announcers of light. **Morning** <note>original: "matutinum"</note> is the time between the departure of darkness and the arrival of dawn; it is called *matutinum* because this time exists at the start of the morning. **Daybreak** <note>original: "diluculum"</note> is, as it were, the small light of day already beginning. This is the **dawn** which precedes the sun. Dawn is the beginning of the brightening day and the first splendor of the air, which in Greek is called *eos* <note>Greek: ἕως</note>. We call it *aurora* by derivation, as if it were *eurora* <note>Isidore suggests a link to the East wind, Eurus</note>. From this comes the line: "And Aurora [with] the horses of the dawn [eois]." And again: "The ranks of the dawn [eoas]."

## On the Week, Chapter 32.

**Week** <note>original: "hebdomada"</note> is named from the number of seven days, by the repetition of which months, years, and ages are completed. For the Greeks call seven *hepta* <note>Greek: ἑπτά</note>. We call this a *septimana*, as if it were "seven lights" [septem luces]. For in the morning there is light. The **eighth day** is the same as the first: it is the day to which the week returns, and from which the series of the week begins again.

## On Months, Chapter 33.

**Month** <note>original: "mensis"</note> is a Greek name derived from the name of the moon. For the moon is called *mene* <note>Greek: μήνη</note> in the Greek language. Hence among the Hebrews, legal months are not counted from the sun's circle but from the moon's course—that is, from one new moon to the next. The Egyptians, however, were the first to use the sun’s course to determine the day of the month; they did this so that errors in calculation would not occur from the faster course of the moon, whereas the slower movement of the sun could be more easily understood.

**January** is named after Janus, to whom it was consecrated by the pagans; or because it is the threshold and "door" [*ianua*] of the year. For this reason, Janus is painted with two faces [bifrons], to show the entrance and exit of the year. **February** is named after Februus—that is, Pluto—to whom sacrifices were made in that month. For the Romans consecrated January to the heavenly gods, but February to the gods of the underworld [manes]. Therefore, February is named after Februus (Pluto), not from *febris* [fever], that is, sickness. **March** is named after Mars, the founder of the Roman race; or because at that time all living things are driven toward the male [*marem*] and the pleasure of mating. It is also called the "month of new things" because March is the beginning of the year. It also signals the "new spring," namely by the appearance of buds; because with new fruits turning green, the end of the previous cycle is proven. **April** is named for Venus, as if "Aphrodit-il"; for in Greek Venus is called Aphrodite <note>Greek: Ἀφροδίτη</note>. Or it is so named because in this month all things "open" [*aperiunt*] into flower, as if it were *Aperilis*. **May** is named after Maia, the mother of Mercury; or from the "elders" [*maioribus*] in age, who were the leaders of the republic. For the Romans consecrated this month to the elders, and the following month to the younger men. Whence also **June** [*iunius*] is named <note>after the *iunioribus* or "juniors"</note>. For previously the Roman people were divided into centuries of seniors and juniors. **July**, however, and **August** were named in honor of the men Julius and Augustus Caesar. Previously they were called *Quintilis* and *Sextilis*. Quintilis because it was the fifth [*quintus*] month from March, which the Romans testify is the start of the year. Sextilis likewise because it is the sixth. **September** takes its name from its number and "rain" [*imber*], because it is the seventh month from March and brings rains. So also October, November, and December from their number and

<column-break/>

rains they received their names, a sequence which December finishes. This is because the "number ten" [denarius] closes the preceding numbers. The **Calends**, **Nones**, and **Ides** were established by the Romans either for feast days or for the duties of magistrates. On these days people would gather in the cities. Some think the Calends are named from "worshiping" [*colendo*]. For among the ancients the beginnings of all months were worshiped, just as they are among the Hebrews. Most Latins think the **Ides** are named from "eating" [*edendo*], because these days were feast-days among the ancients. *Monae* <note>likely referring to the Nones or market-days</note> are named from *nundinae* [market days]; for *nundinae* are public assemblies or trade fairs.

## On Solstices and Equinoxes, Chapter 34.

**Solstice** is so named as if it were "the standing of the sun" [*solis statio*], because then, with the sun standing still, the days or nights grow. It is called **Equinox** because then the day and night consist of an equal space of hours. There are two solstices. One is the **summer solstice** on the eighth day before the Calends of July [June 24], at which time the sun begins to return to the lower circles. The other is the **winter solstice** on the eighth day before the Calends of January [December 25], at which time the sun begins to seek higher circles. Thus the day of the winter solstice is found to be the smallest, just as the summer solstice is the largest. Likewise, there are two equinoxes: one vernal [spring] and the other autumnal, which the Greeks call *isomeria* <note>Greek: ἰσημερία, "equal day"</note>. These equinoxes are on the eighth day before the Calends of April [March 25] and the eighth day before the Calends of October [September 24]. For the year was once divided into only two parts: the summer and winter solstice, and into two hemispheres.

## On the Seasons of the Year, Chapter 35.

The **Seasons** of the year are four: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They are called "seasons" [*tempora*] from a "tempering" [*temperamento*] of the mixture, because they temper each other in turn with moisture, dryness, heat, and cold. These are also called "courses" [*curricula*] because they do not stand still but run [*currunt*]. It is established that after the world was made, based on the quality of the sun's course, the seasons and months were divided for us. The ancients made such a distinction of these seasons that in the first month it is called "new spring," in the second "adult," and in the third "late" <note>original: "praeproprio," meaning very early or premature</note>. So too summer in its three months: new, adult, and late. So too autumn: new, adult, and late. Likewise winter: new, adult, and late or extreme. From this comes the saying of Virgil: "And the trembling fall of winter." **Spring** [*ver*] is so called because it "turns green" [*vireat*]. For then, after winter, the earth is clothed in herbs and all things burst into flower. **Summer** [*estas*] is named from "heat" [*estu*]. Or summer is as if "burnt" [*usta*]—that is, scorched and dry; for heat is dry. **Autumn** is named after the "season" [*tempestate*] when the leaves of the trees fall and all things ripen. **Winter** [*hyemem*] was named by the logic of the hemisphere, because then the sun revolves in a shorter circle. For this reason, the time is also called *bruma*, as if it were *brachia hemera* <note>Greek: βραχεῖα ἡμέρα</note>, that is, "the short day." Or it is named from "food" [*cibo*], because there is then a greater appetite for eating. For "gluttony" is called *bruma* in Greek. From this, those who are disgusted by food are called *imbrumari*. The **wintry** period [*hibernus*] is between winter and spring, as if "two-springed" [*bivernus*], which often signifies the whole of winter by its part. These seasons are also ascribed to individual parts of the sky. Spring is given to the east, because then all things arise from the earth. Summer to the south, because its part is more burning with heat. Winter to the north, because it numbs with cold and perpetual frost. Autumn to the west, because...

### On Years, Chapter 36

A **year** <note>original: "annus"</note> is the circuit of the sun, returning to the same positions among the stars after the 365 days of its ancestral path. It is called a year because it revolves through the months recurring within itself. Hence the word "ring" <note>original: "annulus," meaning a finger-ring</note> is like "annual," meaning a circle that returns into itself, as Virgil says:
> And the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.

This was indicated among the Egyptians before the invention of letters by the image of a dragon biting its own tail, because it recurs into itself. Others say "year" comes from a Greek word <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνανεοῦσθαι, *apo tou ananeousthai*</note> meaning "from renewal," for it is always being renewed. There are three types of years: the **lunar year**, which is 29 days; the **solstitial year**, which contains 365 days <note>Isidore likely means the solar year here</note>; or the **great year**, which occurs when all the planets return to the same place, occurring after many solar years. The **Era** <note>The Spanish Era, a dating system used in Iberia</note> of individual years was established by Caesar Augustus when he first described the Roman world through a newly devised census. It was called an *era* because he claimed to return "bronze" <note>original: "aes," referring to money or taxes</note> to the republic throughout the whole world.

### On Olympiads, Lustrums, and Jubilees, Chapter 37

The **Olympiad** <note>a four-year period</note> was established among the Greeks at Elis, a city in Greece, where they held a five-year contest <note>inclusive counting: the games happened every 4th year, which the ancients often called "five-year" cycles</note> with four intervening years vacant. Because of this, they called the time of the Elid contest an *Olympiad*, calculating four years to one Olympiad. A **Lustrum**, however, is a *penteteris*, which means a five-year period. It is said to be "founded" by the Romans every fifth year because of the Olympiads—for at that time there were consuls, but the "Era" did not yet exist. It is a five-year span, and it is named so because every five years the city of Rome was "purified" <note>original: "lustrabatur"</note> after a census of the republic. **Jubilee** is interpreted as "the year of remission." This is a Hebrew term for a number woven from seven weeks of years—that is, 49 years—in which trumpets were sounded, and ancient possessions returned to everyone, debts were forgiven, and freedoms were confirmed. We also celebrate this number in the days of Pentecost after the Lord’s resurrection, when guilt is remitted and the "handwritten note" of our entire debt is wiped away, leaving us free from every bond to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon us.

### On Centuries and Ages, Chapter 38

**Centuries** <note>original: "secula," also meaning "ages" or "generations"</note> consist of generations; they are called *secula* because they "follow" <note>original: "sequantur"</note> one another. As some depart, others succeed them. Some call a fifty-year period a *seculum*, which the Hebrews call a Jubilee. For this reason, that Hebrew servant who, out of love for his wife and children and his master, had his ear pierced and was subjected to service, is commanded to serve "for a century" <note>original: "in secula"</note>—that is, until the fiftieth year. **Age** <note>original: "etas"</note> is often used for a single year (as in annals), for seven years (as in the stages of a man), for a hundred years, or for any length of time. Hence, an "age" is a time constructed from many centuries. The word *etas* is used as if it were "eternity-likeness" <note>original: "euitas," a pun on *etas* and *aeuitas*</note>, that is, a likeness of eternity. For eternity is a perpetual age, of which neither a beginning

<column-break/>

nor an end is known. The Greeks call these "aeons" <note>Greek: αἰῶνας</note>, which is sometimes used by them for a century and sometimes for the eternal; the Latin word is derived from this. "Age" is properly used in two ways: either for the stages of a man (such as infancy, youth, and old age) or for the ages of the world. The **First Age** of the world is from Adam to Noah; the **Second** from Noah to Abraham; the **Third** from Abraham to David; the **Fourth** from David to the deportation of Judah to Babylon; the **Fifth** from then until the arrival of the Savior in the flesh; and the **Sixth**, which is now passing, until this world is finished. The course of these ages through generations and kingdoms was first drawn out in a simple historical style by Julius Africanus <note>a 3rd-century Christian traveler and historian</note> under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. Then Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, and the priest Jerome of holy memory, published a multifaceted "Canon of Chronicles," an organized history of kingdoms and times together. Then others followed, among whom Victor, Bishop of the Church of Tunnuna <note>original: "Victor Turonensis," though Isidore likely refers to Victor of Tunnuna</note>, having reviewed the histories of his predecessors, completed the deeds of the subsequent ages up to the consulship of the younger Emperor Justin. We have noted the sum of these times from the beginning of the world until the Emperor Augustus Heraclius or King Suinthila of the Goths <note>Isidore's contemporary king</note> with as much brevity as possible, with a descending line of time placed at the side, by whose indication the total past of the century may be known. ### On the Distinction of Times, Chapter 39

The **First Age** contains in its beginning the creation of the world. On the first day, God, under the name of Light, created the angels. On the second, under the name of the Firmament, the heavens. On the third, under the name of Distinction, the appearance of the waters and the earth. On the fourth, the lights of heaven. On the fifth, living things from the waters. On the sixth, living things from the earth and the man whom he called Adam.

### Here begins the sixth book on the Old and New Testament. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large ornamental red initial V, decorated with floral flourishes and intricate penwork extending into the margin.</image-desc>

The **Old Testament** is so called because it ceased when the **New** arrived. Of this the Apostle <note>Paul</note> makes mention, saying: "Old things have passed away, and behold, all things are made new." The **New Testament** is so named because it renews. For no one learns it except people renewed from their old state through grace, who now belong to the New Testament, which is the Kingdom of Heaven. Moreover, the Hebrews, following the authority of Ezra, receive the Old Testament in twenty-two books, according to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: namely, the **Law**, the **Prophets**, and the **Hagiographa** <note>Holy Writings</note>. The first order, the Law, is received in five books, of which the first is *Bresith* <note>original: "bresith"</note>, which is **Genesis**; the second *Elesmoth* <note>original: "elesmoth"</note>, which is **Exodus**; the third *Vagecra* <note>original: "vagecra"</note>, which is **Leviticus**; the fourth *Vagedaber* <note>original: "vagedaber"</note>, which is **Numbers**; the fifth *Elleaddabarim* <note>original: "elleaddabarim"</note>, which is 

<column-break/>

**Deuteronomy**. These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call the *Torah* <note>original: "thorae"</note> and the Latins call the **Law**. It is called the Law by the Prophets because it was given through Moses. The second order is that of the **Prophets**, in which eight books are contained:
<margin>Joshua</margin>
the first of which is **Joshua** the son of Nun <note>original: "bennun"</note>, who in Latin is called *Iesu Naue*. The second is *Sopthim* <note>original: "sopthim"</note>, which is **Judges**. The third is **Samuel**, which is the **First Book of Kings**. The fourth is *Malachim* <note>original: "malachim"</note>, which is the **Second Book of Kings**. The fifth is **Isaiah**. The sixth is **Jeremiah**. The seventh is **Ezekiel**. The eighth is *Tarefra* <note>original: "tarefra," a corruption of the Hebrew for "Twelve"</note>, which is called the **Twelve Prophets**; these books are treated as one because they are joined together for their brevity. The third order is the **Hagiographa**, that is, the "writers of holy things," in which there are nine books: the first of which is **Job**; the second the **Psalter**; the third *Masloth* <note>original: "masloth"</note>, which is the **Proverbs of Solomon**; the fourth *Coeleth* <note>original: "coeleth"</note>, which is **Ecclesiastes**; the fifth *Syrasirim* <note>original: "syrasirim"</note>, which is the **Song of Songs**; the sixth **Daniel**; the seventh *Dabreiamin* <note>original: "dabreiamin"</note>, which is the "Words of the Days" <note>Chronicles</note>, that is, the **Paralipomenon**, which is a "Chronicle" <note>original: "cristonicon"</note> and is divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins; the eighth is **Ezra**; the ninth is **Esther**. Together, these (5, 8, and 9) make twenty-two books, as summarized above. Some, however, add **Ruth** and *Cinoth* <note>original: "cinoth"</note>—which in Latin is called the **Lamentations of Jeremiah**—to the Hagiographa and make twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, according to the twenty-four elders who stand before the sight of the Lord. There is a fourth order among us for the Old Testament, consisting of those books that are not in the Hebrew canon. The first of these is the **Book of Wisdom**, the second **Ecclesiasticus**, the third **Tobit**, the fourth **Judith**, the fifth and sixth **Maccabees**. Although the Jews separate these among the "Apocrypha," the Church of Christ honors and preaches them among the divine books. In the **New Testament** there are two orders: the first is the **Gospel** order, in which are **Matthew**, **Mark**, **Luke**, and **John**. The second is the **Apostolic** order, in which are **Paul** in fourteen epistles, **Peter** in two, **John** in three, **James** and **Jude** in one each, the **Acts of the Apostles**, and the **Revelation** of John.
<margin>of both</margin>
The sum of both Testaments is distinguished in a threefold way: namely, in **history**, in **morals**, and in **allegory**. Again, these three are divided in many ways: namely, what was done and said by **God**, what by **angels**, or by **men**; what was announced by the **Prophets** concerning **Christ** and his **body** <note>The Church</note>; what concerning the **devil** and his **members**; what concerning the **old** and **new temple**; and what concerning the **present age** and the **future kingdom** and **judgment**.

### On the writers and names of the holy books. Chapter II.

<image-desc>A large ornamental red initial V, consistent in style with the first initial, marking the beginning of the second chapter.</image-desc>

According to the tradition of the Hebrews, these are the authors of the **Old Testament**. First, **Moses** published the "cosmography" of divine history in five volumes, which is called the **Pentateuch**. It is called the Pentateuch from its five volumes: for *Penta* in Greek means "five," and *teuchen* is what they call a "volume." The book of **Genesis** is named from the fact that the beginning <note>original: "exordium"</note> of the world and the generation of the age are contained in it. **Exodus** describes the exit from Egypt or the departure of the people of Israel, and took its name from that cause. **Leviticus** is named because it follows the ministries of the **Levites** and the diversity of victims <note>sacrifices</note>, and the entire Levite order is noted in it. The book of **Numbers** is so called because in it those who departed from Egypt

...is counted by tribes. It contains a description of the forty-two stations <note>original: "mansionum"; referring to the encampments of the Israelites</note> through the wilderness. **Deuteronomy** is named from the Greek language; in Latin it is interpreted as the "Second Law," that is, a repetition and a prefiguration of the Gospel law, which contains the former things in such a way that all things repeated in it are nevertheless new. The book of **Joshua** <note>original: "Iosue"</note> takes its name from Joshua son of Nun <note>original: "Iesu filio Naue"</note>, whose history it contains. The Hebrews assert that this same Joshua was its writer. In it, after the crossing of the Jordan, the kingdoms of enemies are overturned, and the land is divided among the victorious people. Through individual cities, villages, mountains, and borders, the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem are prefigured. **Judges** is named for the leaders themselves who presided over Israel after Moses and Joshua, before David and the other kings existed. Samuel is believed to have published this book and **Ruth**. The book of **Samuel** describes the birth, priesthood, and deeds of the same Samuel; therefore it took its name from him. And although this book contains the history of Saul and David, both are referred back to Samuel because he himself anointed Saul to the kingdom and David as the future king. Samuel himself wrote the first part of this book, but David wrote the following parts until the end. The book of **Kings** <note>original: "Malachim"</note> is named because it arranges the kings of Judah and the Israelite nation and their deeds in chronological order. For *Malachim* in Hebrew is interpreted as *Regum* <note>Kings</note> in Latin. Jeremiah first gathered this book into one volume; for previously it was scattered through the histories of individual kings. **Chronicles** <note>original: "Paralypomenon," from the Greek for "things left out"</note> is the Greek name, which we can call the "Omitted" or the "Remaining," because those things which were either omitted or not fully related in the Law or the books of Kings are explained in this one briefly and in summary. Some think Moses wrote the book of **Job**, others one of the prophets; some, however, think that Job himself was the writer after the blow of his suffering, believing that he narrated the struggles of his own particular battle and set forth his victories. Among the Hebrews, the beginning and end of the book of Job are composed in prose; the middle parts, however—from the place where he says: "Let the day perish in which I was born" until the place: "Therefore I reproach myself and do penance"—all run in heroic meter <note>Dactylic hexameter, the standard meter for epic poetry</note>. The book of **Psalms** is called the *Psalterium* in Greek, *nablum* <note>A stringed instrument</note> in Hebrew, and *organum* in Latin. It is called the book of Psalms because, with one prophet singing to the psaltery, the choir responded in harmony. The Hebrew title in the Psalms is <unclear>Tehillim</unclear> <note>Hebrew: תהלים</note>, which is interpreted as the "Volume of Hymns." The authors of the Psalms are those named in the titles: namely Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Heman the Ezrahite, and the sons of Korah and the others, whom Ezra gathered into one volume. All the Psalms among the Hebrews are known to be composed in metric song. For in the manner of the Roman Horace <note>original: "Flacci"</note> and the Greek Pindar, now some run in iambics, now they sound in elegiacs, now they shine in Sapphic meter, walking in trimeter or tetrameter feet. **Solomon**, son of David king of Israel, published three volumes according to the number of his titles. The first of these is *Masloth* in Hebrew, which the Greeks call *Parabolos* and the Latins **Proverbs**, because in it he showed the figures of words and images of truth under comparative likeness,

<column-break/>

but reserved the truth itself for the understanding of readers. The second book he called *Coeleth*, which is called *Ecclesiastes* in Greek and **The Preacher** <note>original: "concionator"</note> in Latin, because his speech is not directed specifically to one person as in the Proverbs, but generally to everyone, teaching that all things in the world are fleeting and brief and for this reason least to be desired. The third book he titled *Sirasirim*, which is translated into the Latin tongue as the **Song of Songs**, where through a wedding song he sings of the mystical union of Christ and the Church. It is called the "Song of Songs" because it is preferred above all the songs found in the Holy Scriptures, just as some things in the Law are called "Holy," while those greater are "Holy of Holies." The songs of these three books are said to be composed among his people in hexameter and pentameter verses, as Josephus and Jerome write. **Isaiah**, more an evangelist than a prophet, published his book, of which the whole text proceeds in the prose of eloquence, but the song runs in hexameter and pentameter verse. **Jeremiah** likewise published his book with his "Threnes," which we call **Lamentations**, because they are used in sorrowful and funeral matters; in these, he composed a fourfold alphabet in different meters. The first two of these are written as if in Sapphic meter, because three small verses which are connected to each other and begin with only one letter are concluded by a heroic comma <note>A short rhythmic phrase or "segment"</note>. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and from three letters—that is, three verses—begin. The fourth alphabet is held to be similar to the first and second. **Ezekiel** and **Daniel** are said to have been written by certain wise men; of these, Ezekiel has the beginnings and ends wrapped in many obscurities. Daniel, however, announces the kingdoms of the world in clear speech and notes the time of Christ’s arrival with the most manifest prediction of years. These are the **four prophets** who are called "Major" because they composed longer volumes. The book of the **Twelve Prophets** is marked by the names of its authors, who are called "Minor" because their speeches are short. Hence they are contained together in one volume; their names are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The book of **Ezra** <note>original: "Esdrae"</note> is marked by the title of its author, in whose text the speeches of Ezra and Nehemiah are contained together. Let no one be moved by the fact that it is called one book of Ezra, because the second, third, and fourth are not found among the Hebrews but are reckoned among the apocrypha. Ezra is believed to have written the book of **Esther**, in which the same queen, under the figure of the Church, is written to have rescued God's people from slavery and death; and having slain the enemy Haman—which is interpreted as "iniquity"—the celebration is sent down to posterity. The book of **Wisdom** is nowhere among the Hebrews; hence the title itself savors more of Greek eloquence. The Jews affirm this book belongs to Philo; it is named Wisdom because in it the arrival of Christ—who is the Wisdom of the Father—and his passion are clearly expressed. <margin>Jesus son of Sirach</margin> Jesus son of Sirach, a Jerusalemite and grandson of Jesus the high priest <margin>Jesus the high priest</margin> (whom Zechariah also mentions), most certainly composed the book of **Ecclesiasticus**. Among the Latins, this book is titled after Solomon because of the similarity of eloquence. It is called *Ecclesiasticus* because the discipline and religious conversation of the whole Church [are treated there] with great care and...

<meta>This page continues Book VI of the *Etymologies*, concluding the discussion of the biblical canon. It transitions from the Old Testament books of Judith and Maccabees to the New Testament Gospels and Epistles, before moving into a historical overview of libraries and the Septuagint translation.</meta>

...order it was published. This book <note>referring to Ecclesiasticus from the previous page</note> is found among the Hebrews and is held among the apocrypha. **Judith**, however, and **Tobit**, or the books of **Maccabees**, it is not at all certain by which authors they were written. They take their titles, however, from the names of those whose deeds they record. The four evangelists wrote the four books of the **Gospels** individually. First, **Matthew** wrote his Gospel in Hebrew letters and speech in Judea, beginning to evangelize from the human birth of Christ, saying: *The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham* <note>Matthew 1:1</note>; signifying that Christ descended according to the flesh from the seed of the patriarchs, just as had been promised in the prophets through the Holy Spirit. Second, **Mark**, full of the Holy Spirit, wrote the Gospel of Christ in the Greek tongue in Italy, having followed Peter as a disciple. He made his beginning from the prophetic spirit, saying: *The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord* <note>Mark 1:3</note>, and so forth, to show that Christ preached the Gospel in the world after the assumption of the flesh. For Christ himself says through the prophet, as it is written: *And I have placed you as a prophet among the nations* <note>Jeremiah 1:5</note>. Third, **Luke**, the most learned in the Greek language among all the evangelists—being indeed a physician—wrote his Gospel in Greece to Bishop Theophilus, beginning from the priestly spirit, saying: *There was in the days of Herod king of Judea a certain priest named Zacharias* <note>Luke 1:5</note>; so that he might manifest that Christ, after the birth of the flesh and the preaching of the Gospel, was made a sacrifice for the salvation of the world. For he is the priest of whom it is said in the Psalms: *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek* <note>Psalm 110:4</note>. For when Christ arrived, the priesthood of the Jews fell silent; the law and prophecy ceased. Fourth, **John** wrote the last Gospel and other things, beginning from the Word, to show that the same Savior who deigned to be born for us from the Father is the Word of God from before the ages; that he himself came from heaven and after death returned again to heaven. These are the four evangelists whom the Holy Spirit signified through Ezekiel in the four animals <note>original: "animalibus"; referring to the "living creatures" in Ezekiel 1:5-10</note>. There are four animals because the faith of the Christian religion was spread through the four parts of the world by their preaching. They are called "animals" <note>original: "animalia"; in Latin, this implies "living beings" possessing an "anima" or soul</note> because the Gospel of Christ is preached through them for the sake of the soul of man. For they were full of eyes inside and out, because they foresee those Gospels which were spoken of by the prophets and which had been promised in former times. Their legs were straight because there is nothing crooked in the Gospels. And they had six wings covering their legs and faces; for the things that were covered have been revealed at the arrival of Christ. *Gospel* <note>original: "Euangelium"</note> is interpreted as "good news." For *eu* means "good," and *angelium* is called "news" or "announcement"; from this, "angel" <note>original: "angelus"</note> is also called "messenger" <note>original: "nuncius"</note>. **Paul the Apostle** wrote fourteen epistles, of which he wrote nine to seven churches, and the rest to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. The **Epistle to the Hebrews**, however, is considered uncertain to be his by many Latins because of the difference in style; some suspect Barnabas wrote it, while others think it was written by Clement. **Peter** wrote two epistles in his name, which are called "canonical" <note>original: "canonice"</note> for this reason: that they were written not to just one people or city, but generally to all nations. **James**, **John**, and **Jude** wrote their own epistles. The **Acts of the Apostles** arranges the history of the beginnings of the Christian faith among the nations and the birth of the Church.

<column-break/>

It is certain that the writer of the **Acts of the Apostles** is Luke the Evangelist; in this work, the infancy of the nascent Church is treated and the history of the apostles is contained. Therefore it is called the *Acts of the Apostles*. John the Evangelist wrote the book of the **Apocalypse** at the time when he was exiled to the island of Patmos on account of his preaching of the Gospel. *Apocalypse* <note>original: "Apocalypsis"</note> from Greek is interpreted in Latin as "revelation" <note>original: "revelatio"</note>. For a revelation is called a manifestation of those things that were hidden, just as John himself says: *The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants* <note>Revelation 1:1</note>. These are the writers of the sacred books who, speaking through the Holy Spirit, wrote for our instruction both the precepts of living and the rule of believing. Besides these, other volumes are called **apocrypha**. They are called "apocrypha" <note>original: "apocrypha"</note>, that is, "secret" <note>original: "secreta"</note>, because they come into doubt. For their origin is hidden, and it is not clear to the Fathers from whom the authority of the true scriptures has come down to us by a most certain and well-known succession. In these apocrypha, even if some truth is found, nevertheless, because of many falsehoods, there is no canonical authority in them; they are rightly judged by the wise as not being the work of those to whom they are ascribed. For many things, both under the names of prophets and more recent works under the names of apostles, are brought forward by heretics; all of these have been removed from canonical authority after diligent examination under the name of "apocrypha."

### Chapter 3: On Libraries

**L**ibrary <note>original: "Bibliotheca"</note> received its name from the Greek because books are stored there. For *biblio* is interpreted as "of books" and *theca* as "storage." **Ezra** the scribe restored the library of the Old Testament after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, when the Jews had returned to Jerusalem; being inspired by the divine Spirit, he compiled all the volumes of the Law and the Prophets that had been corrupted by the nations. He established the whole of the Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there were letters <note>referring to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet</note>. Among the Greeks, **Pisistratus**, the tyrant of the Athenians, is believed to have first established a library; which subsequently, after being increased by the Athenians, **Xerxes** carried off to Persia when Athens was burned. And a long time later, **Seleucus Nicanor** brought it back again to Greece. From this, the zeal was born in kings and other collectors for gathering volumes from various nations and translating them into the Greek language through interpreters. Thereafter, **Alexander the Great** and his successors turned their minds toward organizing libraries for all books. Especially **Ptolemy**, surnamed Philadelphus, the most wise in all literature: while he rivaled Pisistratus in his zeal for libraries, he brought into his library not only the scriptures of the nations but even the divine writings. For seventy thousand books were found in Alexandria in his time.

### Chapter 4: On Interpreters

**H**e <note>Ptolemy Philadelphus</note> also, requesting the scriptures of the Old Testament from the high priest **Eleazar**, arranged for them to be translated from the Hebrew tongue into the Greek language by the **seventy interpreters**; these he kept in the library at Alexandria. Indeed, they each interpreted everything separately in individual cells by the Holy Spirit, so that nothing in any of their [work differed...]
