<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical translations from page 27, focusing on the various Greek versions (the Hexapla) and Jerome's Latin Vulgate. It then moves into a history of libraries, famous prolific authors, and a glossary of literary forms.</meta>

found in their codices which differed from the others in the order of words. There were also other translators who translated the sacred utterances from the Hebrew language into Greek, such as **Aquila**, **Symmachus**, and **Theodotion**, as well as that common "Vulgate" translation whose author is not apparent, and for this reason, being without the name of a translator, it is called the "Fifth Edition" <note>This refers to the anonymous columns in Origen's Hexapla, a massive comparative work of the Old Testament</note>. Furthermore, **Origen** discovered the sixth and seventh editions with wondrous labor and compared them with the other editions. The priest **Jerome**, skilled in three languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note>, converted those same scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech and translated them eloquently. His translation is deservedly preferred over the others, for it is both more tenacious of the words and clearer in the lucidity of its meaning, and, as a Christian interpretation, it is more truthful.

### Of him who first brought books to Rome Chapter V.

**A**emilius Paulus was the first to bring a wealth of books to Rome, after the Macedonian king Perseus was defeated; then Lucullus brought them from the Pontic spoils. After these, Caesar gave Marcus Varro the task of constructing a library. But Pollio was the first to open public libraries in Rome, both Greek and Latin, adding the images of authors in the hall which he had constructed most magnificently from the spoils of war.

### Who established libraries among us Chapter VI.

**A**mong us <note>referring to the Christian community</note>, **Pamphilus** the martyr—whose life Eusebius of Caesarea wrote—was the first who strove to equal **Pisistratus** <note>An ancient ruler of Athens credited with the first public library</note> in the study of the sacred library. For he had nearly thirty thousand volumes in his library. **Jerome** also and **Gennadius** followed the ecclesiastical writers throughout the whole world in order, and they included their studies in a single list of volumes.

### Who wrote many things Chapter VII.

**M**arcus Terentius Varro wrote innumerable books among the Latins. Among the Greeks, **Chalcenterus** <note>Didymus Chalcenterus, whose nickname meant "Brazen-guts" due to his tireless work</note> is extolled with wondrous praises because he published as many books as any of us could hardly write out by hand of someone else's work. Among our own people, **Origen** also surpassed both Greeks and Latins in the number of his works in the labor of the scriptures. Finally, **Jerome** confesses that he had read six thousand of his books. Yet **Augustine** surpassed the studies of all these by his genius or his knowledge. For he wrote so much that it is not possible for anyone not only to write his books day and night, but not even to manage to read them.

### On the kinds of minor works Chapter VIII.

**T**here are three kinds of minor works. The first kind are excerpts, which are called *scholia* <note>original: "scholia"</note> in Greek, in which those things that seem obscure or difficult are touched upon briefly and in summary. The second kind are homilies, which the Latins call "the word" (*verbum*), which they deliver to the people. The third are tomes, which we call books or volumes. For homilies speak to the common people, but tomes—that is, books—are of greater discussion. A **dialogue** is a conference of two or more people, which the Latins call a "conversation" (*sermonem*). For what the Greeks call dialogues, we call conversations. A conversation

<column-break/>

is so called because it is struck between both parties. A **tract** (*tractatus*) is a multifaceted exposition of a single thing, because it "draws" (*trahat*) the sense into many directions while handling the matter with itself. There is a difference between a conversation, a tract, and a word (*verbum*). For a conversation requires another person, a tract is specifically addressed to oneself, but a word is addressed to everyone. Hence it is said: "He made a word <note>i.e., delivered a speech</note> to the people." **Commentaries** are named as if "with the mind" (*cum mente*). For they are interpretations, as in the commentaries on the law or the commentaries on the Gospel. For whatever is composed briefly is called a commentary, but that which is lengthened is named an "exposition." An **Apologetic** is an excuse in which some are accustomed to respond to accusers. For it is placed solely in defense or denial, and it is a Greek name. A **Panegyric** is a licentious and wanton kind of speaking in the praises of kings, in the composition of which men flatter with many lies. This evil arose from the Greeks, whose levity, equipped with the faculty and incredible abundance of speaking, stirred up many clouds of lies. **Books of the Fasti** are those in which kings or consuls are written down, named from the *fasces* <note>bundles of rods symbolizing authority</note>, that is, from powers. Hence also Ovid’s books of the *Fasti* are named because they were published concerning kings and consuls. A **Prooemium** is the beginning of speaking. For prooemia are the starts of books which, before the narration of the case, are adapted to prepare the ears of the listeners; many skilled in Latinity have used this name without translation. This word, however, translated among us, is called a **preface** (*praefatio*), as if a "pre-speaking." **Precepts** are those which teach either what must be done or what must not be done. What must be done, such as: "Love the Lord your God" and "Honor your father and your mother." What must not be done, such as: "You shall not commit adultery," "You shall not steal." Similarly, there are the precepts of the pagans as they command or forbid. They command things to be done, such as: "Plow naked, sow naked." <note>A quote from Virgil's Georgics</note> They forbid, such as: "Do not plant the hazel tree among the vines," or "Do not seek the highest shoots." But **Moses** first wrote precepts among the Hebrews; among the Latins, **Martius Vates** <note>A legendary early Roman seer</note> first composed precepts. Among which is this: "Be the last to speak, the first to be silent." **Parables** and **problems** indicate by their names that it is necessary to search more deeply. A **parable** properly bears before it the likeness of some thing; though it is a Greek word, it is now used as Latin. And it is known that in parables, which are spoken through similarities of things, they are compared to the things being discussed. **Problems**, however, which are called "propositions" in Latin, are questions having something that must be solved by discussion. A **question** is an inquiry when it is asked whether it exists, what it is, or of what kind it is. An **argument** is said to be as if "sharp" (*argutum*), or because it is sharply discovered to prove things. The Greeks properly call an **epistle** that which is translated into Latin as "sent" (*missa*). For *stola* or *stoli* means "sent." Before the use of paper and parchment, the eloquence of letters was written on small tablets carved from wood. Hence their carriers were called *tabellarios* <note>tablet-bearers</note>.

### On Wax Chapter IX.

**W**axes are the material of letters and the nurses of little children. They themselves give genius to boys and the beginnings of perception, the study of which the Greeks are said to have been the first to hand down. For the Greeks and Tuscans first wrote with iron on wax; afterwards, the Romans ordered that no iron stylus <note>the tool used for writing on wax</note> should be...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville's encyclopedic history of the written word, moving from the history of libraries to the physical materials of book production—wax, papyrus, parchment, and the tools of the scribe.</meta>

Hence it was said among the scribes: ¶ Do not cut the wax with iron. <note>original: "Ceram ferro ne cedito"</note> Afterward it was established that they should write on wax with bone, as Atta indicates in his satire, saying: "Let us turn the plowshare into the wax and plow the bone point." <note>Titus Quinctius Atta was a Roman comic poet; he uses the metaphor of plowing a field to describe writing with a stylus.</note> Furthermore, a <term>graphium</term> is called a "writing-tool" in Greek-Latin, for writing is called *graphi*.

<margin>c</margin>
### Of Paper Chapter X.
Egypt first provided the use of paper, beginning in the city of Memphis. For Memphis is a city of the Egyptians where the use of paper was first discovered, as Lucan says: "The Memphite paper is made from thirsty papyrus." He called the papyrus "thirsty" because it drinks up moisture. It is called <term>charta</term> <note>paper</note> because the skin of the papyrus is pulled away piece by piece <note>original: "carptim"</note> and glued together. There are many kinds of this. The first and most excellent is the "Augustan" or "Royal," of a larger size, named in honor of Octavian Augustus. The second is "Libyan," for the honor of the province of Libya. The third is called "Hieratic" <note>sacred</note> because it was chosen for sacred books; it is similar to the Augustan but slightly tinted. The fourth is "Teneotic," from a place in Alexandria so named where it was made. The fifth is "Saitic," from the town of Sais. The sixth is "Cornelian," first made by Cornelius Gallus, the prefect of Egypt. The seventh is "Emporitic" <note>merchant-grade</note> because it is used for wrapping merchandise, being less suitable for writing.

### Of Parchment Chapter XI.
When the kings of Pergamon lacked paper, they first devised <term>membrana</term> <note>parchment</note>. Hence the name "parchment" <note>original: "pergamena"</note> has been preserved for it, handed down to posterity. These are also called *membrana* because they are stripped from the limbs <note>original: "membris"</note> of livestock. At first, they were made of a yellowish color, that is, saffron-colored. Later, however, white parchment was discovered at Rome, but it proved to be impractical because it easily becomes soiled and hurts the eyes of readers. For more skilled architects thought that neither gilded ceilings should be placed in libraries, nor floors of any kind other than Carystian marble, because the brightness of gold dulls the sight, while the greenness of Carystian marble refreshes the eyes. For even those who learn the money-changer's trade place myrtle-colored cloths under the forms of coins, and gemstone engravers frequently look at the backs of beetles—than which nothing is greener—and painters do the same, so that they may restore their eyesight from labor with that greenness. Parchment is either white, yellow, or purple. White occurs naturally. Yellow parchment is two-colored, for it is dyed on one side by the maker, that is, colored like saffron, of which Persius says: "Now the book with its two-colored skin and polished hair." <note>Persius was a Roman satirist; he refers to the common practice of staining the back of a scroll yellow.</note> Those dyed with a purple color are intended for letters of molten gold and silver to stand out upon them.

<margin>q</margin>
### Of the Making of Books Chapter XII.
Certain kinds of books among the pagans were made in specific sizes: poems and letters in a shorter form. But histories were written in a larger size, and not only on paper or parchment, but also on ivory tablets and woven leaves of mallows and palms. Licinius <note>OCR: "Linna"</note> remembers this kind thus: "These many famous poems joined for you by narrow lamps, by which we knew the fires of the air: written on a little book of mallow in dry wool." Physical gifts from a small ship. The trimming and filing of the edges of books became frequent. For in the beginning they were smoothed with pumice, whence Catullus says: "To whom do I give this charming new little book, just now polished with dry pumice?"

<column-break/>

<margin>c</margin>
### Of the Names of Books Chapter XIII.
A <term>codex</term> is composed of many books; a "book" is of a single volume. And it is called a *codex* by a metaphor from the trunks <note>original: "caudicibus"</note> of trees or vines, as if it were a "stem" because it contains a multitude of books within itself like branches. A "volume" <note>original: "volumen"</note> is a book named from rolling up <note>original: "voluendo"</note>, just as among the Hebrews there are volumes of the Law and volumes of the Prophets. A "book" <note>original: "liber"</note> is the inner rind of the bark which clings to the wood, on which the ancients used to write, of which Virgil says: "the bark <note>liber</note> dries on the high elm." Hence that in which we write is called a *liber*, because before the use of paper or parchment, volumes were made—that is, fastened together—from the inner bark of trees. Hence, writers were called *librarios* from these tree barks.

### Of Scribes and Their Tools Chapter XIV.
It is well known that scribes were called "librarians" <note>original: "librarios"</note> before they were called "booksellers" <note>original: "bibliopolas"</note>; for the Greeks call a book *biblum*. These same people are called both *librarii* and *antiquarii*; but *librarii* are those who write both new and old things, while *antiquarii* are those who write only old things, from which they take their name. A scribe <note>original: "scriba"</note> took his name from the act of writing, the office being named from the quality of the word. The tools of a scribe are the reed <note>original: "calamus"</note> and the pen. For by these, words are fixed to the pages. But the reed is from a plant, while the pen is from a bird, the point of which is divided into two while keeping unity in the whole body; I believe this is because of a sacred mystery, so that the Old and New Testaments might be represented by the two tips, through which the sacrament of the Word, poured out by the blood of the Passion, is expressed. It is called a *calamus* because it "sets down" <note>original: "ponat"</note> liquid; hence among sailors *calare* means "to set down." A pen <note>original: "penna"</note>, however, is named from "hanging" <note>original: "pendendo"</note>, that is, flying. For as we said, it belongs to birds. The "leaves" <note>original: "folia"</note> of books are so named either from their resemblance to the leaves of trees, or because they are made from skins <note>original: "follibus"</note>, that is, from the hides stripped from slaughtered livestock. The parts of these are called "pages" <note>original: "pagine"</note> because they are fastened <note>original: "compingantur"</note> to one another. Furthermore, they are commonly called "verses" because the ancients wrote just as a field is plowed. For they first drew the stylus from left to right, then they turned back from the bottom again to the right—rows which even today country folk call "verses." A <term>scheda</term> <note>sheet/draft</note> is that which is still being corrected and not yet reduced into books; it is a Greek name, as is <term>tomus</term> <note>volume/section</note>.

<margin>c</margin>
### Of the Gospel Canons Chapter XV.
Ammonius of Alexandria first devised the Gospel Canons, which Eusebius of Caesarea later followed and composed more fully. They were made so that through them we might be able to find and know what the various Evangelists said that was similar or unique. They are ten in number, the first of which contains the numbers in which four said the same things: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second, in which three: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The third, in which three: Matthew and John <note>Note: text likely omits a name here or refers to specific groupings</note>. The fourth, in which three: Matthew, Mark, and John. The fifth, in which two: Matthew and Luke.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Eusebian Canons, a system for cross-referencing parallel passages between the four Gospels, and moves into the history of Church Councils and the calculation of Easter.</meta>

The sixth [canon] includes two: Matthew and Mark. The seventh includes two: Matthew and John. The eighth includes two: Luke and Mark. The ninth includes two: Luke and John. The tenth includes the unique things each of them said individually. The explanation of these is as follows: A certain number is placed next to the individual chapters for each Evangelist. Beneath these numbers, another number is added, **noted in red** <note>original: "minio notata"; vermilion ink was traditionally used for headings and important markers</note>, which indicates in which canon the number above it is located. For example: if the number below is "one," it is in the first canon; if "two," in the second; if "three," in the third; and so you proceed in order up to ten. Therefore, if you open any Gospel and wish to know which of the other Evangelists said similar things, take the number adjacent to the chapter and look for that same number in its indicated canon. There you will find who said it and what they said. By following those numbers through each Gospel, you will find that they spoke of the same things in the investigated locations.

### Of the Canons of the Councils Chapter 16.

A <term>canon</term> <note>original: "canon"; from the Greek 'kanon' meaning a measuring rod or rule</note> is called a "rule" in Latin. It is called a rule because it leads one rightly and never draws one elsewhere. Others have said a rule is so named because it either governs, or provides a norm for living rightly, or because it corrects what is distorted and wicked. The <term>canons</term> of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. In the preceding years, while persecution was raging, there was very little opportunity to teach the common people. From this, Christianity was split into various heresies because bishops did not have the liberty to come together as one, except during the time of the aforementioned Emperor. He gave Christians the ability to gather freely. Under him also, the holy fathers gathered from the whole world at the Council of Nicaea, following the Evangelical and Apostolic faith, and they handed down the <term>Creed</term> <note>original: "symbolum"; a summary of Christian belief</note> as the second authority after the Apostles. Among the other councils, we know there are four venerable synods that embrace the whole of the principal faith, like the four Gospels or the four rivers of Paradise. Of these, the first is the **Synod of Nicaea**, where 318 bishops gathered during the reign of Constantine Augustus. In it, the blasphemy of the Arian heresy was condemned—which Arius himself asserted regarding the inequality of the Holy Trinity—and the same holy synod defined, through the Creed, that God the Son is **consubstantial** <note>sharing the same fundamental essence or substance</note> with God the Father. The second synod of 150 fathers was gathered at Constantinople under Theodosius the Elder. It condemned Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God, and proved that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving the form of the Creed which the entire confession of Greeks and Latins preaches in the churches. The third is the first **Synod of Ephesus**, issued under Theodosius the Younger with 200 bishops, which condemned Nestorius with a just <term>anathema</term> <note>a formal curse or excommunication</note> for asserting two persons in Christ, showing that the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures. The fourth is the **Synod of Chalcedon**, held under the prince Marcian with 630 priests, in which the fathers condemned Eutyches, the Abbot of Constantinople, who proclaimed one nature for the Lord God and His flesh, as well as his defender Dioscorus, formerly Bishop of Alexandria, and Nestorius again, along with the remaining heretics, by a single sentence.

<column-break/>

This same synod preached that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin in such a way that we confess in Him the substance of both divine and human natures. These are the four principal synods, preaching the doctrine of the faith most fully. Even if there are other councils which the holy fathers, full of the Spirit of God, established, all remain fixed in their vigor after the authority of these four, whose acts are contained within this work. A <term>synod</term> <note>original: "synodum"</note> is interpreted from the Greek as "company" or "assembly." The name "Council" <note>original: "concilium"</note> is drawn from Roman custom. For at the time when legal cases were being conducted, everyone came together as one, and they handled them with common intention. Thus, a "council" is named from "common intention" (*communi intentione*), as if it were a "gathering of minds" (*consilium*). For *cilia* are parts of the eyes <note>eyelashes/eyelids</note>, hence the word "assembly" (*considium*), that is, "council" (*consilium*), by changing the letter "D" to "L". An "assembly" (*coetus*) is a convention or congregation from "coming together" (*coeundo*), that is, meeting as one; hence it is called a "convention" (*conventus*). Just as an assembly is named from a convention, so a council is named from the society of many in one place.

### Of the Easter Cycle Chapter 17.

Bishop Hippolytus was the first to write the **Easter Cycle** during the time of Emperor Alexander. After him, the most esteemed authors—Eusebius of Caesarea, Theophilus of Alexandria, Prosper of the Aquitanian nation, and Victorinus—published multiple cycles, expanding the reasoning of the same festival. The most blessed Cyril, Bishop of the city of Alexandria, noted the logic of the moon for 95 years in a calculation of five times nineteen, recording with great brevity on which Kalends or moon the Easter solemnity ought to be celebrated. It is called a **cycle** because it is arranged in an orbit, and it embraces the order of the years as if arranged in a circle without variation and without any specialized art. Hence it happened that poems of any subject matter made with a simple structure were called "cyclic." From this, in Latin, it is called a "cycle" because it has a set order of years.

From the Creation of the World <note>original: "Ab Conditione mundi"</note> until this most recent cycle, 5,920 years are calculated. After its completion, one must return to the first beginning. In ancient times, the Church celebrated Easter on the 14th moon <note>The "14th moon" refers to the Full Moon, following the Jewish Passover (Pesach) timing.</note> along with the Jews, on whatever day it occurred. This ritual the holy fathers prohibited in the Council of Nicaea <note>Held in 325 AD, this council established the rule that Easter must fall on a Sunday.</note>, decreeing that they should not only seek the Paschal moon and month, but also observe the day of the Lord’s resurrection. For this reason, they extended the Paschal celebration from the 14th moon until the 21st, so that the Lord’s Day (Sunday) would not be omitted.

The name "Pascha" <note>Easter/Passover</note> is not a Greek word, but a Hebrew one. It does not come from "passion" <note>original: "passione"</note>—even though "to suffer" is called *paschein* in Greek—but rather it is named from the Hebrew word for "passage" <note>original: "transitu"</note>, because it was then that God himself passed over out of Egypt. Hence also in the Gospel, when Jesus saw that his hour had come that he should pass <note>original: "transiret"</note> from this world to the Father.

The night of Easter is kept as a vigil for this reason: because of the coming of our King and Lord, so that he may find us not sleeping, but waking at the time of his resurrection. There is a double reason for this night: either because he received life at that same hour in which he had suffered, or because later he is to come to judge at that same hour in which he rose. Moreover, we celebrate Easter in such a way that we not only call to memory the death and resurrection of Christ, but we also look upon the other things attested about him for the significance of the sacraments.

For the sake of the beginning of a new life, and for the sake of the "new man" whom we are commanded to put on and to cast off the old, we "clean out the old leaven" so that we may be a "new batch of dough," since Christ our Passover <note>original: "pasca nostrum"</note> has been sacrificed. Therefore, because of this newness of life, the first month of the new things among the months of the year was mystically attributed to the Paschal celebration.

Furthermore, why is Easter celebrated on the day of the third week? That is, the day which occurs from the fifteenth moon until the twenty-first. It is conducted by this number because now this "third time" has appeared as a sacrament. For the first time was before the Law; the second was under the Law; the third is under Grace, where the sacrament, previously hidden in prophetic riddles, has now been made manifest. Therefore, also because of these three ages of the world, the resurrection of the Lord lasted three days. For this reason, the Paschal day is sought through the seven days from the 14th moon until the 21st; this is done for...

<meta>This page continues a technical discussion on timekeeping (computus), specifically the symbolism of numbers and the moon in relation to the Church, before detailing the specific rules for calculating Easter and other liturgical feasts.</meta>

VI

The number seven itself <note>original: "numerum septenarium"</note>, by which totality is often signified, is also attributed to the Church because it mirrors this totality. This is why the Apostle John in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> writes to the seven churches. The Church, however, while still established in this mortal flesh, is signified in the Scriptures by the name of the "moon" because of its mutability.

Various observances of opinion regarding the Paschal festivities <note>Easter</note> sometimes give rise to error. For the Latins seek the moon of the first month from the 4th of March <note>4th Nones of March</note> until the 3rd of April <note>3rd Nones of April</note>; and if the 15th moon falls on a Sunday, they delay Easter to the following Sunday. The Greeks, however, observe the moon of the first month from the 8th of March <note>8th Ides of March</note> until the 5th of April <note>the Nones</note>; and if the 15th moon falls on a Sunday, they celebrate the holy Easter then. Therefore, this kind of disagreement disturbs the Paschal rule between both groups.

A "common year" is said to be that which has only twelve lunations—that is, 354 days. It is called "common" because often two such years proceed joined together so that they follow one another in the Paschal solemnity. For an "embolismic year" <note>from Greek *embolismos*, meaning "intercalated" or "inserted"</note> is always solitary. An embolismic year is shown to have thirteen lunar months—that is, 384 days. This is the year divinely revealed to holy Moses, in which those who live far away are commanded to celebrate Easter in the second month. "Embolism," moreover, is a Greek name which is interpreted in Latin as "super-augmentation," because it completes the number of the common years, which are seen to lack eleven lunar days. Embolismic and common years are found thus: if from the 14th moon of the preceding Easter to the 14th moon of the following there are 384 days, it is an embolismic year; if 354, it is common.

A leap year <note>original: "Bissextus"</note> is one day added after four years. For one-fourth part of a whole <note>original: "assis," referring to the 'as,' a Roman unit of measure</note> grows through each individual year. When it completes the whole unit in the fourth year, it makes a leap year. It is called *bissextus* <note>literally "twice sixth"</note> because "twice the sixth" leads to the whole unit, which is one day. Just as the quadrant <note>a quarter-day</note> is so called because it is led four times to make a leap day, which it creates over the course of the days in a solar year; or because you cannot introduce the year unless you have computed the *bissextus* on the 24th of February <note>6th Nones of March in the text's slightly idiosyncratic terminology, likely referring to the 6th day before the Kalends of March</note>. That is, you count the first "sixth" day, and by adding the second "sixth" on another day, you repeat it. From the 24th of February until the day before the Kalends of January, the leap day is added to and then subtracted from the course of the moon.

Furthermore, they are called "intercalary days" because they are placed in between, so that the ratio of the moon and the sun may agree. For "calare" is said to mean "to place," and "intercalare" to "place between." The Greeks call them "epacts" <note>original: "epactas"</note>, while the Latins call them "annual lunar additions." These revolve through the number eleven up to thirty. The Egyptians add these so that the lunar measurement may equal the solar calculation. For the moon, according to its own course, is known to shine for 29 and a half days; thus there are 354 lunar days in a year, and 11 days remain to match the course of the solar year, which the Egyptians add; hence they are called additions. Without these, you will not find what day the moon is in any given year, month, or day. These epacts are always found on the 22nd of March <note>11th Kalends of April</note> in whatever moon exists on that day. They are contained in a nineteen-year cycle. When they reach 28 epacts, which is the nineteen-year cycle, then in the following year you do not add

<column-break/>

above 28; but rather, subtract 30, and you return so that you announce 11.

### On the remaining festivities Chapter XVIII.

**F**estivity <note>original: "festivitas"</note> is named from festive days, as if it were "feast-idness," because on those days only divine business is done. To these are contrary the *fasti* <note>legal days</note>, on which it is "fas" <note>lawful</note> to speak law. A Solemnity <note>original: "solennitas"</note> is so named from sacred things, established such that they ought not to be changed for religion's sake; named from "solito," meaning firm and solid, or because it is accustomed to happen in a year. A Celebration <note>original: "celebritas"</note> is so named because not earthly but only heavenly things are conducted there. 

Easter <note>original: "Pasca"</note> is the first of all festivities, about whose name we have already spoken above. Pentecost, just like Easter, was a celebrated day among the Hebrews, because it is celebrated after five decades <note>50 days</note> from Easter; from which it also took its name. For "penta" in Greek is "five." On that day, according to the Law, the loaves of proposition from the new fruits were offered. The Jubilee year in the Old Testament bore the figure of this, which now prefigures the future eternal rest of the promise.

Epiphany <note>original: "Epiphania"</note> is Greek; in Latin it is called "appearance" or "manifestation." For on that day, the King to be adored appeared more clearly by the evidence of a star. That was a figure of the first-fruits of the believing Gentiles. On that day also, the sacrament of the Lord's baptism and the beginnings of the signs performed by the Lord—the water changed into wine—were made known. There are, however, two Epiphanies: the first in which Christ was born and appeared to the Hebrew shepherds by an angel's announcement; the second in which he showed himself from the nation of the Gentiles, with a star as a guide, in the cradle of the manger to the Magi who were to adore him.

*Scenophegia* <note>The Feast of Tabernacles</note>—a solemnity of the Hebrews—is interpreted from Greek into Latin as "dedication of tabernacles." It is celebrated by the Jews in memory of the expedition when, having moved from Egypt, they lived in tabernacles <note>tents</note>; and from that it is called *scenophegia*. For *sceno* in Greek is called "tabernaculum" in Latin. This solemnity was celebrated among the Hebrews in the month of September.

*Neomenia* <note>New Moon</note> is for us the Kalends; but among the Hebrews, because months are calculated according to the lunar course, and in Greek the moon is called *mene*, it is called *neomenia*, that is, "new moon." For among the Hebrews, the days of the Kalends themselves were solemn by legal institution, concerning which it is said in the Psalter: "Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of your distinguished solemnity."

*Encenia* <note>Hanukkah or Feast of Dedication</note>, however, is the "new dedication of the temple." For in Greek, *cenon* means "new." When something new is dedicated, it is called *encenia*. The Jews celebrated this solemnity of the dedication of the temple in the month of October.

Palm Sunday <note>original: "Dies palmarum"</note> is so called because on that day our Lord and Savior, as the prophet sang, is shown to have sat upon a young donkey while heading toward Jerusalem. Then, as he walked, a multitude of people met him with palm branches, crying out: "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, King of Israel!" 

The common people, however, call this day "head-washing" <note>original: "capitilavium"</note> because it is then the custom to wash the heads of the infants who are to be anointed <note>for baptism</note>, lest they should come to the anointing soiled by neglect. On this day, the Creed <note>original: "symbolum"</note> is handed over to those professing, because of the proximity of the Lord's Easter solemnity, so that those who are now hastening to receive the grace of God may know what faith they should profess. 

The Lord's Supper <note>original: "Cena dominica," Maundy Thursday</note> is so called because on that day the Savior celebrated the Passover with his disciples.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the liturgical calendar, specifically focusing on the transition from the Jewish Sabbath to the Christian Sunday (the Lord’s Day), before beginning a detailed glossary of liturgical terms and musical "offices" of the Church.</meta>

...which even today, as it has been handed down, is celebrated, and the holy chrism is prepared on that day. The Sabbath <note>Saturday</note> is named by the Hebrews from the interpretation of its own word as "rest," because God rested on that very day after the world was perfected. Indeed, on that day the Lord also rested in the tomb, so that He might confirm the mystery of that rest, which was commanded to the Jews to be observed as a "shadow of things to come." But after Christ fulfilled its symbolic form by His own burial, its observation ceased. The Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> is so named because on it the joy of our Lord’s resurrection is celebrated. This day was declared not for the Jews but for Christians by the resurrection of the Lord, and from that event it began to have its festive character. For to the Jews only the Sabbath was handed down to be celebrated, which was previously the "rest of the dead"; but the resurrection belonged to Him who, rising from the dead, would die no more. After such a resurrection took place in the body of the Lord—so that it might go before the Head of the Church, which the body of the Church might hope for at the end of time—the Lord’s Day began to be celebrated, which is the eighth day and also the first.

### Concerning the Offices Chapter 19.

**T**here are very many kinds of offices, but the principal one is that which is held in sacred and divine matters. The word "office" <note>original: *officium*</note> is derived from "effecting" <note>original: *efficiendo*</note>, as if it were an "effecting" <note>original: *efficitum*</note>; one letter was changed for the sake of the beauty of the language. Or, certainly, it is so named so that each person might do those things which "obstruct" <note>original: *officiant*</note> no one, but rather benefit everyone. The Evening Office <note>Vespers</note> is at the beginning of the night; it is named after the star Vesper <note>the Evening Star</note>, which rises as the night begins. The Morning Office <note>Matins</note>, however, is at the beginning of the light; it is named after the star Lucifer <note>the Morning Star</note>, which rises as the morning commences. By the significance of these two times, it is shown that God should be praised always, by day and by night. The Mass <note>original: *missa*</note> takes place at the time of the sacrifice, when the <term>catechumens</term> <note>those receiving instruction before baptism</note> are "sent" <note>original: *mittunt*</note> outside, as the <term>levite</term> <note>here meaning a deacon</note> cries out: "If any catechumen has remained, let him go outside." And the "Mass" comes from this, because those who are known to not yet be regenerated <note>baptized</note> cannot be present for the sacraments of the altar. A choir <note>original: *chorus*</note> is a multitude gathered for sacred rites. It is called a "choir" because in the beginning they stood around the altars in the manner of a crown <note>original: *corone*</note> and sang psalms in that way. Others say "choir" comes from "concord," which consists of charity; for if one does not have charity, one cannot respond in harmony. When one person sings alone, it is called a "monody" <note>original: *monodia*</note> in Greek, and in Latin a "sincinium." When two sing, it is called a "bicinium"; when many sing, it is a "choir." For a "chorea" <note>a dance</note> refers to playful songs or the rhythmic movements of groups. An "antiphon" <note>original: *antiphona*</note> is interpreted from the Greek as a "reciprocal voice," namely with two choirs singing psalms alternately in a changing order, or from one person to another. The Greeks are said to have invented this kind of singing. The Italians <note>the Romans</note> handed down the "responsories" <note>original: *responsorios*</note>. They call these "responsive songs" because, as one person stops, another answers him. There is, however, this difference between responsories and antiphons: in responsories, one person says the verse; in antiphons, however, the choirs alternate their voices. A "reading" <note>original: *lectio*</note> is so called because it is not sung like a psalm or a hymn, but is simply read. For in those, melody is sought, but here only pronunciation. Canticles <note>original: *cantici*</note> are the songs of those singing in joy. A "psalm," however, is so called because it is sung to the <term>psalter</term> <note>a stringed instrument</note>, which history reveals David the prophet used in a great mystery. These two terms, in certain titles of the psalms according to the musical art, are placed

<column-break/>

alternately with one another. For a "canticle of a psalm" is when the voice of the singer speaks out after the instrument has played the melody. A "psalm of a canticle" is when the human voice speaks first, and the art of the instrument imitates it as it plays. The "psalm," moreover, is named from the psalter; hence it is not customary for it to be composed from any other work. There are, however, three grades in singing: the first is the <term>succentor</term>, the second the <term>incentor</term>, and the third the <term>accentor</term> <note>these refer to the sub-singer, the lead singer, and the high singer</note>. Some want "diapsalma" <note>often translated as 'Selah' in English Bibles</note> to be a Hebrew word, by which "always" is signified—that is, to confirm that those things between which it is placed are eternal. Others, however, think it is a Greek word signifying an interval in singing—so that the "psalma" is what is sung, but the "diapsalma" is the silence interposed in the singing; just as "sympsalma" <note>original: *sumpsalma*</note> means the joining of voices in singing, so "diapsalma" means their division, where a certain rest is shown by a distinct break in the continuation. From this it is also probable that sentences should not be joined in singing where a "diapsalma" has been interposed, because it is placed there so that a change of meaning or of persons may be recognized. A hymn is a song of those giving praise, which is interpreted from Greek into Latin as "praise" <note>original: *laus*</note>, because it is a song of joy and praise. Properly, however, hymns are those containing the praise of God. If, therefore, there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn; if there is praise and it is of God but it is not sung, it is not a hymn. If, therefore, it is both said in praise of God and it is sung, then it is a hymn. The contrary to this is the "threnody" <note>original: *threnu*</note>, which is a song of lamentation and of a funeral. "Alleluia" is the interpretation of two words, which is "praise God," and it is a Hebrew word. For "Ia" is one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews. "Amen" means "truly" or "faithfully," which is also Hebrew. These two words—"Amen" and "Alleluia"—it is not permitted for Greeks, Latins, or barbarians to translate entirely into their own language or to announce in another tongue. For although they can be interpreted, nevertheless because of their more sacred authority, their original linguistic antiquity has been preserved by the Apostles. For the names are so sacred that even John in the Apocalypse reports that he saw and heard, by the Spirit revealing it, the voice of the heavenly host, like the voice of many waters and of mighty thunders, saying: "Amen and Alleluia." And because of this, it is necessary for both to be said on earth just as they resound in heaven. "Hosanna" <note>original: *osanna*</note> cannot pass entirely into another linguistic interpretation. For *Osi* is interpreted as "save"; *anna* is an interjection, signifying a movement of the soul under the feeling of one praying. It is said in its integrity as *osianna*, which we say as *osanna*, having corrupted the middle vowel and struck it out, as happens in verses when we scan them. For the first letter of the following word, coming upon it, excludes the last letter of the prior word. And it is said in Hebrew "Hosanna," which is interpreted as "save," by understanding either "your people" or "the whole world." The "Offertory" <note>original: *offertorium*</note> took its name for such a reason. For an "offering" <note>original: *fertum*</note> is called an oblation which is offered on the altar and sacrificed by the bishops, from which the offertory is named, as if "on account of the offering." It is called an "oblation" <note>original: *oblatio*</note> because it is offered. "Gifts" <note>original: *dona*</note> are properly called the presents of the good. For "services" <note>original: *munera*</note> are called the duties which the poor pay to the rich in place of gifts. Thus, a *munus* is given to a man, but a *donum* <note>gift</note> to God; whence also in temples we speak of "treasuries" <note>original: *donaria*</note>. Services...

<meta>This page continues the definitions of ecclesiastical "offices" and liturgical terms from the previous page, specifically focusing on the distinctions between types of offerings and the nature of the sacraments.</meta>

...but they are called [offices] because they are either received or given by hands. There are two things that are offered: a **gift** and a **sacrifice**. A **gift** <note>original: *donum*</note> is said to be whatever is produced from gold and silver, or any other material form. A **sacrifice** <note>original: *sacrificium*</note>, however, is a victim, and whatever things are burned or placed upon the altar. A gift is that which is given, dedicated, or consecrated to God. How is it dedicated? By being given through speech; from this, it also takes its name <note>The author links *dedicare* (to dedicate) with *dicere* (to speak)</note>. For this reason, those who think **dedication** means the same as **consecration** <margin>prayer</margin> are in error. 

**Immolation** <note>original: *immolatio*</note> was named by the ancients from the fact that the victim was struck down while placed upon the "mound" <note>original: *mola*</note> of the altar; hence, the **slaughter** <note>original: *mactatio*</note> follows the immolation. Now, however, "immolation" is applied to the bread and the chalice. A **libation** <note>original: *libatio*</note>, however, is specifically the offering of the chalice; hence that phrase: "And he offered a libation of the blood of the grape," just as certain of the secular poets say: "Now," he says, "pour libations from the bowls to Jupiter." For "to libate" <note>original: *libare*</note> properly means to pour out, and the name is taken from a certain **Liber** <note>The Roman god Bacchus/Liber, associated with wine</note>, who is found in Greek tradition to be the one who discovered the use of the vine.

Among the ancients, **sacrifices** <note>original: *sacrificia*</note> were called **hosts** <note>original: *hostiae*</note> when they were performed before they went out against an enemy <note>original: *hostis*</note>. But **victims** <note>original: *victimae*</note> were sacrifices immolated after a victory, once the enemies were defeated. And "victims" were greater sacrifices than "hosts." Others have thought a "victim" was so named because it fell struck by a blow <note>original: *ictu*</note>, or because it was led bound to the <margin>altars</margin> altars. A **holocaust** <note>original: *holocaustum*</note> is that where the whole of what is offered is consumed by fire. For when the ancients performed the greatest sacrifices, they used to consume the entire host in the sacred flame; these were the "holocausts." For in Greek, *holo* <note>original: *holo*</note> means "whole," and *caustis* <note>original: *caustis*</note> means "burning" <margin>az</margin>, and thus a "holocaust" is "entirely burned."

Among the Latins, all sacred rites are called **ceremonies** <note>original: *cerimoniae*</note>, which in Greek are called **orgies** <note>original: *orgia*</note>. However, it has specifically seemed to teachers that ceremonies are named from "lacking" <note>original: *carendo*</note>, as if they were "lack-monies" <note>original: *carimonias*</note>, because humans should lack <note>refrain from</note> the use of those things which are offered in divine rites; this name is also in use in the Holy Scriptures. Others believe ceremonies refer specifically to the observances of the Jews, namely the abstinence from certain foods according to the Old Law, because those observing them "lack" or "deprive themselves" of those things from which they abstain.

A **sacrifice** <note>original: *sacrificium*</note> is so named as if it were a "holy deed" <note>original: *sacrum factum*</note>, because it is consecrated by a mystical prayer in memory of the Lord's passion for us. Hence, by the Lord's command, we call it the **Body and Blood of Christ**, which, though it is made from the fruits of the earth, is sanctified and becomes a **sacrament** by the invisible operation of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and chalice the **Eucharist**, which in Latin is interpreted as "good grace" <note>original: *bona gratia*</note>. And what is better than the Body and Blood of Christ?

A **sacrament** exists in a celebration when a deed is done in such a way that it is understood to signify something that must be received holily. The sacraments are **baptism** and **chrism**, and the **Body and Blood of Christ**. These are called sacraments because, under the guidance of physical things, divine power secretly works the salvation of those same sacraments. Whence they are called "sacraments" from their "secret powers" or "sacred" nature. These are performed fruitfully within the Church because the Holy Spirit, remaining in her, secretly works the effect of these same sacraments. Therefore, whether they are dispensed through good or evil ministers within the Church of God, they are valid because the Holy Spirit mystically gives them life—the same Spirit who once, in the time of the Apostles, appeared in visible works. These gifts are not increased by the merits of good dispensers, nor diminished by the bad, because "neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives

<column-break/>

the increase." Whence in Greek it is also called a **mystery** <note>original: *mysterium*</note> because it has a secret and hidden distribution.

**Baptism** <note>original: *baptismus*</note> in Greek is interpreted as "dipping" <note>original: *tinctio*</note> in Latin; it is called a "dipping" because there a person is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace, and becomes something far different than they were. For previously we were foul with the deformity of sins; in that very dipping, we are made beautiful by the "whitening" of virtues. Whence it is written in the Song of Songs: "Who is she that comes up whitened?" <note>Song of Solomon 8:5</note>. This mystery is completed in no other way than under the designation of the Trinity—that is, by the naming of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit—as the Lord said to the Apostles: "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." For just as every word stands on the evidence of three witnesses, so this sacrament is confirmed by the threefold number of divine names. 

As for why baptism is given through water, this is the reason: the Lord willed that an invisible thing should be bestowed through a fitting and perfectly tangible thing—a visible element upon which the Holy Spirit was also carried in the beginning. For just as water cleanses the body externally, so the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit through its mystery. Its sanctification happens thus: when God is invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having medicated the waters, sanctifies them from Himself; they receive the power of cleansing so that in them both the flesh and the soul, defiled by sins, may be cleaned.

**Chrism** <note>original: *chrisma*</note> in Greek is named "anointing" <note>original: *unctio*</note> in Latin, from whose name both "Christ" is called and a person is sanctified after the washing. For just as the remission of sins is given in baptism, so the sanctification of the Spirit is applied through anointing. This is from the ancient discipline by which men used to be anointed into the priesthood and the kingship, from which Aaron was also anointed by Moses. While this is done physically, it is completed spiritually; just as in the grace of baptism itself, the visible act is that we are immersed in water, but the spiritual effect is that we are cleansed of sins. This is signified by that ointment which the sinful woman is described as having poured over the feet of Jesus, and she who is said not to have been a sinner poured over His head.

The **laying on of hands** <note>original: *manus impositio*</note> is done so that the Holy Spirit may be invited and called down through a blessing. For then that Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit as "Comforter" or "Advocate"</note>, after bodies have been cleansed and blessed, willingly descends from the Father; and, recognizing the baptismal water as if it were His original seat, He rests upon it. For we read that in the beginning, the Holy Spirit was carried over the waters.

**Exorcism** <note>original: *exorcismus*</note> in Greek is a "conjuration" <note>original: *coniuratio*</note> or "word of rebuke" in Latin <margin>exorci-smus</margin> against the devil, so that he may depart; as it is in Zechariah: "And he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you." This is exorcism: to rebuke and to conjure against the devil. Whence it should be known that it is not the creature of God in infants that is exorcised or puffed upon, but rather he [the devil] under whom all those who are born in sin are held. For he is the prince of sinners.

**Symbol** <note>original: *symbolum*</note> is interpreted through the Greek language as a "sign" <note>original: *signum*</note> or "knowledge." For the Apostles, when about to depart to preach the Gospel among the nations, established this for themselves as a sign or indication of their preaching. For it contains the confession of the Trinity, the unity of the Church, and all...

<meta>This page continues the definitions of liturgical and ecclesiastical terms. It moves from the nature of sacrifices and offerings to the core disciplines of Christian life: prayer, fasting, and the process of repentance.</meta>

...the sacrament of Christian dogma. This **symbol** <margin>prayer</margin> of our faith and hope is not written with paper and ink, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart. **Prayer** <note>original: *oratio*</note> is called a petition. For to pray is to ask; thus, to obtain by prayer is to prevail. Prayer consists of place and time. Regarding place: because we are not to pray everywhere, since we are forbidden by Christ to pray in public, but rather where opportunity provides or necessity requires. Nor is what was done by the apostles considered to be against this precept, because they prayed and sang to God in prison while the guards listened. Concerning time, however, it is said: "pray without ceasing" <note>original: *sine intermissione orate*</note>; this applies to individuals. For there is an observation of certain common hours which mark the intervals of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth; and similarly for the night. These hours for praying are divided so that if we happen to be detained by some work, the time itself may remind us of our duty. These times are found in the scriptures. For first, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the gathered disciples at the **third hour** <margin>third</margin>. Peter, on the day he experienced the vision of communion in that vessel <margin>sixth</margin>, had ascended to pray at the **sixth hour**. He also, with John, went to the temple at the **ninth hour** <margin>ninth</margin> when he restored the lame man to health. We also read that Daniel observed these times in prayer, surely according to the discipline of Israel, so that we might pray at least three times a day. For we are debtors to three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—excluding, of course, other legitimate prayers which are owed without any reminder at the onset of light and night, or during the vigils. We also ought not to take food before offering a prayer. For the refreshments of the spirit must come first, since heavenly things take precedence over earthly ones. But whoever wishes their prayer to fly to the Lord should give it two wings: **fasting** and **almsgiving**, and it will ascend quickly and be heard. **Fasting** <note>original: *jeiunium*</note> is a life of thrift and abstinence from food; its name is derived from a certain part of the internal organs <note>The author refers to the *jejunum*, a part of the small intestine often found empty during dissection</note> which is always thin and empty, commonly called the "fast." From this, the name for fasting is believed to be derived, because through their hunger the organs remain empty and hollowed out. Fasting <margin>fasting; station</margin> is also called a **station** <note>original: *statio*</note>. The term "station" took its name from a military example, because no joy coming upon the camp breaks the "station" (duty) of the soldiers. For joy administers discipline more willingly, and sorrow more carefully. Hence soldiers, never forgetful of their oath, are more obedient to their stations. Some, however, distinguish between a fast and a station. For a **fast** is the abstinence of any day indifferently, not according to law but according to one's own will. A **station**, however, is the observation of fixed days or times. Of days: such as the fast of the Wednesday and Friday <note>the fourth and sixth days of the week</note>, commanded by ancient law; concerning which "station" that man in the Gospel said: "I fast twice on the Sabbath," that is, on the fourth and sixth days of the week. Of times: those which were established by legal and prophetic institutions at fixed seasons, such as the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months. Or as in the Gospel, the days in which the bridegroom is taken away, or the observation of **Lent** <note>original: *quadragesima*, the forty days</note> which is observed throughout the whole world by apostolic institution, around the time of the Lord’s Passion. To these, some add a third kind, which they call **xerophagy** <note>from the Greek for "dry eating"</note>,

<column-break/>

which is the abstinence from moist foods. From this the name is given, because they use certain dry foods. **Penance** <margin>penance</margin> <note>original: *penitentia*</note> is so named as if it were "punishment-ness" <note>original: *punitentia*</note>, because the person, by repenting, punishes in themselves what they wrongly committed. For those who truly repent do nothing else but ensure that what they did wrongly does not go unpunished. Indeed, in that way, He spares those who do not spare themselves—He whose high and just judgment no despiser escapes. **Perfect penance** is to weep for past sins and not to commit them in the future. This is a second [cleansing] like a fountain; so that if by chance some sin creeps in through the devil's assault, it may be purged by this **satisfaction**. **Satisfaction** <note>original: *satisfactio*</note> is to exclude the causes and suggestions of sins and not to repeat the sin further. **Reconciliation** <note>original: *reconciliatio*</note>, however, is that which is applied after the completion of penance. For just as we are "conciliated" to God when we are first converted from paganism, so we are "reconciled" when we return through penance after a sin. **Exomologesis** is the Greek word for what is interpreted in Latin as **confession** <margin>confession</margin>. This name has a double meaning. For confession is understood either in **praise**, such as: "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth," or when someone confesses their own sins to be forgiven by Him whose mercy is unfailing. Therefore, from this Greek word, "exomologesis" is expressed and frequently used, by which we confess our fault to the Lord—not indeed as if to one who is ignorant, for nothing is hidden from His knowledge—but confession is the acknowledged awareness of a matter by one who previously ignored it. For one might have thought it useful and pleasant to snatch, to commit adultery, or to steal; but once they realize these things are liable to eternal damnation, having learned this, they confess their error. The **confession** <margin>confession</margin> of error is the profession of ceasing [the act]. Therefore, one must determine to leave sins behind while there is confession. Confession precedes; forgiveness follows. Otherwise, he who knows his sin but does not confess it when known is beyond pardon. Thus, **exomologesis** is the discipline of prostrating and humbling a man, in habit and food: to lie in sackcloth and ashes, to darken the body with filth, to cast down the soul with sorrows, and to change those things in which one sinned by a mournful treatment. **Litanies** <margin>litany</margin> <note>original: *letaniae*</note> is the Greek name for what in Latin are called **rogations** <note>original: *rogationes*, meaning "askings" or "petitions"</note>. The difference between litanies and *exomologesis* is this: *exomologesis* is performed for the confession of sins alone, while **litanies** are said for the sake of asking the Lord and obtaining His mercy in some matter. But now both words are held under a single meaning, and there is no common distinction whether they are called litanies or *exomologesis*. The name **supplication** <note>original: *supplicatio*</note> is in a way retained from paganism. For among them, festivals were either statutory or proclaimed. They were "proclaimed" <note>original: *indictae*</note> because the ancient poverty of the Romans meant they sacrificed either from a collection or certainly from the goods of the condemned. From this, **punishments** <note>original: *supplicia*</note> are called **supplications**, which were made from the goods of those who suffered punishment. For sacred things were made from the property of those who were accursed.

**Prayer, Fasting, Station, Penance, Confession, Exomologesis, Litany, Supplication**

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Christian rituals and repentance to a theological examination of the nature of God, specifically focusing on the names and attributes of the Divine as understood through linguistic study.</meta>

->The Seventh Book Begins<-
->Chapter 1: On God<-

<margin>b</margin>
The most blessed Jerome, a man of great learning and skilled in many languages, was the first to translate the interpretation of Hebrew names into the Latin language. Leaving many of these out for the sake of brevity, I have sought to include certain interpretations in this work. For the explanation of words sufficiently indicates what they wish to be understood. Some names, indeed, have their reasoning based on specific causes. At the start, however, we set down ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

<margin>mighty</margin>
The first name of God among the Hebrews is said to be **El**, which some interpret as "God," and others—expressing its etymology—as **Ischyros**, that is, "Mighty" <note>original: *ischyros*, Greek: ἰσχυρός</note>. This is because He is pressed by no weakness, but is strong and sufficient to accomplish all things. The second name is **Eloi**.

<margin>eloe</margin>
The third is **Eloe**, both of which are called "God" in Latin. However, the name in Latin is translated from a Greek designation. For God is called *Theos* in Greek, as if from <term>δέος (deos)</term>, which means **fear** <note>The author is following a traditional (though linguistically debated) etymology linking the Greek word for God to the word for fear</note>. From this is drawn the name "God," because there should be fear in those who worship Him. "God," however, is properly the name of the Trinity, pertaining to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. To this Trinity, the remaining names of God placed below also refer.

<margin>sabaoth</margin>
The fourth name of God is said to be **Sabaoth**, which is translated into Latin as "of hosts" or "of powers" <note>original: *exercituum sive virtutum*</note>. Concerning this, it is said by the angels in the Psalm: "Who is this King of Glory? The Lord of powers." In such an ordering, there are many "powers," such as angels, archangels, principalities, and authorities, and all the ranks of the heavenly militia, of whom He is nevertheless the Lord. For all are under Him and subject to His lordship.

<margin>elion</margin>
The fifth name is **Elion**, which is translated into Latin as "Most High" <note>original: *excelsus*</note>, because He is above the heavens. Thus it is written of Him: "The Lord is most high: His glory is above the heavens." He is called "Most High" <note>original: *excelsus*</note> as if for "exceedingly high." For *el* is placed for "very," just as we might say "very eminent."

<margin>ehyeh</margin>
The sixth name is **Eieie** <note>Ehyeh</note>, which means "He who is." For God alone, because He is eternal—that is, because He has no beginning—truly holds the name of "Essence." For this name was brought to Saint Moses by an angel. For when he asked what was the name of Him who commanded him to go to the people to deliver them from Egypt, He responded:

<margin>He who is</margin>
"I am who I am," and "You shall say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you." In comparison to Him who truly *is*—because He is unchangeable—those things which were made changeable are as if they are not. For that which is said to have "been" no longer is. That which is said "will be" is not yet. God, however, knows only "to be"; He does not know having been or being in the future. Only the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit truly *is*. Compared to His essence, our "being" is "not being." Whence in conversation we say, "God lives," because Essence lives in a way that death does not possess.

<margin>adonay</margin>
The seventh is **Adonay**, which is generally interpreted as "Lord," because He rules over every creature, or because every creature serves His lordship. He is therefore "Lord" and "God," either because He rules over all or because He is feared by all.

<column-break/>

<margin>8. ia</margin>
The eighth is **Ia**, which is applied to God alone, and which also sounds in the final syllable of **Alleluia**.

<margin>9. tetragrammaton</margin>
The ninth is the **Tetragrammaton**, that is, "of four letters," which is properly applied to God among the Hebrews: *Yod, He, Waw, He* <note>The OCR reads "iode, iode," but the author refers to the four-letter Name of God (YHWH)</note>. These duplicated letters make up that ineffable and glorious name of God.

<margin>ineffable</margin>
He is called **ineffable**, however, not because He cannot be spoken of, but because He can in no way be defined by human sense and intellect; and because nothing can be said of Him that is worthy of Him, He is ineffable.

<margin>10. sadday (almighty)</margin>
The tenth is **Saddai**, that is, "Almighty." He is called Almighty because He can do all things, and because His power comes from doing what He wills, not from suffering what He does not will. If that were to happen to Him, He would by no means be almighty. For He does whatever He wills, and is almighty for that reason. Likewise, He is almighty because all things everywhere are His. For He alone holds command over the whole world. Certain other names are also spoken of God according to His substance, such as immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable, and eternal, whence He is rightly set before all creation.

<margin>immortal</margin>
**Immortal**, as it is written of Him: "Who alone has immortality," because in His nature there is no change. For all mutability is not inappropriately called "mortality," according to which the soul is also said to die—not because it is changed or turned into a body or some other substance, but because in its very substance, whatever it is now or was in another way, it is found to be mortal in that it ceases to be what it was. And for this reason God alone is called immortal, because He alone is unchangeable.

<margin>incorruptible</margin>
He is called **incorruptible** because He cannot be corrupted, dissolved, or divided. For whatever admits division also admits destruction. He can neither be divided nor perish; therefore He is incorruptible.

<margin>un-changeable</margin>
He is **unchangeable** because He remains forever and does not know how to be changed. He does not progress because He is perfect, nor does He fail because He is eternal.

<margin>eternal</margin>
He is **eternal** because He is outside of time <note>original: *sine tempore est*</note>. For He has neither beginning nor end.

<margin>everlasting</margin>
Hence He is also **everlasting** <note>original: *sempiternus*</note>, because He is always eternal. Some believe "eternal" is named after the "ether," just as the heaven holds His seat, whence it is said: "The heaven of heavens is the Lord's." These four terms signify one thing. For one and the same thing is expressed whether He is called eternal, God, immortal, incorruptible, or unchangeable.

<margin>invisible</margin>
He is called **invisible** because the Trinity has never appeared to the eyes of mortals through its own substance, but only through the form of a subject creature or a bodily appearance. For no one can see the very majesty of the essence of God and live, just as was said to Moses. Whence John also says in his epistle: "No one has ever seen God." For the reality is invisible, and therefore He is to be sought not with the eye but with the heart.

<margin>impassible</margin>
He is **impassible** because He is affected by no disturbances to which human fragility succumbs. For no passions reach Him, such as lust, anger, greed, fear, sorrow, envy, and the rest by which the human mind is troubled. When God is said to be "angry" or "jealous" or "grieved," it is said according to our human usage. For in God there is no disturbance; in Him there is the highest tranquility.

<margin>simple</margin>
He is called **simple**, either because He does not lose what He has, or because He Himself is not one thing and what is in Him another—as in a human, whose "being" is one thing and "being wise" is another. For a human can both *be* and *not be wise*. God, however, possesses...

<summary>This page explores the various names of God in Hebrew and their Latin interpretations, as well as the essential attributes of the Divine nature, such as immortality, eternity, and simplicity. It emphasizes that while human language uses many terms, God's essence remains a single, unchangeable, and ineffable reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine names and attributes, moving from the ten names of God in the Hebrew tradition to the nature of His essence, and then specifically to the titles and nature of the Son of God.</meta>

essence. He also has wisdom; what He has, He also is.
And He is one in all things. Therefore He is simple <note>In a theological sense, "simple" means indivisible and not made of parts</note>, because there is nothing of an accidental nature in Him. What He is, and what is in Him, is essentially His, except for those things which are said relatively to any of the Persons <note>Referring to the relationships between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>.
<margin>the highest good</margin>
He is the **highest good**, because He is unchangeable. A **creature**, however, is a good, but not the highest, because it is changeable. And although a creature may indeed be good, it can never be the highest good.
<margin>incorporeal</margin>
God is also called **incorporeal** or **incorporeal**, 
<margin>immense</margin>
so that He may be believed or understood to be a spirit, not a body. For 
<margin>eternal</margin>
when He is called a "spirit," His substance is signified. He is **immense**, because He encompasses all things, and He Himself is encompassed by nothing. Here, all things are confined within His omnipotence. He is called **perfect**, because nothing can be added to Him. However, "perfection" is usually spoken of regarding the completion of some deed. But how can God, who was not made, be "perfected"? Yet, human deficiency has taken this term from our own usage, just like other words, so that what is inexpressible may be spoken of in some way or another. For human speech says nothing of God worthily. There are others of this kind: He is called **Creator** because of the things of the whole world created by Him. For there is nothing that has not drawn its origin from God. He is also **one**, because He cannot be divided, or because nothing else can exist that possesses as much power. Therefore, these things said about God pertain to the entire Trinity, because of the one and co-eternal substance, whether in the Father, or in His only-begotten Son in the form of God, or in the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of God the Father and His only-begotten Son.
<margin>Concerning the unvarying God, such terms are never taken from physical members</margin>
There are also certain terms taken from our own usage and applied to God, such as terms for our limbs or lower parts. Because in His own nature He is invisible and incorporeal, the appearances of things are ascribed to Him according to the effects of His causes, so that He may more easily introduce Himself to us through our manner of speaking. Thus, because He sees all, He is called an **eye**; because He hears all, an **ear**. Because He turns away, He is said to **walk**; because He waits, He **stands**. So it is in other similar cases; a likeness to God is drawn from human minds, such as His being **forgetful** or **remembering**. Hence the prophet also says: "The Lord of hosts has sworn by His soul" <note>Amos 6:8</note>, not because God has a soul, but He speaks this according to our human emotion.
<margin>The face of God is knowledge; God Himself is invisible</margin>
For the **face of God** in the Holy Scriptures is understood not as flesh, but as divine knowledge, for the same reason that anyone is recognized by their face when seen. This is why it is said to God in prayer: "Show us Your face," as if to say: "Give us Your knowledge." In the same way, the **footsteps** of God are mentioned, because now God is recognized "through a mirror" <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note>. Indeed, the Almighty looks toward perfection, when in the future He will present Himself **face to face** to His chosen ones so that they may contemplate that very form whose footsteps they now strive to grasp—that is, the one they are said to see "through a mirror." For **posture, clothing, place, and time** are not spoken of properly in God, but metaphorically through likeness. For He is said to "sit upon the cherubim," which pertains to posture; and the "abyss is like a garment," which pertains to clothing; and "Your years shall not fail," which pertains to time; and "If I ascend into heaven, You are there," which pertains to place. For even in the prophet, the appearance of a "wagon carrying hay" <note>Amos 2:13</note> is applied to God. All these things are said through figures of God, because nothing is equal to the proper nature of His substance.

## Chapter II: On the Son of God

<margin>Christ</margin>
**C**hrist is found to be called by many names in the divine Scriptures. For while He was the only-begotten Son of God the Father and equal to the Father, He took on the form of a servant for our salvation. Therefore, some names in Him are from the substance of His divinity, and some are assumed from the dispensation of His taken humanity. He is called **Christ** from "charisma,"
<margin>anointed</margin>
which is to say, "the Anointed One." For a command had been given to the Jews to prepare a sacred ointment with which those who were called to the priesthood or the kingdom could be anointed. And just as now the garment of purple is the sign of royal dignity for kings, so for them the anointing of the sacred oil conferred the name and power of a king. From this, they were called **christs**
<margin>anointed</margin>
from "charisma," which is anointing. For *charisma* is the Greek name, called *unctio* in Latin. This name was also accommodated to the Lord, made spiritual, because He was anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, as it says in the Acts of the Apostles: "For they were gathered in this city against Your holy Son whom You anointed" <note>Acts 4:27</note>—not anointed with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, which is signified by visible ointment. However, "Christ" is not the
<margin>Christ</margin>
proper name of the Savior, but a common designation of His power. For when "Christ" is said, it is a common name of dignity; when "Jesus Christ" is said, it is the proper name of the Savior.
<margin>m...</margin>
For the name of Christ was nowhere else at all, nor in any
<margin>Jesus...</margin>
nation, except only in that kingdom where Christ was prophesied and from whence He was to come. **Messiah**, moreover, is the Hebrew word, in Greek it is **Christ**, and in the Latin tongue **Anointed**. **Jesus** in Hebrew is **Soter** in Greek, and in Latin is interpreted as **Salvator** (Savior) 
<margin>Jesus b.</margin>
or **Salutaris** (Healer), because He came as the bringer of salvation to all
<margin>Christ...</margin>
nations. For even the Evangelist signifies the etymology of this name, saying: "You shall call His name Savior, for He Himself shall save His people" <note>Matthew 1:21</note>.
<margin>Jesus...</margin>
For just as "Christ" signifies a King, so "Jesus" signifies a Savior. Therefore, it is not just any king who saves us, but this King is the Savior. The Latin language previously 
<margin>salv...</margin>
did not have the word *Salvator*, but it was able to have it, just as it could when it wished. **Emmanuel** from Hebrew into Latin signifies "God with us," namely because God, born of the virgin, appeared to men in mortal flesh so that He might open the way of salvation to heaven for those on earth. Those things which pertain to the substance of His
<margin>Emmanuel...</margin>
divinity are these: **Lord** and **God**. He is called
<margin>God...</margin>
**God** because of His substance being one with the Father.
<margin>man...</margin>
He is called **Lord** because of the creation that serves Him. He is also **God and man**,
<margin>the Word...</margin>
because He is the Word and the flesh. Whence He is also said to be **twice born**: either because the Father begat Him without a mother in eternity, or because His mother begat Him without a father in time. He is called **Only-begotten**
<margin>q...</margin>
according to the excellence of His divinity, because He is without brothers; He is the **First-born** according to the taking up of man, in which He deigned to have brothers through the grace of adoption, among whom He would be the first-born. He is called **Omousion** <note>original: *Omousion*, Greek: ὁμοούσιος (homoousios)</note> with the Father, from the unity of substance. For "substance" or "essence" is called *ousia* in Greek, and *homo* means "one." Therefore, both joined together sound as "one substance." For this is called *homoousion*, which is: "I and the Father are one" <note>John 10:30</note>; that is, of the same substance with the Father. And even if this name is not found written in the Holy Scriptures, it is nevertheless defended in the assertion of the entire Trinity, because the reason is given why it is shown to be rightly said.
