Just as the Father is nowhere read to be "unbegotten" <note>original: *ingenitus*</note> in those books <note>referring to the canonical scriptures</note>, He must nevertheless be so described and believed without doubt.
**Consubstantial** <note>original: *Omousion*</note> means "of the same substance"; for such as God is, 
<margin>image</margin> such also is His **image**. God is invisible, and His **image** is invisible. 
<margin>beginning</margin> **Beginning** <note>original: *principium*</note>, because from Him are all things, and 
<margin>end</margin> because before Him there is nothing. **End**, either because He deigned to be humbly born in the flesh and die at the **end** of time, and to undertake the final judgment Himself, or because whatever we do, we refer back to Him. And when we have reached Him, 
<margin>word</margin> we will have nothing further to seek. He is the **Mouth** of God, because He is His **Word** <note>original: *verbum*</note>. For just as we often say "that and that tongue" <note>referring to languages</note> to mean the things done through the "word" of the tongue, so also the "mouth" is used for the Word of God, because it is the custom for words to be formed by the mouth. He is called the **Word**, however, because through Him the Father established or commanded all things. 
<margin>truth</margin> **Truth**, because He does not deceive, but grants what 
<margin>life</margin> He promised. **Life**, because He created. **Image** of God, because of the 
<margin>image</margin> equal likeness to the Father. He is the **Figure**, because taking on the 
<margin>figure</margin> form of a servant, He marked out the riches and the power of the likeness of the Father, and His image and immense magnitude within Himself. 
<margin>hand</margin> He is the **Hand** of God, because all things were made through Him. Hence 
<margin>right hand</margin> also the **Right Hand**, because of the effect of the work of the whole creation which 
<margin>arm</margin> was formed through Him. **Arm**, because all things are contained by Him. 
<margin>power</margin> **Power** <note>original: *virtus*</note>, for the reason that He holds all the authority of the Father within Himself, and governs, contains, and rules every creature of heaven and earth. **Wisdom**, 
<margin>wisdom</margin> for the reason that He Himself reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. But nevertheless, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom and power, and radiance and light, He is nevertheless called by these names as the Son. He is called **Splendor**, however, 
<margin>light</margin> because of what He makes manifest. **Radiance** <note>original: *lumen*</note>, because He illuminates. **Light** <note>original: *lux*</note>, because He directs the eyes of the heart toward contemplating the truth. 
<margin>sun</margin> **Sun**, because He illuminates all. **Rising** <note>original: *oriens*</note>, because He is the source 
<margin>rising</margin> of light and the illustrator of things, and because He makes us rise to 
<margin>fountain</margin> eternal life. **Fountain**, because He is the origin of all things, or because He satisfies those who thirst. He is the **Alpha and Omega**. For no letter 
<margin>Alpha and Omega</margin> precedes the letter Alpha. For it is the first letter, just as is the Son of God. For He Himself answered the Jews when they questioned Him that He was the "Beginning." Hence also John in the Apocalypse, placing that very letter for Himself, says: "I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last." 
<margin>first and last</margin> **First**, because nothing is before Him. **Last**, because He Himself will undertake the final judgment. **Mediator**, 
<margin>mediator</margin> because He was established in the middle between God and man so that He might lead man to God. Hence the Greeks also call Him the **Mediator** <note>original: *mesiten*</note>. **Paraclete** <note>original: *paraclitus*</note>, that is, **Advocate**, because 
<margin>paraclete</margin> He intercedes for us with the Father, just as John says of Him: "We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." **Paraclete** is a Greek word, which in Latin is called **Advocate**. This name is ascribed to both the Son and the Holy Spirit, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: "I will 
<margin>intercessor</margin> ask the Father and He will give you another Paraclete." He is called **Intercessor**, however, because He takes care to remove our guilt, and bestows care for the washing away of our crimes. 
<margin>bridegroom</margin> **Bridegroom**, because descending from heaven, He adhered to the Church, so that by the peace of the New Testament they might be "two in one flesh." 
<margin>angel</margin> He is called **Angel**, because of the announcement of His Father's and His own will. Hence we also read in the prophet of the "Angel of Great Counsel," though He is God and the Lord of 
<margin>sent</margin> angels. He is called the **Sent One**, because He appeared to this 

<column-break/>

world as the **Word made flesh**. Whence also He says: "I went out from the 
<margin>man</margin> Father and came into this world." He is called **Man**, because 
<margin>prophet</margin> He was born. **Prophet**, because He revealed future things. 
<margin>priest</margin> **Priest**, because He offered Himself as a sacrifice for us. **Shepherd**, 
<margin>shepherd</margin> because He is a guardian. **Teacher**, because He is a shower of the way. 
<margin>teacher</margin> <margin>nazarene</margin> **Nazarene** from the place; **Nazaraean** from merit, that is, holy or pure, because He did no sin. Indeed, Christ draws types of names to Himself even from other lower things, so that He may be more easily understood. For He is called **Bread**, and **Flesh**. 
<margin>bread</margin> <margin>vine</margin> <margin>flower</margin> **Vine**, because we are redeemed by His blood. **Flower**, 
<margin>way</margin> <margin>door</margin> <margin>mountain</margin> because He is chosen. **Way**, because through Him we journey to the Lord. **Door**, 
<margin>rock</margin> <margin>stone</margin> because through Him we enter to the Lord. **Mountain**, because He is strong. **Rock** <note>original: *petra*</note>, because He is the firmness of believers. **Cornerstone**, either because He joins two walls from different directions—that is, coming from the circumcision <note>referring to the Jewish people</note> and the uncircumcision <note>referring to the Gentiles</note>—into one building of the Church, or because He 
<margin>stone of stumbling</margin> makes peace between the Gospels and men. **Stone of stumbling**, because coming humbly, unbelieving men stumbled against Him. And He became a "rock of offense," as the Apostle says: "Indeed, a scandal to the 
<margin>foundation</margin> Jews." He is called **Foundation**, however, because faith is most firm in Him, or because the Catholic Church is constructed upon Him. 
<margin>lamb</margin> <margin>sheep</margin> <margin>ram</margin> For Christ is also a **Lamb** for His innocence; a **Sheep** 
<margin>calf</margin> for His patience; a **Ram** for His leadership; a 
**Goat** <note>original: *hedus*</note> for the likeness of sinful flesh; a **Calf**, because He was sacrificed for us; a **Lion**, for His kingship 
<margin>lion</margin> <margin>serpent</margin> <margin>worm</margin> and strength; and a **Serpent**, for death and wisdom. Likewise, 
<margin>eagle</margin> a **Worm**, because He rose again. **Eagle**, because after the resurrection He returned to the stars. Nor is it strange if He is figured by lowly meanings, He who is known to have descended even to the insults of our passions or of the flesh. Who, though He is the co-eternal Son of God the Father before the ages, after the "fullness of time" came, for our salvation He took the "form of a servant." And the Son of God was made the Son of Man. Hence certain things are said about Him in the Holy Scriptures according to the **form of God**, and certain things according to the **form of a servant**. For the sake of example, two such things are mentioned, so that each may be referred to its own context. According to the **form of God**, He says of Himself: "I and the Father are one." According to the **form of a servant**: "Because the Father is greater than I." Men, however, understanding poorly which thing is said for what purpose, wish to transfer those things which were said because of the "form of a servant" to the "form of God." And again, those things which were said so that the Persons <note>of the Trinity</note> might be referred to each other, they wish to be names of nature and substance, and thus they create an error in the faith. Thus, however, the human nature was joined to the Son of God, so that from two substances one Person was made. Therefore, the man alone bore the cross, yet because of the unity of the person, even God is said to have borne it. This is why it is written: "For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." For we confess the Son of God was crucified, not from the power of His divinity, but from the weakness of His humanity; not from the permanence of His own nature, but from our reception <note>referring to the human nature He took on</note>.

### On the Holy Spirit Chapter III.

The **Holy Spirit** is preached as God because He proceeds from the Father and the Son, and has their substance. For nothing else could proceed from the Father except that which the Father Himself is. He is called the "Holy Spirit," however, according to that which refers to something "breathing" <note>the Latin *spiritus* is derived from *spirare*, to breathe</note>.

<summary>This page provides an extensive catalog of the symbolic and theological names for Jesus Christ—such as Word, Light, Alpha and Omega, and Lamb—explaining their scriptural significance and the relationship between Christ's divine and human natures. It concludes by defining the Holy Spirit as being of the same substance as the Father and Son.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of divine names and roles, moving from the attributes of the Son to the nature and titles of the Holy Spirit. # Book

<margin>The Holy Spirit is a spirit; your name is through... <note>original: "sps sanctus ē spū nōmen tuus per m..."</note></margin>
He is called "Spirit" because He is surely breathing <note>original: *spirans*</note> and inspiring. In a particular way, He is called the **Holy Spirit**, according to how He relates to the Father and the Son, because He is their Spirit. For this name "Spirit" is not always used in a way that refers to His relationship to another, but is sometimes understood as signifying His very nature. Indeed, an incorporeal nature is called "spirit" in the Holy Scriptures. Hence, this term fits not only the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but also every rational creature and the soul. Therefore, He is called the **Holy Spirit of God** because He is the holiness of both the Father and the Son. For since the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, He is nevertheless properly called the **Holy Spirit**, as the co-essential and consubstantial <note>sharing the same fundamental essence or "stuff"</note> holiness of them both.
The Holy Spirit is not said to be "begotten," <note>original: *genitus*</note> lest two sons be suspected in the Trinity. Neither is He proclaimed "unbegotten," <note>original: *ingenitus*</note> lest two fathers be believed in that same Trinity. Instead, He is said to "proceed," <note>original: *procedens*</note> by the testimony of the Lord who says:
> I have many things yet to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. However, when the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father, He will receive from what is mine and will declare it all to you. <note>referring to John 16:12-14</note>
In this case, He does not only proceed by nature, but He always proceeds unfailingly to carry out the works of the Godhead. Now, this is the difference between the Son being "born" and the Holy Spirit "proceeding": the Son is born from one <note>the Father</note>, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. And therefore the Apostle says: *But he who does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His.* <note>Romans 8:9</note>
<margin>Angel: two angels to Lot</margin>
The Holy Spirit is also understood as an **Angel** <note>meaning "messenger"</note>. For it was said of Him: "And He will announce to you the things that are to come." And certainly, "angel" in Greek is translated as "messenger" <note>original: *nuncius*</note> in Latin. Hence, two angels appeared to Lot, in whom the Lord is addressed in the singular; we understand these to be the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Father is never read to have been "sent."
<margin>Paraclete</margin>
The Holy Spirit is also called the **Paraclete**, named from "consolation." For *Paraclisis* in Greek is called "consolation" <note>original: *consolatio*</note> in Latin. Indeed, Christ sent Him to the grieving Apostles after He Himself ascended into heaven from their sight. For a Comforter <note>original: *consolator*</note> is sent to those who are sad, according to that sentence of the same Lord:
> Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
He also says:
> Then the children of the bridegroom will mourn, when the bridegroom has been taken away from them.
<margin>Paraclete, that is, the orator</margin>
Likewise, He is the Paraclete because He provides consolation to souls who lose temporal joy. Others interpret "Paraclete" in Latin as **Orator** or **Advocate**. For the Holy Spirit Himself is said to speak and to teach; through Him the word of wisdom is given, and by Him the Holy Scripture was inspired.
<margin>The sevenfold Spirit</margin>
The Holy Spirit is called **Sevenfold** because of the gifts which those who are worthy merit to receive in parts from His united fullness. For He is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. <note>These are the traditional seven gifts of the Holy Spirit from Isaiah 11</note> Furthermore, the **Principal Spirit** is read of in the fiftieth Psalm, where, because "spirit" is repeated three times, some have understood the Trinity in God. For it is written: "God is a spirit." That which is not a body, and yet exists, is seen to remain as a spirit. Some therefore understand the Trinity to be signified there: the Father in the "principal spirit," the Son in the "right spirit," and the Holy Spirit in the "holy spirit." The Holy Spirit is also called a **Gift** <note>original: *donum*</note> because He is given. He is named a gift from the act of giving. For it is very well known that the Lord Jesus Christ, when He had ascended into heaven after

<column-break/>

His resurrection from the dead, gave the Holy Spirit, by whom the believers were filled and spoke in the tongues of all nations. He is "God's gift" insofar as He is given to those who love God through Him. In Himself, He is God; with us, He is a Gift. Indeed, the Holy Spirit is an eternal Gift, distributing the gifts of graces to individuals just as He wills. For He imparts prophecies to whom He wills, and He dismisses sins for whom He wills. For sins are not forgiven without the Holy Spirit.
The Holy Spirit is therefore properly called **Charity** <note>original: *charitas*; divine love</note>, either because He naturally joins those from whom He proceeds and shows Himself to be one with them, or because He works this in us: that we may abide in God and He in us. Hence, among the gifts of God, nothing is greater than charity, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit. He is also **Grace**, which is so named because it is given freely <note>original: *gratis*</note>, not by our merits but by the divine will. Just as we properly call the unique Word of God by the name of **Wisdom**, though the Holy Spirit and the Father Himself are universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name of **Charity**, though the Father and the Son are universally charity.
The Holy Spirit is most clearly declared to be the **Finger of God** in the books of the Gospels. For when one Evangelist said: "By the finger of God I cast out demons," another said the same thing this way: "By the Spirit of God I cast out demons." <note>Comparing Luke 11:20 and Matthew 12:28</note> Hence also the written Law was given by the "finger of God" on the fiftieth day from the slaying of the lamb <note>Passover</note>, and on the fiftieth day from the Passion of the Lord, the Holy Spirit came <note>Pentecost</note>. He is called the "finger of God" so that His operative power may be signified together with the Father and the Son; hence Paul also says:
> One and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each one as He wills.
Just as we die and are reborn in Christ through baptism, so we are sealed by the Spirit, who is the "finger of God" and a special seal.
The Holy Spirit is written to have come in the **form of a dove** so that His nature might be declared through a bird of simplicity and innocence. Hence the Lord said:
> Be simple as doves.
For this bird physically lacks gall <note>bitterness</note>, possessing only innocence and love.
The Holy Spirit is named by the term **Fire** because of the fact that in the Acts of the Apostles, He appeared through the division of tongues like fire, which sat upon each of them. He gave the grace of diverse languages to the Apostles so that they might be made fit for the instruction of faithful peoples. As for the record that it "sat upon each of them," the reason is so it may be understood that He was not divided among many, but remained whole in each person. This is much like the nature of fires; for a lit fire has this quality: however many look toward it or its purple-splendid glow, it imparts the sight of its light to all of them and grants the service of its gift to all, while it nevertheless remains in its own integrity.
The Holy Spirit is called by the name of **Water** in the Gospel, as the Lord cried out saying:
> If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.
The Evangelist explained what He was talking about, following with:
> But He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in Him were to receive.
However, the water of the sacrament is one thing; the water that signifies the Spirit of God is another. For the water of the sacrament...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Holy Spirit's role in the soul's purification, transitioning into a formal definition of the Trinity as a "tri-unity." is visible; the water of the Holy Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what happens in the soul; through that Holy Spirit, however, the soul itself is cleansed and nourished. The Spirit is also called an **anointing** <note>original: *unctio*</note>, as the apostle John testifies. Just as oil by its natural weight floats above every other liquid, so in the beginning the Holy Spirit hovered over the waters. Thus, the Lord is read to have been "anointed with the oil of gladness," which is the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, the apostle John calls the Holy Spirit an "anointing," saying: "And as for you, let the anointing which you have received from Him remain in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but as His anointing teaches you concerning all things." For the Holy Spirit Himself is the invisible anointing.

### On the same Trinity. Chapter 4.

The **Trinity** is so named because a whole is made one from a certain three, as if it were a "tri-unity"—such as memory, intelligence, and will, in which the mind possesses within itself a certain image of the divine Trinity. For while these are three, they are one, because they both remain individually in themselves and all are in all. Therefore, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are both a Trinity and a Unity. They are the same one thing, and the same three things: one in nature, three in persons. One because of the communion of majesty; three because of the property of the persons. For the Father is one, the Son is another, and the Holy Spirit is another; yet they are "another" <note>referring to distinct persons</note> but not "another thing" <note>referring to their shared substance</note>, because they are equally simple, equally immutable, good, and co-eternal. The Father alone is not from another; therefore He alone is called **unbegotten** <note>original: *ingenitus*</note>. The Son alone is born from the Father; therefore He alone is called **begotten** <note>original: *genitus*</note>. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son; therefore He alone is named the Spirit of them both.

In this Trinity, some names are appellative <note>descriptive titles</note> and others are proper <note>essential names</note>. Proper names are essential, such as **God**, **Lord**, **Almighty**, **Immutable**, and **Immortal**. They are "proper" because they signify the very substance by which the Three are one. However, "Father," "Son," and "Holy Spirit," "unbegotten," "begotten," and "proceeding," are appellative. These are also relative names because they refer to one another. For when "God" is said, it refers to His essence (what He is in Himself); but when "Father," "Son," and "Holy Spirit" are said, they are spoken relatively, as they refer to one another. For "Father" is not said in reference to Himself, but relatively to the Son, because He has a Son; likewise, "Son" is said relatively because He has a Father; and "Holy Spirit" because He is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. By these titles, it is signified that they refer to one another, not to the substance itself by which they are one. Consequently, the Trinity exists in the relative names of the persons. The **Godhead** is not tripled but exists in singularity; for if it were tripled, we would be introducing a plurality of gods.

The name "gods" is used in the plural for angels and holy men, because they are not equal by merit. Concerning them the Psalm says: "I have said, you are gods." But regarding the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, it is shown to be not the name of "gods," but of "God." As the Apostle says: "Yet for us there is one God." Or as it is said by the divine voice: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." This is so that there may be both a Trinity and one Lord God. Among the Greeks, the faith concerning the Trinity is expressed this way: one *ousia* <note>original: *vsia* (Greek: οὐσία)</note>, as if one were to say one nature or one essence; and three *hypostases* <note>original: *hypostases* (Greek: ὑποστάσεις)</note>, which

<column-break/>

translates into Latin as either "three persons" or "three substances." However, the Latin language does not properly speak of "substance" regarding God except in an imprecise way; for among the Greeks, "substance" is properly understood as "person," not "nature."

### On Angels. Chapter 5.

They are called **Angels** in Greek, **Malaoth** <note>original: *malaoth* (Hebrew: malakhim)</note> in Hebrew, and are interpreted as **Messengers** <note>original: *nuncij*</note> in Latin. This is because they announce the will of the Lord to the people. The word "Angel," however, is a name of office, not of nature; for they are always spirits, but when they are sent, they are called angels. Because of this, the artistic license of painters gives them wings, to signify their swift movement through all things, just as in the fables of the poets the winds are said to have wings because of their speed. Hence Holy Scripture says: "He who walks upon the wings of the winds."

Holy Scriptures testify that there are nine orders of angels: namely, **Angels**, **Archangels**, **Thrones**, **Dominions**, **Virtues**, **Principalities**, **Powers**, **Cherubim**, and **Seraphim**. We shall follow by interpreting why the names of their offices are so called.

They are called **Angels** because they are sent from the heavens to announce things to men. For "Angel" in Greek is called "Messenger" in Latin. **Archangels** in the Greek tongue are interpreted as "Highest Messengers" in Latin. For those who announce small or minor things are called angels; those who announce the highest things are named archangels. They are called Archangels because they hold primacy among the angels; for *Archos* in Greek is interpreted as "Prince" in Latin. They are leaders and princes, under whose order the duties of each of the angels are assigned. That archangels preside over angels is testified by the prophet Zechariah, saying: "And behold, the angel who talked with me went forth, and another angel went forth to meet him, and said to him: Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls." For if superior powers did not direct the inferior ones within these angelic offices, the angel would by no means have known from another angel what he was to say to the man.

<margin>Michael</margin>
Certain archangels are called by private names, so that through the names themselves, their power in their work may be designated. **Michael** in Hebrew is translated into our language as "Who is like God?" For whenever something of wondrous power is done in the world, this archangel is sent. His name comes from the work itself, because no one is able to do what God prevails in doing.

<margin>Gabriel</margin>
**Gabriel** is interpreted as "Strength of God." For where divine power or strength is manifested, Gabriel is sent. Hence, at that time when the Lord was to be born and to triumph over the world, Gabriel was sent to Mary to announce Him who deigned to come as a humble man to defeat the powers of the air.

<margin>Raphael</margin>
**Raphael** is interpreted as "Healing" or "Medicine of God." For wherever a work of curing and healing is necessary, this archangel is sent by God, and hence he is called the medicine of God. Thus, this same archangel was sent to Tobias and applied healing to his eyes, restoring his sight after his old blindness. By the interpretation of the name, the office of the angel is designated.

<margin>Uriel</margin>
**Uriel** is interpreted as "Fire [of God]..."

of God. Just as we read that fire appeared in the bush. We also read that fire was sent from above and fulfilled what was commanded. However, **Thrones**, **Dominations**, **Principalities**, **Powers**, and **Virtues**—by which the Apostle <note>referring to St. Paul</note> encompasses the entire heavenly society—are understood as the orders and dignities of angels. Through a peaceful distribution of duties, some are called Thrones, others Dominations, others Principalities, and others Powers, distinguished from one another by certain ranks. The **Virtues** are said to be certain angelic ministries through which signs and miracles are performed in the world; for this reason, they are called "Virtues" <note>original: *virtutes*, meaning powers or strengths</note>. The **Powers** are those to whom the adverse powers <note>demons</note> are subject; they are called by the name of Powers because the malignant spirits are restrained by their authority, lest they harm the world as much as they desire. The **Principalities** are those who preside over the ranks of angels. Because they organize the subordinate angels to fulfill the divine ministry, they received the name "Principalities." For some are those who administer, and others are those who assist, just as it is said through the prophet Daniel: "Thousands of thousands ministered to Him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand assisted Him." **Dominations** are those who even surpass the Virtues and Principalities; they are called "Dominations" because they rule over the other ranks of angels. **Thrones** are the ranks of angels who in the Latin tongue are called "Seats" <note>original: *sedes*</note>; they are called Thrones because the Creator presides over them and through them disposes His judgments. The **Cherubim** are themselves sublime powers of the heavens and angelic ministries. In our language, translated from the Hebrew, the name means "multitude of knowledge" <note>original: *scientiae multitudo*</note>. They are the higher ranks of angels who, because they are placed closer to Him, are filled more fully than the rest with divine knowledge; thus "Cherubim" are called the "fullness of knowledge." These are those two living beings depicted in metal above the mercy seat of the Ark, signifying the presence of the angels, in whose midst God is revealed. The **Seraphim** are a similar multitude of angels; their name in Hebrew is translated into Latin as "burning" or "flaming" <note>original: *ardentes vel incendentes*</note>. They are called "burning" because no other angels stand between them and God, and therefore the closer they stand to God, the more they are inflamed by the brightness of the divine light. Hence, they themselves veil the face and feet of the one sitting on the throne of God; for this reason, the rest of the crowd of angels is not fully able to see the essence of God, because the Seraphim cover it. Therefore, these names for the ranks of angels are specific to each individual order, yet they are to some extent common to all. For although "Thrones" or the "Seats of God" are specifically designated in the order of certain angels, yet the Psalmist says: "He who sits upon the Cherubim." But these orders of angels are called by these private names because they received this specific office more fully within their own rank. And while these traits are common to all, these names are properly assigned to their own orders. To each one, as was said before, specific duties are enjoined, which it is established they earned at the beginning of the world. For the prophet testifies that angels preside over both places and men, saying: "The Prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me." From this, it appears that there is no place over which angels do not preside; for they also preside over the beginnings of all works. This is the order or distinction of the angels who, after the fall of the evil ones, stood firm in heavenly strength. For

<column-break/>

after the apostate angels fell, these were solidified in the perseverance of eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven in the beginning, it is repeated: "Let there be a firmament," and the firmament was called heaven; clearly showing that after the ruin of the evil angels, those who remained attained the firmness of eternal perseverance, no longer turned away by any fall, nor falling through any pride, but remaining firm in the love and contemplation of the world <note>likely meaning the celestial world or God's creation</note>. They find nothing <margin>.6.</margin> else sweet except Him by whom they were created. Furthermore, we read in Isaiah about two Seraphim; figuratively, they show the significance of the Old and New Testaments. They cover the face and feet of God because we cannot know the past things before the world, nor the future things after the world, but we contemplate only the middle things through their testimony. Each has six wings because we know the work of the world in this present age, which was made in six days. That they cry out "Holy, Holy, Holy" to one another demonstrates the mystery of the Trinity within the one Divinity.

### On the men who received proper names. Chapter 6.

Many of the first men have the origin of their names from specific causes. Names were given to them prophetically, so that they might suit either their future or their preceding circumstances. In these names, while a special mystery remains, we are now following only the literal understanding of the history. Where we do not reach the interpretation of the etymology, we place only the etymology itself into Latin. Because one Hebrew name is interpreted in various ways, these names should be reckoned according to their different meanings. **Adam**, as the blessed Jerome hands down, is interpreted as "man," or "earthly," or "red earth." For the flesh was made from the earth, and the soil was the material for making man. **Eve** is interpreted as "life," or "calamity," or "woe" <note>original: *ve*</note>. She is "life" because she was the origin of being born; "calamity" and "woe" because through her transgression she became the cause of dying. For the name "calamity" took its name from "cautioning" <note>original: *a cavendo*</note>. Others say she is called "life" and "calamity" because often a woman is the cause of salvation for a man, and often the origin of calamity and death, which is "woe." **Cain** is interpreted as "possession," wherefore his father, expressing the etymology itself, said: "Cain," that is, "I have possessed a man through God." It also means "lamentation," because he was slain by the one whom Abel slew <note>referring to a tradition where Lamech kills Cain</note>, and he paid the penalty for his crime. **Abel** is interpreted as "grief," by which name he was prefigured as one to be killed. It also means "vanity," because he was quickly released and taken away. **Seth** is interpreted as "resurrection," because he was born following the killing of his brother, as if he were raising up a resurrection of his brother from the dead. It also means "position," because God "positioned" him in place of Abel. **Enos**, according to the variety of his own language, is called "man" or "male." And he held this name fittingly, for of him it is written: "Then was the beginning of calling upon the name of the Lord," although many of the Hebrews think that then for the first time idols were fashioned in the name of the Lord and in His likeness. **Enoch** means "dedication"; for in his name Cain afterwards built a city. **Cainan** means "lamentation" or "possession of them"; for just as Cain is "possession," so the derivative name which is Cainan makes "possession of them." **Methuselah** <note>original: *Matusala*</note> is interpreted as "dead..."

# VII

The etymology of the name <note>referring to Methuselah from the previous page</note> is evident. For some have thought that he was translated with his father <note>Enoch</note> or that he survived the flood. For this reason, the record significantly notes: "he died," to show that he did not live after the flood, but passed away in that same cataclysm. For only eight people escaped the flood in the ark. **Lamech** means "striking." For he struck and killed Cain, which he himself afterwards confessed to his wives that he had perpetrated. **Noah** is interpreted as "rest," because under him all former works rested through the flood. Whence also his father, calling his name Noah, said: "This one shall make us rest from all our works." **Shem** is called "the named one," because he received his name as a presage of his posterity. For from him came the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, and the people of God. From his lineage also comes Christ, whose name is great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting. **Ham** means "hot," because he was so named from a presage of the future. For his posterity possessed that part of the earth which is hotter due to the proximity of the sun. Whence even to this day, Egypt is called "Ham" in the Egyptian language. **Japheth** means "latitude" <note>or width</note>. For from him the multitude of nations is born; and because the multitude of believers from the nations is wide, he was called Japheth from that same latitude. **Canaan**, the son of Ham, is interpreted as "their movement." What is this other than "their work"? For he was cursed for the movement of his father—that is, for his father's deed. **Arphaxad** means "healing depopulation." **Cush** is interpreted in Hebrew as "Ethiopian," having obtained the name from the posterity of his race. For from him the Ethiopians were propagated. **Nimrod** is interpreted as "tyrant." For he was the first to seize an unaccustomed tyranny over peoples, and he himself attempted to build a tower of impiety against God. **Eber** means "passage." His etymology is mystical, because from his lineage God would "pass over," and grace would not remain among them but be translated to the nations. For from him the Hebrews arose. **Peleg** means "division," for his father gave him such a name because it was then that the earth was divided by languages. **Terah** means "exploration of ascent." **Melchizedek** means "just king." He was a "king" because he afterwards ruled Salem; "just" because, discerning the sacraments of the Law and the Gospel, he offered in sacrifice not the victims of cattle, but the oblation of bread and a chalice. **Lot** means "turning away." For he did not consent to the deeds of the Sodomites, but turned away from their illicit fires of the flesh. **Moab** means "from the father," as the whole name contains its etymology. For the firstborn daughter conceived him from her father. **Ammon**, the cause of whose name is rendered "son of my people," is so derived that one part is the sense of the name and the other part is the word itself. For "Ammi," from which the Ammonites are named, is called "my people." **Sarai** is interpreted as "my princess," because she was the matriarch of only one house. Afterward, the reason for the name was changed; the letter *i* was removed from the end and she is called **Sarah**, that is, "princess." For she was to be the princess of all nations, just as the Lord had promised to Abraham: "I will give you a son from Sarah, and I will bless him, and he shall be among the nations, and kings of peoples shall come from him." **Hagar** means "stranger" or "convert." For she was an Egyptian stranger, the handmaid of Abraham for the purpose of procreating, who after her contempt was turned back to Sarah at the angel’s rebuke. **Keturah** is interpreted as "incense." **Ishmael** is interpreted as "the hearing of God," for so it is written: "And he called his name Ishmael, because God heard him." **Esau** is triple-named, and for specific reasons

<column-break/>

is called by various names. For he is called **Esau**, which means "red," on account of the cooking of the red lentils; he was so named when he lost his birthright for a meal. However, he was called **Edom** on account of the redness of his body, which in Latin is called "bloody." He is called **Seir**, however, because he was bristly and hairy; for when he was born, he was entirely hairy like a skin. Thus he is called by three names: **Esau**, that is, "red"; **Edom**, that is, "bloody"; and **Seir**, that is, "hairy," because he did not have smoothness. **Rebecca** means "patience," or "she who received much." **Leah** was "laborious," certainly in giving birth. For she endured many pains because Rachel was blocked from the fruitfulness of bearing. **Rachel** is interpreted as "sheep," for on her account Jacob pastured the sheep of Laban. **Zilpah** means "open mouth." **Bilhah** means "ancient." **Dinah** is translated as "cause," for she stood as the cause of strife in Shechem. **Tamar** means "bitterness" for her dead husbands. She is also "the one changing." For she changed herself into the habit of a harlot when she lay with her father-in-law. **Perez** means "division," from the fact that he divided the membrane of the afterbirth; he obtained the name of "the divider," which is Perez. Whence also the **Pharisees** were called "the divided," because they separated themselves from the people as if they were the only just ones. **Zerah**, his brother, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, is interpreted as "rising," either because he appeared first, or because many righteous ones were born from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles: he was called Zerah, that is, "the rising." **Job** is translated into Latin as "grieving," and rightly grieving for the striking of his flesh and the passions of his sorrows. For the etymology of his name prefigured his calamities. **Pharaoh** is a name not of a man but of an honor <note>a title</note>, just as among us kings are called "Augustus," though they are registered by their own proper names. Pharaoh, however, is expressed in Latin as "denying him"—certainly denying God—or "his dissipator." For he was the afflictor of the people of God. **Jannes** means "marine," or "where his sign is." For his sign yielded and failed before the signs of Moses, whence the magicians said: "This is the finger of God." **Mambres** means "sea of skin," or "sea at the head." Finally, **Moses** is interpreted as "taken from the water." For the daughter of Pharaoh found him exposed on the riverbank, and taking him up, she adopted him for herself and called his name Moses, because she had taken him from the water. **Aaron** is interpreted as "mountain of strength," because taking the censer, he stood in the way between the living and the dead, and excluded the ruin of death like a strong mountain. **Eleazar** means "God’s help." **Balak** means "precipitating" or "devouring." **Balaam** means "vain people." **Phinehas** means "sparing the mouth"; for he pierced Zimri with a dagger along with the Midianite harlot, and appeased the wrath of the Lord so that He might spare them. **Zimri** means "provoking star" or "bitter." For his name is properly called from bitterness, because by sinning he embittered the people. **Rahab** means "width" or "hunger" or "impulse." **Joshua** is interpreted as "savior." For he himself, in the figure of Christ, saved the people from the desert and led them into the land of promise. **Caleb** means "heart" or "dog." **Othniel** means "his time of God" or "the response of God." **Ehud** means "glorious." **Barak** means "flashing" <note>original: *fulgurans*, like lightning</note>. **Deborah** means "bee" or "talkative." She was a "bee" because she was most prompt for war, fighting against Sisera; and she sang a prompt song thereafter, hence "talkative." **Jael** means "ascension." **Gideon** means "testing of their iniquity." For he was informed by frequent proofs through what sort of presage the future victory against the enemies would be.

For this is the one who burned the idols. **Joachaz** means "robust." **Joachim** means "where there is preparation." **Eliachim** means "resurrection of God." **Jechonias** means "preparation of the Lord." **Sedechias** means "the just of the Lord." **Jeroboam** means "judgment of the Lord without cause of the people," or as some say, it is interpreted as "division," because in his kingdom the people of Israel were divided and cut off from the kingdom of the line of David. For he stood as the cause of the division of the people. **Zambri** means "my psalm" or "song" or "hymn." **Amri** means "my curling." **Ahab** means "brother of the father." **Jezabel** means "flow of blood" or "flowing with blood." Or better: "where there is a dunghill." For after being thrown down, dogs ate her flesh, just as Elijah had predicted; and he said, "the flesh of Jezebel shall be as dung upon the face of the earth." **Ochozias** means "apprehending God." **Jehu** means "he is the man." **Joathan** means "robust." **Sella** <note>Shallum</note> means "his shadow" or "petition." **Manaen** means "comforting." **Phaceas** means "opening." **Nabuchodonosor** <note>Nebuchadnezzar</note> means "prophecy of a narrow flask," or the sign of a prophet of this kind and a dream of future things which he is said to have seen and Daniel interpreted; or "session in the recognition of distress," on account of those who were led by him into captivity. **Zorobabel** among the Hebrews is said to be composed of three complete names. *Zor* is "this," *ro* is "master," and *babel* sounds like "Babylonian," and it makes the name Zorobabel: "this master from Babylon." For he was born in Babylon, where he also stood as the prince of the Judean nation.

### On the Patriarchs, Chapter 7.

<margin>q</margin> The etymologies of certain Patriarchs must be noted, so that we may know what they resonate in their own vocabulary. For many of them received names based on specific causes. **Patriarch** is interpreted as "prince of fathers." For *archos* in Greek is "prince." **Abram** was first called "father seeing the people," specifically not just the Israelites; later he was called **Abraham**, which translates as "father of many nations," which was still to come through faith. However, "of nations" is not in the name itself, but is understood, according to that text: "Your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations." **Isaac** received his name from "laughter." For his father laughed when he was promised to him, wondering in joy. And his mother laughed when he was promised through those three men, doubting in joy. For this cause he received the name Isaac, for it is interpreted as "laughter." It should be known that four people in the Old Testament were called by their names without any veil before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah. Read the scriptures. **Jacob** is interpreted as "supplanter," either because at birth he gripped the heel of his brother as he was being born, or because he later deceived his brother by artifice. Whence Esau said: "Rightly is his name called Jacob, for behold, he has supplanted me twice." **Israel** means "a man seeing God." For he received this name at the time when, having wrestled all night, he overcame the angel in the struggle and was blessed as the morning star rose. Thence, on account of the vision of God, he was called Israel, just as he himself said: "I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved." **Ruben** <note>Reuben</note> is interpreted as "son of vision" or "seeing the son." For thus, when Leah bore him, she called his name Reuben, saying: "Because God has seen my humility." **Symeon** is interpreted as "hearing of God." For thus Leah said when she bore him: "Because God has heard me."

**Levi** means "added." For Leah said when she bore him—not doubting her husband's love—"Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons" <note>Genesis 29:34</note>. **Judah** is called "confession." For when Leah bore him, she gave praise to the Lord, saying: "Now because of this I will confess to the Lord" <note>original: "confitebor dño"</note>. And for this reason he was called Judah. His name was therefore derived from "confession," which is "thanksgiving." **Issachar** is interpreted as "there is a reward." For *Is* indeed means "is" and *achar* means "reward." This was because Leah had bought the entry of her husband—which was owed to Rachel—for herself using the mandrakes of her son Reuben; whence also when he was born, Leah said: "God has given me my reward" <note>Genesis 30:18</note>. **Zebulun** is interpreted as "dwelling." For Leah had borne this sixth son; therefore, now secure, she said: "My husband will dwell with me." Whence also her son was called "dwelling." **Naphtali** [comes] from "conversation" or "comparison." This is the cause of his name; hence Rachel said when her handmaid Bilhah bore him: "God made me dwell in a dwelling with my sister." **Dan** is interpreted as "judgment." For when Bilhah bore him, Rachel, her mistress, said: "The Lord has judged me, and hearing me, gave me a son." She expressed the cause of the name so that from the fact that the Lord had judged, she might impose the name of "judgment" on the son of the handmaid. **Gad** was named from "event" or "girded." For when Zilpah bore him, Leah, her mistress, said: "Good fortune," that is, what is called "in readiness" or "event." **Asher** is called "blessed." For when Zilpah bore him, Leah said: "Blessed am I, and women call me blessed." And from the fact that she said she was blessed, she called him "blessed" by the etymology of the name. **Joseph**, because his mother had hoped another son would be added to her, she called "increase." Pharaoh called him *Zaphenath* <note>Zaphenath-Paneah</note>, which in Hebrew sounds like "finder of hidden things," because he revealed obscure dreams and predicted sterility. However, because this name was given by an Egyptian, it must have a reason in that language. In the Egyptian tongue, *Zaphenath* is interpreted as "savior of the world," because he freed the globe from the imminent destruction of famine. **Benjamin** is interpreted as "son of the right hand," which is "of strength." For the right hand is called *jamin*. Indeed, his mother, while dying, had called his name *Ben-oni*, that is, "son of my sorrow." But his father changed it, naming him "son of the right hand." **Manasseh** is so called because his father had "forgotten" his labors. For thus it is called "forgetfulness" in Hebrew. **Ephraim** [is named] because God "takes him away," and from this word "increase" is translated into our language.

### Concerning the Prophets, Chapter VIII.

Those whom the pagans call *vates* <note>seers or bards</note>, our people call **prophets**, as if they were "pre-speakers," because they speak from afar <note>Latin: "porro fantur"</note> and predict true things about the future. However, those who are prophets to us were called "seers" in the Old Testament, because they saw those things which others did not see, and they perceived those things which were hidden in mystery. Hence it is written in Samuel: "Let us go to the seer." Hence Isaiah said: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and elevated." And Ezekiel: "The heavens were opened and I saw visions of God." Since the etymologies of the names of the prophets must be noted, for their names sufficiently show what they would pronounce in their future deeds and words. **Elijah** is interpreted as "Lord God." From

<column-break/>

a foreknowledge of the future, therefore, he is so called. For while he was contending in sacrifice with the four hundred priests of Baal, having invoked the name of the Lord, fire descended from heaven upon the holocaust. When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said: "The Lord himself is God" <note>1 Kings 18:39</note>. And for this reason, he received such a name beforehand, because through him the people would later know the Lord God. He is also interpreted as "strong Lord," either because he killed those same priests or because he endured the opposition of Ahab. **Elisha** is interpreted as "salvation of the Lord." He received this name also from a foreknowledge of the future. Finally, he performed many miracles and, by driving away famine, saved the people from death.
<margin>4 Kings 3, 18 <note>Modern 2 Kings 3 and 18</note></margin>
**Nathan** means "he gave" or "of the giver." **Isaiah** is interpreted as "savior of the Lord," and rightly so. For he is the savior of all nations, and he proclaimed his sacraments more fully than the rest. **Jeremiah** means "high one of the Lord," because it was said to him: "Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms." **Ezekiel** means "strength of God." **Daniel** means "judgment of God," either because he exhibited the sentence of divine examination in the judgment of the elders when, their falsehood having been discovered, he freed Susanna from destruction; or because he opened and discerned with a sagacious mind the visions and dreams in which certain future enigmas were shown through individual symbols. He was also called "man of desires" because he did not eat the bread of desire and did not drink the wine of concupiscence. **Hosea** means "savior" or "saving." For while he had prophesied the wrath of God upon the people of Israel on account of the crime of idolatry, he announced salvation to the house of Judah. On account of this, King Hezekiah of Judah, having removed the idols which preceding kings had consecrated, is shown to have cleansed and purified the temple of the Lord. **Joel** means "Lord God," or "beginning in God," or "he was of God." For the etymology of his name resonates with this, though the origin is uncertain. **Amos** means "torn away" or "plucked." For his prophecy was to the people of Israel, who had already been torn away from the Lord and were serving golden calves, or torn away from the kingdom of the lineage of David. **Nahum** means "sprout" or "of the comforters." For he rebukes the city of bloods and, after its overthrow, consoles Zion, saying: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings and announces peace." **Habakkuk** means "embracing," named "embrace" either because he was lovable to the Lord, or because he entered into a contest with God; the name of "embracing"—that is, "wrestling"—was formed. For no one dared to provoke God to a dispute of justice with such a bold voice, asking why such great iniquity was involved in human affairs and this world. **Micah** means "who is here?" or "who is this?" He dominates Samaria because of the cause of those idols in that way about which Elihu says: "Who is this involving sentences?" **Zephaniah** is interpreted as "mirror" or "secret of the Lord." Both fit the prophets. For they know the mysteries of God. Whence it is said to Ezekiel: "I have placed you as a watchman for the house of Israel." And elsewhere: "The Lord will do nothing unless he reveals it to his servants the prophets." **Obadiah** means "his [servant] of the Lord." Just as Moses was the servant of the Lord and an apostle of Christ, so this man is seen as a legate sent to the nations, and he predicts things worthy of prophetic mystery and service; hence "servant of the Lord." **Jonah** is interpreted as "dove" or "grieving." A dove because of the groaning when he was in the belly of the whale for three days. Grieving, however, either on account of the sadness...

### Liber

[The book] which he held concerning the salvation of the Ninevites, or because of the ivy <note>The "gourd" or "ivy" plant that provided shade for Jonah</note> that suddenly withered, by whose shade he was protected against the heat of the sun. He is himself the son of **Amittai**, the widow of Zarephath <note>original: "amathi sareptanē vidue filius"</note>, as the Jews affirm, whom Elijah raised from the dead. Afterward, his mother said to him: "Now I know that you are a man of God, and the word of the Lord in your mouth is true" <note>1 Kings 17:24</note>. For this reason, he was called **Amittai**; for **Amittai** in the Hebrew language is called "Truth" in English. And because he spoke what was true to Elijah, he who was raised was called the "son of truth." **Zachariah** [means] the memory of the Lord. For when the seventy years of the temple's desolation were completed, the Lord remembered His people through the preaching of Zachariah; and by the order of Darius, the people of God returned, and the city and temple were rebuilt. **Haggai** sounds in English as "festive" and "joyful." For he prophesied that the destroyed temple must be built, and after the sorrow of captivity, he preached the joy of the return. **Malachi** is interpreted as "the angel of the Lord," that is, a "messenger." For whatever he spoke was believed to be as if it were commands from the Lord; and thus he was so named. The seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> translated this by saying: "The assumption of the word of the Lord over Israel by the hand of His angel." **Ezra** [means] "helper." **Nehemiah** [means] "consolation from the Lord." By a certain omen of the future, they were allotted these names. For they were a help and a consolation to that people returning to their fatherland. For they also rebuilt the temple of the Lord, and they themselves restored the work of the walls and towers. **Ananias** is interpreted as "the grace of God." He is also **Shadrach** in the Chaldean language, which is interpreted as "my beautiful one." **Azarias** [means] "the help of the Lord." He is also **Abednego**, which translates into English as "serving Tacco" <note>original: "seruiēs tacco," likely a corruption of Nego or Nebo, the Babylonian deity</note>. **Misael** [means] "who is the people of the Lord." He is also **Meshach**, which is interpreted as "laughter" or "joy." **Azia** [means] "my brother." **Shemaiah** [means] "hearing the Lord." **Asaph** [means] "gathering." **Jeduthun** [means] "leaping over them" or "jumping over them." For those who are clinging to the ground, stooped to the earth and thinking of those things which are at the bottom, and placing their hope in passing things—this man, who is called "the leaper," leaps over them by singing. **Heman** [means] "receiving" or "their fear." **Ethan** [means] "robust." **Berechiah** [means] "the blessed of the Lord" or "may the Lord be blessed." **Huldah** [means] "strictness" or "a turning aside." **Judith** [means] "praising" or "confessing to the Lord." **Esther** [means] "hidden." **Zachariah** [means] "the memory of the Lord," on account of what he sang: "the memorial of his holy testament." **John the Baptist** [means] "the grace of the Lord," because he is the limit of prophecy, the herald of grace, and the beginning of baptism, through which grace is administered. These are the prophets of the Old and New Testament, whose end is Christ, to whom it is said by the Father: "And I have placed you as a prophet among the nations." There are, moreover, seven types of prophecy. The first type is **ecstasy**, which is a departure of the mind, just as Peter saw that vessel sent down from heaven in a stupor of mind with various animals. The second type is **vision**, as with Isaiah saying: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne." The third type is a **dream**, just as Jacob, sleeping, saw the ladder leaning into heaven. The fourth type is **through a cloud**, just as God spoke to Moses and to Job after the plague. The fifth type is a **voice from heaven**, just as it sounded to Abraham, saying: "Do not lay your hand upon the boy," and to Saul on the road: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" The sixth type is a **parable received**, as in Solomon in the

<column-break/>

Proverbs, and with Balaam when he was summoned by Balak. The seventh type is the **filling of the Holy Spirit**, as with almost all the prophets. Others have said there are three types of visions. One is according to the **eyes of the body**, as Abraham saw three men under the oak of Mamre, and Moses saw the fire in the bush, and the disciples saw the transfigured Lord on the mountain between Moses and Elijah, and other things of this sort. Another is according to the **spirit**, by which we imagine those things which we perceive through the body, as Peter saw that dish sent down from heaven with various animals, and as Isaiah saw God in the highest seat, not corporally but spiritually. For a corporeal form does not enclose God, but just as many things are said figuratively rather than literally, so also many things are shown figuratively. The third type of vision, however, is that which is perceived neither by the corporeal senses, nor by any part of the soul by which images of corporeal things are received, but through the **intuition of the mind**, by which intellect the truth is beheld; just as Daniel, endowed in mind, saw what Belshazzar had seen with his body. Without this third type, those other two are either fruitless or even lead into error. Yet the Holy Spirit moderates all these types. Moreover, it is possible to have prophecy not only for the good, but also for the evil. For we find that King Saul prophesied; for he was persecuting the holy David and, being filled with the Holy Spirit, he began to prophesy.

### ->Chapter IX. On the Apostles.<-

**Apostles** are interpreted as "those who are sent." For this is what their name indicates. For just as in Greek they are called *angeli* and in Latin *nuncii* <note>In English: messengers</note>, so in Greek they are called *apostoloi* and in Latin *missi* <note>In English: the sent ones</note>. For Christ sent them to evangelize through the whole world, so that some penetrated even to the Persians and the Indians, teaching the nations and performing great and incredible miracles in the name of Christ, so that they might be believed through the attesting signs and wonders in those things which they spoke and had seen. Many of them have the reasons for their names from these causes. **Peter** received his name from the rock <note>Latin: "petra"</note>, that is, from Christ, upon whom the Church is founded. For the rock is not from Peter, but Peter is named from the rock, just as "Christ" is not from "Christian," but "Christian" is called from "Christ." And therefore the Lord says: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church," because Peter had said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Then the Lord said to him: "Upon this rock," He said, "which you have confessed, I will build my Church." For the rock was Christ, upon which foundation Peter himself was also built. He is called **Cephas** because he was established as the head <note>original: "capite"</note> of the Apostles. For in Greek, *cephalin* <note>Greek: kephale</note> is called "head." And the name itself in Peter is Syriac. **Simon Bar-Jona** in our language sounds as "son of the dove," and it is a name equally Syriac and Hebrew. For *Bar* in the Syriac language is "son," and *Iona* in Hebrew is "dove"; in both languages it is called **Bar-Jona**. Others take it simply that **Simon**, that is Peter, was the son of John, according to that questioning: "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" and they maintain it was corrupted by the fault of a scribe, so that for *Bar-Iohanna*—that is, the son of John—*Bar-Jona* was written, with one syllable taken away. **Iohanna**, however, is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord." And it is established that Peter was triple-named: **Peter**, **Cephas**, and **Simon Bar-Jona**. **Simon**, however, is interpreted in Hebrew as "hearing."

# VII

**Saul** is called "Temptation" in the Hebrew tongue <note>original: "Saulus hebraico sermone tentatio dictus"</note>, because he was previously involved in the "temptation" (testing) of the church. For he was a persecutor, and he held that name while he was persecuting the Christians. Later, his name was changed from Saul to **Paul**, which is interpreted as "Wonderful" or "Elect." He is "Wonderful" either because he performed many signs, or because he preached the Gospel of Christ among all nations from the East even to the West. He is "Elect" just as the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have elected them" <note>Acts 13:2</note>. In the Latin tongue, however, **Paul** is derived from "small" <note>original: "paul' a modico dictus"; Latin *paulus* means small or little</note>, wherefore he himself says: "I am the least of all the apostles." For when he was Saul, he was proud; when he was Paul, he was humble and small. This is why we say: "I will see you *paulo post*," that is, after a little while. Indeed, he himself says that he was made small: "For I am the last of all the apostles, and to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given." Furthermore, **Cephas** <note>Saint Peter</note> and **Saul** were called by changed names so that they might be "new" even in their very names, just like Abraham and Sarah.

**Andrew**, the brother of Peter in the flesh and his co-heir in grace, is interpreted as "Comely" or "Responding" according to Hebrew etymology; but in the Greek tongue, he is called "Manly" from the word for man <note>original: "a viro virilis"; from the Greek *aner/andros*</note>. **John** received his name by a certain prophecy based on merit. For it is interpreted as "in whom is grace" or "grace of the Lord." For Jesus loved him more than the other apostles. **James**, the son of Zebedee, is named after his father, whom he left along with John to follow their true Father. These are the "Sons of Thunder," who were also named **Boanerges** because of the firmness and greatness of their faith. This is James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, who was openly killed by Herod after the Lord’s ascension.

**James**, the son of Alphaeus, is named as such to distinguish him from the former James, who is called the son of Zebedee, just as this one is the son of Alphaeus. Therefore, both took their surnames from their fathers. This is "James the Less," who in the Gospel is named the "brother of the Lord," because Mary the wife of Alphaeus was the sister of the Lord's mother; John the Evangelist surnames this Mary "of Clopas," whether after her father or her family's lineage, or for whatever other reason he gave her the name. **Alphaeus**, however, in the Hebrew tongue is expressed in Latin as "Thousandth" or "Learned."

**Philip**: "Mouth of Lamps" or "Mouth of Hands." **Thomas**: "Abyss" or "Twin," whence he is called *Didymus* in Greek. **Bartholomew**: "Son of him who suspends the waters" or "Son of him who suspends me"; this is a Syriac name, not Hebrew. **Matthew** is expressed in Hebrew as "Given." He was also called **Levi** after the tribe from which he originated. In Latin, however, he took his name from his office as a **Publican**, because he was chosen from the tax collectors and transferred into the apostleship. **Simon the Canaanite** is so called to distinguish him from Simon Peter, coming from Cana, a village in Galilee where the Lord changed water into wine. He is the one written of in another Evangelist as the "Zealot" <note>original: "celotes"</note>. Indeed, "Cana" is interpreted as "Zeal." **Judas [son] of James**, who is elsewhere called **Lebbaeus**, has a name formed from "heart" <note>from the Hebrew *lev*</note>, which we can call by the diminutive "Little Heart" <note>original: "corculum"</note>. In another Evangelist, he is written as **Thaddeus**, whom ecclesiastical history records was sent to Edessa to King Abgar.

**Judas Iscariot** took his name either from the village in which he was born, or from the tribe of Issachar, which served as an omen of his future condemnation. For **Issachar** is interpreted as "Reward," to signify the price of the traitor by which he sold the Lord, as

<column-break/>

it is written: "And they took my reward, thirty silver pieces, the price that was valued by them" <note>Zechariah 11:12-13</note>. **Matthias**, who is the only one among the apostles held without a surname, is interpreted as "Given"—it being understood: "instead of Judas." For he was elected by the apostles into his place when the lot was cast between two. **Mark**: "High in Command," surely on account of the most high Gospel which he preached. **Luke**: "Rising" or "Lifting Up," because he raised up the preaching of the Gospel after the others. **Barnabas**: "Son of a Prophet" or "Son of Consolation."

### Concerning the remaining names in the Gospel
### Chapter X

**M**aria (Mary) [means] "Enlightener" or "Star of the Sea." For she brought forth the Light of the World. In the Syriac tongue, however, Mary is called "Lady" and "Fair," because she brought forth the Lord. **Elizabeth**: "Fullness of my God" or "The oath of my Lord." **Magdalene**: "Tower" <note>from the Hebrew *migdal*</note>. **Martha**: "Irritating" or "Provoking," though in the Syriac tongue it is interpreted as "Mistress." **Nathanael**: "Gift of God," because guile—that is, hypocrisy—was not in him through the gift of God. **Zebedee**: "Given" or "Flowing." **Zacchaeus**: "Just," or "Justified," or "He who is to be justified"; this is a Syriac name, not Hebrew. **Lazarus**: "Assisted," because he was raised from death. **Herod**: "Leathern" or "Glorious," by a clear etymology. **Caiaphas**: "Investigator," or "Sagacious," or "Vomiting from the mouth." For with his wicked mouth he condemned the Just One—though he also announced it by a prophetic mystery. **Pontius**: "Turning away from the council," namely that of the Jews. For having taken water, he washed his hands, saying: "I am innocent of the blood of this just man." **Pilate**: "Mouth of the Hammerer," because while he both justifies and condemns Christ with his mouth, he strikes both ways like the stroke of a hammerer. **Barabbas**: "Son of their Master"—without doubt the master of the Jews, who is the Devil, the author of homicides, who reigns in them even to this day.

### Concerning Martyrs
### Chapter XI

**M**artyrs in the Greek language are called "Witnesses" in Latin. Hence "testimonies" are called *martyria* in Greek. They are called witnesses because they endured sufferings for the sake of the testimony of Christ and contended for the truth even unto death. Why do we not call them "Witnesses"—which we certainly could say in Latin—but instead call them "Martyrs" in Greek? This Greek word sounds more familiar to the ears of the Church, just as we use many Greek names instead of Latin ones.

The first martyr in the New Testament was **Stephen**, which in the Hebrew tongue is interpreted as "Standard," because he was the first in martyrdom for the imitation of the faithful. This same name, however, is translated from the Greek tongue into Latin as "Crowned" <note>from *stephanos*</note>. And this was prophetic, so that what would follow in reality—by a certain prophecy of the future—should first resonate in his name. For he suffered and received that which he was called. Indeed, Stephen is called "Crown," being humbly stoned and sublimely crowned.

There are, however, two kinds of martyrdom: one in open suffering, the other in the hidden virtue of the soul. For many, by enduring the snares of the enemy and resisting all carnal desires, have sacrificed themselves to Almighty God in their hearts, [and thus achieved martyrdom] even in [times of] peace.

## XII. On Clerics

**C**lerics and "clergy" are so named because Matthias was chosen by "lot" <note>original: "sorte"</note>, whom we read was the first ordained by the Apostles. For *cleros* in Greek is called "lot" or "inheritance" in Latin. Therefore they are called clerics, because they are of the "lot" of the Lord, or because they have the Lord as their portion. Generally, however, all those who serve in the Church of Christ are called clerics, the names of whose ranks are these: Doorkeeper, Psalmist, Reader, Exorcist, Acolyte, Subdeacon, Deacon, Priest <note>original: "presbyter"</note>, and Bishop. The order of bishops is fourfold: that is, in patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. "Patriarch" in the Greek language is interpreted as "highest of fathers" <note>original: "summus patrum"</note>, because he holds the first, that is, the apostolic place. And therefore, because he performs the highest honor, he is designated by such a name—such as the Roman, the Antiochian, and the Alexandrian. "Archbishop" is a Greek word meaning the "highest of bishops." For he holds the apostolic place and presides over both metropolitans and other bishops. "Metropolitans," however, are named from the measure of cities, for they stand out in individual provinces. The other priests are subject to their authority, teaching, and power, without whom it is not permitted for the remaining bishops to do anything; for the care of the entire province is committed to them. All the orders designated above are named by one and the same term, "bishop," but some use a private name because of the distinction of powers which they have singularly received. A "Patriarch" is the prince of fathers; for *Archon* means prince. An "Archbishop" is the prince of bishops. This "Metropolitan" is from the measure of cities. The term "episcopate," however, is so called because he who is appointed "super-intends," <note>original: "super-intendat"</note> namely carrying the care of those placed under him. For *skopein* in Greek is called "to intend" [or look upon] in Latin. "Bishops" (*episcopi*) in Greek are interpreted as "watchmen" (*speculatores*) in Latin. For a watchman is a leader in the church, so named because he watches over and looks ahead at the habits and life of the people placed beneath him. A "Pontiff" is the prince of priests, like a "way" <note>original: "via"</note> for those following. He is also called the "high priest" and the "greatest pontiff." For he himself makes the priests and Levites; he himself arranges all ecclesiastical orders; he himself shows what each person ought to do. In former times, however, pontiffs were kings. For this was the custom of the ancestors: that the king was also the priest and pontiff. Whence even the Roman emperors were called pontiffs. *Vates* <note>a term for a seer or diviner</note> are named from the force of the mind (*vi mentis*), the meaning of which is manifold. For sometimes it signifies a priest, sometimes a prophet, sometimes a poet. An *Antistes* <note>one who stands before</note> is called a priest from the fact that he "stands before" (*ante stat*). For he is first in the order of the church, and has no one above himself. "Priest" (*sacerdos*), however, has a name composed from Greek and Latin, as if "giving sacred things" (*sacrum dans*). For just as a king is named from "ruling" (*regendo*), so a priest is named from "sacrificing" (*sacrificando*). For he consecrates and sanctifies. The priests of the pagans were called *flamines*. They wore a cap (*pilleus*) on their head in which there was a short rod having a bit of wool on top. When they could not bear to carry this because of the heat, they began to bind their heads only with a thread (*filum*). For it was a sin for them to walk with their heads entirely bare; hence from the "thread" which they used, they were called *flamines*, as if "filamines" [thread-men]. But on feast days, having set aside the thread,

<column-break/>

they put on the cap because of the eminence of the priesthood. "Presbyter" in Greek is interpreted as "elder" (*senior*) in Latin; not because of old age or decrepit senility, but they are named presbyters because of the honor and dignity which they have received. Whence also among the ancients, bishops and presbyters were the same, because the former is a name of dignity, the latter of age. For this reason presbyters are also called priests, because they "give sacred things," just like bishops. Although they are priests, they do not have the peak of the pontificate <note>they do not hold the highest office</note>, because they neither sign the forehead with chrism [oil] nor give the Paraclete Spirit, which the reading of the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates to be owed to bishops alone. "Levites" <note>Deacons</note> are named from the name of their author; for from Levi the Levites arose, by whom the ministries of the mystic sacrament were performed in the temple of God. These are called "Deacons" in Greek and "ministers" in Latin; for just as consecration is in the priest, so the distribution of the ministry is in the deacon. "Hypodeacons" in Greek are those whom we call "Subdeacons," who are so named because they are subject to the commands and offices of the Levites. For they receive the offerings from the faithful in the temple of God and bring them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars. Among the Hebrews, these are called *Nathinnei* <note>Nethinim, or temple servants</note>. "Readers" (*lectores*) are named from reading; "Psalmists" from singing psalms. The former preach to the people what they should follow; the latter sing so that they might stir the minds of the listeners to compunction—though some readers pronounce so miserably that they compel some to grief and lamentation. These same are also called "pronouncers" (*pronunciatores*), because they announce from afar. For their voice shall be so great and so clear that it fills the ears of those placed far away. "Cantors" <note>Singers</note> are so called because they modulate the voice in song. Two kinds of these are spoken of in the musical art, as learned men have been able to say in Latin: "precentors" and "succentors." Precentors, of course, are those who send the voice out first in song. Succentors are those who respond subsequently by singing. Those who sound together are called "concentors." He who does not sound together, nor sing along, shall be neither a cantor nor a concentor. "Acolytes" in Greek are called "taper-bearers" (*ceroferarij*) in Latin, from carrying wax candles when the Gospel is to be read or a sacrifice offered. For then lights are lit by them and carried, not to drive away darkness while the sun is shining at that same time, but to show a sign of joy, so that under the type of physical light, 그 light might be shown of which it is read in the Gospel: "It was the true light which illuminates every man coming into this world" <note>John 1:9</note>. "Exorcists" from Greek into Latin are called "adjurers" or "rebukers." For they invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over the catechumens or over those who have an unclean spirit, adjuring by Him that he should depart from them. "Doorkeepers" (*ostiarij*) are the same as janitors, who were chosen in the Old Testament for the guarding of the temple, so that nothing unclean in any matter might enter it. They are called *ostiarij* because they are in charge of the "doors" (*ostia*) of the temple. For they themselves, holding the key, guard everything inside and out, and having judgment between the good and the bad, they receive the faithful and reject the unfaithful.

## XIII. On Monks

**M**onks are named from a Greek etymology because they are "singular." For *monas* in Greek means "singularity." Therefore, if the word "monk" is interpreted as "solitary," what is he doing in a crowd who is sol—
