is. There are several kinds of monks. **Coenobites** <note>original: "Cẹnobitẹ"</note>, whom we can call those living in common. For a **Coenobium** <term>Coenobium: a monastery where monks live as a community</term> belongs to many. **Anchorites** are those who, after a communal life, seek the deserts and live alone throughout the wilderness; they are called by this name because they have withdrawn far from men. However, while anchorites imitate Elijah and John, coenobites imitate the apostles. **Hermits** are those who, like anchorites, are removed from the sight of men, seeking the desert and abandoned solitudes. For "hermit" is said to mean "remote." **Abba**, moreover, is a Syriac name signifying "father" in Latin; Paul, writing to the Romans, explained this saying: "In which we cry, Abba, Father," using two languages for one name. For he says *Abba* as the Syriac word for father, and again names him father in Latin.

### XIV. On the other names of the faithful

<margin>c</margin> **Christian**, as far as the interpretation shows, comes from "unction" <note>Anointing with oil</note> or from the name of the author and creator. For Christians are named after Christ, just as Jews are named after Judah. Indeed, the surname is given to the followers from the name of the teacher. In the past, Christians were called **Nazarenes** by the Jews as if a reproach, because our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene from a certain village of Galilee. But one should not boast of being a Christian if they have the name but not the deeds. However, where the work follows the name, that person is most certainly a Christian, showing himself a Christian by his actions, walking just as He walked, from whom he took the name. **Catholic** is interpreted as "universal" or "general." For the Greeks call the universal "catholicon." <margin>o</margin> **Orthodox** is one who believes rightly, and lives rightly as he believes. For *ortho* in Greek means "rightly," and *doxo* means "glory," that is, a man of right glory. One who lives differently than he believes cannot be called by this name. **Neophyte** is "newly-planted" <note>original Latin: "novell' "</note> in Greek, and in Latin can be interpreted as a raw believer or one recently reborn. A **Catechumen** is so named because he still listens to the doctrine of the faith, but has not yet received baptism. For "catechumen" in Greek means "listener." One is called **Competent** who, after instruction in the faith, seeks the grace of Christ; they are called "competents" from the word for "seeking together." **Laic** means "one of the people." For *Laos* in Greek is called "people." **Proselyte** means a stranger and one who is circumcised, who was mixed among the people of God; it is a Greek term.

# Here begins the eighth book
## I. On the Church and the Synagogue

<margin>e</margin> **Church** is a Greek word which is translated into Latin as "convocation," because it calls everyone to itself. **Catholic** means "universal," <note>original Greek: κατὰ óλὸν (*kata holon*)</note>, that is, "according to the whole." For it is not restricted to certain parts of regions like the small assemblies of heretics, but is spread and dilated throughout the whole world. This the Apostle also approves, saying to the Romans: "I give thanks to my God for all of you, because your faith

<column-break/>

is proclaimed in the whole world," or because it joins all believers into a unity. Hence also "university" <note>meaning the whole or the collective</note> is named from "one," because it is gathered into a unity. Whence the Lord says in the Gospel: "He who does not gather with me, scatters." Why then, since the Church is one, does John write to seven <note>The seven churches in the Book of Revelation</note>, unless it is to designate the one Catholic church as full of the sevenfold Spirit? Just as we know Solomon said of the Lord: "Wisdom built herself a house, and hewed out seven columns," which seven are nevertheless not doubted to be one, as the Apostle says: "The Church of the living God, which is the column and foundation of truth." Moreover, the Church began from the place where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled those sitting in one place. On account of its present pilgrimage, the Church is called **Sion**, because it is placed far from the length of this pilgrimage, and watches for the promise of heavenly things; and therefore it received the name Sion, that is, "contemplation" or "watchtower." For the future peace of the fatherland, it is called **Jerusalem**. For Jerusalem is interpreted as "vision of peace." For there, all adversity having been swallowed up, it will possess peace, which is Christ, in its present gaze. **Synagogue** is a Greek word, in Latin called "congregation," which name the Jews kept as their own. For their gathering is properly called a synagogue, although it has also been said of the Church. Our Apostles never called our assembly a synagogue, but always the Church; whether for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between a "congregation" (from which "synagogue" comes) and a "convocation" (from which "Church" takes its name). For even cattle are accustomed to be "congregated" (gathered), and we properly speak of their "flocks," but to be "convoked" (called together) is more the trait of those using reason, such as humans are.

### II. On religion and faith

<margin>d</margin> Philosophers named **Dogma** from "thinking," <note>original: "putando"</note> that is: "I think this to be good, I think this to be true." **Religion** is so named because through it we bind <note>original: "religamus"</note> our souls to one God for divine worship, by a bond of service. Which word is composed from "re-electing," that is, choosing again, so that "religion" is seen in Latin just as "I choose." There are three things that are sought in men for the worship of religion to honor God: that is, faith, hope, and charity. In **faith**, what must be believed; in **hope**, what must be hoped for; in **charity**, what must be loved. **Faith** is that by which we truly believe that which we are by no means able to see. For we can no longer "believe" what we see. Properly, however, the name of faith is said to come from this: if that which was said or promised is entirely done. And hence "faith" is named from the fact that what was agreed between two parties is done—as if between God and man—and hence also "treaty" <note>original: "fedus"</note>. **Hope** is named because it is the "foot" <note>original: "pes"</note> of moving forward, as if it is a foot. Whence on the contrary is "despair," for there the "foot" is missing, and there is no faculty of moving forward, because as long as anyone loves sin, he does not hope for future glory. **Charity** is a Greek word, interpreted in Latin as "esteem" or "love" <note>original: "dilectio"</note>, because it binds two in itself. For "esteem" begins from two, which is the love of God and neighbor. Of which the Apostle says: "Love is the fulfillment of the law." Moreover, this is greater than all, because he who loves both believes and hopes. But he who does not love, although he may do many good things, labors in vain. However, carnal "esteem" is not called esteem, but is more usually called "love" <note>original: "amor"</note>. For the name of esteem <note>dilectio</note> is usually accepted only in better things.

# III. On Heresy and Schism

**Heresy** <note>original: "Heresis"</note> is named from the Greek word for "choice," because each person chooses for himself that which seems better to him—just as the Peripatetic, Academic, Epicurean, and Stoic philosophers did, or as others who, conceiving perverse doctrines, have withdrawn from the Church by their own will. Thus, heresy is named from the Greek word meaning "choice" <note>original: "electionis"</note>, because each person selects for himself by his own judgment what he will establish or adopt. However, we are not permitted to introduce anything by our own will, nor to choose what others have introduced by theirs. We have the apostles of God as our authorities, who did not choose to introduce anything by their own judgment, but faithfully passed on to the nations the teaching they received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should preach another gospel, he shall be called "anathema" <note>An "anathema" is a person or thing cursed or consigned to damnation.</note>. A **Sect** <note>original: "Secta"</note> is named from "following" and "holding." For we call "sects" the dispositions of minds and the institutions regarding a teaching or purpose which they follow by holding to it, having opinions regarding religious worship far different from others. **Schism** <note>original: "Scisma"</note> takes its name from a "tearing" <note>original: "scissura"</note> of minds. For a schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as others, but is delighted solely by the discord of the gathering. A schism occurs when men say: "We are the righteous," "We sanctify the unclean," and other similar things. **Superstition** is so named because it is a "superfluous" or "super-established" observation. Others say it comes from the elderly <note>original: "a senibus"</note>, because after surviving for many years, they become delirious through age and err in a certain superstition, not knowing which ancient things they worship or which things they ignorantly adopt. Lucretius, however, says superstition is the study of "standing above" <note>original: "superstantium"</note> things, that is, celestial and divine things which stand above us; but he says this wrongly. In order that the dogmas of heretics may be easily recognized, it is necessary to demonstrate their causes or names.

# IV. On the Heresies of the Jews

**Jews** are interpreted as "confessors." For a profession of faith follows many of them who were previously held by perfidy. **Hebrews** are called "passers-by" <note>original: "transitores"</note>. By this name they are warned to pass from worse things to better, and to leave behind their former errors. The **Pharisees** and **Sadducees** are contrary to one another. For "Pharisees" is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as "the divided," because they claim justice for themselves from their traditions and observations—which they call "secondary laws" <term>deuterosīs: a Greek term for the rabbinic oral traditions</term>—whence they are called "divided" from the people as if by their justice. **Sadducees** are interpreted as "the just," for they claim for themselves what they are not; they deny the resurrection of bodies and preach that the soul perishes with the body. These accept only the five books of the Law <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy</note> and reject the prophecies of the prophets. The **Essenes** <note>original: "Esneī"</note> say that Christ himself taught them all abstinence. The **Merobonites** <note>original: "Merobonęi"</note> say that he taught them to keep the Sabbath in every matter. The **Benistes** <note>original: "Benistęi"</note> are so called because they boast that they are of the lineage of Abraham. For when the people of God came into Babylon, many left their wives and clung to Babylonian women. But some, content only with Israelite marriages, or those born from them when they returned from Babylon, divided themselves from the whole people and took up this name of boasting. The **Meristites** <note>original: "Meristęi"</note> are so named because they "divide" the scriptures, not believing in all the prophets, saying that they prophesied by different spirits. For *meris* in Greek is called "part" in Latin. **Samaritans** are so called because

<column-break/>

they guard the law alone. For they do not receive the prophets. **Hemerobaptists** <note>literally "day-baptizers"</note> are so called because they wash their clothes and bodies every day.

# V. On the Heresies of the Christians

Certain heretics who have withdrawn from the Church are named after their founders; others, however, from the causes or ideas they chose to establish. The **Simonians** are named after Simon Magus, a man skilled in the [magic] arts whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he wished to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit from the apostles with money. These say that the creation was not made by God, but by a certain heavenly power. The **Menandrians** are named after Menander the magician, a disciple of Simon, who asserted that the world was made not by God but by angels. The **Basilidians** are named after Basilides, who among other blasphemies denied that Jesus suffered. The **Nicolaites** are named after Nicolas, a deacon of the church of Jerusalem who was appointed with Stephen and the others by Peter; because of her beauty, he left his wife and said that whoever wished might use her. This custom turned into debauchery, such that they exchanged marriages with one another. John disapproves of these in the Apocalypse, saying: "But this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaites." The **Gnostics** <note>from the Greek *gnosis*, meaning "knowledge"</note> wished to call themselves this because of their "excellent knowledge." They say the soul is of the nature of God, and they fashion a good and an evil god in their dogmas. The **Carpocratians** are named after a certain Carpocrates, who said that Christ was a man only, and born from both sexes. The **Cerinthians** <note>original: "Chirinthiani"</note> are named after a certain Cerinthus. Among other things, they observe circumcision and preach that there will be a thousand years after the resurrection in the pleasures of the flesh. Whence they are called **Chiliasts** <note>original: "ciliastę"</note> in Greek and **Millenarians** <note>original: "miliciastę"</note> in Latin. The **Nazarenes** are so called because, while they confess Christ (who is called a Nazarene from the village) to be the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all the things of the Old Law. The **Ophites** are named after the serpent. For a serpent is called *ophis* in Greek. They worship the serpent, saying that it introduced the knowledge of virtue in Paradise. The **Valentinians** are named after a certain Valentinus, a follower of Plato, who introduced "Aeons" <note>original: "eonas"</note>, that is, certain ages as the origin of God the Creator; he asserted that Christ took nothing of a body from the Virgin, but passed through her as if through a pipe. The **Apellites**, whose leader was Apelles, claimed that the creator was some glorious angel of the superior God; he made the God of the law of Israel out of fire. The Apellites' founder, Apelles, said that Christ did not appear as God in truth, but as a man in a phantom <note>original: "fantasia"</note>. The **Archontics** <note>original: "Archonciaci"</note> are named after "Archons" <note>Rulers or powers</note>, for they defend the idea that the universe which God established is the work of archangels. The **Adamians** are named because they imitate the nakedness of Adam; hence they pray naked, and men and women meet together naked. The **Cainites** <note>original: "Lainani," likely a scribe's error for Cainani</note> are so called because they worship Cain. The **Sethians** took their name from the son of Adam called Seth, saying that he is the Christ. The **Melchisedechians** are so named because they think that Melchizedek, the priest of God, was not a man but a power of God. The **Angelics** are so called because they worship angels. The **Apostolics** <note>original: "Aplici"</note> presumed this name for themselves because they possess nothing of their own and do not receive those who [own] anything...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of groups considered heretical by the early Church, moving from general definitions of heresy and schism into a specific list of sects, their founders, and their specific deviations from orthodox doctrine.</meta>

in this world. **Cerdonians** <note>original: "Cerdoniani"</note> are named after a certain Cerdo, who asserted two contrary principles <note>Cerdo was a 2nd-century Gnostic who taught that there were two gods: one unknown and good, the other known and the creator of the world.</note>. The **Marcionites** <note>original: "Marcioniste"</note> are named after Marcion, the Stoic philosopher, who followed Cerdo’s dogma and asserted that one god is good and the other is just, as if there were two principles—one of the Creator and one of Goodness. The **Artotyrites** <note>original: "Artoterite"</note> are named from their offering. For they offer bread and cheese <note>The name comes from the Greek "artos" (bread) and "tyros" (cheese).</note>, saying that the first humans celebrated offerings from the fruits of the earth and the fruits of sheep. The **Aquarians** <note>original: "Aquarij"</note> are so named because they offer only water in the chalice of the sacrament. The **Severians** <note>original: "Seueriani"</note> arose from Severus; they do not drink wine, and they do not accept the Old Testament or the resurrection. The **Tatians** <note>original: "Taciani"</note> are named after a certain Tatian, who are also called the **Encratites** <note>Meaning "the continent" or "the self-controlled."</note>; they abominate meat. The **Alogi** <note>original: "Alogi"</note> are so called as if "without the Word." For *Logos* <note>original: "Logos"</note> in Greek means "Word." They do not believe that God is the Word, rejecting the Gospel and Apocalypse of John. The name **Cataphrygians** <note>original: "Cataphrigis"</note> was given by the province of Phrygia, where they emerged; their founders were Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. There they asserted that the coming of the Holy Spirit was handed down to themselves rather than to the apostles. The **Cathars** <note>original: "Catharos"</note> named themselves after "purity" <note>original: "mundicia"</note>. Boasting of their own merits, they deny forgiveness of sins to the penitent. They condemn widows if they remarry, as if they were adulteresses. They proclaim themselves "cleaner" than others. If they wished to know their own name, they would call themselves "worldly" rather than "pure" <note>This is a pun in the original Latin between "mundos" (pure/clean) and "mundanos" (worldly).</note>. The **Paulians** <note>original: "Pauliani"</note> arose from Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ did not always exist but took his beginning from Mary. The **Hermogenians** <note>original: "Hermogeniani"</note> were named after a certain Hermogenes, who, introducing uncreated matter, compared it to the uncreated God and asserted that matter was the mother of the elements and a goddess; the Apostle condemns those serving the elements. The **Manichaeans** <note>original: "Manichei"</note> emerged from a certain Persian who was called Mani. He introduced two natures and substances, that is, good and evil, and asserted that souls flow from God as if from some source; he rejected the Old Testament and partially accepted the New. The **Canonians** <note>original: "Canoniani"</note> are called in Latin "those without law." The **Anthropomorphites** <note>original: "Anthropomorphite"</note> are so named because, with rustic simplicity, they think God has human members which are written of in the divine books; for *Anthropos* <note>original: "Anthropos"</note> in Greek is interpreted as "man" in Latin. They are ignorant of the voice of the Lord, who says: "God is Spirit." For He is incorporeal, and is neither distinguished by members nor measured by the mass of a body. The **Heraclites** <note>original: "Heraclite"</note> arose from their founder Heraclius; they receive only monks, reject marriages, and do not believe that children possess the kingdoms of heaven. The **Novatians** <note>original: "Nouatiani"</note> arose from Novatian, a priest of the city of Rome, who, attempting to seize the priestly chair against Cornelius, established a heresy, refusing to receive apostates and rebaptizing those already baptized. The **Montanists** <note>original: "Montani"</note> were called heretics because they hid in the mountains <note>original: "montibus"</note> during the time of persecution, by which occasion they divided themselves from the body of the Catholic Church. The **Ebionites** <note>original: "Ebionite"</note> are named after Ebion, or from "poverty." For they think Christ became the true and just one only through his own progress. Thus they are appropriately called "Ebionites" for the poverty of their understanding. These are semi-Jewish, and they hold the Gospel in such a way that they observe the Law carnally; the Apostle is found writing to the Galatians against them. The **Photinians** <note>original: "Fotmiani"</note> are named after Photinus, bishop of Sirmium in Gallo-Graecia, who,

<column-break/>

reviving the heresy of the Ebionites, asserted that Christ was conceived from the nuptial union of Mary and Joseph. The **Aerians** <note>original: "Aeriani"</note> were named after a certain Aerius. These people scorn the offering of sacrifice for the deceased. The **Aetians** <note>original: "Ethiani"</note> were named after Aetius. These same people are called **Eunomians** after a certain dialectician named Eunomius, a disciple of Aetius, by whose name they became better known; they assert that the Son is unlike the Father, and the Holy Spirit is unlike the Son. They also say that no sin is imputed to those remaining in faith. The **Origenists** <note>original: "Origeniani"</note> arose from their founder Origen; they say that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit see the Son. They say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world and, according to the diversity of their sins, fell from the heavens to the earth and earned various bodies as if they were chains; and for that reason, the world was made. The **Noetians** <note>original: "Noetiani"</note> are named after a certain Noetus, who said that Christ was the same as the Father and the Holy Spirit, and they accept the Trinity itself in the names of the offices, not in persons. Hence they are also called **Patripassians**, because they say the Father suffered. The **Sabellians** <note>original: "Sabelliani"</note> are said to have sprouted from the same Noetus, whose disciple they claim Sabellius was, and by whose name they became most known; hence they are called Sabellians. They maintain one person for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The **Arians** <note>original: "Arriani"</note> arose from Arius, a priest of Alexandria, who, not acknowledging the Son as co-eternal with the Father, asserted different substances in the Trinity, against that which the Lord says: "I and the Father are one." The **Macedonians** <note>original: "Macedoniani"</note> were named after Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, denying that the Holy Spirit is God. The **Apollinarists** <note>original: "Apollinariste"</note> were named after Apollinaris; they say that Christ took up only a body without a soul. The **Antidicomarites** <note>original: "Antidicomarite"</note> were so named because they contradict the virginity of Mary, asserting that she had relations with her husband after the birth of Christ. The **Metangisimonites** <note>original: "Metangisimonitę"</note> received such a name because *angios* <note>original: "angios"</note> in Greek means "vessel." For they assert that the Son is in the Father just as a smaller vessel is inside a larger vessel. The **Patricians** <note>original: "Patriciani"</note> were named after a certain Patricius; they say that the substance of human flesh was created by the devil. The **Collythians** <note>original: "Coliuthiani"</note> were named after a certain Collythus, who says that God does not make evil, against that which is written: "I am the Lord creating evils." The **Florians** <note>original: "Floriani"</note> from Florinus, who conversely say that God created evils, against that which is written: "God made all things good." The **Donatists** <note>original: "Donatiste"</note> are named after a certain Donatus from Africa, who, coming from Numidia, deceived nearly all of Africa with his persuasion, asserting that the Son is lesser than the Father, and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son, and rebaptizing Catholics. The **Bonosians** <note>original: "Bonosiani"</note> emerged from a certain bishop Bonosus; it is taught that they assert Christ is the adoptive son of God, not his own. The **Circumcellions** <note>original: "Circūcelliones"</note> are so called because they are rustic people, whom they call *cotopitae*, holding the doctrine of the aforementioned heresy. These people, out of a love for martyrdom, kill themselves so that, departing from this life violently, they may be named martyrs. The **Priscillianists** <note>original: "Priscillianiste"</note> were named after Priscillian, who in Spain composed a dogma mixed from the error of the Gnostics and Manichaeans. The **Luciferians** <note>original: "Luciferiani"</note> arose from Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari <note>The OCR says "syrmie" (Sirmium), but Lucifer was Bishop of Cagliari; this might be a scribal error or a reference to the councils at Sirmium.</note>, who condemned Catholic bishops who had suffered under the persecution of Constantius and had consented to the Arian heresy, even though they later chose to return to the Catholic faith...

<meta>This page continues a list of Christian heresies before transitioning into Book VIII, Chapter 6 of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, which discusses the origins and sects of pagan philosophy.</meta>

->Liber<-

...what they had believed, or which they pretended to have believed; these the Catholic Church received into her motherly bosom like Peter after his weeping for his denial. Proudly rejecting this motherly charity and refusing to receive them, they withdrew from communion, and with Lucifer himself, their leader who rose in the morning <note>A reference to Isaiah 14:12; "Lucifer" here refers to the "morning star" or the fallen angel.</note>, they deserved to fall. The **Jovinianists** <note>original: "Jouinianiste"</note> are named after a certain monk Jovinian; they assert there is no difference between marriage and virginity, and no distinction between those who fast and those who feast simply. The **Helvidians** <note>original: "Eluidiani"</note> are named after Helvidius; they say that after the birth of Christ, Mary bore other children to her husband Joseph. The **Paterniani** <note>original: "Paterniani"</note> arose from a certain Paternus; he thinks the lower parts of the body were made by the devil. Those called the **Arabics** <note>original: "Arabici"</note> are so named because they arose in Arabia; they say the soul dies with the body and both will rise at the very end. The **Tertullianists** <note>original: "Tertullianiste"</note> are named after Tertullian, a priest of the African province from the city of Carthage; they preach that the soul is immortal but corporeal <note>meaning having a physical substance</note>, and they think the souls of sinful men turn into demons after death. The **Quartodecimans** <note>original: "Tesseresdecaditę"</note> are so called because they contend that Easter <note>original: "pasca"</note> should be observed on the fourteenth moon with the Jews. For *tesseres* <note>original: "tesseres"</note> signifies four and *deca* <note>original: "deca"</note> signifies ten. The **Nyctages** <note>original: "Nyctages"</note> are named after sleep <note>from the Greek word for night</note>, for they reject the vigils of the night, saying it is superstition to violate the divine laws that gave the night for rest. The **Pelagians** <note>original: "Pelagiani"</note> arose from the monk Pelagius; these place free will before divine grace, saying that the human will is sufficient for fulfilling divine commands. The **Nestorians** <note>original: "Nestoriani"</note> are named after Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that the Blessed Virgin Mary was not the mother of God, but only of a man, so that he made one person of the flesh and another of the divinity; nor did he believe there was one spirit in the Word of God and the flesh, but preached separately and disjointedly one son of God and another son of man. The **Eutychians** <note>original: "Euticiani"</note> are named after Eutyches, an abbot of Constantinople, who denied that Christ existed from two natures after his human assumption, but asserted that there was only a divine nature in him. Those called the **Acephali** <note>original: "Acephali"</note>—that is, "without a head"—are heretics who follow no known leader; no author is found from whom they arose. These are attackers of the three chapters of Chalcedon <note>A complex theological controversy regarding the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD).</note>; they deny the property of two substances in Christ and preach one nature in his person. The **Theodosians** and **Gaianites** <note>original: "Theodosiani ⁊ gaianitę"</note> are named after Theodosius and Gaianus, who in the times of Prince Justinian were ordained bishops on the same day in Alexandria by the election of a perverse people. These, following the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus, reject the Council of Chalcedon and assert one nature in Christ from two; the Theodosians contend this nature is corruptible, while the Gaianites contend it is incorruptible. The **Gnoetae** and **Tritheists** <note>original: "Gnoitę ⁊ tritoitę"</note> arose from the Theodosians. Of these, the Gnoetae are named from "ignorance" <note>from the Greek word "agnoia"</note> because they add to the perversity from which they arose the idea that Christ's divinity is ignorant of future things written concerning the last day and hour, not remembering the person of Christ speaking in Isaiah: "The day of judgment is in my heart." The **Tritheists** <note>original: "Tritoitę"</note> are so called because, just as there are three persons in the Trinity, they claim there are also three gods, contrary to what is written: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." There are also other heresies without an author and without names, of which some think God is triform; others say Christ's di-

<column-break/>

-vinity is passible <note>meaning God is capable of suffering</note>; others give a beginning of time to Christ’s birth from the Father; others do not believe the liberation of men in the underworld was accomplished by Christ’s descent; others deny the soul is the image of God; others think souls are turned into demons and into various animals; others disagree on the state of the world; others imagine innumerable worlds; others make water co-eternal with God; others walk with bare feet; others do not eat with other humans. These are the heresies that have arisen against the Catholic faith and were pre-condemned by the apostles and the holy fathers or councils. While they are divided among themselves by many errors and disagree with each other, they nevertheless conspire under a common name against the Church of God. But whoever understands Holy Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit (by whom it was written) requires, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church, he can nonetheless be called a heretic.

### Chapter VI: On the Philosophers of the Gentiles

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'P' in red ink with ornamental flourishes.</image-desc>

**Philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> are called by a Greek name which in Latin is interpreted as **lovers of wisdom**. For a philosopher is one who has knowledge of divine and human things, and holds to the entire path of living well. The name of "philosophers" is said to have first arisen from **Pythagoras**. For while the ancient Greeks previously called themselves "Sophists"—that is, "wise men" or "teachers of wisdom"—this man, when asked what he professed, answered with a modest name that he was a "philosopher," that is, a lover of wisdom; for to profess oneself a "wise man" seemed most arrogant. Thus it pleased later generations that, no matter how much doctrine anyone seemed to excel in (either to himself or others) regarding things pertaining to wisdom, he should only be called a "philosopher." These same philosophers are divided into a threefold kind. For they are either **Physicists**, **Ethicists**, or **Logicians**. They are called **Physicists** <note>meaning natural philosophers</note> because they treat of nature. For "nature" in Greek is called *physis* <note>original: "physis"</note>. **Ethicists** <note>meaning moral philosophers</note> are so called because they dispute concerning morals. For among the Greeks, morals are called *ethis* <note>original: "ethis"</note>. **Logicians**, however, because they join reason to nature and morals. For "reason" in Greek is called *logos* <note>original: "logos"</note>. These were also divided into their own heresies <note>The author uses the same word for philosophical "sects" as he does for religious "heresies."</note>, having names from their authors, such as **Platonists**, **Epicureans**, **Pythagoreans**; others from the places of their assemblies and stations, such as **Peripatetics**, **Stoics**, and **Academics**. The **Platonists** are named after the philosopher Plato. These assert that God is the creator of souls, but angels are the creators of bodies, and they say that after circles of many years, souls return into different bodies. The **Stoics** are named after a place. For there was a porch in Athens which they called *pifianactia* <note>The "Stoa Poikile" or Painted Porch.</note>, in which were painted the deeds of the wise and histories of brave men. In this porch the wise men would philosophize, from which they were also called "Stoics." For in Greek, a porch is called a *stoa* <note>original: "stoa"</note>. **Zeno** first established this sect. These deny that anyone can be made happy without virtue. They assert that every sin is uniform <note>meaning all sins are of equal gravity</note>, saying: "He who steals straw will be as guilty as he who steals gold; he who kills a diver-bird as he who kills a horse." For it is not the animal that makes the crime, but the mind. These also say the soul perishes with the body. They deny that the soul is the virtue of continence; they affect eternal glory while they confess they are not

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville's survey of philosophical schools, moving from the definition of the Academy to the various sects of pagan thought, their influence on Christian heresies, and finally beginning a new chapter on the nature and origins of poets.</meta>

...to be eternal. The **Academics** <note>original: "Achademici"</note> were named after Plato's villa, the Academy in Athens, where Plato himself used to teach. These thinkers believe that all things are uncertain. While it must be admitted that many things are indeed uncertain and hidden—as God willed them to exceed human intelligence—it is also true that very many things can be understood through the penetration of the senses. This sect was founded by Arcesilaus the Cyrenaic <note>Arcesilaus was a leader of the "New Academy" who emphasized skepticism.</note>, whose follower was Democritus; he said that truth lies hidden as if in a deep well that has no bottom.

The **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripatetici"</note> are so named from "walking about" <note>from the Greek 'peripatētikos'</note>, because their founder, Aristotle, was accustomed to walk around while he disputed. These men say that a certain part of the soul is eternal, but as for the rest, it is for the most part mortal.

The **Cynics** <note>original: "Cinici"</note> are named for the "filth of their impudence." For it was their custom to engage in sexual intercourse with their wives in public, contrary to human shame. They judged it to be lawful and honorable to lie with their wives openly because marriage is just, and they preached publicly that it should be done just as dogs do in the streets or squares. Hence, they took their name from dogs <note>original: "canibus"</note>, whose lives they imitated.

The **Epicureans** <note>original: "Epicurei"</note> are named after a certain philosopher, Epicurus, a lover of vanity rather than wisdom. Even the philosophers themselves called him a "pig," as if he were wallowing in the mud, because he asserted that the carnal pleasure of the body is the highest good. He also said that the world is neither constructed nor ruled by any divine providence; he assigned the origin of things to "atoms," that is, indivisible and solid bodies, from whose accidental collisions all things are born and have been born. He asserted, moreover, that God does nothing, that all things consist of bodies, and that the soul is nothing other than a body. Whence he also said: "I shall not exist after I have died."

The **Gymnosophists** <note>meaning "naked wise men"</note> are said to philosophize naked throughout the shaded solitudes of India, using coverings only for their genitals. For they are called "Gymno" from the fact that young men used to exercise naked in the field, where they covered only their private parts. These men also restrain themselves from procreation.

**Theologians** <note>original: "Theologi"</note> are the same as the "physicists" <note>natural philosophers</note>. They are called theologians because in their writings they spoke about God. There are various opinions among them as to what God might be when they sought Him out. For some, using their bodily senses, said that this visible world made of the four elements is God, such as Dionysius the Stoic. Others, however, understood spiritually that God is a Mind, such as Thales of Miletus. Some thought He was a luminous soul remaining in all things, like Pythagoras. Some thought God was timeless and immutable, like Plato. Some a detached Mind, like Cicero. Some both spirit and mind, like Varro. For although they found God, they did not explain Him as they found Him, because they "became vain in their thoughts." For "professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" <note>A quotation from Romans 1:21-22.</note>.

Likewise, certain **Platonists** assert that God is a caretaker, an arbiter, and a judge. The **Epicureans** say He is idle and unengaged. Regarding the world, the Platonists affirm it is incorporeal, while the Stoics say it is corporeal. Epicurus says it is made of atoms, Pythagoras from numbers, Heraclitus from fire; whence Varro also says that fire is the soul of the world, because in the world fire governs all things, just as the soul

<column-break/>

does in us. This he said most vainly, for he says: "While it is in us, we exist; when it leaves, we die." Therefore, when fire departs from the world by way of lightning, the world should die!

These errors of the philosophers also introduced **heresies** into the Church. From them come "aeons" and various "forms," I know not what; from them comes the Trinity of mere names in Arius <note>Arius taught that the Son and Spirit were subordinate to the Father, rather than being one substance.</note>, and the Platonic madness in Valentinus. From them comes Marcion's "better god" of tranquility, for he had come from the Stoics; and that the soul should be said to perish, Epicurus is followed. And when the resurrection of the flesh is denied, it is taken from the vain school of all the philosophers. Where matter is equaled with God, it is the discipline of Zeno; and where anything is read concerning a "fiery god," Heraclitus intervenes. The same material is tossed about among heretics and philosophers, and the same arguments are entangled.

### Chapter 7: On the Poets.

**Poets** <note>original: "Poete"</note> are so named as Tranquillus <note>Suetonius</note> says: when men first began to have a rational way of life after abandoning their wildness, and began to know themselves and their gods, they devised a modest cult and necessary speech. They thought of a certain magnificence for both in honor of the religion of their gods. Therefore, just as they made temples more beautiful than their own houses and statues larger than human bodies, so also they thought the gods should be honored with a more august eloquence, and they extolled their praises with more illustrious words and more pleasant rhythms. Because that genre is produced in a certain form, which is called *poesis* <note>meaning 'making' or 'composition'</note>, it was called a poem, and its makers were called poets.

Varro is the authority that they were called **Vates** <note>prophets or bards</note> from the "force of the mind" <note>original: "vi mentis"</note>, or from "weaving songs" <note>original: "viendis carminibus"</note>, that is, bending or modulating them. Hence, poets are called *vates* in Latin. Formerly, their writings were called "prophecies" <note>original: "vaticinia"</note>, because they were moved by a certain force and as if by a madness in writing, or because they connected words in rhythmic modes; for "to weave" <note>original: "viere"</note> was used by the ancients for "to bind." Those in a divine frenzy were called by the same name, because they also expressed many things in verse.

**Lyric** poets are so called "from the lyre" <note>original: "apo tu lyrin" / <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λύρειν"</note></note>, that is, from the variety of their songs. Whence the lyre is also named.

**Tragedians** <note>original: "Tragędi"</note> are so called because in the beginning a goat <note>which the Greeks call 'tragos'</note> was the prize for those singing. Whence Horace says:

> He who competed in tragic song for a cheap goat. <note>original: "Carmine qui tragico vilem certauit ob hircum."</note>

From then on, subsequent tragedians attained much honor, excelling in the plots of their plays which were fashioned into the image of truth.

**Comedians** <note>original: "Comędi"</note> are named either from the place, because they acted around the villages—which the Greeks call *comas* <note>original: "comas" / <note>original: "κώμας"</note></note>—or from "revelry" <note>original: "commessatione"</note>. For people were accustomed to come to hear them after eating. But comedians proclaim the deeds of private men, while tragedians proclaim public affairs and the histories of kings. Likewise, the plots of tragedians are from sorrowful matters, while those of comedians are from joyful ones. There are two types of comedians: the Old and the New. The **Old Comedians** were those who stood out as ridiculous in their jesting, such as Plautus, Accius, and Terence. The **New Comedians** are also the **Satirists**, by whom vices are generally criticized, such as Flaccus <note>Horace</note>, Persius, Juvenal, and others. For these men rebuke the crimes of everyone, and they did not avoid describing even the worst things, nor did they shy away from reprehending the sins and habits of anyone. Whence also...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s discussion of literary and spiritual figures from the previous section. Having defined the nature of poets, he now moves into specific genres like satire, the prophetic role of the Sibylls, and the darker origins of magic and necromancy.</meta>

...they are painted naked because through them individual vices are laid bare <note>original: "denudentur"</note>. But satirists are so named either because they are full of every eloquence, or from "saturity" <note>meaning "fullness" or "abundance"</note> and plenty. For they speak of many things at once, or the name comes from that platter <note>the *lanx satura*</note> which used to be brought to the temples of the pagans with diverse kinds of fruits or apples. Or perhaps the name is drawn from satyrs, who say many things while in a state of drunkenness. 

Certain poets were called theologians because they composed songs about the gods. The office of a poet consists in this: that those things which were truly done are translated into other forms through indirect figures with some beauty. This is why Lucan is not placed in the number of poets; he is seen to have composed histories rather than a poem. 

Among poets, there are three styles of speaking: one in which only the poet speaks, as in the books of Virgil’s *Georgics*; another is the dramatic style, in which no poet speaks, as in comedies and tragedies; and the third is the mixed style, as in the *Aeneid*. For there, both the poet and characters introduced by him speak.

### On the Sibylls Chapter 7

"Sibylls" is the general name for all female seers in the Greek tongue. For *syos* <note>original: "syos"</note> in the Aeolic speech means "god," and *belen* <note>original: "belen"</note> is what the Greeks call "mind," as if to say "the mind of God." Therefore, because they were accustomed to interpret the divine will to humans, they were named Sibylls. Just as every man who prophesies is called a prophet or a seer, so every prophesying woman is called a Sibyll. This name refers to their office rather than being a proper name. Ten Sibylls are handed down by the most learned authors:

<margin>1</margin>
The first of these was from the Persians.
<margin>2-3</margin>
The second was Libyan. The third was the Delphic Sibyll, born in the temple of Delphic Apollo, who prophesied before the Trojan wars; Homer inserted many of her verses into his own work.
<margin>4-5</margin>
The fourth was the Cimmerian in Italy. The fifth was the Erythraean, named Eriphyla, born in Babylon. She prophesied to the Greeks seeking Troy that the city would perish and that Homer would write lies. She is called Erythraean because her songs were found on that island.
<margin>6</margin>
The sixth was the Samian, who was called Phemonoe, named after the island of Samos where she was from.
<margin>7</margin>
The seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, who brought nine books to Tarquinius Priscus <note>The fifth king of Rome</note> in which the Roman decrees were written. She is also the "Cymean" of whom Virgil says: *The final age of the Cymean song has now come.* She is called Cumaean from the city of Cumae in Campania; her tomb still remains in Sicily.
<margin>8</margin>
The eighth was the Hellespontine, born in the Trojan territory, who is written to have lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus.
<margin>9</margin>
The ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra.
<margin>10</margin>
The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea. 

The songs of all these women are circulated, in which they are most clearly proven to have written much about God, about Christ, and about the nations. Among the others, the Erythraean is considered the most celebrated and noble.

### On the Magi Chapter 8

The first of the Magi was Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, whom Ninus, King of the Assyrians, killed in battle. Aristotle writes of him that two million verses composed by him are evidenced 

<column-break/>

by the records of his volumes. Many centuries later, Democritus expanded this art at the time when Hippocrates also flourished in the discipline of medicine. Among the Assyrians, the magical arts were abundant, as Lucan testifies:
> Who can know what the entrails <note>original: "fibra"</note> have done? Who reports what birds or lightning bolts of heaven the Assyrian care observes, as it searches the stars?

Therefore, this vanity of magical arts, stemming from the tradition of evil angels, prevailed throughout the whole world for many centuries. Through a certain knowledge of the future and of the underworld and the invocation of demons, things such as haruspicy <note>divination using entrails</note>, augury, and those things called oracles and necromancy were invented. 

It is no wonder that the deceptions of the magi reached such a point of evil that they even resisted Moses with very similar signs, turning rods into dragons and water into blood. It is said that a certain most famous sorceress, Circe, changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. One also reads of the sacrifice that the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus, and whoever partook of it was converted into the form of a beast. 

From this, it appears not to be entirely doubtful what that noble poet <note>Virgil</note> wrote about a certain woman excelling in magical arts:
> She promises to release minds with her songs as she wishes, but to send harsh cares to others; to stop the water in rivers and turn the stars backward, and to rouse the ghosts of the night. You will see the earth groan under your feet and rowan trees descend from the mountains.

What more is there to say? It is lawful to believe the account of the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor</note> who called the soul of the prophet Samuel from the hidden depths of the underworld and presented him to the sight of the living—if indeed we believe it was the soul of the prophet and not some phantasmic illusion created by the deceit of Satan. Prudentius also says this of Mercury:
> He is said to have recalled souls of the dead back to the light with his rod, while condemning others to death.

And a little later he added:
> For by a magic murmur thin figures go out and know how to enchant the ashes of the grave.

Likewise, this harmful art knows how to rob others of life. Magi are those commonly called "evil-doers" <note>original: "malefici"</note> because of the magnitude of their crimes. These men shake the elements, disturb the minds of men, and kill without any swallow of poison, by the violence of a song alone. Whence Lucan says:
> The mind, polluted by no filth of a swallowed poison, perishes by enchantment.

For with demons summoned, they dare to boast so that each may slay his enemies with evil arts. These men also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead. 

**Necromancers** are those by whose incantations the dead seem to be resuscitated to divine and answer questions. *Necro* in Greek means "dead" and *manteia* means "divination." To rouse these spirits, blood is added to the corpse; for demons are said to love blood. Therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, gore is mixed with water so that they may be more easily provoked by the color of blood. 

**Hydromancers** are named from water. For hydromancy consists of summoning the shadows of demons by inspecting water, and seeing their images or mockeries, where, with blood added, they are even said to consult the inhabitants of the underworld. This genus of divination...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s exploration of the spiritual world, moving from the definitions of poets and the Sibylls into a detailed classification of various forms of divination, the origins of paganism, and the historical reality behind the ancient gods.</meta>

...is said to have been brought from the Persians. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar</note> says there are four types of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. From this, it is established they are called **geomancy**, **hydromancy**, **aeromancy**, and **pyromancy**. Those called **diviners** <note>original: "divini"</note> are so named as if they were "full of God" <note>original: "quasi deo pleni"</note>. For they pretend to be full of divinity and, with a certain fraudulent cunning, they predict the future for men. Moreover, there are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Those called **enchanters** <note>original: "incantatores"</note> are those who perform their work through the art of words. **Soothsayers** <note>original: "arioli"</note> are so named because they utter wicked prayers around the altars <note>original: "aras"</note> of idols and offer death-bearing sacrifices; through these ceremonies, they receive responses from demons. **Haruspices** <note>inspectors of entrails</note> are named as if they were "inspectors of hours" <note>original: "horarum inspectores"</note>. For they observe days and hours in conducting business and works, and they attend to what a man ought to observe during specific times. These also inspect the entrails <note>original: "exta"</note> of cattle and predict the future from them. **Augurs** are those who attend to the flights and voices of birds, and other signs of things or unpolished observations that occur to men. These are the same as **auspices**. For auspices are those things which people on a journey observe. **Auspices** are named as if they were the "watching of birds" <note>original: "avium aspicia"</note>, and **auguries** as the "chatter of birds" <note>original: "avium garria"</note>, that is, the voices and tongues of birds. Likewise, "augury" is like "bird-bearing" <note>original: "avigerium"</note>, which the birds carry out. There are two kinds of auspices: one pertaining to the eyes and the other to the ears. To the eyes belong the flights; to the ears, the voice of the birds. **Pythons** <note>original: "phytones"</note> are named after Pythian Apollo, because he was the author of divining. **Astrologers** are named because they divine by the stars. Those called **genethliacs** <note>original: "genetiaci"</note> are named because of their consideration of birthdays. For they describe the origin <note>original: "genesis"</note> of men through the twelve signs of heaven, and they attempt to predict the behaviors, acts, and outcomes of those being born by the course of the stars—that is, who was born under what sign, or what effect it has on the life of the one being born. These are the people the common folk call **mathematicians** <note>original: "mathematici"</note>. The Latins call this kind of superstition **constellations**, and likewise the **observation of stars**, noting how they stand when someone is born. At first, these same interpreters of stars were called **Magi** <note>Wise Men</note>, as we read concerning those who announced the birth of Christ in the Gospel; afterward, this name remained only for the mathematicians. The knowledge of this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that once Christ was born, no one from then on should interpret the birth of anyone from the heavens. Those called **horoscopists** <note>original: "horoscopi"</note> are so named because they speculate on the hours of men’s births with a varied and diverse fate. **Lot-casters** <note>original: "sortilegi"</note> are those who, under the name of a false religion, profess the science of divination through what they call the "lots of the saints," or who promise the future through the inspection of any scriptures whatsoever. Those called **salisatores** <note>from "salire," to leap or twitch</note> are named because, whenever any part of their limbs twitches, they predict that it signifies something prosperous or sad for them. To all these things belong the **amulets** <note>original: "ligaturae," meaning "bindings"</note> of cursed remedies which the art of medicine condemns, whether in incantations, or in characters <note>mystical signs</note>, or in any things whatsoever to be suspended or bound. In all of these, the art of demons has arisen from a certain pestilential society of men and evil angels. Therefore, all these things must be avoided by a Christian,

<column-break/>

and must be utterly rejected and condemned with every curse. The Phrygians were the first to find the **auguries of birds**. **Mercury** is said to have been the first to find **prestige** <note>original: "prestigium," meaning sleight of hand or illusion</note>. It is called "prestige" because it "dazzles the sight" <note>original: "perstringat aciem"</note> of the eyes. A certain **Tages** is said to have been the first to hand down the art of **haruspicy** to the Etruscans; he dictated haruspicy from the earth and afterward disappeared. For it is told in fables that while a certain countryman was plowing, this Tages suddenly leaped out of the clods of earth, dictated the haruspicy on the day he also died. The Romans translated these books from the Etruscan language into their own.

### On the Pagans Chapter 10

**Pagans** are named from the villages <note>original: "pagis"</note> of the Athenians where they arose. For there, in rural places and villages, the heathens established groves and idols. <margin>heathens</margin> From such a beginning, they obtained the name "pagans." **Gentiles** <note>original: "gentiles"</note> are those who are without the Law and have not yet believed. They are called "Gentiles" because they are just as they were born <note>original: "geniti"</note>; that is, just as they descended in the flesh under sin, serving idols and not yet reborn in the Lord. Therefore, they were originally called "Gentiles." In Greek, they are called **ethnici**. <margin>ethnics</margin> For "ethnici" is translated from Greek into Latin as "Gentiles." In Greek, a nation or people is called *ethnos*. After coming to the faith, however, those from the nations who believe ought not to be called "nations" or "Gentiles," just as after the faith one can no longer be called a "Jew," as the Apostle Paul testifies, saying to the Christians: "Since you were once Gentiles"—that is, infidels. <margin>apostates</margin> Those who return to the worship of idols and the contamination of sacrifices after receiving the baptism of Christ are called **apostates**. This is a Greek name.

### On the Gods of the Nations Chapter 11

Those whom the pagans assert to be gods are revealed to have once been **men**. Because of the life or merits of each one, they began to be worshipped among their own people after death, such as **Isis** in Egypt, **Jupiter** in Crete, **Juba** among the Moors, **Faunus** among the Latins, and **Quirinus** among the Romans. In the same way, **Minerva** at Athens, **Juno** at Samos, **Venus** at Paphos, **Vulcan** at Lemnos, **Liber** <note>Bacchus</note> at Naxos, and **Apollo** at Delos. The poets also joined in their praises and, having composed songs, raised them into heaven. For they say that the inventions of certain arts gave birth to their worship—such as medicine for **Aesculapius** and blacksmithing for **Vulcan**. Others are named from their acts, such as **Mercury** because he presides over merchandise <note>original: "mercibus"</note>, and **Liber** from "liberty." There were also certain strong men or founders of cities for whom, after they died, the men who loved them fashioned images <note>original: "simulacra"</note> so that they might have some solace from the contemplation of the statues. But gradually, through the persuasion of demons, this error so crept into their descendants that they considered and worshipped as gods those whom their ancestors had honored only for the memory of their names. The use of idols <note>original: "simulacrorum"</note> arose when, out of a longing for the dead, they established images or effigies as if they had been received into heaven; in their place, demons stole in to be worshipped on earth and persuaded the deceived and lost to sacrifice to them. <margin>idols</margin> **Idols** <note>original: "simulacra"</note> are named from "likeness" <note>original: "similitudine"</note> because, by the hand of the craftsman, they imitate the faces of those in whose honor they are fashioned from stone or other material. Therefore, they are called *simulacra* either because they are "similar," or because...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s discussion on spiritual entities and pagan worship, transitioning from the methods of divination used by soothsayers to the origins of the objects they worship: idols, demons, and the fallen angels led by the Devil and the Antichrist.</meta>

### Book

...simulated and fabricated; therefore they are false. And it should be noted that the word is Latin and not Hebrew. Among them, an idol or likeness is spoken of only once. The Jews say that Ishmael was the first to make a likeness out of mud. The Gentiles, however, claim that **Prometheus** <note>In Greek mythology, a Titan who created humanity from clay</note> was the first to fashion likenesses of men from mud, and from him was born the art of molding likenesses and statues. Hence, the poets figuratively pretend that the first men were made by him, on account of these images. Among the Greeks, however, it was **Cecrops**—under whom the first olive tree sprang up on the citadel and the city of the Athenians received its name from the title of **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for Athena</note>—who first of all called upon Jupiter, discovered likenesses, set up altars, and sacrificed victims, as such things had never been seen in Greece before.

**Idolatry** is interpreted as the service or worship of idols. For *latria* in Greek is called *servitus* <note>original: "servitus"</note> in Latin, which, as far as true religion is concerned, is owed only to the one and only God. Just as wicked pride, whether of men or of demons, desires or commands this worship to be shown to itself, so pious humility, whether of men or of holy angels, refuses it when offered and points toward the one to whom it is truly owed. An **idol**, moreover, is a likeness which is made and consecrated in a human image, according to the interpretation of the word. For *Idos* <note>original: "eidos"</note> in Greek sounds like "form," and from it the word *idol* <note>original: "idolon"</note> is derived by a diminutive, just as among us the word *formula* <note>original: "formula," a small form</note> is made. Therefore, every form or small formula demands to be called an idol. Hence, all "idolatry" is the attendance and service around every idol. Certain Latins, however, being ignorant of Greek, say unskillfully that "idol" took its name from "guile" <note>original: "dolo"</note>, because the devil introduced the worship of the divine name to a creature.

<margin>
Demons in Greek: knowing and foreknowing
</margin>
They say **Demons** were named by the Greeks as if they were *daimones* <note>original: "δαιμονας"</note>, that is, "skilled" and "foreknowing of things." For they foreknow many future events. Hence, they are also accustomed to give certain responses. For there is in them a greater knowledge of things than in human weakness, partly by the subtlety of their keen senses, partly by the experience of a very long life, and partly because they receive the command of God through angelic revelation. They thrive in the nature of **aerial bodies**. Before their transgression, indeed, they bore celestial bodies; but having fallen, they were changed into an aerial quality. They are not permitted to hold the purer spaces of that air, but these dark ones, which are like a prison for them until the time of judgment. These are the prevaricating angels, of whom the **Devil** is the prince.

<margin>
The Devil. Much "devil," so that there are two "throws" [boly]. A holy body compared to the devil.
</margin>
**The Devil** <note>original: "Diabolus"</note> is said in Hebrew to mean "flowing downward," because he scorned to stand still at the height of heaven, but falling by the weight of his pride, he collapsed downward. In Greek, however, the Devil is called "the accuser," either because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices people, or because he accuses the innocence of the elect with false crimes. Whence also in the Apocalypse, he is called by an angelic voice: "The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them in the sight of our God day and night."

<margin>Satan</margin>
**Satan** <note>original: "Sathanas"</note> sounds in Latin like "adversary" or "transgressor." For he is the adversary who is the enemy of truth and always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints. He is also the transgressor, because having become a prevaricator, he did not stand in the truth in which he was created. He is also the **Tempter**, because he demands that the innocence of the righteous be tested, as is written in the book of Job.

<margin>Antichrist</margin>
He is called the **Antichrist** because he is to come against Christ—not as some simple people understand it, that he is called Antichrist because he is to come "before" Christ <note>confusing the Greek 'anti' with the Latin 'ante'</note>, that is, that Christ comes after him. Not so; but he is called Antichrist in Greek, which in Latin means "contrary to Christ." For *anti* in Greek signifies "against" in Latin. For he will lie that he is Christ when he comes, and he will fight against Him, and he will oppose the sacraments of Christ so that he may dissolve the Gospel of His truth. For he will even attempt to repair the Temple in Jerusalem and restore all the ceremonies of the Old Law. But he is also an Antichrist who denies that the Lord is Christ. For he is contrary to Christ. Indeed, all who go out of the Church and cut themselves off from the unity of the faith are themselves antichrists.

<column-break/>

<margin>Bel</margin>
**Bel** is a Babylonian idol, which is interpreted as "old." For this Belus was the father of Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians, whom some call Saturn; this name was later worshipped both among the Assyrians and among the Africans.

<margin>Baal</margin>
Hence, also in the Punic language, **Baal** means "god." Among the Assyrians, however, he is called **Bel** by a certain reasoning of their sacred rites, and is identified with both Saturn and the Sun.

<margin>Beelphegor</margin>
**Beelphegor** <note>original: "Beelphegoz"</note> is interpreted as the "likeness of ignominy." For it was an idol of Moab with the surname Baal upon Mount Phegor, whom the Latins call **Priapus**, the god of gardens. He was from the city of Lampsacus on the Hellespont, from which he was expelled; on account of the magnitude of his male member, the Greeks transferred him into the number of their gods and consecrated him in the name of gardens. Hence, he is also said to preside over gardens because of their fertility.

<margin>Beelzebub</margin>
**Beelzebub** was an idol of Accaron, which is interpreted as the "man of flies." For *Cebub* means "fly." This most filthy idol is therefore called "man of flies" on account of the filth of idolatry, or on account of uncleanness.

<margin>Belial</margin>
**Belial** means "without a yoke." Belial is called Bel in Hebrew, the idol of the Ninevites.

<margin>Behemoth</margin>
**Behemoth** from the Hebrew voice sounds in the Latin language as "animal" <note>or beast</note>, because he fell from the heights to earthly things, and by his own merit has been made like a brute animal.

<margin>Leviathan</margin>
He is also **Leviathan**, that is, the "serpent of the waters," because he moves with cunning in the turbulent sea of this world. Leviathan, however, is interpreted as "their addition"—namely, of those people to whom he once brought death in Paradise through the fault of prevarication, and he adds to or extends this daily toward eternal death by his persuasion.

There are certain names of gods which the Gentiles try to translate from vain fables into physical explanations, and they interpret them as being composed of the causes of the elements. But this is entirely fabricated by the poets so that they might adorn their gods with certain figures, whom histories confess to have been lost and full of the infamy of disgrace. For there is entirely no room for fabrication where truth ceases.

<margin>Saturn</margin>
**Saturn** is designated by the pagans as the origin of the gods and of all posterity. The Latins say he is named from "sowing" <note>original: "satu"</note>, as if the sowing of all things pertains to him; or from the length of time, because he is "saturated" with years. Hence also the Greeks say he has the name **Cronos**, that is, "Time," because he is said to have devoured his own sons—that is, he rolls back into himself the years which time has produced. Or because the seeds from which they arise return again. He is said to have cut off the genitals of his father, Heaven, because nothing is born in heaven from seeds. He carries a sickle...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of pagan deities and their origins as described by Isidore of Seville in Book VIII of his Etymologies. Having previously discussed the general nature of idols, the text now moves into specific Roman and Greek gods, providing etymological explanations for their names and attributes based on historical and poetic traditions.</meta>

# VIII

<column-break/>

They say he holds [a scythe] to signify agriculture, or because of the times and years that return upon themselves, or for the sake of wisdom, which is sharp within. In certain cities, the pagans used to sacrifice their own children to Saturn, as the poets recorded that Saturn was accustomed to devouring his own children.

**Jove** is said to be named from "helping" <note>original: "a iuvando"</note>, and **Jupiter** is as if he were a "helping father" <note>original: "iuvans pater"</note>; that is, one who excels over all. They also gave him the private title of "Jupiter the Best" <note>original: "Iovem Optimum"</note>, even though he was incestuous toward his own kin and immodest toward strangers. They depict him now as a bull, on account of the rape of Europa—for he was on a ship whose figurehead was a bull—and now as having sought a sexual encounter with Danae by means of a golden shower, which is understood to mean that the woman’s modesty was corrupted by gold. At other times he is shown in the likeness of an eagle, because of a boy <note>Ganymede</note> whom he snatched away for debauchery; sometimes as a serpent, and sometimes as a swan because he sang. Therefore, these are not mere figures of speech, but clearly crimes of truth. Hence it was shameful for such beings to be believed as gods, when men ought not to be like them.

**Janus** they describe as being the "door" <note>original: "ianuam"</note> of the world, or of heaven, or of the months. They make two faces for Janus to represent the east and the west. When they make him with four faces and call him "Double Janus," they refer this to the four parts of the world, or to the four elements or seasons. But while they invent this, they create a monster rather than a god.

**Neptune** they proclaim to be the waters of the world; he is named by them "Neptune" as if he were "thundering from a cloud" <note>original: "nube tonans"</note>. They want **Vulcan** to be fire, and he is called "Vulcan" as if he were "flying brightness" <note>original: "volans candor"</note>, or as if he were "flying through the air" <note>original: "volicanus"</note>. For fire is born from the clouds; hence even **Homer** says he was cast down from the air to the earth, because lightning falls from the air. For that reason, Vulcan is also imagined to be born from the thigh of **Juno**, because lightning is born from the lower air. Vulcan is said to be "lame" <note>original: "Claudius," related to "claudus"</note> because fire is never straight by nature, but has a kind of limping appearance and motion. Furthermore, they say this same Vulcan is the author of the blacksmiths' forge, because no kind of metal can be melted or worked without fire.

**Pluto** in Greek is "Diespiter" <note>Father of Day</note> or "Dis Pater" <note>Father of Riches</note> in Latin. Others call him **Orcus**, as if he were a "receiver of the dead" <note>original: "receptorem mortuorum"</note>. From this, the vessel that receives water is also called an "orca" <note>a jar or butt</note>. He is also called **Charon** in Greek.

They want **Liber** <note>Bacchus/Dionysus</note> to be named from "liberation" <note>original: "liberamento"</note>, because through his benefit, males are "liberated" by the emission of seed during intercourse. This same Liber is depicted with a feminine and delicate body. For they say that women were attributed to him, and wine for the sake of arousing lust. Hence his brow is encircled with vine-leaves. For this reason, he has a headband <note>original: "coronam vitteam"</note> and horns, because when wine is drunk gratefully and in moderation, it provides joy; but when drunk beyond measure, it excites strife—that is, it gives "horns." He is also called **Lyaeus** from the Greek word *lyin* <note>original: "apo tu lyin"</note>, that is, from "dissolution," because the limbs are loosened by too much wine. He is also **Dionysus** in Greek, named from Mount Nysa in India, where he is said to have been nursed. Moreover, there is also a city of Nysa in which this same Liber is worshipped, from which he is also called **Nyseus**.

**Mercury** is interpreted as "speech" <note>original: "sermo"</note>. For Mercury is said to be named as if "running in the middle" <note>original: "medius currens"</note>, because speech runs in the middle between men. He is also called **Hermes** in Greek, which means "speech" or "interpretation"; the word for interpretation, which pertains to speech on both sides, is called *hermenia* <note>original: "hermenia," i.e., hermeneutics</note>. Therefore, he also presides over merchandise <note>original: "mercibus"</note>, because speech is the intermediary between sellers and buyers. He is depicted as having wings because words run swiftly; hence he is introduced as "fast" and "wandering." The wings on his head and feet signify that speech becomes a bird flying through the air. He is called a messenger because all thoughts are announced through speech. For this reason, they call him the master of thieves, because speech deceives the minds of listeners. He holds a wand with which he separates serpents—that is, poisons. For those who are fighting and disagreeing are calmed by the oration of interpreters; hence, according to **Livy**, ambassadors of peace are called *caduceatores* <note>heralds carrying the caduceus staff</note>. For just as wars were declared by the *feciales* <note>priests of diplomatic law</note>, so peace was made through the *caduceatores*. Hermes in Greek is named from *hermenias*, and in Latin is "interpreter," who on account of his virtue and knowledge of many arts was named **Trismegistus**, that is, "Thrice-Greatest." When he is depicted with a dog’s head, this is the reason given: that among all animals, the dog is the most sagacious and perceptive breed.

<margin>Mars</margin> They say **Mars** is the god of war, named because the fight is carried out "by men" <note>original: "per viros"</note>, so that Mars is as if he were "male" <note>original: "mas"</note>. However, there are three types of customs: like the **Scythians**, where both women and men go into battle; the **Amazons**, where only women go; and the **Romans** and other nations, where only males go. Likewise, they call him Mars as if he were the "worker of death" <note>original: "effectorem mortuum"</note>. For death is named from Mars. 

<margin>Death is named from Mars</margin> Hence they also call him an adulterer, because he is uncertain to those waging war. He stands with a naked chest so that everyone might throw themselves into war without fear in their hearts. Mars is called **Gradivus** among the Greeks because those who fight "advance in step" <note>original: "gradu inferant"</note> in war, or because they "step" <note>original: "gradiantur"</note> vigorously.

Although they want **Apollo** to be a diviner and a healer, they also said he was the Sun itself—named as if "alone" <note>original: "solum"</note>. He is called **Titan**, as the one among the Titans who did not act against Jove. He is called **Phoebus**, as if he were an *ephebus* <note>Greek for a youth</note>, that is, a young man. Hence the Sun is depicted as a boy, because he rises daily and is born with new light. They say this same Apollo is also called **Pythian**, from **Python**, a serpent of immense mass, whose size was no less terrifying than its venom. Apollo, striking this serpent with hits from his arrows, carried back the spoils of the name, so that he was called Pythian. On account of this mark of victory, he established the **Pythian Games** to be celebrated.

They say **Diana**, his sister, is the Moon and the guardian of roads. Hence they want her to be a virgin, because a road produces nothing. Both are depicted holding arrows because these two stars emit rays from the sky down to the earth. She is called Diana as if "two-natured" <note>original: "duanam"</note>, because the moon appears by day and night. They also assert she is **Lucina** because she shines <note>original: "luceat"</note>. She is also **Trivia** <note>Of the Three Ways</note> because she is imagined in three forms. Concerning her, **Virgil** says: "the three faces of the virgin Diana." She is called the Moon, Diana, and **Proserpina**. When she is the Moon, she shines in a bright garment; when she is the "Latonian Virgin" <note>daughter of Latona</note>, she is girt and throws arrows; when she is the "Plutonian Wife," she sits supported on a throne. She is called Latonian Diana because she was the daughter of **Latona**.

They assert that **Ceres**, that is the earth, is named from "creating fruits" <note>original: "a creandis frugibus"</note>, calling her by many names. They also call her **Ops** because the earth becomes better by "wealth" <note>original: "opem"</note>. They call her Proserpina because fruits "creep forth" <note>original: "proserpant"</note> from her. They call her **Vesta** because she is clothed in herbs...
