<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s Ninth Book of the Etymologies. Having previously discussed the military and the basic definition of a citizen, he now moves into the hierarchy of Roman social and political life, defining types of groups (family, people, plebs) and the specific titles of officials and workers.</meta>

# IX

...just as a city belongs to a single people, so the world is the dwelling-place of the entire human race. A **household** <note>original: "domus"</note> is a family lineage, or the union of a husband and wife. It begins with two people and is a Greek name <note>Isidore likely associates "domus" with the Greek "domos"</note>. A **family** <note>original: "familia"</note> refers to children born of legal marriages, derived from the "thigh" <note>original: "femore"; Isidore uses a common ancient etymology linking family to procreation</note>. **Lineage** <note>original: "genus"</note>, however, is named from "begetting" <note>original: "gignendo"</note> and "procreating" <note>original: "progenerando"</note>, or from the definition of certain ancestors, such as nations that are called **peoples** <note>original: "gentes"</note> because they are bounded by their own kinships. A **people** <note>original: "populus"</note> is a multitude of humans associated by a consensus of law and a harmonious communion. A "people," however, differs from the **commoners** <note>original: "plebibus"</note> in that the "people" consists of all citizens, including the elders of the city. The "commoners," however, are the remaining crowd without the city’s elders. Therefore, the "people" is the whole city, while the "commoners" are the rabble. The "commoners" <note>original: "plebs"</note> are named for their **plurality** <note>original: "pluralitate"</note>, for the number of lower citizens is greater than the number of elders. A "people," on the other hand, is so called... that is, a gathering... from which it is called a "people" <note>original: "populus"</note>. In Greek, a people is called **laos** <note>original: "laos"</note>, from "stones" <note>original: "lapidibus"; a reference to the myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha, who repopulated the earth by throwing stones</note>. The **crowd** <note>original: "vulgus"</note> is the multitude living here and there, as if each person does what they want. **Tribes** <note>original: "tribus"</note> are named as if they were distinct assemblies and congregations of the people; they are called "tribes" because in the beginning the Romans were divided into three parts by **Romulus** <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note>: into senators, soldiers, and the commoners. Although these tribes are now multiplied, they retain their original name. The name **Senate** <note>original: "senatus"</note> was given by age, because they were the **elders** <note>original: "seniores"</note>. Others accept that they were called **senators** from "limiting" <note>original: "finendo"</note>, for they gave the power to act. A **decree of the senate** <note>original: "senatus consultus"</note> is named from "consulting" and "treating" a matter, because it is done so that it may provide counsel and cannot cause harm. The **Fathers** <note>original: "patres"; a title for senators</note>, as **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian</note> says, were so called from the similarity of their care. For just as fathers nourish their children, so they nourished the republic. They are called **Conscript Fathers** <note>original: "patres conscripti"</note> because when Romulus chose ten groups of senators, he recorded their names in the presence of the people on golden tablets, and from that they were called "enrolled fathers." The first ranks of senators are called **illustrious** <note>original: "illustres"</note>, the second **admirable** <note>original: "spectabiles"</note>, and the third **most distinguished** <note>original: "clarissimi"</note>. Now, there is no fourth kind lower than this. Whoever was of senatorial origin would be a **Roman knight** <note>original: "eques romanus"</note> until they reached the legal age, and then they would receive the honor of the senatorial dignity. **Censors** <note>original: "censores"</note> existed among the ancient Romans. For the name of a "Censor" is a judicial dignity, as to **judge** <note>original: "censere"</note> is to decide. **Predecessors** <note>original: "praecessores"</note> are the judges of estates, named from the **census of money** <note>original: "censu aeris"</note>. **Judges** <note>original: "iudices"</note> are named as if they were "speakers of the law" <note>original: "ius dicentes"</note> to the people, or because they debate by law. To argue by law is to judge justly. He is not a judge if justice is not in him. **Presidents** <note>original: "praesides"</note> were named as the rulers of a province because they "preside" <note>original: "praesunt"</note>. **Praetors** <note>original: "praetores"</note> are like the "teachers" <note>original: "praeceptores"</note> and leaders of the city. The same applies to **quaestors** <note>original: "quaestores"</note>, acting like "inquirers" <note>original: "quaesitores"</note>, because they preside over inquiries; for the counsel and the case are before them. **Chiefs** <note>original: "proceres"</note> are the leaders of the city, as if "going before" <note>original: "procedentes"</note>, because they precede all others in honor. Hence the heads of beams that project out from walls are called "chiefs," because they proceed out first. From this, the word was transferred to the **foremost men** <note>original: "primores"</note> because they stand out from the rest of the multitude. **Tribunes** <note>original: "tribuni"</note> are so called because they "distribute" <note>original: "tribuunt"</note> either laws or aid to the commoners. They were established in the sixth year after the kings were driven out. When the commoners

<column-break/>

were being oppressed by the senate and the consuls, they then created for themselves **tribunes** as their own judges and defenders to protect their liberty and defend them against the injustice of the nobility. Hence they are called **defenders** <note>original: "defensores"</note>, because they defend the commoners committed to them against the insolence of the wicked. But on the contrary, nowadays some exist as **overthrowers** <note>original: "eversores"</note>, not defenders. **Tax-payers** <note>original: "munerarij"</note> are those who bring public money into the treasuries. **Officials** <note>original: "functi"</note> are named from the fact that they "perform" <note>original: "fungantur"</note> some duty or honor. From this we also call the dead **deceased** <note>original: "defunctos"</note> because they have completed the duties of life; for they now do nothing. **Citizens of a municipality** <note>original: "municipes"</note> are those born in the same municipality, named from the performance of "duties" <note>original: "munerū"</note>, because they accept public tasks; for tasks <note>original: "munia"</note> are duties. From this those who hold no office are called **immune** <note>original: "immunes"</note>. **Municipals** <note>original: "municipales"</note> are the original citizens who hold office in a place. **Decurions** <note>original: "decuriones"</note> are so named because they are of the "order of the curia" <note>the local council</note>. They administer the office of the curia; thus one is not a decurion if he has not brought in a sum of money or participated in the curia. **Curials** <note>original: "curiales"</note> are the same as decurions. They are called "curials" because they take care of and execute civil duties. **Principals** <note>original: "principales"</note>, **magistrates** <note>original: "magistratus"</note>, and **universals** are the ranks of the curial offices. They are called "principals" because they preside over the magistrates. "Magistrates" are so called because they are "greater" <note>original: "maiores"</note> than the other offices. **Duovirs** <note>original: "duumuirales"</note> are those who have power over two men. A **notary** <note>original: "tabellio"</note> is so called because he is a carrier of **tablets** <note>original: "tabellarum"</note>. He is the same as an **assistant** <note>original: "exceptor"</note> and a **public scribe** <note>original: "scriba publicus"</note>, because he writes down what is done in public records. **Burgarians** <note>original: "burgarij"</note> are named from "burgs" <note>original: "burgis"</note>, because the dwellings established frequently along the borders are commonly called "burgs"; hence the name remained with the nation of the **Burgundians**, whom the Romans once settled in camps after subduing Germany, and thus they took their name from the locations. **Guild members** <note>original: "collegiati"</note> are so called because they are assigned to a "guild" <note>original: "collegio"</note> along with all those who have committed some crime. For it is a most base class of men, born of an uncertain father. **Private citizens** <note>original: "privati"</note> are those outside of public offices. It is a name contrary to those holding a magistracy, and they are called "private" because they are "released" <note>original: "absoluti"</note> from the duties of the curia. **Mercenaries** <note>original: "mercenarij"</note> are those who serve for a received **wage** <note>original: "mercede"</note>. They are also called **barons** <note>original: "barones"</note> by a Greek name because they are strong in labors. For **barys** <note>original: "barys"</note> is said to be "heavy," which means "strong." The opposite of this is "light," that is, weak. **Publicans** <note>original: "publicani"</note> are the contractors of the treasury's taxes or public property, or those who collect public taxes, or those who seek profit through secular business; hence they are so named. A **steward** <note>original: "villicus"</note> is properly the governor of a **villa**. Hence the steward took his name from the villa. Sometimes, however, according to **Tullius’s** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator</note> interpretation, a "steward" does not mean a governor of a villa, but a manager of the entire house, which is a manager of all possessions and villas. **Agents** <note>original: "actores"</note> and **curators** <note>original: "curatores"</note> are named from "acting" and "caring." **Procurators** <note>original: "procuratores"</note> are so called because they perform the role in place of <note>original: "vice"</note> a curator, as if "on behalf of the curators" <note>original: "propter curatores"</note>, just as a **proconsul** acts in place of a consul. **Tenant farmers** <note>original: "coloni"</note> are foreign cultivators, named from the **cultivation** <note>original: "cultura"</note> of the field. For they are those coming from elsewhere and holding a leased foreign field, and they owe their status to the soil of their birth on account of agriculture...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s exploration of Roman social and legal categories in Book IX. Having defined the "people" and the "commoners" on the previous page, he now moves into more specific legal statuses—ranging from tenant farmers and slaves to the various grades of family lineage and kinship.</meta>

...under the domain of the owner because the land has been leased twice. **Colonists** <note>original: "Coloni"</note>, however, are spoken of in four ways: for they are either Roman colonists, Latin colonists, auxiliary colonists, or colonists of a private countryside. **Tenants** <note>original: "Inquilini"</note> are so called as if "inhabiting the property of others" <note>original: "incolentes aliena"</note>. For they do not have their own seat but live on someone else’s land. There is, however, a difference between a "tenant" and a **newcomer** <note>original: "advena"</note>. For tenants are those who migrate and do not remain forever. Newcomers, or "immigrant inhabitants," are considered those who stay; they are called **inhabitants** <note>original: "incolae"</note> because they are now residents, from the word for "inhabiting" <note>original: "incolendo"</note>. **Natives** <note>original: "Indigenae"</note> are those "born from there" <note>original: "inde geniti"</note> and born in the same place where they live. An "inhabitant," however, indicates a newcomer rather than a native. **Foreigners** <note>original: "Peregrini"</note> are so named because the parents from whom they arose are unknown <note>original: "ignorantur"</note>; for they are from a distant region. Those who lived in Rome were called **Urbanites** <note>original: "Urbani"</note>. Those in other places were called **Townsfolk** <note>original: "oppidani"</note>. For Rome alone is the "City" <note>original: "urbs"</note>; the rest are "towns" <note>original: "oppida"</note>. **Household servants** <note>original: "Famuli"</note> are those born from the master's own family. The term **Slaves** <note>original: "Serui"</note>, however, was derived from the fact that those who could be killed by the law of war were "preserved" <note>original: "conservabant"</note> by the victors and became slaves; they are called *serui* from the act of "preserving" <note>original: "servando"</note>. **Handmaidens** <note>original: "Ancillae"</note> are named from "support" <note>original: "sustentaculo"</note>. For in Greek, an "elbow" <note>original: "cubitus"</note> is called *ancon* <note>original: "ancon"</note>. Hence we also say *ancone* <note>An "ancon" can refer to a bracket or support in architecture, or the bend of the arm</note>. **Property** <note>original: "Mancipium"</note> is whatever can be "taken by the hand" <note>original: "manu capi"</note> and subjected, such as a human, a horse, or a sheep. For these animals are considered "property" as soon as they are born. For even those which are numbered among the wild beasts are seen to be "property" only when they begin to be captured or tamed. The **Free-born** <note>original: "Ingenui"</note> are so called because they have liberty in their lineage <note>original: "genere"</note>, not by a specific deed like freedmen. Hence the Greeks call them *eugenes* <note>original: "eugenes"</note> because they are of "good lineage." A **Freedman** <note>original: "Libertus"</note>, however, is so called as if "liberated." For he was previously bound to the yoke of servitude. The sons of freedmen among the ancients were called **Libertines** <note>original: "libertini"</note>, as if born from freedmen. Now, however, "most free" <note>original: "liberrimus"</note> refers to one either made by or possessed by a free person. One is said to be **Manumitted** <note>original: "Manumissus"</note> as if "sent from the hand" <note>original: "manu emissus"</note>. For among the ancients, whenever they released someone "from the hand," they would turn them around with a slap <note>original: "alapa"</note> and confirm them as free; they were called "manumitted" because they were "sent from the hand." The **Surrenderers** <note>original: "Dedititij"</note> were first named from "surrender" <note>original: "deditione"</note>. For a "surrender" is said to occur when the conquered—or those about to be conquered—hand themselves over to the victors. This was the origin of the name: when slaves once fought with arms against the Roman people, they were defeated and surrendered themselves, and once captured, they were affected by various marks of disgrace. Because of these marks of punishment which they clearly endured, some of these later manumitted by their masters did not arrive at the dignity of Roman citizens. **Latins** <note>original: "Latini"</note> were created among the Latins before the founding of Rome; now they take their liberty through a will or by a letter. Because they were not made through a full Roman testament, they could neither take anything from a testament nor make their own heirs. **Roman citizens** <note>original: "Cives romani"</note> were later made so under the consuls through testaments in the city of Rome. They are called Roman citizens because, having been made free by a testament, they are enrolled into the number of Roman citizens. To these was first granted the right to stay in the city of Rome; other freedmen, however, were prohibited from staying either in the city of Rome or within the seventh mile-marker from the city.

<column-break/>

### Chapter V: On Affinities and Degrees

The name of **Heir** <note>original: "Heres"</note> was imposed by the census of copper <note>original: "census eris"</note>; for he pays the tax of the originator <note>Isidore links "heres" to "aes" (bronze/money), suggesting the heir inherits both the assets and the tax obligations of the deceased</note>. In this word is the first succession of inheritance and lineage, such as sons and grandsons. A **Pro-heir** <note>original: "Proheredes"</note> is one who performs the role of an heir, acting as if "for the heir." For he is either "instituted" or "substituted." A **Father** <note>original: "Pater"</note> is he from whom the beginning of the lineage is born. Therefore he is called the **Head of the Household** <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note>. He is called a father because, after the "accomplishment" <note>original: "patratio"</note> is finished, he procreates a son. For "accomplishment" is the consummation of the venereal act. Lucretius says: "And well the accomplishment of the fathers" <note>original: "Et bene patratio patrum"</note>. **Begetters** <note>original: "Genitores"</note> are named from "begetting" <note>original: "gignendo"</note>, and **parents** <note>original: "parentes"</note> as if "bringing forth" <note>original: "parientes"</note>. They are also **creators** <note>original: "creatores"</note>. For "lomentum" <note>likely a variant of "elementum" or "mentum" in this context</note> is the seed of the male, from which the bodies of animals and humans are conceived; hence parents are called "creators." A **Mother** <note>original: "Mater"</note> is so called because something is "made from her." For "mother" is as if "matter" <note>original: "materia"</note>, while the father is the "cause." A **Head of the Household** <note>original: "Paterfamilias"</note>, however, is so named because he looks after all the slaves placed in his family with fatherly love, just as a father does for his sons, and he does not distinguish the condition of the slaves from the affection for his sons, but embraces them as one member. From this the name of "father of the family" arose. Those who rule unjustly over slaves should by no means think themselves called by this name. A **Mistress of the Household** <note>original: "Materfamilias"</note> is called so because, through a certain legal solemnity, she passes into the family of her husband. For marriage tablets were once instruments of "purchase" <note>original: "emptionis"</note>. Otherwise, just as a **Matron** <note>original: "matrona"</note> is the "mother of any child"—that is, as if "mother of the born"—so a *materfamilias* is she who has given birth to many. For a "family" begins from two people. A **Grandfather** <note>original: "Auus"</note> is the father of the father; he is named from "antiquity" <note>original: "antiquitate"</note>. A **Great-grandfather** <note>original: "Proauus"</note> is the father of the grandfather, as if "near the grandfather" <note>original: "prope auum"</note>. A **Great-great-grandfather** <note>original: "Abauus"</note> is the father of the great-grandfather, now "far from the grandfather" <note>original: "longe ab auo"</note>. An **Atauus** is the father of the *abauus*. A **Tritauus** is the father of the *atauuus*, as if "tetra-uus," that is, the fourth above the *abauus*. But *tritauus* is the final name of kinship. A **Family** <note>original: "Familia"</note>, moreover, arises from the father and ends in the *tritauus*. **Son** and **daughter** <note>original: "Filius et filia"</note> are named from "family"; for they are the first in the order of those being born. Hence the Cornelia family is the entire branch arising from Cornelius. A "family," however, is named from the **thigh** <note>original: "femore"</note>; for the "thigh" shows the race <note>original: "genus"</note> and the branch <note>original: "stirps"</note>. For "family" is used improperly for slaves, not in its strict sense. A **Branch** <note>original: "Stirps"</note> is named from the long-standing significance of the lineage. One is called **Born** <note>original: "Gnatus"</note> because he is "generated" <note>original: "generatus"</note>; hence it is written with a "g." **Offspring** <note>original: "Soboles"</note> is so called because it is a "substitution of the race" <note>original: "substitutio generis"</note>. There is a fourfold order of sons: the **Only-begotten**, the **First-born**, the **Middle**, and the **Last**. The **Only-begotten** <note>original: "Unigenitus"</note> because he is the only one, with none before or after. The **First-born** <note>original: "Primogenitus"</note>, before whom there is none. The **Middle** <note>original: "Medius"</note>, between all others. The **Last** <note>original: "Nouissimus"</note>, after all. The same is also the "smallest" <note>original: "minimus"</note>, from "monad" <note>original: "monade"</note>. He is called "newest" because he is "new" <note>original: "nouus"</note>, while the others are older by preceding him. For sons are named in four ways: by nature, by imitation, by adoption, and by teaching. By nature, as when the Jews are called sons of Abraham. By imitation, as when those from the Gentiles imitate the faith of Abraham himself—as the Gospel says: "God is able to raise up sons of Abraham from these stones"—or as the Lord says the same Jews are sons of the devil, from whom they were not named or born, but whom they followed...

Having touched on servants, Isidore now transitions into the legal and biological definitions of children, the nature of adoption, and the intricate terminology used to map out family trees and degrees of kinship.</meta>

# IX

...to imitate. There is also **adoption** <note>original: "Adoptio"</note>, which by human custom no one is allowed to be ignorant of; it is in this way that we are called "of God," not by nature, but by adoption, as in the prayer: "Our Father, who art in heaven." There is also adoption through **teaching** <note>original: "Doctrina"</note>; in this way, the Apostle calls those to whom he preached the Gospel his "sons." In the laws, however, they are called **children** <note>original: "liberi"</note> to distinguish them from their own slaves by this term; for just as a slave is entirely in the power of the master, so a son is in the power of the father. From this comes the **emancipation** of a son, so that he may be free from his father, just as a **manumission** is performed for a slave, so that he may be freed from his master. For children born of a free man and a female slave are of a "swinish" <note>This refers to the legal status of the child following the "inferior" parent</note> condition. For what is born always takes on the status of the inferior parent. Those called **natural** <note>original: "Naturales"</note> are the sons of free concubines, whom nature alone produced, not the honor of marriage. They are also called **boys** <note>original: "pueri"</note> from the word for "puberty" <note>original: "pube"</note>. An **adoptive son** is one who, having been under a lawful father, grandfather, or great-grandfather, is transferred through emancipation into another’s power. He then bears the name of both, such as Flavius Aemilius or Scipio Paulus. **Twins** <note>original: "Gemini"</note> are not only two born together, but can be more. Of twins, if one is a miscarriage, the other who is born legitimately is called a **vopiscus**. A **posthumous** child is so named because he is born "after the burial" <note>original: "post humationem"</note> of the father—that is, after his death. He also receives the name of the deceased; for the law willed that he who is born of the deceased should be called by the name of the deceased. A **bastard** <note>The OCR reads "mortuus," but the context clearly describes the "nothus" or bastard</note> is said to be one born of a noble father and an ignoble mother, such as from a concubine. This is a Greek name, and the Latin language lacks a specific term for it. Contrary to this is the **spurious** <note>original: "spurius"</note> child, who is born of a noble mother and an ignoble father. Likewise, a spurious child is born of an uncertain father and a widowed mother; the ancients called the female nature *spurius*, as if "from the seed" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ σπόρου"</note>, meaning he is named from the seed, not the father. In the same way, they called them *favonii* <note>referring to the West Wind</note>, because certain animals are thought to conceive by breathing in the breeze of the West Wind. Hence, those who are not from a legitimate marriage follow the mother rather than the father. In Latin, *spurii* are so called as if "outside of purity" <note>original: "extra puritatem"</note>, that is, as if impure. A **grandson** <note>original: "nepos"</note> is one born from a son. He is called *nepos* as if "born after" <note>original: "natus post"</note>. For first a son is born, then a grandson. It is a grade of substitution. From this also comes **posterity**, which is a later age. However, *nepos* can refer to a grandson or a granddaughter <note>original: "nepris"</note>; in law, the term for a granddaughter is admitted for the sake of distinguishing the succession. A **great-grandson** <note>original: "pronepos"</note> is one conceived and born from a grandson. He is called a *pronepos* as if "born further on" <note>original: "porro natus"</note>. At this degree, the line begins to be called **lineage** <note>original: "progenies"</note>, as if "born further after." For sons and grandsons are not called "lineage" because there is no long posterity in them. Just as those born far below are called lineage, so those above—great-grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers—are called **progenitors**, as if "generating further on." The **abonepos** <note>a fourth-degree descendant</note> is so called because he is close to the grandson. The **abnepos** is so called because he is separated from the grandson, for the great-grandson stands between him and the grandson. The **adnepos** is the son of the *abnepos*. The **trinepos** is the son of the *adnepos*; he is fourth in order after the grandson, as if a "tetra-nepos." We do not use the term **minors** except when the names for the degrees run out—for instance, son, grandson, great-grandson, *abnepos*, *adnepos*, *trinepos*. Where these degrees run out, we then rightly say "minors"; likewise, we say **elders** <note>original: "maiores"</note> after the names for the earlier grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, and so on. It is necessary to explain how the degrees of kinship are numbered.

<column-break/>

In this matter, we must first be advised that some **kinships** <note>original: "cognationes"</note> are counted upwards, some downwards, and some transversally—which are also called lateral. Kinship is twofold: the parent's line and the child's line. Transversally, it is that of brothers and sisters and those who are born of them, and consequently paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts. Both the upper and lower kinship begin from the first degree, but the transverse line is counted from the second. In the **first degree**, upwards is the father, downwards is the son or daughter. In the **second degree**, upwards is the grandfather and grandmother, downwards is the grandson and granddaughter. Transversally are the brother and sister. In the **third degree**, upwards is the great-grandfather and great-grandmother, downwards is the great-grandson and great-granddaughter. Transversally are the son and daughter of a brother or sister, and consequently the **paternal uncle** <note>original: "patruus"</note>, **paternal aunt** <note>original: "amita"</note>, **maternal uncle** <note>original: "avunculus"</note>, and **maternal aunt** <note>original: "matertera"</note>. The paternal uncle is the father’s brother, which in Greek is called a <note>original: "πατρως"</note> "paternal uncle." The maternal uncle is the mother’s brother, which among the Greeks is properly called a <note>original: "μητρως"</note> "maternal uncle," and is commonly called <note>original: "θειος"</note> "uncle." The paternal aunt is the father’s sister. The maternal aunt is the mother’s sister. Both are called <note>original: "θεια"</note> "aunt," or among some, <note>original: "τηθις"</note> "aunt." In the **fourth degree**, upwards is the great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother, downwards is the *abnepos* and *abneptis*. Transversally are the grandson and granddaughter of a brother or sister, and consequently the **great paternal uncle** and **great paternal aunt**—that is, the grandfather’s brother and sister. Likewise, the **great maternal uncle** and **great maternal aunt**—that is, the grandmother’s brother and sister. Then there are **first cousins** <note>original: "consobrini"</note>, those who are born from brothers or sisters. But some rightly think that those born of two sisters are properly called *consobrini*, as if "sister-born" <note>original: "sororinos"</note>. Those born of two brothers are properly called **paternal cousins** <note>original: "patrueles"</note>. If, however, daughters are born of two brothers, they are called paternal cousin-sisters. Those born of a brother and a sister are properly called **amitinus cousins**. Your paternal aunt’s sons call you a *consobrinus*, and you call them *amitini*. In the **fifth degree**, upwards is the *attavus* and *attavia*, downwards is the *atnepos* and *atneptis*. Transversally are the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister, and consequently the **pro-paternal uncle** and **pro-paternal aunt**—the great-grandfather’s brother and sister. Also the **pro-maternal uncle** and **pro-maternal aunt**—the great-grandmother’s brother and sister. Also the son or daughter of a paternal cousin, a *consobrinus*, or an *amitinus*—these are **second cousins** <note>original: "sobrinus"</note>. These are the children of the great paternal uncles, aunts, or great maternal uncles and aunts. In the **sixth degree**, upwards is the *tritavus* and *tritavia*, downwards is the *trinepos* and *trineptis*. Transversally are the *abnepos* and *abneptis* of a brother or sister, and consequently the **ab-paternal uncle** and **ab-paternal aunt**—the great-great-grandfather’s brother and sister. Also the **ab-maternal uncle** and **ab-maternal aunt**—the great-great-grandmother’s brother and sister. Likewise the *sobrini* and *sobrinae*, who are born from paternal cousins or second cousins. Let it suffice to have shown this much of how the degrees of kinship are numbered. For from these, it is clearly understood how we ought to count each further degree. Indeed, each named person adds a degree; it is much easier to answer which degree each is in when each is denoted by the proper name of their kinship. The degrees of **agnation** <note>kinship through the male line</note> are numbered in the same way. But since the truth is more deeply fixed in the minds of men by the sight of the eyes than by the ears, we have deemed it necessary that, besides the narration of the degrees, they also be inscribed in the present book, so that through both the ears and the inspection of the eyes, young students may attain the most excellent knowledge of the degrees. **Pedigrees** <note>original: "Stemmata"</note> are called the "little branches" that lawyers make in a family tree when the degrees of kinship are divided—as for instance, this one is the son, that one the father, that one the grandfather, that one the great-great-grandfather, and the others whose figures are these.

It concludes by emphasizing the importance of visual family trees (stemmata) for students to understand these complex relationships.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of human biology and family origins, now focusing specifically on the legal and linguistic distinctions of kinship. The text is taken from Book IX of Isidore of Seville’s "Etymologies," a standard medieval reference for how words reveal the nature of the world.</meta>

<header>IX</header>

### Concerning Paternal and Maternal Kin, Chapter 6.

**Paternal kin** <note>original: *agnati*</note> are so named because they are "added" to those already born as long as there are sons. They are recognized first within a clan because they descend through persons of the male sex, such as a brother born of the same father, or a brother's son, a grandson, or his descendant; likewise, the paternal uncle. **Maternal kin** <note>original: *cognati*</note> are so called because they are joined by the proximity of a shared birth. They hold their place after the paternal kin because they descend through persons of the female sex and are not *agnati*; in other contexts, they are called "cognates" by natural law. The **next of kin** <note>original: *proximus*</note> is so named because of the primacy of his blood. Those who are **consanguineous** <note>original: *consanguinei*</note> are so called because they are born of "one blood," that is, from the single seed of the father. For the seed of a man is the foam of blood, much like water dashed against rocks which creates a white foam, or like dark wine which, when agitated in a cup, turns into a white froth.

**Brothers** <note>original: *fratres*</note> are so named because they are born from the same "fruit" <note>original: *fructu*</note>, that is, from the same seed. **Full brothers** <note>original: *germani*</note>, however, are those who issue from the same mother <note>original: *genitrice*</note>, and not, as many claim, from the same "germ" <note>original: *germine*</note>, which is what brothers in general are called. Therefore, *fratres* come from the same fruit, while *germani* issue from the same mother. Those called **uterine** <note>original: *uterini*</note> are those born from different fathers but from one womb <note>original: *vtero*</note>, for the womb belongs only to the woman.

In the Divine Scriptures, "brothers" are spoken of in four ways: by nature, by nation, by kinship, and by affection. By **nature**, such as Esau and Jacob, Andrew and Peter, or James and John. By **nation**, as all Jews call one another brothers, as it says in Deuteronomy: "If you buy your brother who is a Hebrew." And the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says: "I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites." Furthermore, they are called brothers by **kinship** who are of one family, that is, one "fatherland" <note>original: *patria*, interpreted here as ancestry</note>, which the Latins call "paternities," where a great multitude of people spreads out from a single root. As Abraham said to Lot in Genesis: "Let there be no strife between me and you, nor between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers." And certainly, Lot was not Abraham's brother, but the son of his brother Haran. In the fourth way, they are called brothers by **affection**, which is split into two types: specific and common. **Specific** affection is that by which all Christians are called brothers, as in: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity." In **common** affection, all humans are born from one father, and we are joined by an equal brotherhood, as the Scripture says: "Say to those who hate you, you are our brothers."

A **full sister** <note>original: *germana*</note> is understood similarly to a full brother, as one issuing from the same mother. A **sister** <note>original: *soror*</note> is like a brother, for she is from the same seed; she is called *soror* because she is "alone" <note>original: *sola*</note> alongside the brothers in the lot of paternal kinship. The sons of brothers are called **paternal cousins** <note>original: *patrueles*</note> because their fathers were full brothers to each other. **First cousins** <note>original: *consobrini*</note> are those born either from a sister and a brother or from two sisters, as if they were "co-sisters" <note>original: *consozorini*</note>. **Maternal cousins** <note>original: *fratrueles*</note> are the sons of a maternal aunt. **Second cousins** <note>original: *sobrini*</note> are the children of first cousins.

*Theios* <note>original: *Lbi us*, likely a corruption of the Greek *theios* for uncle</note> is a Greek name. A **paternal uncle** <note>original: *patruus*</note> is a father's brother, acting as "another father." Thus, when a father passes away, the paternal uncle takes up the orphan <note>original: *pupillum*</note> and protects them by law like a son. A **maternal uncle** <note>original: *auunculus*</note> is a mother's brother; his name appears to be a diminutive form because he is shown to descend from the "grandfather" <note>original: *auo*</note>. A **paternal aunt** <note>original: *amita*</note> is a father's sister, acting as another mother. A **maternal aunt** <note>original: *matertera*</note> is a mother's sister, like a "second mother." A **father-in-law** <note>original: *socer*</note> is he who gave his daughter in marriage. A **son-in-law** <note>original: *gener*</note> is he who

<column-break/>

took the daughter. He is called *gener* because he is adopted to "increase the clan" <note>original: *augendum genus*</note>. **Father-in-law** and **mother-in-law** <note>original: *socer & socrus*</note> are so called because they "associate" <note>original: *associat*</note> a son-in-law or daughter-in-law to themselves. A **stepfather** <note>original: *vitricus*</note> is he who has married a wife who already has a son or daughter by another man. He is called *vitricus* as if he were a "new-nourisher" <note>original: *nouitricus*</note>, because he is a new father brought in by the mother. A **stepson** <note>original: *privignus*</note> is one born from another father, and is thought to be called *privignus* as if "born before" <note>original: *priuigenus*</note>, because he was sired earlier; hence he is commonly called "born before" <note>original: *ante natus*</note>.

These terms appear to be declined based on the word for **clan** <note>original: *gente*</note>: male parent (*genitor*), female parent (*genitrix*), male and female paternal kin (*agnati/agnatae*), male and female maternal kin (*cognati/cognatae*), male and female ancestors (*progenitores/progenitrices*), and male and female full siblings (*germani/germanae*). This blood relationship, as it gradually divides itself through the ranks of descendants until it reaches the final degree and ceases to be close proximity, is sought out again by the law of marriage through its bond, and in a certain way calls back that which was fleeing away. Therefore, consanguinity is established up to the **sixth degree** of kinship, so that just as the generation of the world and the state of man is completed in six ages, so too the proximity of the clan is terminated by the same number of degrees.

### Likewise regarding the aforementioned affinities

The author of my clan is my **father**; I am his son or daughter. My father's father is my **grandfather**; I am his grandson or granddaughter. My father's grandfather is my **great-grandfather**; I am his great-grandson or great-granddaughter. My father's great-grandfather is my **ab-grandfather** <note>original: *abauus*</note>; I am his ab-grandson or ab-granddaughter. My father's ab-grandfather is my **ata-grandfather** <note>original: *atauus*</note>; I am his ad-grandson or ad-granddaughter. My father's ata-grandfather is my **tri-grandfather** <note>original: *tritauus*</note>; I am his tri-grandson or tri-granddaughter.

### Concerning paternal uncles

My father's brother is my **paternal uncle**; I am his brother's son or daughter. My paternal uncle's father is my **great-father**; I am the daughter of his son's brother. My paternal uncle's grandfather is my **great-paternal-uncle**; I am the grandson or granddaughter of his son's daughter. My paternal uncle's great-grandfather is my **ad-paternal-uncle**; I am the son or daughter of his granddaughter.

### Concerning paternal aunts

My father's sister is my **paternal aunt**; I am her brother's son or daughter. My paternal aunt's mother is my **great paternal aunt**; I am the son or daughter of her brother's daughter. My paternal aunt's grandmother is my **pro-paternal-aunt**; I am the son or daughter of her granddaughter. My paternal aunt's great-grandmother is my **ab-paternal-aunt**; I am the grandson or granddaughter of her granddaughter.

### Concerning maternal uncles

My mother's brother is my **maternal uncle**; I am his sister's son or daughter. My maternal uncle's father is my **great maternal uncle**; I am the son or daughter of his sister's son. My maternal uncle's grandfather is my **pro-maternal-uncle**; I am the grandson or granddaughter of his son. My maternal uncle's grandfather <note>likely meaning great-grandfather</note> is my **ab-maternal-uncle**; I am the son or daughter of his granddaughter.

### Concerning maternal aunts

My mother's sister is my **maternal aunt**; I am her sister's son or daughter. My maternal aunt's sister is my **great maternal aunt**; I am her sister's grandson or granddaughter. My grandmother's sister is my **ab-maternal-aunt**; I am her sister's great-grandson or granddaughter. My great-grandmother's sister is my **pro-maternal-aunt**; I am the son or daughter of her granddaughter.

It provides a systematic nomenclature for ancestors, descendants, and extended family members like uncles, aunts, and in-laws.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of kinship and biological origins in Book IX of Isidore of Seville’s "Etymologies." Having defined how family members are named based on shared blood and birth, Isidore now transitions to the legal and social structures that create new families: marriage and the specific vocabulary used to describe the participants and the dissolution of unions.</meta>

Book [IX]

<margin>Concerning Marriage, Chapter 7.</margin>
**Man** <note>original: *uir*</note> signifies sex, not marriage, unless you add "her man" <note>original: *vir eius*</note>. However, **Husband** <note>original: *maritus*</note> implies a spouse even without any addition. The word husband comes from "male" <note>original: *mas*</note>, as if it were "manly." For it is a primary noun, which in its diminutive form becomes "little male" <note>original: *masculus*</note> and in its derivative form "husband." The **Betrothed** <note>original: *sponsus*</note> is so named from "promising" <note>original: *spondendo*</note>. For before the use of written marriage contracts, they would issue guarantees to one another in which they promised <note>original: *spondebant*</note> to mutually consent to the laws of marriage, and they provided sureties. From this, it became accepted that we call the man the *sponsus* from promising, and the woman the *sponsa* <note>original: "the promised woman"</note> likewise. Furthermore, to "promise" <note>original: *spondere*</note> is properly to "will." Therefore, he is a *sponsus* not because he merely promises, but because he pledges and provides guarantors. **Earnest money** <note>original: *arrabo*</note> is so named as if it were a "good earnest" <note>original: *arrabona*</note>. For what is given for the sake of marriage is "well given" because marriage is "good" <note>original: *bonum*</note>. However, what is given for the sake of fornication or adultery is "evil," and therefore it is not a "good earnest." The word for pledge <note>original: *arra*</note> is derived from the "thing" <note>original: *res*</note> through which it is handed over. An *arra* is not only a marital promise but is given for any promised thing so that it may be completed. Those who **request a marriage** <note>original: *pronuptiarum petitores*</note> are named from "praying" <note>original: *precando*</note> and "seeking" <note>original: *petendo*</note>. An **attendant** <note>original: *pronuba*</note> is so named because she presides over those "veiling" themselves <note>original: *nubentibus*</note>, and she joins the bride to the man; she is also the **bridesmaid** <note>original: *paranympha*</note>. For a **bride** <note>original: *nympha*</note> is a spouse in the wedding, and the term *nympha* also refers to the duty of washing, which alludes to the name of the one marrying. **Spouses** <note>original: *coniuges*</note> are named for the **yoke** <note>original: *iugum*</note> that is imposed on those who are to be joined in marriage. For those marrying are accustomed to be placed under a yoke for the sake of future harmony, so that they might not be separated. However, they are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, even if marital intercourse is still unknown between them—just as Joseph is called the spouse of Mary, between whom there had been, and was to be, no mixing of the flesh. **Weddings** <note>original: *nuptiae*</note> are so called because the brides "veil" <note>original: *velent*</note> their faces; the name is transferred from the **clouds** <note>original: *nubes*</note> by which the sky is covered. Whence they are called *nuptiae* because there they first "veil" the heads of those marrying. For to "ob-veil" <note>original: *obnubere*</note> is to cover over. The opposite of this is "un-veiled" <note>original: *innuba*</note>, that is, unmarried, who does not yet veil her face. **Wives** <note>original: *uxores*</note> are named as if they were **anointers** <note>original: *unxiores*</note>. For it was the custom in ancient times that girls about to marry would come together to the threshold of the husband, and before entering, they would decorate the doorposts with wool ribbons and anoint them with oil. And thus they were called *uxores* as if *unxiores*; for this reason, they were forbidden to step on the threshold, because there the doors both meet and separate. A **Matron** <note>original: *matrona*</note> is one who has already married, and she is called *matrona* as if "mother of a child" <note>original: *mater nati*</note>, or because she is now able to become a mother; from this, **marriage** <note>original: *matrimonium*</note> is also named. A distinction is made between a matron, a mother, and the "mother of a family." For they are matrons because they have already entered into marriage; mothers because they have given birth; and "mothers of the family" <note>original: *matresfamilias*</note> because they have now passed into the husband's family through a certain legal solemnity. A **monogamist** <note>original: *monogamus*</note> is so named because he married only one. For "mono" <note>original: *mono*</note> among the Greeks means "one," and "gamos" <note>original: *gamos*</note> is interpreted as "marriage." A **bigamist** or **trigamist**, however, is named from the number of his wives, as the husband of two or three. A **widow** <note>original: *vidua*</note> is so named because she is not with a man, nor has she attached herself to the companionship of another man after the death of her first spouse. For those who marry another after the death of the first husband are not called widows. Likewise, she is called a widow because she is "alone" <note>original: *sola*</note>, and does not maintain marital rights through the companionship of another man.

<column-break/>

A brother's wife is called a **sister-in-law** <note>original: *fratissa*</note>. A husband's brother is called a **levir** <note>original: *levir*</note>. The wives of two brothers are called **ianitrices** <note>original: *ianitrices*</note>, as if they are "wearing down the same door" <note>original: *ianuam terentes*</note> or having their path through the same door. A husband's sister is called a **glos** <note>original: *glos*</note>. A sister's husband has no special name, nor does a wife's brother. **Marriage** <note>original: *matrimonium*</note> is the lawful agreement and status of noble persons. **Spousal union** <note>original: *coniugium*</note> is the wedding of legitimate persons joining and coupling with one another. It is called *coniugium* because they are "joined together" <note>original: *coniuncti*</note>, or from the "yoke" <note>original: *iugum*</note> by which they are coupled in weddings, so they cannot be released or separated. **Legal marriage** <note>original: *connubium*</note>, however, is formed not from "the bride" but from "marrying" <note>original: *nubendo*</note>. It is called *connubium* when equals come together in weddings, such as Roman citizens of equal dignity on both sides. However, it is not *connubium* when a Roman citizen is joined with a Latin woman. Whenever there is no *connubium*, the children do not follow the father's status. **The wedding song** <note>original: *hymenaeus*</note> is named after a certain Hymennaeus who first used marriage prosperously, or from the Greek word for a membrane <note>original: *hymen*</note> which is the enclosure of virginity. **Cohabitation** <note>original: *contubernium*</note> is a temporary agreement to come together, from which we also get "tent" <note>original: *tabernaculum*</note>, which moves now here, now there. **Repudiation** <note>original: *repudium*</note> is that which is sent under the testimony of witnesses, whether the party is present or absent. **Divorce** <note>original: *divortium*</note> occurs whenever a marriage is dissolved and one of them seeks another marriage. *Divortium* is named from the "divergence of ways," that is, paths stretching in different directions. **Frivolous separation** <note>original: *frivolum*</note> is when they separate with the intention of returning to one another again. For "frivolous" is like something of a shattered or fluid mind, not stable. Properly speaking, however, "frivola" refers to useless earthenware vessels. A wife is taken for three reasons. The first is for the sake of **offspring**, of which we read in Genesis: "And he blessed them saying: Increase and multiply." The second is for the sake of **help**, of which it is said in Genesis: "It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like unto himself." The third is the cause of **incontinence**, as the Apostle says: "So that he who does not contain himself may marry."

<margin>+</margin> In choosing a husband, four things are usually looked for: **virtue, lineage, beauty, and wisdom**. Among these, wisdom is more powerful in producing love. Virgil records these four regarding Aeneas, by which Dido was driven into love for him. By beauty: "How he carries himself in his countenance!" <note>original: *quem sese ore ferens*</note>. By virtue: "With what a brave heart and arms!" <note>original: *qua forti pectore et armis*</note>. By speech: "Alas, by what fates he was tossed, what exhausted wars he sang of!" <note>original: *heu quibus ille iactatus fatis quae bella exhausta canebat*</note>. 
<margin>d</margin> By lineage: "I truly believe, nor is my faith vain, that his lineage is of the gods" <note>original: *credo equidem nec vana fides genus esse deorum*</note>. Likewise, in choosing a wife, four things drive a man to love: **beauty, lineage, wealth, and character**. 
<margin>m</margin> It is better, however, if character is sought in her rather than beauty. Nowadays, however, those women are sought whom either wealth or form commends, not those whom integrity of character recommends. For this reason, women remain under the power of men, because they are often deceived by the levity of their minds. Whence it was also right for them to be restrained by the authority of the man. Therefore, the ancients willed that all women, of whatever mature age they might be, should remain under guardianship on account of that very levity of mind.

->Here ends the ninth book<-

<meta>This page transitions from Book IX, which covered human relationships and social structures like marriage, into Book X. Here, Isidore of Seville begins an alphabetical dictionary of terms, focusing on the "etymologies" or origins of words to reveal their deeper meanings. This reflects the medieval belief that understanding the history of a word provides insight into the nature of the thing itself.</meta>

# Here begins the tenth book, concerning certain vocabularies of names arranged alphabetically

**The Origin** <note>original: *Origo*</note> of certain names—that is, where they come from—is not clear to almost everyone. Therefore, we have interspersed some of these into this work for the sake of knowledge. Although philosophers maintain that the origin of names follows a logical system—such as "man" <note>original: *homo*</note> being named from "humanity" <note>original: *humanitate*</note>, or "wise man" <note>original: *sapiens*</note> from "wisdom" <note>original: *sapientia*</note>, because wisdom exists first and then the wise man—nevertheless, another specific cause is evident in the origin of certain names. For example, "man" <note>original: *homo*</note> comes from "ground" <note>original: *humo*</note>, which is why he is properly so named. We have placed examples of these in this work.

**Hero** <note>original: *Heros*</note>: a brave and wise man. **Author** <note>original: *Auctor*</note>: named from "increasing" <note>original: *augendo*</note>. An author cannot be referred to in the feminine gender. For there are some words that cannot be inflected into the feminine, such as "runner" <note>original: *cursor*</note>. **Actor**: from "doing" <note>original: *agendo*</note>. **Alumnus** <note>original: *Alumnus*</note>: named from "nourishing" <note>original: *alendo*</note>, although "alumnus" can refer to both the one who nourishes and the one who is nourished <note>Isidore notes the word is passive in form but can be used for both teacher and student</note>; however, it better refers to the one who is nourished. **Friend** <note>original: *Amicus*</note>: by derivation, it is as if it were "guardian of the soul" <note>original: *animi custos*</note>. Properly, however, "friend" is named from "hook" <note>original: *hamo*</note>, that is, from the "chain of charity"; hence "hooks" <note>original: *hami*</note> are so named because they hold fast. **Lover** <note>original: *Amator*</note>: one of baseness, because he is twisted by the love of lust. **Amiable** <note>original: *Amabilis*</note>: because he is worthy of love. **Paramour** <note>original: *Amasius*</note>: because he is prone to love. **Astute** <note>original: *Astutus*</note>: named from "cunning" <note>original: *astu*</note>, which is a name for the clever and cautious person who can do something bravely without danger. **Shrewd** <note>original: *Argutus*</note>: because he quickly finds an "argument" <note>original: *argumentum*</note> in speaking. **Sharp** <note>original: *Acer*</note>: vigorous and intense in every form. **Eager** <note>original: *Alacer*</note>: from speed and running, as if one were to say "winged" <note>original: *aliger*</note>. **Squire** <note>original: *Armiger*</note>: because he carries arms. **Brisk** <note>original: *Alacris*</note>: joyful, gesturing, and not disturbed by the novelty of anything. **Agile** <note>original: *Agilis*</note>: from doing <note>original: *agendo*</note> something quickly, just as "teachable" <note>original: *docilis*</note> comes from learning. **Rival** <note>original: *Aemulus*</note>: zealous for the same thing; like an "imitator" and "amiable," though elsewhere it is found to mean "enemy." **Just** <note>original: *Aequus*</note>: one who is naturally fair; named from "equality" <note>original: *equalitate*</note>, that is, from being equal; hence "equity" is named from a certain equality. **Peer** <note>original: *Aequenus*</note>: because he is equal to another in something, such as being of the same age. **Arrogant** <note>original: *Arrogans*</note>: because he asks <note>original: *roget*</note> for much, and is very disdainful. **Bold** <note>original: *Audax*</note>: properly used for the arrogant. **Spirited** <note>original: *Animosus*</note>: because he is full of spirit and strength. **Animated** <note>original: *Animatus*</note>: as if increased by spirit or strengthened by spirit. **Elated** <note>original: *Aelatus*</note>: for one who lifts himself up beyond measure while he seems great to himself in the things he does. **Extolling** <note>original: *Attollens*</note>: because he lifts and raises himself up. **Ambitious** <note>original: *Ambitiosus*</note>: because he goes around seeking <note>original: *ambiat*</note> honors. **Eager/Greedy** <note>original: *Avidus*</note>: named from "craving" <note>original: *avendo*</note>; for "to crave" is to desire. Hence also "greedy" <note>original: *avarus*</note>. For what does it mean to be greedy? To go beyond what is sufficient. **Greedy** <note>original: *Avarus*</note>: also named because he is "eager for gold" <note>original: *avidus auri*</note> and is never filled by wealth; the more he has, the more he desires. Horace <note>original: *Flacci*</note> agrees with this sentiment, saying:
> The greedy man is always in need.
And Sallust says that greed is diminished neither by abundance nor by want. **Bitter** <note>original: *Amarus*</note>: has a name translated from taste. For he is unpleasant, and does not know how to invite anyone to his company with any sweetness.

<column-break/>

<margin>adulterer</margin> **Adulterer** <note>original: *Adulter*</note>: a violator of marital modesty, because he pollutes another's bed <note>original: *alterius thorum*</note>. <margin>wavering</margin> **Wavering** <note>original: *Anceps*</note>: fluctuating here and there and doubtful whether he should take this or that, and anxious about which side to lean toward. <margin>gloomy</margin> **Gloomy** <note>original: *Atror*</note>: because he is of foul character. <margin>abstemious</margin> **Abstemious** <note>original: *Abstemius*</note>: from "strong wine" <note>original: *temeto*</note>, that is, wine; as if abstaining from wine. <margin>weaned</margin> **Weaned** <note>original: *Ablactatus*</note>: because he has been taken away from milk <note>original: *lacte*</note>. <margin>sick</margin> **Sick** <note>original: *Aeger*</note>: because he is driven <note>original: *agatur*</note> by infirmity or temporary sadness. <margin>chronically ill</margin> **Chronically ill** <note>original: *Aegrotus*</note>: because he is sick more frequently, just as "angry" differs from "irascible." <margin>wretched</margin> **Wretched** <note>original: *Aerumnosus*</note>: named from "rumination" <note>Isidore suggests a link to the throat or hunger</note>; because being made miserable through want, he hungers and thirsts. <margin>soothsayer</margin> **Soothsayer** <note>original: *Auspex*</note>: because he observes the omens <note>original: *auspicia*</note> of birds <note>original: *avium*</note>; just as a "fowler" <note>original: *auceps*</note> captures birds. <margin>unlucky</margin> **Unlucky** <note>original: *Astrosus*</note>: named from "star" <note>original: *astro*</note>, as if born under a bad star. **Enormous**: because it exceeds the "norm" <note>original: *normam*</note> and measure. **Cattle rustler** <note>original: *Abactor*</note>: a thief of beasts and cattle, whom the common people call an "abigeus," specifically from "driving away" <note>original: *abigendo*</note>. <margin>clothed in black/white</margin> **Clothed in black** and **Clothed in white**: the former from a black garment, the latter from a white one. <margin>stranger/foreigner</margin> **Newcomer** <note>original: *Aduena*</note>: because he comes from elsewhere. **Foreign-born** <note>original: *Alienigena*</note>: because he was born of another race and not from the place where he is. Also, foreign-born because he is from another region. <margin>neighbor</margin> **Resident/Neighbor** <note>original: *Accola*</note>: because, arriving as a newcomer, he "tills" <note>original: *colat*</note> the land. <margin>farmer</margin> **Farmer** <note>original: *Agricola*</note>: from tilling the "field" <note>original: *agro*</note>, just as a "forest-dweller" <note>original: *siluicola*</note> inhabits the woods. **Follower** <note>original: *Assecla*</note>: because he follows someone for the sake of gain. <margin>diligent</margin> **Assiduous** <note>original: *Assiduus*</note>: among the ancients, this referred to one who oversaw the payment of coins <note>original: *assibus*</note> to the treasury, or one frequent in public business; hence the "p" should not be written <note>Isidore is debating the spelling *assiduus* vs *adsiduus*</note>. <margin>attendant</margin> **Attendant** <note>original: *Apparitor*</note>: so named because he "appears" <note>original: *appareat*</note> and is seen, and is ready for service. <margin>attentive</margin> **Attentive** <note>original: *Attentus*</note>: so that hearing something, he may hold <note>original: *teneat*</note> it. <margin>thunderstruck</margin> **Thunderstruck** <note>original: *Attonitus*</note>: as if stunned and struck by a certain madness. Named from the "crash of thunder" <note>original: *tonitrui*</note>, as if dazed by thunder and the nearby flash or strike of lightning. **Chosen** <note>original: *Allectus*</note>: because he was openly elected. <margin>aborted/removed</margin> **Driven away** <note>original: *Abactus*</note>: as if removed from action. **Abortive** <note>original: *Abortivus*</note>: because it is not born <note>original: *oriatur*</note>, but miscarries <note>original: *aboriatur*</note> and falls away. <margin>adoptive</margin> **Adoptive**: who is openly adopted as a son. **Both** <note>original: *Ambo*</note>: from the word "both" <note><term>αμφω</term> — Greek: *ampho*</note>; the Latin name was made from the Greek by changing the third letter. <margin>another/the other</margin> **Another** <note>original: *Alius*</note>: said of one among many. **The other** <note>original: *Alter*</note>: used for one of two. **Equal-handed** <note>original: *Aequimanus*</note>: one who uses a sword with either hand without hesitation.

**Blessed** <note>original: *Beatus*</note>: so named as if "well increased" <note>original: *bene auctus*</note>; namely, from having what he wants and suffering nothing he does not want. For he is truly blessed who has all the good things he wants and wants nothing evil. For a man is made blessed from these two things. **Good** <note>original: *Bonus*</note>: believed to be named from the "loveliness" <note>original: *venustate*</note> of the body; later the name was translated to the soul. We call him good in whom evil does not prevail; and the "best" is he who sins the least. **Benign** <note>original: *Benignus*</note>: a man ready to do good of his own accord and sweet in speech. Benign does not differ much from "good," because he himself seems disposed to doing good. But it differs in this: a man can be good but rather somber; doing good indeed, and providing what is asked, yet not knowing how to be pleasant in company. But the benign man knows how to invite everyone with his own sweetness. **Beneficent** <note>original: *Beneficus*</note>: named from "doing good" <note>original: *benefaciendo*</note> to another. Whence also "beneficence" is named, which primarily helps. **Benevolent**: because he "wills well" <note>original: *bene vult*</note>. However, we do not say "benevolus" just as we do not say "malevolus" <note>referring to phonetic shifts in compounding</note>. Often a name composed of two parts corrupts either the first or the following letter. For "benevolentia" sounds absurd <note>Isidore is discussing the vowel change from 'e' to 'i' in *benivolentia*</note>. **Bland**: sweet and inviting to intimacy with himself. **Brutish** <note>original: *Brutus*</note>: as if "overwhelmed" <note>original: *obrutus*</note>, because he lacks sense.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book X of Isidore’s Etymologies, presenting an alphabetical dictionary of terms starting with 'A' and 'B'. # Book X

<column-break/>

For he is without reason and without prudence. Thus, that famous Junius Brutus <note>original: *Iunius Brutus*</note>, born of the sister of Tarquinius Superbus, when he feared the same fate that had befallen his brother—who had been killed by their uncle because of his wealth and prudence—he feigned a "useful foolishness" for the time. Hence he was surnamed **Brutus** <note>original: *Brutus*; meaning "dull" or "stupid"</note>, though he was originally named Junius. **Balbus** <note>stammerer</note> is named from "bleating" <note>original: *balando*</note> rather than "speaking" <note>original: *loquendo*</note>, for he does not explain his words clearly. From this also comes **Blesus** <note>lisping</note>, because he breaks his words. **Bucco** <note>babbler</note> is a chatterbox, because he surpasses others in the talkativeness of his mouth <note>original: *oris*</note>, not in sense. **Biliosus** <note>bilious/irritable</note> is one who is always sad because of the "black humor" which is called bile. **Baburrus** is foolish and inept. **Biothanatos** <note>one who dies a violent death or by suicide</note> is one who is "twice dead." For in the Greek language, *Thanatos* <note>original: *Thanatos*</note> is the word for death.

**Clarus** <note>bright/renowned</note> is from "heaven" <note>original: *caelo*</note> because it shines. From this we also get "clear day" <note>original: *clara dies*</note> for the brightness of the sky. **Celsus** <note>lofty</note> is named from heaven <note>original: *caelo*</note> because he is sublime and high, as if heavenly. **Castus** <note>pure/chaste</note> was first named from "castration" <note>original: *castratio*</note>; later it pleased the ancients that those who promised perpetual abstinence from lust should also be so named. **Celes** <note>heavenly</note> is so called because he makes a path for himself to heaven. **Celebs** <note>celibate/unmarried</note> is one who lacks a marriage partner, just as there are names in heaven <note>original: *caelo*</note> which belong to the holy ones. And a celibate is spoken of as if "blessed in heaven" <note>original: *caelo beatus*</note>. **Celicola** <note>heaven-dweller</note> because he inhabits heaven; for he is an angel. **Continens** <note>temperate/continent</note> refers not only to chastity, but also to restraint in food and drink, in anger, in distress of mind, and in the desire for slander. He is called continent because he withholds himself from many evils. **Clemens** <note>merciful</note> is one who is compassionate; the name comes from "to protect" <note>original: *cluat*</note>, that is, to purge and defend, just as a patron is accustomed to protect a client. **Concord** <note>original: *Concors*</note> is named from the joining of hearts <note>original: *cordis*</note>. For just as a "consort" <note>original: *consors*</note> is one joined by lot <note>original: *sorte*</note>, so a "concordant" person is one joined by heart. **Concianator** <note>haranguer</note> is a speaker to a multitude. **Consolator** <note>comforter</note> is a speaker to a single person. He is called a comforter because he applies himself to the one alone <note>original: *soli*</note> to whom he speaks, and relieves their solitude with his conversation. Hence also comes "solace" <note>original: *solatium*</note>. **Consultus** <note>learned in law/consulted</note> is one who gives counsel; his opposite is the **inconsult**, who does not accept counsel. **Constans** <note>constant/firm</note> is so named because he stands everywhere <note>original: *undique stat*</note> and cannot be turned toward any side. **Confidens** <note>confident</note> because he is full of trust in all things. Hence Lucilius says: "If you have confidence, trust in all things." **Lautus** <note>elegant/refined</note> is named from washing <note>original: *lavando*; OCR reads *cauendo*</note>. **Callidus** <note>clever/cunning</note> is fraudulent, because he knows how to conceal and is wickedly experienced. However, the ancients used "clever" not only for the astute, but also for the astutely learned. This person is also **Versutus** <note>shifty/versatile</note> because he quickly turns his mind <note>original: *animum cito vertat*</note>. **Cupidus** <note>desirous</note> is named from desiring much, that is, from taking. **Clamosus** <note>clamorous</note> is as if "reed-like" <note>original: *calamosus*</note>, namely from the reed <note>original: *calamo*</note>, because it makes a sound. **Calumniator** <note>slanderer</note> is an accuser of a false crime, named from "frustrating" <note>original: *calvendo*</note>, that is, deceiving. **Calculator** <note>accountant</note> is named from "calculi," that is, small pebbles, which the ancients held in their hands to compose numbers. **Compilator** <note>plagiarist/piler</note> is one who mixes the words of others with his own, just as pigment-makers are accustomed to crush diverse mixtures in a mortar <note>original: *pila*</note>. That Mantuan bard <note>The poet Virgil</note> was once accused of this crime when he transferred certain verses of Homer and mixed them with his own; when he was called a "compiler of the ancients" by his rivals, he responded that it required great strength to wrench the club from the hand of Hercules. **Contumax** <note>haughty/stubborn</note> is from the fact that he despises <note>original: *contemnat*</note>. **Chromaticus** is one who does not confuse or change color. For in Greek, *Chroma* <note>original: *chroma*</note> is the word for color. **Contumeliosus** <note>abusive/insulting</note> because he is swift and swells with injurious words. **Contentiosus** <note>contentious</note> is named from

<column-break/>

stretching <note>original: *intentioe*</note>, because he maintains his point not by any reason, but by sheer persistence. **Contemptibilis** <note>contemptible</note> either because he is liable to contempt, or because he is despised and vile, that is, without honor. **Crudelis** <note>cruel</note> is the same as "raw" <note>original: *crudus*</note>, whom the Greeks call *ōmon* <note>original: *homon*</note> by a metaphor; like something not cooked nor fit for food. For he is harsh and hard. **Carnifex** <note>executioner/butcher</note> because he affects the flesh <note>original: *carnem*</note>. **Cruciatus** <note>tortured</note> because he is worthy of the cross <note>original: *cruce*</note>. **Collega** <note>colleague</note> is named from the binding together <note>original: *colligatione*</note> of a society and the embrace of friendship. **Coetaneus** <note>contemporary</note> is as if "of equal age." **Complice** <note>accomplice</note> is one who is joined to another for evil in a single sin or crime. We never use "accomplice" for something good. **Consors** <note>partner</note> because a part of the honors belongs to him. For the ancients used "lot" <note>original: *sortem*</note> to mean "a part." Therefore, he is a consort because he is a partner in a lot, just as "dis-ors" is one who is unlike in lot. **Celer** <note>swift</note> is named from celerity, because he does more quickly what use requires. **Confinialis** <note>neighboring</note> because he is related by kind or by place. **Colonus** <note>tenant farmer</note> is named from a "colony" or from tilling the field <note>original: *agro colendo*</note>. **Curator** <note>guardian</note> because he bears the care <note>original: *curam*</note> for boys who are still of such an age that they cannot sufficiently manage their own affairs. **Cognitor** <note>advocate/attorney</note> is named from "knowing the case" <note>original: *cognoscendo causam*</note>. **Clientes** <note>clients</note> were formerly called *colientes* from "cultivating" <note>original: *colendis*</note> their patrons. **Captus** <note>captured</note> refers to a captive, as if "diminished in head" <note>original: *capite diminutus*</note> regarding his freeborn status; for his fortune has fallen away from him. Thus, by learned men, he is said to be "diminished in status." **Colonus** <note>farmer/inhabitant</note> is also named from "column" <note>original: *columna*</note>, because he is upright and very firm. **Comptus** <note>well-groomed</note> is named from "hair" <note>original: *coma*</note>, because he becomes handsome with his hair, or because he nourishes his hair. **Calamistratus** <note>with curled hair</note> is from the *calamistrum*, which is an iron needle made in the likeness of a reed <note>original: *calami*</note> in which the hair is twisted so that it might be curly; they are accustomed to heat this in ashes to curl the hair. **Corpulentus** <note>corpulent/stout</note> is one who is strong in body <note>original: *corpore*</note> and with tough flesh. **Crassus** <note>thick/fat</note> from a fattened body, from "creating flesh." **Comessor** <note>glutton</note> from "eating enough." For he is immoderately devoted to his gullet and belly. **Caupo** <note>innkeeper/huckster</note> is one who makes water out of wine for the worst people. **Candidus** <note>shining white</note>; the white-haired man is named from "brightness" <note>original: *candore*</note>, or *candidus* as if "given to brightness." For brightness comes from effort, whereas to be called "white" <note>original: *album*</note> belongs to nature. **Clodus** <note>lame</note>, **Curvus** <note>bent</note>, **Crispus** <note>curly</note>. **Cecus** <note>blind</note> is so named because he lacks sight. For his lights are lost. A man is blind who does not see with either eye. **Caducus** <note>falling/epileptic</note> is named from "falling" <note>original: *cadendo*</note>, that is, a "lunatic," because he suffers at a certain time of the moon. **Confusus** <note>confused/shamed</note> is named from the "confession" of a crime. Hence also "confusion." **Convulsus** <note>shattered/plucked away</note> is said of one whose strength is taken away by some force. Hence a "shattered ship" <note>original: *convulsa navis*</note> is one whose prominent parts are taken away by the violence of a storm. Whence Virgil says: "A man with seven ships shattered <note>original: *convulsis*</note> by the waves," as if mutilated. **Consumptus** <note>consumed</note> is one totally taken up and devoured. **Conciliatrix** <note>matchmaker/procurer</note> is so named because of the society of a shameful agreement; because she runs into others and bargains for another's body. They also call her a "pimp" <note>original: *lenonem*</note>. **Circumforanus** <note>market-lounger</note> is one who wanders around the markets <note>original: *fora*</note> and assemblies for the sake of legal advocacy. **Collegiarius** <note>guild member</note>. **Carpentarius** <note>wagon-maker</note>.

**Dominus** <note>lord/master</note> is named by derivation because he presides over a house <note>original: *domui*</note> and rules over the whole family. **Disertus** <note>eloquent</note> means learned, named from "discerning" <note>original: *differendo*</note>; for he discusses things in an orderly way. **Doctus** <note>learned</note> from "speaking" <note>original: *dicendo*</note>; whence also "doctor." **Docilis** <note>teachable</note> is not one who...
