<meta>This page continues Book X of Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*, a specialized dictionary exploring the origins of words related to people and their characteristics. The text follows an alphabetical arrangement. Having concluded the letter ‘C’ on the previous page, this page covers the remainder of ‘D’, all of ‘E’, and the beginning of ‘F’. Isidore’s method often relies on "folk etymologies"—linking words that sound similar to explain their deeper nature, such as linking 'decrepit' to the 'twilight' of life.</meta>

# Book X

...be learned; that is, he who can be taught. For he is ingenious and fit for learning. **Disciple** <note>original: *discipulus*</note> is named from "discipline" <note>original: *disciplina*</note>, and discipline is named from "learning" <note>original: *discendo*</note>. A **Steward** <note>original: *dispensator*</note> is the name given to one trusted with the administration of money; he is called a *dispensator* because formerly those who gave money did not count it, but "weighed" <note>original: *appendebant*</note> it. **Rich** <note>original: *dives*</note> is named from "copper" <note>original: *ere* / *aes*, used for money</note> or from "dining for a long time" <note>original: *diu vescens*</note>. **Becoming** <note>original: *decorus*</note> or perfect is said to come from the number "ten" <note>original: *decem*</note>. **Comely** <note>original: *deces*</note> or composed is also said to come from the number ten. From this we get both *decorous* and *fitting*. **Direct** <note>original: *directus*</note> is so called because he goes in a "straight" <note>original: *rectum*</note> line. **Beloved** <note>original: *dilectus*</note> is from "diligence" <note>original: *diligentia*</note>. For these are the signs of loving. **Diligent**. **Anointed** <note>original: *delibutus*</note> means smeared with oil, as athletes are wont to be, or boys in the wrestling room <note>original: *ceromate*</note>. From this also comes "anointed with joy," meaning infused or full of it. **Delicate** <note>original: *delicatus*</note> because he is fed on "delights" <note>original: *deliciis*</note>, living in feasts and with physical splendor. **Exhausted** <note>original: *defessus*</note> is one who is always weak, as if "tired for a long time" <note>original: *diu fessus*</note>. **Weak** <note>original: *debilis*</note> as if made fragile "through bile" <note>original: *per bilem*</note>. For bile is a humor that affects the body. **Discolored** <note>original: *decolor*</note> because color is lacking to him. **Desperate** <note>original: *desperatus*</note> is commonly called evil and lost, no longer having any hope of success. It is said by analogy to the sick who, being afflicted and without hope, are "laid down" <note>original: *deponuntur*</note>. It was the custom among the ancients for the "desperate" to be placed before their doors, either so they might return their final breath to the earth, or so they might perhaps be cured by passers-by who had once suffered a similar disease. **Degenerate** <note>original: *degener*</note> because he is ignoble, or of an unequal stock, or because even if born of the best stock, he nonetheless lives dishonorably. **Decrepit** <note>original: *decrepitus*</note> because he is closer to dying and turns, as it were, toward the shadows of death, just as **Twilight** <note>original: *crepusculum*</note> is the time of night. Others say one is decrepit not because they are torn away by old age, but because they have "ceased to rattle" <note>original: *crepare desierit*</note>, that is, have ceased to speak. **Depreciated** <note>original: *depreciatus*</note> from being cheap and not worthy of any price. **Dire** <note>original: *dirus*</note> means stingy and foul, and as if driven by "divine wrath" <note>original: *divina ira*</note>. For *dirum* is said of things that divine beings bring; otherwise, *dirus* means "great." **Gaping** <note>original: *debilcens* / *dehiscens*</note> means opening wide. For here the prefix *de-* is an intensifier, as in "to love dearly" <note>original: *deamare*</note> or "to desire greatly" <note>original: *desidere*</note>. **Despising** <note>original: *despiciens*</note> because he looks "downward" <note>original: *deorsum aspiciat*</note> or holds something in contempt. **Deceitful** <note>original: *dolosus*</note> is treacherous or malicious, from the fact that he "deludes" <note>original: *deludat*</note>. For to deceive, he adorns hidden malice with flattering words. **Doubtful** <note>original: *dubius*</note> is uncertain, as if of "two ways" <note>original: *duarum viarum*</note>. **Informer** <note>original: *delator*</note> is so called because he "uncovers" <note>original: *detegat*</note> what was hidden. **Procrastinator** <note>original: *dilator*</note> because he "defers" <note>original: *differt*</note> bringing things forward. **Slothful** <note>original: *desidiosus*</note> means slow and lazy, named from "sitting down much" <note>original: *desidendo* / *valde sedendo*</note>. Likewise **Residing** is from *residendo*; for here *de-* is an intensifier. **Delirious** <note>original: *delirus*</note> is one failing in mind due to age, from the Greek "from the furrow" <note>original: *apo toy liran* / *ἀπὸ τῆς λήρας*</note>, or because he wanders from the right order as if from a "furrow" <note>original: *lira*</note>. A *lira* is a type of plowing where farmers direct the furrows for the sacred seed, into which all the crop runs. **Demented** <note>original: *demens*</note> is the same as mindless, that is, "without a mind" <note>original: *sine mente*</note>, or because he has a "diminution of the mind." **Foolish** <note>original: *desipiens*</note> because he begins to "be less wise" <note>original: *minus sapere*</note> than he used to be. **Condemned** <note>original: *damnatus*</note> and **Damnable** <note>original: *damnabilis*</note>; the first of these is already sentenced, the latter can be sentenced. **Glutton** <note>original: *degulator*</note> because he is devoted to the "throat" <note>original: *gulae*</note>.

**Eloquent** <note>original: *eloquens*</note> means poured out in speech. **Skilled** <note>original: *exertus*</note> is one ready in speaking. To *exerere* is to bring forth or to make ready. **Erudite** <note>original: *eruditus*</note> because he is no longer "rough" <note>original: *rudis*</note> but is now learned. **Expert** <note>original: *expers*</note> is one very skilled. For here *ex-* is used for "very," just as **Exalted** <note>original: *excelsus*</note> is "very high" <note>original: *valde celsus*</note> and **Exemplary** <note>original: *eximius*</note> is "very prominent." **Efficacious** <note>original: *efficax*</note> is so called because...

<column-break/>

...he has no difficulty in doing any whatever thing. From this, **Efficient** <note>original: *efficiens*</note> is named from "doing" <note>original: *faciedo*</note>. **Hopeless** <note>original: *expes*</note> because he is "without hope" <note>original: *sine spe*</note>. **Deceased** <note>original: *expers*</note> because he is "outside the part" <note>original: *extra partem*</note>, for he has lacked his share. **Outside the lot** <note>original: *exorus*</note> because he is outside the draw. **Exile** <note>original: *exul*</note> because he is "outside his soil" <note>original: *extra solum*</note>, as if sent across the soil, or wandering outside it. For they are called exiles who go outside their soil. **Exile** <note>original: *extorris*</note> because he is "outside his land" <note>original: *extra terra*</note>, as if "out of the lands" <note>original: *ex terris*</note>. But properly one is an *extorris* when he is driven out by force and ejected from his fatherland with "terror" <note>original: *terrore*</note>, and *extroris* when driven from his land. **Outside the border** <note>original: *exterris*</note> is "outside the land" or outside his "boundaries" <note>original: *terminos*</note>, because he is terrified. **Exterminator** <note>original: *exterminator*</note> is not what is commonly said; in Greek it is *exoristos* <note>original: *εξοριστος*</note>, that is, one who casts down and expels from the boundaries of the city. **Exterminated** <note>original: *exterminatus*</note> is from being ejected outside his boundaries. Here also is **External** <note>original: *externus*</note> because he is of a foreign land. **Needy** <note>original: *egens*</note> and **Destitute** <note>original: *egenus*</note> are "without a people" <note>original: *sine gente*</note> and "without stock" <note>original: *sine genere*</note>. **Small** <note>original: *exiguus*</note> means very needy, for *ex-* is used for "very." **Slender** <note>original: *exilis*</note> means thin, because one can "exit" <note>original: *exire*</note> through a narrow place, or because he is "without flanks" <note>original: *sine iliis*</note>. **Eaten away** <note>original: *exesus*</note> because he is "eaten through" <note>original: *percomesus*</note>. For he is dry, thin, and slender. **Exhausted** <note>original: *exhaustus*</note> because he is consumed and made empty. **Bloodless** <note>original: *exanguis*</note> because he is "without blood" <note>original: *extra sanguinem*</note>. **Lifeless** <note>original: *exanimis*</note> is one who is dead. However, we say both *exanimis* and *exanimus*, just as we say "unanimous" <note>original: *unanimus* and *unanimis*</note> or "unarmed" <note>original: *inermis* and *inermus*</note>; let this be subject to our own judgment. **Scorched** <note>original: *exustus*</note> is said of one of whom nothing remains, as if "very burned." For *ex-* is used for "very." **Hateful** <note>original: *exosus*</note> is named from "hate" <note>original: *odio*</note>. For the ancients used both *odi* and *osus sum*. Hence the word *exosus* which we use, although we no longer say *osus*. **Destructive** <note>original: *exitiosus*</note> because it leads much to "destruction" <note>original: *exitio*</note>. **Executor** <note>original: *executor*</note> from "carrying out" <note>original: *exequendo*</note>. The same for **Exactor**. **Burglar** <note>original: *effractor*</note> because he is a "conqueror of bolts" <note>original: *expugnator claustrorum*</note>. **Wild** <note>original: *efferatus*</note> means made with a "beastly mind" <note>original: *ferina mente*</note> and exceeding beyond human measure. **Unbridled** <note>original: *effrenatus*</note> because he is headlong and prone, and "without the bridle of reason" <note>original: *sine freno rationis*</note>. **Eunuch** <note>original: *eunuchus*</note> is a Greek name, which means "castrate" <note>original: *spado*</note>. Some of these cohabit, yet there is no power in their seed. For they have and emit fluid, but for procreation it is empty and invalid. **Worn out** <note>original: *exteta*</note> from being "exhausted by frequent offspring" <note>original: *fetu exhausta*</note>. For constant childbirth renders her weak.

**Eloquent** <note>original: *facundus*</note> is so called because he can "speak" <note>original: *fari*</note> easily. **Witty** <note>original: *facetus*</note> is one who commends jokes and play by gestures and "deeds" <note>original: *factis*</note>; named from "doing" <note>original: *faciendo*</note>. **Frugal** <note>original: *frugalis*</note> named from "produce" <note>original: *fruge*</note>, that is, from fruit or parsimony, or as others wish, from the temperance of modesty. **Usurer** <note>original: *fenerator*</note> is one who places money with a debtor as an "agent of interest" <note>original: *fenoris actor*</note>. For *fenus* is money. In Latin, *fenerator* is used for both the one who gives the loan and the one who receives it. **Flamens** <note>original: *flamines*</note> were the priests of idols. **Happy** <note>original: *felix*</note> is said of one who gives happiness, one who receives it, and that through which happiness is given, such as "a happy time" or "a happy place." **Faithful** <note>original: *fidelis*</note> because that which he says or promises is "good" <note>original: *bonum*</note>. **Easy** <note>original: *facilis*</note> from "doing" <note>original: *faciendo*</note> and not being slow. **Firm** <note>original: *firmus*</note>, from which also comes **Beautiful** <note>original: *formosus*</note>. **Strong** <note>original: *fortis*</note> because he "bears" <note>original: *fert*</note> adversities or whatever may happen, or from "iron" <note>original: *ferro*</note> because he is hard and does not soften. **Beautiful** <note>original: *formosus*</note> is named from "warmth" <note>original: *formo*</note>. For the ancients called what was warm and glowing *formum*. For heat moves the blood, and blood moves beauty. **Foul** <note>original: *foedus*</note> has its name from "goat" <note>original: *hirco*</note> and "kid" <note>original: *edo*</note> with the letter 'f' added.

The entries are arranged alphabetically; this page covers the remainder of the letter F, the entirety of G and H, and the beginning of I (often interchangeable with J in this script).</meta>

# Book X

The ancients used this word with a grave significance—as in "he defiled with blood the fires he himself had hallowed." **Fragile** <note>original: *fragilis*</note> is so named because it can be "easily broken" <note>original: *facile frangi*</note>. **Weary** <note>original: *fessus*</note> is as if one were "split" <note>original: *fissus*</note>—no longer whole in health; it is a general term. For we say one is weary in spirit—as Terence says: "Weary, he sat down in the valley"—and weary in body, which is more common, and weary of circumstances coming by chance. **Fatigued** <note>original: *fatigatus*</note>—as if "driven by the fates" <note>original: *fatis agitatus*</note>. **Fearful** <note>original: *formidolosus*</note> is named from *formo*, that is, "blood" <note>original: *sanguine*</note>, specifically when blood, fleeing from the heart, contracts. For fear freezes the blood, and this gathered blood produces "dread" <note>original: *formidinem*</note>; hence that saying: "the chilled blood curdles with dread." A fearful person, while being timid himself, also signifies something to be feared. A **Fool** <note>original: *fatuus*</note> is thought to be so named because he understands neither what he "speaks" <note>original: *fatur*</note> himself nor what others say. Some think fools derive their origin from the admirers of Fatua, the "prophetic" <note>original: *fatidice*</note> wife of Faunus; they say they were first called fools because they were stunned beyond measure by her prophecies, even unto madness. A **Supporter** <note>original: *fautor*</note> is from "favoring" <note>original: *faveat*</note> and consenting. A **Shaper** <note>original: *fictor*</note> is named from "shaping" <note>original: *fingendo*</note> and composing something, such as one who smears, handles, anoints, and polishes the hair of women. **Deceitful** <note>original: *fallax*</note> is so called because he deceives by "speaking" <note>original: *fando*</note>. **Fervent** <note>original: *fervidus*</note> means hot-tempered, for anger inflames. **Gnashing** <note>original: *frendens*</note>—because in threatening he "breaks" <note>original: *frangat*</note> and grinds his teeth. **Raging** <note>original: *fremens*</note>—that is, shouting with fury. **Ferocious** <note>original: *ferox*</note> is from exercising "wildness" <note>original: *feritatem*</note> like a beast. **Thief** <note>original: *fur*</note> is named from "dark" <note>original: *furvo*</note>, that is, from dusky, for he operates in the time of night. **Factious** <note>original: *factiosus*</note> is used among insults when we mean someone is "seditious," but as a compliment when we mean someone is "influential"—powerful and, as it were, belonging to a great faction. **Wicked** <note>original: *facinorosus*</note> is named from the "commission of a deed" <note>original: *facti commisso*</note>—for he does what harms another. **Womanizer** <note>original: *famellarius*</note> is one devoted to women, whom the ancients called *mulierium*. **Disgraceful** <note>original: *flagitiosus*</note> because he more frequently "demands" <note>original: *flagitet*</note> and seeks out lust. A **Scoundrel** <note>original: *furcifer*</note> was once the name for one who, for a minor offense, was compelled by his masters—more for ignominy than for punishment—to carry a "forked yoke" <note>original: *furcam*</note> along the road, proclaiming his sin to warn others not to commit the like. **Futile** <note>original: *futilis*</note> means vain, superfluous, or talkative. It is a metaphor from "clay vessels" <note>original: *vasis fictilibus*</note> which, being hollow and leaky, do not hold what you pour in. **To fornicate** <note>original: *fornicari*</note>. A **Prostitute** <note>original: *fornicatrix*</note> is one whose body is public and common. These women used to prostrate themselves under "arched places" which are called "vaults" <note>original: *fornices*</note>, hence the term *fornicari*. Virgil says, "and under the facing vault." **Fruitful** <note>original: *fecunda*</note> is named from "offspring" <note>original: *fetu*</note>, as if abounding in offspring. For she is frequent in giving birth. **Pregnant** <note>original: *feta*</note> means with child. **Weeping** <note>original: *flens*</note> is as if "flowing with tears" <note>original: *lachrymas fluens*</note>. No one is rightly called a **Fugitive** <note>original: *fugitivus*</note> unless he flees a master. For if a small boy leaves his nurse or his school, he is not a fugitive.

**Glorious** <note>original: *gloriosus*</note> is named from the "frequency of renown" <note>original: *frequentia claritatis*</note>, with the letter *c* changed to *g*. Glorious is also named from the "laurel" <note>original: *laurea*</note> which is given to victors. **Knowing** <note>original: *gnarus*</note> means wise; its opposite is **Ignorant** <note>original: *ignarus*</note>, meaning unknowing. **Grave** <note>original: *gravis*</note> means venerable. Whence we also call contemptible people "light." One is called grave for counsel and constancy, because he does not leap away with a light movement, but stands firm with the weight of fixed constancy. **Great** <note>original: *grandis*</note>. **Slender** <note>original: *gracilis*</note>. **Aged** <note>original: *grandaevus*</note> because he is "great in age" <note>original: *grandis aevo*</note>. **Grateful** <note>original: *gratus*</note> means keeping grace. But while *gratus* refers only to the mind, **Most Grateful** <note>original: *gratissimus*</note> is said of both mind and body. **Gratifying** <note>original: *gratificus*</note> is from the fact that he does good "freely" <note>original: *gratis*</note>. **Gracious** <note>original: *gratiosus*</note> because he gives to each more than

<column-break/>

one deserves. **Talkative** <note>original: *garrulus*</note> is properly the name for one commonly called "wordy," who, with an added joyfulness, is neither able nor willing to be silent—the name is taken from the "jackdaw" <note>original: *graculis*</note> birds, which always chatter with troublesome loquacity and are never quiet. **Wastrel** <note>original: *ganeo*</note> is luxurious, and acts as if in "hidden and subterranean places" <note>original: *occultis locis et subterraneis*</note>, which the Greeks call *ganea*. **Glutton** <note>original: *glutto*</note> is from "throat" <note>original: *gula*</note>—that is, greedy.

**Humble** <note>original: *humilis*</note> is as if "leaning toward the ground" <note>original: *humo acclivus*</note>. **Honorable** <note>original: *honorabilis*</note> is as if "fit for honor" <note>original: *honore babilis*</note>—that is, suitable. **Honest** <note>original: *honestus*</note> is that which has nothing of shamefulness. For what is honesty but "perpetual honor," that is, as it were, a "state of honor" <note>original: *honoris status*</note>. **Humane** <note>original: *humanus*</note> is one who has love and a feeling of pity toward humans. Whence also "humanity" is named, by which we protect one another. **Handy** <note>original: *habilis*</note> is that which is convenient and "fit for having" <note>original: *habendum*</note>. **Full of Honor** <note>original: *honorosus*</note> is more than "honored," just as "full of crime" <note>original: *scelerosus*</note> is more than "criminal." **Shaggy** <note>original: *hirsutus*</note> is from being bristly and "rough with hair" <note>original: *pilis horridus*</note>. **Hypocrite** <note>original: *hypocrita*</note> is a Greek word, interpreted into Latin as "pretender" <note>original: *simulator*</note>: one who, while being evil within, shows himself as good in public. For *hypo* means "false" and *crisin* means "judgment." The name of the hypocrite is drawn from the appearance of those who in theatrical shows, having masks colored with pigments—sometimes of linen, plastered and distinguished by various colors, and sometimes even painting their necks and hands to achieve the color of the person they are portraying—act as the masters of the games and deceive. They appear now in the form of a man, now a woman; now shorn, now long-haired; sometimes appearing as an old woman or a maiden, or a servant, so that they may deceive the people while they act in the games. This type of argument is transferred to those who walk with a false face and pretend to be what they are not. For they cannot be called hypocrites once they have left the public stage. **Buried** <note>original: *humatus*</note> is one who is "covered with earth" <note>original: *humo tectus*</note>, that is, entombed.

**Ingenious** <note>original: *ingeniosus*</note> is so named because he has the "inward power" <note>original: *intus vim*</note> of producing any art. **Inventor** <note>original: *inventor*</note> is so named because he "comes into" <note>original: *venit*</note> those things which he seeks. Whence the very thing called "invention"—if we retract the origin of the word—what else does it resonate but that "to invent" is "to come into" that which is sought? **Interpreter** <note>original: *interpres*</note> is one who is "in the middle" <note>original: *medius*</note> between the parts of two languages while he translates. But also, he who is between God (whom he interprets) and men (to whom he indicates divine mysteries) is called an interpreter. **Juridical** <note>original: *juridicus*</note> is one who "speaks the rights" <note>original: *jura dicit*</note> of the laws. **Natural Talent** <note>original: *indolis*</note> is properly a certain image of future virtue. **Just** <note>original: *justus*</note> is so named because he guards the "rights" <note>original: *jura*</note> and lives according to the law. **Harmless** <note>original: *innocuus*</note> because he does not harm. For "innocuous" and "innocent" were used interchangeably among the ancients. **Cheerful** <note>original: *ilaris*</note> is a Greek name. **Pleasant** <note>original: *jocundus*</note> because he is always "apt for jokes" <note>original: *jocis aptus*</note> and cheerfulness, from frequency, just as "hot-tempered" <note>original: *iracundus*</note>. **Jocular** <note>original: *jocolus*</note> is one accustomed to jokes. **Renowned** <note>original: *inclytus*</note> is a Greek name. For the Greeks call the "glorious" person *clyron*. **Illustrious** <note>original: *illustris*</note> is a name of notoriety because he shines to many with the "splendor of his lineage," or his wisdom, or his virtue; the opposite of this is "born in obscurity." **Suitable** <note>original: *ydoneus*</note> is as if "having a double gift" <note>original: *duplum habens donum*</note>. **Unharmed** <note>original: *incolumis*</note> takes its name from "column" <note>original: *columna*</note>, as if one were upright, strong, and stable. **Unfading** <note>original: *immarcessibilis*</note> means incorrupt and everlasting, because it is without "withering" <note>original: *marcore*</note> or...

<meta>This page continues Book X of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies, an encyclopedic dictionary of terms. This section focuses on adjectives and nouns describing human character and behavior, organized alphabetically. It concludes the section on words beginning with 'I' (including those we now spell with 'J'), covers 'K', and begins the letter 'L'.</meta>

[lan]guor. **Unblemished** <note>original: *intemeratus*</note>: incorrupt and violated by no rashness. **Infirm** <note>original: *infirmus*</note>: so named because he is "without heat" <note>original: *sine formo*; *formus* is an ancient Latin term for warm</note>, that is, without warmth. **Feeble** <note>original: *imbecillis*</note>: as if "without a staff" <note>original: *sine baculo*</note>, fragile and inconstant. **Empty** <note>original: *inanis*</note>: light. **Inconstant** <note>original: *inconstans*</note>: because he is not stable; what pleases him now displeases him later. **Boastful** or **arrogant** <note>original: *iactans uel arrogans*</note>: one who does not submit to the institutions of the ancestors, but seeks out his own particular way of justice and sanctity. **Irascible** <note>original: *iracundus*</note>: so named because when the blood is kindled, it compels one into a fury. For "fire" <note>original: *ur*</note> is what a flame is called, and anger inflames. **Inciter** <note>original: *incentor*</note>: from the one who kindles and inflames. **Inciter**: because by depraved suggestion he kindles others to vice and inflames them through persuasion. **Inexpiable** <note>original: *inexpiabilis*</note>: one who may never be expiated, never purged. **Unpraiseworthy** <note>original: *inlaudabilis*</note>: not because he hasn't been praised, but because he does not deserve to be praised. **Irrate** <note>original: *iratus*</note>: driven by anger. **Impious** <note>original: *impius*</note>: because he is without the piety of religion. **Iniquitous** <note>original: *iniquus*</note>: properly named because he is "not equal" <note>original: *non equus*</note>, that is, uneven. There is often a distinction between the **impious** and the **iniquitous**: for every impious man is iniquitous, but not every iniquitous man is impious. For **impious** is used for an infidel, and is so called because he is alien to the piety of religion. But **iniquitous** is said of one who is not "equal" or fair, but is stained by depraved works and may not even be counted under the name of Christianity. **Enemy** <note>original: *inimicus*</note>: because he is "not a friend" <note>original: *non amicus*</note>, that is, an adversary. Two things make enemies: fraud and terror. Terror, for those who are afraid; the evil of fraud, for those who have suffered it. **Envious** <note>original: *inuidus*</note>: named from "looking upon" <note>original: *inuidendo*</note> the good fortune of another. **Invidious** <note>original: *inuidiosus*</note> is one who suffers envy from another. **Hated** <note>original: *inuisus*</note>: odious, named from envy and zeal. **Intestable** <note>original: *intestabilis*</note>: one whose testimony is not valid, or whatever he says is void and disapproved. **Infamous** <note>original: *infamis*</note>: not of good fame. **Wicked** <note>original: *improbus*</note>: so named because he persists even against one who prohibits him. **Troublesome** <note>original: *importunus*</note>: restless, because he "has no port" <note>original: *non habet portum*</note>, that is, no rest. Hence the troublesome are carried away quickly as if in a shipwreck. **Unbridled** <note>original: *infrenis*</note>: that is, one who is not ruled by reins, like the "unbridled Numidians." **Gnashing** <note>original: *infrendens*</note>: properly one who presses his teeth together. For to "gnash" <note>original: *frendere*</note> means to break with the teeth. Hence "toothless ones" <note>original: *nefrendes*</note> are infants who do not yet have teeth. **Gluttonous** <note>original: *ingluuiofus*</note>: named from the throat <note>original: *gula*</note> and voracity. **Inglorious** <note>original: *ingloriosus*</note>: one who is without glory, that is, without triumphs. Likewise, **inglorious** means "unmindful of glory." **Shapeless** or **huge** <note>original: *informis / ingens*</note>: not because it has no form, but because it has a magnitude "beyond form." **Inveterate** <note>original: *inueteratus*</note>: because he has "much and old usage" <note>original: *multi veterisq' vsus*</note> in malice. **Monstrous** <note>original: *immanis*</note>: one who is not good, that is, cruel and terrible. For "good" used to be called *manum*. Hence, by <term>antiphrasis</term> <note>a figure of speech where a word is used to mean its opposite</note>, the "Manes gods" are the least good. **Exempt** <note>original: *immunis*</note>: "least generous" <note>original: *minime munificus*</note>, as in the old proverb: "His own citizens hate the exempt man." Likewise, **exempt** is one who does not perform duties <note>original: *munia*</note>, that is, does not fulfill an office. For he is "empty" of all privilege. **Scatheless** <note>original: *indemnis*</note>: because he lives "without loss" <note>original: *sine damno*</note>, and without any fault or danger. **Skilless** <note>original: *iners*</note>: "without art" <note>original: *sine arte*</note>, and for this reason not even fit for any work. **Unarmed** <note>original: *inermis*</note>: either "without arms" <note>original: *sine armis*</note> or "without strength" <note>original: *sine viribus*</note>. For "arms" are always understood to mean strength. **Slothful** <note>original: *ignauus*</note>: "ignorant of the way" <note>original: *ignarus vię*</note>, that is, of reason and life. **Ignorant** <note>original: *ignarus*</note>: not "knowing" <note>original: *gnarus*</note>, that is, unskilled. Or it means "without nostrils" <note>original: *sine naribus*</note>, for the ancients said that "to have smelled" was "to have known." Moreover, **ignorant** signifies two things: either one who does not know, or one who is not known. **Forgetful** <note>original: *immemo*</note>: one who has forgotten, for he has "lost memory."

<column-break/>

**Unknowing** <note>original: *inscius*</note>: one who is without knowledge. **Idiot** <note>original: *idiota*</note>: unskilled; it is a Greek word. **Inexperienced** <note>original: *impitus*</note>: without expertise. **Unadvised** <note>original: *inconsultus*</note>: from one who does not receive counsel. Likewise, **unadvised** is one who is without counsel, unknowing of things, and ignorant. **Inept** <note>original: *ineptus*</note>: the contrary of "apt," as if "in-apt." **Needy** <note>original: *inops*</note>: one who is "without land" <note>original: *sine terra*</note>, for we understand "wealth" <note>original: *opem*</note> to be the earth, because it brings wealth by fruiting. Others understand **needy** as "unburied" or "uninterred" <note>original: *inhumatu*</note>, for whom no tomb has risen even though he has a soul. **Ignoble** <note>original: *ignobilis*</note>: because he is unknown, vile, and of obscure birth, whose name is not even known. **Stinking** <note>original: *irrosus*; likely *hircosus*</note>: because he reeks with the foul sweat of the body. **Unknown** <note>original: *ignotus*</note>: ignoble, or one coming unexpectedly. **Unforeseen** <note>original: *improuisus*</note>: so called because it happens suddenly and was not "seen beforehand" <note>original: *ante visus*</note>. **Informer** <note>original: *index*</note>: a betrayer; from "indicating." **Native** <note>original: *indigena*</note>: called so because he was "born from there" <note>original: *inde genitus*</note>, that is, born in that same place. **Impudent** <note>original: *impudēs*</note>: because shame and modesty are far from him. **Lewd** <note>original: *impudicus*</note>: named from the "anus" <note>original: *podice*</note>. For it suggests filth and stench. **Incestuous** <note>original: *incestus*</note>: so called on account of illicit mixing; as if "un-chaste" <note>original: *incastus*</note>, such as one who has defiled a sacred virgin or a close relative. **Internecine** <note>original: *internecida*</note>: one who made a false testament and for that reason killed a man. **Denier** <note>original: *inficiato*</note>: one who does not confess, or who strives with a lie against the truth. **Impostor** <note>original: *imposto*</note>: a lying fabricator. **Intercepter** <note>original: *intercepto*</note>: properly said of one who "takes from the middle" between two people. **Treacherous** <note>original: *insidiosus*</note>: one who "sits in" <note>original: *insideat*</note> wait. For properly "to sit in" is to wait for someone deceitfully. From this, "ambushes" <note>original: *insidię*</note> are named. **Ungirt** <note>original: *incincta*</note>: that is, without a girdle, because the womb does not permit it to be cinched tightly. **Unrobed** <note>original: *investis*</note>: that is, without a robe; for he does not yet have the "stola" <note>the traditional gown of a married woman</note>, which is the sign of marital virginity. **Buffoon** <note>original: *scurra*</note>: so called because he follows anyone for the sake of "food" <note>original: *esce*</note>.

**Catholic** <note>original: *katholicus*</note>: universal. For it is a Greek name. **Dear** <note>original: *karus*</note> is a Greek name, just like **charity** <note>original: *karitas*</note>. Whence also **Eucharist** <note>original: *eukaristia*</note>, the sacrifice, which means "good grace."

**Lucid** <note>original: *luculentus*</note>: from one who is clear in tongue and splendid in speech. **Reader** <note>original: *lecto*</note>: named from "reading" <note>original: *legendo*</note>, that is, traversing. Whence a ship is said to "read" <note>skirt or skim</note> whatever it passes. For it "reads," it passes by, it goes past, as we often read: "he skims the straits stirred by the lands." Likewise, a **reader** is named from "gathering" <note>original: *colligendo*</note> in the mind what he reads, as if a "gatherer," just like that line: "you who gather flowers." **Loquacious** <note>original: *loquax*</note> is not the same as eloquent. **Joyful** <note>original: *letus*</note>: from "width" <note>original: *latitudine*</note>. **Wealthy** <note>original: *locuples*</note>: as if "full of places" <note>original: *locis plenus*</note>, and a possessor of many holdings. As Tullius <note>the Roman orator Cicero</note> teaches in the second book of *The Republic*, many things were given in the "edition of sheep and cattle," for at that time wealth consisted in livestock and in the possession of places, from which they were called "moneyed" and "wealthy." **Liberal** <note>original: *liberalis*</note>: named from the fact that he gives "freely" <note>original: *libenter*</note> and does not murmur. **Bountiful** <note>original: *largus*</note>: abundant, affluent. **Long** <note>original: *longus*</note>: named from a "line" <note>original: *linea*</note>, because it is stretched out. **Long-lived** <note>original: *longęuus*</note>: as if of a "long age" and long time. **Long-suffering** <note>original: *langanimis*</note> or **magnanimous**: because he is disturbed by no passions, or he is patient in sustaining all things. To which the contrary is **faint-hearted** <note>original: *pusillanimis*</note>: narrow and not standing firm in any tribulation. Of whom it is written: "The fool is of a vehement faint-heartedness." **Fickle** <note>original: *leuis*</note>: named for the inconstancy of wandering, who by a slight motion of the mind desires now this, now that. **Slippery** <note>original: *lubricus*</note>: from the fact that he "slips" <note>original: *labitur*</note>.

It highlights Isidore's method of using folk etymology—such as linking 'wealthy' to 'full of places' and 'ignorant' to 'lacking nostrils'—to explain the moral character of individuals.</summary>

### Column 1

<margin>bandit</margin>
Gliding, I am sometimes carried, as a nymph might glide from the sky, and glide on wings. For a slip in a race is faster. **Bandit** <note>original: *latro*</note>: one who waits in ambush on the path, named from "hiding" <note>original: *latendo*</note>. Better yet, a "bandit" <note>original: *latro*</note> is like a "sider" <note>original: *latero*</note>, a waylayer from the side <note>original: *a latere*</note>.
<margin>gladiator-trainer</margin>
**Gladiator-trainer** <note>original: *lanista*</note>: that is, a butcher, named in the Etruscan language.
<margin>butcher</margin>
**Butcher** <note>original: *laniator*</note>: obviously from "tearing" <note>original: *laniando*</note> bodies. **Provoker** <note>original: *lacessitor*</note>: by a metaphor taken from dogs or wild beasts, which are accustomed to provoke others by tearing <note>original: *lacerando*</note> at them.
<margin>pimp</margin>
**Pimp** <note>original: *leno*</note>: a counselor of debauchery, because he [soothes] minds—
<margin>lustful</margin>
[—or rather] from the fact that he does whatever "pleases" <note>original: *libet*</note>. **Lustful** <note>original: *libidinosus*</note>: from "free" <note>original: *libero*</note>,
<margin>luxurious</margin>
one who paints the bodies of girls. **Luxurious** <note>original: *luxuriosus*</note>: as if dissolved in pleasures; hence also dislocated limbs are called "luxed" <note>original: *luxa*</note>.
<margin>lascivious</margin>
**Lascivious** <note>original: *lascivus*</note>: named as if "luxed," that is, dissolved and empty.
<margin>madman</margin>
**Madman** <note>original: *lymphaticus*</note>: one who fears water, which the Greeks call "hydrophobia" <note>original: *hydrophoba*</note>. Strictly, one is called "lymphatic" who contracts a defect from water, when the defect is to run here and there, or from a defect taken from the flow of water. But poets now use this kind of name for those who are furious or insane.
<margin>pale</margin>
**Pale** <note>original: *luridus*</note>: one who becomes pallid, named from "leather" <note>original: *loro*</note>, because they have that kind of skin.
<margin>leprous</margin>
**Leprous** <note>original: *leprosus*</note>: named from the excessive itching of the scab itself; hence
<margin>one-eyed</margin>
it should be written with a 'p'. **One-eyed** <note>original: *luscus*</note>: one who knows the light <note>original: *lucem*</note> only in part, like the "dim-sighted" <note>original: *lusciciosus*</note> who sees nothing in the evening. The ancients called the one-eyed "Coclites." Hence we read that the Cyclopes were called "Coclites," who are said to have had only one eye.
<margin>washed</margin>
**Washed** <note>original: *lotus*</note>: bathed, that is, clean.
<margin>prostitute</margin>
**Prostitute** <note>original: *lupa*</note>: literally "she-wolf," named from her rapacity, because she seizes and catches the wretched.

**Merciful** <note>original: *misericors*</note>: this name is chosen from "compassionating the misery of another." From this, "mercy" <note>original: *misericordia*</note> is named because it makes a "wretched heart" <note>original: *miserū cor*</note> in one grieving over another's misery. However, this etymology does not apply everywhere. For there is mercy in God without any misery of the heart. **Enriched** <note>original: *mactus*</note>: more increased by glory. This name is drawn from sacred rites. For whenever they poured incense or wine over a victim, they would say, "the bull is *mactus* with wine or incense," that is, the sacrifice is accumulated and more increased. **Munificent** <note>original: *munificus*</note>: so called either because he bestows many gifts <note>original: *munera*</note> on someone, or because he fulfills his gift, that is, the duty <note>original: *munus*</note> which he owes. Likewise, a **gift-bearer** <note>original: *munifer*</note> is one who brings gifts. **Magnanimous** <note>original: *magnanimis*</note>: from being of a great mind <note>original: *magni animi*</note> and great virtue. To this, the opposite is the "small-souled" <note>original: *pusillanimis*</note>. **Magnificent** <note>original: *magnificus*</note>: draws its name from doing great things <note>original: *magna faciendo*</note>. **Tame** <note>original: *mansuetus*</note>: mild or mastered, as if "accustomed to the hand" <note>original: *manu assuetus*</note>. **Modest** <note>original: *modestus*</note>: named from "measure" <note>original: *modo*</note> and temperament, doing neither too much nor too death. **Mild** <note>original: *mitis*</note>: gentle and tame, yielding to wickedness and silent in enduring injury, as if "mute" <note>original: *mutus*</note>. **Mute** <note>original: *mutus*</note>: because his voice is not speech but a lowing <note>original: *mugitus*</note>. For he emits the vocal breath through the nose as if lowing. **Mindful** <note>original: *memor*</note>: either one who holds a memory, or who is held in memory. **Master** <note>original: *magister*</note>: greater in standing <note>original: *maior i statione*</note>. For *steron* in Greek is called "station" <note>original: *statio*</note> in Latin. **Servant** <note>original: *minister*</note>: lesser in standing <note>original: *minor in statione*</note>, or because he executes his due duty with his hands <note>original: *manibus*</note>. **Greater, lesser, least** <note>original: *maior, minor, minimus*</note>: from the number of the unit <note>original: *monadis*</note>, because after it there is no other. **Greatest** <note>original: *maximus*</note>: most eminent either in merits, age, honor, eloquence, virtue, or in all things. **Moderate** <note>original: *modicus*</note>: "small" here is used loosely; otherwise, it means "reasonable." **Moderated** <note>original: *moderatus*</note>: from "measure" <note>original: *modo*</note> and temperament. **Middling** <note>original: *mediocris*</note>: one for whom a moderate amount suffices.

<column-break/>

### Column 2

**Wretched** <note>original: *miser*</note>: strictly one who has lost all happiness. But according to Cicero, it strictly means "dead," for in his *Tusculan Disputations* he calls the dead "wretched" because they have already lost their life. **Miserable** <note>original: *miserabilis*</note>: one who is capable of <note>original: *habilis*</note> misery. **Sorrowful** <note>original: *maestus*</note>: naturally sad, not by chance. For it is from the nature of the mind <note>original: *mentis*</note> and spirit <note>original: *animi*</note>; hence also "sorrowful." **Beggar** <note>original: *mendicus*</note>: so named because he has "less" <note>original: *minus*</note> of that by which he might live; or because it was the custom among the ancients for the needy to close the mouth and extend the hand, as if to speak with the hand <note>original: *manu dicere*</note>. **Liar** <note>original: *mendax*</note>: because he deceives the mind <note>original: *mentem*</note> of another. **Malignant** <note>original: *malignus*</note>: because he carries out a vow or work of malice. **Bad** <note>original: *malus*</note>: named from "black bile," which the Greeks call *melan* <note>original: *μέλαν*</note>. From this, people are called "melancholic" who flee human interaction and are suspicious of the company of friends. **Malicious** <note>original: *malitiosus*</note>: worse than "bad," because he is frequently bad. From "bad" <note>original: *malus*</note> one is called "worse" <note>original: *peior*</note>; from "good," "inferior" <note>original: *deterior*</note>. **Better** <note>original: *melior*</note>: named as if "softer" <note>original: *mollior*</note>; not hard or iron-like, for "better" is as if "softer." **Threatening** <note>original: *minax*</note>: from the appearance of the eyes when one burns with fury so that, seeing more broadly, he may press upon others. **Threatener** <note>original: *minator*</note> and **advisor** <note>original: *monitor*</note>. But an "advisor" is said when he announces good things; a "threatener" when he announces adverse things. **Softener** <note>original: *mulcator*</note>: because he soothes with flattering words to bend the mind. This is a metaphor from "honeyed wine" <note>original: *mulsum*</note>, that is, something which, when taken, is accustomed to soothe the throat of one in pain, or to fill a stomach [disturbed] with impurities. **Surveyors** <note>original: *metatores*</note>: they are named because they mark out camps, specifically from "measuring" <note>original: *metiendo*</note>, as Lucan says: "The bold surveyor comes into the Hesperian fields." **Effeminate** <note>original: *mollis*</note>: one who disgraces the vigor of his sex with an enervated body, and is made soft like a woman. **Lean** <note>original: *macer*</note>: from "leanness" <note>original: *macie*</note>, and leanness from "wasting" <note>original: *macia*</note> because immoderate lust makes people lean; or from "maceration." **Maimed** <note>original: *mancus*</note>: "crippled in the hand" <note>original: *manu ancus*</note>. **Dying** <note>original: *moribundus*</note>: similar to one dying, just as "avoiding" <note>original: *vitabundum*</note> is similar to one who avoids. For when do we say "he is about to die"? He truly is about to die. But "dying" <note>original: *moribundus*</note> is not truly [dead], but truly similar to one dying. **Prostitute** <note>original: *meretrix*</note>: named because she earns <note>original: *mercat*</note> the price of lust. Hence also "earning-houses" <note>original: *meritoriae*</note>, that is, taverns. For soldiers also, when they receive their pay, are said "to earn" <note>original: *mereri*</note>. **Fool** <note>original: *morio*</note>: named after "death" <note>original: *mortem*</note>, because he does not thrive in intellect. **Mule-driver** <note>original: *mulio*</note>: named from "mules," because he presides over those same vehicles. **Manifest** <note>original: *manifestum*</note>: that which is "ready in the hand" <note>original: *in manu promptum*</note>.

**Noble** <note>original: *nobilis*</note>: "not base" <note>original: *non vilis*</note>; one whose name and lineage are known. **Marriageable** <note>original: *nubilis*</note>: ready for "veiling" <note>original: *nubendum*</note> [marriage]. **No one** <note>original: *nemo*</note>: drawn from "man," that is, "not a man" <note>original: *ne homo*</note>, which is "no person." **None** <note>original: *nullus*</note>: as if "not any" <note>original: *ne ullus*</note>. **Nothing** <note>original: *nihil*</note>: composed of "not" <note>original: *ne*</note> and "a whit" <note>original: *hilum*</note>. Varro says "a whit" <note>original: *hilum*</note> signifies the marrow of that stalk which the Greeks call "asphodel" <note>original: *asphodelon*</note>; and thus "nothing" is said among us as "emptiness" <note>original: *keneryma*</note> is among the Greeks. Many distinguish the **worthless** <note>original: *nequam*</note> from the "bad," considering one pernicious and the other a trifler, as Donatus says: "This youth is worthless, not bad," that is, a trifler, not pernicious. Others confuse them, as if both signify one and the same thing. **Wickedness** <note>original: *nequitia*</note>: the ancients wanted it to be named from "not being anything" <note>original: *nec quicquam*</note>, that is, from being nothing. **Neither** <note>original: *neuter*</note>: not that one nor this one, as if to say "not either." **Nefarious** <note>original: *nefarius*</note>: not worthy of "grain" <note>original: *far*</note>, which was the first kind of food by which the life of men was sustained. **Unspeakable** <note>original: *nefandus*</note>: that is, "not to be named" <note>original: *nec nominandus*</note>, because it should not be spoken. **Nourisher** <note>original: *nutritor*</note>: as if "educated by a nod" <note>original: *nutu eruditor*</note>. **Messenger** <note>original: *nuncius*</note>: is both the one who announces and that which is announced, that is, an "angel" <note>original: *angelus*</note> and "the message" <note>original: *angeleia*</note>. "Messenger" <note>original: *nuncius*</note> is the man himself in the masculine gender; that which he announces is in the neuter gender, as "the message" <note>original: *nuncium*</note> or "the news" <note>original: *nuncia*</note>. **Nazarene**: that is, the holy one of God. Nazarene was formerly—

# Book X

### Column 1

...was so called because he nurtured holy hair and accepted nothing contaminated, abstaining from wine and every strong drink <note>original: *sicera*</note> which perverts the mind from sound health. **Trifles** <note>original: *Nugae*</note>, however, is a Hebrew name. For it is explained in the prophets where Zephaniah says: "The trifles <note>original: *Nugae*</note> who had receded from the law." This allows us to know that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages. **Tattler** <note>original: *Nugigerulus*</note> is named from being a messenger of shameful news. **Negligent** <note>original: *Negligens*</note> is as if "not reading" <note>original: *nec legens*</note>. **Spendthrift** <note>original: *Nepos*</note> is named from a certain kind of scorpion that consumes its own offspring, except for the one that sits upon its back; for that one in turn, having been saved, consumes the father. From this, men who consume the goods of their parents through luxury are called "spendthrifts" <note>original: *nepotes*</note>. Hence also "luxury/extravagance" <note>original: *nepotatio*</note> is used for excess, and certainly for things that consume. **Black** <note>original: *Niger*</note> is as if "cloud-bearer" <note>original: *nubiger*</note>, because it is not clear but covered in darkness. Whence we also call a gloomy day "cloudy" <note>original: *nubilum*</note>.

**Orthodox** <note>original: *Orthodoxus*</note> means of right glory. **Orator** is named from the "mouth" <note>original: *os/oris*</note>, or named from "pleading" <note>original: *orando*</note>, that is, from speaking. For to plead <note>original: *orare*</note> is to speak. **Obedient** <note>original: *Obaudiens*</note> is from the "ear" <note>original: *auris*</note>, because he hears the one commanding. **Guest/Host** <note>original: *Hospes*</note> is because he places his "feet in the doors" <note>original: *ostijs pedes*</note>. A "ready host" <note>original: *hospes facilis*</note> is one open to the door <note>original: *ostio patens*</note>. From this, a man is called "well-traveled" <note>original: *orbitalis*</note>. **Hater** <note>original: *Osor*</note>, an enemy, is named from "hatred" <note>original: *odium*</note>, just as a lover is named from love; and it is of common gender. **Hateful** <note>original: *Odibilis*</note> means fit for hatred. **Beset** <note>original: *Obsitus*</note> means besieged, that is, surrounded on all sides by ambushes. **Obscene** <note>original: *Obscenus*</note>, of impure lust, is named from an "obscure vice" <note>original: *obscuro vitio*</note>. **Obtuse** <note>original: *Obtusus*</note> means duller and more shut out, as if "beaten" <note>original: *tunsus*</note> from every side. **Striving** <note>original: *Obnixus*</note> is said of one who is contrary and struggling. **Obnoxious** <note>original: *Obnoxius*</note> is one who is bound by the "knots of fault" <note>original: *nexibus culpae*</note>. **Delighter/Enticer** <note>original: *Oblectator*</note> is as if "with milk" <note>original: *cum lacte*</note> and fraud, as Terence says: "unless you had enticed <note>original: *lactasses*</note> me as a lover"; whence the word "to delight" <note>original: *oblectare*</note> is derived. **Detractor** <note>original: *Obtrectator*</note> is a malicious person who, by hindering and obstructing, does not allow anyone to advance and grow. **Bereft** <note>original: *Orbus*</note> is one who has no children, as if with "eyes lost." **Help-bringer** <note>original: *Opifer*</note> is so called because he does some "work" <note>original: *opus*</note>. **Shepherd** <note>original: *Opilio*</note> is a guardian of sheep, as if "sheep-keeper" <note>original: *ovilio*</note>.

**Modest** <note>original: *Pudens*</note> is as if "seeing far" <note>original: *porro videns*</note>; for he is insightful and investigates the outcomes of uncertain things. **Fearful** <note>original: *Pavidus*</note> is named from "striking" <note>original: *pavendo*</note>. For "to fear" <note>original: *pavere*</note> is to strike; for fear both strikes and endures. **Perfect** <note>original: *Perfectus*</note> is that to which nothing can now be added. Among grammarians, no comparison is added to this name, for if you say "he is more perfect," then this one will not be perfect. **Beautiful** <note>original: *Pulcher*</note> is named from the appearance of the skin, because it is "reddish skin" <note>original: *rubens pellis*</note>; later this name passed to the whole kind. For the beauty of a person is either in the face, as in: "in face and shoulders like a god" <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.589</note>; or in the hair, as in: "he himself with beautiful locks" <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.147</note>; or in the eyes, as in: "he had breathed joyous honors upon his eyes" <note>original: Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.591</note>; or in brightness, as in: "such beauty as hands add to ivory"; or in the features, as in: "the figure and features of the guest delighted him much more"; or in height, as in: "Turnus moves in their midst... and is a whole head above them." **Mistress/Seductress** <note>original: *Pellex*</note> is from "enticing" <note>original: *pelliciendo*</note>. **Perspicacious** <note>original: *Perspicax*</note> is bright, because he strikes the mind. **Leader** <note>original: *Praesul*</note> is so called because he "presides" <note>original: *praeest*</note> with care. **Provost/Overseer** <note>original: *Praepositus*</note> is named from being the ordainer of subjects and servants, or of the upright. **Patrons** <note>original: *Patroni*</note> are named from "fathers" <note>original: *patribus*</note>, because they show this kind of affection to their clients, as if they rule them like fathers. **Pedagogue** <note>original: *Pedagogus*</note> is one to whom little ones

<column-break/>

are assigned. It is a Greek name, and is composed from the fact that he "leads boys" <note>original: Greek *pais* (boy) + *agein* (to lead)</note>, that is, he teaches them and restrains their wanton age.
<margin>present</margin>
**Present** <note>original: *Praesens*</note> is so called because it is "before the senses" <note>original: *prae sensibus*</note>, that is, before the eyes, which are the senses of the body.
<margin>powerful power</margin>
**Prior** is because he is first in order, and **first** <note>original: *primus*</note> is as if pre-eminent. First, **Posterior**, **Last**. **Powerful** <note>original: *Potens*</note> is wide-reaching in affairs, whence also **power** <note>original: *potestas*</note>, which lies open to him as much as he wishes, and no one may shut him out or be able to resist.
<margin>near next</margin>
**Exceedingly wealthy** <note>original: *Praecopiosus*</note> is more "abundant" <note>original: *copiosus*</note> than other resources. **Moneyed** <note>original: *Pecuniosus*</note>: Cicero records that those who had the most "cattle" <note>original: *pecora*</note> were first called this. For so the ancients named them. Gradually, however, through misuse it devolved into another name. **Persistent/Stubborn** <note>original: *Pervicax*</note> is properly said of one who perseveres in his purpose until "victory" <note>original: *victoriam*</note>. For the ancients used to say *vicia* for what we call victory; I believe the herb *vicia* <note>vetch</note> is named from this, that is, "victorious." **Swift** <note>original: *Pernix*</note> is drawn from "striving hard" <note>original: *pernitendo*</note>, that is, persevering in efforts. Others understand *pernix* as swift of feet. For "pernicity" belongs to the feet, as in: "with swift <note>original: *pnicibus*</note> fiery soles," just as "celerity" belongs to wings, as in: "gliding in swift <note>original: *celeri*</note> flight beneath the stars."
<margin>lazy</margin>
**Lazy** <note>original: *Piger*</note> is as if "sick in the feet" <note>original: *pedibus aeger*</note>. For he is slow to walk, which name through use passed to the mind. **All-night** <note>original: *Pernox*</note> means staying awake through the night. **Persevering** means burning, vigorous, hardworking.
<margin>pertinacious</margin>
**Pertinacious** <note>original: *Pertinax*</note> means shamelessly holding on, as if "thoroughly holding" <note>original: *per-tenens*</note>. **Petulant** <note>original: *Petulans*</note> is now indeed used for the bold and wicked; formerly it referred to harsh demanders of debt, and specifically the boys of money-collectors who demanded the prices of things more frequently and sharply; they were called petulant from "asking/demanding" <note>original: *petendo*</note>. **Bold/Procacious** <note>original: *Procax*</note> is properly the same as "demanding" <note>original: *petax*</note>. For "to ask" <note>original: *procare*</note> is to demand. Whence also seekers of marriage are called "suitors" <note>original: *proci*</note>.
<margin>prodigal fugitive</margin>
**Prodigal** <note>original: *Prodigus*</note> means sumptuous and consuming; one who drives everything "far away" <note>original: *porro*</note> or as if he "throws it forth." **Fugitive/Exile** <note>original: *Profugus*</note> is properly said of one who wanders "far from his home" <note>original: *procul a sedibus*</note>, as if "put to flight far away" <note>original: *porro fugatus*</note>. **Foreigner/Pilgrim** <note>original: *Peregrinus*</note> is one placed far from his fatherland, like an alien. **Cast out** <note>original: *Proiectus*</note> is as if thrown far and wide; just as "he led forth" <note>original: *perduxit*</note> means he led him far away, and "he provoked" <note>original: *provocauit*</note> means he called him far away.
<margin>projected</margin>
**Projected** <note>original: *Proiectus*</note> is as if ejected and cast far out. Whence also "the projected rocks of Pachynus," that is, thrown far out. **Proscribed** <note>original: *Proscriptus*</note> is one whose goods are openly and publicly "written down" <note>original: *scribuntur*</note> and added to the goods of the treasury.
<margin>prescribed prompt</margin>
**Prescribed** <note>original: *Praescriptus*</note> signifies order, just as "prescriptions" <note>original: *praescriptiones*</note> among legal experts. **Girded/Ready** <note>original: *Procinctus*</note> means unencumbered and armed. Whence also "in readiness" <note>original: *in procinctu*</note>, that is, when they took up arms for the cause of war. **Girded** <note>original: *Praecinctus*</note> because he places something "before" <note>original: *prae*</note> himself with which he is girded. Whence it is said of the Lord: "He was girded <note>original: *Praecinctus*</note> with a towel and washed the feet of his disciples." **Plunderer** <note>original: *Praedo*</note> is one who invades a foreign province by ravaging it. A plunderer is named from "driving away spoils" <note>original: *abigendo praedas*</note>, and a plunderer is one who has "spoils" <note>original: *praedam*</note>. A **Predator** is one to whom something of the spoil is owed. **Kidnapper/Plagiary** <note>original: *Plagiator*</note> is from "oblique" <note>original: *plagio*</note>, because he does not walk by a certain path, but by enticing with deceits.
<margin>pirate</margin>
**Pirates** <note>original: *Piratae*</note> are maritime robbers; they are named from the "burning" <note>original: *incendio*</note> of the ships they captured. For *pira* <note>Greek: *pyr*</note> is fire. **Swindler** <note>original: *Pugillator*</note> is one who subtracts something from the coins passed from hand to hand. **Embezzler** <note>original: *Peculator*</note> is one who defrauds the "money" <note>original: *pecuniae*</note> he oversees.
<margin>traitor perfidious perjurer</margin>
**Traitor** <note>original: *Proditor*</note> because he "uncovers" <note>original: *detegit*</note>. Also traitor <note>original: *perditor*</note> as in "we are betrayed <note>original: *perdimur*</note> by the wrath of one." **Perfidious** <note>original: *Perfidus*</note> is one who is fraudulent and without faith <note>original: *fides*</note>, as if "destroying faith." **Perjurer** <note>original: *Periurus*</note> because he "swears perversely" <note>original: *perperam iurat*</note>, that is, he swears wrongly.

<meta>This page continues Book X of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, continuing the alphabetical list of terms describing human character. The text moves through the letters P, Q, R, and S, explaining the origins of words for legal roles, moral vices, and social virtues.</meta>

...has none. For we say "to perjure" <note>original: *pejero*</note> and "to swear falsely" <note>original: *deiero*</note>. <margin>prevaricator</margin> **Prevaricator** is a lawyer of bad faith, who either passes over things in an accusation that would harm the opponent or things in a defense that would help the client, or uselessly places them everywhere for the sake of a bribe, though he is corrupt. Cicero says: "What indeed is so prevaricating?" that is, exceedingly crooked. <margin>deceiver</margin> **Deceiver** <note>original: *Pellax*</note> is deceitful and false, named from the "skin" <note>original: *pelle*</note>, that is, the face. For outwardly he smiles to deceive, but carries wickedness within. <margin>profane</margin> **Profane** is as if "far from the temple" <note>original: *porro a fano*</note>. For it is not permitted for such a person to take part in sacred rites. <margin>parricide</margin> **Parricide** is properly said of one who kills parents. Some of the ancients called him a "parent-killer" <note>original: *parenticida*</note> who had killed a man, since parricide and homicide can be understood in either case, as men are equal <note>original: *pares*</note> to men. <margin>persecutor</margin> **Persecutor** is not always understood in a bad sense; hence "prosecutor" <note>original: *persecutor*</note> means one who followed through perfectly. <margin>publican</margin> **Publican** is one who collects public taxes, or who pursues the gains of the world through public business, from which he is also named. <margin>sinner</margin> **Sinner** <note>original: *Peccator*</note> is named from a "mistress" <note>original: *pellex*</note>, that is, a harlot, as if "committing adultery" <note>original: *pellicato*</note>; which name among the ancients signified only a shameful person. Afterwards, this name passed into a designation for all the unjust. **Sinners** are also named from a "crowd of the breast" <note>original: *pectoris caterua*</note>, because the secrets of crimes are hidden therein. **Prostitutes** <note>original: *Prostitute*</note> are harlots, named from "presiding" <note>original: *presidendo*</note> in brothels or in vaults. **Concubine** <note>original: *Peller*</note> is properly so called by the Greeks, and by the Latins is called a bedfellow. It is named from "deception" <note>original: *fallacia*</note>, that is, craftiness under deceit or a lie. **Procurve** is as if "curved for a long way" <note>original: *pro longum curvum*</note>. **Fearful** <note>original: *Pavidus*</note> is one whom a trembling of the mind agitates; for he has a pulsing of the heart and a movement of the heart. For "to fear" <note>original: *pavere*</note> is to strike. From this also comes "pavement" <note>original: *pavimentum*</note>. **Rocks** <note>original: *Petre*</note> and crags are named from the hardness of stones <note>original: *saxorum*</note>. **Pusillanimous** is from a "tiny soul" <note>original: *pusillo animo*</note>. **Petulant** is named from "seeking out" <note>original: *appetendo*</note>. Whence we also call harlots petulant. **Produced** is as if "led forth" <note>original: *porro ductus*</note>. **Small** <note>original: *Pisinnus*</note> is named from a "little boy" <note>original: *pusione*</note>. <margin>pelican</margin> **Pelican** is a holy man devoted to solitude.

### **Questor**
named from "seeking" <note>original: *querendo*</note>, as if a "seeker" <note>original: *quesitor*</note>.
**Profitable** <note>original: *Questuosus*</note>, **Complaining** <note>original: *Querimoniosus*</note>. **Quarrelsome** <note>original: *Querulus*</note>,
because he brings a complaint <note>original: *querelam*</note>. **Quiet** is one who is
himself secure in his mind, touching no one.

### **Religious**
Cicero says he is named from "re-reading" <note>original: *relegendo*</note>,
one who treats again and as if re-reads those things which pertain to divine worship. These were called **religious** from re-reading, just as from "electing" <note>original: *eligendo*</note> come "choosers" <note>original: *eligentes*</note>, from "loving" <note>original: *diligendo*</note> come "diligent ones" <note>original: *diligentes*</note>, and from "understanding" <note>original: *intelligendo*</note> come "intelligent ones" <note>original: *intelligentes*</note>. **Reasoning** <note>original: *Ratiocinatio*</note>: a great man is so called because he can give a reason <note>original: *rationem*</note> for all things which are known to be marvelous. **Retractor** is a re-finder. For to "retract" <note>original: *retractare*</note> is to repeat what you had omitted. **Coming to one's senses** <note>original: *Resipiscens*</note> because one recovers the mind as if after madness, or because one recovers wisdom <note>original: *sapere*</note> which he had ceased to have. For he chastises himself for his madness and strengthens his soul toward living rightly, taking care lest he fall again. **Sudden** <note>original: *Repentinus*</note> is from "suddenly" <note>original: *repente*</note>. "Suddenly" can be both an adverb and a noun. **Robust** means strong, powerful, named from the strength <note>original: *robore*</note> of the oak tree. **Rapid** means swift of feet. **Ravisher** <note>original: *Rapto*</note>, because he is a corrupter. Hence also a **ravished woman** <note>original: *rapta*</note>, because she has been corrupted. **Defendant** <note>original: *Reus*</note> is named from the "matter" <note>original: *re*</note> for which he is liable; and "guilt" <note>original: *reatus*</note> is named from the defendant. One was first called a "defendant of majesty" <note>original: *reus maiestatis*</note> who had done something against the republic or had conspired with enemies. He was called a "defendant of majesty" because it is a greater <note>original: *maius*</note> thing to harm the fatherland than a single citizen. Afterwards, however, those were also called "defendants of majesty" who were seen to have acted against the majesty of the prince, or who brought useless laws

<column-break/>

to the republic, or abolished useful ones. **Snarling** <note>original: *Rirosus*</note> is named from a dog's "grin" <note>original: *rictu*</note>. For he is always ready to contradict, delights in strife, and provokes a challenger. **Rustic** is one who works the "countryside" <note>original: *rus*</note>, that is, the land.

### **Wise**
<note>original: *Sapiens*</note> is named from "flavor" <note>original: *sapore*</note>, because just as the taste is suited to the discretion of the flavor of foods, so the wise man is suited to the discernment of things and causes, because he discerns each thing and perceives the truth by sense. The opposite is the **foolish** <note>original: *insipiens*</note>, who is without flavor, nor of any discretion or sense. **Studious** is as if curious in "study" <note>original: *studio*</note>. **Holy** <note>original: *Sanctus*</note> is named from an ancient custom, because those who wished to be purified were touched by the blood of a "victim" <note>original: *hostie*</note>, and from this they received the name of holy. **Sincere** is as if without corruption. The opposite is **insincere**, tainted and corrupt. **Supreme** is the highest, from that which stands above. Whence we also say "supreme father." **Sweet** <note>original: *Suavis*</note>. **Sublime** is named from the height of honor. For "sublime" is properly said of that which is on high, as in "bearing himself sublime to the stars of heaven." **Beautiful** <note>original: *Speciosus*</note> is from "appearance" <note>original: *specie*</note> or from sight; likewise "handsome" <note>original: *formosus*</note> is from "form" <note>original: *forma*</note>. **Skilled** <note>original: *Solers*</note> means one who is anxious in art and useful. For among the ancients, one was called skilled who was instructed in every good art. Terence says: "I will give a skilled youth." **Superstitious**, Cicero says, is the name given to those who prayed and sacrificed all day so that their children might be "survivors" <note>original: *superstites*</note>. **Solicitous** <note>original: *Sollicitus*</note> because he is skilled <note>original: *solers*</note> and quick <note>original: *citus*</note> and restless. **Diligent** <note>original: *Sedulus*</note> is a familiar word of Terence; this is "without guile" <note>original: *sine dolo*</note>. Otherwise it means assiduous. **Companions** <note>original: *Sodales*</note> are so called because they were accustomed to come together for a "contribution" <note>original: *symbolum*</note>, as if persuading; otherwise companions are those who "sit together" <note>original: *simul sedeant*</note>. **Partners** <note>original: *Socij*</note> are so called because of a fellowship of danger or work, as if remaining in "one boot" <note>original: *vna caliga*</note> and in one footprint. **Stupid** <note>original: *Stultus*</note> is one with a dull heart, as someone said: "I confess myself to be stupid, but I do not think I am a fool," that is, with blunt senses indeed, but not with none. A stupid person is one who is not moved by injury through numbness; for he bears an insult and is neither avenged, nor is he moved to pain by any ignominy. **Slothful** <note>original: *Segnis*</note> is "without fire" <note>original: *sine igne*</note>, lacking talent. For "se" signifies "without," as "diligent" <note>original: *sedulus*</note> is without guile. **Secure** is as if "without care" <note>original: *sine cura*</note>, that is, cold, which we take as useless. **Dazed** <note>original: *Stupidus*</note> is one who is frequently stunned. **Proud** <note>original: *Superbus*</note> is so called because he wants to seem "above" <note>original: *super*</note> what he is. For he who wants to go beyond what he is, is proud. **Whisperer** <note>original: *Susurro*</note> is named from the sound of speech, because he does not speak in anyone's face but in the ear, disparaging another. **Seditious** is one who makes a dissension of minds and begets discords, which the Greeks call "separation" <note>original: *diastasin*</note>. **Severe** is as if "sufficiently true" <note>original: *satis verus*</note>; for he holds justice without pity. **Simulator** is named from a "likeness" <note>original: *simulacro*</note>. For he bears the likeness of that which he himself is not. **Persuader** <note>original: *Suasor*</note> is a deceiver, that is, drawing someone into his own lot. **Scrupulous** is of a minute and rough mind. For a **scruple** <note>original: *scrupo*</note> is a harder grain of sand. **Sacrilegious** is named from this, that he "gathers sacred things" <note>original: *sacra legit*</note>, that is, he steals them. **Assassin** <note>original: *Sicarius*</note> is the name for one who is armed with weapons to commit a crime. For a **dagger** <note>original: *sica*</note> is a sword, named from "cutting" <note>original: *secando*</note>. **Sinister** <note>original: *Scevus*</note> is left-handed and perverse, that is, from perversity. For he is of a very bad and cruel mind. **Stage-actor** <note>original: *Scenicus*</note> is one who acts in a theater. For the theater is a "scene" <note>original: *scena*</note>. **Prostitutes** <note>original: *Scorta*</note> were called "Scythians" by the Greeks, who rub "skins" <note>original: *pelles*</note>, by which corruption occurs. **Filthy** <note>original: *Spurcus*</note> because he is impure. **Wicked** <note>original: *Scelerosus*</note> from crimes...

Isidore uses "folk etymologies" to connect moral qualities to physical actions or root words, such as linking wisdom to the sense of taste.</summary>
