<meta>This page concludes Book X of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies, which functions as a dictionary of human types and character traits. It then transitions into the opening of Book XI, "On Man and His Parts," where Isidore explores the origins of the word "man," the nature of the soul, and the anatomical design that distinguishes humans from animals.</meta>

...full. Like a stony or sandy place. A **wicked person** <note>original: *scelerosus*</note> is more than a **criminal** <note>original: *sceleratus*</note>. **Sower** <note>original: *Sator*</note>: a planter, or a father from his seed. A **buffoon** <note>original: *Scurra*</note> is one who is accustomed to follow someone for the sake of food; it is certain they are named from "following" <note>original: *sequendo*</note>. Likewise, an **attendant** <note>original: *assecla*</note> is from following. An **attendant** <note>original: *Satelles*</note> is one who stays close to another, or named from "guarding the side" <note>original: *lateris custodia*</note>. **Substituted** <note>original: *Suffectus*</note> is one put in the place of another, as if "made under" <note>original: *suffactus*</note>. Hence we also call a **suffect consul** <note>A consul elected to finish the term of one who died or resigned.</note> one who is substituted for another. **Second** <note>original: *Secundus*</note> is from "following" <note>original: *sequendo*</note>; the word is drawn from the "footmen" <note>original: *pedisequis*</note> who follow. Hence "second fortune" is also mentioned, which is "according to us," that is, near us. From this also "favorable things" <note>original: *res secundae*</note>, that is, prosperous. Moreover, "favorable" things are named from following. **Stipulation** <note>original: *Stipulatio*</note>: a promise. For to stipulate is to promise, from the words of legal experts who also called something firm "stipulum." **Healthy** <note>original: *Sanus*</note> is from "blood" <note>original: *sanguine*</note>, because such a person is without paleness. **Safe** <note>original: *Sospes*</note>, **health** <note>original: *salus*</note>, **guest** <note>original: *hospes*</note>. **Health** is thought to have taken its name from "salt" <note>original: *sale*</note>. **Subtle** <note>original: *Subtilis*</note> is named from "thinning out." A **mediator** <note>original: *Sequester*</note> is one who intervenes as a middle party between contenders; among the Greeks he is called an *homelos* <note>original: *omelus*; likely referring to a common or impartial person</note>, with whom pledges are usually deposited. This name is made from "following" <note>original: *obsequendo*</note> because both parties follow the faith of the one who was chosen. **Sessile** <note>original: *Sessilis*</note>: one who does not seem to stand but to "sit" <note>original: *sedere*</note>. **Deaf** <note>original: *Surdus*</note> is from the "filth" <note>original: *sordibus*</note> of moisture collected in the ear; although the name may happen from many causes, the sufferer nevertheless retains the name from the aforementioned defect. **Dry** <note>original: *Siccus*</note> is one who is "sucked out" <note>original: *exsucatus*</note>, or by antiphrasis <note>A figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its meaning.</note> because he is "without light" <note>original: *sine luco*</note>. **Buried** <note>original: *Sepultus*</note> is so called because he is without "palpitation" or without "pulse," that is, without motion. **To perceive** <note>original: *Sagio*</note> is named from "raising up." A **shoemaker** <note>original: *Sutor*</note> is named from "sewing" <note>original: *suendis*</note> skins. A **swineherd** <note>original: *Subulcus*</note> is a shepherd of pigs, just as a **cowherd** <note>original: *bubulcus*</note> is from the care of oxen.

**Guardian** <note>original: *Tutor*</note>: one who "protects" <note>original: *tuetur*</note> a ward; that is, watches over him. Concerning this, it is said in common custom: "Why do you advise me? My guardian and my teacher were buried long ago." **Witnesses** <note>original: *Testes*</note> are those who are usually present for a "testament" <note>a will</note>, just as **signers** <note>original: *signatores*</note> are those who sign a testament. **Terricus** is a very rough mountain in the Sabine territory. Hence we call sad or harsh men *terricos*. **Taciturn** <note>original: *Taciturnus*</note> is one who is "long-lasting" <note>original: *diuturnus*</note> in "silence" <note>original: *tacendo*</note>. **Weighed** <note>original: *Trutinata*</note>: examined; the judgment hanging straight like a scale, by a correct metaphor from the "balance" <note>original: *trutina*</note>, which is a double-pan scale for weights. **Sad** <note>original: *Tristis*</note>. **Tenacious** <note>original: *Tenax*</note>: one greedy for coins, because he "holds" <note>original: *teneat*</note> them; sometimes also "stubborn." **Truculent** <note>original: *Truculentus*</note>: grim and terrible, because he has a "grim face" <note>original: *toruo vultu*</note> or a "turbulent appearance," like a "grim lioness," or as we see those standing by "lest they look with a grim eye." **Turbid** <note>original: *Turbidus*</note>: terrible. **Foul** <note>original: *Teter*</note> is from a dark and "gloomy" <note>original: *tenebrosa*</note> life. **Most foul** <note>original: *Teterrimus*</note>. For the ancients used *tetram* for "fierce" <note>original: *feram*</note>, as Ennius says: "the foul elephants." **Terrible** <note>original: *Terribilis*</note>: one who has fear or is feared. A **shuffler** <note>original: *Tergiuersator*</note> is one who turns his "back" <note>original: *tergum*</note> this way and that, and it is not easily understood what kind of person he is. **Intoxicated** <note>original: *Temulentus*</note> is named from *temetum*, that is, wine. **Timid** <note>original: *Timidus*</note> is one who fears for a long time; from "blood" <note>original: *sanguine*</note>, for fear freezes the blood, which when constrained produces fear. **Base** <note>original: *Turpis*</note> is one who is "unshapely" <note>original: *informis*</note> or sluggish.

**Force** <note>original: *Vis*</note> is from "virtue" <note>original: *virtute*</note>. **Useful** <note>original: *Utilis*</note> is from "using" <note>original: *utendo*</note> his own things well, or one who can use something well, just as **teachable** <note>original: *docilis*</note> is one who can be taught. **True** <note>original: *Verus*</note> is from "truth" <note>original: *veritate*</note>. Hence also "verified." Truth is greater than the true, for truth is not from the true, but the true descends from truth. **Veridical** <note>original: *Veridicus*</note> is one who speaks the truth, or asserts the truth. **Modest** <note>original: *Verecundus*</note> is one who blushes at a "true deed" <note>original: *verus factum*</note>. **Green** <note>original: *Viridis*</note> is full of "force" <note>original: *vi*</note> or sap, as if "raw with force" <note>original: *vi rudis*</note>. **Charming** <note>original: *Venustus*</note>: beautiful, from "veins" <note>original: *venis*</note>, that is, from blood. **Living**

<column-break/>

that is, alive. **Various** <note>original: *Varius*</note> is as if "not of one way" <note>original: *non unius viae*</note>; from this come uncertain and mixed opinions. **Shifty** <note>original: *Versutus*</note>: because his mind "turns" <note>original: *vertitur*</note> easily in any act toward any fraud. Hence a contorted opinion is also called "shifty." Plautus says: "Shifty is he who is like a potter's wheel." **Vile** <note>original: *Vilis*</note> is from "vileness"; for he has no refinement. **Turncoat** <note>original: *Versipellis*</note>: because he turns his face or mind into different things. From this also "shifty" or "shrewd." **Violent** <note>original: *Violentus*</note>: because he applies "force" <note>original: *vim*</note>. **Evil-hearted** <note>original: *Veors*</note>: of a bad heart or bad conscience. **Wandering** <note>original: *Vagus*</note>: because he is "without a way" <note>original: *sine via*</note>. **Mad** <note>original: *Vecos*</note> draws its etymology from Venus <note>Isidore implies the madness of passion</note>. Likewise **vain** <note>original: *vanus*</note>: empty, false, because it vanishes without memory. **Swift** <note>original: *Velox*</note>: one who drinks enough but is difficult to intoxicate. **Carried** <note>original: *Veratus*</note> that is, "ported," from that which is *veho*, *vero*, *vecto*, as *verrasse* would be to have carried. **Poisoner** <note>original: *Veneficus*</note>: because he prepared, provided, or sold "poison" <note>original: *venenum*</note> for the sake of death. **Carrier** <note>original: *Vector*</note> is as if "one who carries" <note>original: *vebitor*</note>. A carrier is both one who carries and one who is carried. **Hunter** <note>original: *Venator*</note> is as if "a spear-man" <note>original: *venabulator*</note>; namely from "hunting," because he pursues beasts. There are four duties of hunters: trackers, investigators, drivers <note>original: *alatores*</note>, and cutters.

### Here begins the eleventh book
#### Chapter 1: On man and his parts.

**Nature** <note>original: *Natura*</note> is named from this: that she makes something "to be born" <note>original: *nasci*</note>. For she is the sign and the power of making. Some have said that she is God, by whom all things were created and are seen. **Kind** <note>original: *Genus*</note> is named from "begetting" <note>original: *gignendo*</note>, whose name is derived from the "earth" <note>original: *terra*</note> from which all things are begotten. For in Greek, the earth is called *Ge*. **Life** <note>original: *Vita*</note> is named on account of "vigor," or because it holds the "force" <note>original: *vim*</note> of being born and growing. Hence even trees are said to have life, because they are begotten and grow. **Man** <note>original: *Homo*</note> is so named because he was made from the "soil" <note>original: *humo*</note>, just as it says in Genesis:
> And God created man from the mud of the earth.

But it is pronounced loosely: the "whole man" is from both substances, that is, from the society of soul and body. For properly, "man" is from the "soil." The Greeks, however, called man *anthropos*, because he "looks upward," raised from the soil to the contemplation of his Maker. This the poet Ovid describes when he says:
> While other animals look down toward the earth, He gave to man a sublime face, and ordered him to see the sky, and to lift his upright countenance to the stars.

He who, being upright, looks at the sky for this reason: that he may seek God, not that he should intend for the earth like the cattle, whom nature made "prone" <note>looking downward</note> and obedient to the belly. Moreover, man is double: the **inner** and the **outer**. The inner man is the **soul**; the outer man is the **body**. The **soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note>, however, took its name from the "winds" <note>original: *ventis*</note>, because it is like wind. Hence also in Greek wind is called *anemos*. Because we seem to live by drawing in air through the mouth, this is most clearly a mistake, because the soul is begotten long before air can be conceived by the mouth, since it already lives in the mother's womb. Therefore, the soul is not air, as some have thought who could not imagine its incorporeal nature. The Evangelist announces that the **spirit** is the same as the soul, saying:
> I have the power to lay down my soul, and again I have the power to take it up.

Concerning this, the soul of the Lord itself is mentioned at the time of the Passion; the Evangelist brought it forth thus, saying:
> And with his head bowed, he gave up his spirit.

For what is "to give up the spirit" if not to lay down the soul?

<meta>This page continues the transition into Book XI, "On Man and His Parts." Having previously discussed the name "man," Isidore now delves into the metaphysical and physical components that constitute a human being: the soul, the mind, the body, and the sensory organs.</meta>

# Book XI

The **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note> is so called because it lives. The **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note> is named either for its spiritual nature or because it breathes <note>original: *spiret*</note> within the body. Likewise, the **intellect** <note>original: *animus*</note> is the same as the soul, but the soul pertains to life, while the intellect pertains to counsel. Hence, philosophers say that life remains even without the intellect, and the soul endures without the mind; thus we have the "mindless" <note>original: *amentes*</note>. For the **mind** <note>original: *mens*</note> is so named so that it may know, and the **intellect** <note>original: *animus*</note> so that it may will. The **mind** <note>original: *mens*</note> is called such because it stands out <note>original: *emineat*</note> in the soul, or because it remembers <note>original: *meminit*</note>. Hence, those who are forgetful are called "mindless" <note>original: *amentes*</note>. It is called the mind not because it is the whole soul, but because it is that which excels in the soul, acting as its head or eye. For this reason, man himself is said to be the "image of God" according to his mind. However, all these things are joined to the soul so that it remains one thing. For the soul has received various names according to its functions. For **memory** is also the mind, which is why the forgetful are called mindless.

Thus, while it gives life to the body, it is the **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note>. While it wills, it is the **intellect** <note>original: *animus*</note>. While it knows, it is the **mind** <note>original: *mens*</note>. While it recollects, it is **memory**. While it judges rightly, it is **reason**. While it breathes, it is the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note>. While it feels something, it is **sense**. For the intellect is called "sense" according to the things it feels; from this, the word **opinion** <note>original: *sententia*</note> received its name. The **body** <note>original: *corpus*</note> is so called because, being corrupted, it perishes; for it is soluble and mortal, and must eventually be dissolved. **Flesh** <note>original: *caro*</note>, however, is named from "creating" <note>original: *creando*</note>. For the **seed** of the male is an "increase" <note>original: *crementum*</note>, from which the bodies of animals and men are conceived. From this, parents are called **creators**. Flesh is composed of four elements: earth is in the flesh, air in the breath, moisture in the blood, and fire in the vital heat. For each of the elements has its own part in us; when the structure is dissolved, they return what they owe. **Flesh** and **body**, however, signify different things. There is always body in flesh, but not always flesh in a body. For flesh is that which lives, and it is also a body. A body that does not live is not flesh. For a body is called such either because it is dead after life, or it was created without life. Sometimes there is a body with life that is not flesh, such as grass or wood.

The **senses of the body** are five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Of these, two are opened and closed, while two are always open. They are called "senses" because through them the soul agitates the whole body with the vigor of feeling in a very subtle way. Hence they are also called "presences" <note>original: *praesentia*</note> because they are "at the senses" <note>original: *prae sensibus*</note>, just as things "before the eyes" <note>original: *prae oculis*</note> are placed before the eyes. **Sight** <note>original: *visus*</note> is what philosophers call the "glassy humor." Some assert that sight occurs either from external ethereal light, or from an internal shining spirit coming from the brain through thin veins, penetrating the membranes and going out into the air, and then giving sight through the mixing of similar matter. Sight is so named because it is more alive <note>original: *vivatior*</note> than the other senses, more excellent, or swifter; it flourishes more as memory does among the other duties of the mind. For it is closer to the brain, from which everything flows. From this it happens that we say we "see" things that pertain to other senses, as when we say: "See how it sounds," or "See how it tastes," and so on. **Hearing** <note>original: *auditus*</note> is named because it "drinks in" <note>original: *hauriat*</note> voices; that is, it receives sounds from the struck air. **Smell** <note>original: *odoratus*</note> is as if attracted by the "odor of air" <note>original: *aeris odore*</note>; for it feels the air it touches. Likewise, **olfaction** is named because it is affected by odors. **Taste** <note>original: *gustus*</note> is named from the throat <note>original: *gutture*</note>. **Touch** <note>original: *tactus*</note> because it handles <note>original: *pertrectet*</note> and touches, and spreads the vigor of sense through all the members. For by touch we prove whatever we cannot judge by the other senses. There are two kinds of touch: for either that which strikes comes from without,

<column-break/>

or it arises within the body itself. To each sense its own nature is given. For what is to be seen, the eye captures; what is to be heard, the ears; soft and hard things are estimated by touch; flavor by taste; and odor is drawn in by the nostrils.

The first part of the body is the **head** <note>original: *caput*</note>; this name was given to it because all the senses and nerves take their beginning from there, and from it arises every cause of flourishing. For all the senses appear there. Hence, it acts as a kind of "mask" or persona for the soul itself, which provides counsel for the body. The **crown** <note>original: *vertex*</note> is that part where the hairs of the head gather and where the hair turns; hence it is so named. The **skull** <note>original: *calvaria*</note> is named from the "bald bones" <note>original: *ossibus caluis*</note>; it is pronounced as a deficiency and in the neutral gender. The **occiput** <note>original: *occipitiū*</note> is the back part of the head, as if "against the head-piece" <note>original: *contra capitium*</note>, or because it is at the back of the head. **Hairs** <note>original: *capilli*</note> are named as if they were "hairs of the head" <note>original: *capitis pili*</note>. They are made to provide beauty, to fortify the brain against the cold, and to defend it from the sun. **Hairs** <note>original: *pili*</note> are named from the skin <note>original: *pelle*</note> from which they proceed, just as a pestle <note>original: *pilum*</note> is named from the mortar <note>original: *pila*</note> where pigment is crushed. **Chesary locks** <note>original: *cesaries*</note> are named from "cutting" <note>original: *cedendo*</note>, and therefore this term is only for men. For it is becoming for a man to be shorn, but it is not becoming for a woman. **Locks** <note>original: *comae*</note> are specifically hair that is not cut, and it is a Greek word. For the Greeks call locks *caimos* from "cutting." Hence they also say *cirin* for "to shear," from which **curls** <note>original: *cirri*</note> are named, which the same Greeks also call *mallone*. **Tresses** <note>original: *crines*</note> specifically belong to women. They are called *crines* because they are distinguished by ribbons <note>original: *vittis*</note>. Hence they are also called *discriminalia* <note>hair-dividers or hairpins</note>, by which the divided hairs are bound back. The **temples** <note>original: *tempora*</note> are those parts that lie beneath the skull on the right and left. They are so named because they move; by that very mobility they are changed at certain intervals, as if by "times" <note>original: *temporibus*</note>.

The **face** <note>original: *facies*</note> is named from the "likeness" <note>original: *effigie*</note>; for there the entire figure of a man is made and the recognition of each person. The **countenance** <note>original: *vultus*</note>, however, is so named because through it the **will** <note>original: *voluntas*</note> of the soul is shown; for it is changed into various movements according to the will. Hence they differ from each other: for "face" is simply used for the natural appearance of each person, while "countenance" signifies the qualities of the minds. The **forehead** <note>original: *frons*</note> is named from the "openings" <note>original: *foraminibus*</note> of the eyes; it is a certain image of the soul, expressing the movement of the mind by its appearance, whether it is joyful or sad. The **eyes** <note>original: *oculi*</note> are so called either because the coverings of the eyelashes hide <note>original: *occultant*</note> them, lest they be hurt by any offense of an incident injury, or because they have a "hidden light" <note>original: *lumen occultum*</note>, that is, a secret light placed within. These exist as the closest to the soul among all the senses. For in the eyes is every indication of the mind; hence the perturbation or cheerfulness of the soul appears in the eyes. The eyes are also called **lights** <note>original: *lumina*</note>. They are called lights because light flows from them, or because they hold a closed light from their beginning, or because they reflect the light received from without for the purpose of sight. The **pupil** <note>original: *pupilla*</note> is the middle point of the eye in which the power of seeing resides; because small images <note>original: *parvae imagines*</note> are seen by us there, they are therefore called pupils. For small children are called *pupilli*. Most people call this the pupil. It is also called *pupilla* because it is pure and unpolluted, as young girls <note>original: *puellae*</note> are. Physicians say that these same pupils that we see in the eyes are absent three days before death; when they are not seen, despair of life is certain. The **circle** <note>the iris</note> by which the white parts of the eye are separated from the pupil with a distinct blackness is called the **crown**...

--- Page 121 ---
<meta>This page continues Isidore’s anatomical survey from Book XI of the Etymologies. Having discussed the soul and the mind on the previous page, he now moves to the physical structure of the head, focusing on the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and throat, before descending to the neck and shoulders. He relies heavily on the "etymological" method—explaining the nature of a thing through the perceived origin of its name.</meta>

...[the author] says that by its roundness it adorns the circuit of the pupil. Some call the very corners <note>original: *vertices*</note> of the eyes **rollers** <note>original: *volui*</note> because of their likeness to rollers. The **eyelids** <note>original: *palpebrae*</note> are the folds of the eyes, named from "palpitation" <note>original: *palpitatio*</note> because they are always moving. For they constantly run together so that by their steady motion they may refresh the sight. They are fortified with a "rampart" of hairs <note>the eyelashes</note> so that even when the eyes are open, anything that might fall in is repelled; and when they close in sleep, the eyes may rest as if hidden under a covering. At the edge of the eyelids, where they touch when closed, hairs stand out in a preserved order, providing a defense for the eyes. This prevents injuries from easily rushing in and causing harm; it wards off the touch of dust or any thicker material, and by "cutting" the very air, it makes the vision thin and clear.

Some think **tears** <note>original: *lachrymae*</note> are named from the "laceration of the mind" <note>original: *laceratione mentis*</note>; others think they are named because the Greeks call them *dakrua* <note>original: *daffiria* (OCR error for *dakrua*)</note>. The **eyelashes** <note>original: *cilia*</note> are the coverings by which the eyes are sheltered; they are called *cilia* because they "conceal" <note>original: *celent*</note> the eyes and keep them in safe custody. The **eyebrows** <note>original: *supercilia*</note> are so named because they are placed "above the eyelashes" <note>original: *superposita sunt ciliis*</note>; they are clothed with hair for this reason: to provide a defense for the eyes and to divert sweat flowing down from the head. The **space between the eyebrows** <note>original: *intercilium*</note> is that middle area between the brows which is without hair.

The **cheeks** <note>original: *genae*</note> are the lower parts of the eyes where the beard begins. For in Greek, a jaw or chin is called *genys*. Hence they are called *genae* because the beard begins to be "born" <note>original: *gigni*</note> there. The **cheekbones** <note>original: *malae*</note> are the prominent parts beneath the eyes, positioned for their protection. They are called *malae* either because they stand out in a round shape like "apples" <note>original: *mela* in Greek</note>, or because they sit above the jaws. The **jaws** <note>original: *maxillae*</note> are named as a diminutive of *malae*, just as a small stake <note>original: *paxillus*</note> comes from a pole <note>original: *palus*</note>. The **mandibles** <note>original: *mandibulae*</note> are parts of the jaws, from which the name is derived <note>likely from *mandere*, to chew</note>. The ancients called it the **beard** <note>original: *barba*</note> because it belongs to men <note>original: *viri*</note>, not women.

The name for the **ears** <note>original: *aures*</note> was given from the "drinking in" of voices <note>original: *vocibus hauriendis*</note>, as Virgil says:
> And he drank in the voice with these ears.
Or perhaps because the Greeks call the voice itself *auden*, from "hearing" <note>original: *auditu*</note>. By a change of letters, ears (*aures*) were called as if they were *audes*. For the voice, repelled through their winding passages, creates the sound by which they receive the sense of hearing. The **earlobe** <note>original: *pinnula*</note> is the highest part of the ear, named from its "sharpness" <note>original: *acumine*</note>. For the ancients called anything sharp *pinnum*, which is where the "double-edged axe" <note>original: *bipennis*</note> gets its name.

**Nostrils** <note>original: *nares*</note> are so named because through them the flow of odors or breath does not cease <note>original: *non desinit manare*</note>, or because they "warn" <note>original: *admonent*</note> us of odors so that we may recognize and know them. Hence, conversely, the ignorant and unrefined are called "un-scenting" <note>original: *in-sciti*</note>. For the ancients used "to scent" <note>original: *olfecisse*</note> to mean "to have known." Terence says:
> They had scented out <note>i.e., known</note> something before he took it.
The **nose** <note>original: *nasus*</note> is the straight part; the portion that is extended equally in length and roundness is called the **column**. Its tip is the **pear-tip** <note>original: *pyrula*</note>, from the shape of a pear fruit. The two parts on the right and left are the **little wings** <note>original: *pinnulae*</note> from their likeness to wings, and the middle is the **partition** <note>original: *interfinium*</note>.

The **mouth** <note>original: *os*</note> is so called because through it, as if through a "door" <note>original: *ostium*</note>, we send food in and cast spit out; or because food enters there and speech exits. The **lips** <note>original: *labia*</note> are named from "licking" <note>original: *lambendo*</note>. We call the upper one the *labium*, while the lower, because it is more prominent and thicker, is the *labrum*. Others say *labia* refers to men and *labra* to women. Varro thinks the name for the **tongue** <note>original: *lingua*</note> was given from "licking" <note>original: *lingendo*</note> food. Others say it is because it "binds" <note>original: *ligat*</note> words together through articulated sounds.

<column-break/>

For just as a plectrum strikes the strings, so the tongue strikes against the **teeth** and produces the vocal sound. The Greeks call teeth *odontes*, and the Latin name seems to be drawn from that. The front teeth are called **incisors** <note>original: *praecisores*</note> because they are the first to cut into whatever is taken. The following are called **canines** <note>original: *canini*</note>, of which there are two in the right jaw and two in the left. They are called canine because they resemble the teeth of dogs; a dog breaks bones with them just as a man does, and because the front teeth cannot cut through tough things, they pass them to the canines to be crushed. The common people call these **little columns** <note>original: *colomellos*</note> due to their length and roundness. The last are the **molars** <note>original: *molares*</note>, because they process and grind down what has been cut and broken by the front teeth; they "mill" <note>original: *molunt*</note> and gather the food into a mass, which is why they are called molars. The number of teeth is distinguished by age and sex. For there are more in men and fewer in women. The **gums** <note>original: *gingivae*</note> are named from the "begetting" <note>original: *gignendis*</note> of teeth. They were also made for the beauty of the teeth, lest they should appear naked and cause horror rather than being an ornament.

Our **palate** <note>original: *palatum*</note>, like the sky, is positioned high up, and thus the name *palatum* is derived from the "pole" <note>original: *polus*, the sky</note>. The Greeks have a similar word for the palate, calling it *ouranon* <note>heaven</note>, because through its concavity it bears a likeness to the heavens. The **throat** <note>original: *fauces*</note> is named from "pouring out" <note>original: *fundendis*</note> voices, or because we "speak" <note>original: *famur*</note> voices through them. The **arteries** <note>here referring to the windpipe</note> are so called either because air—that is, breath—is carried through them from the lungs, or because they retain the vital spirit in narrow and tight passages, whence they emit the sounds of the voice. These sounds would ring in only one way if the motion of the tongue did not create the distinctions of the voice.

In the Gallic language, they are called **toles**, which the common people call **tonsils** <note>original: *tussillas*</note> by diminutive, which are accustomed to swell in the throat. The **chin** <note>original: *mentum*</note> is so called because the mandibles "arise" <note>original: *oriantur*</note> from there, or because they are joined there. The **windpipe** <note>original: *gurgulio*</note> draws its name from the throat <note>original: *gutture*</note>; its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils, having a way by which the voice is transmitted to the tongue so that it can strike out words. Hence we also say "to chatter" <note>original: *garrire*</note>. The **gullet** <note>original: *rumen*</note> is the first part of the windpipe through which food and drink are swallowed. From this, animals that bring back and re-chew their food are said to "ruminate" <note>original: *ruminare*</note>. The **epiglottis** <note>original: *sublinguium*</note> is the lid of the windpipe, like a little tongue, which closes and covers the opening of the tongue.

The **neck** <note>original: *collum*</note> is so called because it is rigid and round like a "column" <note>original: *columna*</note>, carrying and sustaining the head as if it were a capital. Its front part is called the **throat** <note>original: *gula*</note> and the back is the **nape** <note>original: *cervix*</note>. It is called *cervix* because through that part the brain is directed toward the marrow of the spine, acting as the "way of the brain" <note>original: *cerebri via*</note>. The ancients used to speak of *cervices* only in the plural; Hortensius was the first to use the singular *cervicem*. However, *cervix* in the singular refers to the limb itself, whereas in the plural it often demonstrates "stubbornness" <note>original: *contumacia*</note>. Cicero says in the *Verrines*:
> You accuse the Praetor of breaking necks <note>original: *cervices*</note>.

The **shoulders** <note>original: *humeri*</note> are named to distinguish man from mute beasts; thus men are said to have *humeros*, while beasts have *armos* <note>forequarters</note>, for strictly speaking, *armi* belong to quadrupeds. The **armpit** <note>original: *ala*</note> is the back part of the top of the shoulder. The **arms** <note>original: *brachia*</note> are named from their "strength" <note>original: *fortitudine*</note>. For in Greek, *barys* means heavy and strong. In the arms are the cords of the **muscles** <note>original: *lacertorum*</note>, and the notable strength of the muscles exists there. These are the *tori*—that is, the muscles—and they are called *tori* because the flesh there seems "twisted" <note>original: *torta*</note>. The **elbow** <note>original: *cubitus*</note> is so called because we "lie down" <note>original: *cubamus*</note> on it to take food. The **forearm** <note>original: *ulna*</note>, according to some, is the extension of both hands; according to others, it is the elbow.

<summary>This page catalogs the anatomy of the human head, mouth, and neck, providing etymological explanations for terms like eyelashes, teeth, and shoulders. Isidore combines physical description with linguistic origins, often linking human anatomy to architectural terms like "columns" or "ramparts."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the anatomical survey from Isidore of Seville’s Book XI. Following the description of the head and neck, Isidore now moves down the body to describe the arms, hands, torso, and the skeletal structure of the back. He continues to use etymologies—often based on phonetic similarities rather than modern linguistics—to explain the function and nature of human body parts.</meta>

# Book XI

...which is more true; for in Greek the elbow is called *olenos* <note>original: *olenos*</note>.
The **armpits** <note>original: *alę*</note> are named from "wings" <note>original: *alae*</note>, because the movement of the arms begins there in the manner of wings. Some call them *ascellas* <note>little wings</note>, because from these the arms are "swung" <note>original: *cillentur*</note>, that is, they move. Hence the "little bones" <note>the jawbones</note> are called *ossicilla* from the fact that they "move" <note>original: *cillent*</note> the mouth. For *cillere* means to move. Some call these armpits "little goats" <note>original: *subhircos*</note> because in many men they give off the rank odor of he-goats <note>original: *hircos ferorem*</note>.

<margin>
Hands through common use.
The **right hand** is named from "giving" <note>original: *dando*</note>.
The **left** <note>original: *leua*</note> for "lifting" <note>original: *leuandum*</note>.
The **sinister** <note>original: *sinistra*</note> because it "allows" <note>original: *sinat*</note> things to be done.
</margin>
The **Hand** <note>original: *manus*</note> is so named because it is the "service" <note>original: *munus*</note> of the whole body. It dispenses; through it we receive and give. Figuratively, however, "hand" also refers to art or a craftsman; hence we call the price of labor the "hand-price" <note>original: *manus precium*</note>. The **Right hand** <note>original: *dextra*</note> is named from "giving" <note>original: *dando*</note>. For it gives the pledge of peace; it is used as a witness of faith and for greetings. And what is that saying in Tully <note>Cicero</note>: "I gave the public faith by order of the senate," that is, I gave my right hand. Whence the Apostle also says: "James and John gave me the right hands [of fellowship]," and so forth. The **Left** <note>original: *leua*</note> is so called because it is more fit for "lifting" <note>original: *leuandum*</note>. The **Sinister** <note>original: *sinistra*</note> however is named as if it were "without the right" <note>original: *sine dextra*</note>, or because it "allows" <note>original: *sinat*</note> things to be done. For from *sinendo* <note>allowing/permitting</note> the "sinister" is named. The **Palm** <note>original: *palma*</note> is the hand with fingers spread out, just as the **fist** <note>original: *pugnus*</note> is the hand contracted. The fist is named from the "handful" <note>original: *pugillo*</note>, just as the palm is named from the spread-out branches of a palm tree. The **Fingers** <note>original: *digiti*</note> are so named either because there are ten <note>original: *decem*</note> of them, or because they exist "decently" <note>original: *decenter*</note> joined. For they possess in themselves both a perfect number and a most decent order. The first is called the **Thumb** <note>original: *pollex*</note>, because it "prevails" <note>original: *polleat*</note> over the others in strength and power. The second is the **Index** and the "saluter" or "pointer," because with it we usually salute or point out something. The third is the **Shameless** <note>original: *impudicus*</note> finger, because very often an insulting mockery is expressed by it. The fourth is the **Ring-finger** <note>original: *anularis*</note>, because the ring is worn on it. It is also the "medical" finger, because doctors use it to gather ground-up eye-salves <note>original: *collyria*</note>. The fifth is the **Ear-finger** <note>original: *auricularis*</note>, because we scratch our ears with it. We call the **Nails** <note>original: *ungulas*</note> after the Greek, for they call them *onyches*. The **Trunk** <note>original: *truncus*</note> is the middle part of the body from the neck to the groin. Concerning which Egidius says: "the head is carried by the neck, the trunk is sustained by the hips, knees, and legs." The **Thorax** is what the Greeks call the front part of the trunk from the neck to the stomach, which we call the **Chest** <note>original: *archam*</note>, because in it there is a "secret" <note>original: *archanum*</note>, that is, a hidden thing that is "locked away" <note>original: *arcet*</note>. Whence both *archa* <note>chest/box</note> and *ara* <note>altar</note> are named as if for secret things; its prominent fleshy parts are called **breasts** <note>original: *mamillę*</note>. Between these, that bony part is called the **breastbone** <note>original: *pectus*</note>, while on the right and left are the **ribs**. The *pectus* is named because it is between the prominent parts of the breasts; whence we also say "comb" <note>original: *pectinem*</note> because it makes the hair "distinct" <note>original: *peros* - OCR error for *puros*?</note>. The **Breasts** <note>original: *mamillę*</note> are named because they are round like "apples" <note>original: *mala*</note>, used as a diminutive. **Nipples** <note>original: *papille*</note> are the tips of the breasts, which nursing infants grasp. They are called *papille* because infants "eat" <note>original: *pappant*</note> from them while they suck milk. Thus the *mamilla* is the whole protrusion of the breast, but the *papilla* is that small part from which the milk is drawn. The **Teats** <note>original: *ubera*</note> are named either because they are "fruitful" <note>original: *vberta*</note> with milk, or because they are "moist" <note>original: *vuida*</note>, full of the moisture of milk in the manner of grapes <note>original: *vuay*</note>. **Milk** <note>original: *lac*</note> draws the force of its name from its color, because it is a white liquid. For in Greek, *leucos* means white. Its nature is changed from blood. For after birth, if any blood has not yet been consumed by the nourishment of the womb, it flows by a natural passage into the breasts and, whitening by their power, takes on the quality of milk. **Skin** <note>original: *cutis*</note> is the name for the first layer in the body, because it is the first to suffer an "incision" <note>original: *incisione*</note> when placed over the body. For in Greek, *cutis*

<column-break/>

means "incision." The same is also called the **Hide** <note>original: *pellis*</note> because it "drives away" <note>original: *pellat*</note> external injuries by governing the body, and endures rains, winds, and the heat of the sun. The hide, when moved, stripped off, and worked, is then called **Leather** <note>original: *coriũ*</note>. Leather is named by derivation from "flesh" <note>original: *caro*</note> because the flesh is covered by it; this term is proper to brute animals. The **Pores** <note>original: *pozi*</note> of the body are named by a Greek word; in Latin they are properly called **breathing-holes** <note>original: *spiramenta*</note>, because through them the life-giving spirit is administered from the outside. **Fat** <note>original: *arvina*</note> is the grease adhering to the skin. **Flesh** <note>original: *pulpa*</note> is the meat without fat; it is named because it "palpitates" <note>original: *palpiter*</note>, for it often springs back; many also call this "glue" <note>original: *viscum*</note> because it is sticky. **Members** are the parts of the body. **Joints** <note>original: *artus*</note> are those things by which the members are joined together, named from "fitting tightly" <note>original: *artando*</note>. **Nerves** <note>original: *nerui*</note> are named by a Greek derivation, which they call *neura*. Others think they are called *nernos* in Latin because they adhere invisibly to the connections of the joints. It is most certain that the nerves make up the greatest substance of strength. For the denser they are, the more readily firmness increases. **Joints** <note>original: *artus*</note> are so called because, bound together by nerves, they are "tightened" <note>original: *artentur*</note>, that is, bound. Their diminutives are the **small joints** <note>original: *articuli*</note>. For we call the larger members *artus*, such as arms, and the smaller members *articuli*, such as fingers. **Compagines** <note>fastenings/structures</note> are the heads of the bones, so called because they are joined together by nerves as if by some glue. **Bones** <note>original: *ossa*</note> are the solid supports of the body. For in them all posture and strength subsists. Bones are named from "burning" <note>original: *vsto*</note>, because they used to be burned by the ancients, or as others think, from the "mouth" <note>original: *oze*</note> because they appear there. For everywhere else they are hidden, covered by flesh and viscera. **Marrow** <note>original: *medullę*</note> is so named because it "moistens" <note>original: *madefaciãt*</note> the bones. For it irrigates and comforts them. **Vertebrae** <note>original: *vertibula*</note> are the uppermost parts of the bones, rounded into thicker nodes; they are so called because they "turn" <note>original: *vertanť*</note for the bending of the members. **Cartilage** <note>original: *cartillagines*</note> consists of soft bones without marrow; this type is found in the ears, the partition of the nostrils, and the ends of the ribs, as well as the coverings of bones that move. They are called cartilage because they lack the pain of "grinding" <note>original: *artritu*</note> when they are bent. Some think the **Ribs** <note>original: *costas*</note> are named because the internal organs are "guarded" <note>original: *custodiantur*</note> by them; the whole soft part of the belly is saved by being walled in. The **Side** <note>original: *latus*</note> is named because it is "hidden" <note>original: *latet*</note> when we are lying down. For the left is a part of the body, but the right side is more fit for movement, stronger than the left, and better accommodated for carrying a burden. Whence the left is named *leua* because it is more fit for "lifting" <note>original: *leuandũ*</note> and carrying something. For it carries the shield, the sword, the quiver, and other burdens, so that the right hand may be free for action. The **Back** <note>original: *dorsũ*</note> is from the neck to the kidneys. It is called *dorsum* because it is the "harder" <note>original: *durio2*</note> surface of the body, in the manner of a strong stone, both for carrying and for enduring. They are called **Terga** because on them we lie "supine" on the ground <note>original: *terra*</note>, which only man can do. For mute animals lie only on the belly or on the side; whence in animals they are called *terga* improperly. The **Shoulder blade** <note>original: *scapula*</note> is named from "climbing" <note>original: *scandendo*</note>. The **interscapilium** is the space between the shoulder blades, hence its name. The **shoulder-points** <note>original: *palę*</note> are the protruding members on the right and left of the back, named because we press them in wrestling, which the Greeks call *palin*. The **Spine** <note>original: *spina*</note> is the joint of the back, named because it has sharp "thorns" <note>original: *radiolos acutos*</note>. The joints of this are called **vertebrae** <note>original: *spondilia*</note>, apart from the part of the brain which is carried through them in a long tract to the other parts of the body. The **Sacred spine** <note>original: *sacra spina*</note> is the bottom-most part of the continuous spine, which the Greeks call *ironostoin*, because it is the first to be born when an infant is conceived; and therefore it is the first "sacrifice" <note>original: *hostia*</note>...

It highlights the medieval view of the body as a purposefully designed "ark" or "chest" containing vital secrets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s anatomical survey from Book XI of the Etymologies. Having previously discussed the upper body and arms, he now moves to the lower torso, reproductive organs, legs, feet, and finally the internal organs like the heart and lungs, explaining their names through a mix of physiological function and symbolic etymology.</meta>

XI 56

...was given by the pagans to their gods. For this reason, it is also called the **sacred spine** <note>original: *spina sacra*</note>. Varro says the **kidneys** <note>original: *renes*</note> are so named because "streams" <note>original: *rivi*</note> of foul fluid arise from them. For the veins and the marrow exude a thin liquid into the kidneys, which, once thinned again by the heat of lust, flows down from the kidneys. The **loins** <note>original: *lumbi*</note> are named for the "lewdness of lust" <note>original: *libidinis lasciviam*</note>, because in men the cause of physical pleasure resides in them, just as it resides in the navel for women. Hence, it is said to Job at the beginning of the Lord’s speech: "Gird up your loins like a man" <note>Job 38:3</note>, so that the preparation for resistance might be in that place where the usual opportunity for lust to dominate exists. The **navel** <note>original: *umbilicus*</note> is the central point of the body, named because it is the "boss of the flanks" <note>original: *umbus iliorum*</note>. From this also the name **boss** <note>original: *umbo*</note> is given to the place in the middle of a shield that hangs out. For the infant hangs from it in the womb, and is also nourished by it. Some say it is named in the Greek language because we "envelop ourselves" there; for behold, the flanks are said to "envelop" <note>original: *obvolvere*</note> it. The **buttocks** <note>original: *clunes*</note> are named because they are near the "lower part" <note>original: *colum*, likely referring to the colon or the "neck" of the bladder</note> which is a long cavity. The **haunches** <note>original: *nates*</note> are so named because we "lean" <note>original: *innitimur*</note> on them while we sit; hence the flesh in them is gathered into a mass, so that the bones do not ache under the pressing weight of the body. The **genitals** <note>original: *genitalia*</note> are parts of the body that, as the name itself teaches, received their title from "begetting offspring" <note>original: *gignendae sobolis*</note>, because through them one is procreated or begotten. These are also called the **shameful parts** <note>original: *pudenda*</note>, either for "modesty" <note>original: *verecundia*</note> or from the "pubic hair" <note>original: *pube*</note>, which is why garments cover them. They are also called "dishonorable" because they do not have that appearance of beauty like the members located in plain sight. Likewise, they are called the **member** <note>original: *veretrum*, the penis</note> because it belongs only to the male <note>original: *viri*</note>, or because "fluid" <note>original: *virus*</note> is emitted from it; for *virus* properly refers to the fluid flowing from the nature of a man. The **testicles** <note>original: *testiculi*</note> are named as a diminutive of "witnesses" <note>original: *testibus*</note>, whose number begins at two. These provide the seed to the "reed" <note>the penis</note>, which they receive from the marrow of the spine, or the kidneys, or the loins, for the sake of procreation. The **scrotum** <note>original: *viscus*</note> is the skin in which the testicles are contained. The **posterior parts** are so called because they are "behind" <note>original: *retro*</note> or turned away from the face, so that while we are purging our bowels, we do not defile our sight. The **anus** is named from this, because through it things "pass" <note>original: *meant*</note>, that is, they discharge dung. The **thighs** <note>original: *femora*</note> are named because in that part the male sex is "distinguished from the female" <note>original: *a femina sexus viri discrepet*</note>. They extend from the groin down to the knees. The **inner thighs** <note>original: *femina*</note>, by a derivation of the word, are the parts by which we adhere to the backs of horses when riding. Hence, it was once said that warriors in battle "lost their horses from under their thighs." The **hips** <note>original: *loxe*</note> are, as it were, "joined axes" <note>original: *coniuncte axes*</note>. For in them the thighs move, and their hollows are called **vertebrae** because the heads of the thighs "turn" <note>original: *vertunt*</note> in them. The **hamstrings** <note>original: *suffragines*</note> are so named because they "break under" <note>original: *subfranguntur*</note>, that is, they bend downward, not upward like the arms. The **knees** <note>original: *genua*</note> are the joints of the thighs and shins, and are called *genua* because in the womb they are "opposite the cheeks" <note>original: *genis opposita*</note>. For they cling to each other there, and are "kindred" to the eyes, which are the indicators of tears and mercy. For *genua* are named from *genae* <note>cheeks</note>. Finally, they say that a man is "folded up" as he is begotten and formed, so that the knees are held upward, by which the eyes are formed so that they may become hollow and recessed. Ennius says: "And we press the knees against the cheeks" <note>original: *Atque genua comprimit arra gena*</note>. This is why men, when they prostrate themselves at the knees of others, immediately weep. For nature wished them to be reminded of the maternal womb, where they sat as if in darkness before they came into the light. The **shins** <note>original: *crura*</note> are named because with them we "run" <note>original: *currimus*</note> or make our "step" <note>original: *gressum*</note>. They are below the knees down to the calves. The **shinbones** <note>original: *tibiæ*</note> are named as if they were "trumpets" <note>original: *tubae*</note>; for they are similar in both length and appearance. The **ankle** <note>original: *talus*</note> is named from *tolus* <note>a dome or round hill</note>, for a *tolus* is a protruding roundness. Hence also the...

<column-break/>

...summit of a round temple is called a *tholus*. The ankle, however, is below the shin, and below the ankle are the heels. The **feet** <note>original: *pedes*</note> obtained their name from a Greek etymology. For the Greeks call them *podas* <note>original: *podas*</note>, because with alternating movements they walk "fixed to the soil" <note>original: *solo fixi*</note>. The **soles** <note>original: *plantæ*</note> are named from "flatness" <note>original: *planitie*</note>, because they are not round as in quadrupeds—lest a two-legged man be unable to stand—but are formed flat and longer so they might make the body more stable. The *plantae* are the forward parts, which also consist of many bones. The **heel** <note>original: *calcis*</note> is the first part of the sole; the name is imposed from the "callus" <note>original: *callo*</note> with which we "tread" <note>original: *calcamus*</note> the earth. Hence also the **heel bone** <note>original: *calcaneus*</note>. The **sole** <note>original: *solum*</note> is the lower part of the foot, so called because with it we imprint "footprints" <note>original: *vestigia*</note> on the ground. But *solum* is also said of anything that sustains something else, as it is "solid"; hence the earth is called *solum* because it sustains all things, and the *solum* of the foot because it carries the whole mass of the body. We call **viscera** not only the intestines, but whatever is beneath the "hide" <note>original: *corium*</note>, from the "gristle" <note>original: *visco*</note> which is between the skin and the flesh. Likewise, the **vital organs** <note>original: *viscera vitalia*</note> are the places surrounding the heart, called *viscera* because life—that is, the soul—is contained there. Also, *viscera* are the "heads of the nerves" <note>nerve endings or origins</note>, joined by blood and nerves. The **muscles** <note>original: *lacerti* or *mures*</note> are so called because they are in the individual limbs just as the heart is in its place; they are rounded like a heart in the middle part, and are named after "similar animals" <note>mice</note> that hide under the earth. For from this, **muscles** <note>original: *musculi*</note> are named for their resemblance to **mice** <note>original: *muri*</note>. These same are also called *tori* <note>bulges/cords</note> because the viscera there seem "twisted" <note>original: *tozta/torta*</note>. The **heart** <note>original: *cor*</note> is derived from a Greek name, for they call it *kardia* <note>original: *cardian*</note>; or it is named from "care" <note>original: *cura*</note>. For in it all "solicitude" and the cause of "knowledge" remain. It is placed near the lungs for this reason: so that when "anger" flares up, it may be tempered by the moisture of the lungs. From here there are two **arteries**, of which the left has more blood and the right has more "spirit" <note>original: *spiritum*, breath or life-force</note>; hence we also examine the **pulse** in the right arm. The **precordia** are the places near the heart where "sensation" is perceived; they are called *precordia* because the beginning of the heart and "thought" is there. The **pulse** <note>original: *pulsus*</note> is so called because it "palpitates," by the evidence of which we understand either sickness or health. It has a double movement: either simple or composite. A simple pulse consists of a single leap. A composite one is that which, from many movements, exists as "disordered" and "uneven." These movements have certain intervals; they are called a **dactylic pulse** <note>rhythmic like a poetic foot</note> as long as they are without fault. However, if they are swifter, such as the "leaping gazelle" <note>original: *doxcadaçontes*, from Greek *dorkadizontes*</note> type, or slower, like the "creeping ant" <note>original: *mirmicicōtes*, from Greek *myrmekizontes*</note> type, they are signs of death. **Veins** <note>original: *venæ*</note> are so called because they are "ways" <note>original: *viæ*</note> of swimming blood and "streams" divided through the whole body by which all the members are irrigated. **Blood** <note>original: *sanguis*</note> took its name from a Greek etymology because it "enlivens" <note>original: *vegetetur*</note>, sustains, and lives. It is called *sanguis* while it is in the body, but when shed it is called **gore** <note>original: *cruor*</note>. For *cruor* is named because it "flows out" <note>original: *de-currit*</note> when shed, or because it "falls" <note>original: *corruat*</note> by flowing. Others interpret *cruor* as blood that is "corrupt" when emitted. Others call it *sanguis* because it is "sweet" <note>original: *suavis*</note>. Blood is not "complete" except in the young; for physicians say blood "diminishes" through age, which is why there is "trembling" in the elderly. Properly, however, blood is the "possession of the soul." This is why women are accustomed to "tear their cheeks" <note>lacerate their faces</note> in mourning. From this also, "purple garments" and "purple flowers" are offered to the dead. The **lung** <note>original: *pulmo*</note> draws its title from the Greek; for the Greeks call the lung *pleumon* <note>original: *pleumon*</note>, because it is the "fan of the heart," in which the *pneuma* <note>original: *pneuma*</note>, that is, the "spirit," resides, by which they are agitated and moved. From this also the lungs were named.

It highlights medieval medical theories regarding the heart as the center of emotion and the role of blood and "spirit" in the arteries.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Isidore of Seville completes his description of the lower torso (the loins and navel) and now turns to the internal organs—the lungs, liver, spleen, and digestive tract—before discussing the reproductive system, conception, and the physical differences between the sexes.</meta>

# Book XI

For in Greek, **spirit** <note>original: *pneuma*</note> is so called because by blowing and agitating it emits and receives air. From this, the **lungs** <note>original: *pulmones*</note> move and palpitate; they open themselves to take in breath and contract to eject it. It is, in fact, the organ of the body. The **liver** <note>original: *iecur*</note> has its name because fire <note>original: *ignis*</note> has its seat there, which flies up to the brain; from there it diffuses to the eyes and other senses and members. By its heat, it turns the juice drawn from food into blood, which it provides to each member for the purpose of feeding and nourishing. In the liver, however, resides pleasure and desire, according to those who dispute on physical matters. The **lobes** <note>original: *fibrae*</note> of the liver are the extremities, like the outermost parts of leaves on stalks, or like protruding tongues. These are called *fibrae* because among the pagans they were carried to the altars of Apollo <note>original: *Phoebus*</note> during sacrifices by the soothsayers, and when offered, they received responses regarding success. The **spleen** <note>original: *splen*</note> is named from "supplement" <note>original: *supplementum*</note>, being on the opposite side of the liver so that the space would not be empty. Some also think it was made for the sake of laughter. For with the spleen we laugh, with the **gall** <note>original: *fel*</note> we are angry, with the heart we are wise, and with the liver we love. When these four elements are consistent, the animal is healthy. The gall is so named because it is a small sac <note>original: *folliculum*</note> carrying the fluid called bile. The **stomach** <note>Isidore notes the Greek origin *stoma* meaning mouth</note> is called "mouth" in Greek because it is the door to the belly; it receives food and transmits it to the intestines. The **intestines** <note>original: *intestina*</note> are so called because they are contained in the interior part of the body; for this reason, they are arranged in long coils of circles so that they may digest the received food little by little and not be blocked by the supplied nourishment. The **omentum** <note>the fatty tissue covering the bowels</note> is the membrane that contains the greater part of the intestines, which the Greeks call the *epiploon*. The **diaphragm** <note>original: *disseptum*</note> is the internal partition that separates the belly and the rest of the intestines from the lungs or the heart. The **cecum** <note>original: *lecum*, the "blind" intestine</note> is so called because it is without an opening or exit; the Greeks call this the *typhlon enteron*. The **jejunum** <note>original: *ieiuna*</note> is the thin intestine, from which the word "fasting" <note>original: *ieiunium*</note> is derived. Now, the **belly** <note>original: *venter*</note>, the **paunch** <note>original: *alvus*</note>, and the **womb** <note>original: *uterus*</note> differ among themselves. The *venter* is that which digests the food it has received and is visible from the outside, extending from the chest to the groin; it is called *venter* because it transmits the nourishment of life through the whole body. The *alvus* is that which receives food and is accustomed to be purged. Sallust says: "He feigned that his *alvus* was being purged." It is called *alvus* because it "washes" <note>original: *abluat*</note>, that is, purges; for from it the filth of dung flows down. Only women have a **womb** <note>original: *uterus*</note>, in which they conceive, similar in shape to a small stalk. However, authors often use *uterus* for the belly of either sex, and not only poets but others as well. It is called *uterus* because it is double and divides itself into two parts from both sides, which, being spread out and filled in different directions, fold around in the manner of a ram's horn; or perhaps because it is filled with offspring within. Hence also a **leather bottle** <note>original: *uter*</note> is named because it contains something inside, like members and viscera. The **small gut** <note>original: *aqualiculus*</note> properly belongs to a pig, but the term is transferred to the belly of humans. The **matrix** <note>original: *matrix*</note> is so called because offspring are generated in it. For it cherishes the received seed, gives it body when cherished, and distinguishes it into members when embodied. The **vulva** <note>original: *vulva*</note> is named as if it were a "folding door" <note>original: *valva*</note>, that is, the gate of the belly, either because it receives the seed or because the offspring proceeds from it. The **bladder** <note>original: *vesica*</note> is named as if it were a "vessel of water" <note>original: *vas aquae*</note>, because just as a vessel is filled with water, so the bladder is filled with urine collected from the kidneys and is distended by the fluid. This organ is not found in birds. **Urine** <note>original: *urina*</note> is so named either because it "burns" <note>original: *urat*</note> or because it is ejected from the kidneys. By its indication, both health and

<column-break/>

sickness are shown. This fluid is commonly called **laundry-water** <note>original: *lotium*</note> because with it they make "thongs" <note>original: *lora*</note>, that is, clean garments. **Seed** <note>original: *semen*</note> is that which, once cast, is taken up either by the earth or by the womb for the purpose of producing either fruit or offspring. For it is a liquid made from the decoction of food and the body, diffused through the veins and marrow; from there it is exuded like bilge-water and thickens in the kidneys, and when ejected during intercourse and received in the woman's womb, it is formed into a body by a certain heat of the viscera and by the irrigation of the menstrual blood. **Menstruation** <note>original: *menstrua*</note> is the superfluous blood of women. It is called *menstrua* because of the circuit of the light of the moon <note>called *mene* in Greek</note>, by which this flow is accustomed to occur. These are also called the "womanly things." For the woman is the only animal that menstruates. By contact with this blood, crops do not germinate, new wine turns sour, grasses die, trees lose their fruit, rust corrupts iron, and copper turns black. If any dogs eat of it, they are driven into madness. Even bitumen, like asphalt, which is dissolved neither by iron nor water, is scattered of its own accord when polluted by this blood. After many days of menstruation, the seed is not germinable because there is no longer menstrual blood by which it may be flooded and irrigated. Thin seed does not stick in the woman's places; for it slips out and has no power of adhering. Similarly, thick seed has no power of generating because it cannot be mixed with the woman's seed due to its excessive density. Hence, they say both sterile men and women are made, either through excessive thickness of the seed or blood, or through excessive thinness. They say the **heart** of a man is formed first, because in it is the life and wisdom of the man; then on the fortieth day, the whole body is completed, as is gathered from cases of abortion. Others say the offspring takes its beginning from the head; hence, in the offspring of birds, we see the eyes formed first in the eggs. It is called **offspring** <note>original: *fetus*</note> because it is still cherished <note>original: *foveatur*</note> in the womb. The **afterbirth** <note>original: *secundae*</note> is the name for the small sac that is born together with the infant and contains it; it is so named because it follows <note>original: *sequitur*</note> the infant when it is brought forth. They say children are born resembling their fathers if the paternal seed is stronger, and their mothers if the maternal seed is stronger; by this reasoning, similar faces are expressed. Those who represent the figure of both parents are conceived from an equal mixture of paternal and maternal seed. Children become like grandfathers and great-grandfathers because, just as many seeds are hidden in the earth, so seeds are hidden in humans that will return the figures of ancestors. They say girls are born from paternal seed and boys from maternal seed, because every birth consists of a double seed; whichever part prevails in strength, it claims the likeness of that sex. In our body, some things are made only for the sake of utility, such as the internal organs; some for both utility and beauty, such as the senses in the face and the hands and feet on the body. Of these members, the utility is great and the appearance most decent. Some things are only for beauty, such as the nipples in men and the navel in both sexes. Some are for distinction, such as the genitals in men, the beard, the hair, and the broad chest; in women, smooth cheeks and a narrow chest, but with the kidneys and sides widened for the purpose of conceiving and carrying offspring. As for man and his parts...

It focuses on the etymologies of organs like the liver and spleen and explains conception, menstruation, and sex determination through the balance of "seeds."</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Isidore of Seville concludes his discussion on the physical components of the human body and now transitions to the various stages of human life, from birth to the final years of old age.</meta>

XI

What pertains to the body has been partially discussed. Now I shall add its various ages.

### The Ages of Man, Chapter II.

There are six **stages of age**: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity <note>original: *grauitas*, literally "gravity" or "seriousness"</note>, and old age. The first age is **infancy**; it is the child being born into the light, which extends for seven years. The second age is **childhood** <note>original: *pueritia*</note>; that is, the "pure" stage, not yet fit for procreation, lasting until the fourteenth year. The third is **adolescence**, adult enough for procreation, which extends until twenty-eight years. The fourth is **youth**, the strongest of all ages, ending in the fiftieth year. The fifth age is that of the **senior**, that is, maturity; this is the decline from youth into old age—not yet old age, but no longer youth. This is the age of the senior which the Greeks call *presbyter* <note>original: *pręsbyten*</note>. Thus, among the Greeks, an old man is not called a *presbyter* but a *geron* <note>original: *geron*</note>. This age begins from the fiftieth year and ends at the seventieth. The sixth age is **old age** <note>original: *senectus*</note>, which is not finished by any span of years; rather, whatever life remains after those five stages is assigned to old age. **Senility** <note>original: *senium*</note>, however, is the final part of old age, so called because it is the limit of the sixth age. In these six spans, the philosophers have described human life, in which it changes, runs its course, and reaches the boundary of death. Let us therefore proceed briefly through the aforementioned stages of age, demonstrating their etymologies <term>etymologia: the study of the origins of words to find their true meaning</term> in man. A human of the first age is called an **infant**. He is called "infant" because he does not yet know how to speak <note>original: *fari*, from which *infans* is derived</note>, that is, he is not able to talk. For as his teeth are not yet well-ordered, his outpouring of speech is diminished. A **boy** <note>original: *puer*</note> is named from purity, because he is pure and does not yet have the downy bloom of the cheeks. These are the **ephebes** <note>original: *ephebi*</note>—so called from Phoebus—not yet men, but smooth youths. Furthermore, "boy" is used in three ways: by birth, as Isaiah says: *A child* <note>original: *puer*</note> *is born to us*; by age, such as those of eight or ten years, from which comes the phrase: *Already he ruled the boyish yoke with his tender neck*; and by service and purity of faith, as the Lord said to the prophet: *You are my servant* <note>original: *puer meus*</note>, *do not fear*, even though Jeremiah had long since exceeded the years of childhood. A **girl** <note>original: *puella*</note> is a little one, like a "chick" <note>original: *pulla*</note>. From this we also call **wards** <note>original: *pupillos*</note> not by their legal condition, but by their childish age. They are called *pupilli* as if they were "without eyes" <note>original: *sine oculis*</note>, that is, bereaved of their parents. Those whose fathers died before they could receive a name from them are truly called *pupilli*. Others are called "bereaved" <note>original: *orbi*</note>. **Orphans** are the same as wards; for the former is a Greek name, the latter Latin. Indeed, in the Psalm where it is read: *you will be a helper to the ward* <note>original: *pupillo*</note>, the Greek has *orphan*. The **pubescent** are named from *pubes*, that is, from the shameful parts of the body, because these places then first produce downy hair. Some, however, judge puberty by years, namely that he is pubescent who has completed fourteen years, even if he reaches puberty very slowly. It is most certain, however, that one is pubescent who shows puberty from the habit of the body and is now able to procreate. **Young mothers** <note>original: *puerperę*</note> are those who give birth in their "boyish" <note>meaning: youthful</note> years, whence Horace says: *The young mother is praised for her first-born offspring.* They are called *puerperae* either because they are burdened by their first birth, or because they bear "boys" <note>children</note> for the first time. The **adolescent** is so named because he is adult enough for pro-

<column-break/>

<margin>woman</margin>
-creating, or from "growing" and "being increased." A **youth** <note>original: *iuuencis*</note> is so called because he begins to be able to "help" <note>original: *iuuare*</note>, just as among cattle they are called *iuuenci* when they have departed from being calves. For a youth <note>original: *iuuenis*</note> is placed in the very increase of age and prepared for assistance. For to "help" <note>original: *iuuare*</note> is the work of a person contributing some labor. Just as the thirtieth year is the year of perfected age in humans, so in livestock and beasts of burden the third year is the most robust. A **man** <note>original: *uir*</note> is so named because there is greater "force" <note>original: *uis*</note> in him than in women—whence "virtue" <note>original: *uirtus*</note> also took its name—or because he rules the woman by force. A **woman** <note>original: *mulier*</note>, however, is named from "softness" <note>original: *mollities*</note>, as if the word were *mollior* <note>softer</note> with a letter removed or changed. For both are separated by the strength and weakness of their minds or bodies. But for this reason the virtue of the man is greatest and that of the woman is less, so that she might be subject to the man, specifically lest, with women resisting, lust should force men to seek something else or rush into the other sex. She is called a **woman** <note>original: *mulier*</note> according to the female sex, not according to the corruption of her integrity <note>meaning: loss of virginity</note>, and this is from the language of Holy Scripture. For immediately after Eve was made from the side of the man, and not yet touched by the man, she was called *mulier*, with the Scripture saying: *And He formed her into a woman* <note>original: *mulierem*</note>. A **virgin** <note>original: *uirgo*</note> is named from her "greener" <note>original: *uiridior*, meaning fresher/younger</note> age, just as a "rod" <note>original: *uirga*</note> or a "heifer" <note>original: *uitula*</note>. Others say it is from her incorruption, as if she were a **virago**, because she is ignorant of female passion. She is called a *virago* because she acts like a man <note>original: *uir*</note>, that is, she performs manly deeds and is of masculine vigor. For the ancients called strong women by this name. However, a virgin is not correctly called a *virago* if she does not perform the office of a man. But a woman is correctly called a *virago* if she performs manly deeds, like an Amazon. She who is now called **female** <note>original: *femina*</note> was called *uira* in ancient times; just as *serua* from *seruus* <note>female slave from male slave</note> or *famula* from *famulus* <note>female servant from male servant</note>, so *uira* from *uir* <note>man</note>. Some think the name of "virgin" comes from this as well. **Female** <note>original: *femina*</note> is named from the parts of the "thighs" <note>original: *femora*</note>, where the appearance of the sex is distinguished from the man. Others, by a Greek etymology, think "female" is named from "fiery force" <note>original: *ignea ui*</note>, because she desires vehemently. For females are more lustful than males, both among women and among animals. Hence, among the ancients, excessive love was called "feminine." A **senior** is still somewhat "greener" <note>meaning: more vigorous</note>; Ovid says in his sixth book: *A senior between a youth and an old man.* Terence says: *By what right are we...* A **younger one** <note>original: *adolescentio?*</note> is not one who is *more* of an adolescent, but *less*; just as a *senior* is *less* of an old man, where the comparative degree signifies less than the positive. Therefore, a "senior" is not quite an old man, just as a "youth" <note>original: *iuuenior*</note> is between a youth and an old man, and a "poorer person" <note>original: *pauperior*</note> is between poor and poorest. Some think **old men** <note>original: *senes*</note> are so called from the "diminution of the senses" <note>original: *sensus diminutione*</note> because they already lose their wits due to age. For natural philosophers say that foolish men have colder blood, while the prudent have warm blood. Hence both the old, in whom the blood is already cold, and children, in whom it is not yet warm, possess less wisdom. This is why it is appropriate if they rave with age; children through playfulness and infancy do not know what they are doing. "Old man" <note>original: *senex*</note> is only of the masculine gender, just as "old woman" <note>original: *anus*</note> is feminine. For only a woman is called *anus*. Moreover, she is called *anus* from "many years" <note>original: *multis annis*</note>, as if full of years <note>original: *annosa*</note>. For if the name were common to both, why would Terence say "an old woman" <note>original: *senem mulierem*</note>? From this also comes "little old woman" <note>original: *uetula*</note>, because she is "ancient" <note>original: *uetusta*</note>. So it is from the old man...
