old age. Thus, "dotage" <note>original: *anilitas*</note> is named from the "old woman" <note>original: *anu*</note>. Gray hair <note>original: *canicies*</note> is called so from its whiteness <note>original: *candore*</note>, as if it were "white-saying" <note>original: *canidicies*</note>; hence that saying: "Flowering youth, milky gray hair," as if one were to say "white." Old age brings many goods and many evils with it. The **goods**: because it frees us from the most powerful masters (the passions), it imposes a limit on pleasures, breaks the impulse of lust, increases wisdom, and gives more mature advice. The **evils**: because old age is most wretched due to weakness and decline. For diseases steal in, and "gloomy old age" <note>a reference to Virgil’s *Georgics*</note>. For there are two things by which the strength of the body is diminished: old age and disease.

<margin>bitter death</margin>
**Death** is said to be so called because it is "bitter" <note>original: *amara*; a folk etymology connecting *mors* (death) and *amara* (bitter)</note>, or from Mars, who is the effector of deaths, or from the "bite" <note>original: *morsu*</note> of the first man, by which he earned death through the eating of the fruit.

<margin>three kinds of death</margin>
There are three kinds of death: bitter, premature, and natural. "Bitter" is for infants; "premature" for youths; "mature," which is natural, for the elderly.

<margin>dead</margin>
From which part of speech "dead" <note>original: *mortuus*</note> is derived is uncertain. For as Caesar says: "a dead man cannot do anything after his death"; likewise a man cannot know his origin. That is, the word "dead" should have ended in a single 'u' as a past participle. Where the letter 'u' is doubled, it is a noun and not a participle, such as "foolish" <note>original: *fatuus*</note> or "steep" <note>original: *arduus*</note>. It is fittingly done so that, just as the one it signifies cannot act, the noun itself cannot be declined in speech. A deceased person is either "dead," a "funeral," or a "corpse."

<margin>funeral</margin>
It is a **funeral** <note>original: *funus*</note> if he is buried. And it is called *fua* from the "ropes" <note>original: *funibus*</note> or torches which were carried before the bier, made of papyrus surrounded by wax.

<margin>corpse</margin>
It is a **corpse** <note>original: *cadaver*</note> if it lies unburied. For "corpse" is named from "falling" <note>original: *cadendo*</note>, because it can no longer stand. While it is being carried, we call it the "funeral rites" <note>original: *exequias*</note>; when burned, the "remains" <note>original: *reliquias*</note>; when hidden away, it is "buried." By custom, it is called a "body,"

<margin>deceased</margin>
as in: "Then the bodies of those lacking light." He is called "deceased" <note>original: *defunctus*</note> because he has completed life's duty. For we say they have "discharged" <note>original: *defunctos*</note> their duty because they have completed the duties they owed; hence one is also "discharged from honors."

<margin>buried</margin>
Hence also "deceased," because he is set down from the duty of life, or because he is "done." He is called "buried" <note>original: *sepultus*</note> because he is now without pulse and palpitation <note>original: *sine pulsu*</note>, that is, without movement. To bury is to hide the

<margin>interred</margin>
body. For to "inter" <note>original: *humare*</note> we say is to cover over, which is to cast "earth" <note>original: *humum*</note> upon it.

### On Portents, Chapter III.

Varro says that **portents** are those things which seem to be born against nature. But they are not against nature, because they happen by the divine will, since the will of the Creator is the "nature" of every created thing. Hence even the pagans sometimes call God "Nature" and sometimes call Nature "God." A portent, therefore, does not happen against nature, but against what is *known* nature. Portents and "shows" <note>original: *ostenta*</note>, monsters, and prodigies are so named because they seem to "portend," "show," "demonstrate," and "predict" some future things. For portents are said to be named from "portending," that is, from "foreshowing." "Shows" are named because they seem to show what is to come. "Prodigies" are so named because they "speak far off" <note>original: *porro dicant*</note>, that is, they predict the future. "Monsters" <note>original: *monstra*</note> are named from "warning" <note>original: *monitu*</note> because they demonstrate something by signifying it, or because they immediately show <note>original: *monstrent*</note> what appears. This is the proper sense, though the usage is often corrupted by the misuse of writers. Certain creations of portents seem to be established for future significations.

<column-break/>

For God sometimes wishes to signify things to come through some signs in those being born, just as he warns and signifies through dreams and oracles the future slaughter of certain nations or people. This has been proven by much experience. For example, in the time of a certain king, a fox was born from a mare, which portended the dissolution of his kingdom. For Alexander, a monster was born from a woman; because the upper parts of the body were human but dead, while the lower parts were various beasts and living, it signified the sudden killing of the king—for the worse parts had outlived the better. But these monsters which are given as signs do not live long, but die as soon as they are born. However, there is a difference between a "portent" and something "portentous." For **portents** are those things which are transformed, as it is said a woman in Umbria gave birth to a serpent. Hence Lucan says: "And her own infant terrified the mother." But **portentous** things take on a slight mutation, for example, those born with six fingers. Therefore, portents or portentous things exist: some by the magnitude of the whole body beyond the common measure of men, like Tityus who lay across nine acres, as Homer testifies. Others by the smallness of the whole body, like dwarfs, or those whom the Greeks call **Pygmies**, because their stature is only a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>. Others by the magnitude of parts, such as an informed head, or with superfluous limbs like those with two heads or three hands, or **scinopoda** <note>literally "shadow-feet"</note> in whom double rows of teeth proceed. Others by a deficiency of parts, in which one part is greatly lacking compared to the other, like a hand from a hand or a foot from a foot. Others by "division" <note>original: *diffissione*</note>, such as those born without a hand or head, which the Greeks call *steresios* <note>deprived</note>. Others by number, when only a head or a leg is born. Others which are transformed in part, such as those who have the face of a lion or a dog, or a bull's head or body—as they remember the Minotaur born from Pasiphae, which the Greeks call *etheremorphia* <note>other-formed</note>. Others which are transformed in every part into the portent of a different creation, as history says a calf was born from a woman. Others which, without transformation, have a change of place, such as eyes in the chest or in the forehead, ears above the temples; or as Aristotle recorded, a certain person had the liver on the left side and the spleen on the right. Others by "con-naturation," such as when several fingers are found joined and clinging together on one hand or foot. Others by premature and intemperate creation, such as those who are born with teeth, or bearded, or with gray hair. Others by a complex of many differences, such as that multiform portent we mentioned in Alexander's time. Others by a mixture of gender, such as those called **androgynes** and **hermaphrodites**. They are called hermaphrodites because both sexes appear in them. For "Hermes" among the Greeks is male, and "Aphrodite" is female. These, having the right breast of a man and the left of a woman, by turns in cohabitation both beget and give birth. Just as there are certain monsters of men in individual nations, so in the whole human race there are certain **monstrous nations**, such as giants, dog-headed people <note>original: *cinocephali*</note>, cyclopes, and others. Giants are called so according to the etymology of the Greek language, who call them *gegenes* <note>earth-born</note>...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s discussion on the "monsters" or "portents" of the human race, moving from general definitions of human anomalies to specific legendary races and mythological figures, which he often interprets through natural or historical explanations.</meta>

# XI

...they are thought to be "earth-born" <note>original: *terrigenas*</note>, because fables claim the immense mass of the earth brought them forth, and she generated those similar to herself. For in Greek, *Ge* is the name for "earth" <note>original: *Ge enim terra appellatur*</note>, and the common people call those whose parentage is unknown "sons of the earth." However, certain people unskilled in the Holy Scriptures wrongly believe that the transgressing angels had intercourse with the daughters of men before the Flood, and from this, giants were born—that is, exceedingly large and strong men—by whom the earth was filled.

**Cynocephali** <note>literally "Dog-heads," from the Greek *kyon* (dog) and *kephale* (head)</note> are so named because they have canine heads, and their very barking proves they are more like beasts than humans. These are born in India. India also produces the **Cyclopes**, who are called such because they are said to have a single eye in the middle of their forehead. These are also called **Agriophagitae** <note>literally "wild-eaters"</note> because they eat only the flesh of wild beasts.

In Libya, it is believed that the **Blemmyes** <note>OCR reads "Lemnias," likely a transcription error for *Blemmyas*</note> are born as trunks without heads, having their mouths and eyes in their chests. Others are born without necks, having eyes in their shoulders. At the furthest reaches of the East, monstrous faces of nations are described. Some are without noses, having shapeless, flat faces. Others have a lower lip so prominent that, while sleeping in the burning heat of the sun, they cover their entire face with it. Some have closed mouths, sucking in their nourishment through a small hole using oat straws. Quite a few are said to be without tongues, using nods or movements in place of speech.

The **Panothiosi** in Scythia are said to have ears of such sprawling magnitude that they cover their entire bodies with them. For in the Greek language, *pan* means "all" and *othi* means "ears." The **Arrabaritae** in Ethiopia are said to walk prone like cattle; none of them live past their fortieth year.

**Satyrs** are small men with hooked noses; they have horns on their foreheads and feet like those of goats, such as the one Saint Anthony saw in the desert. When questioned by the servant of God <note>Saint Anthony</note>, he is said to have replied:
> I am a mortal, one of the inhabitants
> of the desert, whom the pagans, deceived by various
> errors, worship as Fauns and Satyrs.
Certain "wild men" are also spoken of, whom some call **Fauni Ficarii** <note>Fig-Fauns, often associated with wild or lustful spirits of the woods</note>. The race of **Sciopodes** <note>literally "Shadow-feet"</note> is said to live in Ethiopia, having only one leg but a marvelous swiftness. The Greeks call them *Sciopodes* from this: because in the heat, they lie on their backs on the ground and are shaded by the great size of their feet. The **Antipodes** in Libya have the soles of their feet turned backward behind their legs, and eight toes on each sole. The **Hippopodes** in Scythia have human forms but horse-like feet. In India, they say there is a race called the **Macrobii** <note>literally "long-lived"</note>, who are twelve feet tall. There is also a race there a cubit <note>a unit of length based on the forearm, about 18 inches</note> in stature, whom the Greeks call **Pygmies** from the word for "cubit," of whom we have spoken above. These hold the mountains of India near the ocean. It is also claimed that in India there is a race of women who conceive at age five and do not exceed the eighth year of life.

Other fabulous things are told of men which do not exist but are fictions interpreted to explain the causes of things, such as **Geryon**, the king of Spain, who was said to have a triple form. For there were three brothers of such great harmony that it was as if one soul existed in three bodies. They say the **Gorgons** were harlots with hair like snakes, who turned those looking at them into stone; they had one eye which they used in turn. But there were actually three sisters

<column-break/>

of such beauty that they made those who looked upon them so stunned that they were thought to turn into stone.

Fables say there were three **Sirens**, part virgin and part bird, having wings and talons; one sang with her voice, the second with flutes, and the third with a lyre. They drew sailors, enticed by their song, into shipwrecks. According to the truth, however, they were harlots who led passers-by to poverty, and thus were fictionally said to cause "shipwrecks." They are said to have had wings and talons because love both flies and wounds. They are said to have lived in the waves because the waves created Venus <note>the goddess of love, born from sea foam</note>.

They also say **Scylla** was a woman girded with barking dogs. She is actually a strait in the Sicilian sea where sailors, terrified by the whirlpools of clashing waves, imagine the waves are barking—waves which the heat of the swallowing vortex causes to collide.

They also invent certain monsters from irrational animals, such as **Cerberus**, the dog of the underworld, having three heads; through him they signify the three ages through which death devours man—that is, infancy, youth, and old age. Some think he is called Cerberus as if he were *creoboros*, which means "flesh-devouring" <note>original: *creobozos id est carnē vozās*</note>.

They also say the **Hydra** was a serpent with nine heads, which in Latin is called an *excetra* <note>Isidore's term for a multi-headed water snake</note>, because when one head was cut off, three more grew. But it is established that the Hydra was a place vomiting out water that devastated a nearby city; when one opening was closed, many more burst out. Seeing this, Hercules burned the area and thus closed the water passages. For "Hydra" is named from "water" <note>Greek: *hydor*</note>. Ambrose makes mention of this in a comparison to heresies, saying:
> For heresy, like a certain Hydra of the fables,
> grew through its own wounds; and while it was often
> cut back, it sprouted, destined to perish by the fire
> of a deserved burning.
They also invent the **Chimera**, a three-formed beast: a lion in its face, a dragon in its hind parts, and a goat in the middle. Certain naturalists say this was not an animal, but a mountain in Cilicia, which in some places nourished lions and goats, in some was burning, and in others was full of snakes. Bellerophon made this mountain habitable, and for this reason he is said to have "slain the Chimera."

The name **Centaur**—that is, a man joined with a horse—was given to a marvelous species; some say these were Thessalian horsemen, because as they rode about in war, they seemed to have one body of horse and man; thus the fiction of Centaurs was asserted. Furthermore, the **Minotaur** took its name from a bull and a man; fables say such a beast was shut in the Labyrinth. Of which Ovid says:
> A man half-bull,
> and a bull half-man.
The **Onocentaur** is so called because it is said to be half-man and half-donkey; just as the **Hippocentaur**, in which the nature of horses and men is thought to have been joined.

### Chapter 4: On Transformed Beings

Certain monstrous transformations of men and changes into beasts are also written about, such as that most famous sorceress **Circe**, who is said to have changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts; and concerning the **Arcadians** who, chosen by lot, swam across a certain pond and were there converted into wolves. Indeed, they confirm that the companions of **Diomedes** were changed into birds, not by a fabulous lie, but by historical affirmation.

But some also assert that witches <note>original: *strigae*</note> are made from human beings. For the forms of the wicked are changed for many acts of robbery; whether by magic incantations or by the poison of herbs, they pass into wild beasts with transformed bodies. Indeed, many things undergo change by their very nature and, once corrupted, are transformed into different species: just as bees come from the putrid flesh of calves, so beetles <note>original: *scarabaei*</note> come from horses, locusts from mules, and scorpions from crabs. Ovid says: "If you remove the hollow claws of a shore-crab, a scorpion will emerge, and threaten with its hooked tail."

### Here begins the twelfth book
### Concerning cattle and beasts of burden. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop-cap O, colored in red. The interior of the letter contains a circular diagram resembling a T-O map (orbis terrarum), a medieval world map where a T-shape divides the world into Asia, Europe, and Africa.</image-desc>

Adam was the first to bestow names upon all living creatures, calling each one by a name according to its present status, following the condition of the nature it was meant to serve. However, the various nations gave names to each of the animals in their own languages. Adam did not impose those names according to the Latin or Greek languages, or those of any barbarian nations, but in that language which was the single tongue of all before the Flood, which is called Hebrew. In Latin, "animals" <note>original: *animalia*</note> or "living things" <note>original: *animantia*</note> are so called because they are animated by life and moved by spirit. They are called "quadrupeds" because they walk on four feet; while these may be similar to cattle, they are not under human care, such as deer, does, wild asses, and others. These are neither "beasts" <note>original: *bestiae*</note>, like lions, nor "beasts of burden" <note>original: *iumenta*</note> that can assist human use. We call "cattle" <note>original: *pecus*</note> everything that lacks human language and form. Properly, however, the name of "livestock" <note>original: *pecorum*</note> is usually applied to those animals that are either fit for eating, such as sheep and pigs, or useful for human service, such as horses and oxen. There is a difference between "cattle" <note>original: *pecora*</note> and "beasts" <note>original: *pecudes*</note>; for the ancients used "cattle" generally for the meaning of all living animals, but "beasts" only for those animals that are eaten, as if the word were *pecuedes* <note>a false etymology suggesting "cattle that are eaten"</note>. Generally, however, every animal is called *pecus* from "grazing" <note>original: *pasco*</note>. "Beasts of burden" <note>original: *iumenta*</note> drew their names from the fact that they help <note>original: *iuvent*</note> our labor or burden by carrying it or by plowing. For the ox draws wagons and turns the hardest clods of earth with the plowshare. The horse and the donkey carry loads and ease the labor of humans in walking. Hence they are called *iumenta*, from the fact that they "help" <note>original: *iuvent*</note> humans; for they are animals of great strength. These same are called "herds" <note>original: *armenta*</note>, either because they are fit for "arms" <note>original: *arma*</note>—that is, for war—or because we use them in "armaments." Others understand "herds" to mean only oxen, from "plowing" <note>original: *arando*</note>, as if they were *aramenta*, or because they are "armed" with horns. There is a distinction between "herds" <note>original: *armenta*</note> and "flocks" <note>original: *greges*</note>. For herds consist of horses and oxen, while flocks are of goats and sheep. The sheep <note>original: *ovis*</note> is a soft creature with wool, defenseless in body, placid in spirit; it is named from "offering" <note>original: *oblatio*</note>, because among the ancients, in the beginning, they did not slaughter bulls but sheep in sacrifice. Some of these they call "two-toothed" <note>original: *bidentes*</note>, because among their eight teeth they have two higher ones; these the pagans especially offered in sacrifice. The wether <note>original: *vervex*</note> is named either from its

<column-break/>

strength <note>original: *vires*</note>, because it is stronger than other sheep, or because it is a "male" <note>original: *vir*</note>, or because it has a "worm" <note>original: *vermis*</note> in its head; excited by the itching of these worms, they strike each other and hit with great force when fighting. The ram <note>original: *aries*</note> is named either from "Ares" <note>the Greek god of war</note>, that is, from the male, which is why among us the males in flocks are called *mares*; or because this animal was first sacrificed on "altars" <note>original: *aris*</note> by the pagans. It is a ram <note>original: *aries*</note> because they would place it on altars <note>original: *aris*</note>. Hence the saying: "The ram is slaughtered at the altar." The Greeks call the lamb <note>original: *agnus*</note> *apo tou agnou* <note>from 'the holy/pure'</note>, as if it were pious; the Latins, however, think it has this name because it "recognizes" <note>original: *agnoscat*</note> its mother more than other animals, so much so that even if it wanders in a large flock, it immediately recognizes the voice of its parent by its bleating. Kids <note>original: *haedi*</note> are named from "eating" <note>original: *edendo*</note>. For the small ones are very fatty and pleasant in flavor; hence the word for "to eat" <note>original: *edere*</note> and "edible" <note>original: *edulium*</note> comes from this. The he-goat <note>original: *hircus*</note> is a lecherous and butting animal, always burning for mating; its eyes look sideways because of its lust, from which it also takes its name. For *hirci* are the corners of the eyes, according to Suetonius. Its nature is so extremely hot that only its blood can dissolve the "adamant" stone <note>the diamond</note>, a material which neither fire nor iron has the power to master. Older he-goats are called *cinifi* from the Cinyps river in Libya, where large ones are born. Some have said "goats" <note>original: *capros* and *capras*</note> are named from "plucking" <note>original: *carpendo*</note> twigs. Others because they "seize" <note>original: *captent*</note> rough places. Some from the "cracking" <note>original: *crepitu*</note> of their legs, which is why they are called *creas*—these are wild goats. Because they are said to see very sharply, the Greeks called them *dorcas*, from "to see clearly" <note>original: *apo tou derkesthai*</note>. For they dwell in high mountains, and although they are far away, they see everyone who is coming. These are the same as the "roe-deer" <note>original: *capreae*</note> and the "ibexes" <note>original: *ibices*</note>, as if they were "birds" <note>original: *avices*</note>, because like birds they hold to steep and high places and inhabit the heights, so that from the height they are barely visible to human eyes. Hence, in the southern parts, the ibexes are called birds that inhabit the flows of the Nile. These animals, as we have said, stay on the highest rocks, so that if they sense the hostility of wild beasts or humans, they throw themselves down from the highest peaks of the rocks and catch themselves unharmed on their own horns. Deer <note>original: *cervi*</note> are named *apo ton keraton* <note>from 'the horns'</note>, for in Greek, horns are called *kerata*. These are enemies of serpents; when they sense they are weighed down by infirmity, they draw them out of their dens with the breath of their nostrils and, having overcome the danger of their poison, they are restored by eating them. They themselves discovered the herb "dittany." For having eaten it, they shake out the arrows they have received. They marvel at the whistling of pipes and listen sharply with upright ears. It is also remarkable how, when they swim across immense rivers or seas, they place their heads upon the haunches of those going before them, and succeeding each other in turn, they feel no labor from the weight. "Goat-stags" <note>original: *tragelaphi*</note> are named by the Greeks; while they are of the same species as deer, they have shaggy shoulders like goats and chins hairy with long beards. These are found nowhere else but near the Phasis river. Fawns <note>original: *hinnuli*</note> are the offspring of deer, named from "hinting" <note>original: *innuere*</note>, because they hide themselves at the mother's signal. The doe <note>original: *damula*</note> is so called because it flees from the "hand" <note>original: *manu*</note>; a timid and defenseless animal, about which Martial says: "The boar is feared for its tusk; horns defend the stag. We, the defenseless does, what are we but prey?" The hare <note>original: *lepus*</note> is as if it were "light-footed" <note>original: *levipes*</note>, because it runs swiftly. Hence in Greek it is called *lagos* for its running; for it is a swift and very timid animal. The rabbit <note>original: *cuniculus*</note> is a kind of wild animal, named as if it were a "little dog" <note>original: *caniculus*</note> because...

# XII

<margin>q</margin> is caught by a pack of dogs or driven from its caves. The **sow** <note>original: *sus*</note> is named because it turns up <note>original: *subigat*</note> the pastures; that is, it seeks food by overturning the earth. The **boar** <note>original: *verres*</note> is so called because it possesses great strength <note>original: *vires*</note>. The **pig** <note>original: *porcus*</note> is, as it were, "filthy" <note>original: *sporcus*</note>. For it gorges itself on filth, submerges itself in mud, and smears itself with slime. As Horace says: "And the sow is a friend to the mud." From this also comes the name "squalor" or "filth." We call the hair of pigs "bristles" <note>original: *setas*</note>, and these are named from the sow <note>original: *suant*</note>; from which also "furies" <note>original: *furores*</note> are named, because they "sew" or bristle up. The letter *f* was added and *p* was substituted. Hence, among the Greeks it is called a **wild boar** <note>original: *fyagros* (suagros); from the Greek roots for "pig" and "wild"</note>. For everything that is wild and untamed is loosely called "of the fields." The **steer** <note>original: *juuencus*</note> is so named because it begins to help <note>original: *iuuare*</note> in the use of men for tilling the earth, or because among the pagans a steer was always sacrificed to Jupiter <note>original: *ioui*</note>, never a bull. For even among the victims, age was considered. **Bull** <note>original: *taurus*</note> is a Greek name, as is **ox** <note>original: *bos*</note>. The color of Indian bulls is tawny, and they have the speed of birds; their hair is turned in the opposite direction, and they can turn their heads with whatever flexibility they wish. Because of their royal hardness, they reject every weapon with their untamed ferocity. <margin>b</margin>The Greeks call the **ox** *boeren*; the Latins call this a *trio*, because it treads <note>original: *terat*</note> the earth, as if it were a *terio*. Menius says: "Here is the rustic master of the *triones*." Its width of hide extends from the shoulder to the flanks. They are called **dewlaps** <note>original: *palearia*</note> from the skin <note>original: *pelle*</note> itself, as if they were "skin-flaps," which is a sign of noble breeding in an ox. Among cattle, there is a pious bond between companions. For one seeks the other with whom it has been accustomed to pull the plow by the neck, and it testifies to its pious affection with frequent lowing if by chance its partner is missing. <margin>v</margin>The **cow** <note>original: *uacca*</note> is named as if it were a *boacca*. For it is formed from the quality of movable names, just as lion and lioness, or dragon and dragoness. The **calf** and **heifer** <note>original: *vitulus & vitula*</note> can be named from "greenness" <note>original: *viriditate*</note>, that is, from a green age, just as a virgin <note>original: *virgo*</note>. A *vitula* is small and has not yet given birth. For once she has given birth, she is a steer or a cow. <margin>b</margin>**Buffaloes** <note>original: *bubali*</note> are named by derivation because they are similar to oxen, yet so untameable that out of ferocity they do not receive the yoke on their necks. Africa produces them. <margin>v</margin>**Aurochs** <note>original: *uri*</note> are wild oxen in Germany, having horns so large that they are made into drinking vessels of remarkable capacity for royal tables. <margin>c</margin>A reason gave the name to **camels** <note>original: *camelis*</note>: either because they lie down when being loaded so that they become shorter and lower—since the Greeks call what is low and short *camai*—or because it has a curved back. For *camus* in a Greek word signifies "curved." Although other regions send these, Arabia sends the most. They differ from one another; for the Arabian ones have two humps on the back, while those of other regions have one. <margin>d</margin>The **dromedary** <note>original: *dzomeda*</note> is a type of camel of smaller stature, but of swifter course, from which it takes its name. For *dromos* in Greek is called "running" and "speed." Indeed, it is accustomed to travel a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal, like the ox, sheep, and camel, ruminates. Now, **rumination** is named from the *rumen*, a protruding part of the throat through which food that has been swallowed is called back by certain animals. <margin>a</margin>The **donkey** <note>original: *asinus*</note> and the **little donkey** <note>original: *asellus*</note> are named from sitting <note>original: *sedendo*</note>, as if it were "seater." But this name, which was more suitable for horses, this animal took because men began to ride this before they captured horses. For being a slow animal and resisting for no reason, man immediately placed himself upon it as he wished. <margin>o</margin>The **onager** is interpreted as

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin>a wild donkey. For the Greeks call the donkey *on* and the wild *agria*. Africa has these, large and untamed, wandering in the desert. Individuals lead herds of females. They are jealous of newborn males and bite off their testicles; as a precaution, the mothers hide them in secret places. **Arcadian donkeys** are so called because they were first brought from Arcadia, being large and tall. However, the smaller donkey is more necessary in the field <note>original: *on agro*</note>, because it both tolerates labor and almost does not refuse neglect. <margin>e</margin>**Horses** <note>original: *equi*</note> are so named because when they were joined in four-horse teams they were "leveled" <note>original: *equabantur*</note>, and they coupled those equal in form and similar in speed. The **nag** <note>original: *caballus*</note> is named from "hollowing" <note>original: *cauando*</note>, because as it walks, its pressed hoof hollows the earth, which other animals do not have. Hence also they are called **noisy-footed** <note>original: *sonipes*</note> because they sound with their feet. The liveliness of horses is great. For they exult in the fields; they scent war; they are stirred by the sound of the trumpet to battle; and roused by the voice, they are provoked to the race. For they grieve when they have been defeated, and exult when they have won. Some sense enemies in war to the extent that they attack adversaries with a bite. Others recognize their own masters; they forget their gentleness if they are changed. Some receive no one on their back except their master. Many shed tears for their masters when they are killed or dying. It is unique to the horse to cry for a human being and to feel the affection of grief. Hence, in centaurs, the nature of horses and humans is mixed. From the sadness or eagerness of horses, those about to fight are also accustomed to gather the future outcome. The lifespan is long for Phrygian, Epirean, and Sicilian horses: upwards of fifty years. However, the common opinion is that it is shorter for Spanish, Numidian, and Gallic horses. In noble horses, as the ancients say, four things are looked for: form, beauty, merit, and color. **Form**: that the body be strong and solid for vigor, with a suitable height, a long side, lean belly, very large and round haunches, a wide-spreading chest, the whole body knotty with a density of muscles, and a dry foot consolidated with a concave hoof. **Beauty**: that the head be small and lean, with the skin adhering closely to the bones, short and sharp ears, large eyes, wide nostrils, and an erect neck, a thick mane and tail, and a firm roundness in the solidity of the hooves. **Merit**: that it be bold in spirit, swift of foot, with trembling limbs (which is a sign of strength), and that it may be easily stirred from deep quiet, or not easily held back once haste is excited. The movement of a horse is understood in its ears; its virtue in its trembling limbs. <margin>c</margin>**Color**: this especially is expected—bay, golden, rosy, myrtle-colored, fawn, yellow-gray, gray, checkered, hoary, shining-white, pure white, spotted, and black. Following in order is the "variegated" distinguished from black and bay; the remaining variegated color or ash-colored is the worst. The ancients used to call **bay** "vadium," because among other animals it "goes" <note>original: *vadat*</note> more strongly. It is also <margin>s</margin>called **chestnut** <note>original: *spadix*</note>, which they call "date-red," and is named *spadix* from the color of the palm branch, which the Sicilians call *spadica*. <margin>b</margin>The **bright-white** <note>original: *blancus*</note> is as if having painted eyes, and infused with a certain splendor. For the ancients used to call the gray-white "shining." <margin>s</margin>**Yellowish-white** <note>original: *siluus*</note> is a honey-colored, whitish hue.

# Book Twelve

A **spotted** horse is white with black dots interspersed. However, **brilliant white** <note>original: *candidus*</note> and **plain white** <note>original: *albus*</note> differ from each other. For "plain white" has a certain paleness, while "brilliant white" is snowy and infused with pure light. **Gray** <note>original: *canus*</note> is said to be a mixture of brilliant white and black. **Dappled** <note>original: *scutulatus*</note> is named for the white circles it has among purple tones. **Variegated** <note>original: *varius*</note> is so called because it has divided paths of colors. Those that have only white feet are called **white-footed** <note>original: *petuli*</note>; those with a white forehead are called **blazed** <note>original: *calidi*</note>. **Stag-colored** <note>original: *cervinus*</note> is what the common people call **dun** <note>original: *guaranem*</note>. The same common folk use the term **copper-colored** <note>original: *eranem*</note> because it is like the color of bronze. **Myrtle-colored** <note>original: *myrteus*</note>, however, is essentially purple. **Ashen** <note>original: *dosinus*</note> is so named because it is the color of a donkey <note>original: *asino*</note>, that is, ash-gray. These are descended from a wild race which we call **wild horses**; and therefore they cannot transition to the dignity of the city. **Black** in Greek is *mauros* <note>original: *mauron*</note>. For the Greeks call the black horse *mauros*. A **pony** <note>original: *mannus*</note> is a shorter horse, which the common people call a **brownie** <note>original: *brunicum*</note> or **brunitius**. The ancients called **post-horses** <note>original: *veredos*</note> by that name because they "carried carriages" <note>original: *veherent redas*</note>, that is, they led them, or because they ran the public ways through which carriages were accustomed to travel. There are three kinds of horses. One is noble, fit for battles and burdens. The second is common and for the herd, fit for carrying but not for riding. The third is born from a mixture of different kinds, which is called **hybrid** <note>original: *bigenerum*</note> because it is born from diverse parents, like the **mule**. The word "mule" is drawn from the Greek; specifically because, subdued by the yoke of the bakers, it leads the slow **millstones** <note>original: *molas*</note> in a circle by grinding. The Jews assert that Anah, the descendant of Esau, was the first to have herds of mares covered by donkeys in the desert, so that from there new animals, the mules, were born against nature. They say that **wild asses** <note>original: *onagros*</note> were also admitted to female donkeys, and they discovered this kind of intercourse so that very swift donkeys were born from them. Indeed, human industry forced different animals into coitus, and thus by adulterous mixing found another race, just as Jacob procured similarities of colors against nature. For those sheep conceived such offspring as the shadows of the rams climbing above them which they contemplated in the mirror of the waters. Finally, this very thing is said to happen in a herd of mares: that they place noble horses before the sight of those conceiving, so that they might conceive and create foals similar to them. For lovers of **doves** also place painted, very beautiful doves in the same places where the birds live, so that by catching their sight, they generate similar ones. This is why some command pregnant women not to look upon any very ugly faces of animals, such as **dog-headed creatures** <note>original: *cenocephalos*</note> and apes, lest meeting them with their sight, they give birth to similar offspring. For they say this is the nature of women: that whatever they look upon, or conceive in their mind at the extreme heat of pleasure while they are conceiving, such offspring they procreate. For the animal in the sexual act transmits external forms inward, and its heart, seized by these patterns, pulls the species into its own quality. Among living beings, those are called **hybrids** <note>original: *bigenera*</note> which are born from diverse parents: like the **mule** from a mare and a donkey; the **hinny** <note>original: *burdo*</note> from a horse and a female donkey; **hybrids** <note>original: *hybaide*, likely a corruption of *hybridae*</note> from wild boars and pigs; the **tityrus** from a sheep and a buck; the **musimon** from a goat and a ram. Now, the **leader of the herd** is...

<column-break/>

->Chapter II. Concerning Beasts.<-

The term **beasts** <note>original: *bestiarum*</note> properly applies to lions, pards, tigers, wolves, foxes, dogs, and similar creatures that rage either with tooth or claw, except for snakes. They are called "beasts" from the "force" <note>original: *vi*</note> with which they rage. They are called **wild animals** <note>original: *fere*</note> because they enjoy natural liberty and are "carried" <note>original: *ferantur*</note> by their own desire. Their wills are free; they wander here and there, and wherever their spirit leads, there they are carried. <margin>Lion</margin> The word **lion** was inserted into Latin from a Greek origin. For in Greek it is called *leon*, and it is a "bastard" name because it is partially corrupted. **Lioness** <note>original: *leena*</note>, however, is entirely Greek, just as is **female dragon** <note>original: *dracena*</note>. That a lioness might be called a *lea* is a usage taken from the poets. "Lion" in Greek is interpreted as "King" <note>original: *rex*</note> in Latin, because he is the prince of all beasts. His kind is said to be threefold. Of these, those that are short and have a curly mane are peaceful; those that are long and have a simple mane are more fierce. Their foreheads and tails indicate their moods. Their strength is in their chest, and their firmness in their head. When surrounded by hunters, they look at the earth, so that they are less terrified by the sight of hunting spears. They fear the clatter of wheels, but they fear fires more. When they sleep, their eyes remain vigilant. When they walk, they cover their tracks with their tail so that the hunter cannot find them. When they have given birth to a cub, the cub is said to sleep for three days and three nights. Then, by the father's roar or bellowing, the place of the den is said to be shaken as if by a tremor, waking the sleeping cub. Around humans, the nature of lions is kind, so that they cannot be angry unless harmed. Their mercy is shown by constant examples. For they spare the prostrate; they permit captives they meet to return home; they do not kill a human except in great **hunger** <note>original: *fama*, likely a misspelling of *fame*</note>. Regarding them, Lucretius says: "And the breeds of lions," etc. <margin>Tiger</margin> The **tiger** is named because of its swift flight. For so the Persians and Medes name an **arrow**. For it is a beast distinguished by various spots, wonderful in strength and speed. From its name, the river **Tigris** is called, because it is the most rapid of all rivers. <margin>panther</margin> It is mostly produced in **Hyrcania**. The **panther** is so called either because it is the friend of all animals except the dragon, or because it delights in the society of its own kind, and whatever it receives, it returns to the same likeness. For in Greek, *pan* means **all**. This beast is marked with tiny little circles, so that with eye-like circles it is distinguished by a variety of black or white on a tawny background. This animal gives birth only once. The reason for this is manifest. For when the cubs have grown together in the mother's womb and the mother's strength is ready for birth, they hate the delay of time. And so they tear the womb burdened with offspring with their claws as if it were an obstacle to their birth; she pours forth the birth, or rather loses it, driven by pain. Thus, afterward, with the places corrupted and scarred, the received seed does not stick when infused, but jumps back in vain. For **Pliny** says that animals with sharp claws cannot give birth frequently. For they damage themselves internally as the cubs move. The **pard** is second after the panther; it is a variegated and very swift kind, headlong for blood. For it rushes to death with a leap. The **leopard** is born from the adultery of a lioness and a pard, and it creates a third origin, as Pliny also says in his *Natural History*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of animals from Book 12, Chapter 2 ("On Beasts"), specifically detailing hybrids like the leopard before moving into a catalog of exotic and wild animals, including the rhinoceros, elephant, and various predators.</meta>

...lions mate with pards, or pards with lionesses, and from both matings "degenerate" offspring are created—just as the mule is born from a horse and a donkey. The **Rhinoceros** <note>original: *Rhinoceron*</note> is named by the Greeks; in Latin this is interpreted as "horn on the nose" <note>From Greek *rhis* (nose) and *keras* (horn)</note>. The same animal is also called the **Monoceros**—that is, the **Unicorn**—because it has a single horn in the middle of its forehead, four feet in length. It is so sharp and strong that whatever it attacks, it either tosses into the air or pierces through. It often engages in combat with **elephants**, wounding them in the belly and throwing them down. It is of such great strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters; but as those who have written on the natures of animals assert, a young **virgin** is placed before it. As it approaches, she opens her gown to her breast, and there the animal, putting aside all its ferocity, places its head and is thus lulled to sleep, and is captured as if unarmed.

The Greeks think the **Elephant** <note>original: *Elephantem*</note> is named for its massive body, because it presents the form of a mountain; for in Greek, a mountain is called *elepho* <note>This is a false etymology common in the medieval period; the Greek word for mountain is actually *oros*</note>. Among the Indians, however, it is called *barro* from its voice. Thus its cry is called a **barritus**, its teeth are **ivory**, and its snout is called a **proboscis** <note>original: *promoscida*</note> because it uses it to move food to its mouth; it is like a snake, protected by an ivory wall <note>referring to the tusks</note>. The ancient Romans used to call these animals **Lucanian oxen**; "oxen" because they had seen no larger animal, and "Lucanian" because Pyrrhus first deployed them against the Romans in battle in Lucania. This type of animal is well-suited for warfare, for the Persians and Indians place wooden towers upon them and fight with javelins as if from a wall. They are very strong in intellect and memory. They travel in herds and greet humans with whatever movement they can. They flee from **mice**. They mate back-to-back. When they are about to give birth, they release their young in the water or on islands because of **dragons**, which are their enemies and kill them by entangling them. They carry their young for two years and give birth only once; they do not have multiple offspring, but only one. They live for three hundred years. Previously, elephants were born only in Africa and India; now India alone produces them.

The **Griffin** <note>original: *Gryphes*</note> is so called because it is a winged and four-footed animal. This kind of beast is born in the Hyperborean mountains; they are lions in every part of their body, but similar to eagles in their wings and faces, and they are fiercely hostile to horses. They will even tear living men to pieces. The **Chameleon** does not have a single color but is sprinkled with various patterns, like a leopard. It is so named because it has the likeness of a camel and a lion <note>From Greek *chamai* (on the ground) and *leon* (lion)</note>; the small body of this chameleon changes to whatever colors it sees with very easy conversion. The bodies of other animals are not so easily changed. The **Giraffe** <note>original: *Cameleopardus*</note> is so called because, while it is covered in white spots like a leopard, it has a neck like a horse, feet like an ox, and a head like a camel. Ethiopia produces this animal. The **Lynx** is so named because it is counted among the genus of wolves; it is a beast with a spotted back like a leopard, but similar to a wolf—hence the wolf is *lykos* and this is the *lynx*. Those who speak of it say its urine turns into the hardness of a precious stone called **lyngurium** <note>also known as lyncurium or amber in some traditions</note>. It is proved by evidence that the lynxes themselves are aware of this, for they cover the excreted liquid with sand as much as they can out of a certain natural envy, so that such an excretion does not pass into human use. Pliny says that lynxes never have more than one offspring. **Beavers** <note>original: *Castores*</note> are named from "castrating" <note>original: *castrando*</note>. For

<column-break/>

their testicles are suitable for medicines, because of which, when they sense a hunter, they castrate themselves and cut off their own strength with their bites. Regarding them, **Cicero** says in the *Scauriana*: "they ransom themselves with that part of the body for which they are most sought." **Juvenal** says: "He who makes himself a eunuch, desiring to escape by the loss of a testicle." They are the same as **fiber-beavers**, which are also called Pontic dogs. The **Bear** <note>original: *Ursus*</note> is said to be named because it "shapes" <note>original: *orsus*</note> its offspring with its mouth. For they say bears give birth to unformed offspring; a certain mass of flesh is born which the mother, by licking, composes into limbs. Thence comes the saying: "Thus the tongue forms the offspring which the mother bear brought forth." But this is caused by the immaturity of the birth. Finally, she gives birth on the thirtieth day; hence it happens that the rushed fertility brings forth an unformed creature. The head of bears is weak; their greatest strength is in their arms and loins. Thus they sometimes stand upright.

<margin>the wolf</margin>
**Wolf** <note>original: *Lupus*</note> is a Greek derivation transferred into our language. For they call wolves *lykos*. However, it is called *lykos* in Greek from its bites, because in its rabid greed it slaughters whatever it finds. Others say they are called "wolves" as if they were "lion-footed" <note>original: *leopos*</note> because, like a lion, their strength is in their feet; thus, whatever it presses with its foot does not live. It is a predatory beast and hungry for blood. Of it, the country folk say that a man loses his voice if the wolf sees him first. Hence, if someone is suddenly silent, it is said: "The wolf in the fable." Certainly, if it perceives it is seen first, it lays aside its bold ferocity. Wolves mate for no more than twelve days in the whole year; they endure hunger for a long time, and after long fasts, they devour much. Ethiopia sends wolves with maned necks and so many colors that they say no color is missing from them.

The name **Dog** <note>original: *Canis*</note> seems to have a Greek etymology in Latin. For in Greek it is called *kyon* <note>original: *cinos*</note>, although some think it is named from the "sound" <note>original: *canore*</note> of its barking, because it makes a sound; hence also "to sing" <note>original: *canere*</note>. Nothing is more sagacious than dogs, for they have more sense than other animals. For they alone recognize their own names, love their masters, defend their masters' homes, throw themselves into death for their masters, and voluntarily run to the hunt with their master; they do not even leave their master’s body when he is dead. Finally, it is their nature that they cannot exist apart from humans. In dogs, two things are to be expected: either strength or speed. **Puppies** <note>original: *Catuli*</note> is a term used loosely for the young of any beasts. Properly, however, "puppies" refers to dogs, distinguished by the diminutive form. **Hybrids** <note>original: *Licisci*</note>, as Pliny says, are dogs born from wolves and dogs when they happen to mix. It is also common for female dogs to be tied up in the woods at night to be mated with **tigers**; from this mating are born dogs so fierce and strong that they can strike down lions in a fight.

The **Fox** <note>original: *Vulpes*</note> is named as if it were "twisty-foot" <note>original: *volupes*</note>. For it is nimble with its feet and never runs in a straight path, but travels in twisted turns. It is a fraudulent animal, deceiving with ambushes. When it has no food, it feigns death; thus it seizes and devours the birds that fly down to it as if to a carcass. **Ape** <note>original: *Simia*</note> is a Greek name, meaning "with pressed nostrils." Whence we call them *simias* because they have flattened noses and ugly faces, with foully sagging wrinkles; though she-goats also have pressed noses. Others believe they are called *simia* in the Latin language because they [imitate] much in them...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of animals from Book 12, specifically moving from large land beasts like the elephant and rhinoceros to primates, small mammals, and the beginning of the section on serpents.</meta>

...the similarity to human reason is perceived, but it is false. 
These clever creatures of the elements exult at the new moon, but are saddened by the half and waning moons. They carry the offspring they love in front of them, while those they neglect cling to the mother's back. There are five kinds of these creatures. Of these, the **Cercopitheci** <note>original: *cercopetici*; monkeys with tails</note> possess tails. For the **Ape** <note>original: *Simia*</note> with a tail is what some call the "dura."
**Sphinxes** <note>original: *Sphinge*</note> are shaggy with hair and have prominent breasts; they are easily tamed into forgetting their wildness. The **Cynocephali** <note>original: *Cenocephali*; literally "dog-heads"</note> are themselves similar to apes, but with a face like a dog's, from which they receive their name. **Satyrs** <note>original: *Satyri*</note> have quite pleasing faces and are restless with gesturing movements. The **Callitrices** <note>original: *Callitrices*; literally "beautiful hair"</note> differ from the others in nearly their whole appearance, for they have a long beard on their face and a broad tail. The **Leontophontes** <note>original: *Leontofonos*; "lion-killer"</note> is a small beast, and is so named because if it is captured and burned, and its ashes are sprinkled on meat placed at crossroads, it kills lions if they consume even the smallest amount of it. 
The **Ictis** <note>Likely a species of mongoose or weasel</note> is an animal in Africa similar to a hedgehog, named for the screeching of the spines which it sends out from its back to wound pursuing dogs. The **Hydrus** <note>original: *Enydros*; likely the otter or a water-snake</note> is a small beast so named because it lives in the water, especially in the Nile. If it finds a sleeping crocodile, it first rolls itself in mud, enters the crocodile's mouth into its belly, and by consuming all its inner parts, it emerges alive from the crocodile's vitals once the creature is dead. This is called the **Ichneumon** in Greek <note>original: *neomon gręce*</note> because it reveals both healthy and poisonous foods by its scent. Regarding this, Draconntius says: "The little pig-animal <note>original: *suillus*</note> predicts the power of any poison." It is called "suillus" because of its bristles. This animal also hunts serpents; when it fights against an asp, it raises its tail, which the asp watches most closely as if it were a threat. While the asp directs its force there, it is deceived and destroyed. 
The **Cat** is called *musio* <note>original: *Musio*</note> because it is an enemy to mice <note>original: *muribus*</note>. The common people call it a "catcher" <note>original: *captum*</note> from the act of catching. Others say it is because it "catches with its eyes," that is, it sees. For it sees so keenly that it overcomes the darkness of night with the brilliance of its eyes. From this also comes the Greek name *catus*, meaning ingenious or "from burning" <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ καίειν* (apo tou kaiein), referring to the glowing of eyes</note>. The **Ferret** <note>original: *Furo*</note> is named from "darkness" <note>original: *furuo*</note>, which is also the root of the word "thief" <note>original: *fur*</note>. For it digs out dark and hidden burrows and throws out the prey it finds. The **Badger** <note>original: *Melo*</note> is so named either because it has very round limbs or because it seeks out honeycombs <note>original: *fauos*</note> and constantly hunts for honey <note>original: *mella*</note>.

### On Small Animals: Chapter III.

The **Mouse** <note>original: *Mus*</note> is a tiny animal; its name is Greek, and whatever is derived from it becomes Latin. Others say mice are so named because they are born from the moisture of the earth, for *mus* means earth <note>Isidore connects *mus* to *humus*</note>. In these creatures, the liver grows during the full moon, just as certain sea creatures increase, and then decrease again as the moon wanes. The **Shrew** <note>original: *Sorex*</note> is a Latin name because it gnaws <note>original: *rodat*</note> and cuts in the manner of a saw. The ancients used to call the shrew *saurix*, just as they said *clodus* for *claudus* <note>lame</note>.
The **Weasel** <note>original: *Mustela*</note> is named as if it were a "long mouse" <note>original: *mus longus*</note>, for a spear <note>original: *telum*</note> is named for its length. This creature is deceitful by nature; in the houses where it raises its young, it transfers them and changes its nest. It also hunts serpents and mice. There are two kinds of weasels: one is a forest type, differing in size, which the Greeks call *ictidas*; the other wanders in houses. Those who say the weasel conceives through its mouth and gives birth through its ear are mistaken. 
The **Shrew-mouse** <note>original: *Musaraneus*</note>, whose bite is like a spider's, is a very small animal in Sardinia <column-break/> with the shape of a spider; its bite causes straight cuts. It is called the **Solifuga** <note>sun-fleer</note> because it avoids the day. It is very common in silver mines, crawling in secret, and it brings a plague upon those who step on it unawares. 
The **Mole** <note>original: *Talpa*</note> is so named because it is condemned to perpetual blindness and darkness. It is without eyes; it always digs the earth, casts out soil, and eats the roots beneath the crops. The Greeks call it *asphala*. 
**Dormice** <note>original: *Glis*</note> are so named because sleep makes them fat. For we say "to grow" <note>original: *gliscere*</note> is to increase. They sleep through the whole winter and lie motionless as if dead; they come back to life in the summer time. 
The **Hedgehog** <note>original: *Heritius*</note> is an animal covered in spines, and its name is derived from the way it "bristles up" <note>original: *subrigit*</note> when it is enclosed by its spines, by which it is protected on all sides against ambushes. For as soon as it senses anything, it first bristles up and, turning into a ball, withdraws into its own weapons. It possesses a certain cleverness: when it has cut a grape from the vine, it rolls onto its back over it and thus carries it to its young.
The **Cricket** <note>original: *Grillus*</note> gets its name from the sound of its voice. It walks backward, bores into the earth, and chirps at night. It is hunted by putting an ant tied to a hair into its burrow, after blowing in a little dust so it doesn't hide; thus it is dragged out by many ants. 
The **Ant** <note>original: *Formica*</note> is so named because it carries crumbs of grain <note>original: *ferat micas farris*</note>. Its cleverness is great, for it provides for the future and prepares in summer what it may eat in winter. During the harvest, it chooses wheat and does not touch barley. When it rains upon its grain, it throws it all out. They say that in Ethiopia there are ants shaped like dogs which dig up golden sands with their feet; they guard these so no one may take them, and they pursue those who seize them to the death. 
The **Ant-lion** <note>original: *Formicoleon*</note> is so called because it is either a "lion of ants" or certainly part ant and part lion. It is a small animal, quite hostile to ants, which hides itself in the dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is called a "lion" because it is to ants what a lion is to other animals, though it is itself like an ant to others.

### On Serpents: Chapter IIII.

**Snake** <note>original: *Anguis*</note> is the name for the whole genus of serpents because they can be folded and twisted; hence "anguis" because it is angular <note>original: *angulosus*</note> and never straight. Among the ancients, snakes were always held as the guardian spirits of places <note>original: *genijs locoz*</note>. Thus Persius says: "Paint two snakes; boys, the place is sacred." It is established that the **Coluber** <note>adder/snake</note> is so named because it "inhabits shadows" <note>original: *colat vmbras*</note> or because it glides in slippery <note>original: *lubricos*</note> paths with sinuous bends. For whatever slips while being held is called "slippery," such as a fish or a serpent. The **Serpent** <note>original: *Serpens*</note> took its name because it "creeps" <note>original: *serpint*</note> by hidden approaches; it does not crawl with obvious steps, but by the smallest pressures of its scales. Those animals which move on four feet, such as lizards and newts, are not called serpents but "reptiles." However, serpents are reptiles because they crawl on their belly and breast. There are as many poisons as there are kinds; as many destructions as there are species; and as many pains as there are colors.
The **Dragon** <note>original: *Draco*</note> is the largest of all serpents, or indeed of all living things on earth. The Greeks call this *drakon* <note>original: *δρακοντά*</note>. From this it was derived into Latin as *draco*. Frequently drawn out from caves, it is carried into the air, and the air is stirred up because of it. It is also crested.

### XII

...with a small mouth and narrow pipes through which it draws breath and sticks out its tongue. Its power is not in its teeth, but in its tail, and it causes harm by striking rather than by its bite. It is, however, harmless against poisons; thus, poisons are not necessary for it to cause death, because if it binds anything, it kills it. From it even the elephant is not safe, despite the greatness of its body. For hiding around the paths through which elephants usually walk, it binds their legs with knots and kills them by suffocation. It is born in Ethiopia and in India, in the very heat of perpetual summer.

The **Basilisk** <note>original: *Basiliscus*</note> in Greek is interpreted as "Little King" <note>original: *regulus*</note> in Latin, because it is the king of serpents, so much so that when they see it, they flee, because it kills with its smell. For it even kills a person if it looks at them. Indeed, no flying bird passes unharmed by its sight; although it may be far off, the bird is devoured, consumed by the creature's mouth. It is nevertheless conquered by weasels, which people place there in the caverns in which the basilisks hide. And so, having seen the weasel, the basilisk flees, but the weasel pursues and kills it. For the parent of all things <note>referring to the Creator</note> established nothing without a remedy. It is half a foot in length and marked with white spots. Like the "little kings," scorpions seek out dry places, and after they come to water and bite someone there, they cause them to become hydrophobic and frenzied. The **Sibilus** <note>literally "the Hisser"</note> is the same as the "little king," for it kills with a hiss before it bites or burns.

The **Viper** <note>original: *Vipera*</note> is so named because it gives birth by force <note>original: *vi pariat*</note>. For when its belly has swollen for birth, the young, not waiting for the timely release of nature, burst forth by force, gnawing through the mother's sides, resulting in the mother's death. As Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD) often quoted in medieval texts</note> says: "The viper’s offspring are born by breaking the body." It is said, moreover, that the male spits his seed into the viper's mouth. She, turned to madness by the pleasure of lust, cuts off the male's head, which she has received in her mouth. Thus it happens that both parents perish: the male while mating, the female while giving birth. From the viper are made medicinal lozenges which are called "tyriaci" <note>Theriac; a famous ancient and medieval panacea</note> by the Greeks.

The **Asp** <note>original: *Aspis*</note> is so called because it injects and sprinkles poison with its bite. For the Greeks call poison *ios*, and from this comes "aspis," because it kills with a poisonous bite. There are diverse kinds and species of this creature, with different effects for causing harm. It is said that when the asp begins to suffer the enchanter who calls it forth with certain specific songs to draw it out of its cavern, it—not wishing to come out—presses one ear against the earth and covers and blocks the other with its tail; and so, not hearing those magical voices, it does not go to the enchanter.

The **Dipsas** is a kind of asp, which in Latin is called "the pail" <note>original: *situla*</note>, because whoever it bites perishes from thirst. The **Hypnalis** is a kind of asp named because it kills by sleep; Cleopatra applied this to herself, and thus she was released by a death like sleep. The **Emorrois** asp is so named because whoever is bitten by it sweats blood, so that, with the veins being dissolved, whatever life there is is drawn out through the blood. For in Greek, blood is called *hema*. The **Prester** asp always runs with its mouth open and steaming. Of which the poet <note>Lucan</note> remembers: "And the greedy prester stretching its steaming mouth." This creature, whomever it strikes, causes them to swell up, and kills them with enormous corpulence; for rot follows the distension. The **Septabisicus** asp is one that, when it bites a person, immediately consumes them so that the whole person melts away in the mouth of the serpent.

The **Cerastes** serpent is so named because it has horns on its head similar to those of rams; for the Greeks call horns *kerata*.

<column-break/>

They have four small horns, which they show as a sort of bait to entice and kill animals that are provoked by them. For the serpent hides its whole body in the sands and offers no sign of itself, except for that part by which it captures birds or animals by imitation. It is, moreover, more flexible than other serpents, so much so that it seems not to have a spine.

The **Scitalis** serpent is so named because it shines with such variety on its back that the beauty of its markings slows down those who look upon it. And because it is slower at crawling, it captures those whom it cannot overtake because they are stunned by the wonder of it. It is of such great heat that even in the time of winter it sheds the skin of its burning body. Of which Lucan says: "And the scitalis, alone even now when the frosts are scattered, about to lay aside its skin."

The **Amphisbaena** <note>original: *Amphibena*</note> is so named because it has two heads: one in its proper place and the other at the tail. It runs from both heads with a circular pull of its body. This alone among serpents commits itself to the cold, preceding all others. Of which the same Lucan says: "And the heavy amphisbaena turning toward its twin heads." Its eyes shine like lamps.

The **Enidris** is a water-snake living in the water; for the Greeks call water *hydor*. The **Hydros** is a water-serpent from whose strike people swell up. A certain disease of this is called "boa," because it is cured by the dung of an ox <note>original: *bos*</note>. The **Hydra** is a dragon of many heads, such as was in the Lernean swamp in the province of Arcadia. This is called *excedra* in Latin, because when one head was cut off, three heads grew back. But this is a fable. For it is established that the "Hydra" was a place vomiting forth waters that wasted the neighboring city, in which, when one channel was closed, many broke out. When Hercules saw this, he burned the places and closed the water channels. For "hydra" is named from "water" <note>original: *aqua*</note>.

The **Chelydros** serpent is called as if it were a "land-water" snake <note>original: *chersydros*</note>, because it dwells both in waters and on land. For the Greeks call the land *chersos* and water *hydor*. This serpent makes the earth smoke through which it glides. Thus Macer <note>Aemilius Macer, a Roman didactic poet</note> describes it: "Whether the foaming backs exhale poison, or the foul snake smokes where it glides." And Lucan: "And the path of the chelydros with a smoking track." For it always walks straight; if it twists itself while running, it immediately cracks.

The **Rinatris** is a serpent that infects water with poison. In whatever spring it has been, it mixes its poison with it. Of which Lucan says: "The Rinatris, the violator of water." The **Cenchris** is a wandering serpent that always makes its way straight. Of which Lucan: "And the cenchris always about to glide in a straight path." The **Parias** is a serpent that always walks on its tail and seems to make a furrow. Of which the same Lucan: "The parias, content to plow its path with its tail."

The **Boas** is a snake of Italy of immense mass; it pursues herds of cattle and buffalo, and it attaches itself to udders flowing with much milk and kills them by sucking; and from this "depopulation of cattle" <note>original: *boum populatione*</note> it received the name *boas*. The **Iaculus** <note>literally "the Javelin"</note> is a flying serpent, of which Lucan says: "And the winged iaculi." For they leap from trees, and when any animal comes their way, they hurl themselves upon it and kill it. Thus they are called "iaculi" <note>darts or javelins</note>. In Arabia, moreover, there are serpents with wings which are called **Sirens**, which run faster than horses; it is also said that they fly. Their poison is so great that death follows the bite before the pain. The **Dipsas** is so named because it has the color of sand. Of which the poet: "And the dipsas painted with small spots..."

<meta>This page continues the catalog of serpents from the previous page, specifically detailing smaller varieties like the seps and dipsas, before moving on to lizards, the general nature of venom, and the beginning of a new chapter on "worms" (invertebrates).</meta>

...of a uniform color; it is found among dug-up and mixed sands. The **Seps** <note>A legendary snake whose venom was said to decompose the body instantly</note> is a tiny creeping thing, which consumes not only the flesh but even the bones with its venom. The poet Lucilius mentions it thus: "The wasting seps, dissolving bones along with the body." <note>original: *Ossaqué dissoluens cum corpore tabificus seps*</note> The **Dipsas** <note>From the Greek word for "thirst"; its bite was famously said to cause unquenchable thirst</note> is a serpent reported to be of such smallness that it is not even seen when stepped upon. Its venom kills before it is felt, so that the face of the deceased is calm and does not show the sadness of one about to die. Concerning this, the poet says: "Aulus, a standard-bearer of Tyrrhenian blood, stepped on and was bitten by a **Dipsas** with its head twisted back. Scarcely was there pain or the feeling of a tooth." <note>A reference to Lucan’s *Pharsalia*</note> The **Salpinga** is a serpent that is not seen. The **Blind-worm** <note>original: *Lęcula*, likely a corruption of *Caecilia*</note> is so named because it is small and has no eyes. The **Centipede** is named for its multitude of feet. The **Caterpillar** <note>original: *Brucus*; often referring to a locust in its wingless stage</note> is a creature whose nearly entire body is gathered into its belly.

The **Lizard** <note>original: *Lacertus*</note> is a genus of reptile, so named because it has "arms" <note>original: *brachia*; a play on the word *lacertus*, which can mean 'upper arm' in Latin</note>. There are many kinds of lizards, such as the **Botrax**, the **Salamander**, the **Saura**, and the **Stellio**. The **Botrax** is named because it has the face of a frog; for the Greeks call a frog *botracam* <note>original: *botrachos* / βάτραχος</note>. The **Salamander** is so named because it is strong against fires; among all venomous creatures, its power is the greatest. For while others strike individuals, this one kills many at once. For if it crawls into a tree, it infects all the fruit with venom and kills those who eat them; even if it falls into a well, the power of its venom kills those who drink from it. This creature, resisting fire, is the only animal that extinguishes flames. Indeed, it lives in the midst of flames without pain or being consumed, and not only does it not burn, but it puts out the fire. The **Saura** lizard is so called because when it grows old, its eyes fail; it then enters a hole in a wall facing the east, and stretching its eyes toward the sun, it is restored to sight. The **Stellio** <note>Likely a gecko or a starred lizard</note> takes its name from its color. For its back is painted with shining spots in the manner of stars. Concerning this, Ovid says: "It has a name suited to its color, its body starred with various spots." <note>original: *Aptumqué colori nomen habet. varijs stellatus corpore guttis*</note> This creature is said to be so contrary to scorpions that its mere sight brings them fear and paralysis. There are also other kinds of serpents, such as the **Admodice**, the **Elephantie**, and the **Chamedracontes**. Ultimately, there are as many types of deaths as there are names for these creatures.

However, all serpents are cold by nature, and they do not strike except when they are warm. For when they are cold, they touch nothing. Thus, their venom is more harmful by day than by night. They are sluggish in the chill of the night, and rightly so, because they are cooled by the nocturnal dew. They draw into themselves the vapor of a frozen plague's body and are cold by nature. For this reason, they are twisted into knots in winter and loosened in summer. This is why, when someone is struck by a serpent's venom, they are first numbed, and later, when the poison itself has flared up and warmed within them, it kills the person immediately. **Venom** <note>original: *Uenenum*</note> is so called because it travels through the **veins** <note>original: *venas*</note>. For the assault of its plague runs through the veins, increased by the heat of the body, and extinguishes the soul. Thus, venom cannot cause harm unless it touches a person's blood. Lucan says: "The harm of serpents is a plague only when mixed with blood." <note>original: *Noxia serpentium est admixte sanguine pestis*</note> Furthermore, all venom is cold, and therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees the cold venom. Among the natural gifts that we see are common

<column-break/>

to us and to irrational animals, the serpent excels in a certain liveliness of the senses. Hence we read in Genesis: "Now the serpent was wiser than all the beasts of the earth." <note>Genesis 3:1</note> Pliny says, if it is to be believed, that a serpent’s head lives on even if it escapes with only two fingers' width of its body. For this reason, it offers its whole body to those who strike it, in order to protect its head. All snakes have dim vision. They rarely look straight ahead, and not without reason, since they do not have eyes in their forehead but in their temples, so that they hear sooner than they see. No animal moves its tongue with such speed as the serpent, so much so that it seems to have a triple tongue when it is actually only one. The bodies of serpents are moist, so that they mark their path with moisture wherever they go. The tracks of serpents are such that, although they seem to lack feet, they crawl by the effort of their ribs and scales, which they have arranged in an even manner from the top of the throat to the bottom of the belly. They lean on their scales as if on claws, and on their ribs as if on legs. Hence, if it is struck in any part of its body from the belly to the head, it is rendered weak and cannot run, because wherever that blow falls, it breaks the spine, which acted as the "feet" of the ribs and the movement of the body. Serpents are said to live a long time, so much so that they are reported to put away old age and return to youth by shedding their old skin. The skins of serpents are called **sloughs** <note>original: *exuviae*</note> because they strip themselves <note>original: *exuunt*</note> of these when they grow old; having stripped them off, they return to youth. They are also called *induvię*, because they strip off and are clothed again. Pythagoras says that a serpent is created from the marrow of a dead man's spine; Ovid also mentions this in the books of the *Metamorphoses*, saying: "There are those who believe human marrow turns into a snake when the spine has rotted in a closed tomb." This happens rightly, so that just as man's death came through a serpent, so through man's death a serpent is produced. It is also said that a serpent does not dare to touch a naked man.

### On Worms Chapter 5

<image-desc>A large rubricated initial letter U (V), containing a woodcut-style illustration of a figure standing beside a tall narrow structure, possibly a tomb or a hive.</image-desc>

**A** **worm** <note>original: *Uermis*</note> is an animal that is mostly born from flesh, or wood, or any earthly thing without any mating, although sometimes they are born from eggs, such as the scorpion. Worms are either of the earth, the water, the air, the flesh, the leaves, the wood, or of clothing. The **Spider** <note>original: *Aranea*</note> is a worm of the air, named after its nourishment from the air; with its tiny body, it draws out long threads and, always intent on its web, never ceases to work, enduring a perpetual suspension in its labor. The **Leech** <note>original: *Sanguisuga*, literally "blood-sucker"</note> is a water worm: so named because it sucks blood. For it lies in wait for those drinking, and when it glides into their throats or attaches anywhere else, it draws blood. When it is soaked with too much gore, it vomits what it has swallowed so that it may suck fresh blood again. The **Scorpion** is an earth worm, which is ascribed to the worms rather than the serpents; it is an animal armed with a sting, and from this it is named in Greek because it strikes with its tail and spreads venom through a curved wound.
