<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of serpents and small reptiles, concluding the section on worms (invertebrates) before transitioning to a major new chapter on the nature and classification of fishes and sea creatures.</meta>

It is a characteristic of the **scorpion** <note>original: *scorpionis*</note> that it does not strike the palm of the hand. The **cantharid** <note>original: *cantareda*; the blister beetle or Spanish fly</note> is an earth-worm which, as soon as it is applied to the human body, produces blisters full of fluid by its burning nature. The **millipede** <note>original: *multipos*; literally 'many-footed'</note> is an earth-worm named for its multitude of feet; when touched, it curls itself up into a ball. It is born under stones from moisture and earth. The **slug** <note>original: *limax*</note> is called a "worm of the mud" <note>original: *limi*</note> because it is born in or from the mud; hence it is always filthy and unclean. The **silkworm** <note>original: *bombyx*</note> is a worm of the leaves, from whose weaving "bombycine" <note>silk</note> fabric is made. It is called by this name because it "empties" itself while producing threads, and only air remains within it. The **caterpillar** <note>original: *eruca*</note> is a worm of the leaves, found wrapped in vegetables or vine-shoots; it is named from "gnawing" <note>original: *erodendo*</note>. Plautus mentions it, imitating a wicked and harmful beast wrapped in a vine-shoot. It folds itself up and does not fly like the locust, running here and there and leaving its work half-eaten; instead, it remains upon the crops destined to perish, consuming everything with its slow crawl and sluggish habits. The Greeks call "wood-worms" **teredonans** <note>original: *teredonas*</note> because they eat by "boring" <note>original: *terendo*</note>. We call these **termites**. For among the Latins, wood-worms are called those which trees produce when cut at an inopportune time. The **moth** <note>original: *linea*; likely clothes moth larvae</note> is a worm of garments, so named because it "holds" <note>original: *teneat*</note> and settles there until it gnaws through. Hence it is "persistent" because it remains active in the same thing repeatedly. Worms of the flesh include the **migraine-worm** <note>original: *emigraneus*</note>, the **earthworm** <note>original: *lumbricus*</note>, **pinworms** <note>original: *ascaride*</note>, **maggots** <note>original: *costi*</note>, **lice** <note>original: *pediculi*</note>, **fleas** <note>original: *pulices*</note>, **nits** <note>original: *lender*</note>, the **lard-worm** <note>original: *tarmus*</note>, the **tick** <note>original: *ricinus*</note>, the **pig-worm** <note>original: *usia*</note>, and the **bedbug** <note>original: *cimex*</note>. The **migraine-worm** is called a worm of the head. The **intestinal worm** is called *lumbricus* as if it were "slippery" <note>original: *lubricus*</note> because it glides, or because it lives in the "loins" <note>original: *lumbis*</note>. Pinworms, maggots, and lice are worms of the skin; lice are named from "feet" <note>original: *pedibus*</note>, hence those in whose bodies lice swarm are called "pediculous." **Fleas** are so named because they are nourished more by "dust" <note>original: *puluere*</note>. The **lard-worm** is a worm of bacon. The **tick** is a worm of the dog, so named because it clings to the ears of dogs; for in Greek, a dog is called *linos* <note>original: *lykos* or *kyon*; the text likely contains a scribal error or folk etymology here</note>. The **usia** is a worm of the pig, so named because it "burns" <note>original: *urit*</note>. For where it bites, the place burns so much that blisters immediately form there. The **bedbug** is named from the similarity to a certain herb whose stench it possesses. Properly speaking, a **worm** <note>original: *vermis*</note> is born in putrefied flesh, a **moth** <note>original: *tinea*</note> in clothes, a **caterpillar** in vegetables, a **wood-worm** in wood, and a **lard-worm** in bacon. A worm does not crawl with open steps or the thrust of scales like a serpent, because it lacks the stiffness of a spine; like the snake, it moves the parts of its little body forward step by step, stretching out those that were contracted and contracting those that were stretched, and so, once set in motion, it glides along.

## On Fishes Cap. VI.

**Fishes** <note>original: *pisces*</note> are named from "pasture" <note>original: *pasciendo*</note>, just as "livestock" <note>original: *pecus*</note> is. These creatures that swim are called **reptiles** because they have the appearance and nature of creeping; for although they immerse themselves in the depths, they "creep" while swimming. Hence David says: **"This great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number."** <note>A quote from Psalm 104:25</note> **Amphibians** <note>original: *anfinia*</note> are certain kinds of fish so named because they have the habit of walking on land and the duty of swimming in the waters. For "amphi" in Greek means "both," that is, they live in both water and land, such as seals, crocodiles, and hippo-

<column-break/>

-potami, which are "river horses." Men gave names to livestock, beasts, and birds before they did to fishes, because the former were seen and known earlier. Later, as the types of fishes were gradually recognized, names were established either from a similarity to land animals, or from their appearance, habits, color, shape, or sex. From similarity to land animals come: **sea-frogs**, **sea-lions**, **sea-calves** <note>seals</note>, **black sea-merles**, and **sea-peacocks** which are multicolored on their backs and necks, **sea-thrushes** with white spots, and others which claimed names for themselves based on species of land animals. From the habits of land animals: **sea-dogs** <note>sharks</note> are named after land dogs because they bite, and **sea-wolves** because they pursue others with wicked voracity. From color: **shadow-fish** <note>original: *umbrae*</note> because they are the color of a shadow; **gilt-heads** <note>original: *auratę*</note> because they have a gold color on their heads; and **trout** <note>original: *varij*</note> from their variety of spots, which the common people call *tructas*. From shape: the **orb-fish** <note>pufferfish/sunfish</note>, because it is round and consists almost entirely of a head; and the **sole** <note>original: *solea*</note> because it is like the "soles" <note>original: *solijs*</note> of shoes. From sex: the **musculus** <note>pilot fish</note>, because it is said to be the male of the whale; for it is said that the whale conceives through its mating. Hence also the "muscles" of snails, from whose milk oysters are said to conceive. **Whales** <note>original: *balenę*</note> are beasts of immense size, named from "emitting" and "pouring out" water; for in Greek, *ballein* <note>original: βάλλειν</note> means "to throw." They are called **cete** <note>original: τò κῆτος καὶ τὰ κήτη</note> because of their monstrous size. For they are a massive kind of sea-monster with bodies equal to mountains, such as the whale that swallowed Jonah, whose belly was of such great size that it held the likeness of the underworld, as the prophet said: "He heard me from the belly of hell." **Sea-horses** are like horses in their front part, but the back part ends in a fish. They say **bocas** are sea-oxen <note>original: *boacas*</note>. **Azure-fish** <note>original: *cerulei*</note> are named from their color, for azure is green mixed with black, like the sea. **Dolphins** <note>original: *delphines*</note> have a specific name because they follow the human voice, or because they gather together at the sound of music. Nothing in the sea is swifter than they. For they often fly over ships by leaping. When they play in the waves and throw themselves with headlong leaps through the movement of the waters, they are seen to signal storms. These are specifically called "Simons." There is also a kind of dolphin in the Nile with a saw-like back that kills crocodiles by cutting their soft bellies. **Sea-pigs**, commonly called "swinish," dig up the earth under the water like pigs while seeking food. They have the function of a mouth near the throat, and unless they submerge their snouts in the sands, they cannot gather food. **Sea-ravens** <note>original: *lozui*, likely a corruption of *corvi*</note> are named from the sound of their "heart" <note>original: *cordis*</note>, because they grunt from their chest, and are caught when betrayed by their own voice. **Tuna** <note>original: *tinni*</note> have a Greek name. They enter [the Mediterranean] in the springtime; they enter on the right side and exit on the left. This is believed to be because they see more sharply with their right eyes than with their left. The **swordfish** <note>original: *gladius*</note> is so called because it is born with a large snout, and because of this, it sinks ships by piercing them. The **sawfish** <note>original: *serra*</note> is so named because it has a serrated crest, and swimming under a ship, it cuts it. The **sea-scorpion** <note>original: *scorpio*</note> is so called because it stings when picked up by hand. They say that if ten crabs are tied with a handful of basil, all the scorpions that are there will gather in that place. The **spider-fish** <note>original: *aranea*; weaver fish</note> is so called because it strikes with a "sting" <note>original: *aure* - likely a corruption of *aculeo*</note>. For it has spikes with which it strikes. The **crocodile** is named from its "saffron" <note>original: *crocco*</note> color.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion of terrestrial "worms" and insects into the vast world of aquatic creatures, beginning with the crocodile and the hippopotamus before detailing various species of fish and shellfish. It follows the encyclopedic tradition of explaining an animal's nature through the origin of its name.</meta>

### Book on the Nature of Aquatic Creatures

[The **crocodile**] is born in the Nile. It is a four-footed animal that is powerful both on land and in the water. It usually grows to a length of twenty cubits and is armed with a terrifying array of teeth and claws. Its skin is of such great hardness that it does not even feel the blows of heavy stones bouncing off its back. It rests in the water at night and on the ground by day. While brooding on land, the male and female take turns guarding the spot. Certain fish with serrated dorsal fins kill it by slicing open its soft belly. It is said to be the only living creature that moves its upper jaw.

The **hippopotamus** <note>original: *Hippotamus*</note> is so called because it resembles a horse in its back, its mane, and its neighing. It has a snout that turns upward from its front teeth, a twisted tail, and cloven hooves. It stays in the waters during the day and grazes on crops at night; it, too, is produced by the Nile.

The **sea-bream** <note>original: *Pagrum*</note>, which the Greeks call *fagron*, is so named because it has such hard teeth that it feeds on oysters in the sea.

The **dentex** <note>original: *Dentix*</note> is named for the multitude and great size of its teeth.

The **sea-hare** <note>original: *Lepus*</note> is named for the resemblance of its head to that of a land hare.

The **sea-wolf** <note>original: *Lupus*; likely the European sea bass</note> is named, as has been said, for its greed; it is a very clever fish at avoiding capture. Indeed, it is said that when surrounded by nets, it plows the sand with its tail and, having hidden itself thus, allows the net to pass over it.

The **mullet** <note>original: *Mullus*</note> is so called because it is soft <note>original: *mollis*</note> and very tender. It is said that eating it inhibits lust and dulls the sharpness of the eyes. Men who have frequently eaten it smell of fish. If a mullet is killed in wine, those who drink from it will develop a loathing for wine.

The **mugil** <note>original: *Mugilis*; a grey mullet</note> takes its name from being very agile <note>original: *agilis*</note>. For when it senses the traps set by fishermen, it immediately turns back and leaps over the net so that you would think the fish was flying.

The **blacktail** <note>original: *Melanurus*</note> is so named because it has a black tail, black fins, and black lines along its body. For the Greeks call black *melan*.

The **glaucus** is named for its color, because it is white. For the Greeks call white *glaucon*. This fish rarely appears in summer, except in cloudy weather.

The **grayling** <note>original: *Timallus*</note> takes its name from a flower; for thyme <note>original: *Timum*</note> is what the flower is called. While it is pleasing in appearance and delightful in flavor, it also smells like the flower and emits a fragrant odor from its body.

The **parrot-fish** <note>original: *Escarus*</note> is so named because it is said to be the only fish that chews the cud <note>ruminates</note>. Indeed, other fish do not ruminate. It is also said to be very clever; for when trapped in wicker baskets, it does not try to break out head-first or stick its head into the dangerous gaps, but instead uses repeated strikes of its tail to loosen the opening and thus escapes backward. If another parrot-fish on the outside sees its struggle, it helps the one breaking out by gripping its tail in its mouth and pulling.

The **sparus** <note>a species of sea-bream</note> takes its name from a throwing spear <note>original: *sparus*</note> because it is of the same shape. For terrestrial things were discovered before marine ones. A *sparus* is a rustic missile weapon, named from "scattering" <note>original: *spargendo*</note>.

The **southern fish** <note>original: *Australis piscis*</note> is so called either because it takes in the waves of water with its mouth or because it rises at the time when the Pleiades begin to set toward the west.

The **amio** is marked on its left and right sides with continuous purple stripes and other different colors. It is called *amio* because it is not caught except by a hook <note>original: *hamo*</note>.

The **remora** <note>original: *Echinus*; likely a confusion with the *Echeneis* or 'ship-holder'</note> is a tiny fish only half a foot long. It takes its name from the fact that it holds back a ship by clinging to it. Though winds may rage and storms howl, the ship nevertheless seems to stand rooted in the sea and cannot be moved—not by being held back, but merely by the fish clinging to it. The Latins called this fish *mora* <note>delay</note> because it forces vessels to stand still.

The **stargazer** <note>original: *Uranoscopus*</note> is named from the

<column-break/>

eye which it has on its head, with which it always looks upward.

The **flying fish** <note>original: *Millago*</note> is named because it flies above the water. Whenever it is seen flying out of the water, it indicates that the weather is changing.

The **angelshark** <note>original: *Squatus*</note> is named because it has sharp scales <note>original: *squamis*</note>. Because of this, wood is polished with its skin.

The city of Syria which is now called Tyre was formerly called *Sarra*, after a certain fish which is abundant there, which they call *sar* in their own language. From this similarity is derived the names of the small fish called **sardas** and **sardines**.

The **allec** is a tiny fish suitable for making a salty liquid <note>original: *salsamento*; likely referring to garum or fish sauce</note>, which is why it is so named.

The **affozus** is a tiny fish which, because of its smallness, cannot be caught with a hook.

The **eel** <note>original: *Anguille*</note> is given its name from its resemblance to a snake <note>original: *anguis*</note>. Its origin is from mud <note>original: *limo*</note>. Thus, when it is caught, it is so slippery that the harder you press it, the more quickly it slips away. They say that the Ganges river of the East produces eels thirty feet long. If eels are killed in wine, those who drink of it will develop a loathing for wine.

The **sea dragon** <note>original: *Draco marinus*</note> has spikes on its gills pointing toward the tail. When it strikes, it pours out venom wherever it hits; thus it is so named.

The **moray eel** <note>the Greeks call it *mirenam*</note> is so named because it coils itself into circles. They say that this fish is only of the female sex and conceives from a serpent. For this reason, it is called out and caught by fishermen by a whistling sound, as if by a serpent. It is killed with difficulty by a blow from a club, but instantly by a light rod <note>original: *ferula*</note>. It is certain that its life is in its tail; for if struck on the head, it is hardly killed, but if struck on the tail, it dies immediately.

The **conger** <note>original: *Congrus*</note> is similar to an eel but large; it dwells in the hollows of rocks under the water.

The **octopus** <note>original: *Polipus*</note>—that is, "many-footed"—for it has many nerves. This clever creature, when seeking the hook, embraces it with its gills <note>arms</note> rather than biting it, and does not let go until it has gnawed the bait all around.

The **torpedo** <note>the electric ray</note> is so called because it causes the body to grow numb <note>original: *torpescere*</note> if anyone touches it while it is alive. Pliny the Elder tells of the Indian Sea that the torpedo can numb even the strongest arms from a distance and far away, even if touched only by a spear or a rod, and can bind feet however fast they are at running. So great is its power that it affects the limbs even by the "aura" of its body.

The **cuttlefish** <note>original: *Sepia*</note> is so named because it is more easily caught when it is enclosed. In mating, it is a shameful kind; for it conceives through the mouth just like a viper. Its ink <note>original: *attramenti*</note> is of such great power that some claim that if it is added to a lamp, the people present seem to look like Ethiopians once the primary light is removed.

The **squid** <note>original: *Lulligo*</note>: they say that in the ocean of Mauritania, not far from the Lirus river, such a great multitude of squid fly out of the water that they can even sink ships.

**Shellfish** <note>original: *Conche* and *concleae*</note> are named for this reason: they are hollowed out <note>original: *cauantur*</note>—that is, emptied—when the moon wanes. For the limbs of all enclosed sea animals and shells swell with the waxing of the moon and are emptied at its waning. For the moon, when it is increasing, increases moisture, but when it begins to wane, the moisture decreases. This is what the natural philosophers say. *Conche* is the name of the primary form, while *concleae* is the diminutive, as if "little shells."

There are many kinds of shells, among which are the pearl-bearers called *celoe*. In their flesh, a precious stone solidifies. Regarding these, those who have written on the nature of animals say that they seek the shores at night and conceive the **pearl** from the dew of heaven; hence they are named *celoe* <note>heavenly</note>.

The **murex** is a sea-shell, named for its sharpness <note>original: *acumine*</note> and roughness; it is known by another name as the *conchilium* <note>the source of purple dye</note>.

<keywords>crocodile, hippopotamus, fish etymology, mullet, eel, octopus, torpedo ray, pearls, shellfish, Isidore of Seville, marine biology</keywords>

--- Page 137 ---
<meta>This page continues the encyclopedic survey of the animal kingdom, transitioning from the description of sea-wolves (bass) and predatory fish to the classification of shellfish, frogs, sponges, and finally the vast world of birds.</meta>

...on account of which, when it is cut with iron, it emits tears of a purple color, from which purple dye is stained. From this, it is called *ostrum* <note>purple dye or shell</note> because this dye is drawn from the moisture of the shell.

**Crabs** <note>original: *Cancros*</note> are so called because they are shellfish with legs. They are animals that are enemies to oysters. Indeed, they live off their flesh with remarkable ingenuity. Since the oyster's strong shell cannot be forced open, the crab waits for when the oyster opens its gates. Then, the crab secretly throws in a small stone, and with the closing hindered, it devours the oyster's flesh. Some say that if you carry ten crabs tied with a handful of basil <note>likely *ocimum* (basil), though the OCR reads *optimi*</note>, all the scorpions in that place will gather together. There are two kinds of crabs: river and sea.

The **oyster** <note>original: *Ostrea*</note> is named after its shell <note>Latin: *testa*</note>, which protects the softness of the inner flesh. The Greeks call a shell *ostrea*. The word *ostrea* is neuter, but they refer to its flesh in the feminine gender.

**Mussels** <note>original: *Musculi*</note> are, as we said before, shellfish of the waters; they are called *musculi* as if they were "little males" <note>Latin: *quasi masculi*</note> because oysters conceive from their milt <note>Latin: *lacte*, literally "milk"</note>.

**Pelozides** <note>likely a variety of clam</note> are named after Cape Pelorus in Sicily where they are abundant. Whence Virgil says: "Behold, the North Wind from the narrow seat of Pelorus."

**Ungues** <note>literally "nails," referring to razor clams</note> are named for their resemblance to human fingernails.

The **turtle** or **tortoise** <note>original: *Testudo*</note> is named because it is covered by the protection of a shell in the manner of a vaulted chamber <note>Latin: *camerae*</note>. There are four kinds: land, sea, mud-dwellers (those living in filth and marshes), and the fourth kind are river-dwellers that live in fresh water. Some report—though it is incredible—that ships carrying the right foot of a sea turtle travel more slowly.

The **sea urchin** <note>original: *Icinus*</note> takes its name from the land urchin, which common people call a hedgehog <note>original: *heritius*</note>. Its small shell is double and prickly with spines like chestnuts when they fall from trees while still covered. Its flesh is soft and similar to vermilion.

The term **Tris** is said in three ways: tortoise, *pelozus*, and shell. For both the thing we eat and the place where the meat is are called *pelozus*.

**Frogs** <note>original: *Ranae*</note> are named for their chattering <note>Latin: *garrulitate*</note>, because they make a noise around the marshes where they breed and produce sounds with annoying cries. Some are called aquatic, some marsh-frogs, and some "bramble-frogs" <note>original: *rubetae*</note> because they live among brambles; these are the largest of all. Others are called *calamites* <note>reed-frogs</note> because they live among reeds and shrubs; they are the smallest of all, very green, and are mute without a voice. **Agridulae** are small frogs that stay in dry places or fields, which is how they got their name. Some say that dogs will not bark if a live frog is given to them in a piece of food.

The **sponge** <note>original: *Spungia*</note> is named from *fingere*, which means to make neat and to wipe. Afranius says: "I come to you to 'mold' your neck with a cloth," meaning to wipe it. Cicero says: "And he 'molded' the blood with sponges," meaning he wiped it away. That it is an animal is shown by the blood that clings to the rocks; when it is cut away, it emits blood. Some things live in the water and run about like fish; others are fixed, like oysters, urchins, and sponges. Of these, some are called "males" because their tubes are thin and denser; others "females," which have larger and continuous tubes; others are harder, which the Greeks call *tragos* <note>literally "goats"</note>, and we can call "goat-like" due to their roughness. The softest kind is called **penicilli** <note>little brushes</note> because they are suitable for swelling of the eyes and for wiping away discharge.

<column-break/>

They are useful. White sponges are made through care. During the summer, they are spread out in the sun and, like Punic wax, they drink in the whiteness.

Chapter 57. The names of all animals living in the waters. Pliny says: they are divided into types of sea monsters, serpents common to land and water, crabs, shells, lobsters, pelozides, octopuses, soles, lizards, and squids, and others like these. Many of these, through a certain natural understanding, recognize the order of their own seasons; others wander in their own places without change. Among fish, some females conceive and give birth to young through mating with a male. Others lay eggs without having mated; these eggs are then fertilized by the male's milt being cast over them in the following discharge. Those that have been breathed upon by this gift become capable of life; those not covered remain sterile or rot.

### On Birds, Chapter 7.

"Bird" is a single name, but the kind is diverse. For just as they differ from each other in appearance, so they differ in the diversity of their natures. Some are simple, like doves; others are cunning, like the partridge; some submit themselves to the hand, like the hawk; others are fearful, like the *garamantes*; some delight in the company of men, like the swallow; others love a secret life in the wilderness, like the turtledove; some feed only on found seeds, like the goose; others eat meat and focus on prey, like the kite. Some are residents that always stay in their places, like the ostrich; others are visitors that return at their proper times, like storks and swallows. Some eat together and fly in flocks, like starlings and quails; others are solitary wanderers for the purpose of ambushing prey, like the eagle and the hawk, and whatever others are like that. Some chatter with voices, like the swallow; others produce the sweetest songs, like the swan and the blackbird. Others imitate the words and voices of humans, like the parrot and the magpie. But there are countless others, differing in both kind and character. No one can find out how many kinds of birds there are. For who could penetrate the deserts of India, Ethiopia, or Scythia to know their kind or differences?

**Birds** <note>original: *Aves*</note> are so named because they do not have fixed paths, but wander wherever they go through trackless places <note>Latin: *pavia*</note>. They are called *alires* because they head for the heights with wings <note>Latin: *alis*</note> and ascend to the heavens by the rowing of their wings. **Winged creatures** <note>original: *Volucres*</note> are named from flying (*volando*); for we say "walking" from where we walk, and "flying" from where we fly. For the middle part of the foot or hand is called the *vola* <note>the palm or sole</note>, and in birds, the *vola* is the middle part of the wings by whose motion the feathers are moved. Hence they are called *volucres*.

**Chicks** <note>original: *Pulli*</note> is the name for the offspring of birds. But the offspring of four-footed animals are also called *pulli*, and a small person is called a *pullus*. Therefore, the newly born are called *pulli* because they are "polluted" <note>original: *polluti*; referring to the state of being wet or stained at birth</note>. From this, black clothing is also called *pulla*.

There are others in which the feathers do not provide the use of flying. These are called *alae* <note>wings</note>. The **feather** <note>original: *Penna*</note> is named from "hanging" (*pendendo*), that is, from flying; hence also "to hang" (*pendere*). For winged creatures are moved by the help of feathers when they entrust themselves to the air.

**Plumage** <note>original: *Pluma*</note> is like *piluma*. For just as there is hair <note>Latin: *pili*</note> on the bodies of four-footed animals, so there is plumage on birds. It is certain that many names of birds are composed from the sound of their voice, such as the crane (*grus*), the crow (*corvus*), the swan (*cygnus*), the peacock (*pavo*), the kite (*miluus*), and the owl (*ulula*).

<summary>This page concludes the study of aquatic life, including the ingenious hunting methods of crabs and the biological nature of sponges, before beginning a detailed classification of birds based on their behavior and the etymology of their names.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medieval encyclopedia's bestiary, moving from aquatic life to the nature and lore of birds. It begins by discussing the origins of bird names based on their vocalizations before detailing specific species starting with the eagle.</meta>

Cuckoos, jackdaws, and others; for the variety of their voices taught men what to name them. The **eagle** <note>Latin: *aquila*</note> is named for the sharpness <note>Latin: *acumen*</note> of its eyes. For it is said to have such great vision that when it hovers over the seas with motionless wings, invisible to human sight, it sees small fish swimming from such a great height, and descending like a sea-diver <note>original: *rosmēri*; likely referring to a diving bird or the sea spray</note>, it drags the seized prey to the shore with its wings. For it is also said not to turn its gaze away from the rays of the sun; hence it even holds its chicks suspended by its claws against the sun's rays. Those it sees keeping a steady gaze, it preserves as worthy of the lineage; if any turn their gaze away, it casts them out as degenerate.

The **vulture** <note>Latin: *vultur*</note> is thought to be named for its slow flight <note>Latin: *volatu tardo*</note>. Because of the great size of its body, it does not have swift flight. Some say of these that they do not engage in mating, but conceive and give birth without intercourse, and that their offspring live for nearly a hundred years. Vultures, like eagles, can sense carcasses even beyond the seas. Indeed, flying higher, many things hidden by the darkness of the mountains they perceive from on high.

The bird called **gradipes** <note>literally "step-foot"</note> by the Greeks is called the **bustard** <note>original: *tarda*</note> among us, because, held back by its heavy flight, it is by no means lifted up by the speed of its wings like other birds.

**Cranes** <note>Latin: *grues*</note>, however, took their name from their own voice, for they murmur with such a sound. When they hurry, they follow one another in the formation of letters. Concerning which Lucan says: "And the letter, disturbed, perishes as the wings are scattered." They seek high places so they may more easily see which lands they are heading toward. The leader encourages the flock with a voice that gathers the line. But when it becomes hoarse, another succeeds it. At night they divide the watches and take turns as sentries, holding small stones in their lifted feet <note>This myth suggests that if the bird falls asleep, the stone drops and wakes it up</note> to ward off sleep. Whatever must be guarded against, a cry indicates. Their color betrays their age, for they turn black in old age.

**Storks** <note>Latin: *ciconię*</note> are named from the sound with which they chatter, as if *cicaniae*; it is established that this is a sound of the mouth rather than the voice, which they make by shaking their beak. These are messengers of spring, companions of society, and enemies of serpents. They fly across the seas and travel into Asia in a gathered flock. **Crows** precede them as leaders, and they follow like an army. They have extraordinary devotion <note>Latin: *pietas*</note> toward their children. For they cherish their nests so dearly that they shed their feathers through constant brooding. However much time they spend in rearing their young, they themselves are fed in turn by their chicks for the same amount of time.

The **swan** is a bird that the Greeks call *cygnus*. It is called **olor** <note>in Latin</note> because it is entirely white in its feathers. For no one remembers a black swan. Indeed, "whole" <note>original: *olos*</note> in Greek means "all." The *cygnus* is named from "singing" <note>Latin: *canēdo*</note> because it pours forth the sweetness of song in modulated tones. They say it sings so sweetly because it has a long and curved neck, and it is inevitable that the voice, struggling through a long and winding path, should produce varied modulations. They say that in the Hyperborean regions <note>the far north</note>, when the lyre-players sing, many swans fly toward them and sing along quite harmoniously. *Olores* is the Latin name, for in Greek they are called *cygni*. Sailors say that this bird provides a good omen for them, as Aemilius says: "The swan is always the most joyful bird in omens; sailors desire it because it does not submerge itself in the waves."

The **ostrich** <note>Latin: *strutio*</note> is called by a Greek name. This animal appears to have feathers like a bird, yet it does not lift itself high from the ground. Because

<column-break/>

it neglects to hatch its own eggs, these, having been cast aside, are brought to life only by the warmth of the dust.

The **heron** is called **ardea**, as if "lofty" <note>Latin: *ardua*</note>, on account of its high flights. Lucan says: "whichever heron dared to fly." For it fears rain and flies above the clouds so that it cannot feel the storms of the clouds. When it flies higher, it signifies a storm. Many call this bird the *tantalus*.

The **phoenix** is a bird of Arabia, named because it has a Phoenician <note>purple-red</note> color, or because it is singular and unique in the whole world. For the Arabs call what is singular and unique "phoenix." Living for five hundred years and more, when it sees that it has grown old, it builds a funeral pyre for itself from gathered twigs of spices. Turning toward the rays of the sun, with a flapping of its wings, it nourishes a voluntary fire for itself, and thus it rises again from its own ashes.

The **cinnamolgus** is also a bird of Arabia, so named because it builds its nests in high groves from cinnamon shrubs. And since men cannot climb there because of the height and fragility of the branches, they bring down those nests with lead-weighted darts, and thus they gather that cinnamon and sell it for higher prices, because merchants value that cinnamon more than others.

The **parrot** <note>Latin: *psitacus*</note> is produced on the shores of India; it is green in color with a purple collar, possessing a large tongue that is wider than other birds'. Whence it expresses articulate words, so that if you did not see it, you would think a human was speaking. By nature, it greets by saying "Hail" <note>original: *aue*</note> or "Greetings" <note>original: *chere*</note>. Other names it learns by instruction. Hence the saying: "I, a parrot, shall learn from you the names of others; this I have learned to say by myself: 'Hail, Caesar!'"

The **halcyon** <note>the kingfisher</note> is a bird of the sea, called as if "ocean bird" because in winter it makes its nests in the still waters of the ocean and rears its chicks. While it broods, it is said that the sea becomes calm over the vast expanse with silent winds for a continuous seven days of tranquility. Nature herself provides this favor for the rearing of the offspring.

The **pelican** is an Egyptian bird living in the solitude of the Nile River, from which it took its name. For "Canopus" <note>a city in the Nile delta</note> is a name for Egypt. It is said—if it be true—that it kills its own young and mourns them for three days; then it wounds itself and, by the sprinkling of its own blood, brings its children back to life.

The **Stymphalian birds** are named after the Stymphalian islands where they are most abundant; Hercules used arrows against them. For they are sea-birds living on islands.

The **birds of Diomedes** are named after the companions of Diomedes, whom legends say were transformed into these very birds; they are similar in form to a coot, the size of swans, white in color, with hard and large beaks. They fly among the cliffs of the shores and rocks around Apulia on the Diomedian island; they distinguish between their own people and strangers. For if someone is Greek, they approach closely and fawningly; if a foreigner, they attack with bites and wound them, grieving with tearful voices, either for their own transformation or for the death of their king. For Diomedes was killed by the Illyrians. These birds are called *diomediae* in Latin; the Greeks call them *herodii*.

The **Memnonides** are Egyptian birds named from the place where Memnon died. For they say they fly in flocks from Egypt to Troy <note>original: *Ilium*</note> near the tomb of Memnon, and hence they call them the "Memnonian birds of Troy" <note>original: *ilicnfes memnonias*</note>. In the fifth year, they come to Troy, and when they have circled for two days, on the third day they enter into battle...

...in turn, it tears itself apart with its talons and beak. **Hercynian birds** <note>original: *Mercynę*; refers to birds of the Hercynian Forest in Germany</note> are named for the Hercynian woods of Germany where they are born. Their feathers shine so brightly through the darkness that, however much the night is shrouded in thick shadows, they light the way to guide one's journey; the path of the road is made clear by the sign of their glowing plumage. The Greeks call the **pelican** <note>original: *Onocrotalon*; literally 'ass-trumpeter'</note> a bird with a long beak. Of these, there are two kinds: one of the water, the other of the desert. The **ibis** is a bird of the Nile river, which purges itself with its beak by pouring water into its anus. It feeds on the eggs of serpents, carrying the most welcome food from them back to its nest. The **meropes** <note>bee-eaters</note>, also called *gauli*, are said to hide and nourish their own parents. The **lozedulus** <note>a bird name possibly corrupted from *acredula* or *regulus*</note> is a winged creature whose name implies "eating the heart." The **jackdaw** <note>Latin: *monedula*</note> is named as if it were a "money-taker"; for whatever gold it finds, it carries off and hides. *Cicero in Pro Valerio Flacco:* "No more gold should be entrusted to you than to a jackdaw." The **bat** <note>Latin: *vespertilio*</note> received its name from the time it appears, because it flies about in the evening twilight <note>Latin: *crepusculo vespertino*</note> while fleeing the light. It is driven by a headlong motion and suspended by the thinnest membranes of its arms; it is a creature similar to a mouse, making a sound not so much with a voice as with a screech. It is a species that is both winged and a quadruped, which is not usually found in other birds. The **nightingale** <note>Latin: *luscinia*</note> took its name because it is accustomed to signal the rising of the new day <note>Latin: *lucis*</note> with its song, as if it were the "light-bringer" <note>Latin: *lucinia*</note>. The same bird is also called the **acredula**, about which *Cicero* writes in the *Prognostics*: "And the morning singer <note>original: *acredula*</note> practices her dawn songs." The **screech owl** <note>Latin: *ulula*</note> is named from the Greek word *ololyzein* <note>original: ἀπό τοῦ ὀλολύζειν</note>, that is, named from wailing and mourning. For when it cries out, it either imitates weeping or groaning. Whence among augurs, if it laments, it is said to show sadness; if it is silent, it is said to show prosperity. The **eagle owl** <note>Latin: *bubo*</note> has a name composed from the sound of its voice. It is a bird of ill omen, burdened indeed with feathers, but always held back by a heavy sluggishness. It dwells in sepulchers day and night and always lingers in caverns; of which *Ovid* writes: "A foul bird, the messenger of coming grief; the lazy owl, a dire omen to mortals." Finally, among augurs it is said to portend evil. For when it is seen in a city, they say it signifies desolation. The **little owl** <note>Latin: *noctua*</note> is so called because it flies about at night <note>Latin: *nocte*</note> and cannot see during the day. For when the brightness of the sun arises, its vision is dimmed. The island of Crete does not have this bird. And if it should come from elsewhere, it dies immediately. Now, the little owl is not the eagle owl. For the eagle owl is larger. The **night-raven** <note>original: *nycticorax*</note> is the little owl itself, so called because it loves the night. For it is a bird that flees the light and cannot endure to see the sun. The **strix** <note>a legendary screech owl or vampire-bird</note> is a nocturnal bird having its name from the sound of its voice. For when it cries out, it shrieks <note>Latin: *stridet*</note>. Of which *Lucan* writes: "The sound of the owl, and what the nocturnal strix laments." This bird is commonly called the "Amma" <note>nurse</note>, from "loving" <note>Latin: *amando*</note> little children; whence it is also said to offer milk to infants. The **raven** <note>Latin: *corvus*</note> or *corax* has its name from the sound of its throat, because it croaks with its voice. It is said of this bird that when its chicks are hatched, it does not fully provide them with food until it recognizes in them the likeness of its own color through the blackness of their feathers. But after the black feathers have appeared on them, recognizing them fully, it feeds them more abundantly. When it encounters corpses, it first seeks out the eyes. The **crow** <note>original: *corix*</note>, a long-lived bird, is called by the Latins by its Greek name; the augurs say it concerns itself with the cares of men through its signs, showing the paths of ambushes and predicting the future. It is a great wickedness

<column-break/>

to believe this: that God would entrust his counsels to crows. Among many auspices, it is also credited with portending rain with its voice; whence comes that saying: "Then the wicked crow calls for rain with a full voice." The **jackdaw** <note>Latin: *graculus*</note> is named for its chatter <note>Latin: *garrulitate*</note>, not, as some wish, because they fly in flocks <note>Latin: *gregatim*</note>, since it is clearly named from its voice. It is a most talkative genus and troublesome with its cries. **Magpies** <note>Latin: *picae*</note> are as if "poetic" <note>Latin: *poetice*</note>, because they express words with a distinction of voice like a human. For they sound with troublesome chatter hanging among the branches of trees. And even if they cannot explain tongues in speech, they nonetheless imitate the sound of the human voice. Concerning which, someone aptly said: "As a magpie I speak, and with a certain voice I greet you as master; if you did not see me, you would deny I am a bird." The **woodpecker** <note>Latin: *picus*</note> took its name from Picus, the son of Saturn, because he used it in auspices. For they say this bird has something divine in it, evidenced by this: that in whatever tree it has nested, a nail or whatever else has been fixed there cannot remain long without immediately falling out when the bird sits upon it. This is the woodpecker of Mars; for the magpie is another thing. The **peacock** <note>Latin: *pavo*</note> has its name from the sound of its voice; its flesh is so hard that it hardly feels decay nor is it easily cooked. Of which someone said: "You admire him whenever he unfolds his gem-like wings; yet you can hand him over to a cruel, hard cook." The **pheasant** <note>Latin: *fasianus*</note> is named from the Phasis, a river of Greece <note>actually in Colchis/modern Georgia</note>, from where it was first brought. That old couplet testifies to this: "I was first transported by an Argive ship; before that, nothing was known to me but the Phasis." The **rooster** <note>Latin: *gallus*</note> is named from castration <note>a medieval etymological pun linking *gallus* to the *Galli*, the castrated priests of Cybele, or to the verb *castrare*</note>. For among all other birds, for this one alone the testicles are removed. For the ancients called those who were cut "galli." Just as from a lion comes a lioness, and from a dragon a dragoness, so from a rooster <note>Latin: *gallus*</note> comes a hen <note>Latin: *gallina*</note>. Her limbs, as some say, if mixed with molten gold, are consumed. The **duck** <note>Latin: *anas*</note> received an appropriate name from its constancy <note>Latin: *assiduitate*</note> in swimming. From this genus, certain ones are called "germane" because they nourish more than the others. The **goose** <note>Latin: *anser*</note> was given its name derived from "duck" or from similarity, or because it also has a frequency for swimming. It testifies to the watches of the night by the persistence of its honking. No animal senses the scent of a man like the goose; hence by its honking, the ascent of the Gauls <note>Latin: *gallorum*</note> upon the Capitol was discovered. The **coot** <note>Latin: *fulica*</note> is so called because its flesh tastes like a hare. For *lagos* means hare; hence among the Greeks it is called *lagos*. It is a bird of the marshes, having its nest in the middle of the water or on rocks surrounded by water; it is always delighted by the deep sea. When it senses a coming storm, it plays in the shallows while fleeing. The **diver** <note>Latin: *mergus*</note> has its name from its habit of diving <note>Latin: *mergendi*</note>. Often, with their heads dipped into the deep, they gather signs of the winds beneath the waves, and foreseeing a storm of the sea, they head for the shores with a cry. For it is certain that a most severe storm is already on the open sea when the divers have fled to the shores. The **hawk** <note>Latin: *accipiter*</note> is a bird armed more by spirit than by talons, carrying a greater virtue in a smaller body. It took its name from "seizing" <note>Latin: *accipiendo*</note>, that is, taking. For it is a bird greedy for seizing other birds. Therefore it is called *accipiter*, that is, a "snatcher"; whence also the Apostle Paul says: "For you endure it if someone seizes <note>Latin: *accipit*</note> you." For where he might have said "if someone snatches," he said "if someone seizes."

<meta>This page continues the medieval natural history catalog, moving from predatory birds to domestic fowl, migratory species, and finally into the world of insects, specifically bees. ...who receives it. For the **hawk** <note>original: *accipitres*</note> acts thus around its own chicks: when it sees that they are able to attempt flight, it provides them with no food, but beats them with its wings and casts them from the nest, compelling them from a tender age to hunt for prey, lest they perhaps grow lazy as adults. The **shrike** <note>original: *lanius*</note> is named in the Italian tongue from "catching." Our people call this the **falcon**, because its toes are curved <note>The Latin *falx* means sickle, referring to the hooked talons</note>. The **kite** <note>original: *milvus*</note> is soft both in strength and in flight, as if it were a "soft bird" <note>original: *mollis avis*</note>; for this reason it is also called most greedy, and always lies in wait for domestic birds. The **bone-breaker** <note>likely the ossifrage or bearded vulture</note> is commonly called the bird that drops bones from a height to break them. Thus it received its name from "breaking bones." The **turtle-dove** <note>original: *turtur*</note> is named from its voice; it is a modest bird, always dwelling on the peaks of mountains and in desert solitudes. It flees the roofs of men and their company, dwelling in the woods. It is said that in winter, having lost its feathers, it lives in the hollow trunks of trees. In contrast, the **dove** <note>original: *columba*</note> loves human hospitality, a gentle inhabitant of the home. Doves are so named because their necks change colors with every turn; they are tame birds, living among a multitude of men and lacking "gall" <note>Ancient science believed doves lacked a gall bladder, making them incapable of bitterness or anger</note>. The ancients called them "birds of Venus" because they frequent their nests and conceive love through a kiss. The **wood-pigeons** <note>original: *palumbes*</note> are named because they are stuffed with fodder <note>etymology from *pabulo*, fodder</note>; the common people call them "recruits" <note>original: *tiros*</note>. It is called a chaste bird because of its habits, for it is a companion of chastity. It is said that if its mate is lost, it walks alone and never again seeks a physical union. The **partridge** <note>original: *perdix*</note> has its name from its voice; it is a deceitful and unclean bird. For the male rises up against the male, and headlong lust forgets its sex. It is so fraudulent that it steals the eggs of another to brood upon them, but this fraud has no fruit. Finally, when the chicks hear the voice of their true mother, they leave the one who brooded them by a certain natural instinct and return to the one who gave them birth. **Quails** <note>original: *coturnices*</note> are named from the sound of their voice, which the Greeks call *ortygias* because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. These have specific times for arriving. For when summer is driven away, they cross the seas. The **leader-quail** <note>original: *ortygometra*</note> is the bird that leads the flock; when a hawk sees it approaching the land, it seizes it, and for this reason the flock takes care to seek a leader of a different species to guard against the first dangers. They find the seeds of poisonous plants most pleasing, for which reason the ancients forbade eating them. For only this animal, like man, suffers from the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>. The Greeks call the **hoopoe** the *upupa* because it considers human dung and feeds on stinking manure; it is a most filthy bird, helmeted with wandering crests, always dwelling in tombs and human filth. If anyone smears themselves with its blood when going to sleep, they will see demons suffocating them. The **cuckoos** <note>original: *cuculos*</note>, which the Spanish call *lucos*, are named from their own voice. They have a specific time for coming, carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and small flights, lest they fail from fatigue over long spaces of air. Their saliva gives birth to cicadas. It eats the eggs found in a sparrow's nest and puts in its own, which the sparrow receives, broods, and nourishes. **Sparrows** <note>original: *passeres*</note> are tiny winged creatures named from "purity" <note>Latin *puritate*, though likely a corruption of *parvitate* meaning smallness</note>, from which also come the words for "slight" and "small." The **blackbird** <note>original: *merula*</note> was called *medula* in ancient times because it "modulates" its song. Others say it is called *merula* because it flies alone, as if "flying pure" <note>original: *mera volans*</note>. Although it is black in all other places, in Achaia

<column-break/>

it is white. The **swallow** <note>original: *hirundo*</note> is so named because it does not take its food while sitting, but catches its meals in the air and eats them; it is a talkative bird, flying in twisted circles and winding paths, and is most skillful in building nests and raising its offspring. It even has a certain foresight, for it deserts buildings about to fall and never approaches their heights. It does not rule over other birds, nor is it ever prey. It flies across the seas and dwells there in winter. **Thrushes** <note>original: *turdia*</note> are named for their slowness <note>original: *tarditate*</note>. They return at the edge of winter. The **large thrush** <note>original: *turdela*</note> is like a greater thrush; it is thought that mistletoe <note>original: *viscum*</note> is generated from its droppings. Whence there was a proverb among the ancients: "The bird shits its own evil" <note>Mistletoe was used to make birdlime, a sticky substance used by hunters to catch birds; thus the bird provides the means of its own capture</note>. The **furfurio** is so named because it feeds on bran <note>original: *furfur*</note> reduced to flour. **Fig-eaters** <note>original: *ficedulae*</note> are named because they eat figs above all. As is explained in that ancient verse: "Since the fig feeds me, and since I feed on sweet grapes, why did the grape not give its name to me instead?" The **goldfinch** <note>original: *carduellus*</note> feeds on thorns and thistles <note>original: *carduis*</note>. For this reason it is called *achantis* among the Greeks, from *achantis*, that is, the thorns on which it is nourished. **Augurs** <note>religious officials in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods from the behavior of birds</note> say that signs are established in the gestures, motion, flight, and voice of birds. They call those birds **song-birds** <note><term>oscines</term>: birds that provide omens via their song or speech</note> which provide an omen by mouth and song, such as the raven, the crow, and the woodpecker. **Wing-birds** <note><term>alites</term>: birds that provide omens through their flight</note> are those seen to show the future by their flight. If these are unfavorable, they are called "inhibiting" <note>original: *inhibę*</note> because they inhibit, that is, forbid. If they are favorable, they are called "prosperous" <note>original: *prapetes*</note>, because all flying birds seek the things ahead of them. They make a third type of augury which they call "common," promising from both; that is, when birds provide auguries by both mouth and flight; however, this is not held in faith <note>The author likely means this is not a Christian belief</note>. Indeed, the types of winged creatures are born twice. For first they produce eggs, then they are formed and animated by the heat of the mother's body. **Eggs** <note>original: *oua*</note> are so named because they are "moist" <note>original: *vuida*</note>. Whence also the word for grape <note>original: *vua*</note>, because it is full of moisture inside. For that is "humid" which has moisture on the outside, but "moist" <note>original: *vuidum*</note> which has it on the inside. Some think the name of the egg has a Greek origin. For they call them *oa*, with the letter 'u' removed. Indeed, they conceive some eggs from empty wind, but these are not capable of generating life unless they have been conceived by masculine lying-together and penetrated by the seminal spirit. They say the power of egg whites <note>original: *duo* refers to the albumin</note> is so great that wood soaked in it will not burn, nor will a garment even be singed. It is said that when mixed with lime, it glues together fragments of glass.

### Concerning Minute Flying Creatures Chapter viii.

**Bees** <note>original: *apes*</note> are so named either because they bind themselves together by their feet <note>original: *pedibus invicem alligent*</note> or because they are born without feet. For afterwards they receive both feet and wings. These, skillful in the duty of generating honey, inhabit assigned seats and compose their dwellings with unspeakable art. From various flowers they build the comb, and with rubbed waxes they fill innumerable camps. They have an army and kings, they move into battles, they flee smoke, and they are exasperated by noise. Many have found that these are born from the carcasses of oxen. For to create them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, so that from the putrefied blood worms are created, which afterwards become bees. Properly then, they are called bees when born from oxen, just as **hornets** come from horses, **drones** from mules, and **wasps** from donkeys. The Greeks call them **castors** which create larger bees in the outermost parts of the combs, which some think are kings; they are named because they lead the camps <note>original: *castra*</note>. The **drone** <note>original: *fucus*</note> is larger than a bee and smaller than a hornet. It is called *fucus* because it eats the labors of others, as if it were a "glutton" <note>original: *fagus*</note>.

<summary>This page catalogs various bird species and insects, focusing on their etymological origins, behavioral traits, and superstitious associations, such as the use of hoopoe blood for seeing demons. It also describes the "spontaneous generation" of bees and wasps from the carcasses of larger animals.</summary>

<meta>This page completes the catalog of insects from the previous discussion on bees and begins Book 13, which transitions from the study of living creatures to the study of the physical universe (the cosmos, atoms, and elements).</meta>

For he <note>Referring to the drone bee</note> feeds on that for which he did not labor. Concerning which Virgil says: "Drive the lazy herd of **drones** from the stalls." **Hornets** <note>original: *crabrones*</note> are named after the "nag" <note>original: *cabo*, meaning a pack-horse</note>, because it is from these that they are created; for just as hornets are born from the putrid flesh of horses, so too are **beetles** <note>original: *scarabei*</note> often born from them, which is how they got their name. **Bull-beetles** are what they call terrestrial beetles that resemble a tick. The **Buprestis** <note>literally "cow-burster"</note> is a small animal in Italy similar to a beetle, but with long legs. It hides among the grass and especially deceives cattle; it gets its name because if it is swallowed, it touches the gall and causes such inflammation that the animal bursts. The **glow-worm** <note>original: *cicindela*</note> is a type of beetle, so named because it shines <note>original: *lucet*</note> while walking or flying. **Cockroaches** <note>original: *blattae*</note> are named for their color; indeed, if caught, they stain the hands, which is why we speak of the color "blatta-purple." This animal cannot endure seeing the light, being the opposite of the fly. For the fly is a light-seeker, while the cockroach is a light-fleeer; it walks only through the night. **Butterflies** <note>original: *papiliones*</note> are small "birds" <note>In the medieval system, flying insects were often grouped with small birds</note> that are most abundant among flowering mallows, and they cause little worms to be born from their droppings. The **locust** <note>original: *locusta*</note> is so called because it has legs as long as a spear <note>original: *hasta*</note>; for this reason, the Greeks call both the marine and terrestrial varieties *astagon*. **Cicadas** <note>original: *licades*</note> are born from the "spit" of the cuckoo. These are numerous in Italy among the people of Rhegium, and nowhere else. The word for **fly** <note>original: *musca*</note> comes from the Greek; just like bees, if they are killed in water, they sometimes revive after the space of one hour. The **horse-fly** is called *linomia* in Greek, which means "dog-fly," for *cynos* is the Greek word for dog. The **gnat** <note>original: *culex*</note> is named from its "sting" <note>original: *aculeo*</note> because it seeks out blood. It has a tube in its mouth like a needle, which pierces the flesh so that it may drink blood. **Scinifes** <note>biting midges or gnats</note> are very tiny flies with extremely annoying stings, which were the third plague that struck the proud people of Egypt. The **gadfly** <note>original: *oestrus*</note> is an animal very troublesome to herds because of its stings. *Oestrus* is the Greek name, which in Latin is called *asilus*, and commonly *tavanus*. **Wine-gnats** <note>original: *bibiones*</note> are those born in wine, which people commonly call *musciones* from "must" <note>original: *musto*, or unfermented wine</note>; hence the poet Afranius says: "When you look at me and begin to chatter, wine-gnats fly from your mouth into your eyes." The **weevil** <note>original: *gurgulio*</note> is so named because it is almost nothing else but a throat <note>original: *guttur*</note>.

### A Brief Preface to the Following Book

In this little book, as if in a brief table, we have noted certain causes of the heavens, the sites of lands, and the spaces of the sea, so that the reader may run through them in a small compass and learn their etymologies and causes with concise brevity.

## Here begins the thirteenth book.
### On the World, Chapter 1.

<margin>m</margin>
The **World** <note>original: *mundus*</note> consists of the heavens, the earth, the sea, and those things within them which are the works of God, of which it is said: "And the world was made through Him." The world is called *mundus* in Latin by philosophers because it is in eternal motion, such as the heavens, the sun, the moon, the air, and the seas. For no rest is granted to its elements, and therefore it is always in motion. For this reason, the elements seemed like living animals to Varro <note>A famous Roman scholar</note>, because, as he says, they move by themselves. The Greeks, however, took the name for the world from 

<column-break/>

"ornament," <note>original: *ornamento*</note> because of the diversity of the elements and the beauty of the stars. For among them, it is called ***cosmos***, which signifies ornament. For we see nothing more beautiful than the world with the eyes of the flesh. It is established that there are four climates of the world—that is, regions: East, West, North, and South. The **East** <note>original: *oriens*</note> is named from the rising <note>original: *exortu*</note> of the sun. The **West** <note>original: *occidens*</note> is so called because it makes the day "fall" <note>original: *occidere*</note> and perish; for it hides the light from the world and brings on the darkness. The **North** <note>original: *septentrio*</note> is named from the seven stars of the axis <note>the Big Dipper</note> which turn in a circle there. This is also properly called the "vertex," because it turns; here the poet says: "Meanwhile the heaven turns." The **South** <note>original: *meridies*</note> is so called either because the sun makes the "mid-day" <note>original: *medi-dies*</note> there, or because the ether then shines more purely; for *merum* means "pure." There are two gates of heaven: the East and the West. For through one gate the sun comes forth, and through the other it returns. There are also two "hinges" <note>original: *cardines*</note> of the world: North and South, for upon these the heavens revolve.

### On Atoms, Chapter 2.

Philosophers call **Atoms** certain parts of bodies in the world so extremely minute that they are neither visible to the sight nor can they receive a "cutting" <note>Greek: *tomos*</note>; hence they are called *atomi* <note>indivisible</note>. These are said to fly through the void of the entire world with restless motions, carried hither and thither like the finest dust seen in sunbeams streaming through windows. Certain pagan philosophers thought that from these atoms arise trees, fruits, and all grasses; and from these, fire and water and all things are born and consist. Atoms exist in body, in time, in number, or in letters. In **body**, like a stone: you divide it into parts, and those parts into grains like sand; again, divide those grains of sand into the finest dust, until if you could, you would reach some tiny point that can no longer be divided or cut. This is an atom in bodies. In **time**, the atom is understood thus: you divide a year, for instance, into months, months into weeks, weeks into days, and days into hours. The parts of hours still admit of division until you come to such a point of time and a "drop" of a moment that it cannot be drawn out by any delay, and therefore can no longer be divided. This is the atom of time. In **numbers**, for example, eight is divided into four; four into two; then two into one. One, however, is an atom because it is indivisible. So it is with a **letter**: for you divide a speech into words, words into syllables, and a syllable into letters. The letter is the smallest part—the atom—and cannot be divided. An atom, therefore, is that which cannot be divided, like a "point" in geometry. For in Greek *tomos* means division, and *atomus* means indivision.

### On the Elements, Chapter 3.

The Greeks call a certain primary matter of things ***hyle*** <note>original: *ylen*</note>, which is formed by no prior means, but is capable of all bodily forms, and from which these visible elements were shaped; hence they took their name from its derivation. The Latins called this *hyle* "**matter**" <note>original: *materia*</note>, because anything unformed from which something is to be made is always called "matter." Accordingly, the poets also wished to call it "the woods" <note>original: *silva*</note>, and not inappropriately, because woods provide the material <note>wood/timber</note> for things. The Greeks, however, call the elements *stoicheia*, because they [join] in a fellowship...

<summary>This page concludes a bestiary of insects (detailing creatures like hornets, beetles, and gnats) and begins Book 13 of the Etymologies, which defines the physical world, its celestial regions, and the concept of indivisible atoms in physics, time, and grammar.</summary>
<keywords>insects, hornets, beetles, locusts, gnats, world, cosmos, four directions, atoms, matter, hyle, elements, Isidore of Seville</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on insects, concluding the study of living creatures and moving into Book 13 of the encyclopedia. It marks a transition to "On the Universe and Its Parts," beginning with a philosophical overview of the elements and then focusing on the heavens, the celestial circles, the nature of air, and meteorological phenomena like thunder.</meta>

...meet in a certain harmony and communion. For they are said to be joined to one another by a certain natural reason, so that they follow a cycle: now repeating their origin from fire down to earth, and now from earth back up to fire. Thus, fire ends in air, air thickens into water, and water becomes heavy in earth; and conversely, earth is dissolved into water, water thins into air, and air is refined into fire. Therefore, it is certain that all elements are present in all things, but each takes its name from the element it possesses in greater abundance. Moreover, they are distributed by divine providence to their own living beings. For the Creator himself filled the heaven with angels, the air with birds, the sea with fish, and the earth with humans and other animals.

### Chapter 4: On the Heavens

The sky <note>original: *celum*</note> is so called because, like an engraved <note>original: *celatum*</note> vessel, it has the lights of the stars impressed upon it like designs. For a vessel is said to be "engraved" when it shines with prominent figures. For God distinguished it with bright lights and filled it with the glowing orbs of the sun and moon, and adorned it with the shining signs of twinkling stars. Others, however, say it is named from "hiding" <note>original: *celando*</note> higher things from us. In Greek, it is called *uranos* <note>original: *ουρανος*</note>, from "seeing" <note>original: *απο του οραν* — "from the act of seeing"</note>, because the air is transparent and clear for gazing. In the Holy Scriptures, the sky is called the "firmament" <note>original: *firmamentum*</note> because it is strengthened <note>original: *firmatum*</note> by the fixed course of the stars and by established, firm laws. Sometimes "sky" is also used to refer to the air, where winds, clouds, storms, and whirlwinds occur. Lucretius says: "the sky which is called air." And the Psalm calls them "birds of the sky," though it is clear that birds fly in the air. We also commonly call this air "the sky." For when we ask about clear or cloudy weather, we sometimes say: "how is the air?" and sometimes: "how is the sky?"

### Chapter 5: On the Parts of the Sky

**Ether** <note>original: *aether*</note> is the place where the stars are. It signifies that fire which is separated from the whole world in the heights. Indeed, *ether* is the element itself, while *ethera* is the splendor of the ether; it is a Greek term. The **sphere of the sky** is so called because its appearance is formed into a round shape; and anything of such a kind is called a sphere by the Greeks because of its revolving nature, just like the balls children play with. For philosophers say the sky is turned on every side into the figure of a sphere, enclosing the earth in an equal way on all sides, balanced in the middle mass of the world. They say this is moved, and with its motion the stars fixed in it circle from east to west, with the **Great Bears** <note>original: *septentrionibus*, literally "the seven oxen"</note> performing shorter revolutions near the pole. The **axis** is the straight line of the north which extends through the middle of the sphere. It is called the axis because the sphere turns on it like a wheel, or because the "Wain" <note>The constellation of the Big Dipper, often visualized as a wagon</note> is located there. The **hinges** <note>original: *cardines*</note> are the extreme parts of the axis; they are so named because the sky turns <note>original: *vertitur*</note> through them. The **poles** are the circles that run through the axis. One of these is the northern pole which never sets, called *boreas*; the other is the southern pole which is never seen, called *austronotus*. They are called poles because they are the cycles of the axes, named from "polishing" <note>original: *poliendo*</note> in the manner of wagons. But the northern pole is always visible, while the southern is never seen, because the earth suppresses the lower parts of the sky in the south. The **convexities** are the extremities of the sky, named for their curvature. For "convex" means curved, inclined, and bent in the manner of a circle. The **Milky Way** <note>original: *lacteus*</note> is a circle, a path that

<column-break/>

is seen in the sphere, named for its whiteness because it is white. Some say it is the path along which the sun travels, and that it shines from the passage of the sun's own splendor.

### Chapter 6: On the Circles of the Sky

This habitation of the sky, divided by circles, has permitted certain parts to be inhabited because of their temperate nature, while denying others due to the enormity of cold or heat. These zones <note>original: *zonae*</note> are five in number. They are called zones or circles because they exist in the circuit of the sphere. The first circle is called **Arctic** because the signs of the Bear <note>original: *arcturi*</note> are seen enclosed within it, which are called the "Seven Oxen" <note>original: *septentriones*</note> by our people, fashioned in the likeness of bears. The second circle is called the **Tropic** boundary because in that circle the sun, bringing summer to the northern borders, does not pass beyond that circle but immediately returns; thus it is called "tropic" <note>from the Greek word for "turning"</note>. The third circle is the **Equinox**, which is called "equinoctial" by the Latins because when the sun reaches it, it creates an equal night. For "equinox" <note>original: *himerinus*, from Greek *hemerinos*</note> means "day and night" in Latin; half of the sphere is seen established in this circle. The fourth circle is called **Antarctic** because it is opposite to the circle we call Arctic. The fifth circle is the **Winter Tropic**, which is called "wintry" or "brumal" by the Latins, because when the sun reaches that circle, it creates winter for those in the north and summer for those dwelling in the southern parts. The **Zodiac** circle is that which contains the twelve signs; it is named from "living things" <note>original: *απο του ζωον* — "from the animal"</note>.

### Chapter 7: On Air and Clouds

**Air** is an emptiness having a much greater admixture of thinness than the other elements. Concerning this, Virgil says: "Following through the long void." Air is named from "lifting" <note>original: *απο του αιρειν* — "from lifting up"</note>, either because it carries the earth or because it is carried itself. Part of it pertains to the heavens, and part to earthly matter. The subtle part, where windy and stormy motions cannot exist, belongs to the celestial part. But this more turbulent part, which grows thick from moist exhalations, is assigned to the earth; it takes many forms. When moved, it makes winds; when more vehemently stirred, it makes fires and thunders; when contracted, it makes clouds; when thickened, it makes rain; when the clouds freeze, it makes snow; when more dense clouds freeze in a turbulent way, it makes hail; when stretched out, it makes clear weather. For it is certain that a dense air is a cloud, and a thinned and dissolved cloud is air. **Clouds** <note>original: *nubes*</note> are named from "veiling" <note>original: *obnubendo*</note>, that is, covering the sky; hence also brides <note>original: *nuptae*</note> are named because they veil their faces. From this also Neptune is named, because he "veils," that is, covers the sea and land. The density of the air makes clouds. For winds mass the air together and make a cloud; hence the saying: "and the air is gathered into a cloud."

### Chapter 8: On Thunder

**Thunder** <note>original: *tonitruum*</note> is so called because its sound terrifies <note>original: *terreat*</note>. For *tonus* means sound. This sometimes clashes all things so heavily that the sky seems to have split apart; for when a storm suddenly thrusts a most vehement wind into the clouds, the whirlwind growing strong and seeking an exit rips through the cloud it has hollowed out with great force, and thus it is carried to the ears with a horrific crash.
