<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on atmospheric phenomena in Book 13. The previous section concluded with the nature of thunder, explaining it as the sound of clouds crashing together. This page expands on lightning, the rainbow, various forms of precipitation, and the system of the twelve winds.</meta>

Which no one should wonder at, since even small carriages emit a great sound when they break apart. Lightning and thunder are produced at the same time, but the lightning is seen sooner because light is faster, or because the sound reaches the ears more slowly. The light that appears before the thunder is elsewhere called "flashes" <note>original: *fulgetra*</note>. As we have said, these are seen first because light is clear and bright, while thunder reaches the ears more slowly.

### On Lightning Bolts, Chapter 9

"Flash" <note>original: *fulgur*</note> and "lightning bolt" <note>original: *fulmen*</note> are named for the striking of a heavenly dart, derived from "to strike" <note>original: *feriendo*</note>. For to flash is to strike and hit. Moreover, colliding clouds create lightning bolts; for the collision of all things creates fire, as we see in stones, or the friction of wheels, or trees in the forest. In the same way, fire is created in the clouds; hence clouds are formed first, then fire. It is certain that lightning bolts are created in the clouds from wind and fire, and are cast out by the force of the winds. For this reason, the fire of a lightning bolt has a greater power for penetrating because it is made of subtler elements than our fire—that is, the fire we use. There are three names for it: *fulgur*, *fulgor*, and *fulmen*. It is a *fulgur* when it touches; *fulgor* when it sets on fire and burns; and *fulmen* when it cleaves or splits. For this reason, they are depicted with three rays <note>This refers to the "thunderbolt" icon often held by Jupiter in classical art</note>.

### On the Rainbow and the Effects of Clouds, Chapter 10

The "heavenly bow" <note>the rainbow</note> is named from its similarity to a curved bow. Its proper name is *Iris*. It is called *Iris* as if it were "of the air" <note>original: *aeris*</note>, because it descends to the earth through the air. It reflects from the sun when hollow clouds directly receive the sun's rays and form the appearance of a bow. That phenomenon gives it various colors because the thin water, the bright air, and the dark clouds together create various colors when irradiated. "Rains" <note>original: *pluviae*</note> are so named because they flow <note>original: *fluant*</note>, as if they were "flowings" <note>original: *fluviae*</note>. For they are born from the breath of the earth and the sea. When these breaths are raised higher, they are either dissolved by the heat of the sun or condensed by the force of the winds, and they drip onto the earth. A *nimbus* <note>storm cloud</note> is a density of cloud that is dark and stormy; the word *nimbus* comes from *nubes* (cloud). *Nimbi* are sudden and headlong rains. We call "rains" <note>original: *pluvias*</note> those that are slow and continuous, as if they were "flowing" <note>original: *fluvias*</note>. "Showers" <note>original: *imbres*</note>, however, pertain to both clouds and rains; they are named from a Greek word because they "intoxicate" <note>soak</note> the earth for sprouting. For all things are created from these. Hence Lucretius says: "Fire, earth, soul, and shower are born." <note>original: *Et igni terra atqz anima nascuntur et imbri*</note> It is a Greek name. "Hail" <note>original: *grando*</note> is so named because its form has a similarity to "grains" <note>original: *grano*</note>. These harden in the cloud by the rigor of the winds and solidify into snow; they are released when the air is broken. Snow comes from the cloud from which it originates. Ice <note>original: *glacies*</note> comes from frost <note>original: *gelu*</note> and water, as if it were "frost-water" <note>original: *gelacies*</note>; that is, frozen water. It is called *gelu* because it binds the earth; for *Ge* <note>original: *Γῆ*</note> is the Greek word for earth. The earth is bound by a greater frost when the night is clear. "Hoarfrost" <note>original: *pruina*</note> is the cold of the morning time; it took its name from the fact that it burns like fire, for *pyr* <note>original: *πῦρ*</note> is Greek for fire. To "burn" <note>original: *urere*</note> pertains to both cold and the sun. For one word signifies two different things because they have one effect. For the power of heat and cold is similar; whence both can break rocks. For heat burns, as in: "unhappy Dido burns" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* regarding Dido's passion</note>. Likewise, cold burns, as in: "the piercing cold of the North Wind may burn" <note>original: *boreae penetrabile frigus adurat* — a reference to Virgil's *Georgics*</note>. "Dew" <note>original: *ros*</note> is a Greek word which they call *drosos*. Others think *ros* is so named because it is "rare" <note>sparse</note> and not thick like 

<column-break/>

rain. "Mist" <note>original: *nebula*</note> is named from the same root as clouds <note>original: *nubila*</note>, from "veiling" <note>original: *obnubendo*</note>, that is, covering the earth; or because a flying cloud creates it. For humid valleys exhale mists and they become clouds. From this comes "cloudy weather," and from this "snows." Mists seek the lowest places when it is clear, and the highest when it is cloudy. "Gloom" <note>original: *caligo*</note> or "shadow" is produced from the thickness of the air. It is called *caligo* because it is mostly produced by the heat <note>original: *calore*</note> of the air. "Darkness" <note>original: *tenebrae*</note> is so called because it "holds shadows" <note>original: *teneant umbras*</note>. Darkness is not a thing in itself, but the absence of light is called darkness. Just as silence is not a thing, but where there is no sound it is called silence; so darkness is not anything, but where there is no light it is called darkness. A "shadow" <note>original: *umbra*</note> is air lacking sun; it is so called because it occurs when one is placed against the sun's rays. It is mobile and uncertain, both from the sun's circuit and from the movement of places. For as often as we move in the sun, it seems to move with us, because in every place we block the rays of the sun; therefore we take away the light from that spot. Thus the shadow seems to walk with us and imitate our gestures. "Light" <note>original: *lux*</note> is the substance itself; "illumination" <note>original: *lumen*</note> is what flows from the light, that is, the brightness of the light. But authors often confuse these terms.

### On the Winds, Chapter 11

Wind is moved and agitated air, and it receives different names according to the different parts of the heaven. It is called "wind" <note>original: *ventus*</note> because it is vehement and violent. For its force is so great that it not only uproots rocks and trees, but even disturbs the heaven and earth and moves the seas. There are four principal spirits of the winds. The first of these, from the east, is *Subsolanus*; from the south, *Auster*; from the west, *Favonius*; from the north, a wind of the same name <note>Septentrio</note> breathes. These have twin spirits of winds on either side. *Subsolanus* has *Vulturnus* on its right side and *Eurus* on its left. *Auster* has *Euroauster* on its right and *Austroafricus* on its left. *Favonius* has *Africus* on its right and *Chorus* on its left. Furthermore, *Septentrio* has *Circius* on its right and *Aquilo* on its left. These twelve winds circle the globe of the world with their blasts. Their names are designated for specific reasons. For *Subsolanus* is so called because it is born "under the rising of the sun" <note>original: *sub ortu solis*</note>. *Eurus* is named because it blows from there, that is, from the East. For it is joined to *Subsolanus*. *Vulturnus* is named because it thunders on high, of which Lucretius says: "High-thundering Vulturnus and Auster powerful with lightning." <margin>auster</margin> *Auster* is named from "drawing up" <note>original: *hauriendo*</note> waters; whence it also makes the air thick and nourishes clouds. This is called *Notus* in Greek because it sometimes corrupts the air. For the pestilence that is born from corrupted air is transmitted to other regions when *Auster* blows. But just as *Auster* generates pestilence, so *Aquilo* repels it. *Euroauster* is so named because it has *Eurus* on one side and *Auster* on the other. *Austroafricus* because it is joined on either side to *Auster* and *Africus*. It is also called *Libonotus* because it is the "Southern wind of Libya" from both sides. *Zephyrus* is called by a Greek name because flowers and seeds are brought to life by its breath. In Latin, this is called *Favonius* because it "favors" <note>original: *foveat* — warms or nourishes</note> those things that are being born; whence the saying: "And the clod of the countryside relaxes itself for Zephyrus." Flowers are dissolved by *Auster*, but they are created by *Zephyrus*. *Africus* is named from its own region; for it takes the beginning of its blowing in Africa. *Chorus* is that which blows from the northwest in summer; it is called *Chorus* because it closes the circle of the winds and makes, as it were, a "choir" <note>original: *chorum*</note>.

It transitions into a detailed classification of the winds and their natures, followed by a new section on hydrology (the study of water), describing the properties of water and a catalog of remarkable springs and lakes known to the medieval world.</meta>

Liber

This wind was previously called *caurus* <note>the northwest wind</note>, which most call *argestes*—though not as the unlearned commoners do, who call it *agresten* <note>original: "agresten," meaning "rustic" or "country-like," a folk etymology Isidore corrects</note>. The North Wind <note>original: *septentrio*</note> is named because it rises from the circle of seven stars <note>the Big Dipper or Ursa Major</note>, which are seen to be carried along as the world turns with its head tilted back. The *Circius* <note>west-northwest wind</note> is named because it is joined to the "chorus" <note>the northwest wind group</note>. The Spanish call this the "Gallic" wind because it blows to them from the direction of Gaul. The wind *aquilo* <note>north-northeast</note> is so named because it "binds the waters" <note>original: *aquas stringat*</note> and dissipates clouds; for it is a cold and dry wind. It is the same as *boreas*, which blows from the Hyperborean mountains <note>legendary mountains in the far north</note>. Indeed, the origin of this wind is from there, which is why it is cold. For the nature of all northern winds is cold and dry, while the southern winds are moist and warm. Of all the winds, however, two are "cardinal" <note>principal or hinge-points</note>: the North and the South. The Etesian winds are blasts of the north wind, given their name because they begin to blow at a certain time of the year. For *eniautos* in Greek is called "year" <note>original: *annus*</note> in Latin. These carry a straight course from the north into Egypt, and the South Wind is their opposite. Besides these, there are two others everywhere that are more like breezes than winds: the *aura* and the *altanus*. The *aura* <note>breeze</note> is named from the air <note>original: *aer*</note>, as if it were "aerial," because it is a gentle movement of the air. Indeed, agitated air creates a breeze; hence Lucretius says: "Aerial breezes." The *altanus* is the wind on the open sea, named by derivation from the "deep" <note>original: *altum*</note>, that is, the sea. For there is one blast on the shores which they call a breeze, and a whirlwind <note>original: *turbo*</note> is named from the earth <note>original: *terra*</note> whenever the wind rises and throws the earth into a circle. A "tempest" <note>original: *tempestas*, a storm</note> is named for "time" <note>original: *tempus*</note>, just as historians are accustomed to say when they mention "at that time" <note>original: *ea tempestate*</note>; or it is named from the state of the sky, because it rises over many days by its own magnitude. Tempests happen most often in the spring and autumn, when it is neither fully summer nor fully winter; hence, the middle and boundary of either time creates tempests from the joining of contrary airs. A "crash" <note>original: *fragor*</note> is named from the sound of things breaking <note>original: *fractarum*</note>, because it easily breaks anything dry and parched. A "gale" <note>original: *procella*</note> is named from the fact that it "prostrates" <note>original: *procellat*</note>, that is, it runs forth and uproots. For it is the force of wind combined with rain. Gales occur either from rivers or from winds. Nothing is faster than the winds; hence, because of their speed, poets depict both the winds and lightning with wings, as in "with the winged strengths of the South Wind."

### On Waters, Chapter 12

Water <note>original: *aqua*</note> is so named because its surface is level <note>original: *equalis*</note>. From this, the word for "the level sea" <note>original: *equor*</note> is also derived, because it is equally flat. There are two elements most powerful for human life: fire and water. Thus, those who are "interdicted from fire and water" <note>a form of Roman legal banishment or excommunication</note> are most severely condemned. The element of water commands all others. For waters temper the heavens, fertilize the earth, and incorporate the air into their own exhalations. They climb into the heights and claim the heavens for themselves. For what is more marvelous than waters standing in the sky? It would be a small thing to have reached such a height; they even carry swarms of fish with them. When poured out, they become the cause of all things growing on the earth. They bring forth fruits, produce trees, shrubs, and herbs; they wash away filth, cleanse sins <note>a reference to baptism</note>, and provide drink to all living creatures.

### On the Diversity of Waters, Chapter 13

The nature of waters is of great diversity. For some are of salt, some of soda <note>original: *nitri*</note>, some of alum, some of sulfur, and some of bitumen. Some provide cures for diseases

<column-break/>

For near Rome, the *Albulae* waters heal wounds. In Italy, Cicero's spring cures wounds of the eyes. In Ethiopia, there is a lake where bodies, when bathed in it, shine as if with oil. The Zama spring in Africa makes voices melodious. Those who drink from the Clitorius lake of Italy lose their taste for wine. They say there is a spring on the island of Chios that makes people dull-witted. In Boeotia there are two springs: one brings memory, the other brings oblivion. The spring of Licici takes away the love of Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. There is a lake in Boeotia that is "furious"; whoever drinks from it burns with the heat of lust. In Campania, there are waters said to banish the sterility of women and the insanity of men. In Ethiopia, whoever drinks from the Red Spring becomes frantic <note>original: *lymphaticus*, meaning crazed or "water-mad"</note>. The Lechnus spring of Arcadia does not allow miscarriages to happen. In Sicily, there are two springs: one makes the sterile fertile, and the other makes the fertile sterile. In Thessaly, there are two rivers; they say sheep drinking from one become black, from the other white, and from both, variegated. Lake Clitumnus in Umbria produces the largest oxen. It is said the hooves of pack animals are hardened in the Reatine marshes. In the Asphalt Lake of Judea <note>the Dead Sea</note>, nothing that has life can be submerged. In the Indies, there is a pond called Side in which nothing floats, but all things sink. But on the contrary, in Lake Alce <note>perhaps the "Asci" or a similar legendary lake</note> through Pozidamus, everything floats and nothing is submerged. The Marside spring in Phrygia produces stones. In Achaia, water flows out of the rocks called "Styx," which kills immediately when drunk. The Seloniun pond of Sicily drives away those who approach with a foul odor. There is a spring in Africa near the temple of Ammon <note>the Oracle of Siwa</note> which binds the soil with its moisture. *Faustlas* <note>an unclear or local name</note> also solidifies into turf. Job's spring in Idumea is said to change color four times a year: that is, dusty, bloody, green, and clear, holding one of these colors for three months of the year. Among the Troglodytes <note>Cave-dwellers</note> there is a lake that becomes bitter three times a day and then sweet as many times. The spring of Siloam at the foot of Mount Zion does not flow with continuous water, but bubbles up at certain hours and days. In Judea, there was once a stream that dried up every Sabbath. In Sardinia, hot springs heal the eyes and expose thieves, for their crime is revealed by blindness. In Epirus, they say there is a spring in which lit torches are extinguished, and extinguished ones are lit. Among the Garamantes <note>a Saharan people</note>, there is a spring so cold by day that one cannot drink it, and so hot by night that one cannot touch it. Now indeed, in many places, waters flow out extremely hot with such force that they can heat baths. For there are certain lands that have much sulfur and alum. Thus, when cold water comes through hot veins and is touched by the neighboring heat of sulfur, it glows hot. It does not flow out such from its origin, but the waters pass through both materials full of fire and grow hot from the movements.

### On the Name of the Sea, Chapter 14

The sea <note>original: *mare*</note> is a general collection of waters. For every congregation of waters, whether they are salt or fresh, is called "seas" by common usage, according to the passage: "And the gatherings of the waters he called Seas" <note>Genesis 1:10</note>. Properly, however, it is called *mare* because its waters are bitter <note>original: *amare*</note>. It is called *equor* <note>the level sea</note> because it is equally flat, even though the fluctuating waters rise up like mountains.

...when the storms are stilled again, they are leveled. For the depth of the sea is varied, and yet its equality is seen as indistinguishable. However, the sea does not grow larger even though it receives all the rivers and all the springs. This cause is partly because its very magnitude does not feel the incoming waves. Furthermore, the bitter water <note>meaning salt water</note> consumes the fresh flow. Or perhaps the clouds themselves attract much of the water to themselves, or the winds carry part of it away, or part of it filters through certain hidden openings in the earth and flows back, returning to the head of all springs <note>Isidore here reflects the ancient theory of a subterranean water cycle where seawater is filtered into fresh water through the earth</note>. The sea has a certain color, but it changes through the quality of the winds. For now it is yellow, now muddy, now black.

### Chapter 15: Concerning the Ocean

<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing to the title</image-desc></margin>
The Greeks and Latins name the Ocean thus because it encircles the world in the manner of a ring; or from its speed, because it runs quite swiftly <note>original: "ocius," meaning more swiftly</note>. Likewise, because it shines with a purple color like the sky, "ocean" is as if it were "cyan" <note>original: "quasi cianeus." Isidore is making a word-play connecting Oceanus to the color cyan/blue</note>. It is this which embraces the borders of the lands, and approaches and recedes with alternating tides. For when the winds breathe into the depths, it either pushes the seas out or sucks them back. It has taken diverse names from the regions it first touches: such as the Gallic, German, Scythian, Caspian, Hyrcanian, Atlantic, and Gaditan <note>referring to the area around Cadiz, Spain</note>. For the Gaditan strait is named from Gades <note>modern Cadiz</note>, where the threshold of the Great Sea first opens from the Ocean. From which also Hercules, when he had reached Gades, placed columns there, hoping that there was the end of the world <note>these are the "Pillars of Hercules," marking the entrance to the Mediterranean</note>.

### Chapter 16: Concerning the Mediterranean Sea

<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing to the title</image-desc></margin>
The Great Sea is that which flows from the Ocean at the setting of the sun <note>the West</note> and turns toward the south; then it stretches toward the north. It is called "Great" because the other seas are smaller in comparison to it. It is also the "Mediterranean" because it is poured through the middle of the land as far as the East, determining the boundaries of Europe, Africa, and Asia. The gulf of its first part, which is poured into the Spanish regions, is called the Iberian and Balearic. Then the Gallic, which washes the province of Narbonne. Soon the Ligustican, which is first near where Genoa is. After these is the Tyrrhenian, which touches Italy, which the Greeks call the Ionian and the Italians call the "Lower Sea." Then the Sicilian, which goes from Sicily as far as Crete. Then the Cretan, which extends toward Pamphylia and Egypt. Then the Hellespont, which, turning back toward the north with great windings near the Greek lands and Illyricum, is narrowed into a space of seven stadia <note>about 0.8 miles</note>, across which Xerxes crossed into Greece by a bridge made of ships; Abydos is located there. Then, spread out from the open water, it is narrowed again and makes the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note>, which soon is cramped into narrow passages and becomes the Thracian Bosphorus, across which Darius transported his troops. Then the Pontic gulf <note>the Black Sea</note>, very vast, with the Meotian marshes <note>the Sea of Azov</note> at its back. This sea is sweeter than the others because of the multitude of rivers, and it is misty and shallower; for this reason it is called "Pontic" because it is shallower <note>original: "breuius," meaning shorter or shallower</note>, and for that reason it does not allow for other greater beasts besides seals, tunas, and dolphins. Just as the land, while it is one, is called by various names in different places, so also this Great Sea is named by different names throughout the regions. For the Iberian and Asiatic...

<column-break/>

...are named from the provinces. From islands, it is called the Balearic, Sicilian, Cretan, Cypriot, Aegean, and Carpathian. For between Tenedos and Chios there is a landmark <note>original: "farum," usually a lighthouse, but here likely a rock or landmark</note> in the sea rather than an island, which is believed to be like a goat <note>original: "capre"</note> to those seeing it from a distance, which the Greeks call *ega*; hence the Aegean Sea is named. So also the Carpathian Sea between Egypt and Rhodes is named from the island of Carpathos placed there. From peoples, it is called the Gallic, Ausonian, Dalmatian, and Libustican. From towns, the Argolic, Corinthian, Tyrian, and Adriatic. For Adria was once a certain primary city on the Illyrian sea, which gave its name to the Adriatic Sea. From the position of the sky, it is called the "Upper" or "Lower," because the East is of the higher regions and the West is of the lower. There is also the Tuscan and the Adriatic. From the memory of a leader, like the Ionian; for Ion was a Greek leader, from whom came the Ionian Athenians. This sea is also called the Tyrrhenian, either because it washes Tuscany (that is, Tyrrhenia) or from the Tyrrhenian sailors who threw themselves headlong into the sea. And it should be known that the Ionian gulf is immense from Ionia as far as Sicily, and its parts are the Adriatic, Achaean, and Epirotic. From the character of those living near it, the "Hospitable" <note>original: "euxinus"</note> was previously called "Inhospitable" <note>original: "arenus"</note>. From the accidents of men who fell into the sea, such as the Hellespont, Icarian, and Myrtoan. For the Myrtoan sea is named from the fall of Myrtilus, because he was thrown headlong there by Oenomaus. Icarus the Cretan, as the fables tell, seeking higher things with wings melted by the heat of the sun, gave his name to the sea in which he fell. Phrixus, fleeing the snares of his stepmother with his sister Helle, boarded a ship having the sign of a ram, because of which he was delivered. But Helle his sister, driven by the storm, fell in a shipwreck into the sea and, having died, gave her name to the Hellespont Sea. From the order of the flow, the Propontis; for it is called Propontis because it comes before the Pontus <note>from Greek "pro" meaning before</note>. It is also named from a crossing, as the Bosphorus is named "the ox-passage" <note>from Greek "bous" (ox) and "poros" (passage)</note> because of its narrow channels. The Egyptian sea is the African; the Dalmatian and Gallic are of Europe; the African of Libya. These parts came to be as each was first reached. *Pelagus* <note>open sea</note> is the width of the sea without a shore; and *pontus* is named from the Greek name "from the sides" <note>term: <term>apo tu plagia</term> original Greek: ἀπὸ τὰ πλάγια; Isidore interprets this as being named for its "width" or "breadth"</note>, from which also comes the word "slopes" <note>original: "plagia"</note>, because they are without harbors.

### Chapter 17: Concerning the Boundaries of the Sea

<margin><image-desc>red paraph mark</image-desc></margin>
Gulfs <note>original: "sinus," literally "folds"</note> are what the larger recesses of the sea are called, such as the Ionian in the Great Sea, or in the Ocean the Caspian, Indian, Persian, and Arabic, which is also the Red Sea ascribed to the Ocean. It is called the Red Sea because it is stained with rose-colored waves. However, it does not have such a nature as it seems to show; this whirlpool is spoiled and stained by the neighboring shores, because all the land that stands around the sea is red and prime with a blood-like color. And therefore the sharpest cinnabar <note>original: "minium"</note> is gathered from there, and other colors by which painting is varied. Therefore, since the earth has this nature, it is constantly washed away by the waves, and whatever has adhered to them falls into that color. Because of this, red gems are also found on these shores. For a pebble of this kind, wrapped in such soil when it has been rubbed among the sands, takes on both the color of the earth and the sea. This sea is split into two gulfs. Of these, the one from the east is called Persian, because the Persians inhabit its coast. The other is called Arabic because it is around Arabia.

### Chapter 18: Concerning Tides and Straits

Tide <note>original: "aestus"</note> pertains to the ocean, a strait <note>original: "fretum"</note> to both seas. For a tide is the approach or recession of the sea, that is, its restlessness. From which also estuaries...

--- Page 146 ---
<meta>This page continues Isidore’s exploration of the hydrosphere. Following his general introduction to the Ocean, he now moves to specific geographical features of the Mediterranean, the properties of inland lakes like the Dead Sea and Galilee, and the etymology of water in its various states—from the deep abyss to the falling drip.</meta>

...through which the sea both approaches and recedes in turn. A strait, however, is so named because the sea there always "seethes" <note>original: "ferveat"</note>. For a strait is narrow, and like a boiling sea, it is named from the "fervor" or seething of the waves, such as the Strait of Gades <note>the Strait of Gibraltar</note> or the Sicilian Strait. For Varro says that straits are so named as if they were "fervid," that is, seething and having the motion of boiling. Sallust writes that the Sicilian Strait, which is called *Regium* <note>modern Reggio Calabria</note>, is named for this reason: that Sicily was once joined to Italy, and while it was a single land, the middle space was either broken off by the moisture of the waters or cut through by the narrowness, and from this it was named *Regium*, which in Greek is called "abrupt" or "broken off" by this name <note>original: "rhegnymi," meaning to break or shatter</note>. It is a very narrow space of three miles dividing Sicily from Italy, famous for the legendary monsters which it displays on either side: Scylla and Charybdis. The inhabitants call Scylla a rock overhanging the sea, resembling a well-known form to those seeing it from afar. From this, legends gave it a monstrous appearance, as if it were a human form girt with dog heads, because the waves crashing there seem to mimic the sound of barking. Charybdis is so named because it swallows ships in its hidden whirlpools. For it is a swirling sea, and from there, mangled shipwrecks emerge from the deep. Three times a day it raises its waves and three times it swallows them; for it takes in the waters to vomit them out, and vomits them to take them in again. The Syrtes, however, are sandy places in the sea. Sallust says they are called *Syrtes* from "drawing" <note>original: "tractu"</note> because they draw everything to themselves, and those approaching the shallow sea get stuck. These are near the Egyptian sea and are mixed with it. Shallows, truly, are those places through which men or animals cross through the sea or rivers on foot; Virgil calls these "shallows" <note>original: "brevia," literally "briefs" or "shorts"</note>, and the Greeks call them *bacia*.

->### Chapter 19: Concerning Lakes and Pools<-

There are, moreover, certain seas which do not mix with the waves of the ocean or the Great Sea, and they are called lakes and pools. A lake is a reservoir in which water is held, nor does it mix with the waves, such as Lake Asphaltites <note>the Dead Sea</note>, Lake Benacus <note>Lake Garda</note>, Lake Larius <note>Lake Como</note>, and others which the Greeks call *limen*, that is, pools. For springs flow into rivers, and rivers run down into straits. A lake stays in its place and does not flow through, and it is called a "lake" <note>original: "lacus"</note> as if it were a "place of water" <note>original: "aquae locus"</note>. Lake Asphaltites is also called the Dead Sea, because it produces nothing living, and receives nothing of a living kind. For it neither has fish, nor birds accustomed to the water and happy in the use of diving. Moreover, whatever living things you attempt to submerge by any art, once dipped, they immediately bounce back; and if they are forcefully struck in, they are immediately cast out. It is not moved by winds, as the bitumen resists whirlwinds, by which all the water is made stagnant. Nor is it capable of navigation, because all things lacking life sink to the bottom, nor does it support any timber unless it is smeared with bitumen. They say that a lit lamp floats on top, but once extinguished, it sinks. This is also called the Salt Sea, or the Lake of Asphalt—that is, of bitumen—and it is in Judea between Jericho and Zoara. Its length extends as far as Zoara in Arabia for seven hundred and eighty stadia <note>about 90 miles</note>. Its width is one hundred and fifty stadia <note>about 17 miles</note> up to the vicinity of Sodom. Lake Tiberias <note>the Sea of Galilee</note> is named from the town of Tiberias, which Herod once built in honor of Tiberius Caesar. It is, however, the most healthy of all the lakes in Judea, and in a certain way more effective for the health of bodies.

<column-break/>

The Lake of Gennesaret is a very large lake in Judea, extending one hundred and forty stadia in length and forty in width. It spreads out with rippling waters, creating a breeze for itself, not from the winds, but from its own nature. From this it is called *Genesar* in the Greek vocabulary, as if it were "generating a breeze for itself" <note>Isidore is using a creative etymology here, linking the name to "generans auram"</note>. Finally, throughout its wider spaces, the lake is agitated by frequent blowing breezes. Hence its draught is purer, and it is sweet and suitable for drinking. Benacus is a lake of Italy in Venetia, from which the river Mincius is born; this lake mimics marine storms in its magnitude. Lucrinus and Avernus are lakes of Campania. Lucrinus is so named because it once provided great revenues <note>original: "lucra," meaning profits</note> due to its abundance of fish. Avernus, however, is called a lake because birds cannot fly over it <note>Isidore connects Avernus to the Greek "a-ornos," meaning "without birds"</note>. For previously it was surrounded by such a density of woods that the sulfurous waters exhaling through the narrows killed the birds flying over with the weight of their stench. Augustus Caesar, understanding this matter, cut down the woods and rendered the locations pleasant instead of pestilential. A lake and a pool are the same, where an immense amount of water gathers. For it is called a pool <note>original: "stagnum"</note> from the fact that the water "stands" there <note>original: "stet"</note> and does not run down.

->### Chapter 20: Concerning the Abyss<-

The abyss is an impenetrable depth of waters, or the caverns of hidden waters from which springs and rivers proceed, or those which run secretly underneath; hence it is called the abyss. For all waters or torrents return through hidden veins to the mother abyss. Waves <note>original: "fluctus"</note> are so called because they are made by "blasts" <note>original: "flatibus"</note>. For the waters fluctuate when agitated by the impulse of the winds. *Aqua* <note>water</note> is stationary and level without motion. A wave <note>original: "unda"</note>, however, is the rising part of the liquid which is always in motion. Lucretius says: "Aerial waves," that is, the motions and that body which flows back. For a wave is not water by itself, but water in a certain motion and agitation; it is called *unda* as if from "abounding" and "returning." *Latex* is properly the liquid of a spring, and it is called *latex* because it "lies hidden" <note>original: "lateat"</note> in the veins of the earth. A drop <note>original: "gutta"</note> is that which stays; a drip <note>original: "stilla"</note> is that which falls. From this also comes "dripping" <note>original: "stillicidium"</note>, as if it were a "falling drip." For *stiria* is Greek, meaning a drop; from this comes the diminutive we use, *stilla*. While it either stays or hangs from roofs or trees, it is a kind of sticky drop; when it has fallen, it is a drip. Foam <note>original: "spuma"</note> is named from the fact that it "spits" <note>original: "spuat"</note>; for it is the dregs of the waves. From this also comes "must" <note>new wine</note> and those things which are purged of foam when they are cooked; hence also comes "spittle."

->### Chapter 21: Concerning Rivers<-

A river <note>original: "fluvius"</note> is a perennial downward flow of waters, named specifically from "flowing" <note>original: "fluendo"</note>. Strictly speaking, the "stream" <note>original: "flumen"</note> is the water itself; the "river" <note>original: "fluvius"</note> is the course of the water. However, "stream" is used more properly than "river," meaning the water before the downward flow. There are two kinds of rivers: one is a torrent, the other is "living." Concerning which Virgil says: "Until I wash myself in the living stream." A torrent is water coming with force. It is called a torrent because it increases with rain and "is scorched" <note>original: "torrescit," meaning dries up</note> by drought—that is, it withers. Concerning which Pacuvius says: "The torrent is scorched by flaming vapor." The Greeks gave it a name from winter; we give it a name from summer—they from the time it flows, we from the time it dries up. An *amnis* is a river wreathed in groves and foliage, and it is named *amnis* from its very "pleasantness" <note>original: "amoenitate"</note>. A "downward course" <note>original: "decursus"</note> is properly the end of a course, whether it be of waters or...

<meta>This page continues the encyclopedic description of the world's waters, moving from the general nature of straits and seas on the previous page to the specific etymologies and geography of the world's most famous rivers. # XIII

...of any king whatsoever. **Streams** <term>original: *rivus*; a small flow of water</term> are so named because they are "derived" to irrigate—that is, to lead water into the fields—for to irrigate is to lead in. A **whirlpool** <note>original: *gurges*; the OCR reads *burges*</note> is strictly a deep place in a river. A **well** is a place dug out from which water is drawn, named from the act of "drinking" <note>original: *potatio*</note>. A **spring** is the source of rising water, as if it were "pouring out" <note>original: *fundens*</note> waters.

Some rivers, however, received names from specific causes, and several of these are noteworthy as they are celebrated in historical accounts. The **Gihon** river, rising from Paradise and encircling all of Ethiopia, is called by this name because it irrigates the land of Egypt with the increase of its flood. For *Ge* in Greek signifies "earth" in Latin. Among the Egyptians, this is called the **Nile** because of the silt <note>original: *limus*</note> it carries, which produces fertility. From this, it is called the Nile, as if to say "new silt" <note>original: **νέα ἰλὺϛ** (nea ilus)</note>. Previously, the Nile was called the *Melo* in Latin. It appears, moreover, in the Nilid lake, from which it heads south towards Egypt; there, pushed back by the blasts of the North wind, it swells as the waters struggle backward and creates the inundation of Egypt.

The **Ganges** river, which Holy Scripture calls the **Pishon**, rises from Paradise and proceeds to the regions of India. It is called *Phison*, meaning "a multitude" <note>original: *caterva*</note>, because it fills and forms a single body with ten great rivers joined to it. It is called the *Ganges*, however, after Gangaro, a king of India. Like the Nile, it is known to rise and burst over its banks.

The **Tigris**, a river of Mesopotamia rising from Paradise, flows against the Assyrians and, after many windings, flows into the Dead Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, similar to the beast known as the **tiger**, which runs with excessive swiftness.

The **Euphrates**, a river of Mesopotamia rising from Paradise, is very rich in gems and flows through the middle of Babylon. This river took its name from "crops" or "fertility," for in Hebrew, *Euphrata* is interpreted as "fertility." Indeed, in certain places, it irrigates Mesopotamia just as the Nile does Alexandria.

**Sallust**, a most reliable author, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from a single source in Armenia, and though they go their separate ways, they divide a long space, leaving many miles in between; yet the land surrounded by them is called Mesopotamia <note>meaning "the land between rivers"</note>. From this, **Jerome** observes that the rivers of Paradise must be understood differently.

The **Indus** is a river of the East which is received by the Red Sea. **Istaspes** was a very ancient king of the Medes, from whom the river of the East took its name, which is now called the **Hydaspes**, of which **Lucan** says: *Where the Median Hydaspes approaches the sea from the fire of the rising sun*. When it becomes a river of the Persians, it is said to run toward the East.

The **Arar** <note>modern Saône</note> is a river of Germany, of which **Virgil** says: *Either the Parthian shall drink of the Arar, or Germany of the Tigris*. For it runs through Parthia and Assyria.

The **Bactrus**, a river of the East, is said to be named after King Bactrus, from whom both the Bactrians and their city are named.

The **Choaspes** is a river of the Persians, named in their language because it has a wonderful sweetness of water, so much so that the Persian kings, even when far from its banks, claimed cups of it for themselves. Some think the **Cydnus**, a river of Cilicia, is derived from this stream.

The **Araxes** is a river of Armenia which rises from the same mountain as the Euphrates, but in a separate direction; it is named for its "rapacity" because it overthrows all things. Hence, when **Alexander** wished to cross it and built a bridge, it flooded with such force that it destroyed the bridge. In a short...

<column-break/>

...valley, it raises its head from the source of the Euphrates and then is carried into the Caspian Sea.

There is a river of Syria called the **Orontes**, running by the walls of Antioch, which, rising from the sunrise, is buried in the sea not far from the city. Because of the course of its origin, the ancient Latins called it the "Orient" <note>meaning "the rising sun" or "the East"</note>. Because of the force of its flowing and the West winds <term>zephyrs</term> constantly blowing there, the whole city is cooled at all times.

The **Jordan**, a river of the Jews, is named from two springs, one called *Jor* and the other *Dan*. These, though starting far from each other, join into one alliance and are thereafter called the Jordan. It rises under Mount Lebanon and divides Judea and Arabia; after many windings, it flows into the Dead Sea near Jericho.

The **Phasis** <note>OCR reads *Eusio*</note>, poured out from the Caucasus Mountains, throws itself into the Euxine Sea with many others, from which it also takes its name.

The **Cydnus** is a river of Cilicia, coming from Mount Taurus, having water of wonderful sweetness; and because anything that is white is called *cydnus* in the native Syrian tongue, this name was given to the river. It swells in summer when the snows melt; in other times of the year, it is thin and quiet. These are the rivers of Asia.

The **Pactolus** is a river of Asia carrying golden sands, of which **Virgil** says: *And the Pactolus irrigates with gold*. Because of its golden flow, others call it the *Chrysorrhoas* <note>Greek for "Stream of Gold"</note>.

The **Hermus** <note>OCR reads *Erinus*</note> is a river of Asia that cuts through the fields of Smyrna, and it is also full of golden flows and sands, from which Smyrna was also named.

The **Meander** is a winding river of Asia, which, with its banks running back on themselves through Phrygia and Ionia, throws itself into a bay that divides Miletus and Priene. It is called Meander because it is winding and never runs straight. Of which **Ovid** says: *Whatever the Meander plays in its backward-turning waves*.

**Tanus** was the first king of the Scythians, from whom the **Tanais** <note>the Don</note> river is said to be named; coming from the Riphean forests, it divides Europe from Asia, running in the middle between the two parts of the world and flowing into the Black Sea.

The **Inachus** is a river of Achaia irrigating the Argive fields, which King Inachus named after himself; he was the first to give origin to the Argive people. There also is the **Erymanthus**, sent down from Mount Erymanthus.

The **Po** <term>Latin: *Padus*</term> is a river of Italy, poured from the ridges of the Alps, rising from three springs, one of which is named *Padus*; spreading out like a pool, it directs the stream into a bend, from which it is named *Padus*. Among the Greeks, this is known as the **Eridanus**, after Eridanus the son of the Sun, whom they call **Phaethon**, who was struck by lightning and cast into this river and killed. It increases at the rising of the Dog Star from the melting snows, and with the addition of thirty rivers, it is carried into the Adriatic Sea near Ravenna.

The **Tiber**, a river of Italy, is said to be named after **Tiberinus**, a king of the Albans, who fell into this river and gave it his name upon his death. For previously its ancient name was **Albula**, named for its color because it becomes white with snow. It is the same as the *Tybris*, which is also called *Tyberis*; it is called *Tyberis* in daily speech, but *Tybris* in poetic use.

The **Danube**, a river of Germany, is said to be named from the "abundance of snow" <note>original: *nivium copia*</note> by which it is greatly increased. This is the river that has the greatest fame of all in Europe. It is also called the **Ister**, because as it passes through numerous nations, it changes its name and gathers greater strength by surrounding others. It rises from the German ridges and the western parts of the barbarians, and proceeding toward the East, it receives sixty rivers into itself and flows into the Black Sea through seven mouths.

It covers prominent waterways across Africa, Asia, and Europe, including the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, Jordan, Tiber, and Danube.</summary>

# Book

The **Rhone** <note>original: *Rhodanus*</note>, a river of Gaul, is named after the town of Rhodes, which was founded by Rhodian colonists. It rushes with a rapid and violent course, cutting into the waves of the Tyrrhenian Sea; it often poses a significant danger to sailors where the sea's waves and the river's current struggle against one another. The **Rhine** is said to be named from its "association" with the Rhone <note>original: *societate*</note>, because they both arise from the same province. It is a river of Germany, counted among the three greatest rivers of Europe, directing its course from the ridge of the Alps all the way into the depths of the Ocean. The **Ebro** <note>original: *Iberus*</note> is the stream that once gave its name to all of Hispania. The **Abintus** <note>likely the Miño; original: *Minius*</note>, a river of Galicia, took its name from the color of the pigment <note>vermilion or red lead</note> which is found there in great abundance. The **Duero** <note>original: *Durius*</note> is nicknamed "the Dorian" by the Greeks. Carthage named the river **Tagus** in Hispania, from whose source it proceeds; it is a river rich in gold-bearing sands and, for this reason, is more famous than the other rivers of Hispania. The **Guadalquivir** <note>original: *Baetis*</note> is the river that gave its name to the province of Baetica. Regarding it, the poet Martial wrote: 

->*Baetis, your hair wreathed in an olive-bearing crown,*<-
->*who tints the golden fleeces with your bright waters.*<-

This refers to the fact that the wool there is dyed a beautiful color <note>The river water was thought to naturally stain the wool of sheep</note>. It is called the **Baetis**, however, because it flows through low-lying ground; for the Greeks call "low" or "submerged" *bathyn* <note>original: **βαθύν**</note>. Some rivers were released during the Flood and then blocked by masses of earth, while others, which were not previously part of the "abyss" <note>the subterranean deep</note>, burst forth when their channels were broken open.

### Concerning Floods, Chapter 22

A **flood** <note>original: *diluvium*</note> is so called because it "deletes" <note>original: *deleat*</note> everything it inundates by the destruction of the waters. The first flood occurred under **Noah**, when the Almighty, offended by the sins of humanity, corrected the whole world by destroying everything; the sky and the sea became a single space. We see evidence of this even now in the stones we often see in remote mountains, which contain hardened shells and oysters, and are often hollowed out by water. The second flood occurred in Achaia during the times of the patriarch **Jacob** and of **Ogygus**, who was the founder and king of Eleusis; he gave his name to both the place and the time. The third flood was in Thessaly in the times of **Moses** or Amphictyon, who reigned third after Cecrops. In his time, a deluge of water consumed the greater part of the people of Thessaly, though a few were liberated by the refuge of the mountains, especially on Mount Parnassus. In that region, **Deucalion** then held the kingdom; he took in those who fled to him on rafts and cared for and nourished them between the twin peaks of Parnassus. Because of this, Greek fables say the human race was "repaired from stones," due to the innate hardness of the human heart. But rivers also, when increased beyond their custom by unusual rains—whether by duration or magnitude—overflow and destroy many things; these too are called floods. It should be known, however, that when rivers grow beyond measure, they do not only bring present damage but also signify something for the future.

### Here begins the Fourteenth Book
### Concerning the Earth, Chapter 1

The **Earth** is positioned in the middle region of the universe, standing at an equal interval from all parts of heaven in the manner of a center point. In the singular num-

<column-break/>

ber, the word signifies the whole world; in the plural, it signifies individual parts. Reason gives it various names. For it is called *terra* from its upper part which is "trodden upon" <note>original: *teritur*</note>. It is called *humus* from the lower part or from "moist earth" <note>original: *humida terra*</note>, as under the sea. It is called *tellus* because we "take" <note>original: *tollimus*</note> its fruits. It is also called *Ops* <note>the Roman goddess of resources</note> because it brings "help" <note>original: *ope*</note> to the crops. Likewise, it is called *arva* <note>plowland</note> from "plowing" <note>original: *arando*</note> and cultivating. Strictly speaking, however, the earth is called "the dry land" to distinguish it from water, as Scripture says: "Which God called the dry land." For the natural property of earth is dryness; that it is moist is something it gains from its affinity with waters. Some say its **motion** <note>earthquakes</note> is caused by wind in its hollows, which moves it. Sallust says: "Winds, having been plunged through the hollows of the earth and having broken through, caused several mountains to collapse and the ground to sink." Others say that a general body of water moves within the earth and they collide together, like a vessel, as Lucretius says. Others call the earth *seismon* <note>original: **σεισμόν**; Greek for 'shaking'</note>, whose hidden collapses often shake everything placed above them. The gaping of the earth is caused either by the motion of the water below, or by frequent thunders, or by winds bursting out from the hollows of the earth.

### Concerning the World, Chapter 2

The **World** <note>original: *orbis* (literally "circle" or "orb")</note> is named for the roundness of a circle, because it is like a wheel. From this, a small wheel is also called an "orbicule." For the Ocean, flowing around it on all sides, encompasses its boundaries in a circle. It is divided into three parts: one part is **Asia**, the second is **Europe**, and the third is **Africa**, which is also called Libya. The ancients did not divide these three parts of the world equally. For Asia reaches from the south through the east all the way to the north; Europe, however, reaches from the north to the west; and from there, Africa reaches from the west to the south. From this, it is evident that Europe and Africa together occupy one half of the world, while Asia alone occupies the other half. These two parts <note>Europe and Africa</note> were made so because the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> enters from the Ocean between them and intersects them. Therefore, if you divide the world into two parts, East and West, Asia will be in one, and in the other will be Europe and Africa.

# Book 14

### Concerning Asia and its Parts, Chapter 3

<margin>a</margin> **Asia** was named after a certain woman who, among the ancients, held the empire of the East. It is situated in the third part of the world: bounded on the east by the rising sun, on the south by the Ocean, on the west by our sea <note>original: *nostro mari*, referring to the Mediterranean</note>, and it is terminated on the north by Lake Maeotis <note>The Sea of Azov</note> and the river Tanais <note>The Don</note>. It contains many provinces and regions, whose names and locations I will briefly explain, beginning with Paradise. <margin>paradise</margin> **Paradise** is a place established in the eastern parts; its name is translated from Greek into Latin as "garden" <note>original: *hortus*</note>. Furthermore, in Hebrew it is called **Eden**, which in our language is interpreted as "delights" <note>original: *delitiae*</note>. When joined together, they form a "garden of delights." For it is planted with every kind of wood and fruit-bearing tree, possessing also the Tree of Life. There is neither cold nor heat there, but a perpetual temperate air. From its center, a fountain breaking forth waters the entire grove, and is divided into four burgeoning rivers. Access to this place was closed off after the sin of man. It is hedged about on all sides by a flaming sword <note>original: *romphea flammea*</note>; that is, it is girt with a wall of fire, so that its heat almost reaches the heavens. The **Cherubim** as well—that is, a guard of angels—is stationed above the flashing of the sword to keep away evil spirits, so that the flames might repel men, and the good angels might remove the evil ones, lest any path to Paradise lie open for fleshly or spiritual transgression. **India** is named after the Indus River, by which it is closed on the western side. This land extends from the southern sea all the way to the rising sun, and from the north it reaches as far as Mount Caucasus. It has many nations and towns, and the island of **Taprobane** <note>Modern Sri Lanka</note>, which is filled with gems and elephants; as well as **Chryse** and **Argyre**, fertile with gold and silver; it is a useful land, and its trees never lack leaves. It also has the rivers Ganges, Nidus, and Hypanis, which distinguish the Indians. The land of India is very healthy due to the breath of the west wind; it yields crops twice in a year. It experiences a cycle of winter and summer together in the air. It produces men of a tinted color, huge elephants, and the **monoceros** <note>The unicorn</note> beast. Also the parrot, ebony wood, cinnamon, pepper, and aromatic reed. It sends forth ivory and precious stones: beryls, chrysoprase, and adamant <note>diamond</note>; carbuncles, ligures <note>possibly amber or zircon</note>, pearls, and large "union" pearls, for which the ambition of noble women burns. There also are mountains of gold which it is impossible to approach because of dragons, griffins, and monsters of immense men. **Parthia** is generally named from the borders of India all the way to Mesopotamia. For on account of the unconquered valor of the Parthians, both Assyria and the other neighboring regions took its name. For in it are Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Media, and Persis; these regions are joined to one another and take their beginning from the Indus River. They are closed in by the Tigris, situated in mountainous and rugged places, having the rivers Hydaspes and Arar. They are distinct among themselves by their own borders, drawing their names from their own founders in this way: **Arachosia** is named from its own town. The Parthians, coming from Scythia, occupied **Parthia** and called it after their own name. To its south is the Red Sea; to the north the Hyrcanian thicket; and to the west lies the central region of the sun. There are eighteen kingdoms within it,

<column-break/>

stretching from the Caspian shore all the way to the lands of the Scythians. **Assyria** is named after Asshur, the son of Shem, who was the first to inhabit that region after the Flood. It touches India on the east, Media on the south, the Tigris on the west, and Mount Caucasus on the north, where the Caspian Gates are located. In this region, the use of purple dye was first discovered. From there first came ointments for the hair and body, and the scents with which the luxury of the Romans and Greeks overflows. **Media** and **Persis** were named after the kings Medus and Perses, who attacked those provinces in war. Of these, Media, lying crosswise from the west, embraces the Parthian kingdoms; it is surrounded by Armenia on the north, sees the Caspians on the east, and Persis on the south. This land produces the **Median tree** <note>The citron tree, valued for its medicinal properties and fruit</note>, which no other region brings forth. There are, however, two Medias: the Greater and the Lesser. **Persis** <note>Persia</note> extends from the east all the way to the Indians; on the west it has the Red Sea; on the north it touches Media; and on the south Armenia, which is annexed to Persis. In these lands is Susa, a most noble town. <margin>magical arts</margin> In Persis the **magical art** first arose, to which Nimrod the giant went after the confusion of languages; there he taught the Persians to worship fire. For all in those parts worship the sun, which in their language is called **El**. **Mesopotamia** possesses a Greek etymology: it is surrounded by two rivers. For on the east it has the Tigris, and on the west the Euphrates. It begins on the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus. To its south follows **Babylonia**, then **Chaldea**, and finally **Arabia**. The head of the Babylonian region is the city of **Babylon**, from which it is named; it was so noble that Chaldea, Assyria, and Mesopotamia once passed into its name. <margin>Arabia i.e. sacred</margin> **Arabia** is so named, meaning "sacred." For this is what the name is interpreted to signify, because it is a region bearing frankincense and producing scents. Hence the Greeks named it *Eudaimon* <note>Greek for "Happy" or "Fortunate"</note> and our people call it "Blessed" <note>Arabia Felix</note>. In its thickets, myrrh and cinnamon grow. There the **Phoenix** bird is born; the sardonyx gem and the *biris melocides* <note>possibly a type of yellow gem</note> and *pedorata* are found there. <margin>saba</margin> This same land is also called **Saba** <note>Sheba</note>, after the son of Cush who was named Saba. It extends in a narrow tract of land toward the east to the Persian Gulf; its northern parts are closed by Chaldea, and its western side by the Arabian Gulf. A certain native named Syrus is said to have named **Syria** from his own name. It is bounded on the east by the river Euphrates, on the west by our sea and Egypt, having Armenia and Cappadocia to the north, and the Arabian Gulf to the south. Its site is stretched out to an immense length, but is narrower in width. It contains within itself the provinces of **Commagene**, **Phoenicia**, and **Palestine**, a part of which is **Judea**, aside from the Saracens and Nabataeans. **Commagene**, the first province of Syria, is named from the city of Commage, which once held the status of a metropolis there. To its north is Cappadocia, to its east Mesopotamia, to its south Syria, and to its west the Great Sea. **Phoenix**, the brother of Cadmus, setting out from Egyptian Thebes for Syria, reigned at Sidon, and named that province **Phoenicia** after his own name.

# Book 14

This is the region where Tyre is located, to which the prophet Isaiah speaks. It has Arabia to the east and the Red Sea to the south. The province of Palestine once had the city of Ascalon as its metropolis—from which the entire region around it was named Palestine. To the east of this land, the Red Sea is found; on the southern side it is bordered by Judea; on the northern side it is enclosed by the borders of the Tyrians; and to the west it is bounded by the Egyptian border. The region of **Judea**, a part of Palestine, was named after Judah, from whose tribe it drew its kings. This land was previously called **Canaan**, either after the son of Ham or after the ten Canaanite nations; once they were expelled, the Jews took possession of the land. The beginning of its length stretches from the village of Arsa to the village of Julia, where Jews and Tyrians live together in a shared settlement. Its width extends from Mount Lebanon to the Lake of Tiberias. In the middle of Judea is the city of **Jerusalem**, which is like the navel <note>original: "umbilicus"; a common medieval metaphor for the center of the world</note> of the entire region and the whole earth. It is rich in diverse resources, fertile in crops, famous for its waters, and abundant in balsams. Therefore, according to <term>fm</term> <note>original abbreviation for "secundum," meaning "according to"</note> the favor of the elements, the Jews judged it to be the land promised to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey, since it was from here that the privilege of the resurrection of God was promised to them. **Samaria** is a region of Palestine that took its name from a certain town called Samaria, once a royal city in Israel, which is now called **Sebastia** in honor of Augustus <note>Sebastos is the Greek equivalent of the Latin name Augustus</note>. This region lies in the middle between Judea and Galilee, beginning from the village named Eleas and ending in the land of Acrabat. Its nature is very similar to Syria, and it does not differ at all from Judea. **Galilee** is a region of Palestine so named because it produces people who are whiter <note>original: "candidiores"; Isidore falsely links "Galilee" to the Greek word "gala," meaning "milk"</note> than those in the rest of Palestine. This region is twofold, Upper and Lower, which are connected to one another and border Syria and Phoenicia. The land is rich and fertile, and it is abundantly productive with fruits.

<margin>Concerning Sodom, consumed by fire</margin>
**Pentapolis** <note>literally "Five Cities"</note> is a region located on the border of Arabia and Palestine, named after the five cities of the impious which were consumed by celestial fire. This land, once the most fertile beyond Jerusalem, is now a desert and burnt. For because of the crimes of its inhabitants, fire descended from heaven and dissolved that region into eternal ashes. A certain shadow and appearance of this remains even now in the embers and the trees themselves. For green apples grow there with such an appearance of ripeness that they create a desire to be eaten; but if you pluck them, they crumble and dissolve into ash, exhaling smoke as if they were still burning.

<margin>Nabataea</margin>
The region of **Nabataea** is named after Nebaioth, the son of Ishmael. It lies between Judea and Arabia, and rising from the Euphrates, it stretches to the Red Sea; it is considered a part of Arabia.

<margin>Egypt</margin>
**Egypt**, which was previously called Aeria, later received its name from Egyptus, the brother of Danaus, who reigned there. To the east, it is joined to Syria and the Red Sea; to the west it has Libya; to the north the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>; and to the south it recedes inland, reaching all the way to the Ethiopians. This region of the sky is unaccustomed to storms and ignorant of rain. Only the **Nile** irrigates it as it flows around it, making it fertile by its inundation. Thus, it is so productive in crops that it feeds a great part of the earth with grain; it is also so abundant in other business that it fills the whole world with necessary merchandise.

<margin>Canopus</margin>
The boundary of Egypt is **Canopus**, named after Canopus, the pilot of Menelaus, who was buried on that island which

<column-break/>

marks the beginning of Libya and forms a mouth of the Nile. The **Seres** <note>A name used for the people of China, derived from the word for silk</note> is a town of the East from which both the silk people and their region are named. This land curves from the Scythian Ocean and the Caspian Sea toward the Eastern Ocean. It is fertile with noble leaves from which fleeces <note>original: "vellera"; the author believes silk grows on trees like wool</note> are gathered, which the Seres sell to other nations for the making of garments. The river Bactros gave its name to the region of **Bactria**. Those parts of it that are flat are surrounded by mountain ridges; the parts facing them are bounded by the headwaters of the river Indus. The rest is enclosed by the river Oxus. Bactria produces the strongest camels, which never wear down their feet. **Scythia**, like **Gothia**, is said to be named after Magog, the son of Japheth. Its land was once immense; for it stretched from India in the east, through the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov</note> in the north, between the Danube and the Ocean, all the way to the borders of Germany. Later, however, it was made smaller, extending from the right side of the East, where the Syrian Ocean goes, to the Caspian Sea which is to the west; from there it extends south to the Caucasus ridge. Below this lies **Hyrcania**, having many small nations to the west that wander widely because of the infertility of the lands. Some of these inhabit fields; others are monstrous and fierce, living on human flesh and blood. Many parts of Scythia are wealthy, yet many are uninhabitable. For while in most places they abound in gold and gems, because of the cruelty of the **griffins** <note>mythical creatures with the body of a lion and wings of an eagle</note>, the access of humans is rare. This is the homeland of the best emeralds. The *liancus* stone <note>possibly lyncurium, a legendary gemstone</note> and the purest crystal are also found in Scythia. It has great rivers: the Oxus, the Phasis, and the Araxes. **Hyrcania** is named after the Hyrcanian forest, which lies below Scythia, having the Caspian Sea to the east, Armenia to the south, Albania to the north, and Iberia to the west. It is rugged with forests and full of monstrous wild beasts: tigers, panthers, and leopards. Concerning this, **Virgil** wrote: *Hyrcanian tigers gave you suck.* **Albania** is named for the color of the people, because they are born with white hair. Rising in the east below the Caspian Sea, it extends along the shores of the Northern Ocean all the way to the Maeotian marshes through desert and uncultivated lands. There are huge dogs in this land, of such ferocity that they can pin down bulls and kill lions. **Armenia** is named after Armenus, the companion of Jason the Thessalian; after King Jason was lost, Armenus gathered a multitude of people who were wandering about, took Armenia, and named it after himself. It is situated between the Taurus and Caucasus mountains, stretching from Cappadocia to the Caspian Sea. It has the Ceraunian mountains to the north, from whose hills the river Tigris is born, and upon whose mountains the **Ark** is said to have rested after the Flood. Armenia is twofold, Upper and Lower, just like the two Pannonias. **Iberia** <note>referring to Caucasian Iberia, modern Georgia</note> is a region of Asia, joined to Armenia near the Black Sea. Useful dye-herbs grow here. **Cappadocia** was named after its own city. Situated at the head of Syria, it touches Armenia to the east, Asia Minor to the west, and the Cimmerian Sea to the north, as well as the Themiscirian plains which the **Amazons** once held. To the south it has the Taurus mountain, below which lie Cilicia and Isauria as far as the Cilician Gulf, which looks toward the island of Cyprus. Its land nurtures horses more than any other. The river Halys flows through it, which once divided the kingdoms of Lydia from Persia.

<meta>This page continues a geographical survey, likely from Isidore of Seville's "Etymologies." It transitions from the provinces of Asia Minor to the beginning of a description of Europe, focusing heavily on the origins of place names and the legendary history of their inhabitants.</meta>

Asia Minor is bounded on the east by Cappadocia; on all other sides it is surrounded by the sea. To the north it has the Euxine Sea <note>original: "pontū euxinū"; now known as the Black Sea</note>; to the west the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>; and to the south the Egyptian Sea. It contains the provinces of Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycia, and Cilicia. The first of Asia Minor is Bithynia at the beginning of the Euxine Sea toward the rising sun, lying opposite Thrace. It was called by many names previously: for it was first called Bebrytia, then Mygdonia, and soon named Bithynia after King Bithynus. This is also Greater Phrygia. The city of Nicomedia is in it, where the fleeing Hannibal died by drinking poison. Galatia was named after the ancient tribes of the Gauls <note>original: "galloꝝ" / "Gallorum"</note> by whom it was occupied. For the Gauls, summoned to help by the king of Bithynia, divided the kingdom with him after a victory was agreed upon; thus later mixed with Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks, but now from the ancient name of the Gauls they are called Galatians, and their region is called Galatia. Phrygia was named after Phrygia, the daughter of Cecrops. It was also called Dardania after Dardanus, the son of Jupiter, of whom Homer says:
> Whom Jupiter first begat in the celestial citadel. <note>original Latin: "Quē primū genuit celesti iupiter arce." This refers to a passage in the Iliad describing the lineage of the Trojan kings.</note>
For this man, setting out from the city of Corinth, first came to Phrygia. This region of Troas lies below Galatia to the north; to the south it is near Lycaonia; to the east it borders Lydia; and to the west it is bounded by the Hellespont sea. The region of Troy is here, which Tros, the king of the Trojans and father of Ganymede, named after himself. There are two Phrygias: Greater and Lesser. Greater Phrygia contains Smyrna; Lesser Phrygia contains Ilium <note>Troy</note> and Lycaonia. The river Herinus separates Caria from Phrygia. Lydia was the seat of ancient kings, which the waters of the Pactolus made wealthy with its golden torrents. This was previously called Maeonia. Because it could not support two brother kings, Lydus and Tyrrhenus, due to its small size, Tyrrhenus set out from here by lot with a vast multitude, occupied parts of Italy, and named it Tyrrhenia <note>The land of the Etruscans</note>. Lydia, however, was named after Lydus, the king's brother, who had remained in the province. It joins Lesser Phrygia to the west and has the city of Smyrna to the east, which the river Melas surrounds. The Pactolus and Herinus rivers flow around its fields, very rich in golden sands. Isauria is said to be named from the nature of the place, because it is open on all sides to the blowing of the winds <note>original: "aurarū flatibus"; the author is making a word-play between "Isauria" and "aura," the Latin word for breeze</note>. It has the city of Seleucia as its metropolis. Cilicia took its name from a certain Cilix, whom they say was the son of Phoenix and assert was older than Jupiter. Much of it lies in plains, meeting Lycia from the west, the Persian Sea from the south, and the ridges of the Taurus Mountains from behind. The river Cydnus intersects it, and its mother-city is Tarsus. In it is also the town of Corycus, from which comes the most and best saffron <term>crocum: a spice and dye derived from the crocus flower</term>, with a fragrant breath and a color more beautiful than gold. Lycia is so named because it is joined to Cilicia from the east. For it has Cilicia to the east, the sea to the west and south, and Caria to the north. There is Mount Chimera, which breathes out fire in nocturnal heats, just as Etna does in Sicily and Vesuvius in Campania.

### Chapter 4: On Europe

After Asia, we turn our pen to Europe. Europe was indeed the daughter of Agenor, king of Libya,

<column-break/>

whom Jupiter carried away from Africa to Crete, and he named the third part of the world after her name. This Agenor was the son of Libya, from whom Libya—that is, Africa—is said to have been named. From this it appears that Libya received its name first, and Europe afterwards. Europe, divided into the third part of the world, begins from the Tanais river <note>The Don river</note>, descending from the west through the northern ocean as far as the borders of Spain, whose eastern and southern part, rising from the Euxine Sea, is entirely joined to the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> and ends at the islands of Gades <note>Cadiz</note>. The first region of Europe is Lower Scythia, which, beginning from the Maeotian marshes <note>Sea of Azov</note>, extends between the Danube and the northern ocean as far as Germany; this land is generally called "Barbarica" because of the barbarian tribes by which it is inhabited. The first part of this is Alania, which reaches the Maeotian marshes. After this is Dacia, where Gothia is also located; then Germany, where the Suebi inhabited a large part. Germany is after Lower Scythia, enclosed by the Danube between the Rhine river and the ocean; it is girded by the ocean to the north and west, by the Danube to the east, and is separated by the Rhine river to the south—a land rich in strength, and with numerous and immense peoples. Therefore, it is called Germany <note>original: "Germania"</note> because of the fecundity <note>original: "fecunditatē"</note> of germinating <note>original: "gignendoꝝ" / "gignendorum"; the author incorrectly derives the name from "germinate"</note> peoples. It produces Hyrcanian birds, whose feathers shine at night <note>A legendary bird often mentioned in medieval bestiaries</note>. It gives birth to bisons, wild beasts, bears, and elks. It also yields gems: crystal, amber <note>original: "sucinū" / "succinum"</note>, and green callais <note>a turquoise-colored stone</note>, as well as white ceraunium <note>literally a "thunder-stone," believed to be created by lightning</note>. There are two Germanies: Upper, near the northern ocean, and Lower, near the Rhine. As for the provinces which the Danube separates from the barbarian lands toward the Mediterranean Sea, the first is Mysia, named from the abundance of harvests <note>original: "messiū ꝓuētu" / "messium proventu"</note>. Whence the ancients used to call it the granary of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture</note>. This is joined to the mouths of the Danube from the east, to Thrace from the southeast, to Macedonia from the south, and to Istria from the west. After Mysia is Pannonia. Then comes the Norican land, cold and sparingly fruitful. After that is Raetia, fertile in crops, which leads into Belgic Gaul. Tiras, the son of Japheth, is said to have come and given his name to Thrace. Others say Thrace was named from the Scythian character of its inhabitants. To its east is the Propontis and the city of Constantinople; to the north the Ister <note>The Danube</note> stretches out; to the south it borders the Aegean Sea; and to the west Macedonia lies beneath it. Many nations once inhabited its region: the people of the Bessi, the Massagetae, Sarmatians, Scythians, and many others. For it is vast, and therefore contained many tribes. Thrace pours forth the Hebrus river, which touches many barbarian nations. Greece is named after King Graecus, who inhabited that entire region during his reign. There are seven provinces of Greece: the first from the west is Dalmatia, then Epirus, then Hellas, then Thessaly, then Macedonia, then Achaia, and two in the sea, Crete and the Cyclades. All of Greece is generally called Illyricus. Dalmatia is thought to have taken its name from Delminium, the largest city of that province. It borders Macedonia on the east, Mysia on the north, is bounded by Istria on the west, and is enclosed by the Adriatic Gulf on the south. Epirus is named after Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles...
