part of which is Chaonia, which was previously called Molossia after Molossus, the son whom Pyrrhus had by Andromache. <note>Pyrrhus is another name for Neoptolemus, son of Achilles; Andromache was the widow of the Trojan hero Hector.</note> But after Pyrrhus was killed by the treachery of Orestes, Helenus <note>a brother of Hector</note> took Andromache as his wife. He held the kingdom of his stepson, who had succeeded his father, and from him a part of Epirus was called Molossia. Later, Helenus named it Chaonia after his brother Chaon, whom he is said to have killed by accident while hunting, naming it thus as a consolation for his lost brother. **Hellas** was named after King Hellen, the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, from whom the Greeks were also called "Hellenes." This same land is **Attica**, which was first called Atta. For there was a certain Cranaus <note>OCR reads "gran'"; Cranaus was a legendary king of Athens</note>, a native of Greece, from whose daughter, named Attis, the land was called Attica. This lies in the middle between Macedonia and Achaia, joined to Arcadia on the northern side. This is "True Greece," where the city of **Athens** was, the mother of liberal arts and the nurse of philosophers; Greece had nothing more famous or noble than her. In it is also the plain of **Marathon**, famous for a once very bloody battle. There are two provinces of Hellas: **Boeotia** and the **Peloponnese**. Boeotia was named for this reason: when Cadmus, son of Agenor, was searching for his sister Europa (who had been abducted by Jupiter) by his father's command and could not find her, he chose exile, fearing his father's anger. By chance, having followed the tracks of a cow <note>original: "bouis" / "bovis"</note>, he took up residence where she had lain down; thus he named the place Boeotia from the name of the cow <note>The Greek word for cow is "bous."</note>. There he also built the city of **Thebes**, where civil wars once thundered and where Apollo and the Great Hercules—the Theban—were born. This same land is called **Aonia** from a certain fountain consecrated to Apollo and the Muses, which is in that same Boeotia. The **Peloponnese** is the second part of Hellas, ruled by and named after Pelops. **Thessaly** was named after King Thessalus; it is joined to the southern region of Macedonia, while Pieria is behind it. There are many rivers and towns in Thessaly, most notably **Thessalonica** and **Thebes**. There also is Mount **Parnassus**, once consecrated to Apollo. Thessaly was the homeland of Achilles and the origin of the **Lapiths**, of whom it is said they were the first to tame horses with bridles, which is why they were called "Centaurs." In Thessaly, solid gold coins were first made, and the use of the horse for taming was also first discovered there. In the beginning, **Macedonia** was called Emathia after King Emathius, but Macedon, the maternal grandson of Deucalion, changed the name and called it Macedonia after his own name after he took leadership there. It is bounded on the east by the Aegean Sea, on the south by Achaia, on the west by Dalmatia, and on the north by Moesia; it is the homeland of Alexander the Great and a region rich with veins of gold and silver. It produces the stone they call "paeanite." Mount **Olympus** is within it, which rises with such an excellent peak that neither clouds nor winds are felt at its summit. **Achaia** was named both a city and a province after King Achaeus. This is almost an island, for except for the northern part where it joins Macedonia, it is surrounded by sea on all sides. To the east it has the Myrtoan Sea, to the southeast the Cretic Sea, to the south the Ionian, and to the southwest and west the Cassiopian islands; only on the northern side is it joined to Macedonia or the land of Attica. Its capital is the city of **Corinth**, the

<column-break/>

glory of Greece. The Inachus is a river of Achaia. **Arcadia** is a fold of Achaia, shaped like a plane tree leaf, situated between the Ionian and Aegean seas. Arcas, the son of Jupiter and Callisto, brought the Pelasgians under his rule and named it Arcadia after himself. This is also **Sicyonia**, named after King Sicyon, from whom the kingdom of the Sicyonians was named. Arcadia has a great river, the Erymanthus, and the stone "abeston" <note>asbestos</note>, which, once set on fire, is never extinguished. Most praised blackbirds are also born there. **Pannonia** was named from the "Apennine Alps" <note>The author likely refers to the Eastern Alps or Julian Alps</note> by which it is separated from Italy; a region strong and joyful in its soil, walled by two very swift rivers, the Drava and the Sava. It joins with Noricum and Raetia, having Moesia to the east, Istria to the southeast, the Apennine Alps to the southwest, Belgic Gaul to the west, and to the north the source or boundary of the Danube, which separates Germany and Gaul. **Istria** was named by the river Ister, which flows into its land; this is the same as the Danube. To the north, Istria has Pannonia. **Italy** was once occupied by the Greeks themselves and was called "Magna Graecia" <note>Great Greece</note>. Then, from the name of a king, it was called **Saturnia**, and also **Latium**, because the same Saturn, driven from his home by Jupiter, hid <note>original: "latuerit"</note> there. Finally, it was named Italy after Italus, king of the Sicels, who reigned there. Its site extends further in length than in width, from the northwest to the southeast; it is enclosed to the south by the Tyrrhenian Sea and to the north by the Adriatic; it is bounded on the west by the ridges of the Alps. It is a land most beautiful in all things, most pleasing in the fertility of its soil and the richness of its pasture. It has lakes Benacus, Avernus, and Lucrinus; the rivers Eridanus <note>The Po</note> and Tiber; and the warm springs of Baiae. It produces gemstones, silk, the "ligurium," and coral; also the "boa" serpent, the lynx, and "Diomedian" birds. Both Italy and Spain are called **Hesperia** because the Greeks sail by the star Hesperus <note>The Evening Star</note>. There are two Hesperias—in Italy and in Spain—which are distinguished in this way: either "Hesperia" is said alone, signifying Italy, or "Ultimate" is added, signifying Spain, because it is at the end of the West. **Tuscany** <note>original: "Tuscia"</note> is a part of Italy, and **Umbria** is a part of Tuscany. Tuscany was named from the frequency of its sacred rites and incense: "from sacrificing." <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν" (apo tou thyein). The author is linking the name 'Tuscia' to the Greek word for sacrifice/incense.</note> Umbria is so called, as histories tell, because it survived the rains <note>original: "imbribus"</note> during the time of the watery disaster <note>the Great Flood</note>, and for this reason it was named "Umbria" in the Greek manner. It is situated on the ridges of the Apennine mountains in the part of Italy toward the south. **Etruria** <note>original: "Hetrruria"</note> is a part of Italy so named because its boundaries extended all the way to the bank of the Tiber, as if "another boundary." <note>original: "ἕτερος ὅροος" (heteros oros). The author is providing a folk etymology for Etruria.</note> For *heteros* means "another," and *oros* is called "boundary." For previously the boundaries of Rome held only one bank of the Tiber. Others think Etruria was named after Prince Etruscus. It is the same as **Tyrrhenia**, named after Tyrrhenus, the brother of Lydus, who came to Italy from Maeonia with a part of his people by lot. This is also Tuscany; however, we ought not to say "Tusciam," as we never read it <note>The translator notes a grammatical preference here</note>. Tuscany was named from the frequency of sacrifice and incense: "from sacrificing." <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θύειν" (apo tou thyein)</note> There, the arts of the soothsayers <note>haruspices</note> are said to have been discovered. **Apulia** is where Brundusium is, which those who followed the leader Diomedes founded long ago. **Campania** has lands that are green in winter and summer alike. The sun there is mild, the temperature pleasing, the air pure and gentle. **Gaul** <note>original: "Gallia"</note> was named from the whiteness <note>original: "candore"</note> of its people.

<meta>This page continues the geographical survey of the world, moving from the regions of Greece into Western Europe (Gaul and Spain) and then across the Mediterranean to Northern Africa (Libya/Africa). For *gala* <note>original: "gala"; the Greek word for milk</note> in Greek means milk. For the mountains and the coldness of the climate in that part of the world shut out the heat of the sun, which results in the whiteness of people's bodies not being darkened by color. This land is protected on the east by the peaks of the Alps; it is enclosed on the west by the Ocean; to the south it is bounded by the steep Pyrenees; and to the north by the flows of the Rhine and by Germany. Its beginning is **Belgica** and its end is **Aquitania**. It is a region with fertile soil and rich pastures, well-suited for the use of living creatures, and watered by rivers and springs; it is bathed by two great rivers, the **Rhine** and the **Rhone**. **Belgis** is a city in Gaul from which the province of Belgica is named. **Cisalpine** <note>literally "this side of the Alps"</note> is on this side of the Alps, while **Transalpine**—that is, "across the Alps"—lies toward the north. **Rhaetia** is located near the Rhine. **Aquitania**, however, is named after the "slanting waters" <note>original: "obliquis aquis"</note> of the river Loire, which forms most of its boundary and surrounds it almost in a circle. **Spain** was first called **Iberia** after the river Ebro, and was later named **Hispania** after Hispalus <note>a legendary founder associated with the city of Seville</note>. It is also the true **Hesperia**, named after Hesperus, the evening star. It is situated between Africa and Gaul, closed off to the north by the Pyrenees mountains and surrounded on all other sides by the sea. It is equal in the healthfulness of its climate, fertile in all kinds of crops, and very rich in stores of gems and metals. Great rivers flow through it: the **Baetis** <note>the Guadalquivir</note>, the **Minho**, the **Ebro**, and the **Tagus**, which carries gold like the river Pactolus. It has six provinces: Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, Galicia, Baetica, and—across the straits in the region of Africa—Tingitana. There are two "Spains": **Nearer Spain** <note>original: "citerior"</note>, which stretches in the northern region from the Pyrenees to Cartagena; and **Further Spain** <note>original: "ulterior"</note>, which extends in the south from the Celtiberians to the Strait of Gades <note>the Strait of Gibraltar</note>. They are called "Nearer" and "Further" as if to say "on this side" and "beyond"; "on this side" as if it were around the lands, and "beyond" either because it is the furthest or because there is no other land after this one.

### Concerning Libya, Chapter 5

**L**ibya is so named because the *libs* <note>the southwest wind</note> blows from there. Others say that Epaphus, the son of Jupiter who founded Memphis in Egypt, fathered a daughter named **Libya** by his wife Cassiotis, and she later possessed a kingdom in Africa. The land was named Libya after her. Some think **Africa** was named as if it were *aprica* <note>sunny or open to the sun</note>, because it is open to the sky or the sun and is without the dread of cold. Others say Africa is named after one of the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, who was called **Afer**, whom we mentioned above. It begins from the borders of Egypt, proceeding toward the south through **Ethiopia** as far as Mount Atlas. On the northern side, joined to the Mediterranean Sea, it is enclosed and ends at the Strait of Gades. It contains the provinces of Libya Cyrenensis, Pentapolis, Tripolis, Byzacena, Carthage, Numidia, Mauritania Sitifensis, Mauritania Caesariensis, Mauritania Tingitana, and, near the heat of the sun, Ethiopia. **Libya Cyrenensis** is the first part of Africa, named after the metropolitan city of Cyrene, which is within its borders. To its east is Egypt; to its west are the Greater Syrtes <note>a gulf on the Libyan coast</note> and the Troglodytes; to the north is the Libyan Sea; to the south are various nations of Ethiopians and barbarians, and inaccessible solitudes that even produce basilisk serpents. **Pentapolis** is named in the Greek language from five

<column-break/>

cities: that is, Cyrene, Berenice, Teuchira <note>OCR reads "centria"</note>, Apollonia, and Ptolemais. Of these, Ptolemais and Berenice were named after kings. Pentapolis is joined to Libya Cyrenensis and is considered part of its territory. The Greeks also designate the province of **Tripolitana** in their language from the number of three great cities: Oea, Sabratha <note>OCR reads "taba"</note>, and Leptis Magna <note>OCR reads "celepris magnę"</note>. This province has the Greater Syrtes and the Troglodytes to the east, the Adriatic Sea <note>referring generally to the Mediterranean south of Italy</note> to the north, Byzacena to the west, and to the south the Gaetulians and Garamantes reaching as far as the Ethiopian Ocean. The region of **Byzacena** obtained its name from two very noble towns, one of which is called Hadrumetum and the other Byzacium. This lies below Tripolis, extending two hundred miles or more; it is a land of such rich soil that seeds cast there return a harvest of almost a hundred-fold. **Zeugis**, where Great **Carthage** is, is the "True Africa," situated between Byzacena and Numidia; it is joined to the Sicilian Sea on the north and stretches south as far as the region of the Gaetulians. Its interior is fruitful, but the further parts are full of beasts and serpents and large wild donkeys wandering in the desert. **Gaetulia** <note>OCR reads "Setulia"</note> is the inland part of Africa. **Numidia** was so called by its inhabitants who wandered everywhere, because they had no fixed home. Indeed, in their language, "Numidia" means unstable and wandering homes. It begins from the river Ampsaga and ends at the border of Zeugitana, having the Lesser Syrtes to the east, the sea facing Sardinia to the north, Mauritania Sitifensis to the west, and the Ethiopian tribes to the south. It is a region of very rich plains. Where it is forested, it rears wild beasts; where it is mountainous and steep, it produces horses and wild donkeys. It is also celebrated for its excellent marble, which is called "Numidian." It has the principal cities of Hippo Regius and Rusicade <note>OCR reads "fusicadam"</note>. **Mauritania** is named from the color of its people, for the Greeks call black *mauros*. For just as Gaul was named for the whiteness of its people, so Mauritania obtained its name from their blackness. Its first province is **Mauritania Sitifensis**, which had the town of Sitifis, from which the region is said to have taken its name. **Mauritania Caesariensis** had the city of Caesarea, a colony, and the name of the province was given from it. Both of these joined together have Numidia to the east, the Great Sea to the north, the river Moulouya <note>original: "malua"</note> to the west, and Mount Astrixis to the south, which separates the fertile land from the lying sands, extending to the Ocean. **Mauritania Tingitana** is named after Tingi <note>Tangier</note>, the metropolitan city of this province. This last part of Africa rises from the Seven Mountains, having the river Moulouya to the east, the Strait of Gades to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and to the south the Gaetulian tribes wandering as far as the Western Ocean. It is a region producing wild beasts, monkeys, dragons, and ostriches. It was also once full of elephants, which now only India produces. The capital of the region of the **Garamantes** was the town of Garama. It is located between Cyrenensis and Ethiopia, where there is a spring that is cold during the heat of the day and hot during the cold of the night. **Ethiopia** is named from the color of its people, whom the proximity of the sun scorches. Finally, the power of the star...

Around the west, however, it is mountainous; in the middle, it is sandy; and toward the eastern region, it is a desert. Its location extends from the western Atlas Mountain to the east, as far as the borders of Egypt. It is bounded on the south by the Ocean and on the north by the river Nile, containing many nations with diverse faces and a horrible, monstrous appearance. It is also fertile and filled with a multitude of serpents. Indeed, the rhinoceros beast, the camelopard <note>original: "camelopardus"; the giraffe, named for having features of both a camel and a leopard</note>, the basilisk, and huge dragons are found there; it is from the brains of these dragons that gems are extracted. Hyacinths and "gold-opals" <note>original: "chrysolopallus"</note> are found there. Cinnamon is also gathered there. There are, however, two Ethiopias: one near the rising sun, and the other near its setting in Mauritania. 

Beyond the three parts of the world <note>The three parts being Asia, Europe, and Africa</note>, there is a fourth part across the interior Ocean in the south, which is unknown to us because of the sun's heat; in its lands, the **Antipodes** <note>literally "those with opposite feet"</note> are fabulously said to dwell. Closest to Spain is **Mauritania**, then **Numidia**, then the region of **Carthage**; after that we find **Gaetulia**, then **Ethiopia**, and then places scorched by the heat of the sun. It should certainly be known that certain provinces were first named after the name of an author <note>a founding figure or ruler</note>, and later the name of the people was made from the province. For from **Italus** came **Italia**, and again from Italy comes the "Italian," and thus we use the name of the nation in the same way the name of the founder was, from which the name of the province was derived. And thus it happens that from one man, a city, a region, and a people are named. 

**Provinces**, however, received their name from a cause. For when the Romans, by conquering <note>original: "vincendo"</note>, brought the leadership of nations that belonged to other kings under their own law, they called those distantly placed regions "provinces" <note>Isidore derives *provincia* from *pro* (before/far) and *vincere* (to conquer)</note>. A **fatherland** <note>original: "patria"</note> is so called because it is common to all who are born in it. **Land** <note>original: "terra"</note> signifies the element, as we said before, while "lands" <note>original: "terras"</note> refers to individual parts, such as Africa or Italy. These are the same as **places**. For places and spaces of lands in the circle of the earth contain many provinces within them, just as a "place" in the body is one part containing many members within itself, or as a house contains many rooms; so lands and places are called "spaces of lands," of which the parts are provinces, such as **Phrygia** in Asia, **Rhaetia** in Gaul, or **Baetica** in Spain. For Asia is the place, but Phrygia is the province, **Troy** is the region of Phrygia, and **Ilium** is the city of Troy. 

Furthermore, **regions** are parts of provinces, which the common people call "districts" <note>original: "conventus"</note>, such as Troy in Phrygia, or **Cantabria** and **Asturia** in **Galicia**. A region is named after its rulers <note>Isidore links *regio* to *rector* (ruler)</note>, and its parts are **territories**. A **territory** is so called as if it were a "bull-tory" <note>original: "tauritorium"</note>, worn down <note>original: "tritum"</note> by oxen and the plow. For the ancients, by drawing a furrow, designated the limits of both possessions and territories.

### On islands Chapter 6.

<image-desc>A small red decorative drawing of a leafy branch or plant, serving as the base for the initial letter 'I'.</image-desc>
**Islands** <note>original: "insulae"</note> are so called because they are in the salt-water <note>original: "salo"</note>, that is, in the sea. Of these, the most well-known and greatest, which many of the ancients investigated with skillful zeal, should be noted. **Britain**, an island of the Ocean, is divided from the whole world by the intervening sea; it is named after the name of its own people. This is situated opposite the part of the Gauls, facing toward Spain. Its circumference is forty-eight times seventy-five miles <note>approximately 3,600 miles</note>. There are many large rivers in it,

<column-break/>

hot springs, and a large and varied supply of metals. The **jet** stone <note>original: "gagates"</note> is very abundant there, as are pearls. **Thanatos** <note>the Isle of Thanet</note> is an island of the Ocean, separated from Britain by a narrow channel of the Gallic sea, with grain-producing fields and fertile soil. It is called *Thanatos* <note>Greek for "death"</note> because of the death of serpents; although it has none of its own, soil carried from there to any other nation kills snakes instantly. **Thule** <note>original: "Tile"</note> is the furthest island of the Ocean, between the northern and western regions beyond Britain, taking its name from the sun because the sun makes the summer solstice there, and there is no day beyond it. Hence its sea is sluggish and frozen. The **Orkneys** are islands of the Ocean positioned beyond Britain, thirty-three in number, of which twenty are deserted and thirteen are inhabited. **Scotia** is the same as **Hibernia** <note>Ireland</note>; it is the nearest island to Britain, narrower in the space of its lands, but more fertile in its location. This extends from the southwest to the north. Its earlier parts look toward Iberia and Cantabria across the Ocean, which is why it is called Hibernia. It is called **Scotia**, however, because it is inhabited by the tribes of the Scots. There are no snakes there, birds are rare, and there are no bees; so much so that if dust or pebbles brought from there are scattered among beehives elsewhere, the swarms desert the honeycombs. 

**Gades** <note>Cádiz</note> is an island situated at the end of the province of Baetica, which divides Europe from Africa, in which the **Pillars of Hercules** are seen, and where the tide of the Ocean is sent into the mouth of the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is divided from the mainland by one hundred paces; the Tyrians, coming from the Red Sea, occupied it and called it *Gades* in their own language, which means "enclosed," because it is surrounded by the sea. A tree grows there similar to a palm, whose gum, when used to stain glass, produces the "thunder-gem" <note>original: "ceraunium"</note>. The **Fortunate Isles** <note>the Canary Islands</note> signify by their name that they produce all good things, as if happy and blessed with an abundance of fruits. By their own nature, they produce precious fruits of the forests; the ridges of the hills are clothed with spontaneous vines. Instead of common grass, there is harvest-grain and vegetables. Hence the error of the pagans and the songs of the secular poets, who, because of the fertility of the soil, thought these same islands were Paradise. They are situated in the Ocean against the left side of Mauritania, nearest to the west, and separated from each other by the intervening sea. 

The **Gorgodes** are islands of the Ocean facing the promontory called the "Horn of the West" <note>original: "Hesperu-ceras"</note>, which the Gorgon women once inhabited—tall of agility, with hairy and rough bodies; the islands are named after them. They are two days' sail from the mainland. The **Hesperides** islands are named after the city of Hesperis, which was in the territory of Mauritania. They are located beyond the Gorgodes at the foot of Mount Atlas in the deepest reaches of the sea; in their gardens, fables imagine a dragon acting as a guardian, watching over the golden apples. For it is said that an estuary of the sea there is so winding with twisted sides that to those looking from afar, it mimics the coils of snakes. **Chryse** and **Argyre** are islands situated in the Indian Ocean, so fertile with a supply of metals that many have claimed they have a surface of gold and silver, from which they received their names. **Taprobana** <note>Sri Lanka</note> is an island lying off India to the southeast, from where the Indian Ocean begins; it extends eight hundred and seventy-five miles in length and six hundred and twenty-five thousand stadia in width. It is split by a river flowing through it and is entirely filled with pearls and gems. Part of it...

# XIIII

b 3

...is filled with beasts and elephants. Part of it, however, is held by men. In this island <note>This refers to Taprobane, modern-day Sri Lanka, described at the end of the previous page</note> they say there are two summers and two winters in one single year, and that the place blooms twice with flowers. **Tylos** is an island of India <note>Now identified with Bahrain in the Persian Gulf</note> bearing leaves at all times. So far, these are the islands of the Ocean. Likewise, there are islands situated in the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> from the Hellespont to Gades <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain</note>. The island of **Cyprus** took its name from the city of Cyprus which is within it. This same island is Paphos, consecrated to Venus, located in the Carpathian Sea near the south; it was once famous for its riches and especially for copper <note>original: "ęris"; the word "copper" is actually derived from "Cyprus"</note>. For the first discovery and use of this metal was there. The island of **Crete** is a huge part of Greece opposite the Peloponnese. This was first called *Macaroneson* <note>original: "macaroneson"; Greek for "Islands of the Blessed"</note> because of the mildness of its climate. Then it was called Crete after a certain native named Cres, who they say was one of the Curetes <note>original: "cretarū"; referring to the mythological guardians</note> by whom Jupiter was hidden and nourished there. It is an island of Greece stretched out in a very long tract between the east and the west, bathed by the heat of Greece from the north and by the Egyptian waves from the south. It was once noble for its hundred cities, from which it was also called *Hecatompolis* <note>original: "hecatompolis"; Greek for "hundred-city"</note>. It first became famous for oars and arrows. It first fashioned laws with letters and was the first to teach cavalry troops. Musical study was begun there by the Idaean Dactyls <note>Mythical craftsmen and healers</note>. It is abundant in goats and lacks stags. it produces no wolves or foxes, nor any other harmful beasts; no serpent is there, and no owl; and if one is brought in, it dies immediately. It is large in its strengths and trees. The herb **Dittany** <note>original: "Dictamus"</note> grows in Crete, as does *alimos* <note>A plant said to prevent hunger</note>, which prevents daily hunger for those who chew it. However, it also produces venomous spiders <note>original: "Sphalangos"</note> and the stone called the Idaean Dactyl. **Abydos** is an island in Europe positioned above the Hellespont, separated by a narrow and dangerous sea; it is called Abydos in Greek because it is the entrance to the Hellespont sea, where Xerxes made a bridge from ships and crossed into Greece. The island of **Cos** lies adjacent to the province of Attica, in which the physician Hippocrates was born; as Varro <note>A famous Roman scholar</note> testifies, it first became famous for the art of wool-working for the adornment of women. The **Cyclades** were islands of Greece in ancient times, which they think are called "Cyclades" because, although they are protected at longer distances from Delos, they are situated in a circle around Delos. For the Greeks call a circle a *kyklon* <note>original: "κὐκλον"</note>. Some, however, think they are called Cyclades not because they are arranged in a circle, but because of the rocks <note>original: "scopulos"</note> which are around them. These are situated in the Hellespont between the Aegean and the Malean sea, and are also surrounded by the Myrtian sea. They are all fifty-two in number, stretching five hundred miles from north to south, and two hundred miles from east to west. Their metropolis is Rhodes. The island of **Delos** is situated in the middle of the Cyclades. It is said to be called *Delos* because after the flood which is noted in the times of Ogygus, when a continuous night had shadowed the world for many months, it was illuminated by the rays of the sun before all other lands, and took its name from that fact: because it was the first to be manifested to human sight. For the Greeks call "manifest" *delos* <note>original: "Δῆλος"</note>. It is also called **Ortygia**, because quails were first seen there, which the Greeks call *ortygias*. On this island, Latona gave birth to Apollo and Diana. Delos is the name of both a city and the island. **Rhodes** is the first of the Cyclades from the east, in which a "head of a rose" <note>original: "rosę capitulū"</note> is said to have been found while the city

<column-break/>

was being founded, from which both the city and the island were named Rhodes <note>A reference to the Greek word "rhodon" for rose</note>. In this city was the bronze **Colossus of the Sun**, seventy cubits in height. There were also one hundred other smaller colossi on the same island. **Tenedos** is one of the Cyclades situated to the north, in which a city was once founded by a certain Tenes, from whom the name of that city, or rather the island, came. For this Tenes, having been slandered <note>original: "insamatus"; likely a typo for "infamatus"</note> for having slept with his stepmother, fled to this island and took possession of it when it was empty of inhabitants; hence it was called the island of Tenedos. So says Cicero: "Tenes himself, from whose name Tenedos is called." **Carpathos** is one of the Cyclades positioned to the south opposite Egypt, from which the Carpathian Sea is named; it was called so because of the rapid ripening of its fruits. It is between Egypt and Rhodes. From this island, they say, come the "Carpathian ships," which are great and spacious. **Cythera** is one of the Cyclades situated on the western side, whose name was previously *Porphyris*. It was called Cythera, however, because Venus was said to have emerged there <note>Venus is often called "Cytherea"</note>. **Icaria** is one of the Cyclades which gave its name to the Icarian Sea; this island is inhospitable due to rocks running between Samos and Mykonos and has no harbors in its bays. It is said that Icarus the Cretan died there in a shipwreck, and the name was given to the place from the death of the man. The island of **Naxos** was named by Dionysus, as if "Dionaron," because it surpasses others in the fertility of its vines; it is separated from Delos by eighteen miles. It is from here that Jupiter is said to have set out against the Tyrrhenians. **Melos**, one of the number of the Cyclades, is the roundest of all islands, from which it was named <note>A pun on the Greek "melon" for apple/round fruit</note>. History says that Philomelus and Plutus were born of Iason, and from Philomelus was born Paron, who called the island and town **Paros** after his own name. It was previously called Minoa, then Paros. Of this Virgil says: "and snowy Paros." For it produces the whitest marble, which they call Parian. It also sends the sardius stone <note>A type of carnelian</note>, which is more excellent than marble, but among gems it is the cheapest. The island of **Chios** is named in the Syrian language because **mastic** <note>A resin</note> is produced there. For the Syrians call mastic *chion*. **Samos** is an island in the Aegean Sea where Juno was born; from here was the Samian Sibyl and Pythagoras the Samian, by whom the name "philosophy" was invented. It is handed down that earthenware vessels were first found on this island, which is why they are called Samian ware. **Sicily** was surnamed *Sicania* after King Sicanus, then *Sicilia* after Siculus, the brother of Italus. It was also called **Trinacria** because of its three "acres" <note>points</note>, that is, capes: Pelorus, Pachynus, and Lilybaeum. For *Trinacria* is Greek, which in Latin is called "tri-cornered" <note>original: "triquadra"</note>, as if divided into three squares. This is separated from Italy by a narrow strait, facing the African sea, very fruitful, and abundant in gold. However, it is full of caverns and pipes and full of winds and sulfur. For this reason, the fires of Mount **Etna** wander there; in its strait are **Scylla and Charybdis**, by which ships are either swallowed or dashed together. It was once the homeland of the Cyclops, and later the nourisher of tyrants; fertile in crops, and the first of all lands to be plowed with a furrow to receive seeds. It has Syracuse as the chief of its cities, the fountain of Arethusa, and the river Alpheus, the generator of great horses. Comedy was first invented on that island. It first produced the Agate stone from the river Achates...

<meta>This page continues the geography of Mediterranean islands, specifically moving through the central and western Mediterranean (Sicily, the Aeolian Islands, Sardinia, Corsica, and the Balearics) before transitioning into a new section on Promontories and then Mountains of the world.</meta>

by a river. It also produces coral. It even produces **Agrigentine salt**, which dissolves in fire and crackles in water <note>original: "sales agrigentinos"; a famous natural wonder cited in antiquity where the salt behaved contrary to its nature</note>. Its entire circumference covers three thousand stadia. **Sallust**, however, says that Sicily was once joined to Italy, but that the middle space was divided by the force of the sea and cut into a narrow passage. The island of **Lapsus** lies ten stadia away from Sicily; it is flatter than Sicily, which is why it was so named. Concerning this, **Virgil** wrote: "And the low-lying Lapsus" <note>original: "Lapsūq iacente"; likely referring to the Pelorian shore or a specific sandbank</note>. The **Aeolian Islands** are named after Aeolus, the son of Hippotes, whom the poets imagined to be the king of the winds. As **Varro** says, he was the ruler of these islands, and because he could predict the future blowing of the winds from the clouds and smoke of these islands, he appeared to the unskilled to have held the winds in his own power. These same islands are also called the **Vulcanian Islands**, because they themselves burn just like Mount Etna. There are nine of them, each having its own name. Some call the first of these **Lipara**, after a certain Liparus who ruled it previously. Another is called **Hiera**, because it has very high hills. The others are named **Strongyle**, **Didyme**, **Eriphusa**, **Phestias**, **Phenicusa**, **Euonymos**, **Ericodes**, and **Phęcicodes**. Because they burn at night, they are called the Aeolian or Vulcanian islands. Some of these did not exist from the beginning, but were later brought forth from the sea and remain until now. The **Stoechades** islands of the people of Marseilles are sixty miles from the continent, in front of the province of Narbonne where the river Rhone enters the sea. They are called "Stoechades" in Greek <note>original: "stoechades"; from the Greek *stoichas*, meaning "arranged in a row"</note> as if they were placed in an orderly arrangement. **Sardus**, the son of Hercules, set out from Libya with a great multitude and occupied **Sardinia**, giving the island its name from his own. This island, located in the African Sea, is shaped like a human footprint; it is wider in the east than in the west, with nearly equal sides facing south and north. Because of this, before trade began, it was called *Ichnusa* by Greek sailors <note>original: "ichnos"; Greek for "footprint"</note>. The land extends 140 miles in length and 40 in width. In it, neither serpent nor wolf is produced, but only the *solifuga* <note>original: "solifuga"; literally "sun-fleer," likely a type of venomous spider or solifuge</note>, a tiny animal that is ruinous to men. No poison grows there except for a herb mentioned by many writers and poets, similar to celery, which causes a contraction of the mouth in men, killing them as if they were laughing <note>This is the origin of the term "sardonic grin" or *risus sardonicus*</note>. Sardinia has hot springs that offer healing to the sick, but cause blindness in thieves if they touch the water to their eyes after swearing a false oath. The inhabitants of the island of **Corsica** originated from the Ligurians, naming it after their leader. For a certain Ligurian woman named Corsa saw a bull from the herd she tended near the shore frequently swim across and return after a time with its body enlarged. Desiring to know the unknown pastures, she followed the bull as it departed from the others in a boat all the way to the island. Upon her return, the Ligurians, learning of the fertility of the island, traveled there on rafts and called it by the name of the woman who was their founder and leader. This island is called *Cyrne* in Greek <note>original: "cyrne"</note>, inhabited by Cyrnus the son of Hercules. Concerning this, **Virgil** says: "Cyrnean yews." It is divided from Sardinia by twenty miles, surrounded by a strait, in the bay of the Ligurian Sea within sight of Italy. It is angular with many promontories, producing very lush pastures and the stone which the Greeks call *cacociren*. The island of **Ebissus** <note>Modern Ibiza</note> is said to be Spanish because it is not far from the city of Dianium <note>original: "çomo"; likely a corruption of Dianium</note>, as if in a dance. For it is seventy stadia distant from it. Snakes flee from its soil. Opposite this is **Colubraria**, which is filled with snakes. The **Balearic** 

<column-break/>

Islands of Spain are two: the **Aphrodysiades** and the **Gymnesidae**, the greater and the lesser. Hence the common people call them **Majorca** and **Minorca**. In these islands, the sling which hurls stones was first invented, from which they are called "Balearic." For in Greek, <term>Βάλλειν</term> <note>original: "ballein"; to throw</note> means to hurl. From this also comes the *ballista*, as if sent forth, and the *fundibulum* <note>A type of sling or siege engine</note>. **Virgil** wrote: "The Balearic thongs of the sling."

### Concerning Promontories, Chapter VII

It is common for islands to project outward. From this, their locations are called **promontories**. Thus **Sallust** says of Sardinia: "It projects wider in the east than in the west." The **Sigeum** promontory widens before the Hellespont opens. It is called Sigeum because of the silence of Hercules <note>original: <term>σιγή</term> (*sigē*); silence</note>, because after he was received as a guest by Laomedon, king of the Trojans, he feigned departure and then came silently against Troy. **Malea** is a promontory of Greece which enters the sea and extends for fifty miles, where the waves are so fierce that they seem to pursue sailors. This promontory received its name from Maleus, king of the Argives. **Pelorus** is a promontory of Sicily facing the north wind. According to **Sallust**, it was named after Hannibal’s pilot who was buried there. **Pachynus** is a promontory of Sicily looking toward the south wind, named for the thickness of the air. For <term>παχύς</term> <note>original: "pachys"</note> means fat and thick. For the south wind blows through it. **Lilybaeum** is a promontory of Sicily, stretching toward the setting sun, named after the city of the same name which is situated there. **Bozion** is a promontory of Numidia, so named because it stretches toward the north wind. This was later called Hippo Regius because it is interrupted by the waters. **Calpe** is a promontory of Spain <note>Modern Gibraltar</note>.

### Concerning Mountains and Other Terms of the Earth, Chapter VIII

**Mountains** are the highest swellings of the earth, so called because they are eminent. Some have been named for specific reasons; among these, those most celebrated in opinion should be noted. **Mount Caucasus** extends from India all the way to the Taurus; according to the variety of nations and languages, it goes in every direction and is called by various names. Where it rises to a peak in the east, it is called Caucasus because of its extreme whiteness. For in the Oriental language, "Caucasus" signifies white, that is, whitening with very thick snows. Hence, even the Scythians who are joined to the same mountain called it *Croacasin*. For in their language, "whiteness" or "snow" is so called. **Mount Taurus** is called by many the same as the Caucasus. **Lebanon** is the highest mountain of the Phoenicians, which the prophets remembered; it is named from incense <note>original: "thure"; Latin *thus* (incense) relates to the white resin or the snowy peaks</note>, because it is gathered there. That part of it which looks above the peak toward the eastern region is called **Antilibanus**, that is, "opposite Lebanon." **Ararat** is a mountain of Armenia where history testifies that the Ark rested after the flood. Even to this day, traces of its wood are seen there. The **Acroceraunian** mountains are so called because of their height and the hurling of lightning bolts. For in Greek, lightning is called <term>ceraunios</term>. They are in Armenia and Iberia, beginning from the Caspian Gates all the way to the source of the river Tigris. The **Hyperborean** mountains of Scythia are so named because the north wind <note>original: "boreas"</note> blows above, that is, beyond them. The **Riphean** mountains are at the head of Germany, named from the perpetual blowing of winds. For in Greek, <term>ριφή</term> <note>original: "ripē"</note> means impetus and <term>ὁρμή</term> <note>original: "hormē"</note> means rush. **Mount Olympus** in Macedonia is so exceedingly high that clouds are said to be below it. Concerning which **Virgil** wrote: "Olympus surpassed the clouds."

<meta>This page continues the geographic descriptions of the world, transitioning from the islands of the Mediterranean to the notable mountains of Europe and Africa, followed by a glossary of landscape features and maritime terms. The text follows the etymological style of Isidore of Seville, explaining the origins of names through history and poetry.</meta>

# XIIII

**Olympus** is so named as if it were *ololampus* <note>original: "ololampus"; a Greek-derived pseudo-etymology suggesting "wholly shining"</note>, which is to say, like heaven. This mountain divides Macedonia from Thrace. **Mount Athos** is in Macedonia; it too is higher than the clouds, and so sublime that it casts its shadow upon Lemnos, which is separated from it by eighty-seven miles. **Parnassus** is a mountain in Thessaly, near Boeotia, which rises into the sky with twin peaks. It is divided into two ridges, **Cirrha** and **Nysa**, from which it receives its name, because Apollo and Liber <note>Liber is another name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note> were worshipped on each respective ridge. These ridges are named **Cithaeron** and **Helicon** after two brothers. For Helicon was named after the brother of Cithaeron. Likewise, the **Ceraunian** mountains are in Epirus; they are named for the frequent lightning strikes, for in Greek lightning is called *ceraunos*. The **Apennine** mountain is named as if it were the "Punic Alps" <note>original: "alpes penice"</note>, because Hannibal, coming to Italy, opened those very Alps. Regarding this, **Virgil** says: "He sends forth the opened Alps." For Hannibal, after the Spanish wars, broke through these mountains with vinegar. **Juvenal** says: "And he broke the mountain with vinegar." <note>A famous legend that Hannibal used fire and vinegar to shatter the rocks blocking his path through the Alps.</note> And from this, the places he broke through are called the Apennine Alps. **Mount Etna** is named from fire and sulfur, which is also the origin of Gehenna <note>hell</note>. It is established that on the side where the east and south winds blow, it has caves full of sulfur reaching down to the sea; these caves, taking in the waves, create a wind which, being agitated, generates fire from the sulfur, which is why the burning is seen. **The Pyrenees** are also named from the frequent fires of lightning; for in Greek, fire is called *pyro*. This is the range that lies between Gaul and Spain, as if acting as a deliberate fortification. **Soluntus** is named for its singularity, either because it alone appears higher than all the mountains of Spain, or because when the sun rises, its rays are seen upon it before they are seen elsewhere. **Mount Calpe** is at the furthest limits of the ocean, separating Europe from Africa; they say it is the end of Atlas, of which **Lucan** writes: "He filled Hesperian Calpe and highest Atlas." **Atlas** was the brother of Prometheus and a king of Africa, by whom the art of astrology is said to have first been devised. For this reason, he was said to have held up the heavens. Therefore, on account of his learning in that discipline and his knowledge of the sky, his name was transferred to a mountain in Africa, which is now called Atlas, and which, because of its height, seems to support the machine of heaven and the stars. The **Alps**, however, are properly the mountains of Gaul. Of these, **Virgil** says: "The airy Alps." And by saying "airy," he expressed the word from the word itself. For in the language of the Gauls, "Alps" means high mountains. These are the ones that serve as walls for Italy. **Hills** <note>original: "lolles/colles"</note> are the more prominent ridges of mountains, like "necks" <note>original: "colla"</note>. **Ridges** <note>original: "juga"</note> of mountains are so called because they are joined by their proximity. A **mound** <note>original: "tumulus"</note> is a short mountain, like "swelling earth" <note>original: "tumēs tellus"</note>. Likewise, a mound is a heap of earth where there is no memorial. **Valleys** are low-lying places, as if "torn away" <note>original: "vulsa"</note>. From this come **dales** <note>original: "convalles"</note>, which are sunken places of the earth between mountains. A **field** <note>original: "campus"</note> is a level expanse of land. It is called a field because it is low to the feet <note>original: "breuis sit pedibus"</note> and not upright like mountains, but lying open and stretched out in its space; hence in Greek it is called *pedion*. It took its name from Greek etymology, for in Greek *lami* means "brief" or "low." **Soil** <note>original: "solum"</note> is everything that supports, named for its solidity. Regarding this, **Virgil** says of the sea: "The surface [soil] is withdrawn." **Glades** <note>original: "saltus"</note> are vast wooded places where the trees "leap" <note>original: "exiliunt"</note> high. **Passes** <note>original: "fauces"</note>

<column-break/>

are the approaches to narrow places between steep mountains—narrow and short places, named from their resemblance to "throats" <note>original: "fauces"</note>, as if they were gullets. **Crags** <note>original: "confraga"</note> are places where the winds rush from every side and break themselves, as **Ennius** says: "Into the mountains where the winds broke the place." **Rough places** <note>original: "scabra"</note> are sites harsh in their situation; from this "scabies" <note>the itch or mange</note> is named, from the roughness of the body. **Dens** <note>original: "lustra"</note> are dark hiding places for wild beasts and the beds of wolves; hence brothels are called *lustra* by the opposite meaning, because they are poorly "illuminated" <note>original: "lustrantur"</note>. A **grove** <note>original: "lucus"</note> is a place enclosed by dense trees, taking away the light <note>original: "luce"</note> from the ground. It can also be named from the "shining" <note>original: "collucendo"</note> of frequent lights that were made there on account of the religious worship of the pagans. **Deserts** are so called because they are not "sown" <note>original: "seruntur"</note> and therefore are as if "deserted," such as forest and mountain places, the opposite of fertile lands, which are of the richest soil. **Devious places** are secret and hidden, as if "outside the path" <note>original: "extra viam"</note>. These are also **impassable** <note>original: "invia"</note>. From this also come **remote paths** <note>original: "avia"</note>, secret places and those removed from the path, or at least inaccessible to anyone. From this comes that saying: "The wild remote paths blush with berries." **Pleasant places** <note>original: "amęna"</note>, **Varro** says, are so named because they provide only "love" <note>original: "amorem"</note> and entice one to love them. **Verrius Flaccus** says it is because they are "without duty" <note>original: "sine munere"</note>, and nothing is required of them, as if they were *amunia*, that is, without fruit, from which no profit is gathered. From this also those who provide nothing are called "exempt" <note>original: "imunes"</note>. **Sunny places** <note>original: "aprica"</note> are those that rejoice in the sun, as if from the Greek *aneu psychros*, that is, "without cold," or because they are open to the sky. **Shady places** <note>original: "opaca"</note> are as if "covered," the opposite of a sunny sky. It is established that a place is called **slippery** <note>original: "lubricum"</note> from the fact that someone "slips" <note>original: "labitur"</note> there; and it is called slippery not because it slips, but because one slips on it. **Summer pastures** <note>original: "estiua"</note> are shady places where cattle avoid the heat of the sun during summer. **Statius** says: "The summer pastures of shady Lycaeus lay open." **Docks** <note>original: "navalia"</note> are places where ships are built. This is also called a *tertrinum*. A **station** <note>original: "statio"</note> is where ships stay for a time. A **harbor** <note>original: "portus"</note> is where they spend the winter. **Inconvenient** <note>original: "importunū"</note> however, is a place where there is no refuge, as if there were "no harbor." A harbor is a place removed from the reach of the winds, where they are accustomed to set up winter quarters. And a harbor (*portus*) is named from "carrying" <note>original: "deportandis"</note> commerce. The ancients called these *baiae* from "carrying" <note>original: "baiulādis"</note> merchandise, with that declination from *baia* to *baias*, just as from *familia* to *familias*. The **shore** <note>original: "littus"</note> is the land that is near the sea. And it is called *littus* because the wave is "dashed" <note>original: "eliditur"</note> there, or because the water "washes" <note>original: "alluitur"</note> it. **Cicero** says in his *Topics*: "The shore is where the wave plays upon the water." A **circumluvium** is a place which the water flows around. **Alluvium** is the wearing away of banks by water. A **margin** is the edge of any place, such as the sea, from which it took its name. **Maritime** is as if "innermost to the sea" <note>original: "maris intima"</note>. **Mouths** <note>original: "ostia"</note> are named from the entrance and exit of a river into the sea. The **mainland** <note>original: "continēs"</note> is continuous land not separated by any sea, which the Greeks call *pyron* <note>perhaps a corruption of "epeiron"</note>.

<margin>Chapter 9</margin>
**A** **cave** <note>original: "specus"</note> is a ditch under the earth through which one can look out. It is *spelca* in Greek, *spelunca* in Latin. **Vents** <note>original: "spiracula"</note> are what all places of pestilential breath are called, which the Greeks call *paronia* or *acherontea*. Even **Varro** calls a place of this kind a *spiraculum*; and places are called *spiracula* because there the earth gives forth "breath" <note>original: "spiritum"</note>. A **chasm** <note>original: "hiatus"</note> is a deep breaking-open of the earth, as if a "gaping." Strictly speaking, however, a *hiatus* is the opening of a human mouth.

<meta>This page concludes the glossary of underworld terms and theological geography from Book XIV of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, then begins Book XV, which focuses on the history and founding of famous cities. It maintains the same encyclopedic tone, blending biblical history with Greco-Roman myth.</meta>

...metaphorically applied from wild beasts, whose greed is shown by the opening of their mouths. **The Deep** <note>original: "profundum"</note> is properly named as if its bottom <note>Latin: "fundus"</note> were far off. In common usage, however, "the deep" is used for either what is above or below, such as the sea, the earth, or the deep sky. **Barathrum** is a name for a place of immense depth, and is called "barathrum" because it is a dark whirlpool <note>original: "vorago atra"</note>, specifically because of its profound depth. **Erebus** refers to the depth and hidden recesses of the lower world. **Styx** is named from the Greek *apo tou stygos* <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ στυγός</note>, which is to say, from sadness, either because it makes people sad or because it generates sadness. **Cocytus** is a place in the underworld of which Job speaks thus: "The gravel of Cocytus was sweet to him" <note>A reference to Job 21:33, though usually translated as "the clods of the valley."</note>. Cocytus received its name from the Greek interpretation for mourning and groaning. **Tartarus** is so named either because all things there are troubled <note>from the Greek "tarattein", to disturb</note>, or, as is more likely, from the Greek *apo tes tereseos* <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς τηρήσεως</note>, which refers to the trembling of cold—that is, to be chilled and stiff—because it lacks the light of the sun. For there are neither vapors there, which are generated by the sun's light, nor winds, which are stirred by its movements, but rather a perpetual stupor. Indeed, in Greek writings, "Tartarus" is read as meaning to shiver and tremble. "There shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth" <note>Matthew 8:12</note>. **Gehenna** is a place of fire and sulfur, which they believe was named after a valley consecrated to idols near the wall of Jerusalem, which was once filled with the corpses of the dead. For there, the Hebrews sacrificed their own sons to demons, and the place itself was called Gehennon. Therefore, the place of future punishment where sinners are to be tortured is designated by the name of this location. We read in Job that Gehenna is twofold: both of fire and of cold. It is called **the Underworld** <note>original: "inferus"</note> because it is below <note>Latin: "infra"</note>. Just as in the physical world all heavier things occupy the lower space according to the order of their weight, so in the spiritual world all sadder things are lower. From this, even in the Greek language, the origin of the name for the underworld comes from the fact that nothing pleasant is allowed to sound from it. Furthermore, just as the heart of an animal is in its middle, so the underworld is said to be in the middle of the earth. Whence we also read in the Gospel: "in the heart of the earth" <note>Matthew 12:40</note>. They are called the *inferi* <note>the lower ones/the dead</note> because souls are brought into that place from here.

**F**rom the authors
of city foundations, much
disagreement is found, so much so that
the origin of even the city of Rome 
cannot be diligently identified.
For Sallust says: "The city of
Rome, as I have understood, was
founded and inhabited in the
beginning by Trojans and with
them the Aborigines." Others say it was by
Evander, as Virgil says: "Then King Evander, the
founder of the Roman citadel." Others say it was by Romulus, as Ennius says: "From this man’s
auspices, that illustrious Rome was born." If, therefore, the certain reason for so great a city
does not appear, it is no wonder if there is doubt regarding the opinion of others. Thus, we
should not condemn the ignorance of historians nor of commentators who say different things,
because antiquity itself created the error.
Indeed, concerning those cities for which either the Holy Scriptures or the histories of the
nations report a certain origin, it is fitting to report them in a few

<column-break/>

words. First, before the flood, Cham <note>The text says "Cham" (Ham), but the Bible and other versions of Isidore state "Cain" founded the first city.</note> founded the city of Enoch, named after his son, in India; he filled this city with the sheer multitude of his own posterity. First after the flood, the giant Nimrod founded the city of Babylon in Mesopotamia; later the queen of the Assyrians, Semiramis, enlarged it, and made the wall of the city with bitumen and baked brick. Its name was taken from "confusion," because there the languages of those building the tower were confused and mixed. The height of this tower was five thousand one hundred and seventy-four paces. The Jews assert that Shem, the son of Noah, whom they call Melchizedek, was the first after the flood to found the city of Salem in Syria, in which was the kingdom of the same Melchizedek. Later, the Jebusites held this city, from whom it also received the name Jebus; thus, with the two names joined together—Jebus and Salem—it was called Jerusalem. Later, it was called Hierosolyma by Solomon, as if it were "Hierosalomonia." This name was also corrupted by the poets and called Solyma, and later it was frequently called Aelia by Aelius Hadrian. Within it is also **Sion**, which in Hebrew is interpreted as "watchtower" <note>original: "speculatio"</note>, because it was constructed in a high place and looks out upon things coming from afar. "Jerusalem," however, is translated into our language as "peaceful" <note>original: "pacifica"</note>. Regarding noble towns, and who or what established them: Dionysus, who is also Father Liber, when he traveled through India as a victor, founded the city of Nysa after his own name near the Indus River and filled it with seven thousand men. Medus, the son of Aegeus, built Media, from which his region also took the name Media. Perseus, the son of Danae, founded the city of Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom, most famous and crowded with riches, from whom Persia is also named. The Parthians built Ctesiphon in Parthia in emulation of the city of Babylon. They say the brother of Memnon established the town of Susa in Persia. It is called Susa because it stands over the River Susa. There is the palace of Cyrus, made of white and variegated stone, with golden columns and ceilings adorned with gems, containing even a likeness of the sky, marked out with shining stars, and other things incredible to human minds. The Bactrians founded the town of Bactra, naming it after their own river, which is called the Bactrus. Carrhae is a city of Mesopotamia founded by the Parthians across the Edissa, where once the Roman army was slaughtered and the leader Crassus was captured. Nimrod, the son of Cush, founded the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia after he migrated from Babylon, in which he also reigned; it was previously called Iare. He also constructed Calanne, which was later called Seleucia by King Seleucus after a change of name. The Raphaim, a most ancient people whom the sons of Lot killed, founded Philadelphia, a city of Arabia. Seleucus, one of the attendants of Alexander, after the death of the same Alexander and having occupied the kingdom of the East, founded a city in Syria and named it Antioch after the name of his father, Antiochus, and established it as the capital of Syria. He also constructed Laodicea and Seleucia, as well as the cities of Apamea and Edessa. Damascus, a city of Syria, was founded and named by Damascus, the son of Abraham’s steward. This city formerly held the leadership in all of Syria. The Macedonians...

<meta>This page transitions from the final descriptions of the underworld and theological geography into the beginning of Book XV of the *Etymologies*, which details the history and founding of famous cities of the ancient world. The text moves from the depths of the Earth to the civilizations of the East and the Mediterranean.</meta>

...flourished there: Antioch, Laodicea, and Apamea. We know that these cities were constructed by Alexander the Great. This is Damascus, of which Abraham had said would be his future heir, before Isaac was first born to him. The Aeneadae <note>original: "enei"; possibly referring to the descendants of Aeneas, though the historical connection to Gaza is mythic</note> founded Gaza, a town of Palestine, in which the Cappadocians lived after the former inhabitants were killed. It was called Gaza because Cambyses, King of the Persians, placed his treasures there when he brought war upon the Egyptians. For in the Persian language, a treasure is called a <term>gaza</term>. The "Foreigners" <note>original: "allophili"; the standard Latin term for the Philistines in biblical translations</note> founded the city of Philistim; this is Ascalon, of which we made mention above, named after the name of Casluhim, who was the grandson of Ham and the son of Mizraim. Dor: a city that was once most powerful; in turn it became Strato’s Tower, and was afterwards named Caesarea by Herod, King of Judea, in honor of Caesar Augustus. In this city is the church of the house of Cornelius, and the small shrines of Philip, and the chamber of the four virgin prophetesses. Joppa, a coastal town of Palestine, was built by these same Palestinians; there a rock is shown which still retains the marks of Andromeda's chains <note>A reference to the myth of Perseus and Andromeda; Isidore blends biblical and classical history</note>. The form of the sea-monster there was more massive than an elephant. Jericho is said to have been founded by the Jebusites, from whom it is also forbidden to have drawn its name; Jesus [Joshua] overthrew this city. Afterward he built another from Bethel from the tribe of Ephraim. But this one too was captured and destroyed at the time Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans because of the treachery of its citizens. After this, a third city was built which remains to this day. Shechem, a city of Samaria which is called *Sichima* in Latin and Greek, was built by Hamor; he called it by the name of his son, Shechem. This is now Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans. The Jebusites founded Bethel, a city of Samaria, which was previously called Luz. But after Jacob, while sleeping there, saw a ladder leaning against heaven and said: "Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven," the place received the name Bethel, which means "House of God" <note>Hebrew: *Beth-El*</note>. However, when the golden calves were fashioned there by Jeroboam, it was called *Beth-aven*, which means "House of the Idol," though it was previously called the House of God. Bethlehem in Judah, the city of David, which brought forth the Savior for the world, is said to have been founded by the Jebusites and first called Ephrata. However, because Jacob pastured his flocks there, he gave the same place the name Bethlehem as a certain prophecy of the future; it is interpreted as "House of Bread" <note>Hebrew: *Beth-Lechem*</note>, because of that Bread [Christ] who descended from heaven at that place. Hebron, a city of Judea which was once called Arba, was founded by giants seven years before the city of Tanis in Egypt was founded by them. It is called Arba from the number <note>The Hebrew word "Arba" means "four"</note> because three patriarchs are buried there, and the fourth is Adam. It is also called Mamre, after one of the friends of Abraham. Samaria, from which the entire region around it took its name, was built by Sennacherib, King of the Assyrians; he called it Samaria, which means "Watch-tower" <note>original: "custodiam"</note>, because when he moved Israel, he stationed Medes there as guards. Antiochus leveled this city to the ground after capturing it by siege. Afterward, Herod restored it from its foundations and called it *Augusta*—which is *Sebastia* in the Greek language—in honor of Augustus. The prophets Elisha and Obadiah are buried there, as is John the Baptist, than whom no one greater was born among the sons of women. Another Herod founded Tiberias in Judea in the name of Tiberius Caesar. Tyre, a city of the Phoenicians, was founded by the Phoe-

<column-break/>

nicians. This is the city from which gold was brought to King Solomon, and in which the finest purple is dyed; hence the noble purple is called "Tyrian." The Phoenicians, coming from the Red Sea <note>original: "rubro mari", referring here to the Persian Gulf/Indian Ocean area</note>, founded Sidon, a most opulent city, which they named Sidon from the abundance of fish. For the Phoenicians call a fish a <term>sidon</term>. They also founded Tyre in Syria, Utica in Africa, Hippo, Leptis, and other cities on the sea coast. They founded Thebes in Boeotia under the leadership of Cadmus; finally, stretching out to the ends of the earth, they founded a city on the Ocean and named it Gades [Cadiz] in their own language. For it was the custom of the ancient Phoenician people for many to set out from home together for the sake of trade, and when they had won over the minds of the inhabitants by the commerce of things previously unknown to them, they would take possession of places that seemed suitable for founding cities. Setting out from these people, Dido also founded a city on the African shore and named it *Carthada*, which in the Phoenician language expresses "New City" <note>original: "ciuitatem nouam"</note>; soon, with the word altered, it was called Carthage. Scipio destroyed this city. The one which exists now was later founded by the Romans. Carthage, however, was previously called *Byrsa*, then *Tyre*, and finally Carthage. Epaphus, son of Jupiter, built Memphis, a city of Egypt, when he was reigning in the second [part of] Egypt. This is the city in which papyrus <note>original: "charta"</note> is born, and where there were also the best mathematicians. For the ancient remains of this city show traces of error dedicated to the magic arts even up to the present time. Tanis is the metropolis of Egypt, where Pharaoh was, and where Moses performed all the signs that are written in Exodus. They claim the *Tyrannoi*—that is, the giants—built this city and named it from their own name. Heliopolis is a city of Egypt, which is interpreted in Latin as "City of the Sun" <note>Greek: *Helios* (Sun) + *Polis* (City)</note>, as the seventy translators [of the Septuagint] believe. It was built by the sons of Israel, in which Potipherah was priest, whom Ezekiel mentions. Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria, which still retains his name. For he established it on the borders of the regions of Africa and Egypt, and ordered it to be the capital of the region of Egypt. It lies between Egypt and the sea, like a harborless barrier. This was [previously] a city of Egypt, later turned into Alexandria. Cadmus founded Egyptian Thebes, which are more noble among the Egyptian cities for their number of gates, to which the Arabs bring trade from all sides. Hence the region of Egypt is called the Thebaid. There are Thebes in both Boeotia and Egypt; however, they were founded by the same author. Ptolemais and Berenice were named after the kings [and queens] of Egypt by whom they were also built. Philip built Caesarea in Cappadocia in honor of Caesar. Perseus, the offspring of Danae, built Tarsus in Cilicia; the Apostle Paul was from this city. "Born," he said, "in Tarsus of Cilicia." A certain place in India is also called Tarsus. Seleucus founded Seleucia in Isauria, the same who founded Antioch. Ilus, the son of Apollo, founded Ilium [Troy] in Phrygia. The Amazons constructed Ephesus in Asia. Theseus, however, built Smyrna, which was the homeland of the poet Homer; it was called Smyrna because of the fields which the river Hermus cuts through. Amphitus and Cercius, the charioteers of Castor and Pollux, built Dioscurias, a city of the Colchians, naming it from their name. For in Greek, Castor and Pollux are called the <term>Dioscuri</term> <note>meaning "Sons of Zeus"</note>.

# Book XV

He calls them. Nicomedia was built by Nicomedes, the King of Bithynia. Bithynia was founded by Phoenix; it was first called Mirandina. The city of Constantinople in Thrace was established by Constantine, named after himself; it is the only city equal to Rome in merit and power. This city was first founded by Pausanias, the King of the Spartans, and was called Byzantium—either because it lies so wide between the Adriatic Sea and the Propontis <note>original: "poponridē"; the Propontis is the modern Sea of Marmara</note>, or because it is a storehouse for the wealth of both land and sea. For this reason, Constantine judged it the most suitable place to establish <note>original: "constantinop'lissimā"; a play on the name of the city and the superlative for 'most constant' or 'most fitting'</note> his city, so that it might become a storehouse for him of both land and sea. Hence, it is now the seat of the Roman Empire and the head of all the East, just as Rome is of the West. Epirus, a city of Thrace, was founded by Pyrrhus and named after him. Cecrops founded Athens in Hellas and named it Cecropia after himself. This city was later consecrated to Minerva <note>the Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena</note> by Assyrius, who reigned in Greece as the third king after Cecrops, and he gave the city the name Athens. For in Greek, Minerva is called <term>Athena</term> <note>original: "athenas"</note>; thus the Greeks assert that Minerva was the inventor of many arts, which is why letters, the arts of various studies, and even Philosophy itself have held Athens as their temple. Corinth in Achaia was founded by Corinthus, the son of Orestes. The Greeks call this city *Corintheba*, which means "the administration of the republic." Cadmus, coming from the Phoenicians, founded Thebes in Boeotia, having previously constructed the Egyptian Thebes. Mycenae in Lacedaemonia was founded by Lacedaemon, the son of Semele. Sparta was named after Spartus, the son of Phoroneus, who was the son of Inachus. However, that same Sparta is also the city of Lacedaemonia; therefore, the Lacedaemonians are also called Spartans. Achaia was constructed by Achaeus. Pelops, who reigned at Argos, founded the city of Peloponnesus. Cecrops built Rhodes on the island of Rhodes. Carpathus founded Cos. Acus, the son of Typhon, founded Paphos. Angeus, the son of Lycurgus, founded Samos. Dardanus founded Dardania. Thessalus, the son of Graecus, built Thessalonica, where he also reigned. The Greeks constructed Brundisium <note>modern Brindisi</note>. It is said to be called Brundisium because in the Greek language <term>brunda</term> means "the head of a stag"; for the position of the city is such that the head and tongue seem to form horns. In Italy, Janiculum was named after Janus, and Saturnia after Saturn; Latium was also founded there, named because Saturn had "lain hidden" <note>original: "latuisset"; a popular medieval etymology for Latium from *latere*, to hide</note> while fleeing. Hercules founded Pompeii in Campania, as he had led a "procession of oxen" <note>original: "pompa boum"; another folk etymology connecting the word *pompa* to Pompeii</note> there after conquering them in Spain. Aeneas, however, coming into this same Italy after the destruction of Troy, founded Lavinia, named after his wife. Ascanius, having left the kingdom to his stepmother Lavinia, built Alba Longa. It was called <term>Alba</term> because of its white color, and <term>Longa</term> because it is a long town, following the length of the hill on which it is placed. From this city, the kings of the Albans began to be named. Capys Silvius, King of the Albans, constructed Capua, named after its founder—although there are those who say it is called Capua from its "capacity" <note>original: "capacitate"</note>, because that land can hold <note>original: "capiat"</note> every fruit of life. Others say it is from the "level plains" <note>original: "campestribus"</note> in which it is situated. It is the capital of the cities of Campania, numbered among the three great maritime cities alongside Rome and Carthage; from it, the province of Italy was called Campania. When Romulus had killed Amulius at Alba and restored his grandfather as the builder of the kingdom, he came to the place where Rome is now—there he established his seat and built the wal-

<column-break/>

-ls, and called the city Rome after his own name. However, Evander is said to have founded this city previously, as it is written: "Then father Evander, the founder of the Roman citadel." <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid* (8.313)</note> Ancus Marcius, born of the daughter of Numa Pompilius, founded this city at the exit of the Tiber, both to receive foreign merchandise and to delay the enemy; he called it Ostia from its very location <note>from *ostium*, meaning 'mouth' or 'entrance'</note>. Certain Gauls, stirred up by internal discord and constant dissensions among their own people, set out for Italy seeking new homes; having expelled the original Tuscans from their seats, they founded Milan <note>original: "mediolanū"</note> and other cities. It is called *Mediolanum* because a "half-woolly" <note>original: "medio lanea"</note> sow was found there by their people. History records that the origin of Messapia was given by Melapus the Greek; it was later changed to the name Calabria, which Peucetius, the brother of Oenotrus, had named Peucetia in the beginning. Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, after the destruction of the Thebans, was brought to Italy and founded Mantua. It is in Venetia, which is called Cisalpine Gaul. It is called Mantua because it "protects the spirits of the dead" <note>original: "manes tueat'"; another typical Isidorean etymology</note>. Parthenopeia was named after a certain virgin, Parthenope, who was buried there; later Augustus preferred that the town be called Neapolis <note>meaning "New City" in Greek</note>. Near the promontory of Leucate, where there was a temple of Actian Apollo, Augustus waged war against Antony. Having conquered him, he founded a city on the Actian Gulf, which he called Nicopolis after his "victory" <note>from the Greek *nike* (victory) and *polis* (city)</note>. Palantus, the leader of the Partheniae, established the Partheniae. Taras was the son of Neptune, after whom the city of Tarentum was both founded and named. When Cyrus was occupying the maritime cities of Greece, the Phocaeans, who were under attack and pressed by every hardship, swore an oath to flee as far as possible from the unholy land where even their name would not be heard; thus they set out by ship for the furthest bays of Gaul, and protecting themselves with arms against Gallic ferocity, they founded Massilia <note>Marseille</note> and named it after the name of their leader. Varro says these people are "trilingual," because they speak Greek, Latin, and Gallic. Colonists founded Narbonne, Arles, and Poitiers for themselves. They say Bordeaux <note>original: "Burdegala"</note> was so named because it first had Gallic "townsmen" <note>original: "burgos gallos"</note> as colonists, by whose cultivation it was previously filled. The Scipios constructed Tarragona in Spain; therefore, it is the capital of the province of Tarraconensis. Zaragoza <note>original: "Cęsaraugusta"</note> is a town in Tarraconensian Spain named after and situated by Caesar Augustus; it excels all cities of Spain in the pleasantness of its location and its delights, and is even more illustrious for the flowering of the burials of the holy martyrs. The Africans under Hannibal, occupying the maritime parts of Spain, constructed Carthage Spartaria <note>Cartagena</note>, which was soon captured by the Romans and made a colony; it even gave its name to the province. Now, however, it has been overthrown by the Goths and reduced to desolation. Greeks setting out from the island of Zacynthos founded Saguntum in Spain, which the Africans later destroyed in an uncommanded war. Caesar Augustus built Mérida <note>original: "Emeritā"</note>, after which he took Lusitania and certain islands of the ocean, giving it its name from the fact that he had settled veteran soldiers there. For veterans released from military service are called <term>emeriti</term>. Lisbon <note>original: "Ulyxbona"</note> was founded and named by Ulysses; at which place, as historians say, the sky is separated from the earth and the seas from the land. Julius Caesar founded Seville <note>original: "Hispalim"</note>, which he named from his own name and that of the city of Rome.
