# Book XV

He named it with the title Julia Romula <note>original: "iulia romula"; this refers to Seville, which Julius Caesar granted colonial status</note>. **Hispalis**, however, was named for its situation, because it is located on marshy soil supported by poles driven deep into the ground <note>Isidore links the name *Hispalis* to *palus* (marsh) and *palis* (poles)</note>, lest it fall due to a slippery and unstable foundation. **Gades** <note>modern Cadiz</note> is a town founded by the Phoenicians, who also founded Carthage of the Broom-field <note>original: "carthaginem spartariam"; referring to Cartagena in Spain, named for the esparto grass in the region</note>. The town of **Septem** <note>modern Ceuta</note> is named from the seven mountains which, by their similarity, are called the Brothers; they loom over the Strait of Gades. Of the city of **Lingis** and the city of **Liris**, Antaeus is the founder, whom Hercules is said to have killed after overcoming him in a wrestling match. **Lix**, however, is named after the Lixus river of Mauritania, where there was formerly a palace; and **Sala**, which looms over the river Sala. King Juba of the Moors founded **Caesarea** in Mauritania in honor of Caesar Augustus, and they called it Caesarea by his name—just as Herod founded another **Caesarea** in Palestine, which is now a most famous city. Twenty men from the company of Hercules, as he was passing through there, constructed **Icosium**, a town of Caesarean Mauritania. Lest anyone should glory privately in a name imposed by himself, the name **Icosium** was given to the city from the number of its founders <note>original: "icosium"; from the Greek *eikosi*, meaning twenty</note>. **Cyrene** was the queen of Libya, who founded the city of Cyrene from her own name, and for whom he also called the region Cyrenaic Libya.

->## Chapter II: On Public Buildings<-

A **city** <term>civitas</term> <note>original: "Ciuitas"</note> is a multitude of humans joined together by a bond of society. It is named from the citizens—that is, from the inhabitants of the city themselves—because it gathers and contains the lives of very many people. For the **urban center** <term>urbs</term> <note>original: "urbs"</note> refers to the walls themselves, but a "city" refers not to the stones, but to the inhabitants. There are three types of society: of families, of urban centers, and of nations. The word *Urbs* is derived from the circle <term>orbis</term>, because ancient cities were made in a circle; or from the *urbum*, the part of the plow by which the walls were marked out. From this comes the phrase: *He chose a place for his kingdom and marked it with a furrow* <note>original: "Oprauitqȝ locũ regno ⁊ cõcludere ſulco"; a reference to Virgil's Aeneid</note>. For the site of a future city was marked by a furrow—that is, by a plow. Cato says: "He who founds a new city plows with a bull and a cow; where he has plowed, let him make a wall; where he wants a gate to be, let him lift up the plow and carry it, and let him call it a 'gate' <note>original: "porta"; from *portare*, to carry</note>." Therefore, the city was surrounded by the plow using a pair of different sexes because of the mixing of families and the image of one who sows and returns fruit. A city is established by the plow and overturned by the plow. Hence Horace says: *And the hostile plow might press upon the walls* <note>original: "Imprimeretqȝ muris hoſtile aratrũ"</note>. Some have called it a **town** <term>oppidum</term> from the "opposition" of walls; others from the "wealth" <term>opes</term> to be stored within it, because it is fortified. Others say it is because the inhabitants meet there to provide "aid" <term>ops</term> to one another against an enemy. For at first, humans were naked and unarmed; they had no such defenses against wars, nor shelters from cold and heat. Finally, through natural cleverness, they wove together huts for themselves in caves and forest covers, and cottages made of brushwood and reeds, so that life might be safer and no access would be easy for those who could do harm. This is the origin of towns, which were to give aid; for this reason, they said they were named *oppida*. A town differs from a **village** <term>vicus</term>, a **stronghold** <term>castellum</term>, and a **rural district** <term>pagus</term> in its size and its walls. Settlements are called either cities, colonies, municipalities, villages, strongholds, or rural districts. A "city" is properly called that which was founded not by foreigners, but by those born in the same soil. Therefore, cities founded by their own citizens are called *civitates*, not colonies. A **colony** <term>colonia</term>, however, is that which is filled with new

<column-break/>

cultivators because of a lack of native inhabitants; hence "colony" is named from the cultivation of the field <note>original: "colonia a cultu agri"</note>. A **municipality** <term>municipium</term> is where, while the status of the city remains, some right of a minor or major office is obtained from the prince. It is called a municipality from the duties <term>munia</term>, that is, the offices—because they return duties, that is, owed taxes or gifts. For the liberal and most famous causes and whatever proceeds from the prince are not conducted there; for these belong to the dignity of cities. **Villages**, **strongholds**, and **rural districts** are those which are adorned by no dignity of a city, but are inhabited by a common gathering of men, and because of their smallness, they are attributed to larger cities. A village <term>vicus</term> is named from "neighboring" <term>vicinus</term> habitations, or because it has "ways" <term>vias</term> although without walls. It is without the protection of walls, even though the habitations of an urban center are themselves called *vici*. A village is also called a *vicus* because it stands in the place <term>vice</term> of a city, or because it has ways without walls. The ancients called a **fortress** <term>castrum</term> a town situated in a very high place, as if it were a "high cottage" <term>casa alta</term>; its plural number is *castra* <note>military camp</note>, and its diminutive is *castellum*. It was so named because the license of those living there was "castrated" <note>original: "castrabatur"; Isidore uses a word-play suggesting their freedom was restricted or fortified</note> so that they would not lie open to a wandering enemy. **Rural districts** <term>pagi</Term> are places suitable for buildings among those living in the fields. These are also called **meeting-places** <term>conciliabula</term> from the gathering and society of many into one. **Crossroads** <term>competa</term> are where it is customary for gatherings of rustics to occur; they are called *competa* because many places in the fields "meet" <term>competant</term> at the same spot where the rustics assemble. **Suburbs** <term>suburbana</term> are the buildings surrounding a city, as if "under the city" <term>sub urbe</term>. **Moenia** <note>the fortifications</note> are the walls of the city, named from the fact that they "fortify" <term>muniant</term> the city, as if they were the city's "fortifications" <term>munimenta</term>, that is, protections. A duty <term>munium</term> is so called as if it were "made by hand" <term>manu factum</term>; likewise, "walls" <term>muri</term> are named from "fortification" <term>munitio</term>, as if they were for fortifying, because they fortify and protect the interior of the city. *Moenia*, however, has a double meaning. For sometimes, by misuse of the term, all the public buildings of a city are called *moenia*, as in: *We divide the walls and open up the moenia of the city* <note>original: "diuidimus muros ⁊ menia pandimus urbis"; from Virgil's Aeneid</note>. Properly, however, *moenia* are only the walls. The wall is adorned with towers and battlements. **Towers** <term>turres</term> are named because they are "tapered" <term>teretes</term> and long. For something *teres* is round with height, like a column. For even if they are constructed square or wide, they are nevertheless thought to be round by those seeing them from afar, because every image of an angle vanishes and is consumed through a long space of air, and it appears round. **Battlements** <term>propugnacula</term> are called the "pinnacles" of the walls, because from these one "fights forward" <term>propugnatur</term>. A **forewall** <term>promurale</term> is so named because it is for the protection of the wall; it is the first wall before the main wall. A **gate** <term>porta</term> is so named because something can be "carried in" <term>importari</term> or "carried out" <term>exportari</term> through it. Properly, it is called the gate of either a city or a camp, as was said above. A **village-street** <term>vicus</term>, as was said before, refers to the habitations of the city themselves, from which "neighbors" <term>vicini</term> are named. **Ways** <term>viae</term> are the narrow spaces themselves that are between the streets. **Plazas** <term>plateae</term> are the continuous and wider ways of cities, named according to the property of the Greek language from "width." For the Greeks call width <term>platos</term>. The **quintana** is a part of the plaza, a fifth part, through which a carriage can pass. **Sewers** <term>cloacae</term> are named because waters are "filtered through" <term>percolantur</term> them. They say Tarquinius Priscus first made these in Rome, so that whenever an inundation of rains occurred, the waters would be sent out of the city through them, lest the floods and sudden storms soak the level ground...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s exploration of the physical and legal components of a city, moving from specific geographical names to the common terms for public infrastructure and private dwellings.</meta>

...or the foundations of cities might be overthrown by the flooding of waters.

The **Insubres** <note>original: "Insubuli"; a Celtic people of northern Italy</note> are so named either because they are "under the scrolls" <note>original: "subuolumina"</note>, or because they walk "under the open air" <note>original: "sub hiō"; likely a corruption of "sub dio"</note>. For there are porticos on either side of the streets. A **Forum** is a place for conducting lawsuits; it is named from "speaking" <note>original: "a fando"</note>, or from King Phoroneus, who first gave laws to the Greeks. These places are also called **Rostra** <note>the speaker's platform in the Roman Forum</note> because the beaks <note>original: "rostra"; the bronze prows of ships</note> were taken from the captured ships of the Carthaginians during the Punic War and fixed in the Roman forum as a sign of this victory. A **Curia** <note>the senate house</note> is so called because the "care" <note>original: "cura"</note> of all things is administered there. A **Praetorium** <note>a general's tent or a governor's residence</note> is so named because the praetor sits there for legal discussion. A **Gymnasium** is a place for exercise. Hence, there was a place in Athens where philosophy was learned and the study of wisdom was practiced. For "gymnasium" is the Greek word for what is called "exercise" <note>original: "exercitium"</note> in Latin; this is a form of practice or meditation. There are also baths and places for running, and there are gymnasia for athletes, so that everyone may be trained there in the studies of their own art. 

The **Capitol** in Rome is so named because it was the supreme "head" <note>original: "caput"</note> of the Roman city and religion. Others say that when Tarquinius Priscus was opening the foundations of the Capitol in Rome, he found a human head in the location of the foundation marked with Etruscan letters, and he named it the Capitol from that. **Citadels** <note>original: "arces"</note> are the high and fortified parts of the city. For whatever parts of the cities are most secure are called "citadels" from "warding off" <note>original: "arcendo"</note> the enemy. Hence also "arcus" <note>a bow</note> and "arca" <note>a chest or ark</note>. The Romans believe the **Circus** is named from the "circuit" <note>original: "circuitu"</note> of horses, because the horses run there around the turning-posts <note>original: "metas"</note>. A **Theater** is named from the spectacle, from the Greek word "to gaze at" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θεάσθαι"</note>, because in it the people, standing above and watching, might contemplate the stage plays. An **Amphitheater** is so named because it is composed of two theaters. For an amphitheater is round, while a theater, being half of an amphitheater, has the shape of a semicircle. 

A **Labyrinth** is a building with tangled walls, such as the one made by Daedalus in Crete, where the Minotaur was shut in; if anyone enters it without a ball of linen thread, they cannot find the way out. The layout of this building is such that to those opening the doors, a terrible thunder is heard within. It descends more than a hundred steps; inside are images and monstrous figures, with innumerable passages through the darkness into various parts, and other things made for the terror of those entering, so that it seems impossible to come from the darkness back to the light. There are four labyrinths: the first in Egypt, the second in Crete, the third in Lemnos, and the fourth in Italy; all are so constructed that no age could ever dissolve them. 

A **Pharos** is a marine tower, which the Greeks and Latins together called "pharos" from the use of the thing itself, because it is seen from afar by sailors by the sign of its flames. Ptolemy is said to have built such a tower near Alexandria for eight hundred talents. Its use is to show fires for the nighttime course of ships, to announce shallows, harbors, and entrances, so that sailors, deceived by darkness, do not fall upon the rocks. For Alexandria has treacherous approaches due to deceptive shallows. Hence also the machines built in harbors for the service of shining light are called "pharos." For *phos* is "light" and *oros* is "vision." Hence the morning star is called *phosphoros* <note>light-bringer</note> in Greek. **Spiral towers** <note>original: "cochleae"</note> are other round towers, and are called "cochleae" as if they were "cyclical" <note>original: "cyclaeae"</note>, because one ascends in them as if through a circle and a globe; such a tower in Rome is 175 feet high.

<column-break/>

**Thermae** <note>public hot baths</note> are so named because they are warm. For they call heat *thermon* in Greek. The name **Baths** <note>original: "balnea"</note> was given from the "washing away of sorrow" <note>original: "lauatione męroris"</note>. For the Greeks used the word *balanion* because it takes away the anxiety of the mind. These are also called gymnasia, because there athletes exercise their bodies, having been anointed and rubbed with hands. For "gymnasium" in Greek is called "exercise" in Latin, while *gymnos* means "naked." An **Apodyterium** <note>changing room</note> is where the clothing of those washing is placed; it is named from "stripping off" <note>original: "ἀποδύειν"</note>. 

**Popina** <note>a cookshop or eating house</note> is a Greek word which is corruptly called *perpina* among us. It is a place next to the public baths, where after the bath they are refreshed from hunger and thirst. Hence it is called *perpina* and *perpinare*. For *pina* <note>from the Greek 'peina'</note> signifies "hunger," because this place takes away hunger. **Tabernae** <note>booths or shops</note> were once the names of the small and simple dwellings of the common people in the streets, closed with boards and planks. Hence also "tavern-keepers" <note>original: "tabernarię"</note> because they are accustomed to sit together. They were called "tabernae" because they were constructed from "boards" <note>original: "tabulis"</note> and wood; although they do not have that appearance now, they still retain their ancient name. A **Macellum** <note>meat market</note> is so called because cattle which are sold to merchants are "slaughtered" <note>original: "mactent"</note> there. A **Market** <note>original: "mercatum"</note> is named from "commerce" <note>original: "commertio"</note>; for there it is customary to sell or buy things. So also it is called a **Teloneum** <note>custom house</note> where the merchandise of ships and the payments of sailors are rendered. For there the collector of taxes sits, about to impose a price on things and demanding payment with his voice from the merchants. A **Carcer** <note>prison</note> is that from which we are prohibited from leaving, and it is called "carcer" from "restraining" <note>original: "coercendo"</note>. Hence Fronto said that they might seem to wander through pleasant places rather than be restrained in a prison.

### On Dwellings Chapter III

A **habitation** <note>original: "habitatio"</note> is named from "having" or "holding" <note>original: "habendo"</note>, as in "to inhabit cottages." **House** <note>original: "domus"</note> is also called by a Greek name. For the Greeks call roofs *domata*. A house is the dwelling of one family, just as a city is the dwelling of one people, and as the world is the domicile of the entire human race. 

The ancients called every building an **Aedes** <note>originally meaning a sanctuary or hearth</note>. Others think that "aedes" took its name from "eating" <note>original: "edendo"</note>, giving the example from Plautus: "If I had invited you into the house for lunch." Hence also "edificium" <note>building</note>, because it was first a sacred place for eating. An **Aula** <note>palace or courtyard</note> is a royal house, or a spacious dwelling enclosed by four porticos. An **Atrium** <note>central hall</note> is a large building or a more ample and spacious house; and it is called an "atrium" because "three porticos" <note>original: "tres porticus"</note> are added to it on the outside. Others have said "atrium" as if it were "blackened" <note>original: "atrum"</note> by fire and wood. For blackness comes from smoke. 

A **Palace** <note>original: "palatium"</note> is named after Pallas, the prince of the Arcadians, in whose honor the Arcadians built the town of Pallanteum and called the royal residence built in his name a "palatium." They say the **Thalamus** <note>bridal chamber</note> was named for this reason: when the Sabine women had been seized by the Romans, and when one among them, noble in appearance above the others, was being carried off to the great wonder of all, the response of an oracle was given that she should be given to the leader Thalassius. And because these nuptials had turned out happily, it was established that in all weddings the name of Thalassius should be repeated. The Egyptians also, in their own language, call the places in which those marrying go and lie down "thalamus." 

A **Cenaculum** <note>dining room, often upstairs</note> is named from the "communion of eating" <note>original: "coione vescendi"</note>; hence also "coenobium" <note>a monastery or communal living</note> is a congregation. For the ancients ate publicly in common, nor was the banquet of anyone private, lest in secret they might produce the luxury of madness. A **Triclinium** is a dining room named from the "three small couches" <note>original: "tribus lectulis"</note> of those reclining.

<summary>This page explains the etymological origins of Roman public architecture and private dwellings. It defines spaces ranging from the forum and theater to the labyrinth and lighthouse, concluding with a breakdown of domestic spaces like the atrium and dining room.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s discussion of human habitats, transitioning from the public squares and administrative buildings mentioned on the previous page to private dwellings, hospitality structures, and finally, sacred architecture.</meta>

...to be said. Among the ancients, in the place where the banquet apparatus was displayed, three small couches were spread out, upon which those reclining would feast. In Greek, a couch or a place for reclining is called a **clinon** <note>original: "clinon"; from the Greek κλίνη (klīnē)</note>; from this, the term **triclinium** <note>a dining room with three couches</note> was fashioned. A **cella** <note>cell or storeroom</note> is so named because it conceals or hides us <note>original: "celet"</note> in private. A **cubiculum** <note>bedroom</note> is so named because we "lie down" <note>original: "cubemus"</note> there and rest while sleeping; thus, a cubiculum is a place for lying down. A **secessus** <note>retreat or privy</note> is a secret place, that is, one without access. A **diversorium** <note>inn</note> is so called because people from "diverse" paths come together there. **Hospitium** <note>guest house or hospitality</note> is a Greek term where someone dwells for a time by right of hospitality and then, passing from there, moves on. From this comes the term **metatum** <note>quarters/lodging</note>, because it is changed. Whence it is read: "They moved their camp" <note>original: "Ex castra metati sunt"</note>, meaning they moved their walls; for the army does not remain there, but passes through. **Meniana** <note>balconies or galleries</note> are named from "remaining" <note>original: "maneamus"</note>. Maenius, a colleague of Crassus, projected wooden beams into the forum so that there would be places for those waiting to stand; these were called *meniana* from his name. These are also called **solaria** because they are open to the sun. Later, some built these with stone and others with wood, adding *meniana* to porticos, doors, and houses. **Tabulata** <note>storeys or floors</note> were once made in wooden houses; from this, the name for floor-levels <note>original: "tabulatorum"</note> remains. An **apogeum** <note>underground chamber</note> is a building constructed under the earth, which we call a cave or a cavern. A **solarium** <note>sun terrace</note> is open to the sun and air; such was the place from which David saw Bathsheba washing and fell in love with her. When Antiochus was besieging Jerusalem, Hyrcanus, the prince of the Jews, opened the tomb of David and took from it three thousand talents of gold, from which he gave three hundred to Antiochus so that he would abandon the siege and to remove the resentment regarding the sacred site. It is said that from the remaining money he was the first to establish **xenodochia** <note>hostels for strangers</note>, where arriving paupers and pilgrims might be received; from this, it took its name. For translated from Greek into Latin, a *xenodochium* is called a "reception of strangers." However, where the sick are gathered from the streets, it is called a **nosocomium** in Greek, in which the limbs of the wretched, wasted by languor and hunger, are nourished.

### On Sacred Buildings, Chapter 4

Sacred places are those established for divine worship, such as those in which altars are consecrated by bishops for those offering sacrifices. According to the ancients, the **sancta** <note>holy places</note> were the exterior parts of the temple. However, the **sancta sanctorum** <note>Holy of Holies</note> was the more secret place of the temple to which none had access except the priest alone. They are called the *sancta sanctorum* because they are holier than the outer oracle, or because they are holier in comparison to other holy things, just as the "Song of Songs" excels all other songs. **Sanctum** <note>holy/sacred</note>, however, is named from the blood <note>original: "sanguine"</note> of the victim; for among the ancients, nothing was called "sacred" unless it had been consecrated by the blood of a victim. To **sancire** is to confirm and to defend from injury by the imposition of a penalty; thus, laws are said to be "sanctioned" and customs are called "holy." The **propitiatorium** <note>mercy seat or place of atonement</note> was the oracle between two cherubim. It is called *propitiatorium* as if it were the "oratory of atonement" <note>original: "propitiationis oratorium"</note>; for atonement is a pacification. They are called **oracula** <note>oracles</note> because responses are given from there, and *oracula* comes from the "mouth" <note>original: "ore"</note>. The **penetralia** are the secret parts of the oracles; they are named from that which is "deeply within" <note>original: "penitus"</note>, that is, almost inside. An **oratorium** <note>oratory or chapel</note> is consecrated for prayer <note>original: "orationi"</note> alone, in which no one ought to do anything else but that for which it was made, from which it also received its name. A **monasterium** <note>monastery</note> is the habitation of a single monk.

<column-break/>

For **mono** in Greek means "alone" and **sterium** means "station," that is, the habitation of a solitary person. **Cenobium** <note>monastery for a community</note> seems to be composed of Greek and Latin; for it is the dwelling of many living in common. For in Greek, **leno** <note>likely a scribal error for "koinos"</note> means "common." **Templum** <note>temple</note> is a general name for places; for the ancients called any large places temples. They were called *templa* as if they were "ample roofs" <note>original: "tecta ampla"</note>; also, a place designated toward the east for contemplation was called a *templum*. It had four parts: the **atria** <note>courtyards</note> looking toward the sunrise, the **postica** toward the sunset, the left toward the north, and the right toward the south. Hence, when they constructed a temple, they looked toward the equinoctial east so that lines sent from the east to the west would make the parts of the sky, right and left, equal, so that he who consulted or prayed would look directly toward the east. **Fana** <note>shrines</note> are named from the Fauns <note>original: "fannis"</note> for whom the temples of the gentiles' error were constructed, from whence they would hear the responses of consulting demons. The ancients called **delubra** those temples having springs <note>original: "fontes"</note> in which they washed <note>original: "diluebant"</note> before entering; and *delubra* are named from "washing away" <note>original: "diluendo"</note>. These are now the churches with sacred fonts in which the faithful, having been reborn, are purified; and it is well that by a certain omen they were called *delubra*, for they are for the washing away of sins. The **fons** <note>font/spring</note> in the *delubra* is the place of those being reborn, in which seven steps are formed in the mystery of the Holy Spirit: three in the descent and three in the ascent. The seventh is the same as the fourth, that is, like the "Son of Man" extinguishing the furnace of fire, a stabilizer of the feet, a foundation of water, in which the fullness of the divinity dwells bodily.

<margin>
Why kings are called *basilici*: just as the king touches the *basilici* people <note>the royal subjects</note>, he is sustained, and therefore he is called *basil...* stoned in the deep between columns and in the place of the crown... he takes it... Book 9, Chapter 3.
</margin>
**Basilicae** were formerly the habitations of kings, from which they have their name. For **basileus** means "king," and *basilicae* are royal dwellings. Now, however, divine temples are called *basilicae* because there, worship and sacrifices are offered to the King of all, God. A **martyrium** is the place of a martyr, a Greek derivation because it is constructed in memory of a martyr or because the tombs of the holy martyrs are there. Some have said an **ara** <note>altar</note> is so called because the victims' incense burns <note>original: "ardeant"</note> there. Others say *arae* are named from "imprecations" <note>original: "preprecationibus"</note>, which the Greeks call *aras*; from which a satire of counter-imprecation is spoken. Others want *arae* to come from "altitude," which is incorrect. **Altare**, however, is known to be named from "altitude" <note>original: "altitudine"</note>, as if it were a "high altar" <note>original: "alta ara"</note>. A **pulpitum** <note>pulpit/lectern</note> is so named because the lector or psalmist placed upon it can be seen in public by the people so they may hear more freely. <margin>see tribunal</margin> A **tribunal** is so named because from there, the precepts for living are "distributed" <note>original: "tribuantur"</note> by the priest. For it is a place established on high from which all things can be heard. Otherwise, a *tribunal* is named from the "tribes," because the tribes are called together to it. An **analogium** <note>ambo or lectern</note> is so called because the word <note>original: "sermo"</note> is preached from there. For in Greek, **logos** means "word" <note>original: "sermo"</note>; it is also situated in a higher place.

### On Repositories, Chapter 5

A **sacrarium** <note>sacristy</note> is properly the place of the temple in which sacred things are stored, just as a **donarium** is where offerings are placed, or as **lectisternia** are named where men are accustomed to gather. From the bringing in <note>original: "inferendis"</note> and carrying away of sacred items, it is called a *sacrarium*. **Donaria** are so called because gifts <note>original: "dona"</note> are stored there which are customarily offered in temples. It was called an **erarium** <note>treasury</note> because formerly bronze <note>original: "æo"</note> was stored there before it was stamped. For this was once in use before gold and silver were stamped, from which metals someone later...

<meta>This page continues the transition from describing general types of buildings to the specific rooms, storage areas, and architectural components of a Roman or medieval estate, focusing heavily on the etymological origins of terms for storehouses, workshops, and doorways.</meta>

->Book<-

Once money was minted from bronze, the name **treasury** <note>original: "erarium" (aerarium)</note> remained, taking its name from that metal where currency had its beginning. A **cupboard** <note>original: "armarium"</note> is a place where the instruments of any art are placed. An **armory** <note>original: "armamentarium"</note>, however, is only for weapons. Thus Juvenal says: "Whatever weapons the armories of heaven possess." Both are named from **arms**—that is, the "arms" <note>original: "brachijs"</note> of the body by which they are wielded. A **library** <note>original: "bibliotheca"</note> is a place where books are stored; for in Greek, *biblio* means "book" and *theca* means "repository." A **pantry** <note>original: "promptuarium"</note> is so called because the necessities for life are "brought forth" <note>original: "promunt"</note> from it. A **cellar** <note>original: "cellarium"</note> is so named because in it are gathered the services of the table, or the leftovers necessary for food. However, there is this difference between a pantry and a cellar: a cellar is for a few days' use, but a pantry is for a long duration. A **storehouse** or **granary** <note>original: "apotheca uel hozea" (horrea)</note> can be called "repositories" or "hidden-stores," a word for word translation from the Greek, because in these places men store the fruits of their labor. From this we also call a plentiful substance of stored things an **entheca** <note>original: "entheca"; from the Greek 'entheke'</note> in the Greek language.

### Chapter 6: On Workshops

A **workshop** <note>original: "ergasteriū"</note> is a place where any work is done. In the Greek tongue, *erga* means "works" and *sterio* means "station"—that is, a "work station." **Work-prisons** <note>original: "ergastula"</note> are also named from a Greek word; they are where the guilty are assigned to perform some task, as is common for gladiators and exiles who cut marble while bound by the guards in chains. **Women's quarters** <note>original: "gyneciū"</note> are so called in Greek because a gathering of women meets there to carry out the work of spinning wool. For in Greek, a woman is called a **gyne** <note>original: "γύνη"</note>. A **mill** <note>original: "pistrinū"</note> is named as if it were a "pestle-place" <note>original: "pilistrinum"</note>, because they used to pound the grain with a pestle <note>original: "pilo"</note> before. Hence among the ancients they were not called "millers" but **pounders** <note>original: "pistoꝛes"</note>, as if they were "pinchers" from the "pinching" or crushing of grain; for the use of the millstone did not yet exist, but they crushed the grain with a pestle. Whence Virgil also says: "Now toast the fruits with fire, now break them with a stone." An **oven** <note>original: "clibanus"</note> is a furnace named from a "slope" <note>original: "cliuo"</note> because it is built in an upright shape; for we call a steep ascent a "slope" <note>original: "cliuū"</note>. A **furnace** <note>original: "furnus"</note> is named by derivation from **spelt** <note>original: "farre"</note>, because bread is made from it and cooked there. A **wine-press** <note>original: "torcular"</note> is so called because there the grapes are trodden and squeezed out. A **vat** <note>original: "foꝛus"</note> is the place where the grapes are trodden, named because the grapes are "carried" <note>original: "feratur"</note> there, or because the grape is "struck" <note>original: "feriatur"</note> by the feet; hence it is also called a **treading-floor**. But this name has many meanings. The first kind of *forum* is a place left in a city for holding markets. The second is where a magistrate is accustomed to judge. The third is what we mentioned above, which we call a treading-floor. The fourth are the flat spaces on ships, of which Virgil says: "And he loosens the hatches." A **vat** <note>original: "lacus"</note> is so called because the liquid of the fruits runs down into it.

### Chapter 7: On Entrances

An **entrance** <note>original: "aditus"</note> is named from "going" <note>original: "eūdo"</note>, through which we enter and are admitted. A **vestibule** is either the entrance of a private house or the space adjacent to public buildings. And it is called a "vestibule" because they "clothe" <note>original: "vestiūt"</note> the doors there, or because it "clothes" the direct entrance, or from "standing." A **portico** is so called because it is more of a passage and one must stand there, like a **gate** <note>original: "poꝛta"</note>; and a portico is so named because it is open. A **doorway** <note>original: "janua"</note> is named from a certain Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance and exit. Whence Lucan says: "He closes the iron thresholds of warring Janus."

<column-break/>

Indeed, the *janua* is the first entry into a house; all other doors between the *janua* are generally called **openings** <note>original: "ostia"</note>. An **opening** <note>original: "ostiū"</note>, however, is that by which we are barred from some entry, named from "standing against" <note>original: "obstando"</note>; or it is an "opening" because it "shows" <note>original: "ostendit"</note> something inside. Others say it is called an *ostium* because it "delays the enemy" <note>original: "hostē moꝛat̃"</note>. For there we place ourselves against adversaries; hence the **mouths of the Tiber** <note>original: "ostia tyberina"</note> are so named because they are set against enemies. **Outer doors** <note>original: "foꝛes"</note> and **folding doors** <note>original: "ualuę"</note> are barriers. But those are called "outer doors" which open outward, while "folding doors" are those which revolve inward and are double and folding; however, general usage confuses these terms. **Enclosures** <note>original: "claustra"</note> are so called because they are "closed." **Windows** are those where the exterior part is narrow and the interior is wide, such as we see in granaries; they are so named because they "yield light" <note>original: "lucē fene/rent"</note>. For in Greek, light is called **phos** <note>original: "fos"</note>; or they are so named because a person placed inside sees "outdoors" <note>original: "foꝛas" - Isidore is punning on *fenestra* and *foras*</note>. Others think a "window" is so called because it provides light to the house, a name composed from Greek and Latin speech; for in Greek, light is **phos**. A **hinge** <note>original: "cardo"</note> is the place in which a door turns and always moves, named **from the heart** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς καρδίας" (apo tēs kardias)</note>; because just as the heart rules the whole man, so the hinge rules and moves the entire door. From this also comes the proverb: "The matter is on the hinge" <note>meaning a matter is at a critical turning point</note>. The **thresholds** <note>original: "limina"</note> of doors are so called because they are transverse like a **boundary path** <note>original: "limes"</note>, and through them, as in a field, one either enters or goes out. **Doorposts** <note>original: "postes"</note> and **front-pillars** <note>original: "antes"</note> are named as if standing "behind" <note>post</note> and "before" <note>ante</note>. And they are called *antes* because they stand "before," or because we come to them "before" we enter the house. They are called *postes* because they stand "after" <note>post</note> the door.

### Chapter 8: On Parts of Buildings

A **foundation** is so named because it is the "bottom" <note>original: "fundus"</note> of the house. The same is also called **masonry** <note>original: "cementū"</note>, named from "cutting" <note>original: "cedendo"</note>, because it rises from broken stone. A **wall** <note>original: "paries"</note> is so named because there are always two as "pairs" <note>original: "pares"</note>, either from the front or the side. Whether it is a square or a hexagon, those that face each other will be equal. Otherwise, the structure would be built deformed. We call **ruined walls** <note>original: "parietinas"</note> the "ruins of walls"; for they are walls standing without a roof and without inhabitants. A **corner** <note>original: "angulus"</note> is what joins two walls into one. **Roof-tops** <note>original: "culmina"</note> were so named because among the ancients roofs were covered with **straw** <note>original: "culmo"</note>, as they are now in the countryside; hence the summit of a roof is called a *culmen*. **Vaults** <note>original: "camerę"</note> are arched structures looking inward, named from "curved." For in Greek, **camur** means "curved." **Panelled ceilings** <note>original: "laquearia"</note> are those which support and adorn the vault, which are also called "hollowed ceilings" <note>original: "lacunaria"</note> because they have certain square or round "lakes" <note>original: "lacos"</note> <note>coffers or recessed panels</note> depicted in wood, plaster, or colors with shining decorations. Originally, however, they were called "lakes," as Lucilius says: "The houses and the lakes [recessed ceilings] resound." The diminutive of this makes **lacunar**, as Horace says: "No golden panelled ceiling <note>original: "lacunar"</note> shines in my house." From this comes another diminutive, *lacunarium*, and by a change of letters, *laquearium*. An **apse** <note>original: "absida"</note> in the Greek tongue is interpreted in Latin as **bright** <note>original: "lucida"</note>, because it shines when light is received through the arch. But whether we ought to say *absida* or *absis*, some teachers consider this kind of word ambiguous. A **vaulted roof** <note>original: "testudo"</note> is the slanted chamber of a temple. For the ancients made the roofs of temples in the manner of a "tortoise-shell" <note>original: "testudinis"</note>, which were made that way so they might reflect the image of heaven, which is known to be convex. Others want a *testudo* to be a place in the part of the courtyard facing those who enter. The **arches** of buildings are so called because they are curved by a "tight" <note>original: "arta"</note> enclosure. They are also called **vaults** <note>original: "foꝛnices"</note>. **Pavements**...

<meta>This page continues Book XV of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies, moving from the specific rooms and tools of a building to the architectural features of floors, columns, and materials, followed by sections on military fortifications, tombs, and rural structures.</meta>

# XV

Among the Greeks, the origins of the art of painting were highly elaborate. **Mosaic floors** <note>original: "Lithostrata"</note> are made from small crusts and tiles dyed in various colors. These are also called **pavements** <note>original: "pavimenta"</note>, because they are "beaten down" <note>original: "paviant"</note>, that is, struck. From this also comes the word "dread" <note>original: "pavor"</note>, because it strikes the heart. An **earthenware pavement** <note>original: "ostracus"</note> is one made of pottery, because it is struck from broken shards mixed with lime. Indeed, the Greeks call roofs *ostra*. The **compluvium** <note>an opening in the roof of a Roman atrium</note> is so named because the waters that are around it gather there. **Tesserae** <note>small square tiles</note> are the pieces with which homes are paved, named from "dice" <note>original: "tesseris"</note>, which are small square stones, by way of a diminutive.

**Bases** are the supports of columns which rise from the foundation and sustain the weight of the structure placed upon them. In the Syrian language, the name for a base is *fortilline*, meaning "rock." **Columns** are named for their length and roundness; the entire weight of a building is raised upon them. Among the ancients, the height of a column was three times its width. There are four types of round columns: **Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Tuscan**, differing from one another in the measure of their thickness and height. There is a fifth type called **Attic**, which has four angles or more, with equal intervals between the sides. **Capitals** <note>original: "capitolia"</note> are so called because they are the "heads" of the columns, just as the head is above the neck. **Architraves** <note>original: "epistylia"</note> are those beams placed above the capitals of the columns; it is a Greek word meaning "placed upon." **Roof tiles** <note>original: "tegule"</note> are so named because they "cover" <note>original: "tegant"</note> the house, and **gutter tiles** <note>original: "imbrices"</note> because they receive the "rain showers" <note>original: "imbres"</note>. **Bricks** and **tiles** <note>original: "lateres et laterculi"</note> are named because they are "wide" <note>original: "lati"</note>, formed on all four sides by four wooden boards. A **channel** <note>original: "canalis"</note> is named from the fact that it is hollow like a "reed" <note>original: "canne"</note>. Indeed, we prefer to use the feminine gender for channel rather than the masculine. **Water pipes** <note>original: "fistule"</note> are so named because they "pour out" and "emit" water. For in Greek, *stola* means "to send." Their shapes are made according to the volume of water and the measure of their capacity.

### Chapter 9: On Fortifications

A **fortification** <note>original: "munitio"</note> or defense is so called because it is "made by hand" <note>original: "manu factum"</note>. These places are called fortifications either because they enclose everything that is inside—that is, they shut it in—or because they restrain outsiders by their presence and prevent them from entering. A **rampart** <note>original: "vallum"</note> is that which is raised as a mass of earth to provide protection. It is named *vallum* from "valleys" <note>original: "vallis"</note>. For the stakes with which a rampart is fortified are called *valli*. These stakes are so named because they are "fixed" or "uprooted." **Intervals** are the spaces between the tops of the stakes—that is, the posts from which the rampart is made; from this, other spaces are also named, specifically from these posts. A **mound** <note>original: "agger"</note> is a heap of any material from which ditches or valleys can be filled. Properly speaking, an *agger* is the earth brought together and placed near a rampart once it is made, but we loosely call all walls and fortifications *aggers*. **Stone walls** <note>original: "macerie"</note> are long walls with which certain vineyards are enclosed. For the Greeks call "long" *makron*. Walls made of earth in Africa or Spain are called **rammed-earth walls** <note>original: "formatum" or "formatium"</note>, because they are inserted into a "frame" <note>original: "forma"</note> surrounded by two boards on either side, rather than being built up. These last for ages, undamaged by winds or fire, and are stronger than any cement. **Hedges** are the defenses of fields, and from this they take their name. **Courtyards** <note>original: "laulas" (aulas)</note> are defenses for everything or enclosures for sheepfolds. For the name is Greek; the Greeks call the shelters for animals *aulas*.

### Chapter 10: On Tents

**Tabernacles** are the tents of soldiers, in which they avoid the heat of the sun, storms of rain, and the injuries of the cold while on a journey. They are called tabernacles because cords stretched by ropes were hung from poles <note>original: "rabulis"</note> to support the tents. A **tent** <note>original: "tentorium"</note> is so called because it is "stretched" <note>original: "tendatur"</note> by ropes and stakes; from this, we still say "to extend" <note>original: "pretendere"</note> today. **Pavilions** <note>original: "papiliones"</note> are named from their resemblance to the flying creature, the butterfly, which is especially abundant among flowering mallows. These are the little creatures that fly toward a lit lamp and, fluttering around it, are forced to perish in the fire.

<column-break/>

### Chapter 11: On Tombs

A **sepulcher** is named from the "buried" <note>original: "sepulto"</note>. Formerly, everyone was buried in their own house. Later, it was forbidden by law so that the stench of the bodies would not infect the health of the living. A **monument** is so named because it "warns the mind" <note>original: "mentem moneat"</note> to remember the deceased. For when you do not see a monument, you forget the dead. From this comes that which is written: "I have been cut off from the heart like one who is dead." But when you see it, it warns the mind and brings you back to memory, so that you recall the dead. Therefore, monuments and **memorials** <note>original: "memorie"</note> are named for the admonition of the mind. A **mound** <note>original: "tumulus"</note> is named as if it were "swelling earth" <note>original: "tumens tellus"</note>. **Sarcophagus** is a Greek name because bodies are consumed there; for in Greek *sarx* means "flesh" and *phagein* means "to eat." **Mausoleums** are the tombs or monuments of kings, named after Mausolus, a king of the Egyptians <note>Isidore mistakenly identifies the Carian king as Egyptian</note>. For when he died, his wife built a tomb of marvelous size and beauty, so much so that to this day all precious monuments are called mausoleums after his name. **Pyramids** are a type of tomb, square and tapering to a point, beyond all height that can be made by hand; hence they are said to exceed the measure of shadows and to have no shadow. They rise in such a building that they begin wide and end narrow, like fire. For *pyr* means "fire." Egypt has these. Among the ancestors, the powerful were buried either under mountains or in mountains. From this it was derived that either pyramids were made over corpses or huge columns were placed there.

### Chapter 12: On Rustic Buildings

A **hut** <note>original: "casa"</note> is a rural dwelling woven together from stakes, brushwood, and reeds, by which men can protect themselves from the force of the cold or the injury of the heat. A **shack** <note>original: "tugurium"</note> is a little hut that guardians of vineyards make for their own governance—as if it were a "covering" <note>original: "tegurium"</note>—either to turn away the heat and rays of the sun, or so that they may drive away men or little beasts that tend to lie in wait for the ripening fruit. The peasants call this a **cabin** <note>original: "capana"</note> because it holds only one "head" <note>original: "caput"</note>. Some think **lescua** are shacks, while others think they are steep and rugged places. **Magalia** are the buildings of rural Numidians; they are oblong with curved sides and roofs, as if they were the hulls of ships, or round in the manner of ovens. They are called *magalia* as if they were *magaria*, because in the Punic language *magar* means a "new village," with one letter changed, L for R.

### Chapter 13: On Fields

A **field** <note>original: "ager"</note> is said to be named in Latin because something is "done" <note>original: "agatur"</note> in it. Others believe it is clearly named from the Greek; hence a village in Greek is called *cozagros*. A **villa** is named from a "rampart" <note>original: "vallum"</note>, that is, a mound of earth, because it is usually established along a boundary. **Possessions** are widely extending fields, both public and private, which in the beginning someone occupied and possessed as they were able, rather than by formal hand-transfer <note>original: "mancipatio"</note>; hence the name. An **estate** <note>original: "fundus"</note> is so called because the patrimony is "founded" or made stable there. *Fundus* can be understood as both an urban and a rural building. A **farm** <note>original: "predium"</note> is so called because it is especially "provided for" <note>original: "pervidet"</note>—that is, it is visible—out of all the things belonging to the head of a family.

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s "Etymologies," specifically Book XV on buildings and fields. Having previously discussed the components of houses and architectural materials, the text now transitions into the classification of rural lands, the methods of surveying boundaries, and the specific units of measurement used in the Roman world.</meta>

# XV

An **estate** <note>original: "praedium"</note> is named either from the land itself or because the ancients held fields they had captured in war in the name of **booty** <note>original: "praeda"</note>. This land, as Varro teaches, is divided fourfold: it is either **arable** <note>original: "arvus"</note> land, which is for sowing; or **planted** <note>original: "consitus"</note>, which is suitable for trees; or **pasture** <note>original: "pascuus"</note>, which is available only for grass and animals; or **flowery** <note>original: "floridus"</note>, which are gardens suitable for bees and flowers—a distinction which Virgil also followed in the four books of the *Georgics*. The ancients used to call uncultivated fields the **countryside** <note>original: "rura"</note>, meaning the woods and pastures, while they called the land that was worked a **field** <note>original: "ager"</note>. For the "countryside" is where honey, milk, and cattle can be had; from which the word **rustic** <note>original: "rusticus"</note> is also named. This is the primary and leisurely happiness of country folk. A **crop-field** <note>original: "seges"</note> is the field in which one sows; whence Virgil says: "That crop at last answered the prayers of the greedy farmer." A **common pasture** <note>original: "compascuus"</note> field is so named because it was left by the surveyors of fields for the neighbors to graze their livestock in common. An **alluvial** <note>original: "alluvius"</note> field is land that a river gradually returns to the field. An **undetermined** <note>original: "arcifinius"</note> field is so named because it is not contained by certain measurements of lines, but bars <note>original: "arcet"</note> its borders by the obstruction of rivers, mountains, or trees; for this reason, nothing in the way of "leftovers" is found in these fields. **Fallow** <note>original: "novalis"</note> land is that which is first ploughed, or because it lies empty in alternate years for the sake of **renewing** <note>original: "novandarum"</note> its strength. For fallow lands will be fruitful once and empty once. A **neglected** <note>original: "squalidus"</note> field is as if it were "ex-cultivated" <note>original: "excolidus"</note>, because it has already departed from cultivation, just as an "ex-consul" has departed from the consulship. A **marshy** <note>original: "uliginosus"</note> field is always wet. For "wet" <note>original: "uvidus"</note> is the term used for that which is sometimes dried, but **moisture** <note>original: "uligo"</note> is the natural humor of the earth that never leaves it. **Leftovers** <note>original: "subseciva"</note> are first what a cobbler, cutting from material, throws away as if superfluous. From this, "leftover fields" are those which those dividing a territory into **measuring-poles** <note>original: "pertica"</note> reject as being sterile or swampy. Likewise, "leftovers" are those bits which, in the division of a field, do not make up a **century** <note>original: "centuria"</note>, that is, 200 **iugera** <note>the standard Roman unit of land area, roughly 0.6 acres</note>. A **threshing floor** <note>original: "area"</note> is a level surface of boards. It is named *area* from its flatness and equality, whence also the word **altar** <note>original: "ara"</note> is derived. Others say it is called *area* because it gives "wealth" <note>original: "era"</note> through the threshing of crops, or because nothing is threshed in it unless it is **dry** <note>original: "arida"</note>. A **meadow** <note>original: "pratum"</note> is that from whose abundance of hay the herds are maintained. The ancient Romans "envied" <note>original: "inviderunt"</note> this name <note>Isidore is making a pun on 'pratum' and 'paratum'</note>, because it is **immediately ready** <note>original: "protinus paratum"</note> and does not require great labor of cultivation. Meadows are those lands which can be mown. **Marshes** <note>original: "paludes"</note> are named from Pales, the pastoral goddess, because they nourish **chaff** <note>original: "paleas"</note>, which is fodder for beasts of burden.

### On the Borders of Fields, Chapter 14.

**Borders** <note>original: "fines"</note> are so called because fields are divided by **cords** <note>original: "funiculis"</note>. For lines of measurement are stretched in the partitioning of lands so that equality of dimension may be maintained. The ancients used a word for "transverse" to call these **boundaries** <note>original: "limites"</note>. For the ancients called all transverse things *luma*, from which are derived the **thresholds** <note>original: "limina"</note> of doors through which one goes out and in, and "boundaries" <note>original: "limites"</note> through which one goes out into the fields. From this also the word **apron** <note>original: "limus"</note> was taken for the belt with which public servants were girded with a slanted purple stripe. **Boundary markers** <note>original: "termini"</note> are so called because they distinguish and declare the measurements of the land. For by these the evidence of the borders is understood, and contention and strife over fields are removed. There are two primary boundaries in fields: the **axis** <note>original: "cardo"</note> and the **cross-path** <note>original: "decumanus"</note>. The *cardo* is that which is directed from the north, from the "hinge" <note>original: "cardine"</note> of heaven. For without doubt the heaven turns upon the northern pole. The *decumanus* is that which is directed crosswise from east to west; it is called *decumanus* because it forms the shape of the Roman numeral X <note>meaning 'ten'</note>. For a field divided twice <note>by the north-south and east-west lines</note> produces the figure of the number ten. A **boundary stone** <note>original: "arca"</note> is named from "warding off" <note>original: "arcendo"</note>. For it guards the borders of the field and prohibits people from entering them. A **triple-border** <note>original: "trifinium"</note> is so called because it joins the bor-

<column-break/>

-ders of three possessions. From this also comes the **quadruple-border** <note>original: "quadrifinium"</note> for four. The remaining boundaries are narrower and stand apart from each other by unequal intervals and designated names.

### On the Measurements of Fields, Chapter 15.

**Measurement** <note>original: "mensura"</note> is whatever is limited by weight, capacity, length, height, width, and the mind. The ancients therefore divided the world into parts, the part into provinces, the provinces into regions, the regions into places, the places into territories, the territories into fields, the fields into **centuries**, the centuries into **iugera**, the *iugera* into **plots** <note>original: "climata"</note>, and then the plots into **tracts** <note>original: "actus"</note>, **poles** <note>original: "perticae"</note>, **paces**, **steps**, **cubits**, **feet**, **palms**, **ounces**, and **fingers**. Such was their ingenuity. A **finger** <note>original: "digitus"</note> is the smallest part of rural measurements. Next is the **inch** <note>original: "uncia"</note>, having three fingers. A **palm** <note>original: "palmus"</note> has four fingers. A **foot** <note>original: "pes"</note> has sixteen fingers. A **pace** <note>original: "passus"</note> has five feet. A **pole** <note>original: "pertica"</note> has two paces, which is 10 feet. The *pertica* is named from "carrying" <note>original: "portando"</note>, as if it were a "portable-pole" <note>original: "portica"</note>. For the preceding measurements are based on the body: like the palm, the foot, the pace, and the rest; only the pole is carried. It is ten feet long, like the reed in Ezekiel that measures the temple.

But a **porca** <note>ridge</note> is what stands out in ploughing; that which is dug out is called a **lyra** <note>furrow</note>. A **century** <note>original: "centuria"</note> is a field of two hundred *iugera*, which among the ancients was named from one hundred *iugera*. Later this measurement was doubled, but it retained its original name. For although the centuries were multiplied in number, they did not lose the name.

<meta>This page concludes the final chapter of Book XV, regarding roads and pathways, and begins Book XVI, which focuses on the nature of the earth, its minerals, and its various substances. The transition moves from man-made infrastructure and navigation of the landscape to the physical properties of the soil and stone itself.</meta>

### On Roads Chapter xvi.

We call the measurements of roads **miles** <note>original: "miliaria"</note>; the Greeks call them **stadiums** <note>original: "stadia"</note>; the Gauls, **leagues** <note>original: "leuuas"</note>; the Egyptians, **signs** <note>original: "signos"</note>; and the Persians, **parasangs** <note>original: "parafangas"</note>. Yet all of these are determined by a specific space, with a **mile** <note>original: "miliarium"</note> being defined by one thousand paces. It is called a "mile" as if to say "a thousand acts" <note>original: "mille adtu," likely a folk etymology for "mille passuum"</note>, consisting of five thousand feet. A **league** <note>original: "leuua"</note> is finished in one thousand five hundred paces. A **stadium** <note>original: "stadium"</note> is the eighth part of a mile, consisting of one hundred twenty-five paces. They say that **Hercules** <note>the Roman hero and god</note> first established this measurement, determining it by the distance he could cover in a single breath; he then called it a "stadium" because he had breathed again <note>original: "respirasset"</note> and stood still <note>original: "stetisset"</note> at its end.

A **road** <note>original: "via"</note> is where a vehicle can go. It is called "via" from the "incursion of vehicles" <note>original: "vehiculorum incursu"</note>. For it contains two **tracks** <note>original: "actus"</note> for the sake of vehicles meeting as they go and come. Every road is either **public** or **private**. A public road is that which is on public soil, open to the people between various districts; these lead either to the sea or to towns. A private road is one granted to a neighboring municipality. A **paved road** <note>original: "strata"</note> is so called because it is "strewn" or worn down by the feet of the common people. Lucretius <note>Roman poet and philosopher</note> says: "And the paved roads of the ways now swept by the feet of the common people." This is also called **dilapidated** <note>original: "dilapidata"</note>, which means "paved with stones" <note>original: "lapidibus strata"</note>. The **Carthaginians** <note>original: "poeni"</note> are said to have been the first to pave roads with stones; later, the Romans laid them out across nearly the whole world for the sake of direct travel and to keep the common people from being idle.

An **embankment** <note>original: "agger"</note> is the central elevation of a paved road, built up with piled-up stones; it is named from *agger*, meaning a heap or "accumulation." Historians call this a **military road**, such as the "serpent often seen hanging on the embankment of the road." A **way** or **path** <note>original: "iter" or "itus"</note> is a road where a person can go in any direction. However, "iter" and "itiner" have different meanings. For an **iter** is a place easy to cross, from which we also get the word "entrance" <note>original: "aditum"</note>. An **itiner**, however, is the journey of a long road and the labor of walking itself, so that you may arrive where you wish. A **footpath** <note>original: "semita"</note> is half of a journey, named from "half-way" <note>original: "semi itu"</note>. A "semita" belongs to humans, while a **track** <note>original: "callis"</note> belongs to wild beasts and cattle. A "callis" is a narrow and worn path for cattle among the mountains, named from the "callousness" <note>original: "callo"</note> of their feet, or because it is hardened by the "callus" of the livestock.

**Cross-paths** <note>original: "tramites"</note> are transverse roads in the fields, or a straight way, so called because they "transmit" or cut across. **Forks** <note>original: "divortia"</note> are the bends of roads, that is, roads stretching in different directions; these are the same as **diversions** <note>original: "diverticula"</note>, which are diverse and divided ways or transverse footpaths that serve as alternative routes. A **two-way** <note>original: "bivium"</note> is so named because the road is double. **Crossroads** <note>original: "compita"</note> are where many roads "compete" or meet in it, such as three-way or four-way junctions. A **perimeter** <note>original: "ambitus"</note> is a space of two and a half feet left between neighboring buildings for the ability to walk around them, named from "walking" <note>original: "ambulando"</note>. A **rut** <note>original: "orbita"</note> is the track of a wagon, named from the "orbit" or circle of the wheel. Furthermore, a **cattle-path** <note>original: "actus"</note> is where livestock are usually driven. A **sloping road** <note>original: "clivosum iter"</note> is one that is winding or steep. **Footprints** <note>original: "vestigia"</note> are the marks of feet pressed by the soles, so called because they "investigate" <note>original: "instigent"</note> or make known the ways of those who have run before.

## Here begins the sixteenth book
### On the dust and clods of the earth Chapter i.

**Dust** <note>original: "pulvis"</note> is so called because it is "driven" <note>original: "pellatur"</note> by the force of the wind. For it is lifted by its blast, and it neither resists nor knows how to stand still. As the Prophet says: "Like the dust which the wind casts away from the face of the

<column-break/>

earth." **Mud** <note>original: "limus"</note> is named because it is "smooth" <note>original: "lenis"</note>. *Lenum* is a term for slime. **Ash** <note>original: "favilla"</note> is said to come from a fire. For it is made by fire. For *fox* is fire. A **clod** <note>original: "gleba"</note> is so called because it is a "globe." For it is compacted by a collection of dust and united in a single mass. Earth that is bound together is a clod; when loosened, it is dust. A **landslide** <note>original: "labina"</note> is so named because it brings a "slip" <note>original: "lapsum"</note> to those walking, a word derived from "fall" <note>original: "labe"</note>. Some think **dirt** <note>original: "lutum"</note> is named by "antiphrasis" <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</note>, because it is *not* clean; for everything that is "washed" <note>original: "lotum"</note> is clean. **Wallows** <note>original: "volutabra"</note> are named because boars "roll" <note>original: "volutentur"</note> there. **Moisture** <note>original: "uligo"</note> is the filth of mud or water. **Sand** <note>original: "sabulum"</note> is the lightest kind of earth.

**Clay** <note>original: "argylla"</note> is named from the Argives, among whom vessels were first made from it. **Chalk** <note>original: "creta"</note> is named from the island of Crete where the best kind is found. **Cimolian chalk** is white, named from the island of Cimolus in Italy <note>actually Greece, but Isidore identifies it here with Italy</note>; one kind of it softens the precious colors of garments, and when sulfur is rubbed on, it brightens them with a certain luster; the other kind provides a polish for gemstones. **Silver chalk** <note>original: "creta argentarea"</note> is also called white because it restores luster to silver. **Samian earth** is named from the island of Samos; it is glutinous, white, and smooth to the tongue, necessary for medicines and small vessels. **Puteolan dust** <note>volcanic ash from Pozzuoli used in Roman concrete</note> is collected in the Puteolan hills of Italy; it is set against the sea to withstand its force and break the waves. For when submerged in water, it immediately becomes stone, and becoming stronger every day on all sides, it is transformed into rock, just as clay is turned into stone by fire.

**Sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"</note> is so called because it is kindled by fire; for *ur* means fire. Indeed, its power is felt in boiling waters, and no other substance is more easily ignited. It is born in the Aeolian Islands between Sicily and Italy, which are said to burn. It is also found dug up in other places. There are four types of this: one that is dug up, translucent and green, which is the only one used by physicians. The second is what they call **clod** <note>original: "glebam"</note>, which is familiar for the uses of fullers <note>those who clean cloth</note>. The third is a liquid, used for whitening wool, as it provides whiteness and softness. The fourth is especially suitable for making lamps. The power of sulfur is so great that it can detect the "comitial disease" <note>epilepsy</note>; when placed on fires, it burns with its luster in a cup of wine, and by its smell and the smoke it gives off, it causes a dreadful paleness like that of the dead to spread over those it affects.

### On clods from water Chapter ii.

**Bitumen** <note>asphalt or tar</note> emerges in the Lake of Asphalt <note>the Dead Sea</note> in Judea; sailors approaching in boats collect its floating clods. In Syria, it is a slime that bubbles up everywhere from the earth. Both types thicken and unite when they settle. The Greeks call both of these thick substances **asphalt** <note>original: "asphalton"</note>. Its nature is fiery and kin to flames; it is broken neither by water nor iron, except by womanly stains <note>referring to a historical myth regarding menstrual blood</note>. It is useful for the joints of ships. **Alum** <note>original: "alumen"</note> is named from "light" <note>original: "lumine"</note> because it provides brightness to colors for dyeing. It is a saltiness of the earth, and it is produced in winter from water and mud and matured by the summer sun. There are two species of this: liquid and thick. Some think **salt** <note>original: "sal"</note> is so named because it "leaps" <note>original: "exiliat"</note> in the fire. It flees fire even though it is of a fiery nature; but it follows nature, because fire and water are always enemies to each other. Others believe salt is named from the **sea** <note>original: "salo"</note> and the **sun** <note>original: "sole"</note>. For it is born spontaneously from the waters of the sea as foam left on the furthest shores or rocks.

<meta>This page transitions from the geography and man-made structures of Book XV to the natural properties of the earth's substances in Book XVI. It specifically begins the exploration of minerals, starting with salt and nitre, then moving to common stones and the remarkable properties of the magnet.</meta>

& boiled by the sun. There are also lakes, rivers, and wells from which it is drawn; then, poured into salt-pans, it dries in the sun. There are also rivers that thicken into salt while the rest of the stream flows beneath the ice. Elsewhere, it is gathered by removing sand; it grows with the waxing of the moon. For in Cyrenaica <note>a region in modern-day Libya</note>, "Hammoniac" salt <note>original: "bammmoniacus," likely "hammoniacus"</note> is found under the sands. There are also mountains of native salt which is cut with iron as if it were stone; it regrows, and in some places is of such hardness that they make walls and houses from blocks of salt, as in Arabia. In the nature of salt, there are also differences. For in some places it is mild; in others, very salty. Common salt crackles in the fire. Tragasean salt <note>from Tragasae in the Troad</note> neither crackles in the fire nor leaps out. Agrigentine salt from Sicily endures flames, but leaps in water; in fire, it flows, contrary to its nature. There are also differences in colors. "Mephitic" salt is red. In a certain part of Sicily where Mount Etna is, it is purple. Likewise in that same Sicily, at Pachynum <note>the southeastern tip of Sicily</note>, it is so splendid and bright that it reflects images. In Cappadocia, it is dug up with a saffron color. The nature of salt is necessary for every food. For it gives flavor to dishes; it excites greed and creates an appetite for all foods. Indeed, from it comes all the delight of nourishment and the greatest cheer. Hence, the word for "health" <note>original: "salus"</note> is thought to have taken its name from "salt" <note>original: "sale"</note>. For nothing is more useful than salt and sun. Finally, we see this in the diet of sailors; even cattle, herds, and beasts of burden are greatly provoked to pasture by salt, producing much more milk and making cheese much more pleasing by its gift. Salt also astringes, dries, and binds the body. It even protects the deceased from the decay of putrefaction so that they might endure. **Nitre** <note>original: "Nitrum," likely natron/sodium carbonate</note> took its name from a place. For it is produced in a town or region of Egypt called Nitria, from which medicines are made and the filth of bodies and clothes is washed. Its nature does not differ much from salt; for it has the power of salt, and similarly arises on whitening shores through dryness. **Aphronitrum** <note>original: "Aphronitrū"</note> is called so in Greek; in Latin it is "froth of nitre" <note>original: "spuma nitri"</note>. Regarding this, someone said: "You are a rustic, you do not know what I am called by a Greek name; I am called the froth of nitre. You are a Greek, and it is Aphronitrum." It is collected in Asia, dripping in caves; then it is dried by the sun. It is considered best if it is least heavy and most brittle, with a color almost purple. **Chalcanthum** <note>original: "Chalcanthū," likely blue vitriol or copperas</note> is so called because it is the "flower of copper" <note>original: "chalcidis... id est flos"</note>; hence among the Latins it is called "flower of brass" <note>original: "aeris flos"</note>. It is now produced in many regions; formerly in Spain from wells or pools containing that kind of water, which they would boil and pour into wooden tanks, hanging ropes stretched with small stones over them, to which the slime adhered in the likeness of green grapes; thus cast out, it would dry for thirty days. It is now also produced elsewhere in caves, where the collected liquid solidifies into certain clusters; it is also formed in hollowed pits where falling drops on the sides coalesce. It is also formed in the manner of salt by the most scorching sun. It is of such a constricting power that, if sprinkled into the mouths of lions and bears, it has such great force for binding that they are unable to bite.

## On Common Stones Chapter iii.

**Stone** <note>original: "Lapis"</note>, being denser than a tract of earth, is distinguished even by the common people. It is called "lapis" because it "hurts the foot" <note>original: "ledat pedem," a folk etymology</note>. A soft stone is scattered. **Rocks** <note>original: "Saxa"</note> stick together and are cut from mountains. **Petra** is the Greek word <note>for rock</note>. **Siler** is a stone 

<column-break/>

that is hard; it is so named because fire leaps forth from it. A **Crag** <note>original: "Scopulus"</note> is named after a prominent lighthouse <note>original: "faro"</note>, as if from "looking out" <note>original: "speculando"</note>; or from the steering of ships, from the Greek <term>to protect <note>original: "σϰεπαζειν" (skepazein)</note></term>. **Spelea** is the Greek word, **cave** <note>original: "spelunca"</note> the Latin. It is a hollowed part of a cliff. A **brink** <note>original: "Crepido"</note> is the edge of a broken rock; hence it is called "crepido" because it is the height of a broken rock; thus: "foot sticks to foot, thick and fast" <note>likely a poetic quote or mnemonic</note>, whence it is named. **Reefs** <note>original: "Cautis"</note> are rough rocks in the sea, named from "taking care" <note>original: "cauēdo"</note>, because they must be handled cautiously. **Murices** are rocks on the shore, similar to the shells of the murex with very sharp points, and are perilous to ships. **Echo** <note>original: "Ycho"</note> is a stone that, catching the sound of the human voice, even imitates the words of those speaking. In Greek it is called "Icon," in Latin "image," because by responding to the voice, it becomes an image of another's speech; although this happens both from the nature of places and often in valleys. A **Pebble** <note>original: "Calculus"</note> is a small stone mixed with the earth, round and very hard, and very smooth in its cleanliness. It is called "calculus" because it is trodden upon <note>original: "calcetur"</note> without discomfort due to its smallness. Contrary to this is the **scruple** <note>original: "scrupus"</note>, a minute and sharp stone; if it falls into a shoe, it hurts and is a trouble to the mind—whence we call mental trouble a "scruple." Hence also "scrupea" rocks, that is, rough ones. A **Whetstone** <note>original: "Cos"</note> received its name because it sharpens for cutting. For in Greek speech, "Cos" signifies "incision." Of these, some are for use with water; others require oil for sharpening, but oil makes the edge smooth, while water makes the edge very sharp. **Pumice** <note>original: "Pumex"</note> is so called because it is formed from the density of froth <note>original: "spumę"</note> being hardened; it is dry, small in its whiteness, and has such a nature for cooling that, if placed in a vessel, new wines <note>original: "musta"</note> cease to boil over. Craftsmen call **rubble** <note>original: "Rudus"</note> stones that are mixed and mingled with lime, which they pour over in making floors; hence they call them "rudera." **Gypsum** is related to lime, and its name is Greek; there are many kinds of it. But the best of all is **mirror-stone** <note>original: "lapis specularis," likely mica or selenite</note>. It is famous for buildings and very pleasing for ornaments. **Quicklime** <note>original: "Calx viua"</note> is so called because, while it is cold to the touch, it contains a hidden fire within. Whence, when water is poured over it, the latent fire immediately breaks out. Its nature does something wondrous. For after it has burned, it is ignited by water, by which fire is usually extinguished; and it is extinguished by oil, by which fire is usually kindled. Its use is necessary for the structures of building. For stone cannot adhere strongly to stone unless joined by lime. Lime from white and hard stone is better for structure; that from soft stone is useful for plastering. **Sand** <note>original: "Arena"</note> is named from "aridity" <note>original: "aridita/ te"</note>, not from "adhering" <note>original: "adherendo"</note> in buildings as some would have it. The proof of this: if it creaks when pressed by the hand, or if it leaves no filth when sprinkled on a white garment.

## On More Notable Stones Chapter iiii.

The **Magnet** stone <note>original: "Magnes"</note> is named after its discoverer. It was first found in India, with the nails of the shepherd's sandals and the tip of his staff sticking to it while he, also named Magnes, was pasturing his herds; later it was found everywhere. It is of a rusty color. Its proof is this: when applied to iron, it causes its capture. For it so seizes iron that it makes a chain of rings, which is why the common people call it "living iron." It is also believed to draw the liquid of glass just as it draws iron. There is such great force in it, as the most blessed **Augustine** reports, that someone held that same magnet stone under a silver vessel and placed iron upon the silver; then, as the hand moved underneath with the stone, the iron moved its course above. Whence it happened that in a temple...
