<meta>This page continues the catalog of stones and minerals from the previous discussion on salt. It transitions from common minerals to stones with wondrous or medicinal properties, such as the magnet, jet, and various gemstones, concluding with the introduction to marbles.</meta>

...that an image made of iron seemed to hang in the air. There is indeed another **magnet** in Ethiopia that does not attract iron but repels it. Every magnet is better the more blue <note>original: "ceruleus"</note> it is. **Jet** <note>original: "Gagates"</note> stone was first found in Sicily, cast out by the flow of the Gages River, from which it is named; however, it is most abundant in Britain. It is black, flat, light, and burns when brought to fire. Writing made on pottery with it cannot be erased; when burned, it puts serpents to flight, exposes the possessed <note>original: "demoniacos .pdit."</note>, and tests virginity. Remarkably, it is ignited by water and extinguished by oil.

**Asbestos** <note>original: "Abeston"</note> from Arcadia is a stone of iron color, named from fire <note>original: "ab igne nomē sortitus"</note> because once lit, it is never extinguished. Human art has fashioned a mechanical device from this stone, which the pagans marvel at as a sacrilege <note>likely referring to perpetual lamps in pagan shrines</note>. Indeed, they say there was a shrine of Venus in a certain temple, and in it was a candelabrum with a lamp under the open sky that burned so that no storm or rain could put it out.

**Pyrite** is a tawny stone, sharp and smoky in quality; it is so named because it contains much fire <note>Greek "pyr" means fire</note>, so that it easily emits sparks. If someone holds it and presses it hard, it burns the hand; for this reason, it took its name from fire. There is another common pyrite which they call **living stone** <note>original: "viuū lapidē" – referring to flint</note>, which when struck by iron or stone emits sparks that are caught by sulfur, fungi, or leaves, providing fire faster than a word. The common people call this "hearth stone" <note>original: "focare petrā"</note>.

**Selenite** is interpreted as "lunar" in Latin <note>original: "lunaris"</note> because they say its internal whiteness waxes and wanes with the moon; it is born in Persia. The **Dionysius** stone is dark and sprinkled with red spots. It is so called because if it is ground and mixed with water, it smells like wine, and—what is wondrous in it—it resists drunkenness. The **Thracian** stone is black and resonant; it is born in a river whose name is Pontus in Equitria. The **Phrygian** stone took its name from its location. For it is born in Phrygia; it is pale in color and moderately heavy. It is a pumice-like clod. It is prepared by being soaked in wine and blown with bellows until it glows red, then dipped again in sweet wine three times; it is only useful for dyeing clothes.

The **Syrian** stone is named from Syria where it is found; it is said that when whole it floats, but when crushed it sinks. **Arabian** stone is similar to ivory without any spots. When rubbed against the skin, it leaves a juice like saffron. The **Jewish** stone <note>original: "Judaicus lapis"</note> is white and marked with grand script-like patterns, which the Greeks call *grammata* <note>original: "grāmas"</note>. The **Samian** stone is named from the island of Samos where it is found; it is grainy and white, useful for polishing gold. **Mephitis** is named from a place in Egypt and has the nature of a gem. When ground and smeared with vinegar on parts of the body that must be burned or cut, it so numbs the body that it does not feel the torture.

The **Sarcophagus** stone is so called because bodies of the dead placed in it are consumed within forty days. For in Greek, *sarx* <note>original: "σαρξ"</note> means flesh, and *phagein* <note>original: "φα γειν"</note> means to eat. It is born in the Troad and is split along a fissile vein. There are stones of the same kind that eat away even at living bodies if bound to them; milder ones, however, preserve bodies rather than consuming them. It is called **Hematite** <note>original: "Hemarites"</note> because when dissolved on a whetstone it turns the color of blood. It is quite leaden or rust-colored. It is born in furthest Egypt, Babylon, and Spain.

<column-break/>

**Androdamas** <note>original: "Androdamantus"</note> is black in color, remarkable for its weight and hardness, from which it takes its name <note>Greek for "man-tamer"</note>. It is chiefly found in Africa. It is said to attract silver or copper to itself; when rubbed, like hematite, it turns the color of blood. **Schistos** <note>original: "Jscistos"</note> is found in far Spain, similar to saffron with a light glow, and easily crumbled.

**Amiantus** <note>original: "Amiārbon"</note> is the name given by the ancients because if a garment made of it is touched by fire, it resists it, and placed in fire, it does not burn. Having received splendor, it becomes smooth; it is similar to split alum and resists all sorcery, especially that of magi. The **Batrachites** stone is similar to a layered, splittable shell <note>named for its resemblance to a frog</note>. **Galactite** is ash-colored and sweet to the taste; it is so called because when rubbed, it gives off a milky fluid.

**Obsidian** <note>original: "Obsius"</note> stone is black and translucent, having the appearance of glass; it is placed in wall mirrors to reflect shadows of images. Many make gems from it. It is born in India and in Samos, Italy. The **Mithridax** stone of the Euphrates, when struck by the sun, sparkles with various colors. **Eagle-stones** <note>original: "Ethyres"</note> are found in the nests of eagles; they say two are found, a male and a female, and without these, eagles do not give birth. The male of these is hard, reddish like a gall-nut; the female is small and soft. Bound to the body, they cause speed in childbirth; indeed, the wombs of some may even fall out unless the stones are removed quickly after birth.

**Phengite** <note>original: "Fingites"</note> is a stone of Cappadocia with the hardness of marble, white and translucent, from which a certain king once constructed a temple with golden doors; when these were closed, the brightness inside remained as if it were day. The **Ennydros** <note>original: "Emites"</note> stone is like ivory in which a wandering fluid is said to be contained; it is similar to Parian marble in whiteness and hardness, but less heavy. **Ostracites** is so called because it has the likeness of a shell; its use is in place of pumice. **Adeltanis** <note>original: "Adelanites"</note> stone is so called because it emits a honey-sweet juice. **Hilaris** stone is rough and indomitable, wearing down all things; gems are ground with this stone.

**Sapphire** <note>original: "Zephyres"</note> is similar in color to yellow ochre; it is found in Egypt. **Amires** is like nitre, but harder; it is produced in Egypt and Arabia. In Ethiopia, it is born green, but turns milky when dissolved, stinging vehemently. **Coral** is white and harder than Parian marble. **Allochros** is green and large; it is found in Egypt. **Lucullan** marble is named from a place in Italy; it is said to split in fire. **Sabinian** stone is dark; with oil added, it is said even to shine. There is also a certain green stone that vehemently resists fire. **Siphnian** stone is soft and white, but when heated in oil, it turns black and hardens. Stones are also fit for the use of medicinal mortars and pigments; the **Aedesian** is excellent, and from it comes the **Colaric**. **Thebaic** and **Balanites** stones lose nothing of themselves <note>i.e., they do not wear down into the medicine</note>. **Specular stone** <note>Mica or Selenite</note> is so called because it is translucent like glass; it was first found in Hither Spain near the city of Segobriga. It is found underground; when dug up, it is cut and split into very thin sheets of any size.

### Chapter 5: On Marbles

After the types of stones, we come to **marbles**. For there is a difference between stones and marbles. Marbles are called "exceptional stones" which are commended for their spots and colors. "Marble" is a Greek word <note>marmaros</note>, named from its brightness <note>original: "a viriditate" - though usually brightness, the author links it to "greenness"</note>, and although afterwards...

It concludes by defining marble as a distinct class of "exceptional" stones known for their color and luster.</summary>

...and other colors may be found; nevertheless, they retain their ancient name from their greenness <note>This likely refers to *Prasinos* or "leek-green" stones mentioned on a previous page</note>. The colors and types of **marbles** are innumerable. Not all, however, are cut from cliffs; many are found scattered under the earth and are of the most precious kind. Such is **Lacedaemonian green**, more cheerful than all others; it was first found among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, from whom it took its name. **Ophites** <note>original: "Ophites"; from the Greek "ophis" for snake</note> is similar to the spots of serpents, from which it took its name. There are two kinds: a soft white and a hard black. **Augustan** and **Tiberian** marbles were first found in Egypt during the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius. They differ from Ophites because while that stone, as we said, is like snake spots, these gather spots in a different way. For Augustan marble is wavy with curls at the top, while Tiberian is scattered with gray <note>original: "canitie" – grayness or hoariness</note> rather than coiled patterns.

**Porphyry** <note>original: "Purpurites"</note> from Egypt is reddish with white dots interspersed. Its name comes from the fact that it is red like purple. **Basanite** <note>original: "Basanites"</note> is of an iron color without variety, from which its name was given; it is found in Egypt and Ethiopia. **Alabaster** <note>original: "Alabastrites"</note> is a white stone tinged with various colors, from which that Gospel vessel of ointment was made <note>referring to the "alabaster box" of ointment used to anoint Jesus</note>. It is used for ointment vessels because it is said to preserve them best from corruption. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria; it is whiter than others, but the most highly prized is found in India.

**Parian marble** is of exceptional whiteness, also known as **Lychnites** <note>original: "lychnites"; from the Greek "lychnos" for lamp, as it was quarried by lamplight</note>. This is produced on the island of Paros, whence it is called Parian. Its size does not exceed that of plates or mixing bowls. It is also suitable for ointments. **Proconnesian** <note>OCR: "Pozalliticus"</note> marble, found in Asia, does not exceed two cubits in measure; it is white on the surface but black on the opposite side. **Alabandic** is named after its native land <note>Alabanda in Caria</note> and is similar in appearance to purple. In the East, it is melted by fire and poured for the use of glass. **Thebaic** is found with golden drops in the Egyptian region; it is suitable for grinding **eye-salves** <note>term: <term>collyria</term>—medicinal cakes or pastes used to treat eye ailments</note> due to a certain natural utility. **Syenite** is produced around Syene or Thebes; it is said that kings made beams from it. The marbles found in workshops are born from cliffs, of which this Syenite is one, distinct with spots of various colors; the Cyclades islands first provided its use. **Lesbian** is a little paler than this, also having spots of different colors. **Corinthian** is similar to a drop of ammonia <note>original: "ammoniacę guttę"</note> with a variety of different colors; it was first found in Corinth, and from it, huge columns, thresholds, and beams are made. **Carystian** <note>original: "Charysteū"</note> is a most excellent green, taking its name from its appearance <note>possibly linked to the Greek "charis" for grace</note>; it is pleasing to those who carve gems, for its greenness refreshes the eyes.

**Numidian marble** <note>original: "Humidicu marmo"</note> is sent from Numidia; it releases a juice like saffron to the skin, from which it took its name; it is found in masses rather than crusts and is fit for use in thresholds. **Lucullan marble** is produced on the island of Chios, which the consul Lucullus named, who first brought it to Rome; it is almost the only marble to take its name from an admirer. There is also **Luni marble**, called **Tephria**, the color of ash; wearing this stone as an amulet is praised as a defense against serpents. **Ivory** <note>original: "Ebur"</note> is named from *barrus*, which is the elephant. Horace says: *"What do you want, woman, most worthy of black elephants?"* <note>original: "barris"</note>

<column-break/>

## Chapter VI. On Gems

After the types of marbles, **gems** follow, which add much beauty to gold with their charm of colors. Their origins are from the cliff of the Caucasus. Fables say that Prometheus first enclosed fragments of that rock in iron and circled it around his finger; from these beginnings, the ring and the gem started. They say the kinds of gems are innumerable, of which we will note only those that are principal or most well-known. They are called "gems" <note>original: "Gemme"</note> because they are translucent like **gum** <note>original: "gummi"</note>. They are called **precious stones** because they are of great value, or to distinguish them from common ones, or because they are rare. For everything that is rare is called "great" and "precious," just as it is read in the Book of Samuel: *And the word of the Lord was precious in Israel*, which means it was rare.

## Chapter VII. On Green Gems

Of all green gems, the **emerald** <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> holds the first rank. The ancients gave it the third rank of dignity after pearls and "unions" <note>term: <term>uniones</term>—large, unique pearls found solitary</note>. The emerald is named for its excessive greenness. For in the language of Syria, a green thing is called an emerald <note>original: "smaragdū"</note>. No gems or herbs have a greater intensity than this. Indeed, it surpasses green herbs and leaves, staining the air around it with its reflected greenness. For those who carve gems, there is no more pleasant refreshment for the eyes. Its body, if extended like a mirror, returns images. Indeed, Nero used to watch gladiator fights in an emerald.

There are twelve kinds, but the most noble are the **Scythian**, found among the Scythian people. The **Bactrian** hold the second place. These are collected in the crevices of rocks when the North Wind blows. For then, as the earth is uncovered, they shine through, because the sands are moved most by these winds. The **Egyptian** hold the third place. The rest are found in copper mines, but they are flawed. For they have marks like copper, lead, stones, or salt. Emeralds, however, are improved by pure green oil, which helps their natural quality. The **Copper-emerald** <note>original: "Calcosmaragđ’"</note> is so called because it is green but turbid with copper veins. This is produced in Egypt or the island of Cyprus. The **Prase** <note>original: "Prasius"</note> is named for its leek-green color, but it is cheap. One kind of it is mottled with blood-red spots. A third kind is distinguished by three white stripes.

The **Beryl** is produced in India, taking its name from the language of its own people; it is similar in greenness to the emerald, but with a paleness. They are polished by the Indians into hexagonal forms so that the dullness of the color is excited by the reflection of the angles. Another kind, though polished, has no luster. There are nine kinds of it. The **Chrysoberyl** is so named because its pale greenness shines into a golden color; India also sends this. The **Chrysoprase** is Indian, resembling the juice of a leek in color with intervening golden drops, from which it took its name; some have judged this to be a kind of beryl. **Jasper** <note>original: "Jaspis"</note> is interpreted from Greek into Latin as "green gem." For *ias* means green, and *pin* <note>original: "pinnasin"</note> means gem. It is somewhat similar to the emerald but of a thicker color. There are seventeen species of it. Some wish the jasper gem to bring both grace and protection to those wearing it; to believe this is not a matter of faith, but of superstition. The **Topaz** <note>original: "Lopazion"</note> is of the green kind and [of every color]...

resplendent. It was first found on an island in Arabia where troglodyte <note>A term used by ancient writers for "cave-dwellers."</note> pirates, exhausted by hunger and storms, unearthed it while digging for the roots of herbs. This island, subsequently searched for and often hidden by clouds, was finally found by sailors. For this reason, both the place and the gem received their name from the circumstance; for **Topaz** <note>original: "topazin"</note> in the language of the Troglodytes signifies "seeking." It is the largest of the gems and the only noble stone that can be felt by a file <note>Meaning it is soft enough to be worked with metal tools compared to harder stones.</note>. There are two kinds: the **Lallaic**, which is green in color but pale and very dense—nothing is more pleasant, and it suits gold well, hence its name. It is born in India or Germany in cold cliffs, glowing like an eye. **Malachite** <note>original: "Molochites"</note> is a thicker green and denser than emerald; it takes its name from the color of the mallow plant. It is praised for its use in making seals and is found in Arabia. **Heliotrope** <note>original: "Eliotropia"</note> is green and cloudy, sprinkled with crimson spots and blood-red veins. The reason for its name comes from the effect of the stone; for if thrown into bronze basins, it changes the rays of the sun with a blood-red reflection. Outside of water, it receives the sun like a mirror and reveals its eclipses, showing the moon passing under it. In this, there is a most wondrous example of the impudence of mages <note>The author is skeptical of magical claims.</note>, for they claim that if the herb heliotrope is added with certain incantations, the wearer is rendered invisible. It is found in Cyprus and Africa, but the best is in Ethiopia. **Sagda** is a gem of leek-green color among the Chaldeans, which has such great power that it seeks out ships covered in pitch from the deep and adheres so tenacily to their hulls that it can scarcely be separated unless the wood is scraped away. **Myrrh-stone** <note>original: "Myrrhites"</note> is so called because it has the color of myrrh. When pressed, it breathes out the sweetness of an aromatic fragrance like nard. It is found in Arabia or Egypt, having the color and scent of myrrh, from which it takes its name. **Adeleros** is bicolor: green on one side and like honey on the other. **Jasper** <note>original: "Iaspis"</note> is named after a river of the Persians, known for its greenness with a golden glow.

### On Red Gems, Chapter 8

<margin>c</margin> **Coral** <note>original: "Corallius"</note> is produced in the Red Sea in a branched form. It is green in color and reddish from the sea. Its berries or paths <note>referring to the branches</note> are white and soft under the water; once pulled out, they immediately harden and turn red, and at the first touch, they turn to stone. Therefore, it is usually seized and pulled up with nets or cut with sharp iron tools, for which reason it is called "coral." Just as the Indian pearl is precious to us, so is coral to the Indians. Mages affirm that it resists lightning, if it can be believed. **Sard** <note>original: "Sardius"</note> is so named because it was first found by the people of Sardis. It has a red color, prized for marbles, but is the cheapest among gems. There are five kinds. **Onyx** is so named because it has a mixture of whiteness in it like a human fingernail; for the Greeks call a nail *onyx*. India or Arabia produces this. They differ from one another: the Indian variety has little sparks surrounded by white zones, while the Arabian is black with white zones. There are five kinds. **Sardonyx** is named from the union of two names, for it consists of the whiteness of onyx and the sard. It consists of three colors: black at the bottom, white in the middle, and vermilion on top. This stone alone, when used for sealing, pulls away no wax. It is found among the Indians and Arabs, revealed by mountain torrents. There are five kinds.

<column-break/>

**Hematite** <note>literally "bloodstone"</note> is so called because of its blood-red color; for *haema* <note>original: "hama"</note> indeed is blood. It is produced in Ethiopia, but the principal kind is found in Arabia and Africa. Concerning this stone, the mages promise something for exposing the traps of barbarians. **Amber**, which the Greeks call *electron*, is of a tawny and wax-like color; it is said to be the sap of a tree, and for that reason is called "succinus" <note>from "succus," meaning juice or sap</note>. A mythical argument gave it the name *electrum*: for they say that when Phaethon was killed by a lightning bolt, his sisters, changed into poplar trees by their grief, shed "tears" of amber every year along the river Eridanus. Many poets have said it was called *electrum* because the sun was called *Elector*. However, it is certain that it is not the sap of a poplar but of a pine tree; for when lit like a torch, it smells of resin. it is born in the islands of the Northern Ocean, like a gum, and it hardens like crystal by cold or heat. From it are made necklaces for the adornment of rustic women. It is called by some *harpaga* <note>the "snatcher"</note> because, when warmed by the rubbing of fingers, it catches up leaves, chaff, and the fringes of clothes, just as a magnet attracts iron. It can be dyed in whatever way one pleases; for it is stained with the root of alkanet and purple dye. **Lyncus-stone** <note>original: "Ligurius"</note> is so named because it is said to be made from the urine of the lynx beast, hardened over time. It is tawny like amber, attracting nearby leaves with its breath.

### On Purple Gems, Chapter 9

Among purple gems, the Indian **Amethyst** holds the primary place. The amethyst is purple, mixed with a violet color, and with something of a rosy brightness, gently sending out certain little flames. Another kind, however, descends from the **hyacinths**. The cause of its name is asserted as if there were something in its purple that is not entirely fiery but has the color of wine. It is easy to carve. There are five kinds. **Sapphire** <note>Ancient "sapphire" often refers to Lapis Lazuli, hence the "gold dust."</note> is blue with purple, having scattered golden dust. The best is found among the Medes, yet it is nowhere transparent. The **Hyacinth** <note>likely a sapphire or blue zircon</note> is named after the flower of its own name. This is found in Ethiopia. Having a blue color, the best is that which is neither rare nor dulled by density, but shining from a balance of both and glowing with purple. This stone, however, does not glow equally but changes with the appearance of the sky. For in clear weather it is transparent and pleasing; in cloudy weather, it fades before the eyes and wilts. Put in the mouth, it is cold; in carvings, it is very hard, yet not invincible, for it is inscribed and sealed by diamond. The **Hyacinthiconta** is Indian, surpassing the hyacinth. Some of them, however, are similar to crystals but are obscured by internal filaments; from this defect, they also get their name. It is called **Amethisticon** because its outermost spark turns into the violet of an amethyst. **Celandine-stone** <note>original: "Celidonia"</note> is named from the color of swallows <note>Greek "chelidon" means swallow</note>, and it is of two kinds: one is purple on one side, and the other is purple with black spots intervening. **Lyanea** is a gem of Scythia, shimmering with a blue brightness, sometimes varying with purple and golden dust-like spots flashing between. **Roditis** is rosy, and from that it took its name.

### On White Stones, Chapter 10

**Pearls** <note>original: "Margarita"</note> are the first among white gems. They are called *margarita* because they are found in sea shells <note>original: "conculis marinis"</note>. Indeed, a pebble is born within the flesh of the shell, just as the most precious pearl is said to be found in the flesh of the oyster, or a small stone in the brain of a fish. They are a sign of celestial dew, which the shells drink in at a certain time of year. Some of these pearls are called **Unions** <note>original: "vniones"</note>, a fitting name because only one is ever found at a time, never two or more together. White pearls are better than those that turn yellow; for youth or the conception of morning dew makes them white, while old age or the evening air produces dark ones. **Hedora** is second among white gems after the pearl; there is a question as to which color category it belongs, as its name is so often associated with the beauty of others that the name itself has become a mark of excellence. **Asterites** is a white gem containing an enclosed light, like a star wandering within, and it reflects the whitening rays of the sun, from which it also took its name. **Galactites** <note>literally "Milk-stone"</note> is milky; when rubbed, it gives off a white juice with a milky taste. Bound to nursing women, it makes their breasts fertile with milk. Tied around an infant's neck, it is said to create saliva, but it is said to melt in the mouth and take away the memory. The Nile and Acheloas rivers provide them. Some also call an emerald with white veins a *galactites*. **Salarias** has the whiteness and shape of hail; its hardness is invincible like a diamond, and even when placed in fire, it maintains its own coldness. The **Sun's Gem** <note>original: "Solis gemma"</note> is white, and took its name because it scatters rays shining in a circle like the appearance of the sun. **Selenites** <note>Moon-stone</note> is translucent with a white and honey-like glow, containing an image of the moon, which they say decreases and increases daily according to the course of that star; it is born in Persia. **Lymedia** is found in the brain of the fish of the same name; it is white and oblong. Mages claim these stones provide signs of tranquility or storms. **Beloculus** <note>Eye of Belus</note> is whitish and surrounds a black pupil, shining from the middle with a golden glow; it was dedicated to Belus, the King of the Assyrians, because of its beauty, and was named after him. **Epimelas** <note>meaning "black on top"</note> is so called when a white gem is black on the upper surface, from which it takes its name. **Erebenus** is beautiful and white, which goldsmiths use to polish gold.

### On Black Stones, Chapter 11

**Agate** <note>original: "Achates"</note> was first found in Sicily near the river of the same name, and afterwards in many lands. It is black, having black and white circles joined and varied in the middle, similar to a goatskin. If believed, mages turn away storms and stop rivers with the smoke of these stones. **Absictos** is black and heavy, marked with reddish veins. If heated by fire, it holds its heat for seven days. **Egypilla** is black at the base with a sky-blue face; it is named after Egypt, where it is found. **Medea** is black, found by the legendary Medea. It has saffron-colored veins and gives off a sweat the color of saffron and the taste of wine. **Vicientana** is an Italian gem found by the Vicienti; it has a black face with shimmering white marks. **Bariptos** is black with blood-red and white

<column-break/>

marks. **Merameas** has a black vein, whatever its color, cutting through the middle. **Venus’s Hair** <note>original: "Veneris crinis"</note> is of the blackest brilliance, containing within itself the appearance of red hair. **Tricuus** from Africa is black; it gives off three juices: black from the base, blood-red from the middle, and yellow <note>original: "ocreũ"; ochre-colored</note> from the top. **Dionysia** is black with red spots; when ground with water, it smells of wine and is thought to resist drunkenness by its scent. **Pyrites** is black; when rubbed, it burns the fingers.

### On Various Stones, Chapter 12

**Pangrus** is variegated, consisting of almost all colors, from which it takes its name <note>likely from the Greek "pan," meaning "all"</note>. **Oleas**, a foreign name, is made of tawny, black, green, and white. **Mitridar**, when struck by the sun, shines with various colors; it is produced in Persia. **Dyoselitus** is variegated; it is so named because if it is placed near a fire, it gives off a sweat. **Opal** <note>original: "Opalus"</note> is marked with the colors of diverse gems. For in it is the softer fire of the carbuncle, the shining purple of the amethyst, the glowing green of the emerald, and all things shining together in a certain variety. It takes its name from its homeland, for India alone produces it. **Pontic stones** <note>original: "Ponticę"</note> are named from Pontus; they are of diverse kinds, sometimes shimmering with blood-red or golden drops, others having a star, others marked with long lines of color. **Herocontatithus** is multi-colored despite its small size, from which it adopted its name. It is sprinkled with such diverse marks that the colors of sixty gems can be detected in one small orb. It is born in Libya among the Troglodytes <note>Cave-dwellers</note>. **Murrine** <note>original: "Murina"</note> is produced among the Parthians, but is especially found in Germany; it is thought to be moisture thickened by heat under the earth, from which it took its name. Its variety lives in purple, white, and fire, with certain reflections of colors such as are seen in a rainbow <note>original: "cęlesti arcu"</note>. The opposite cause produces crystal: by a more powerful freezing of ice.

### On Crystals, Chapter 13

**Crystal** <note>original: "Crystallus"</note> is described as resplendent and watery in color; it is said to be snow hardened into ice over many years, from which the Greeks gave it its name. It is produced in Asia and Cyprus, but especially in the northern Alps, where the hottest sun of summer is not found. Therefore, this long-lasting and ancient hardness produces this appearance which is called crystal. When placed opposite the rays of the sun, it captures the flame so effectively that it provides fire to dry fungi or leaves. It is also used for drinking cups. It can endure nothing but the cold. The Indian **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> is a small and unsightly stone, having a rusty color and the brilliance of crystal. It is never found larger than the kernel of a hazelnut. This stone yields to no material, neither iron nor fire, nor does it ever grow hot; from which it received its name by Greek interpretation, "indomitable force." But though it be an unconquered scorner of iron and fire, it is broken by goat's blood; it is softened when soaked in fresh, warm blood, and thus it is shattered by many blows. Engravers use its fragments for marking and boring gems. However, it disagrees with the magnet stone to such an extent that, if placed nearby, it does not allow iron to be pulled away by the magnet; or if the magnet has already gripped the iron, the diamond seizes it.

...and takes it away. It is said that, like amber <note>original: "electri"</note>, it can detect poisons, dispel empty fears, and resist the arts of sorcerers. There are six types of this stone. The **Galatias** <note>literally "hailstone"</note> has the whiteness and shape of hail and the hardness of a diamond. Even when placed in a fire, it remains cold. There are two types of **Thunderstones** <note>original: "Ceraunioꝝ"</note>. One, which Germany sends, is similar to crystal but shines with a blue tint; if placed under the open sky, it captures the brilliance of the stars. Spain produces the second type of Thunderstone on the Lusitanian <note>modern-day Portugal</note> shores; its color is like glowing red-gold <note>original: "pyropo"</note> and its quality is like fire. This stone is said to help against the force of lightning, if we believe the tales. They are called *ceraunia* because they are found nowhere else but in places where a lightning bolt has first struck; for in Greek, lightning is called *ceraunos*. The **Iris** is born in the Red Sea near Arabia; it is crystal-colored and six-sided. It is named "Iris" by reasoning: for when struck by the sun under a roof, it imitates the appearance and colors of a heavenly rainbow upon the nearby walls. The **Astrion** <note>literally "star-stone"</note> comes from India and is close to crystal; in its center, a star shines with the brilliance of a full moon. It took its name from the stars because, when held opposite them, it captures and reflects their brilliance. The **Electria** <note>more commonly "Alectoria"</note> is named as if it were the "rooster-stone." For it is found in the gizzards of roosters; it looks like crystal and is the size of a bean. Magicians claim that those who carry this become invincible in contests, if we believe them. The **Enidros** <note>literally "water-stone"</note> is named from water. For it flows with water so much that you would think a bubbling spring was enclosed within it. Among all the glowing gems, the **Carbuncle** <note>literally "little coal"</note> holds the leadership. It is called a carbuncle because it is fiery like a coal, and its brilliance is not overcome even by night. Indeed, it shines in the darkness so much that it vibrates flames before the eyes. There are twelve types of it, but the most excellent are those that appear to glow and pour out fire as if it were a flame. In Greek, the carbuncle is called an *anthrax*. It is born in Libya among the Troglodytes <note>cave-dwellers</note>. The **Anthracites** is so named because it is of a fiery color like the carbuncle; it is surrounded by a white vein. Its unique property is that when thrown into a fire, it is extinguished as if among the dead, but conversely, when drenched with water, it blazes up. The **Sandastros** is born in India in a place of the same name. Its appearance is like a glowing fire within, with golden drops shining inside. It is agreed among all that as the number of "stars" within it increases, so the price increases. The **Lychnis** <note>from the Greek for "lamp"</note> is of the same genus of glowing stones; it is named for the brightness of lamps. It is born in many places, but the most prized are among the Indians. Some have said it is a milder form of carbuncle. It has two appearances: one radiates with purple, the other with a scarlet redness. When heated by the sun or by the rubbing of fingers, it is said to draw chaff and threads of paper to itself. It resists engraving, and if it is ever engraved, it clings to the wax as if with a living bite while the seal is being pressed. There are four types of it. The **Larcedonia** is said to do what the Lychnis does, though it is much cheaper than those mentioned above; it is born among the Nasamones. It is found, as they say, by divine shadow at the reflection of the full moon. Both types resist engraving. The **Alabandina** is named after Alabanda, a region of Asia; its color tends toward chalcedony, but it is rare. The **Dragon-stone** <note>original: "Dracontides"</note> is extracted from the brain of a dragon; it does not "ignite" unless it is cut from the living creature. Therefore, magicians cut them from sleeping dragons. Brave men explore the caves of dragons and scatter

medicated herbs there to induce the dragons to sleep; and thus, while they are lulled in slumber, they cut off their heads and pull out the gems. These stones are of a translucent whiteness. The kings of the East especially glory in their use. The **Chrysoprase** <note>original: "Chrysopassus"</note> is Ethiopian; it is a stone that light hides but darkness reveals. Its color is saffron, containing faint stars within that shine even under a cloud. The **Ermiscion** is seen among the most pleasing gems; it radiates with a golden light from a fiery color, carrying a white light at its edges.

### On Golden Stones, Chapter 13

**T**here are certain types of gems named after the appearance of metals or stones. The **Chrysopis** is that which appears to be gold. The **Chrysolite** <note>literally "gold-stone"</note> is similar to gold, with a likeness to the color of the sea; Ethiopia produces this. The **Chrysoplectrus** is similar to gold; it has a color verging toward amber, pleasing only in the morning light. it is most greedy for fire, and if fire is near, it ignites very quickly. The **Chrysolanis** is named from gold and fire; for it is golden by day and fiery by night. Ethiopia produces this. The **Leucochrysus** <note>literally "white-gold"</note> is golden in color with an intervening white vein. The **Melectritis** is so named because, just like pure gold, this gem is translucent. **Chrysocolla** <note>literally "gold-glue"</note> is born in India, where ants dig up gold. It is similar to gold and has the nature of a magnet, except that it is said to "increase" gold, from which it takes its name. The **Argyrites** <note>literally "silver-stone"</note> is similar to silver, having golden spots. The **Chalcitis** is the color of copper. The **Chalcophanos** is black; it returns the ringing sound of that copper stone. There are two types of **Balanites**: one is greenish, and the other is like Corinthian bronze with a flaming vein cutting through the middle. The **Sideritis** <note>literally "iron-stone"</note> does not differ at all from the appearance of iron. In sorcery, it excites discords in whatever way it is used. The **Idaean Dactyl** is from the island of Crete and is iron-colored; the reason for its name is that it expresses the shape of a human thumb. The **Arabian stone** is named after its homeland; it is ivory in appearance. The **Ostracites** is stony and shell-colored, but harder. Another type is like an agate, except that agate becomes greasy with polishing. This harder stone has such power that other gems are engraved with its fragments. The **Tongue-stone** <note>original: "Glossa petra"</note> is similar to a human tongue, from which it took its name. Practitioners of magic attribute power [to it]. For they think lunar movements are stirred by it. There are also certain kinds of gems named after animals. **Echites** <note>literally "viper-stone"</note> expresses the spots of a viper. **Larcine** <note>likely *carcinis*, "crab-stone"</note> is the color of a sea crab. **Scorpites** <note>scorpion-stone</note> resembles a scorpion in both color and image. **Mirmicites** <note>ant-stone</note> imitates the appearance of a crawling ant. **Tao** <note>peacock-stone</note> is similar to a peacock. **Hieracites** <note>hawk-stone</note> is the color of a hawk. **Ethites** <note>eagle-stone</note> is the color of an eagle. **Egophthalmus** <note>goat-eye</note> is like a goat's eye. **Lycophthalmus** <note>wolf-eye</note> has four colors: from glowing red it becomes bloody; it is black in the center, and a white circle surrounds it like a wolf's eye. **Meconites** <note>poppy-stone</note> expresses the poppy. There are also certain gems which the pagans use in certain superstitions. By the **Anancitide**, they say the images of demons are called forth in necromancy. Pagans say that by the **Sinocitide**, the shadows of the underworld are held fast once summoned. The **Celonites** <note>turtle-stone</note> is the eye-marker of a turtle, variegated and purple. Through this, the magicians pretend that by placing it under the tongue, future things can be foretold. **Bronia** <note>from the Greek word for "thunder"</note> is thought to fall from the heads of turtles during thunderstorms and to extinguish the strikes of lightning. The **Hienia** stone is found in the eyes of the hyena beast. They say that if it is placed under a man's tongue, he will foretell future events. But even **Coral** <note>original: "corallius"</note> is said to resist storms and hail. **Pontica** is a certain gem, clear in its bluish hue, having red stars and sometimes golden ones. They say it interrogates demons and puts them to flight. Among certain kinds of gems, there is great difficulty in discerning true ones from false. Indeed, it has been discovered how to transform one type into another false one from a true kind, such as **Sardonyx** stones, which are glued together from three gems so that they cannot be detected. For they fashion them from different types: black, white, and vermillion <note>original: "minio"</note> in color. For even instead of the most precious stone, the **Emerald** <note>original: "smaragdo"</note>, some people artificially stain glass and a certain crafty, false greenness deceives the eyes, until someone tests and exposes the imitation. So too are others faked in one way or another. For no life of mortals is without any fraud. Furthermore, they call all gems that are not translucent "blind," because they are darkened by their own density.

### On Glass. Chapter 15.

**Glass** <note>original: "Vitrum"</note> is so named because it shines through with transparency to the sight <note>suggesting a derivation from "videre," to see</note>. For in other metals, whatever is contained inside is hidden; but in glass, any liquid or appearance that is on the inside is declared on the outside, and in a way, what is enclosed is open. This was its origin: in a part of Syria which is called Phoenicia, bordering Judea, near the base of Mount Carmel, there is a swamp from which the river Belus is born; it flows into the sea for a space of five miles near Ptolemais, and its sands are washed clean of filth by the flow of the torrent. The story goes that a ship of nitre <note>natron or soda</note> merchants was driven ashore here; while they were preparing a feast along the beach and there were no stones to prop up their vessels, they placed blocks of nitre from the ship beneath them. When these were set on fire, the sand of the shore mixed with the nitre and clear streams of a new liquid flowed out; and this was the origin of glass. Soon, as ingenious skill is never content with nitre alone, it studied this art with other mixtures. For it is cooked with light and dry wood, with copper and nitre added, in continuous furnaces so that

<column-break/>

the bronze melts and masses are formed. Afterward, it is melted again from these masses in workshops; some is shaped by blowing, some is smoothed on a lathe, and some is engraved like silver. It is also stained in many ways so that it imitates hyacinths, sapphires, emeralds, and onyx, or the colors of other gems. Nor is there any material more suitable for mirrors or more accommodating for painting. However, the greatest value is in white glass, and especially that which resembles crystal. Hence, it has even pushed back the metals of silver and gold for use in drinking vessels. Glass was formerly made in Italy, through Gaul, and in Spain; white and very soft sand was ground with a pestle and mill. Then it was mixed with three parts of nitre by weight or measure, and once melted, it was poured into other furnaces. This mass was called *admonitrum*, and when remelted, it became pure and white glass. In the category of glass, the **Obsidian** <note>original: "obsianus"</note> stone is also numbered. It is sometimes green and sometimes black, and occasionally translucent, though thicker to the sight; it is used in wall-mirrors, reflecting shadows instead of an image. Many make gems from it. They say this stone is born in India, in Italy, and by the ocean in Spain. It is reported that under Tiberius Caesar, a certain craftsman devised a tempering for glass so that it was flexible and ductile. When he had been admitted to Caesar, he handed a vial to Caesar. He, being angry, threw it onto the floor. The craftsman, however, picked up the vial from the floor, which had bent itself like a bronze vessel. Then he took a hammer from his pocket and fixed the vial. This done, Caesar said to the craftsman: "Does anyone else know this composition for glass?" After he swore that no one else knew it, Caesar ordered him to be beheaded, lest if this became known, gold would be held as cheaply as mud and the value of all metals would be stripped away. And truly, if glass vessels did not break, they would be better than gold and silver.

### On Metals. Chapter 16.

**Metals** <note>original: "Metallis"</note> are so named in Greek from the phrase *apo tou metallan* <note>original: "απο του μεταλλαν," meaning "from searching"</note> because its nature is such that where one vein appears, there is hope of finding another. There are seven kinds of metals: gold, silver, bronze <note>original: "aes"</note>, electrum <note>an alloy of gold and silver</note>, tin, lead, and that which conquers all things, iron.

### On Gold. Chapter 17.

**Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> is named from "aura," that is, from splendor, because it shines more when reflecting the air. Hence also Virgil says: "From which the *aura* of gold reflected through the branches with a different color" <note>Aeneid VI, 204</note>; this is the splendor of gold. For it is natural that the splendor of metals shines more when struck by another light. From this also, goldsmiths are named, whose brilliance makes them splendid. **Obrycum** <note>refined</note> gold is so named because it "radiates" <note>original: "obradiet"</note> with splendor, for it is of the best color; the Hebrews call it *orbaz* and the Greeks *cairon*. **Gold leaf** <note>original: "Brachtea"</note> is a very thin plate, named from *brachein* <note>original: "βραχειν"</note>, which is *echein* <note>original: "ηχε ν," meaning to rattle or ring out</note>, that is, from its rattling sound. <margin>a plate.</margin> **Money** <note>original: "Pecunnia"</note> was formerly named from cattle <note>original: "pecudibus"</note>, and it held both the property and the name. For coins were cut and marked from the hides of cattle. Later, the bronze coin was invented by Saturn. He himself ordained that coins be marked and inscribed. For this reason, the treasury <note>original: "aerarium"</note> was consecrated to Saturn by the pagans. Others, as mentioned above, say money comes from cattle...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on materials, transitioning from precious stones to the origins of money and the properties of metals. It defines the etymological roots of financial terms and begins a detailed survey of silver and copper.</meta>

...they called it, just as beasts of burden <note>original: *iumenta*</note> are named from "helping" <note>original: *iuuando*</note>. For among the ancients, all inheritance was called "private property" <note>original: *peculium*</note> from "flocks" <note>original: *pecudibus*</note>, in which their entire substance consisted. From this, one who was rich was called a "cattleman" <note>original: *pecuarius*</note>, whereas now he is called "moneyed" <note>original: *pecuniosus*</note>. The most ancient people, before gold and silver were discovered, used bronze. For first bronze money was in use, later silver, and then gold followed; but money retained its name from that with which it began. From this also the "treasury" <note>original: *erarium*</note> is named, because at first only bronze was in use, and it alone was stored there, before gold and silver were yet stamped. Although money was later made from those other metals, the name "treasury" remained from that metal from which it took its beginning. "Treasure" <note>original: *thesaurus*</note>, according to the Greek property *from the setting down* <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως</note>, is named from "positioning" <note>original: *a positione*</note>, that is, from "gold stored away." For *thesis* is called "positioning," and it is a name composed from Greek and Latin speech. For the Greek *thesis* means "placed," which the Latin joins to sound like "stored gold." "Gold-mine" <note>original: *auraria*</note> takes its name from gold. Tributes <note>original: *tributa*</note>, however, are so called because they were previously levied through individual "tribes" <note>original: *tribus*</note>, just as they are now through individual territories. It is well known that the Roman people were divided into three parts, so that those who presided over the individual parts were called "tribunes." From this also the expenses that the people gave are called "tributes." "Taxes" <note>original: *uectigalia*</note> are tributes named from "carrying" <note>original: *uehendo*</note>. A "stipend" <note>original: *stipendium*</note> is named from "weighing a small payment" <note>original: *stipe pendenda*</note>. For the ancients were accustomed to weigh out money rather than count it. The "mint" <note>original: *moneta*</note> is so called because it "warns" <note>original: *monet*</note> lest any fraud be committed in the metal or the weight. A "coin" <note>original: *numisma*</note> is a gold or silver or bronze *solidus*, which is called *numisma* because it was marked with the names <note>original: *nominibus*</note> and likenesses of rulers. Previously, money was called *argirus* <note>from the Greek word for silver, *argyros*</note>, because it was mostly struck from silver. A "coin" <note>original: *nummus*</note>, however, was named after Numa, the king of the Romans, who was the first among the Latins to mark them with images and prescribe the title of his own name. They call them *folles* <note>small copper coins or bags of coins</note> from the small sack in which they are stored; the contents are named from the container. In a coin, three things are required: the metal, the figure, and the weight. If any of these is missing, it will not be a coin. There are three kinds of silver, gold, and bronze: stamped, fashioned, and raw. "Stamped" is that which is in coins; "fashioned" is that which is in vessels and statues; "raw" is that which is in masses, which is also called "heavy" <note>original: *graue*</note>, that is, a mass. In the knowledge of forms, metals were discovered in this way: when, for whatever reason, burning forests scorched the earth, the heated veins flowed in streams of whatever structure was there. Whether it was copper or gold, when it ran down into the lower depressions of the earth, it took the shape of the flowing stream or the hollow that received it. Men, captivated by the splendor of these things, when they picked up the solidified masses, saw in them the shaped traces of the earth; from this they realized that these metals, when melted, could be brought into any form.

### On silver, Chapter 18.

Silver <note>original: *argentum*</note> does not differ far from its Greek name, for they call it *argiron*. But in a marvelous way, though it is white, it leaves black lines when pressed against the body. "Quicksilver" <note>original: *argentum uiuum*, or mercury</note> is so named because it surpasses the materials in which it is found, 

<column-break/>

and quickly runs through liquids. It is found specifically in mines or clinging to the roofs of silver-smelting furnaces in the form of thickened drops; often also in the very old filth of sewers or the mud of wells. It is also made from cinnabar <note>original: *minio*</note> placed in an iron bowl with a clay dish placed beneath it; when the small vessel is surrounded by coals and sealed, the quicksilver drips out from the cinnabar. Without this, neither silver nor copper can be gilded. It is of such great power that if you place a hundred-pound stone upon a pint of quicksilver, it immediately resists the burden. But if you place a tiny scruple of gold, it rapidly receives its lightness into its bosom; from this it is understood that it is not weight but nature to which it yields. It is better preserved in glass vessels, for it bores through other materials. If taken as a drink, it kills because of its weight. The dross of silver is called "litharge" <note>original: *lithargyros*</note>, which we call silver-foam. It is made from a mixture of silver and lead.

### On copper, Chapter 19.

Copper <note>original: *aes*</note> is named from the "splendor of the air" <note>original: *aeris*</note>, just as gold and silver are. Among the ancients, the use and knowledge of copper came before that of iron. Indeed, with copper they first tilled the earth and waged the contests of war. Copper was held in greater value, while gold and silver were rejected because of their uselessness. Now, by a turn of fate, copper lies neglected, and gold has attained the highest honor. Thus, the rolling age changes the seasons of things, and that which was in value finally becomes of no honor. The use of copper later transitioned into statues, vessels, and the structures of buildings, and especially for the permanence of monuments; even public laws were written upon them. Cyprian copper <note>original: *cyprium aes*</note> was first found on the island of Cyprus, from which it is named. It is made from a corroded stone which they call "cadmia" <note>calamine or zinc ore</note>, and it is ductile. If lead is added to this, it becomes a purple color. "Orichalcum" <note>original: *auricalcum*</note> is so called because it possesses the splendor of gold and the hardness of copper. It is a name composed of the Latin and Greek languages. For copper is called *chalchos* in the speech of the Greeks. It is made from copper and much fire and chemical treatments, brought to a golden color. "Corinthian bronze" is a mixture of all metals, which chance first mixed at Corinth when it was captured and set on fire. For when Hannibal <note>The author likely means the Roman general Mummius, who destroyed Corinth in 146 BC; Hannibal never captured Corinth</note> had captured this city, he heaped all the bronze, gold, and silver statues into one pyre and burned them. Thus, from this mixture, craftsmen took it up and made side-dishes. So Corinthian vessels were born from all metals in one, being neither this nor that. Wherefore even to this day, whether from the original or in imitation of it, they call it Corinthian copper or Corinthian vessels. There are three kinds of this: one white, approaching the brightness of silver; a second in which the yellow nature of gold itself is present; a third in which there is an equal tempering of all. "Coronary" <note>original: *coronarium*</note> copper is made from ductile copper thinned into leaves and dyed with the gall of bulls; it provides the appearance of gold in the crowns of actors, from which it is named. "Pyropus" <note>a red gold-copper alloy</note> is named for its fiery color. For when six scruples of gold are added to each ounce of copper, it ignites in a very thin foil and imitates flames, hence it is called pyropus. "Regulated" copper is that which others call "ductile," such as all Cyprian copper is. It is called ductile because it can be drawn out by a hammer, as opposed to "cast" copper which is only melted. For "cauldron-copper" <note>original: *caldarcium*</note> is only melted...

<keywords>money, cattle, treasury, minting, coinage, silver, quicksilver, mercury, copper, bronze, Corinthian bronze, orichalcum, metallurgy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on metallurgy, specifically the properties and origins of bronze, iron, lead, tin, and electrum, following the previous section on silver and the history of coinage.</meta>

For under the hammer it is fragile. Indeed, all bronze is made more workable <note>original: *regulare*</note> if it is carefully purified by fire and soda and thoroughly smelted. Campanian bronze, which among all types of bronze is named after the province of Campania in the parts of Italy, is most highly approved for all utensils and vessels. All bronze is cast better in great cold. Bronze is quickly drawn into rust unless it is smeared with oil; however, they say it is best preserved in liquid pitch. Among all metals, bronze is the most resonant <note>original: *vocalissimum*</note> and of the greatest power; hence there are also bronze thresholds. Wherefore Virgil says:
> The hinge creaked upon the bronze doors. <note>original: *In foribus cardo stridebat aeneis*</note>
The origin of bronze is cadmia <note>zinc ore or calamine</note> and copper-stone <note>original: *calcitcus*</note>. The purifications of bronze are cadmia, and also the origin and the flower of bronze. Cadmia is produced in the furnaces of bronze and silver metals, appearing as a shining residue. For just as the stone itself from which bronze is made is called cadmia, so it arises again in the furnaces and receives its name from its origin. The "flower of bronze" <note>original: *flis aeris*</note> is said to be made during the smelting when the bronze is melted and refined, and cold water is poured over it. By sudden condensation, the flower is recovered as if from a juice. Bronze creates verdigris <note>original: *eruginem*</note>. For when bronze plates are placed over a vessel of very sharp vinegar upon brushwood, and that which has fallen into the vinegar itself from the distillation is ground and sifted.

### On Iron Chapter 20

**Iron** <note>original: *ferrum*</note> is so named because it harvests the "spelt" <note>original: *farra*</note>, that is, the seeds of the crops, from the earth. The same is also called *chalybs* <note>steel</note>, from the Chalybes river where iron is tempered to its best edge. From this, the material itself is called *chalybs* by extension, as in "wound-inflicting steel." The use of iron was discovered after other metals, but its appearance was later turned into a source of reproach. For from that which the earth was once worked, now blood is shed. No substance has elements so densely clinging and intertwined with one another as iron, which is why it possesses hardness along with coldness. The metal of iron is found almost everywhere; yet of all kinds, the prize is given to Seric iron <note>Chinese iron</note>. For the Seres <note>the Chinese</note> send this along with their garments and hides. The second prize goes to Parthian iron; nor are other kinds of iron tempered from a pure edge. For in the others, a softer blend is mixed in. There are many differences in iron according to the type of earth. For some is soft and close to lead, fit for the use of wheels and nails. Another is fragile and corroded, suitable for the cultivation of the earth. Another pleases only for its shortness, such as for boot-nails. Another feels rust more quickly. All these are called *stricturae* <note>bars or blooms</note>, a name not used for other metals, appropriately applied from "binding together" <note>original: *stringendo*</note>. There is a great difference in the waters in which glowing iron is immersed to make it more useful, such as Bilbilis in Spain and Turiaso in Italy. In sharpening iron, the edge is improved with oil; hence it is the custom for thinner iron tools to be quenched in oil, lest they harden into brittleness in water. From iron, human blood avenges itself, for when touched, it quickly draws rust. The magnet stone has a concord with iron. For only this material receives power from that stone and retains it for a long time. From the same stone, a certain architect at Alexandria had vaulted a temple so that an iron statue might appear to hang in the air within it. Iron heated by fire is not fit for use unless it is beaten with hard blows. When red, it is not ready for pounding, nor until it begins to turn white. Iron smeared with vinegar or alum becomes similar to bronze. The purifications of iron are

<column-break/>

rust and dross <note>original: *scoria*</note>. Rust is a defect that gnaws iron or crops, as if it were *rudigo* with one letter changed; this is also called *erugo* from "gnawing away" <note>original: *erodendo*</note>. For *erugo* is a defect of iron named from gnawing, not from bronze <note>original: *eramēto*</note>. Dross, however, is the purifications and filth which are smelted out by fire. And it is called *scoria* because it "runs out" <note>original: *excurit*</note> from the iron. Iron lacks rust if it is smeared with white lead, gypsum, and liquid pitch. Likewise, rust does not spoil a tool if it is anointed with deer marrow or white lead mixed with rose oil.

### On Lead Chapter 21

**Lead** <note>original: *plumbum*</note> is so named because the depth of the sea was first tested by lead weights <note>original: *pilis*</note> made from it. There are two kinds of this: black and white—but the white is better, which was first found in the islands of the Atlantic Ocean. Indeed, it is produced in Lusitania and Galicia by taking sandy earth of a black color and heavy weight; small pebbles also intervene, mostly from dried torrents. They wash these sands, and that which settles they cook in furnaces. In gold mines, when water is sent in, black and heavy pebbles are found, and while the gold is being collected, they remain with it; later separated, they are smelted and melt into white lead <note>tin</note>. From this comes the same weight of lead as of gold. Black lead <note>common lead</note> is abundant around Cantabria, and its origin is twofold. For either it comes forth alone from its own vein, or it is born with silver, and is smelted with mixed veins. Of this, the first liquid in the furnaces is *stannum* <note>an alloy of lead and silver</note>, the second is silver; that which remains when a vein is added and smelted again becomes black lead. India has neither lead nor bronze; it exchanges gems and pearls for them. We use black lead for pipes and sheets. Lead is extracted with more labor in Spain and Gaul, but in Britain, it is found in the very top layer of the earth.

### On Tin Chapter 22

The etymology of **Tin** <note>original: *stannum*</note> is *apochoriston* <note>original: ἀποχωριστὸν</note>, that is, it is called "separating" and "discerning." For it dissociates metals that have been mixed and adulterated with one another through fire; and it separates bronze and lead from gold and silver. It also defends other metals from fire; and though the nature of bronze and iron is very hard, if they are without tin, the fire burns and consumes them. Tin smeared on bronze vessels makes the flavor more pleasing and restrains the poison of verdigris. Mirrors are also tempered from it. White lead is also made from it, just as it is from lead.

### On Electrum Chapter 23

**Electrum** is so called because it reflects the sun's ray more brightly than gold or silver. For the sun is called *electron* by the poets. This metal is more purified than all other metals. Of this there are three kinds: One which flows from pine trees, which is called amber <note>original: *sucinum*</note>. Another is a metal which is found naturally and is held in high value. A third is that which is made from three parts of gold and one of silver. You will find these same proportions even if you melt natural electrum. Wherefore it makes no difference whether it is born or made, for both are of the same nature. Electrum which is natural is of such a nature that at a banquet and by the light of lamps, it shines more brightly than all metals and reveals poison. For if you pour poison into it, it emits a hissing sound.

<margin>☿</margin> <note>The symbol for Mercury or Quicksilver.</note> It emits various colors in the manner of a rainbow.

### On Weights Chapter 24

It is helpful to know the system of weights and measures. For all physical things, as it is written, from the highest to the lowest, have been arranged and formed in "measure, number, and weight." <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note> Nature has given weight to all physical things: its own weight governs all things. First, Moses gave weights and measures to the children of Israel in the desert. Pheidon of Argos <note>original: *sidon argiuus*</note> first established the system of weights in Greece. Although others may have existed earlier, he was more experienced in this art. Weight <note>original: *pondus*</note> is so named because it hangs in the balance of pounds <note>original: *librarum*</note>; hence also the word for "weighing" <note>original: *pensum*</note>. Loosely, however, a "weight" is one pound. Whence also the *dipondium* is named: as if "two weights," a name which it still retains in use today. The *trutina* <note>scales</note> is a pair of pans for weights, hanging with an equal balance; besides the weighing of talents and hundreds, it is like the *momentana* used for small and modest amounts of money. This is also called *moneta* <note>coinage</note>. The same also has the name *statera* <note>steelyard or balance</note> from "number," because balanced by two pans and one central needle, it stands equally. The *examen* is the middle thread by which the balance of the scale is governed and the pans are leveled. Whence it is also called the *amentum* of the pan. The *campana* <note>a type of balance, or steelyard</note> took its name from the region of Italy <note>Campania</note> where its use was first discovered. This does not have two pans; rather, it is a rod marked with pounds and ounces and measured by a moving weight. For each weight, however, there is a fixed limit designated by its own names.

The *calculus* is the smallest part of a weight, the fourth part of an *obolus*, consisting of two grains of lentil. It is called *calculus* because it is very small; just like 
<margin>☿</margin> the *calculus* stone <note>a pebble</note>, which is so small that it does not hurt the heel <note>original: *calce*</note>. The *siliqua* <note>the carat, originally the seed of the carob tree</note> is the twenty-fourth part of a *solidus*, taking its name from the seed of a tree. The *cerates* <note>original: *lerates*</note> is the middle part of an *obolus*, having one and a half *siliquae*. In Latin, this is called a "half-obolus." However, *cerates* in Greek is interpreted as "horn-shaped siliqua" in Latin. The *obolus* weighs three *siliquae*, having two *cerates* and four *chalcoi* <note>small copper coins</note>. For it was once made of bronze in the likeness of an arrow; whence it also received its name from the Greeks—that is, "arrow." The *scrupulus* <note>scruple</note> consists of the weight of six *siliquae*. Among the Greeks, this is called a *gramma*. However, it is called a *scrupulus* as a diminutive from the small stone which is called a *scrupus*. The *drachma* is the eighth part of an ounce and the weight of a silver *denarius*, consisting of three *scrupuli*—that is, 18 *siliquae*. The *denarius* is so named because it is counted for ten coins. The *solidus* is so named because it seems that nothing is missing from it. For the ancients called that which was whole and complete "solid." It is also called a *nomisma* <note>coin</note> because it is marked with the names and images of princes. From the beginning, however, one *nomisma* was one silver piece. For this began with the Assyrians; indeed, the Jews say that Abraham first brought this form into the land of Canaan. Among the Latins, the *solidus* is called by another name, the *sextula*, because six of these complete an ounce. To distinguish it from common use, the crowd calls it a "gold solidus" <note>the *aureus*</note>. They called the third part of this a *tremissis* because it makes a *solidus* when sent three times. A *sextula* taken twice 

<column-break/>

makes a *duella*; placed three times, it returns a *stater*. The *stater*, however, is half of an ounce, weighing three gold pieces; whence it is also called a *stater* because it "stands" for three *solidi*. Hence also the *semiuncia* <note>half-ounce</note>, because it has half of an ounce. This is also the *semissis*, because it is half of the weight—as if a "half-as." The Hebrews likewise call the *quadrans* <note>farthing</note> a *quadrans*; and it is called *quadrans* because it weighs the fourth part of an ounce. The *sicel*, which in Latin speech is corruptly called the *siclus* <note>shekel</note>, is a Hebrew name, having among them the weight of an ounce. Among the Latins and Greeks, however, it is the fourth part of an ounce and half of a *stater*, weighing two *drachmas*. Therefore, when the *siclus* is read in the Divine Scriptures, it is an ounce; but when in the writings of the Gentiles, it is the fourth part of an ounce. The *uncia* <note>ounce</note> is so named because by its unity <note>original: *unitate*</note> it conquers—that is, embraces—the whole collection of smaller weights. It consists of 8 *drachmas*, which is 24 *scrupuli*. Therefore it has a "legitimate" weight because the number of its *scrupuli* measures the hours of the day and night <note>24 hours</note>; or because, counted twelve times, it makes a pound. The *libra* <note>pound</note> is completed by 12 ounces; and from this it has its status as a perfect weight, because it consists of as many ounces as there are months in a year. It is called a *libra* because it is "free" <note>original: *libera*</note> and concludes all the aforementioned weights within itself. The *mna* <note>mina</note> among weights weighs one hundred *drachmas* and is a Greek name. The *talentum* <note>talent</note>, however, is said to be the highest weight among the Greeks. For nothing is smaller than a *chalcus* and nothing is greater than a talent. The weight of this varies among different nations. Among the Romans, the talent is seventy-two pounds, as Plautus shows when he says two talents are 144 pounds. It is, however, threefold: that is, the small, the medium, and the highest. The small consists of 50 pounds, the medium of 72 pounds, and the highest of 120 pounds. The *centenarium* is a name of number, because it is of a weight of 100 pounds. The Romans established this weight because of the perfection of the number one hundred.

### On Measures Chapter 25

A measure is some thing circumscribed by its own limit or time. This is either of body or of time. Of the body, such as the length or shortness of men, of wood, 
<margin>☽</margin> <note>The symbol for the Moon.</note> or of columns. But they also say that this sun has a specific measure of its own orbit, which geometricians dare to investigate. Of time, such as the measure of hours, days, and years. Whence we also speak of "measuring the feet of the hours"—that is, to measure. Properly, however, it is called "measure" <note>original: *mensura*</note> because by it crops and grain are measured—that is, liquids and dry goods—such as *modii* <note>pecks</note>, *arrabones*, *uznae*, and *amphorae*. The smallest part of measures is the *cochlear* <note>spoonful</note>, which is the half part of a *drachma*, weighing 9 *siliquae*. This, tripled, makes a *concula*. The *concula* fills one and a half *drachmas*. The weight of a *cyathus* <note>cup</note> weighs 10 *drachmas*; which is also called a *causatus* by some. It becomes an *oxibaphus* <note>original: *oribalus*</note> if five *drachmas* are added to the ten. The *acetabulum* <note>vinegar-cup</note> is the fourth part of an *emina*, weighing 12 *drachmas*. The *cotula* is an *emina* having 6 *cyathi*; it is called *cotula* because in the Greek language it is called the "cutting of a girl" <note>A confused etymology from the Greek *kotyle*</note>. And the *emina* of a *sextarius* is cut into two equal parts and makes a *cotula*. The *emina*, however, weighs one pound, which doubled makes a *sextarius*. A *sextarius* is of two pounds; which, taken twice, is named a *bilibris*; taken four times, it is called by the Greek name *choenix*. Folded five times, it is a *quinarum*...
