<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from Isidore of Seville's *Etymologies*, Book XVII. The previous page concluded a discussion on resins and oils derived from trees. This page begins with the description of sweet cane and the balsam tree, before transitioning into Chapter IX, which covers aromatic and common herbs.</meta>

Liber

...it [may] mix in. **Sweet cane** <note>original: *calamus aromaticus*</note> is so named from its resemblance to the common reed <note>original: *calamus usualis*</note>. It is recognized in India by its many knotted joints, its reddish-yellow color, and its fragrant, sweet scent. When broken, it splits into many parts, similar in taste to cassia but with a mild, stinging sharpness. The **Balsam tree** <note>original: *balsami arbor*</note> was once found in Judea within a boundary of only twenty *jugera* <note>a Roman measure of land, roughly 12 acres</note>. After the Romans took control of that region, it was spread even over the widest hills. Its stem is like a vine, and its leaves are like rue but whiter and evergreen. The tree itself is called balsam; its wood is called **xylobalsamum** <note>literally "wood-balsam"</note>, its fruit or seed **carpobalsamum** <note>literally "fruit-balsam"</note>, and its juice **opobalsamum** <note>literally "juice-balsam"</note>. This last name is given with an addition because when the bark of the wood is struck with iron hooks, a drop of scent distills through the openings. For in the Greek language, an opening is called *opē* <note>original: *oppē*</note>. People adulterate this drop by mixing in cypress oil or honey. But pure balsam is proven by honey if it curdles like milk, and by oil if, when dropped into water or mixed, it easily dissolves. Furthermore, if woolen clothes are stained by it, they are not permanently marked. Adulterated balsam does not curdle with milk, it floats on water like oil, and it stains clothing. Pure balsams have such power that if the sun shines brightly, they cannot be held in the hand.

### Chapter IX: On Aromatic or Common Herbs

There are also names of certain herbs that resonate based on some cause within themselves, having an explanation for their names. However, you will not find the etymology <note>word origin</note> for all herbs, for their names change according to location. **Malabathrum** <note>original: *folium*, meaning "leaf"</note> is so called because it is gathered on the shores of India without any root, growing upon the water. The Indians pierce it with wood, dry it, and store it. It is said to be an herb of Paradise, resembling nard in taste. **Nard** <note>original: *nardus*</note> is a spiked herb; hence it is called *nardostachys* <note>original: *nardos tacos*; literally "spiked nard"</note> by the Greeks. One kind is called Indian, another Syrian—not because it grows in Syria, but because the mountain where it is found faces India on one side and Syria on the other. Indian nard takes many forms, but Syrian is better: light, reddish-yellow, bushy with small spikes, very fragrant, and similar to **cyperus** <note>a marsh grass</note>. If kept in the mouth for a long time, it dries the tongue. **Celtic nard** took its name from the region of Gaul. For it grows in the Ligurian Alps and in Syria, as a small shrub with roots gathered into bundles like ligaments. Its flower is used only for its good scent. Its stems and small roots are found useful for our needs. **Costum** <note>an aromatic root</note> is the root of an herb growing in India, Arabia, and Syria. The Arabian variety is better, being white, light, and of a pleasant, sweet smell. The Indian kind is black and light like a fennel stalk. The Syrian kind is heavy in weight, yellowish in color, sharp in scent, and gives off a cloud when placed on fire. **Saffron** <note>original: *crocum*</note> is named after a town in Cilicia called Corycus <note>original: *coritium*</note>; for although it grows elsewhere, it is not of the same quality as that from Cilicia. Thus it took its name from the superior place. For many things have taken their names from the places where they grow better or more abundantly. The best saffron is that which is fresh, of good scent, with a little whiteness, of extended length, whole and not crumbled into fragments, with a good essence, and which stains the hand when handled and is slightly pungent. If it is not of this sort, it is recognized as either old or tasteless. It is adulterated by mixing in saffron dregs <note>original: *magmate*</note>. To increase the weight, crushed **litharge** <note>original: *spuma argenti*; lead monoxide</note>

<column-break/>

is added, which is a fraud if it is found to be powdery and if, when boiled, its proper scent has vanished. **Saffron dregs** <note>original: *crocum magma*</note> are made by pressing the aromatics for saffron ointment and shaping the sediment into little cloths; thus it is so named. **Asarabacca** <note>original: *asarum*</note> grows in shady mountains, with flowers similar to cassia. Between these is a purple flower near the root which contains a seed like a grape; its roots are numerous, very thin, and sweet-smelling. It is similar in power to nard. **Valerian** <note>original: *fu*</note> grows in Pontus, with leaves like the wild olive. It is called *kyparos* <note>original: *quipaz*</note> by the Greeks because it has a burning quality. The root is like a triangular reed with leaves like a leek; the roots are black and clustered together like olives, very fragrant and sharp. It grows in marshes and empty places. Another species of *kyperos* is mentioned which grows in India and is called **ginger** <note>original: *cinçiber*</note> in their language. **Illyrian Iris** <note>original: *iris illyrica*</note> took its name from its resemblance to the heavenly rainbow <note>original: *iris*</note>. Hence it is also called **gladiolus** <note>original: *argumē*; likely referring to its sword-shaped leaves</note> by the Latins. It is called "Iris" because its flower mimics the same heavenly arc with its variety of colors. It is called "Illyrian" because it is most abundant and potent in Illyria. Its species has leaves like the sword-lily and an aromatic root of good scent. **Sweet Flag** <note>original: *acorum*</note> has leaves like the iris and roots of a very sharp but pleasant smell, for which reason it is aromatic. **Adul** <note>likely *amoum* or a similar aromatic</note> has leaves like parsnips. **Cardamom** <note>original: *cardamomum*</note> is the herb the common people call **watercress** <note>original: *nasturgū*</note>. **Camel grass** <note>original: *squinum*; from *schoenanthos*</note> is better if it grows by the Euphrates than in Arabia; it is reddish-yellow, many-flowered, purple, thin, and has a rose-like scent. When rubbed by hand, its taste burns and bites the tongue significantly. Its flower is called **schoenanthos** <note>original: *squinoantos*</note>. For *anthos* is the Greek name for "flower". **Thyme** <note>original: *thimum*</note> is so called because its flower yields a [sweet] scent. About this, Virgil says:
> And the fragrant honey smells of thyme.
*Epithymum* <note>original: *epirbimū*</note> is the Greek name for what is called "thyme-flower" in Latin. For "flower" is called *thunon* <note>original: *thunū*</note> in Greek. It is a flower similar to **savory** <note>original: *timbzę*</note>. **Marjoram** <note>original: *sālucus*</note> is what the Latins call **amaracus**. Virgil, referring to its use for Venus, says:
> Where soft marjoram embraces him with flowers and sweet, breathing shade.
This herb is suitable for ointments. Hence the name *amaracus* was derived from a boy of a certain king who, having fallen by chance while carrying ointments, created a new and most pleasant scent from the mixture. The **Hyacinth** <note>original: *jacyntb⁹*</note> is an herb having a purple flower. It took its name from a certain noble boy who was found among purple flowers in the woods, stained [with blood]; the accidental death of the boy gave its name to the herb. It is similar in root and flower to the **bindweed** <note>original: *volui*</note>, and it prevents boys from reaching puberty. The herb **Narcissus** has a name assigned by myth from a certain boy whose limbs changed into this flower, which preserves the name of Narcissus in its title and retains the glory of beauty in the whiteness of its petals. The **Rose** <note>original: *rosa*</note> is named from the appearance of the flower, because it is red with a glowing color. **Lilies** <note>original: *lilia*</note> are herbs of a milky flower; hence they are named as if "milk-lilies" <note>original: *liolia*</note>; for while there is whiteness in the petals, a golden appearance shines from within. The **Violet** <note>original: *viola*</note> received its name because of the power <note>original: *vim*</note> of its scent. There are three kinds: purple, white, and yellow-gold <note>original: *mellinum*</note>. **Acanthus** <note>original: *acbant*</note> is an Egyptian herb, always green, full of thorns, with a flexible twig. In imitation of it, clothing is decorated by art and called "acanthine"; otherwise it is called *acanthis*. **Ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note> is so called because it "adheres" <note>original: *adherat*</note> by crawling up trees. Of which Virgil says: To let the ivy creep among your victor's...

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from Book XVII of Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*. Having previously discussed aromatic trees and balsams, the text now transitions into a detailed list of specific herbs, focusing on their medicinal properties, folklore, and the linguistic origins of their names.</meta>

# XVII 88

**Laurels**. Others say that **ivy** <note>original: *hedera*</note>, called *ephedis* <note>likely referring to a variety of ivy or a similar climbing plant</note>, was provided in abundance as food by the ancients. According to natural philosophers, ivies are indicators of cold. Indeed, it serves as a **remedy against drunkenness** <note>original: *antipharmacon ebrietatem*</note> if one wears a crown made of ivy. The Greeks record that a certain type of **hellebore** <note>original: *elleborum*</note> grows in great quantities around a particular river, and it is named after it by the Greeks. The Romans call this by another name, **veratrum**, because when taken, it restores the **mind to health** <note>original: *mentem in sanitatem*; a reference to the belief that hellebore cured madness</note>. There are two kinds: white and black. Experts say this is the food and nourishment of quails, because by a certain natural temperament of their bodies, they can digest the power of this harmful fodder. For if, by the method of medicine, it is often tempered for the health of the human body to which it seems contrary, how much more does it serve as food by its natural properties when it is converted by a medicinal hand for health?

**Acorus** <note>likely Yellow Flag or Sweet Sedge</note> is found especially in Bithynia; it is so famous for the growth of evil weeds that we name the harmful **aconite** herbs from that place. Indeed, **toxic poisons** <note>original: *toxica venena*</note> are so named because they are squeezed from yew trees <note>original: *taxeis*</note>, especially in Cantabria. **Euphorbium** is so named because its sap sharpens the sight of the eyes. Its power is so great that if it is added to tough meats, it compels them to cook more quickly. It grows in many places, but most abundantly in Mauritania. The herb **laser** <note>the resin of the now-extinct Silphium plant</note> grows on Mount Oscobagi, where the river Ganges rises. Its sap was first called *lasir* because it flows in the manner of **milk** <note>original: *lactis*</note>. Then, through common usage, it was named *laser*. This is also called **Cyrenaic opium** by some because it also grows in Cyrene. **Aloe** is an herb of very bitter juice. **Panax** <note>All-heal</note> is an herb of fragrant scent, similar to the stalk of a giant fennel. From it flows a sap called **opopanax**, which is saffron-colored and fatty, heavy in odor and very bitter. **Galbanum** is a type of white pigment growing on Mount Amanus in Syria; otherwise, it is the sap of the giant fennel. **Dicte** is a mountain in Crete from which the herb **dittany** <note>original: *dictamnum*</note> took its name. It is this herb that Virgil describes a wounded doe seeking through the woods. For dittany is of such power that it expels iron from the body and shakes out arrows; hence, wild beasts, when struck by arrows, eat it to eject the shafts sticking in their bodies. Some of the Latins call this **Mars' pennyroyal** <note>original: *polegium martis*</note>, because it shakes out the weapons of war.

**Mandrake** <note>original: *mandragora*</note> is so named because it has sweet-smelling apples <note>original: *mala*</note> the size of "Marian apples" <note>likely a type of quince or citron</note>; hence the Latins also call it the **earth-apple**. Poets call it **human-shaped** <note>original: *anthropomorphos*</note> because it has a root that shows the likeness of a human form. For in Greek, *anthropos* means "human" in Latin. Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink to those whose bodies are to be cut in surgery, so that they may sleep and not feel the pain. There are two species of this: the **female**, with leaves like lettuce, producing apples similar to plums; and the **male**, with leaves like a beet.

**Poppy** <note>original: *papaver*</note> is a sleep-inducing herb. Concerning it, Virgil says: "Poppies steeped in **Lethean sleep**" <note>referring to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>. For it brings sleep to the weary. One kind is the common sort; another is the wild sort, from which flows the sap they call **opium**. **Colocynth** is a wild gourd and is exceedingly bitter; it spreads its runners along the ground just like a gourd. It is called colocynth because it has round fruit and leaves like the common cucumber. **Centaury** is what the Greeks call it because it is said to have been discovered by **Chiron the Centaur**. It is also called *limnisios* because it grows in damp places. It is also called **gall of the earth** <note>original: *fel terrae*</note> because of its bitterness.

<column-break/>

**Licorice** <note>original: *glyciriza*</note> is so named in Greek because it has a **sweet root**; for the Greeks call "sweet" *glykys* <note>original: *γλυκύ*</note>. It is also called *adipsos* <note>thirst-quencher</note> because it settles thirst for those who are thirsty. **Dragon-wort** <note>original: *dracontea*</note> is so named because its stalk is variegated in the manner of a snake <note>original: *colubri*</note>, and it imitates the likeness of a dragon; or because vipers fear this herb. **Celandine** <note>original: *chelidonia*</note> is so named either because it is seen to break forth at the arrival of **swallows** <note>original: *hirundinum*</note>, or because it is said that if the eyes of swallow chicks are taken away, their mothers heal them using this herb.

**Heliotrope** received its name first because it blooms at the summer solstice, or because its leaves turn around following the movements of the sun. For this reason, it is called the **sun-follower** <note>original: *solsequia*</note> by the Latins. For it opens its flowers when the sun rises and likewise closes them late when the sun has set. This is the same herb that the Latins call the **wild nightmare** <note>original: *incubum silvaticum*</note>. It is also called **wart-wort** <note>original: *verrucaria*</note> because it extinguishes warts when drunk with water or applied as a poultice. **Cinquefoil** <note>original: *pentaphilon*</note> is named from the number of its leaves; for the Latins also call it **five-leaf**. It is an herb so clean that it was accustomed to be used by the Pagans for purification and in temples.

**Hyssop** is an herb suitable for purging the lungs. Whence also in the Old Testament, the blood of the lamb was sprinkled with bundles of hyssop by those who wished to be cleansed. It grows clinging to rocks with its roots. **Rhubarb** <note>original: *reubarbarum*</note>: whether it be called *reuponticum* (that which is gathered around the Pontic Sea) or *reubarbarum* (that which is across the Danube in barbarian soil). *Reu* is the word for "root." Thus, *reubarbarum* is like "barbarian root," and *reuponticum* is like "Pontic root."

**Henbane** <note>original: *hyosciamos*</note> is called by the Greeks, but in Latin it is called the **cup-herb** <note>original: *herba calicularis*</note> because its small cups grow in the shape of chalices <note>original: *cantarorum*</note>, like those of a pomegranate, which have serrated mouths containing seeds within similar to the poppy. This herb is called **insane** because its use is dangerous. Indeed, if it is drunk or eaten, it causes madness or a heavy, dream-filled sleep. The common people call it *milimindrum* because it induces an alienation of the mind.

**Saxifrage** is so named because its seed breaks and crushes **stones** <note>original: *petras/saxa*</note> in the bladder. **Gentian** took its name, as physicians record, from its discoverer <note>King Gentius of Illyria</note>; it has roots similar to birthwort. It grows at the foot of the Alps in Galatia and elsewhere. **Savory** <note>original: *satureia*</note> is hot and specifically "ignited." Whence its name is believed to be given because it provokes one to lust <note>original: *venerem*</note>. **Satyrion** is named from the satyrs because of the fire of lust; the common people call it *stincum*, for it arouses sexual desire. It is also called **orchis** because its root is in the shape of **testicles**, which the Greeks call *orcheis* <note>original: *ὄρχεις*</note>. It is also called *leporina* <note>rabbit-herb</note> because it sends out a soft stalk.

**Nettle** <note>original: *urtica*</note> is so named because its touch **burns** <note>original: *adurat*</note> the body. It is indeed of an entirely fiery nature and stings by touch; whence it also causes itching. It is very useful for staunching blood. **Mugwort** <note>original: *artemisia*</note> was an herb consecrated to **Diana** <note>Artemis</note> by the Pagans, whence it was named; for in Greek, Diana is called Artemis. It is suitable for physicians, and when taken in a drink, it takes away pain of the heart. **Lamineos** is the name of an herb in Greek because it has the scent of Marian apples and is short and close to the ground. **Lamidrios** is named by the Greeks because it is short, spread along the ground, and small with very tiny leaves. **Paeon** was a certain physician after whom the **peony** herb is said to have been discovered, as Homer says. Some call this *glesis* because it is of sweet flavor, or *penterobina* from the number of its grains, or as others say, *dactylofam* from...

### Book XVII

...resembling fingers. It grows in the forests. **Bugloss** <note>original: *buglossos*</note> is named by the Greeks because its very rough leaves are like a bull's tongue <note>original: *lingue bouis*</note>. It is remembered by the ancients that this herb, when steeped in wine, is wonderful for nourishing wisdom. It is said to provide joy and cheerfulness; it is also consumed for its fragrance. **Lamb’s Tongue** <note>original: *arnoglossos*; likely Plantain</note> is what the Romans call *plantago*, because its sole <note>original: *planta*; referring to the sole of the foot</note> quickly clings to the earth. Many eat this for its fragrance. **Wild Thyme** <note>original: *erpillos*</note>, which we call *serpillus*, is named because its roots creep far <note>original: *serpiant*</note>. This is also called the **Mother’s Breath** <note>original: *matris animola*</note>, because it moves the menses. **Birthwort** <note>original: *aristolocia*</note> is so named because it is best for women in childbirth. For if it is suspended after birth, it purges the womb <note>original: *matricē*</note> through the benefit of its vapor. There are two kinds of this herb: one is called **Round Birthwort** because it has a round root; the other is **Long Birthwort**, because it has a long root with longer branches and leaves. They also call this **Finger-herb** <note>original: *dactylin*</note> because its root is the thickness of a finger and long. **Groundsel** <note>original: *erigonon*</note> is named by the Greeks because it grows old early in the spring. Hence the Latins call this herb *senerionem* <note>from *senex*, meaning old man, due to its white, downy seed heads</note>. It grows on stone walls. **Fleawort** <note>original: *psillios*</note> is named because its seed is like a flea <note>original: *pulicis*</note>. Hence the Latins call it the **flea-herb**. **Vervain** <note>original: *berabotane*</note> received this name from the Greeks because it was found suitable by the pagans for remedies, bandages for men, and for the purifications performed by priests. Hence the high priests used to call it *sagmen* <note>meaning sacred grass or foliage</note>, as if it were a "consecration" <note>original: *sancimen*</note>. This is also **verbena**, because it is "pure" <note>original: *pura*</note>. It benefits those with fevers if drunk. **Halium** is a very rough and thorny herb, stinging and clinging, wounding anyone who approaches it and seizing them with a hooked tooth. **Soapwort** <note>original: *strutios*</note>, which some call the **wool-herb**, because many wash wool with it. It grows in cultivated places. **Bedbug-herb** <note>original: *limicia*</note> is named for its similarity to a bedbug <note>original: *cimicis*</note>. Hence the Greeks called it *corion* <note>Coriander</note>. It grows in rough and uncultivated places. **Horehound** <note>original: *marubiū*</note>, which the Greeks call *prassium*, is named for its bitterness. It grows in fields. **Pennyroyal** <note>original: *pollegiū*</note> is more precious than pepper among the Indians. It has an emetic power <note>original: *virtutē emanticā*; it induces vomiting</note>; it warms and draws out; it thins, purges, and aids digestion. **Wormwood** <note>original: *absinthiū*</note> is a Greek name, which is likely because it grows in the region of Pontus; hence it is called **Pontic Wormwood**. **Comfrey** <note>original: *simpatur*, for *symphytum*</note> is named in Greek because it has such power in its root that pieces of meat sprinkled with it in a cooking pot will congeal together. **Polypody** <note>original: *polipodion*; a type of fern</note> is a herb whose root is shaggy and hairy, like an octopus <note>original: *polipus*</note>; its name is derived from this. It grows in the thin crevices of rocks or near oaks. **Felwort** <note>original: *polios*</note> is the Greek name; the Latins call it the **all-disease herb** <note>original: *omnimorbia*</note> because it assists in many diseases. It grows on mountains and in hard places; from one root it sends out many thin fibers full of seeds, having at the top certain whitening clusters. It has a heavy and somewhat sweet smell; its juice boiled in water heals those struck by snakes. Scattered in a house or burned, it puts all snakes to flight. **Scammony** <note>original: *scamonea*</note>, which the Latins call **sharp-herb** <note>original: *acridium*</note>, is an herb full of juice, which is collected from below the hollowed-out root. Finally, they dig a round cavity in the earth, and then the juice is caught in shells or nut leaves and dried and taken away. It often comes from Mysia in Asia. A contrary and false version comes from Syria and Judea. **Wild Carrot** <note>original: *daucos*</note> is a herb with leaves like fennel and a stalk two palms high. **Spurge** <note>original: *litocacia*</note> is so named because it quickly

<column-break/>

clears out the belly; the common people call it **the corruptor** <note>original: *corrupticicia*</note>. **Burdock** <note>original: *lapapa*</note> is named because it has a huge stem spread across the ground. This herb is called **the man-lover** <note>original: *philantropus*</note> by the Greeks because it clings to people's clothes due to its roughness. It grows near walls. **Maidenhair** <note>original: *capillum veneris*</note> is so named either because it restores hair after mange <note>original: *alopiciā*</note>, or because it restrains hair loss, or because it has smooth black twigs with a shine, like hair. It grows in watery places. **Madder** <note>original: *rubia*</note> is so named because its root is red <note>original: *rubra*</note>; hence it also provides dye for wool. **Alkanet** <note>original: *ancusa*</note> has a root that, when crushed, stains the fingers. It is indeed of a blood-red color; hence it is also used by painters to make purple. **Chameleon** <note>original: *cameleon*</note>, which is called *vascarago* in Latin because it produces a face <note>original: *vultū*</note> in which birds get stuck when they descend of their own will for food. **Hemlock** <note>original: *cicuta*</note>, because it has hidden knee-like joints in its stalk like a reed; thus a blind ditch that is hidden is called a *cicuta*. Given as a drink, it kills. **Socrates** drank this in prison and died. **Persius** says: "The draft that takes away the dire hemlock." While this is poison to humans, it makes goats fat. **Trefoil** <note>original: *trifoliū*; Clover</note> is what the Greeks call *trifillū*, because it has triple leaves on each stem. **Mullein** <note>original: *flomos*</note> is what the Latins call the **lamp-herb**, because it serves as wicks for lamps <note>original: *lychinia*</note>. It is also called **light-bearer** <note>original: *lucubros*</note> because it provides light in the shadows. **Pellitory** <note>original: *piretron*</note> is named in Greek because it has a burning and sharp root. **Marshmallow** <note>original: *altea*</note> is a wild mallow; it has the name *altea* because it rises high <note>original: *altū*</note>, and it is "viscous" because it is sticky <note>original: *glutinosa*</note>. **Oregano** <note>original: *origanū*</note>, which is interpreted as **coloring** in Latin, because it colors wine when infused. This herb is hot; it also draws out phlegm and is passed in urine. **Sun-spurge** <note>original: *litimallū/titimallū*</note> took its name because it turns the foliage of its leaves to the rays of the sun. For the Greeks call the sun *titan* and hair *mallon*; from this, the name *titimallū* was composed. There are seven species of this growing in different places. **Nightshade** <note>original: *strignos*</note>, which is called the **health-giving herb** in Latin because it mitigates headaches and the burning of the stomach. It is also called **wolf-grape** <note>original: *vua lupina*</note> because of its seed, which is like a grape. **Knotgrass** <note>original: *pilogonos*</note> is what the Latins call **blood-herb**, because put into the nostrils it moves the blood. **Ambrosia**, which the Latins call **wild parsley**, about which **Virgil** says: "And the ambrosias breathed a divine scent from her head." **Bee-herb** <note>original: *apiago*; likely lemon balm</note> is named because bees especially seek its flowers. **Rosemary** <note>original: *rosmarinum*</note> is what the Latins call the **health-giving herb** from its effect; its leaves are like fennel and rough, spread on the ground in a circle. **Wild Mint** <note>original: *menta agrestis*</note>, which the Greeks call *calaminti*, our common people have called *nepera*; it is of greater power and intense in heat. **Groundsel** <note>original: *senicularis*</note> herb is spread out to repel the violence of scorpions. **Sword-lily** <note>original: *gladiolus*</note> is so named because its leaves are like swords, with a stalk a cubit long and purple flowers. **Agaric** <note>original: *agaricū*; a tree fungus</note> is a root of white strength. **Asphodel** <note>original: *assodilos*</note>, which the Latins call *alburium* from its white color. **Squill** <note>original: *scilla*</note> is so named because it is harmful; about which the superstition of the pagans says that if it is hung whole at the threshold, it puts all evils to flight. **Juniper** <note>original: *ianiperora*</note> is so named by the Greeks because it clings to trees and has the smell of pine; the Latins call it **cucumber-herb** because its smell partly resembles a cucumber. **Stavesacre** <note>original: *stafisagria*</note>, that is, the herb of the fingers; its seed, when chewed, draws out excessive humor from the head; it is bitter in taste and grows in pleasant places. **Spleenwort** <note>original: *splenos*</note> is named because...

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from Book XVII of Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies. # XVII

...cures the spleen <note>original: *splenē*</note>. It is also called **Scolopendrios** <note>Hart’s-tongue fern</note> because its leaves are similar to the centipede <note>original: *scolopendro*</note> animal. It grows on damp rocks. It has neither a stem, nor a flower, nor a seed. Its leaves are green on the surface, but reddish and speckled <note>original: *dannosa*</note> underneath; it cures the spleen. **Bindweed** <note>original: *Voluus*</note> is so named because its root is twisting <note>original: *volubilis*</note> and round. **French Lavender** <note>original: *Stroecas*</note> grows in the Stoechades islands, from which it takes its name. **Cyclamen** <note>original: *Cyclaminos*</note> is named in Greek after a certain man called Cyclos who first discovered the power of this herb; or perhaps because it has a round root—for the Greeks call a circle *cyclon*. Its root or juice, if mixed with wine, makes one a drunkard. It grows in wooded and wild places. **White Bryony** <note>original: *Ampelos leuce* or *brionia*</note>, which the Latins call the *white vine*, is named either for the quality of its color or because its root, when crushed and rubbed on the body, makes the skin tenderer and whiter. Indeed, the juice of its berries restores milk to dry breasts. **Black Bryony** <note>original: *Ampelosmelena*</note>—that is, the *black vine*—is the same as the wild vine <note>original: *labrusca*</note>. Its leaves are like ivy in all respects, but larger than those of the white vine. It likewise has berries which turn black when ripe, from which it takes its name. **Clematis** <note>original: *Viticella*</note> is an herb named by the Latins because, like a vine <note>original: *vitis*</note>, it catches hold of whatever it first encounters. **Climbers** <note>original: *Cozimbis*</note> are what we call rings. **Ox-eye** <note>original: *Buptalmon*</note> has a saffron-colored flower resembling an eye, from which it received its name from the Greeks. It has a soft stem and leaves similar to coriander. It grows near city walls. **Mullein** <note>original: *Flomos*</note>, which the Latins call *verbascum*, has two types: one is the male, with whiter and narrower leaves; the other is the female, with broader and darker leaves. **Giant Fennel** <note>original: *Ferula*</note> is named from its pith <note>original: *medulla*</note>. For Varro records that the pith of the fennel is what the Greeks call *oypodelon*. Some call it *ferula* from "striking" <note>original: *feriendo*</note>, because boys and girls are often beaten with it. Its juice is galbanum. **Papyrus** <note>original: *Papyr*</note> is so named because it is suited for fire and wicks; for the Greeks call fire *pyron*. **Rush** <note>original: *Juncus*</note> is named because it is held together by joined roots <note>original: *iunctis radicibus*</note>. **Bulrush** <note>original: *Scyrpus*</note>, from which mats <note>original: *legeres*</note> are woven, is without nodes. Concerning this, Ennius says: "They seek a knot in a bulrush as they are wont to say." And in the proverb: "He who is an enemy seeks a knot even in a bulrush" <note>This proverb refers to looking for difficulties or flaws where none exist, as the bulrush is naturally smooth.</note>. **Orchil** <note>original: *Fucus*</note> is a type of herb from which clothing is dyed; it is so named because it "counterfeits" <note>original: *mentitur*</note> a foreign color. Hence Virgil also says: "The wool learned to counterfeit colors." **Seaweed** <note>original: *Alga*</note> grows in standing waters. It takes its name from the coldness <note>original: *algore*</note> of the water, or because it "binds" <note>original: *alliget*</note> the feet because it is thick, with its leaves partly rising above the water. **Sedge** <note>original: *Ulva*</note> and **Cattail** <note>original: *typ*</note> are herbs that grow around springs, marshes, and pools. From these, *ulva*—that is, soft algae and in a certain way called a "fungus"—is named from moisture <note>original: *uligine*</note>. But the *typus* is that which swells up <note>original: *inflat*</note> from the waters. From this, the swelling of ambitious and self-pleasing men is also called "pride" <note>original: *typus*; likely referring to the Greek *tuphos*, meaning smoke or vanity</note>. **Galingale** <note>original: *Larir*</note> is a sharp and very hard herb similar to esparto. Concerning it, Virgil says: "And fed on sharp sedge." **Esparto** <note>original: *Spartus*</note> is a twiggy, leafless shrub named for its roughness <note>original: *asperitate*</note>. For the coils of rope made from it are rough. **Grass** <note>original: *Gramen*</note> is named rather for its location <note>original: *situ*</note> because it belongs to very many fields <note>original: *agrorum*</note>. Thus the Greeks called it "of the field" <note>original: *agreste*</note>. However, every herb is called *gramen* from the fact that it "germinates" <note>original: *germinetur*</note>, just as the "strength" <note>original: *robur*</note> of all wood is its bark, and it is a "species" from being very firm. **Fern** <note>original: *Filix*</note> is named for the singularity of its leaf. Indeed, from a single twig a cubit in height, a single feathery leaf is produced, an intricate thing like a wing.

<column-break/>

**Oat** <note>original: *Auena*</note> spelled with a "u" is an herb; but with a "b" <note>original: *abena*</note> it is the place where a horse is held <note>reins</note>. The oat is a seed-bearing herb similar to a crop. Virgil says: "For a crop of flax burns the field, and a crop of oats burns it." And sometimes it is named for its stalk <note>original: *chalamo*</note>. **Darnel** <note>original: *Ciçania*</note> is what poets always call "tares" <note>original: *loliū*</note>, because it is useless and prolific. **Hay** <note>original: *Fenū*</note> is so named because the flame <note>original: *flamma*</note> is nourished by it; for *for* means flame. Hay, which is straw <note>original: *palea*</note>, should be written with only an "e" <note>original: *fenum*</note>; profit <note>usury</note>, which is *foenum*, is written with an "o" and "e". We call a bundle of hay a **handful** <note>original: *manipulū*</note>. And it is called a handful because it "fills the hand" <note>original: *manum impleat*</note>.

### On Vegetables Chapter X.

A **Garden** <note>original: *Hortus*</note> is so named because something is always "rising" <note>original: *oriatur*</note> there. For while other land produces something only once a year, a garden is never without fruit. A **Vegetable** <note>original: *Olus*</note> is named from "nourishing" <note>original: *alendo*</note>, because humans were first nourished by vegetables before they ate grains and meat. For they lived only on the fruits of trees and vegetables, just as animals live on herbs. The **Stalk** <note>original: *Caulis*</note> is generally the middle shoot of vegetables, which is commonly called a **thyrsus** <note>original: *tyrsus*</note>, because it climbs upward from the earth. From this is derived the specific name for a certain kind of vegetable called "cabbage" <note>original: *caulis*</note>, because its shoot grows together—that is, increases—more than other vegetables. It is, however, a general name. For every shoot is called a *caulis*. There are five kinds of cabbage: Cuman, Pompeian, Arcinian, Sabellian, and Brucian. **Foliage** <note>original: *Lima*</note> is spoken of as if it were hair <note>original: *coma*</note>. It is the top of vegetables or trees in which the natural vigor is active. **Mallow** <note>original: *Malua*</note> is a genus of garden herb which is partly named from a Greek word meaning "to soften" <note>original: *apo tou malakizesthai*</note>, because it has the nature of softening and loosening the bowels. If someone pricks themselves with a branch of myrtle oil, the bees are said to refuse to sting them. Its leaves, crushed in oil and applied, are believed to take away the numbness from scorpion stings. **Parsnip** <note>original: *Pastinaca*</note> is so named because its root is an excellent "food" <note>original: *pastus*</note> for man. For it is pleasant in scent and delightful as food. The **Turnip** <note>original: *Rapa*</note> is named from "seizing" <note>original: *rapiendo*</note>—that is, grasping. It has a larger root than the rape <note>original: *nape*</note>, a sweeter flavor, and a thinner leaf. The **Rape** <note>original: *Napus*</note> is named from its similarity to the turnip, except that it has broader leaves and is sharper in the taste of its root. The relationship of the name in both is almost common, because each seed is changed into the other in turn. For the turnip in another soil, as Emilianus says, is changed into the rape over two years; in another soil, however, the rape passes into the turnip. **Kohlrabi** <note>original: *Napocaulis*</note> has a name composed of two vegetables, because while it is similar to the rape in flavor, it does not grow in a root but rises in a stalk like a cabbage. **Mustard** <note>original: *Sinapis*</note> is so named because its leaves are similar to the rape <note>original: *napis*</note>. As authors say, this has a hot quality and purges, though it restricts urine. Taken raw in food, it is contrary to the stomach; but cooked as a vegetable, it helps the stomach. Its seed, crushed with vinegar, cures the wounds of serpents. What the Greeks call **Radish** <note>original: *Raphanum*</note>, we call "the root" <note>original: *radicem*</note>, because it pushes entirely downward while other vegetables leap forth more at the top. If anyone stains their hands with its macerated seed, they may handle serpents with impunity. Indeed, even ivory becomes white from its root. In food, it also resists poison. For against poisons, roots, nuts, lupins, citrons, celery, and rue are beneficial—but against a future poison, not against one already taken. Hence, among the ancients, these were usually placed on the table before other feasts. **Lettuce** <note>original: *Lactuca*</note> is named...

# Book XVII

...because it overflows with an abundance of milk <note>original: *abundantia lactis*</note>. Or perhaps because it fills nursing women with milk. In men, however, it restrains the urges of lust. **Wild lettuce** is what we call **sarralia** <note>Sow-thistle</note>, for the reason that its back is shaped like a saw <note>original: *serrae*</note>. **Endive** <note>original: *Intubus*</note> is a Greek name; it is called *intubus* because it is full of strings <note>original: *intus sit tosus*</note> inside. **Lepa** <note>likely a variant of *Lappa*, burdock</note> is so called because it is nothing other than a head. **Shallots** <note>original: *Ascalonia*</note> are named after one of the cities of Palestine called Ascalon, from where they were first brought. **Garlic** <note>original: *Allium*</note> is named because it smells <note>original: *oleat*</note>. **Great Garlic** <note>original: *Ulpicum*</note> is named because it has a high odor. They say **Kidney beans** <note>original: *Faselos*</note> are named after the Greek island of Pharsalus, where Mount Olympus is not far away. **Leeks** <note>original: *Porrum*</note> are of two types: headed and clipped. The headed type is larger and the clipped type is very small. **Beet** <note>original: *Beta*</note> among us is a type of vegetable, but among the Greeks, it is a letter. **Blite** <note>original: *Blitum*</note> is a type of vegetable with a tasteless flavor, like a "vile beet." **Cucumbers** <note>original: *Lucumeres*</note> are so named because they are sometimes bitter; they are said to be born sweet if their seeds are soaked in honeyed milk. **Gourd** <note>original: *Cucurbita*</note>, **Pumpkin** <note>original: *Pepo*</note>, **Honey-melon** <note>original: *Melipepo*</note>, and **Basil** <note>original: *Ocimum*</note> are Greek names and their Latin origins are uncertain. **Orach** <note>original: *Arriplex*</note> is a soft vegetable. **Cabbage** <note>original: *Brassica*</note>, **Alexanders** <note>original: *Olisatrum*</note>, and **Watercress** <note>original: *Nasturtium*</note> are so named because its sharpness "twists the nose" <note>original: *nasum torqueat*</note>. **Fungi** <note>Mushrooms</note> are named because they catch fire when dried; for they are "of fire," which is why they are commonly called "food" <note>original: *esca*</note>, because they are tinder and nourishment for fire. Others say they are called fungi because some of their kind are deadly, hence "the deceased" <note>original: *defuncti*</note>. **Truffles** <note>original: *Tubera*</note> are a "swelling of the earth" <note>original: *tumor terre*</note>, and that cause gave them their name. **Bindweeds** <note>original: *Volui*</note> are named because they are twisting and round. **Asparagus** is named because it is thorny and rough <note>original: *aspera*</note>, as is the shrub from which it grows. **Capers** <note>original: *Lapparis*</note> seem to have taken their name from the Greeks because they have round little heads at the tips of their seeds. **Armozarea**, which is **charlock** <note>original: *lapsana*</note>, **Wild Radish** <note>original: *Lapistrum*</note>, and **Sorrel** <note>original: *Lapatia*</note>: these, when eaten, comfort the stomach and repress lust. **Thistle** <note>original: *Carduus*</note> is a type of thorny herb. Its nature is biting, somewhat harsh, and soft. Its juice, being cold and indigestible, cures hair loss <note>original: *alopicias*</note>. **Rocket** <note>original: *Eruca*</note> is as if it were *uruca*, because it has a "burning" <note>original: *ignita*</note> quality; and when eaten frequently, it stirs the fire of lust. There are two species: one cultivated and the other wild, which is of a sharper quality, yet both stir the practice of lust.

### On Fragrant Vegetables, Chapter XI.

**Celery** <note>original: *Apium*</note> is named because the crown <note>original: *apex*</note>—that is, the head—of ancient conquerors was crowned with it. Hercules was the first to wrap this herb around his head. For at times people preferred the poplar on their heads, at times the olive, and at times celery. Its roots fight effectively against poisonous traps. To this genus belong **Parsley** <note>original: *petrosilenon*</note>, **Horse-parsley** <note>original: *iposilenon*</note>, and **Marsh-parsley** <note>original: *oleosilenon*</note>. **Parsley** is so named because it is similar to celery and grows among rocks <note>original: *petris*</note> and steep mountains; we can call it "rock-celery" <note>original: *petrapium*</note>. In Greek, *silenon* means celery. This is the highest and most approved Macedonian variety, sweet in taste and aromatic in smell. **Horse-parsley** is so called because it is hard and harsh. **Marsh-parsley** is so named because it is softer, with a tender leaf and stalk. **Fennel** <note>original: *Fenuculum*</note> is what the Latins call it because the juice of its stalks or roots sharpens the sight <note>original: *acuat visum*</note>; its power is said to be such that snakes shed their yearly old age by tasting it. The Greeks call this vegetable **marathron**. **Lovage** <note>original: *Ligusticum*</note> took its name from a region, for it grows mostly in Liguria, with an aromatic smell

<column-break/>

and a sharp taste. The Greeks say **aneson**, just as the Latins say **anise** <note>original: *anesum*</note>; it is an herb known to all, burning very sharply. **Coriander** <note>OCR: *Loridandrū*</note> is taken from a Greek name, which they call *corion*. Its seed, given in sweet wine, makes people more prone to lust; if you give it beyond measure, it nourishes madness. It is also recorded that grey hair can be dyed with coriander. **Rue** <note>original: *Ruta*</note> is so named because it is very hot. One variety is wild and sharper in its power, but both are proven to be extremely hot. Weasels teach us that this herb resists poisons; when they fight with a snake, they arm themselves by eating it. **Elecampane** <note>original: *Inula*</note>, which country folk call *ala*, has an aromatic root with a supreme scent and a gentle sharpness. **Mint** is a type of fragrant herb; there are six kinds of it.

### Here begins the eighteenth book.
### On Wars, Chapter I.

**Ninus**, the king of the Assyrians, was the first to bring about wars. For he, by no means content with his own borders, broke the bond of human society and began to lead armies, to devastate the lands of others, and to either slaughter or subjugate free peoples. He subdued all of Asia as far as the borders of Libya into a new servitude. From this point on, the world was eager to rush into mutual bloodshed through reciprocal slaughter. There are, however, four kinds of wars: that is, **just**, **unjust**, **civil**, and **more than civil**. A **just war** is one that is waged by prior declaration to recover property or for the sake of repelling enemies. An **unjust war** is one that is entered into out of madness, not out of lawful reason. Concerning this, Cicero says in *The Republic*: "Those wars are unjust which are undertaken without cause. For no just war can be waged except for the sake of avenging oneself or repelling enemies." And this same Tully <note>Cicero</note> added a few lines later: "No war is considered just unless it has been announced, unless it has been declared, and unless it is for the recovery of property." A **civil war** is a rebellion or an incited riot that has arisen among citizens, such as that between Sulla and Marius, who waged civil war against each other within one nation. A **more than civil war** <note>original: *plus quam civile*</note> is where not only citizens struggle, but also kinsmen, such as occurred between Caesar and Pompey, when a son-in-law and a father-in-law fought each other. Indeed, in this fight, brother fought with brother, and father carried arms against son. Lucan says: "The progeny of a brother fell by a brother's hands." Also: "To whom should the severed neck of a parent fall?" Wars are thus called internal, external, servile <note>slave revolts</note>, social <note>allied</note>, and piratical. For **piratical wars** are those waged by scattered bands of thieves across the seas with light and swift pirate ships <note>original: *myoparonibus*</note>, devastating not only the passage of ships but also islands and provinces. Gnaeus Pompey was the first to crush and overcome them with miraculous speed after the great devastation they had long carried out on land and sea. Just as that which is conducted against enemies is called a "war," so that which is stirred up by civil rebellion is called a "tumult." For **sedition** <note>original: *seditio*</note> is a dissension of citizens, so named because some go "to one side" <note>original: *seorsum*</note> and others to another. Others consider the dissension of minds to be called sedition, which the Greeks call *diastasin* <note>original: *diastasin* - a standing apart</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the agricultural discussion in Book XVII into the opening chapters of Book XVIII, which focuses on war, triumphs, and military equipment. The text continues Isidore of Seville's method of using etymology to explain the nature of human institutions.</meta>

they call it. Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator</note> teaches how these two differ. He says there can be a war <note>original: *bellum*</note> without a "tumult," but a tumult cannot exist without a war. For what is a **tumult** <note>original: *tumultus*</note> other than a disturbance so great that a greater fear arises? Thus, it is called a "tumult" as if it were a "great fear" <note>original: *timor multus*</note>. A tumult is more serious than a war. For in war, exemptions from service are valid, but in a tumult, they are not. Furthermore, "war" (*bellum*), "fight" (*pugna*), and "battle" (*praelium*) differ. For **war** is the name of the whole conflict, such as the Punic War. The parts of this war are **fights**, such as the one at Cannae. Again, in a single fight, there are many **battles**. For one thing happens on the wings, another in the center, and another at the rear of the line. Therefore, war is the whole, a "fight" refers to a single event, and a "battle" is a part of a fight. War was previously called **duellum**, because there are two sides fighting; or because it makes one the victor and the other the vanquished. Later, the letter *d* was removed and the *v* changed to *b*, and it was called *bellum*. Others believe it is called *bellum* through antiphrasis <note>a figure of speech where a word is used to mean its opposite</note> because it is something horrid; hence the phrase: "Wars, horrid wars." In truth, war is the worst of things. **Battles** <note>original: *praelia*</note> are named from "pressing" <note>original: *premendo*</note> the enemy against enemy. From this, the wooden beams used to press grapes are also called *praelia*. A **fight** <note>original: *pugna*</note> is so called because in the beginning, men used to contend in war with their fists <note>original: *pugnis*</note>; or because war first began with fists. Thus, a fight can sometimes be between two people even without weapons. Four things occur in war: the fight, the flight, the victory, and the peace. The word for **peace** <note>original: *pax*</note> seems to be taken from "pact" <note>original: *pactum*</note>. Afterward, however, it is accepted through a treaty; first, a **league** <note>original: *foedus*</note> is entered into. A league is a peace made between combatants; it is named either from "faith" <note>original: *fides*</note> or from the *fetiales*—that is, the priests. For treaties were made through them, just as they were for secular wars. Others think leagues are named after a sow <note>original: *porca*</note> that was struck and cruelly killed, whose death would overshadow anyone who withdrew from the peace. Virgil says: "And having slain a sow, they joined in treaties." Parts of a treaty are **truces** <note>original: *induciae*</note>. They are called truces as if they were "leisure for days" <note>original: *in dies otia*</note>.

### On Triumphs, Chapter 2

Every kingdom of this world is sought through wars and expanded by victories. **Victory** is so named because it is obtained by force <note>original: *vis*</note>, that is, by valor <note>original: *virtus*</note>. For this is the law of nations: to repel force with force. For a victory sought through trickery is shameful. A certain victory is either the killing of the enemy, the plundering, or both. A victory is not joyful if it is achieved with immense loss. And it is well that Sallust <note>Roman historian</note> praises leaders who brought home a victory with a bloodless army. **Pompa** <note>procession</note> is a Greek name meaning "to be shown publicly" <note>original: *pompeuein*</note>. Victory precedes the procession, because the first vow of victory is for a good contest. A **trophy** <note>original: *tropaeum*</note> is named from "turning" <note>original: *trope*</note>, that is, from the turning back and flight of the enemy. For a trophy was earned by the one who put the enemy to flight, but a **triumph** <note>original: *triumphus*</note> by the one who killed them. Triumph is named from "exultation" <note>original: *thriambeuein*</note>. For a triumph is owed to a full victory, and a trophy to a partial one, because the commander has not yet secured a full victory; he did not hold the field but merely put the army to flight. Writers, however, confuse these names. But Suetonius Tranquillus says it is more likely called a "triumph" in Latin because he who entered the city in triumph was honored by a threefold judgment <note>original: *tripartito iudicio*</note>. For first, the army was accustomed to judge whether the triumph should be granted to the leader; second, the Senate; third, the People. It was the custom among the Romans that those triumphing would be carried in four-horse chariots <note>original: *quadrigis*</note>

<column-break/>

because the praetors and leaders used to enter wars in this manner. Whoever had conquered in a conflict was crowned with a golden **palm**, because the palm has prickles. But he who had prostrated a fleeing enemy without a conflict was crowned with **laurel**, because this tree is without thorns. For those triumphing wore both a purple and a palm-embroidered toga, and they carried a staff <note>original: *scipio*</note> with a scepter in their hand, in imitation of the victory of Scipio <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus</note>; although a *scipio* is also a staff upon which men lean. From this, that first Cornelius was called Scipio because his blind father walked in the Forum leaning upon him. Moreover, an eagle hung above the staff as a sign that the victory reached toward a kind of heavenly greatness. For this reason, they were also painted with a red color <note>vermilion</note>, as if they were imitating the appearance of divine fire. The fact that they were touched by an executioner <note>a slave who stood behind the general</note> was a sign so that, having been elevated to such a height, they might be reminded of human mediocrity. An army is destroyed in two ways: either by total destruction <note>original: *internitio*</note> or by scattering <note>original: *dispersio*</note>. Sallust says: "The enemies were either crushed or they slipped away." So also Virgil describes both. Destruction: "and overwhelm the sunken ships." Scattering: "drive them and scatter their bodies over the sea." The things taken from enemies are **spoils** (*spolia*), **booty** (*praeda*), **prize-money** (*manubiae*), and **spoils of war** (*exuviae*). Booty is named from the act of plundering (*praedando*). Prize-money is so called because it is "drawn from the hands" (*manibus*) of the enemy. These are also called *exuviae* from "stripping" (*exuendo*), because the enemies are stripped. These are also called "parts" because of an equal division, through a just decision based on the quality of persons and their labor. Furthermore, **spoils** (*spolia*) are named from "cloaks" (*palliis*), as if they were "un-cloaked" (*expallia*), for they are stripped from the conquered.

### On Military Standards, Chapter 3

They are called **signs** <note>standards</note> of war because from them the army receives the signal for fighting, victory, or retreat. For the army of the legions would be warned either by the sound of the trumpet or by a signal. The principal standards are **eagles**, **dragons**, and **spheres**. Eagles are used because that same bird of Jupiter was seen as an omen in arms. For when Jupiter himself set out against the Titans, they say an eagle appeared to him as an omen; he accepted it as a sign of invincible victory and, having taken it under his protection, gave it to the legion as a standard. Thus it happened that thereafter it was committed to the military standards. Lucan mentions this, saying: "Standards with matching eagles, and spears threatening spears." The **dragon** standards were begun by Apollo after the death of the serpent Python. From then on, they began to be carried in war by the Greeks and Romans. Augustus is said to have established the **sphere** <note>original: *pila*</note> as a standard because of the nations subjected to him in the whole world, so that he might better show the shape of the globe. The **banner** <note>original: *vexillum*</note> itself is also a military sign; its name is derived as a diminutive of "sail" (*velum*), as if it were a little sail. Under Romulus, however, the soldiers had bundles of hay for banners. From this, they are also called **maniples** <note>original: *manipuli*</note>. For we call bundles of hay "maniples" because they fill the hand (*manum*). Other various signs exist for the distinguished ranks according to military custom, through which the army is recognized in the confusion of battles.

### On Trumpets, Chapter 4

The **buccina** is that by which a signal is given against the enemy; it is named from the voice, as if it were a "voice-maker" (*vocina*). For the peasants and country folk used the *buccina* for every purpose, calling together...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of military terminology from Book XVIII of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies. The previous page defined the difference between war, fights, and battles; this page moves into the specific instruments and weapons used in conflict, starting with trumpets and moving through swords and spears.</meta>

Book

They used to call them together; this was specifically a signal for country folk. Concerning this, Propertius says: "The **curved trumpet** <note>original: *buccina*</note> compelled the ancients of old to take up arms as cavalry." But the ringing sound is called a *buccina*. The Tyrrhenians <note>Etruscans</note> first invented the **trumpet** <note>original: *tuba*</note>, as Virgil says: "The Tyrrhenian clangor of the trumpet rings out." For they say this was devised by Tyrrhenian pirates; when they were scattered around the seacoasts, they could not easily be called together for any opportunity for plunder by voice or curved trumpet because the wind often made too much noise. From this, it was later applied to military contests and for announcing the signals of war: so that where a herald could not be heard due to the tumult, the sound of the ringing trumpet might reach them. The trumpet is called *tuba* as if it were "to-sa," that is, "hollow" <note>original: *cava*</note>. Likewise, *tuba* is like *tibia* <note>a pipe or flute</note>. Moreover, the ancients distinguished between the *tuba* and the *buccina*. For the sounding *buccina* announced anxiety or preparation for war. Virgil says: "Where the dread *buccina* gave the signal." But the *tuba* indicated the battle itself, as in: "But the trumpet with its terrible sound." Its sound is varied. For sometimes it is played so that they may join battle; sometimes so that they may pursue those who flee; sometimes for the retreat. For it is called a "retreat" <note>original: *receptus*</note> when the army withdraws itself; from this they are said "to sound the signals for retreat." **Bugles** <note>original: *classica*</note> are horns that were made for the purpose of calling people together; they were called *classica* from "calling" <note>original: *calando*, meaning to summon</note>. Regarding these Virgil says: "Now the bugles sound." Among the Amazons, however, the army of women was called not by a trumpet as by kings, but by the queen using a **sistrum** <note>a metallic rattle used in Egyptian and ritual contexts</note>.

### Of Arms, Chapter 5

**Arms** <note>original: *arma*</note> are generally the instruments of all things; from this, the places where they are stored are called **armories** <note>original: *armaria*, also meaning cupboards or closets</note>. Likewise, "arms" and "missiles" <note>original: *tela*</note> refer to all kinds. But **arms** are those things with which we protect ourselves; **missiles** are those things we send out. For arms are twofold: that is, those with which we strike or those with which we are covered. Arms, however, are properly so called because they cover the **shoulders** <note>original: *armos*</note>. For arms are named either from *armos*, that is, the shoulders—as in: "From this side the spear, driven through the shoulders, trembles"—or from the Greek *ares*, which is Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note>.

### Of Swords, Chapter 6

**Sword** <note>original: *gladius*</note> is the general name for the blade <note>original: *ensis*</note> in battle. *Ensis* refers only to the iron; *gladius* refers to the whole thing. Properly, however, it is called a *gladius* because it "divides the throat" <note>original: *gulam dividit*</note>; that is, it cuts the neck. For it was first made for this purpose. For other members are more often cut by axes, but the neck by the sword alone. The **edge** <note>original: *acies*</note> of the sword is named from its sharpness <note>original: *acumine*</note>. The **hilt** <note>original: *capulus*</note> is so called either because it is the "head" <note>original: *caput*</note> of the sword, or because it is "taken" <note>original: *capitur*</note> there so that it may be held. For elsewhere the sharpness of the iron does not allow it. The **point** <note>original: *mucro*</note> is not only of a sword, but the sharp point of any missile; it is named from its length. For the Greeks call "long" *makron*. From this also comes the **machaera**. A *machaera* is a long sword sharp on one side. A **framea**, however, is a sword sharp on both sides, which the common people call a **spatha**. It is called a *framea* because it is made of iron <note>original: *ferrea*</note>. For just as an iron tool <note>original: *ferreamentum*</note> is named, so it is called a *framea*; and hence every sword is a *romphea*. The *spatha* is named from "suffering" <note>original: *passione*</note> in the Greek word, because in Greek "to suffer" is called *pathein*. From this we also say "passion" and "he suffers." Others think the *spatha* is named in Latin because it is "spacious" <note>original: *spaciosa*</note>, that is, broad and wide. From this also comes the shoulder blades <note>original: *spatulae*</note> in cattle. The **semispathium** <note>half-spatha</note> is a sword named from being half the length of a *spatha*; not, as the ignorant commoners say, "without space," while the ar-

<column-break/>

-row <note>original: *sagitta*</note> is swifter. The **dagger** <note>original: *pugio*</note> is named from "stabbing" <note>original: *pungendo*</note> and piercing through. For it is a small sword, sharp on both sides, adhering to the side. The same is also called a *clunabulum* because it is bound to the **haunch** <note>original: *clunem*</note>. The **celidoniacus** sword is a broad iron blade whose point is double and bifurcated, formed in the manner of a swallow's tail; from which it is called *celidoniacus* <note>from the Greek *chelidon*, swallow</note>. The **sica** <note>a curved dagger</note> is named from "cutting" <note>original: *secando*</note>. For it is a short sword used mostly by those who commit robberies among the Italians, from which they are called **assassins** <note>original: *sicarii*</note>. Suetonius Tranquillus, however, says that when the sword of a certain gladiator had been bent during a game, one man ran up to straighten it from its straight edge; and then it was said in a fighting sense: "I will fight with a *sica*." Thence the name *sica* was given. **Axes** <note>original: *secures*</note> are signs which were carried before the consuls, lest they either lose the use of war or, being idle in peace, lose the sight of swords. These the Spaniards, following the usage of the Franks, call *franciscas* <note>Frankish axes</note> by derivation.

### Of Spears, Chapter 7

A **spear** <note>original: *asta/hasta*</note> is a pole with iron; its diminutive makes *astile* <note>shaft</note>. The name *asta*, however, is taken from "skill" <note>original: *astu*</note>; from which also comes "astuteness." The **contus** <note>a long pole or pike</note> has no iron, but is only sharp at the point. Virgil says: "Iron-shod poles and pikes with a sharp point." A *contus* is as if "pointed" <note>original: *conitus*</note>. For it is a sharp roundness. **Trudes** <note>thrusting-poles</note> are shafts with polished iron, which the Greeks call *aplustria*. They are called *trudes* from the fact that they "thrust" <note>original: *trudunt*</note> and "push down." Virgil: "Iron-shod poles." **Hunting spears** <note>original: *venabula*</note> are so named as if they were "handy for the hunt" <note>original: *venatui habilia*</note>. They "receive" <note>original: *excipiant*</note> what is coming, as if they were "receivable." For they receive boars, and they wait for and catch lions; they even enter bears if the hand is firm. A **lance** <note>original: *lancea*</note> is a spear having a strap <note>original: *amentum*</note> in the middle. It is called a *lancea* because it vibrates balanced with an "equal scale" <note>original: *equa lance*</note>, that is, with an equal strap. The **strap** <note>original: *amentum*</note> is the bond of the javelin shafts which is fitted to the middle of the spears. And from this, *amentum*, because it binds the middle of the spear so that they may hurl it. A **club** <note>original: *claua*</note> is like that which belonged to Hercules; it is named because it is bound together with iron nails <note>original: *clauis*</note>. And it is made a cubit and a half in length. This is also the *cateia* <note>a throwing club</note> which Boethius calls a *caia*. For it is a type of Gallic missile made of the most flexible material; which, when thrown, does not fly far because of its weight, but where it reaches, it breaks through with excessive force; and if it is thrown by a skilled person, it returns again to him who sent it. Virgil mentions this, saying: "Accustomed to hurl the *cateia* in the Teutonic fashion." Whence also the Spaniards and Gauls call them **Teutons**. The **falarica** is a huge missile made on a lathe, having a cubit-long iron and a sphere of lead at the very top. It is also said to have fire attached to it. This weapon is used in fighting from **towers**, which it is clear are called *falae*. Juvenal: "Before the *falae* of the consuls and the dolphins," which are also columns. From *falae*, therefore, it is called a *falarica*, just as from a wall <note>original: *muro*</note> it is called "mural." Lucan says the *falarica* is sent by twisted sinews and a certain machine: "As now the *falarica* is vibrated by the sinews." Virgil, however, says that Turnus hurled a *falarica* by hand. **Javelins** <note>original: *pila*</note> are the arms of throwers and missiles, named from "twisting" <note>original: *torquendo*</note> or sending forth. Concerning which Lucan says: "Standards like to standards, eagles to eagles, and javelins threatening javelins." Lucan uses the singular *pilum*. A **missile** <note>original: *telum*</note> is named according to Greek etymology from "from a distance" <note>original: *apo tou telothen*</note>, whatever can be thrown far. By extension, a sword is also called this, as in: "But not this weapon of mine which..."

<summary>This page catalogs ancient Roman military equipment, explaining the etymological origins of various trumpets, swords, axes, and spears. Isidore links the names of these objects to their physical properties, their inventors (like the Etruscans), or their specific tactical uses in warfare.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of military equipment from Book XVIII of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies. The previous page ended while discussing the spear; this page completes the spear section and moves into missiles, defensive armor, and civil spaces like the Forum.</meta>

the right hand wields. Strictly speaking, a weapon <note>original: *telum*</note> is named for its length. Hence also the weasel <note>original: *mustela*</note> is so called because it is like a "long mouse" <note>original: *longus mus*</note>. The point <note>original: *cuspis*</note> of a spear or shaft is fastened with a strap; it is named from "turf" <note>original: *cespes*</note>, which is a thicket. Virgil says: "Myrtle fixed with a pastoral point." Strictly, however, the *cuspis* is the rear part of the spear.

### Chapter 8: Concerning Arrows

An **arrow** <note>original: *sagitta*</note> is named from a "keen strike" <note>original: *sagax ictus*</note>, that is, a swift strike. It is carried by feathers like a bird, so that death may swiftly run toward a person. The Cretans were the first to use these. Feathers are glued to them, as we have said, so they are light and fly to those protected by shields. Small darts <note>original: *spicula*</note> are arrows or short lances, named from their resemblance to ears of grain <note>original: *spicarum*</note>. The **scorpion** is a poisoned arrow shot from a bow or war engine; when it reaches a person, it pours in the venom with which it stings, from which it took the name scorpion.

### Chapter 9: Concerning Quivers

A **quiver** <note>original: *pharetra*</note> is a case for arrows, named from "carrying" <note>original: *ferendo*</note> javelins; just like a bier <note>original: *pheretrum*</note> where a corpse is carried. These have a common etymology because the quiver carries death, and the bier carries the dead. **Bow-cases** <note>original: *coryti*</note> are strictly the cases for bows, just as quivers are for arrows. A **scabbard** <note>original: *vagina*</note> is so called because the point or sword is carried <note>original: *baiulet*</note> in it. A **case** <note>original: *theca*</note> is named because it covers <note>original: *tegat*</note> what is received, with the letter "c" put in place of "g." Others claim it is called a *theca* from the Greek name, because something is placed back in it. From this, a library <note>original: *bibliotheca*</note> is called a repository for books. **Daggers** <note>original: *dolones*</note> are wooden sheaths, within which a blade lies hidden under the appearance of a staff. They are called *dolones* from "deceit" <note>original: *dolus*</note> because they fail and deceive with iron while showing the appearance of wood. The common people call these by the Greek name *oros*, meaning "sharp." From this, doctors call an acute disease *orea*. A **bow** <note>original: *arcus*</note> is so called because it "fends off" <note>original: *arceat*</note> an adversary. From this, citadels <note>original: *arces*</note> are also named, from which enemies are fended off. Also "bow" because of its appearance, because they are curved tightly <note>original: *artius*</note>.

### Chapter 10: Concerning Slings

A **sling** <note>original: *funda*</note> is so called because stones are "poured out" <note>original: *fundantur*</note> from it, that is, sent forth. Use of these was first found in the islands called the Balearics. Virgil: "The lashes of the Balearic sling." The **ballista** is a type of engine, named from sending out javelins; for *ballein* in Greek means "to throw." It is twisted by the tension of sinews and throws either spears or rocks with great force. From this, the **sling-engine** <note>original: *fundibalus*</note> is like one pouring and sending out. Against the ballista, the **tortoise** formation <note>original: *testudo*</note> is effective; for a sequence of armor is made with shield-bosses joined together.

### Chapter 11: Concerning the Ram

The name was given to the **ram** <note>original: *aries*</note> by its appearance, because it strikes the wall with an impulse in the manner of fighting rams. For the head of a strong and knotty tree is clothed in iron; suspended by ropes, it is driven against the wall by the hands of many. Then, drawn backward, it is aimed with greater force; thus the side of the wall, shaken by frequent blows, gives way, is hollowed out, breaks in, and makes a breach. Against the blow of the ram, the remedy is a sack full of chaff, lowered into the place where the ram strikes. For the blow of that ram is softened by the fold of the sacks. For harder things

<column-break/>

yield more easily to softer things. **Hurdles** <note>original: *plurei*</note> are crates of raw hide woven together, which are placed in the way of the enemy while work is being done. The **musculus** <note>meaning "little mouse," a protective shed for miners</note> is made like a tunnel by which a wall is pierced; from which it is also named as if it were a "little wall" <note>original: *murusculus*</note>.

### Chapter 12: Concerning Shields

The **clypeus** is a larger shield, named from the fact that it "hides" <note>original: *clepet*</note>, that is, conceals the body and withdraws it from dangers <note>Isidore links this to the Greek *kleptein*, "to steal" or "hide"</note>. Placed in front, it protects the body by its defense against spears and javelins. The *clypeus* belongs to infantry; the **scutum** <note>oblong shield</note> to cavalry. It is called a *scutum* because it "shakes off" the blow of weapons from itself. For to resist weapons, the *clypeus* is held in front. The **boss** <note>original: *umbo*</note> is the middle part of the shield, like a navel <note>original: *umbilicus*</note>. The **ancile** is called a short and round shield, about which Virgil says: "And he carried the *ancile* on his left." It is called *ancile* from "cutting around" <note>original: *ancisione*</note> because it is as if cut and rounded on every side. Ovid: "They call it *ancile* because it is cut back on every side, and wherever you look with your eyes, every corner is absent." The **pelta** is a short shield, shaped like the middle of a half-moon. The Book of Kings mentions this: "King Solomon made two hundred shields of pure gold, and three hundred *peltas* of tested gold." The **cetra** is a leathern shield without wood, used by Africans and Moors. Of which the poet says: "The *cetra* covers the left." The **parma** is a light weapon like a small *clypeus*. A shield is also called a **testudo** <note>tortoise</note>. For the *clypeus* is made in the manner of a tortoise. There is also the *testudo* of shields, curved in the manner of a tortoise shell. For in types of armor, soldiers even take names from animals, such as the ram. And Sallust says: "in the manner of a military *beritium*" <note>This term is likely a textual corruption of *testudo* or another formation</note>.

### Chapter 13: Concerning Breastplates

It is called a **breastplate** <note>original: *lorica*</note> because it "lacks thongs" <note>original: *loris careat*</note>; for it is woven only from iron circles. **Scale mail** <note>original: *squama*</note> is an iron breastplate made of iron or bronze plates linked together, in the manner of a fish's scales; it is named from the very brightness and similarity of the scales. From haircloths, breastplates are both polished and guided.

### Chapter 14: Concerning Helmets

The **cassis** is made of metal plate; the **galea** is of leather. For *galeros* refers to leather. They say the *cassis* is named from the "Rusci" <note>Etruscans</note>; for they call a helmet a *cassis*, I believe from the head <note>original: *capite*</note>. The **apex** is what stands out on top of the helmet, where the crest is fixed, which the Greeks call the **cone** <note>original: *conus*</note>. For the cone is the curve that projects on the helmet and above which the crests are.

### Chapter 15: Concerning the Forum

The **forum** is a place for conducting lawsuits, named from "speaking" <note>original: *fando*</note>, or from King Phoroneus, who first gave law to the Greeks. This place is also called the **rostra** <note>the beaks</note> from the fact that in the Punic War, the "beaks" were taken from the captured ships of the Carthaginians and fixed in the Roman Forum, so that it might be a sign of this victory. Moreover, the forum consists of a cause, a law, and a judge. It is called a **cause** <note>original: *causa*</note> from the "event" <note>original: *casus*</note> in which it happens. For it is the matter and origin of a business, not yet revealed by the examination of discussion; while it is proposed, it is a cause; while it is discussed, it is a **judgment**; while it is finished, it is **justice**. A judgment <note>original: *iudicium*</note> is named as if it were a "declaration of law" <note>original: *iuris dictio*</note>, and justice <note>original: *iusticia*</note> as if it were a "standing of law" <note>original: *iuris status*</note>. A judgment used to be called an inquiry. Hence also the "actors" of judgments and the overseers, "questors"...
