# Book

...we call **investigators** <note>original: *quisitores*</note>. The word **business** <note>original: *negotium*</note> signifies many things: sometimes it refers to the performance of some act, the opposite of which is leisure <note>original: *otium*</note>; at other times, it refers to the action of a legal case, which is a **legal quarrel** <note>original: *iurgium*</note>. And it is called *negotium* as if it were *nec otium*, meaning "without leisure." However, in legal cases it is called *negotium*, while in trade it is called **commerce** <note>original: *negotiatio*</note>, where something is given so that greater profits may be gained. A **legal quarrel** <note>original: *iurgium*</note> is so named as if it were the "chatter of the law" <note>original: *iuris garritum*</note>, because those who argue a case debate by the law. A **lawsuit** <note>original: *lis*</note> originally took its name from the contention over a boundary <note>original: *limes*</note>. Regarding this, Virgil says:
> A boundary stone was placed to decide a dispute <note>original: *litem*</note> over a field.

A **case** <note>original: *causa*</note> consists either of an argument or a proof. An **argument** never provides proof by witnesses or by documents, but finds the truth through investigation alone; hence it is called an *argumentum*, meaning a "sharp discovery" <note>original: *argutum inventum*</note>. **Proof**, however, consists of witnesses and the reliability of documents. In every judgment, six persons are required: the judge, the accuser, the defendant, and three witnesses. The **judge** <note>original: *iudex*</note> is so named as one who "speaks the law" <note>original: *ius dicens*</note> properly, or because he debates by the law. To debate by the law is to judge justly. For one is not a judge if justice is not in him. The **accuser** <note>original: *accusator*</note> is so called as if he were a "summoner to the case" <note>original: *adcausator*</note>, because he calls the one he names to the case. The **defendant** <note>original: *reus*</note> is named from the "thing" <note>original: *res*</note> which is being sought; for even if one is not guilty of a crime, he is still called the *reus* as long as he is being petitioned for something in court. In ancient times, **witnesses** were called "survivors" <note>original: *superstites*</note>, because they stood over <note>original: *super statum*</note> the status of the case. Now, with a part of the word removed, they are called **witnesses** <note>original: *testes*</note>. A witness is considered by three things: condition, nature, and life. By **condition**, whether they are free and not a slave; for often a slave suppresses the testimony of truth out of fear of a master. By **nature**, whether a man and not a woman; for "woman is always a various and changeable thing" <note>Isidore quotes Virgil’s Aeneid here to reflect the legal prejudices of his time.</note>. By **life**, whether they are innocent and upright in conduct; for if a good life is lacking, they will lack credibility. For justice cannot have a partnership with a criminal. There are two types of witnesses: those who speak what they saw, and those who offer what they heard. Witnesses fail in two ways: when they either put forth false things, or cover up true things with silence.

### Chapter 16: Concerning Spectacles
**Spectacles**, in my opinion, is the general name for pleasures which do not defile by themselves, but through the things that are done there. They are called *spectacula* because a public inspection <note>original: *inspectio*</note> is provided there for people. These are also called **amusements** <note>original: *ludicra*</note> because they are performed in the games <note>original: *ludi*</note> or on stages. The origin of the games is handed down as follows: the Lydians, crossing from Asia, settled in Etruria under their leader Tyrrhenus, who had succeeded his brother in the kingdom. Therefore, during the conflict in Etruria, they instituted spectacles among the other rites of their superstitions in the name of religion. From there, the Romans summoned craftsmen and borrowed the practice; thus the games <note>original: *ludi*</note> were named after the Lydians <note>original: *Lydis*</note>. Varro, however, says the games are named from **play** <note>original: *lusu*</note>, because young people used to delight the populace with the excitement of play during festival days. Hence they are assigned to the play of youth, festival days, temples, and religions. The reason for the name matters little now, as long as the reason for the thing itself is idolatry. Hence the games were also called **Liberalia** <note>A festival for the god Liber/Bacchus.</note> indiscriminately in honor of Father Liber. For this reason, the stain of their origin must be despised, lest you consider good that which took its beginning from evil. A game is either **gymnic**, **circus-based**, **gladiatorial**, or **scenic**.

<column-break/>

### Chapter 17: Concerning the Gymnic Game
The **gymnic game** is the glory of speed and strength. Its place is called a **gymnasium**, where athletes exercise and the speed of runners is proven. From this, it happens that the exercises of nearly all arts are called gymnasia. Formerly, those competing in these places were belted so they would not be naked. Later, when his belt loosened, a certain runner was suddenly tripped and killed; for this reason, the archon Hippoemenes decreed that everyone should exercise naked from then on. And for that reason it was called a *gymnasium*, because young people exercise naked <note>original: *nudi*; Greek: *gymnos*</note> in the field where only the private parts are covered.

### Chapter 18: Concerning the Types of Gymnic Games
There are five types of gymnic games: **jumping**, **running**, **throwing**, **strength**, and **wrestling**. Hence they say a certain king, having as many young sons, ordered them to contend for the kingdom in as many types of games.

### Chapter 19: Concerning Jumping
**Jumping** <note>original: *saltus*</note> is so named as if to "leap into the high" <note>original: *exilire in altum*</note>. For jumping is to leap higher or further.

### Chapter 20: Concerning Running
**Running** <note>original: *cursus*</note> is named from the speed of the legs. For running is the swiftness of the feet.

### Chapter 21: Concerning Throwing
**Throwing** <note>original: *iactus*</note> is named from "to throw" <note>original: *iaciendo*</note>, from which also the fisherman's net is called a "casting-net" <note>original: *iaculum*</note>. The practice for this art is to strike distant stones, to throw spears with balanced weight, and to release arrows from a bow.

### Chapter 22: Concerning Strength
**Strength** <note>original: *virtus*</note> is the immensity of force in labor and the weight of the body.

### Chapter 23: Concerning Wrestling
**Wrestling** <note>original: *luctatio*</note> is named from the "embrace of the sides" <note>original: *laterum complexu*</note>, because those contending at close quarters lean on each other; those who do this are called **athletes** in the Greek naming. The place of wrestling is called the **palaestra**.

### Chapter 24: Concerning the Palaestra
They say the **palaestra** is named either "from wrestling" <note>original: *apo tou pales*</note> or "from the motion of a mighty fall" <note>original: *apo tou pallein*</note>, namely because in wrestling, when they seize the middle of their opponents, they shake them violently, and this is called *pallein* among the Greeks. Some believe the art of wrestling was shown by the fighting of **bears**. For among other wild beasts, they say only bears stand upright to clash, and crouch down quickly and return, and now test each other with their paws, now drive each other away with an embrace in the manner of wrestlers.

### Chapter 25: Concerning the Contest
What the Latins call **competitions** <note>original: *certamina*</note>, the Greeks call **contests** <note>original: *agones*</note>, from the "multitude" <note>original: *frequentia*</note> because they were celebrated by many. Indeed, every gathering and assembly is called an *agon*. Others think they are called *agones* because they were held in circles and, as it were, "without a corner" <note>original: *aneu gonias*</note>, that is, in places without angles.

### Chapter 26: Concerning the Types of Contests
The types of contests were: immensity of strength, speed of running, skill in archery, endurance in standing, the gesture of walking to the zither or flutes, and some concerning character, beauty, and singing...

Isidore provides a Christian-tinted history of Roman public spectacles, linking their origins and equipment to pagan mythology and natural symbolism.</meta>

XVIII

...by the rhythm and land-based nature of war, as well as naval battle, and also by experiencing the contests of punishments.

### Chapter 27: On the games of the circus

<margin>l</margin> The **games of the circus** <note>original: *ludi circenses*</note> were established for the sake of the sacred rites of the gods and the celebrations of the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the pagan Romans and Greeks</note>. For this reason, those who watch them are seen to be serving the cults of demons. In the past, horsemanship was practiced simply, and the common use of this activity did not carry the same guilt of sin. However, once natural usage was forced into the service of these games, it was diverted into the worship of demons. Thus, these types of displays are assigned to **Castor and Pollux** <note>Twin deities in Roman mythology associated with horsemanship</note>, to whom history teaches that horses were distributed by Mercury. For the same reason, the equestrian game is also associated with **Neptune**, whom the Greeks call **Hippios** <note>original: *ippon*; Neptune was the god of horses as well as the sea</note>. Because of this, horses are also consecrated to Mars and Jove in the games, and they themselves preside over the **four-horse chariots** <note>original: *quadrigis*</note>. The games are called "circus-style" <note>original: *circenses*</note> either from the act of "going around" <note>original: *circumeundo*</note>, or because in the place where the turning posts now stand, swords were once placed around which the chariots would circle; thus they were called *circenses* from the "swords" <note>original: *ensibus*</note> around which they ran. Indeed, when they held races on the shores along the banks of rivers, they would place swords in a row along the bank, and it was a matter of skill to turn the horse around the points of the blades. Therefore, they are thought to be called *circenses*, as if "around the swords" <note>original: *circum enses*</note>.

### Chapter 28: On the circus

<margin>c</margin> The **circus** was primarily consecrated to the **Sun** by the pagans; the Sun's temple is in the middle space, and its image shines out from the peak of the temple, because some people believed it should be consecrated under the open sky, in the open air. The circus is all that space which the horses are accustomed to circle. The Romans believe it is named from the "circuit" <note>original: *circuitu*</note> of the horses, because the horses run there around the turning posts. However, the Greeks assert it was named after **Circe**, the daughter of the Sun, who instituted this kind of contest for her father, and they argue the name of the circus comes from her. She was a mage, a poisoner, and a priestess of demons. In her character and through the work of magic art, the cult of idolatry is recognized.

### Chapter 29: On the ornaments

<margin>o</margin> The **ornaments of the circus** are: the eggs, the turning post, the obelisk, and the starting gates. The **eggs** <note>original: *ova*; large wooden eggs were used as lap counters</note> they assign to the honor of Castor and Pollux, for they are not ashamed to believe that those two were born from an egg produced by a swan and Jove <note>Referring to the myth of Leda and the Swan</note>. The Romans pretend to relate the circus games to the causes of the world, so that under this pretext they might excuse the superstitions of their vanities.

### Chapter 30: On the turning posts

<margin>d</margin> By the name of the **turning posts** <note>original: *metarum*</note>, they specifically wish to designate the boundary and the end of the world, derived from the fact that someone has measured out an end, or as a testimony to the rising and setting of the sun.

### Chapter 31: On the obelisk

<margin>o</margin> **King Mespheres of Egypt** <note>A legendary figure, likely a corruption of a Pharaoh's name such as Thutmose</note> is said to have been the first to make an **obelisk** for the following reason: when the Nile at one time had harmed Egypt with a violent flood, the king, being indignant as if to exact punishment from the river, shot an arrow into the waves. Not long after, he was seized by a grave illness and lost his sight. After he regained his vision following his blindness, he consecrated two obelisks to the Sun. For "obelisk" means "**arrow**," which is why it is placed in the middle of the circus, because the Sun runs through the middle of the world. In the middle space,

<column-break/>

the obelisk is positioned between the two turning posts; it signifies the peak and the heights of heaven, as the sun passes through the middle space at the division of the hours. Placed atop the obelisk is a certain gilded object shaped like a **flame**, because the sun possesses a great deal of heat and fire.

### Chapter 32: On the starting gates

<margin>i</margin> In the circus, the places from which the horses are released are called **starting gates** <note>original: *carceres*</note> for the same reason as the **prison** <note>original: *carcer*</note> which is in the city: because just as condemned and shut-in men are held there, so here the horses are restrained so that they do not rush out before the signal is given.

### Chapter 33: On the charioteers

<margin>a</margin> The participants of the circus: the **charioteer** <note>original: *auriga*</note> and the chariot, the riders, or the footmen. The *auriga* is so called properly because he "drives and rules the chariot," or because he "strikes the joined horses." For we say "he strikes the side" <note>original: *aurit*; Isidore uses an archaic or poetic verb to link *auriga* to striking</note>, as in "he strikes the open side." He is also the **driver** <note>original: *agitator*</note>: that is, the "striker," named from the act of driving <note>original: *agendo*</note>. Charioteers use two colors, with which they clothe the appearance of idolatry: for **Green** <note>original: *prasinus*</note> was dedicated to the Earth and **Blue** <note>original: *venetus*</note> to the Sky and Sea by the pagans.

### Chapter 34: On the four-horse chariots

<margin>e</margin> **Erichthonius**, who reigned at Athens, is said to have been the first to join four horses together, as Virgil is witness, saying:
> Erichthonius was the first who dared to join a chariot and four horses, and to stand victorious upon the rapid wheels.

He was the son of Minerva and Vulcan, created—as the fables tell—from a fallen lust upon the earth; a demonic portent, or rather the Devil himself, who first dedicated the chariot to Juno. By such an author were the **four-horse chariots** <note>original: *quadrige*</note> brought forth.

### Chapter 35: On the chariot

<margin>c</margin> The **chariot** <note>original: *currus*</note> is named from "running" <note>original: *cursu*</note>, or because it is seen to have wheels, whence *currum* is like "curved" <note>original: *curvum*</note>. Formerly, *quadrigae* chariots had a double pole and a continuous one that was placed upon all the horses. **Eristenes of Sicyon** was the first to yoke only the middle ones, and he attached the individual horses on either side with a simple strap. The Greeks call these **trace-horses** <note>original: *siraforos*; Greek *seiraphoroi*</note>, and the Latins call them **rope-horses** <note>original: *funarios*</note> from the type of strap by which they were previously tied.

### Chapter 36: On the horses with which they run

<margin>q</margin> Chariots are called **quadrigae** (four), **bigae** (two), **trigae** (three), and **seiugae** (six) from the number of horses and the yoke <note>original: *iugo*</note>. Of these, they consecrated the four-horse chariots to the **Sun**, the two-horse chariots to the **Moon**, the three-horse to the **gods of the underworld**, and the six-horse to **Jove**. They consecrated the **desultores** <note>trick riders who leapt between horses</note> to the Morning Star and the Evening Star. They join four-horse chariots to the Sun because he turns through the four seasons of the year: spring and summer, autumn and winter. Two-horse chariots to the Moon, because she competes with the sun in a twin course, or because she is seen by both night and day; for they join one black horse and one white horse. Three-horse chariots to the gods of the underworld, because they snatch men to themselves through three ages: that is, through infancy, youth, and old age. The **seiuga** is the greatest chariot for Jove, because they believe him to be the greatest of their gods. They say the *quadrigae* run on wheels either because this world rushes through the speed of its own circle, or because of the Sun, which rotates in a rolling circuit, just as Ennius says:
> Then the white wheel of heaven opened up with rays.

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s Book XVIII of the Etymologies. Having previously discussed the origins and religious associations of the circus games, he now focuses on the specific components of the races—the laps, the participants (riders, leapers, and runners), and the symbolic meaning of the team colors—before transitioning into a description of the theater and its various performers.</meta>

### Chapter 37: On the seven laps
The seven **laps** <note>original: *spacia*; these are the circuits around the track</note> of the four-horse chariot represent the course of the **seven stars** <note>The seven "wandering stars" or planets known in antiquity: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> by which they say the world is ruled, or they refer to the course of the seven days through which the limit of life is reached. Their finish line is the "Bear" <note>original: *arctus*; referring to the constellation Ursa Major, which never sets below the horizon, here used to symbolize judgment or the fixed end of a journey</note>, which signifies judgment.

### Chapter 38: On the horsemen
They say the **individual horsemen** <note>original: *equites singulares*</note> race for this reason: because each person individually completes and passes through the course of this life. One follows another at different times, yet they all travel through the single path of mortality toward the common goal of death.

### Chapter 39: On the leapers
The **leapers** <note>original: *desultores*</note> were so named because formerly, whenever someone reached the end of the course, he would leap down and run; or perhaps because he would leap across from one horse to another.

### Chapter 40: On the foot-racers
Moreover, they say the **foot-racers** <note>original: *pedites*</note> run on foot because mortality is run with feet. For this reason, they run from a higher place to a lower one, that is, from the East to the West, because mortals are born and die. They run **naked**, because there are no possessions remaining to a person in this world. They run in a **straight space**, because there is no distance between life and death. But they devise these explanations merely to try to excuse their vanities and sacrileges.

### Chapter 41: On the colors of the horses
Regarding the elements and their causes, the pagans also assigned **colors** to the horses. They associated **red** <note>original: *rosseos*</note> with the sun (that is, fire); **white** with the air; **green** <note>original: *prasinos*</note> with the earth; and **blue** <note>original: *venetos*</note> with the sea. Likewise, they wanted the **red** to race for summer, because they are of a fiery color and everything then turns golden. **White** for winter, because it is icy and everything grows white with frosts. **Green** for spring, because then the vine leaves grow thick. Again, they consecrated the **red** to race for Mars, from whom the Romans originate, and because the banners of the Romans are decorated with scarlet, or because Mars delights in blood. **White** they dedicated to the Zephyrs <note>Gentle west winds</note> and clear weather; **green** to Flora <note>Goddess of flowers</note> and the earth; **blue** to the waters or the air, because they are of an azure color; **yellow** (that is, saffron) to fire and the sun; and **purple** they sacrificed to Iris, whom we call the **rainbow**, because it possesses many colors. And so, while they are distracted by this spectacle of the cults of gods and the elements of the world, they are clearly recognized as honoring those same gods and elements through these colors. Therefore, Christian, you ought to notice what unclean spirits possess you. For this reason, the place will be foreign to you, as many spirits of Satan have occupied it. For the devil and his angels have filled that entire place.

### Chapter 42: On the theater
The **theater** is where the stage is enclosed; it has the shape of a semicircle, in which everyone standing can look in. Its form was originally round, like that of an amphitheater. Later, the theater was made from half of an amphitheater. The theater is named from the "spectacle," from the Greek *theasthai* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ θεᾶσθαι*; to view or contemplate</note>, because the people standing above would contemplate the games. The theater is also the same as a **brothel** <note>original: *prostibulum*</note>, because after the games were finished, prostitutes were prostituted there. It was also called a **lupanar** <note>A "wolf-den" or brothel</note> because of these

<column-break/>

same prostitutes who, because of the common lightness of their bodies, were called "she-wolves" <note>original: *lupae*</note>. For prostitutes were called *lupae* because of their greed, for they snatch and seize the wretched for themselves. Moreover, these brothels were established by the pagans so that the shame of unfortunate women would be made public there, and both those who committed the act and those who endured it would be held in mockery.

### Chapter 43: On the stage
The **stage** <note>original: *scena*</note> was a place below the theater, built in the manner of a house with a platform. This platform was called the **orchestra** <note>original: *orcistra*</note>, where comic and tragic actors sang, and where performers and mimes danced. It was called *scena* by a Greek name because it was built in the appearance of a house; from this, among the Hebrews, the dedication of tabernacles <note>original: *scenophegia*; the Feast of Tabernacles</note> was so named from the similarity to dwellings.

### Chapter 44: On the orchestra
The **orchestra** was the platform of the stage, where a dancer could perform, or where two people could debate with each other. There the poets, comedians, and tragedians would ascend for competition; and while these were singing, others would perform gestures. The theatrical offices are: **tragedians, comedians, thymelici, actors, mimes, and dancers.**

### Chapter 45: On the tragedians
**Tragedians** are those who sang of the ancient deeds and crimes of wicked kings in mournful song while the people watched.

### Chapter 46: On the comedies
**Comedians** are those who sang of the acts of private men through words or gestures, and they expressed the defilement of virgins and the loves of prostitutes in their stories.

### Chapter 47: On the thymelici
The **thymelici** were the theatrical musicians who played accompaniment on organs, lyres, and harps. They were called *thymelici* because in the past they sang standing in the orchestra upon the platform, which was called the *themele*.

### Chapter 48: On the actors
**Actors** <note>original: *histriones*</note> are those who, in women’s clothing, expressed the gestures of shameless women. These also demonstrated histories and deeds by dancing. They were called *histriones* either because that kind of performer was brought from Istria, or because they expressed many stories in their plays, as if they were "story-performers" <note>original: *historiones*</note>.

### Chapter 49: On the mimes
**Mimes** are named by a Greek term because they are imitators of human affairs. For they had their own author, who would announce the story before they performed the mime. For stories were composed by poets so that they were most fitting for the movement of the body.

### Chapter 50: On the dancers
Varro says the **dancers** <note>original: *saltatores*</note> are named after the Arcadian **Saltius**, whom Aeneas brought with him into Italy, and who first taught the noble Roman youths to dance.

### Chapter 51: What they do for their patron
And clearly in the theatrical arts, they act under the patronage of **Bacchus** <note>original: *Liber*</note> and **Venus**, which are private and specific to the stage, concerning gesture and the flow of the body. For the soft...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s discussion of Roman spectacles. On the previous page, he described the theater and its performers; here, he concludes the section on the theater by explaining its pagan origins before moving on to the amphitheater, the various classes of gladiators, and finally, the origins and symbolism of board games and dice.</meta>

...sacrificed to Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus, the god of wine and theater</note> and Venus, those who were dissolved by their own lust. The things that are carried out there—with voices, musical modes, instruments, and lyres—have Apollo, the Muses, Minerva, and Mercury as their patrons. You, as a Christian, ought to hate the spectacle if you hate those who authored it.

### Chapter 52: On the amphitheater
The **amphitheater** is a place of spectacle where **gladiators** fight. From this, it is called a "gladiatorial game" because in it young men learn the use of arms through various movements, sometimes contending among themselves with swords or fists, and other times advancing against wild beasts. There, they undergo a deadly struggle, enticed not by hatred but by a prize. It is called an "amphitheater" <note>From the Greek *amphi* (around/both) and *theatron*</note> because it is made of **two theaters**. For an amphitheater is round, whereas a theater is a semi-circle, effectively half of an amphitheater.

### Chapter 53: On the equestrian game
There are several types of gladiators. The first of these is the **equestrian game**. Two horsemen would proceed, preceded by military standards; one from the eastern gate and the other from the western gate. They rode on white horses, wearing small golden helmets and carrying light, fluttering armor <note>original: *babilionibus*; likely a corruption of *papilionibus*, referring to light or butterfly-like equipment</note>. With fierce perseverance, they would enter the fight for the sake of their own valor, fighting until one died at the hands of the other—so that he who fell had the "glory" of his fall, and the survivor had the "glory" of the kill. This style of fighting was conducted for the sake of **Mars** <note>The god of war</note>.

### Chapter 54: On the net-fighters
The **net-fighter** <note>original: *retiarius*</note> was named from his type of equipment in the gladiatorial game. While fighting against another, he would secretly carry a net—called a "cast-net"—so that he might cover his adversary as he pursued him with a spear, entangling him to overcome him by force. This style of fighting was sacred to **Neptune** <note>The god of the sea</note> because of the trident he carried.

### Chapter 55: On the pursuers
The **pursuer** <note>original: *secutor*</note> is so named from pursuing the net-fighter. He would aim for the net-fighter's spear-point and carry a lead weight to snag the opponent's net, so that he might overcome him before the net could be cast. This equipment was sacred to **Vulcan** <note>The god of fire</note>. For fire always "pursues" water; therefore, the pursuer was matched against the net-fighter because fire and water are forever enemies to one another.

### Chapter 56: On the lasso-fighters
The fight of the **lasso-fighters** <note>original: *laqueatores*</note> consisted of pursuing men who were fleeing in the game, entangling them by throwing a noose <note>original: *laqueus*</note> to strike them down while they were protected by a leather shield-boss.

### Chapter 57: On the skirmishers
The fight of the **skirmishers** <note>original: *velites*</note> was one where they threw missiles back and forth. Their combat was varied and more pleasing to the spectators than the others. They were called *velites* either from their "flying about" <note>original: *volitatio*</note> or from a city of the Etruscans which was called Veii <note>original: *Veletes*</note>.

### Chapter 58: On the deadly contest
The **beast-fight** consisted of young men receiving and fighting against wild beasts that had been released. They entered this contest of their own accord, struggling not because of a crime they had committed, but out of a wild frenzy.

### Chapter 59: On the execration of these games
Indeed, these spectacles of cruelty and the watching of such vanities were instituted not only by the vices of men but

<column-break/>

by the commands of demons. Therefore, a Christian should have nothing to do with the madness of the circus, the impurity of the theater, the cruelty of the amphitheater, the atrocity of the arena, or the luxury of the games. For he denies God who presumes to take part in such things, becoming a prevaricator <note>A term for someone who betrays a duty or shifts their stance</note> of the Christian faith by seeking again what he once renounced at the baptismal font: that is, the devil, his pomps, and his works.

### Chapter 60: On dice
**Dice** <note>original: *alea*</note>, that is the game of the board, was invented by the Greeks during the leisure of the Trojan War by a certain soldier named Alea, from whom the art took its name. The board is played with a dice-tower, counters, and dice.

### Chapter 61: On the dice-tower
It is called a **tower** <note>original: *pirgus*</note> because the dice "pass through" <note>original: *pergant*</note> it, or because it has the appearance of a tower. For the Greeks call a tower a *pyrgos*.

### Chapter 62: On the counters
They are called **counters** <note>original: *calculi*</note> because they are smooth and round. From this, a *calculus* is also the name for a small stone that is stepped on <note>original: *calcet*</note> without discomfort because of its smallness. Likewise, they are called *calculi* because they move along established paths, as if along footpaths <note>original: *calles*</note>.

### Chapter 63: On the dice
They are called **dice** <note>original: *tesserae*</note> because they are square <note>original: *quadrae*</note> on all sides. Some call these "little hares" because they scurry about by leaping. In the past, dice were called *iacula* from "throwing" <note>original: *iaciendo*</note>.

### Chapter 64: On the figures of dice
Some gamblers think they practice this art "physiologically" as an allegory, feigning a certain similarity to the nature of things. For they claim people play with **three dice** because of the three times of the age—past, present, and future—because they do not stand still but run their course. They even argue that the paths themselves are marked into six spaces because of the ages of man, and into three lines because of the times. Thus, they say the board is described with three lines.

### Chapter 65: On the names of the dice
Among the ancient players, each value was called by a number, such as the one, the two, the three, the four, the five, and the six. Later, the names for each changed: they called the **one** the "dog," the **three** the "sigh," and the **four** the "plain."

### Chapter 66: On the throws of the dice
The throw of the dice is so arranged by skilled gamblers that it brings whatever one wishes—for instance, the **six**, which brings them a good result in the throw. They avoid the **dog**, however, because it is damaging and signifies only a one.

### Chapter 67: On the "death" of the counters
The counters move partly in a fixed order and partly wandering; therefore, they call some "orderly" and others "wandering." But those that cannot be moved at all are called **blocked** <note>original: *incitos*</note>. From this, destitute men are also called *inciti*, because no hope remains for them to move forward.

### Chapter 68: On the prohibition of dice
From this art, fraud, lying, and perjury are never absent; finally, there is also hatred and the loss of property. For this reason, because of these crimes, it has occasionally been forbidden by laws.

# Chapter 69: On the Ball

A **ball** (*pila*) is properly so-called because it is "full of hairs" (*pilis plena*). <note>Isidore suggests the word for ball comes from the animal hair used to stuff it.</note> This is also called a **sphere**, named from either "carrying" (*ferendo*) or "striking" (*feriendo*). Regarding its type and weight, Dorcas <note>A Greek name, possibly referring to a lost grammatical source</note> handed down this: "Do not spare the lively hairs of a deer to stuff inside, until two ounces have been added to the pound." <note>This quote describes the traditional method of stuffing a leather ball with deer hair to a specific weight.</note> Among the types of balls are the **trigonaria** and the **arenata**. The *trigonaria* is that which is played among three people. <note>From the Greek *trigonos*, meaning triangle.</note> The *arenata* (sanded ball) is that which is thrown in a crowd from a circle of bystanders and spectators; they were accustomed to catch the ball beyond the proper distance and enter the game. A **lubitale** is the name of a game where two people strike the ball close at hand, with their elbows almost joined. To **"give the calf"** (*suram dare*) is said of one who offers the ball to be struck with a flat leg by their teammates.

### Here begins the nineteenth book
### Chapter 1: On Ships

The **names of certain arts** by which something is manufactured—or the instruments of craftsmen, or those things which provide service, and other matters of this sort—must now be noted in part. **Craftsman** (*artifex*) is a general name, called so because he "makes art" (*artem faciat*), just as a **goldsmith** (*aurifex*) makes gold. For the ancients used the word *faro* instead of *facio* (to make). A **ship-master** (*nauclerus*) is the owner of the ship; he is called this because the ship is his "lot" (*sorte*). For in Greek, a "lot" is called *cleros*. <note>original: "cleros"</note> The others on the ship are "in contribution" (the crew). The **helmsman** (*gubernio*), who is also the **pilot** (*gubernator*), is named as if he were a "winter-restrainer" (*cohibernator*), because he restrains the "winters" (*hiberna*)—that is, the storms of the sea—with his prudence. **Sailor** (*nauta*) is derived from "ship" (*navis*). Poets use the word *nauita* for sailor, just as they say *Mauors* for Mars. However, *nauta* is the correct form. An **oarsman** (*remex*) is so named because he "carries the oar" (*remum gerit*); *remex* is used in the nominative case just as *tubex* (trumpeter) is. In the Greek tongue, the one who is called **"the newcomer"** in Latin is called an *epipata* <note>original: "epibates"</note>. This person has no business on board but arranges to cross to other lands after paying his fare (*naulum*). Some claim a **ship** (*navis*) is so named because it seeks a "knowing" (*gnarum*) leader—that is, a skilled, wise, and vigorous person who knows how to restrain and pilot it due to the dangers and accidents of the sea. Hence that saying of Solomon: "The man of understanding shall possess the helms." <note>Proverbs 1:5</note> The **Lydians** were the first to build a ship, and seeking the uncertainties of the open sea, they made the sea a path for human use. **Rafts** (*rates*) are the first and oldest type of vessel, fastened together from rough logs and planks. Ships built in their likeness are called *ratariae*. Nowadays, "rafts" is used loosely for any ship. Properly, however, rafts are beams bound together. A **trireme** (*trieris*) is a large ship which the Greeks call a *dromon*. Of which it is said in Isaiah: "The great trireme shall not pass through it." <note>Isaiah 33:21</note> A **Carpasian** <note>OCR: "Larpasia"</note> ship is named from the island of Carpasus, just as a **Rhodian** is from Rhodes and an **Alexandrian** from Alexandria. **Liburnian** ships are named from Libya <note>Actually from the Liburnians of Illyria, but Isidore identifies them with Libya</note>; these are merchant ships. Of which Horace says: "You shall go in Liburnian galleys among the towering ships." <note>Horace, Epodes 1.1</note> **Rostrate** ships are so called because they have bronze **beaks** (*rostra*) on the bow to protect them from rocks and collisions. **Long ships** are those they call 

<column-break/>

**dromones**, named because they are longer than others. The opposite of these is the **musculus** (little mouse): a short vessel. A **dromo** is named from "running down" (*decurrendo*). For the Greeks call a race or a course a *dromos*. <note>original: "dromos"</note> A **fleet** (*classis*) is named from a Greek word, *apo ton kalon*, which means "from the logs" <note>original: "apò tōn kalōn"</note>; from this also come **calones**, little boats that carry wood for soldiers. An **anquiromagus** is so named because its speed makes it suited for carrying **anchors** (*anchoris*) and other ship's gear. A **phasellus** is a vessel which we corruptly call a *baselum*. Of which Virgil says: "With painted skiffs (*phaselis*)." <note>Virgil, Georgics 4.289</note> A **scapha** (skiff), which is also a **calatcopus** vessel, is called a **"scout-ship"** (*speculatorium*) in Latin. For in Greek, *scopos* means "to look at" or "aim." A **barca** (bark) is what carries all the ship's cargo to the shore. The ship takes this boat into its "bosom" while on the open sea due to the excessive waves. When it approaches port, the bark returns the favor to the ship it received at sea. A **paro** is a vessel suitable for pirates, named accordingly. Cicero says: "Then he delivers and commits himself to the wave-bearing *paro*." And elsewhere: "He plays at the shore with swift little *parones*." A **myoparo** is like a "minimal *paro*"—that is, a **carabus**. It is a small skiff made of wicker which, when covered in raw hide, provides a type of vessel. Such are used by the **German pirates** on the shores or marshes of the Ocean because of their agility. Of which history says: "The Saxon people rely on *myoparones*, not on strength, prepared for flight rather than war." **Celones**, which the Greeks call *celetras*, are swift biremes or triremes, agile and suited for the service of a fleet. Ennius says: "The oiled keel of the *celo* glides through the white-foamed waters." **Biremes** are ships having a double row of oars. **Triremes** and **quadriremes** have three and four rows; likewise **penteremes** and **hexeremes** <note>OCR: "hereremes"</note> have five or six rows. **Actuariae** ships are those driven by both sails and oars. An **hippoganus** is a vessel in which they are accustomed to transport horses. A **potonium** is a river vessel—slow and heavy—which can only move by rowing. From this also comes the **ferry** (*traiectus*)—that is, "stretched out." For a rope is broad, whence a stretched rope is called a **transenna**. A **lembus** is a short boat, which by another name is called a **cymba** or **caupillus**. Just like a **lintris** (wherry), that is a **carabus**, which they use in the marshes. A **carabus** is a small skiff made of wicker which, when covered in raw hide, provides a type of vessel. A **pontonia** (pontoon) is a small boat of Syrian origin, broad and without a keel—named from "carrying" (*portando*). They use these in Pannonia. **Trabariae** are river ships which are hollowed out from single logs (*trabibus*); by another name they are called "shore-boats" (*littorariae*). These are also called **caudicae**, made hollow from one piece of wood. They are called *caudicae* because they hold from four to ten men.

# Chapter 2: On parts of ships and their gear

The **stern** (*puppis*) is the rear part of the ship, as if "behind" (*post*). The **prow** (*prora*) is the front—as if "the prior things." The **hull** <note>original: "cumba"; likely "alveus" (hollow/belly) in the original manuscript tradition</note> is the lowest part of the ship, which rests upon the waters. The **keel** (*carina*) is named from "running" (*currendo*), as if it were a *currina*. The **hatches** (*fori*) are the hollow sides of ships, named from "carrying" (*ferendo*) loads; or they are the decks of ships that are spread out, named because they "carry" footsteps, or stand out "outdoors" (*foris*). Of which Virgil says: "And he clears the hatches." <note>Virgil, Aeneid 6.412</note> **Oar-ports** (*columbaria*) are the hollow places on the highest sides of ships...

<meta>The previous page introduced Book 19, beginning with a general definition of craftsmanship and the construction of ships. This page continues the detailed technical vocabulary of maritime vessels, specifically focusing on oars, masts, sails, and rigging, before moving into fishing equipment and the tools of the forge.</meta>

through which the oars protrude, which I believe are named for their resemblance to the nesting holes of pigeons where they make their nests. **Passageways** <note>original: "agea"</note> are the paths or places in a ship through which the rowing master <note>original: "hortator"</note> approaches the rowers. Concerning this, Ennius says: "He places many things in the marketplace, he fills the long **passageways**." **Benches** <note>original: "transtra"</note> are the planks where the rowers sit, named because they are placed "across" <note>original: "in transuerso"</note>; Virgil calls these **yokes**. **Oars** (*remi*) are named from "removing" (*removendis*) or "striking away" (*decutiendis*) the waves, just as barbers (*tonsores*) are named from "clipping" (*tondendis*) or "cutting away" hair. The **blade** is the extreme width of the oar, named from the "palm" (*palma*) of the hand, by which it strikes the sea. **Yardarms** (*antemnae*), however, are so named because they are placed "before the river" (*ante amnem*), for the river <note>meaning the flow of wind or water</note> precedes them. **Tips** <note>original: "lozua"</note> are the extreme parts of the yardarms; they are named by a metaphor from a living creature to an inanimate object. The **mast** is the tree of the ship by which the sails are sustained. It is called a **mast** (*malus*) either because it has the likeness of an "apple" (*malum*) at the top, or because it is surrounded by certain wooden "mallets" (*malleolis*) by whose rotation the sails are easily raised. The **socket** (*modiũ*) is that in which the ship’s mast stands, named for its resemblance to a measuring vessel. **Lookouts** <note>original: "larceria"</note> are at the peak of the mast. **Pulleys** (*troclee*) are those which have holes through which the ropes are pulled. Linna says: "The lookouts of the tall mast shine brightly. They are called **pulleys** because they have little wheels; for in Greek, a wheel is called a *trochos*." **Supports** (*parastatę*) are pairs of standing posts by which the ship's mast is held up. Laro says: "The mast is bound to the joined supports." The **tiller-pin** (*clauus*) is that by which the rudder is steered. Concerning which Ennius says: "That I may hold the tiller-pin straight and steer the ship." The **gavel** (*porticulus*) is a mallet carried in the hand by which the rhythm and signal is given to the rowers. Concerning which Plautus says: "You have a gavel for speaking and for keeping silent." It is called a *porticulus* from "carrying" (*portando*). A **mooring-stake** (*tonsilla*) is an iron or wooden hook fixed in the shore to which the ropes of ships are tied. Concerning which Ennius says: "They seize the mooring-stakes and fasten them to the hooked shore." An **anchor** (*ancora*), an iron tooth, takes its name from Greek etymology, because it "grasps" (*comprehendat*) either rocks or sands like a human hand. For in Greek, a hand is called a *cheir*. Among the Greeks, however, it does not have the aspiration <note>The 'h' sound</note>. It is called *ankyra*, which is why among our ancestors it was pronounced without the aspiration. **Rollers** (*paluini*) are the machines by which ships are drawn down into or hauled up from the harbor. A **gangway** (*pons*) is the ladder of ships.

### Chapter 3: On Sails

The Greeks call **sails** *armena*, because they are moved by the "air" (*aere*). Among the Latins, however, sails (*vela*) are named from "flying" (*volatu*). From this comes that phrase: "We spread the wings of our sails." There are various types: the **acateon**, the **epidromos**, the **dalum**, the **artemon**, the **siparum**, and the **mendicum**. Among these, the *acateon* is the largest sail, placed in the middle of the ship. The *epidromos* is the second sail in size, located at the stern. The *dalum* is the smallest sail, fixed at the prow. The *artemon* is valued more for steering the ship than for speed. The **top-sail** (*siparũ*) is a type of sail having one "foot" <note>one lower corner</note> which ships use for help during navigation whenever the force of the wind weakens. Concerning which Lucan says: "And stretching the highest point, the swift top-sail gathers the painted breezes." Some think it is named from "separation" (*separatio*). The **clew** (*pes*) is the extreme corner of the sail, of which sailors speak in this way.

### Chapter 4: On Ropes

<meta>The guide letter 'f' indicates the start of the section for 'Funes' (Ropes).</meta> **Ropes** (*funes*) are so named because previously they were used for light, being surrounded by wax; from which also comes the term "funeral torches" (*funalia*). 

<column-break/>

**Cords** (*restes*) are those which either hold rafts together or in which nets are stretched. **Halyards** (*rudentes*) are the ropes of ships, so named from their excessive "creaking" (*stridore*). **Coils** (*spirę*), however, are the ropes which are used in storms, which sailors in their own custom call "gourds" (*curcubas*). They are called *spirę* from the "Spanish broom" (*sparto*) grass. The **sheet** (*propes*) is the rope by which the foot of the sail is tied, as if "near the feet" (*prope pedes*). Concerning which Turpilius says: "Just as when a favorable wind carries the ship into the sea, if anyone has let go the sheet or the left sail." A **stay** (*loxmentũ*) is a long rope in ships which is extended from prow to stern so that they may be more tightly bound together. They are called *loxmenta* from "twisting" (*tortura*); they are cords and ropes. The **saphon** is a rope positioned at the prow. Concerning which Caecilius says: "I came on a course of love with a flat foot all the way to the *saphon*." **Braces** (*opisfera*) are ropes which are stretched from the horns of the yardarm to the right and left, facing backward. A **mooring-rope** (*prohnesiũ*) is the rope by which a ship is tied to a post on the shore. A **girdle** (*mitra*) is the rope by which the middle of the ship is bound. A **hoist** (*anqna*) is a rope of the ship which binds the yardarm to the mast. Concerning which Linna says: "And the strongest hoist directs the steady course." A **tow-line** (*remulcum*) is a rope by which a bound ship is pulled in place of an oar (*remi*). Concerning which Valerius says: "Here my prow, following with a long tow-line, stops for free in a guest's harbor." **Straps** (*struppi*) are bonds made of leather or flax by which oars are tied to the thole-pins. Concerning which Livy says: "And then he ordered the oars to be tied with straps." A **sounding-lead** (*catapoꝛates*) is a line with a lead mass by which the depth of the sea is tested. Lucilius says: "A boy will bring down this sounding-lead, a small piece of greased lead and a rod of rough flax."

### Chapter 5: On Nets

**Nets** (*retia*) are named either from "retaining" (*retinendis*) fish or from the "cords" (*restibus*) by which they are stretched. Another type of net is called a **snare** (*simplagiũ*), from "striking" (*plagis*). For properly, *plagae* are those ropes by which nets are stretched around the bottom and top parts. A **casting-net** (*funda*) is a type of fisherman's net, named from the fact that it is "thrown" (*mittat*) to the "bottom" (*fundum*). This same net is also called a **javelin-net** (*iaculũ*) from "tossing" (*iactando*). Plautus says: "Indeed, formerly a good thrower; tomorrow." A **drag-net** (*tragum*) is a type of net named from the fact that it is "dragged" (*trahatur*); it is the same as a **sweep-net** (*verriculũ*). For to sweep (*verrere*) is to drag. A **creel** (*massa*) is woven from osiers like a net. A **pouch-net** (*cassis*) is a type of hunter's net that "captures" (*capiat*). From this, we say "in vain" (*incassum*), that is, without cause, as if "without nets" (*sine cassibus*), without which hunting is useless. A **mosquito net** (*conopeũ*) is a net woven in the likeness of a tent to exclude flies and gnats; it is used mostly by the Alexandrians, because there gnats are born in great numbers from the Nile. From this it is called *conopea*, for Egypt is the land of gnats (*conopea*).

### Chapter 6: On Workshops or Furnaces

A **craftsman** (*faber*) takes his name from "making" (*faciendo*) iron. From this, the name was derived for other materials of the arts, calling them "craftsmen" or "workshops" with an addition, such as a **wood-craftsman** (*faber lignari'*) and others, specifically because of the "firmness" (*firmitatem*) of the work. In the furnace of craftsmen, the pagans say **Vulcan** is the author, signifying fire through the figure of Vulcan, without which no kind of metal can be melted or hammered out. For there is almost nothing which is not brought about by fire. In one place it produces glass, in another silver, in another lead, in another vermilion, in another pigments, in another medicines. By fire, stones are dissolved into bronze; by fire...

It concludes by introducing the concept of the craftsman (faber) and the essential role of fire and the forge in human industry.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book 19 of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies. Following the discussion of maritime tools from the previous page, the author shifts focus to the transformative power of fire, the tools of the blacksmith, and the materials used in masonry and architecture.</meta>

It produces and tames iron; it perfects gold through fire. Through fire-burned stone, cements and walls are bound together. Fire makes black stones white by cooking them, and darkens white wood by burning it. From a glowing ember, it creates black charcoal; from hard wood, it makes fragile charcoal; and it renders perishable things imperishable. It thaws what is frozen, and binds what is loose; it softens the hard and hardens the soft. It also has a use in medicine, for it is often beneficial to cauterize <note>original: "uri"</note>. It is certain that fire provides help against pestilence caused by the darkening of the sun <note>Referring to the ancient belief that solar eclipses caused disease by corrupting the air</note>. In the works of craftsmen, it produces one thing with the first fires, another with the second, and another with the third. Fire also contains within itself another diversity: for there is one fire that serves human use, and another that obeys divine judgment, whether it is the lightning that strikes from heaven or the fire that erupts from the earth through the peaks of mountains. 

Fire (*ignis*) is so named because nothing can be born (*gigni*) from it <note>This is a classic Isidorian etymology: ignis = "is" + "gigni" (nothing is born from it), emphasizing its destructive nature</note>. It is an inviolable element that consumes everything it seizes. The forge consists of two things: winds and flames. A flame (*flamma*) specifically belongs to the furnace, so named because it is excited by the "blast" (*flatu*) of the bellows. The furnace (*fornax*) is named after fire, for "fire" (*fos*) is a word for it. A *lamina* is a furnace; it is a Greek name derived from *cauma*, which means heat. **Embers** (*favilla*) are sparks abandoned by the fire. A **glowing coal** (*pruna*) is what it is called as long as it burns; when it has been extinguished, it is named **charcoal** (*carbo*). The term *pruna* is derived from "burning" (*purendo*), while *carbo* is so called because it lacks a flame. Even when it expires, it is believed to possess greater power, for when reignited, it glows with a stronger light. Its durability is so great even without fire that it is corrupted by no moisture and overcome by no age; indeed, once extinguished, it remains so incorruptible that those who mark boundaries <note>original: "limites"</note> bury them in the earth and set stones over them to convince any litigator, so that they might recognize for as many ages as may pass that the set stone marks the boundary.

<margin>¶</margin>
### Chapter VII: On the tools of blacksmiths

The **anvil** (*incus*) is that upon which iron is beaten; it is named from "striking" (*caedendo*), because we beat something there, that is, we draw it out by striking. For to beat is to strike and hit. The ancients did not call it an *incus*, but an *intus*, because the metal is "beaten" (*tundatur*) upon it, which is to say it is "stretched" (*tendatur*); hence also the **mallet** (*tudis*) is named from beating, which is stretching. The **hammer** (*malleus*) is so called because it strikes and draws out the metal while it is hot and "soft" (*molle*). A **Marcus** is a larger hammer, so named because it is "larger" (*maior*) and stronger for striking. A **Marcellus** is of medium size. A **Marculus** is a very small hammer. As Lucilius says: "And just as in the forge when the little hammer (*marculus*) beats the glowing iron with the great blows of many." **Pincers** (*forceps*) are like "iron-takers" (*ferricipes*), because they take hold of and keep a grip on glowing iron; or because with them we take and hold something from the furnace (*forvus*), as if they were "furnace-takers" (*forvicapes*). For *forvus* means hot, which is where we get the word "fervent" (*fervidus*), and why we call people "beautiful" (*formosos*), for whom the heat of the blood creates beauty out of a reddish glow. The **file** (*lima*) is so named because it makes things smooth (*lene*), for *limus* means smooth. The *lilium* is the tool used by silversmiths, from which engraved (*celata*) vessels are also named.

<margin>¶</margin>
### Chapter VIII: On the construction of walls

In the construction of walls and roofs, the Greeks claim that **Daedalus** <note>The mythical Greek architect and inventor</note> was the inventor. He is said to have been the first to learn the craft of building from Minerva. The Greeks call builders or craftsmen *tectones*, which means "arrangers." **Architects**, however, are the masons who arrange the foundations. Whence also the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in 1 Corinthians 3:10</note> says of himself:

<column-break/>

"As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation." **Masons** (*mationses*) are named after the "machines" (*machinae*) or scaffolds upon which they stand because of the height of the walls.

<margin>¶</margin>
### Chapter IX: On disposition

The parts of buildings are three: **disposition**, **construction**, and **beauty**. Disposition is the plan or description of the area, the ground, and the foundations.

<margin>¶</margin>
### Chapter X: On construction

Construction is the building up of the sides and the height. It is called construction or "instruction" because it binds and holds things together, such as stones with mortar, or wood and stones with each other. For the quenching of iron in water is also called "instruction"; for unless it is quenched while glowing, the iron cannot be bound and held together. Likewise, "construction" is named for the multitude of stones and wood; hence also the term "pile" (*strues*). Building (*aedificatio*) is one thing, and restoration (*instauratio*) is another. For building is new construction, while restoration is that which is repaired to the "likeness" (*instar*) of its former state; for the ancients used *instar* to mean similarity. Construction consists of the foundation, stones, sand, lime, and wood. The **foundation** (*fundamentum*) is so named because it is the "bottom" (*fundus*) of the building. Likewise, **cement** (*cementum*) is named from "cutting" (*caedendo*), because it rises from roughly cut stone. 

In masonry, several types of stone are used: white, Tiburtine, pigeon-colored, river-stone, sponge-stone, red, and others. **White stone** is sometimes hard and sometimes soft. The soft kind is cut with a toothed saw and is so easy to work with that letters can be written on it as if it were wood. **Tiburtine** <note>travertine</note> is named after a place in Italy <note>Tivoli</note>; although it is strong for building, it shatters under the influence of heat. **Tufa** (*tophus*) is useless for buildings but suitable for foundations because of its roughness and softness. It is worn and beaten in the shallows by the heat and the salt-breath of the sea. **Sandy stone** is composed of sea sands; it is also called "thirsty" (*bibulus*) because it retains the moisture it receives. Likewise, the **Gaditanus** stone is named from an island in the ocean <note>Cadiz</note> where it is most frequently quarried. **Pepper-stone** (*piperinus*) is whitish with black spots, hard, and very strong. **Snail-stone** (*concleatius*) is composed of small shells, pebbles, and sand; it is very rough and sometimes porous. **Pigeon-colored stone** (*columbinus*) is named for the color of the bird; it is naturally close to gypsum and very similar in softness. **Millstone** (*molaris*) is useful in walls because its nature is somewhat oily, hard, and rough; it is also the stone from which millstones are made, hence the name. There are four kinds of this: white, black, mixed, and porous. **Sponge-stone** (*spungia*) is a light, porous stone created from water, suitable for vaulted ceilings. **Siler** is a hard stone, of which the best kinds are the black flints found in certain places, as well as the red ones. **White flints** remain uncorrupted against age; likewise, when carved for monuments, they remain undamaged, and even fire cannot harm them. Indeed, molds for casting bronze are made from these. **Green flint** is also very resistant to fire, but it is never found in abundance, and where it is found, it is not a solid mass. **Pale stone** is rarely useful in cement. **Bibulus** <note>literally "drinker"</note> is strong against injury but unreliable in structures unless it is bound by much bracing. **River flint** is always as if it were damp; it must be used cautiously and not before...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s nineteenth book of the Etymologies. Having previously discussed the nature of fire and the tools of the forge, he now transitions into the practical application of these elements in architecture and the decorative arts, specifically focusing on building materials, masonry, and the aesthetics of Roman construction.</meta>

...to allow two years to pass before using timber in the construction of houses. In the making of pottery for walls and foundations, they use baked bricks; for roofs, they employ curved tiles and flat tiles. The flat tiles <note>original: "regulae"</note> are so named because they "rule" or guide the buildings; the curved tiles <note>original: "imbrices"</note> are named because they receive the rains <note>original: "imbres"</note>. "Rule" is the primary name, of which the diminutive is "small rule." Small bricks <note>original: "laterculi"</note> are named because they are formed wide by four wooden boards moved around them. Raw bricks (*lateres*), however, are also named for being wide (*lati*), and are shaped in wooden forms; the frames in which they carry the mud for these raw bricks are called crates. These are connections of reeds, named from the Greek word "to hold" <note>original: "kratein"</note>, because they hold one another together. Some think mud <note>original: "lutum"</note> is named by antiphrasis <note>A rhetorical device where a word is used to mean its opposite</note> because it is not clean; for indeed, all mud is clean <note>Isidore is making a pun: "lutum" (mud) sounds like "lautum" (clean/washed)</note>. Quicklime (*calx viva*) is so named because, while it is cold to the touch, it contains a hidden fire within, so that when water is poured over it, the latent fire immediately erupts. Its nature does something wonderful: after it has burned, it is ignited by water—which usually extinguishes fire—and is extinguished by oil—which usually feeds fire. Its use is necessary in building structures, for one stone cannot adhere strongly to another unless joined by lime. Gypsum is a relative of lime, and the name is Greek. There are several kinds of it, but the best is the "mirror-stone" <note>lapis specularis, likely mica or selenite</note>; it is excellent for buildings and highly prized for decorative moldings. Sand (*arena*) is named for its dryness (*ariditate*), not from "adhering" in buildings as some claim. The test for its quality is if it squeaks when pressed in the hand, or if it leaves no dirt when sprinkled on a white garment. Columns are named for their length and roundness; upon them, the weight of the entire structure is raised. According to the ancient rule, the height of columns was a third of their width <note>Isidore may be misinterpreting Vitruvian proportions here, or referring to a specific archaic style</note>. There are four types of round columns: Doric, Ionic, Tuscan, and Corinthian, differing from each other in the measurement of their thickness and height. A fifth kind is what they call "Attic," which has four angles or more with equal intervals between the sides. Bases are the supports of the columns that rise from the foundation and sustain the weight of the structure placed upon them; in the Syrian language, *base* is the name for a very strong stone. Capitals (*capitella*) are so named because they are the "heads" of the columns, like a head upon a neck. Architraves (*epistylia*) are those things placed above the capitals of the columns; the word is Greek, also called "over-beams." Pavements originated as a craft from the Greeks. They are called pavements (*pavimenta*) because they are beaten down <note>original: "paviant"</note>, that is, struck; from this also comes "terror" (*pavor*), which strikes the heart. An *ostracum* is a pavement made of pottery shards, so called because it is made of broken shells or tiles mixed with lime; for the Greeks call a shell *ostra*. "Rough stones" (*rudos*) is what craftsmen call unsorted stones mixed with lime, which they pour over when making pavements; from this they are called "rubble" (*rudera*). A channel (*canalis*) is named because it is hollow in the manner of a reed (*canna*). We should properly refer to a channel in the feminine gender rather than the masculine. Water pipes (*fistulae*) are so named because they "pour out and send" water; for in Greek, "to send" is *stola*. Their forms are made according to the volume and capacity of the water, through which the water is divided by certain standard measures. Among these are the *uncia* and the *quinaria*, the square digit, the round digit, and other measures for this purpose.

### Chapter XI: On Beauty

This concludes the section on construction; next follows the beauty of buildings. Beauty <note>original: "venustas"</note> consists of whatever ornament and decoration is added to buildings for the sake of elegance, such as ceilings adorned with gold, veneers of precious marble, and the painting of colors.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XII: On Paneled Ceilings

Paneled ceilings (*laquearia*) are those which support and adorn the vault from below; they are also called *lacunaria* because they have certain square or round hollows <note>original: "lacus", literally "lakes"</note> painted with wood, gypsum, or colors, with glittering images interspersed. Properly, however, it is called a "lake," as Lucilius says: "Both the houses and the hollowed ceilings (*lacus*) resound." The diminutive of this is *lacunar*, as Horace says: "No golden paneled ceiling (*lacunar*) gleams in my house." From this comes another diminutive, *lacunarium*, which by a change of letters becomes *laquearium*.

### Chapter XIII: On Veneers

Veneers (*crustae*) are thin slabs of marble. From this, walls are said to be "marbled" or "crusted." It is not certain who first devised the method of cutting marble into thin slabs. They are made using sand and iron; the iron presses the sand in a very thin line, and the dragging motion itself does the cutting, though coarser sand erodes more of the marble. Thin sand is suited for fine work and polishing.

### Chapter XIV: On Mosaic Pavements

Mosaic pavements (*lithostrata*) are works elaborated with the art of painting using tiny veneers and small tiles <note>original: "tessellae"</note> dyed in various colors. These tiles are named after *tesserae*, which are small square stones, by way of diminutive.

### Chapter XV: On Modeling

Modeling (*plasticen*) is the art of expressing the likenesses of figures on walls using gypsum, and painting them with colors. It is called *plasticen* in Greek, which in Latin is "to fashion" (*fingere*) likenesses from earth or gypsum. For to create some form from pressed clay is the work of a modeler (*plastis*). From this, man was called the "first-formed" <note>original: "protoplastus"</note>, because he was the first to be fashioned from the mud.

### Chapter XVI: On Painting

Painting (*pictura*) is an image expressing the appearance of some thing. When it is seen, it brings the mind back to a memory. It is called "painting" as if it were a "fiction" <note>original: "ficura"</note>. For it is a fashioned image, not the truth. Hence it is also called "counterfeit" (*fucata*), that is, smeared with a certain false color, having nothing of faith or truth. Thus there are certain paintings that exceed the bodies of truth out of a zeal for color, and while they strive to increase credibility, they are carried away into falsehood—such as those who paint the three-headed Chimera, or 
<margin>the false</margin>
Scylla as a human above, but girded with dogs' heads below. The Egyptians first devised painting by tracing the shadow of a man with lines. Thus at the beginning it was like that; in the second stage, it used single colors; afterwards, diverse ones. Thus, little by little, the art distinguished itself and discovered light, shadows, and the differences between colors. Therefore, even now, painters first draw the shadows and lines of the future image, and then fill them in with colors, following the order of the invented art.

### Chapter XVII: On Colors

Colors are so named because they are perfected by the heat <note>original: "calore"</note> of fire or the sun, or because they were initially strained <note>original: "colabant"</note> so that they might exist with the highest subtlety. Colors are either natural or man-made. Natural ones include sinopia and red ochre...

Isidore explains the physical properties of materials alongside their linguistic origins and the historical development of artistic techniques.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s encyclopedic survey of the arts. Following the discussion of building materials like bricks and lime, Isidore now catalogs the various pigments used in painting and decoration (Chapter 17), before transitioning into the physical tools required for masonry and construction (Chapter 18).</meta>

Parettonium, Melian white, Eretrian earth, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"</note>. Others are fashioned either by art or by mixing. Sinopia <note>A red ochre pigment</note> was first found in Pontus; from there it took its name from the city of Sinope. There are three kinds: red, less red, and a medium between these two. It is called *rubrica* <note>Red ochre</note> because it is red <note>original: "rubra"</note> and primary for blood-colored work. This is produced in many places, but the best comes from Pontus, which is why it is also called "Pontic." Syrian red <note>original: "Syricum"</note> is a red pigment from which the headings of books <note>The "rubrics"</note> are written. It is the same as Phoenician red, so named because it is gathered in Syria on the shores of the Red Sea where the Phoenicians live. *Seric* is one thing; *Syric* is another. For *Seric* <note>Silk</note> spelled with an 'e' is the wool that the Seres <note>The Chinese</note> send; *Syric* with a 'y' is the pigment that the Syrian Phoenicians gather on the shores of the Red Sea. There is also an artificial version; for it is often made by mixing sinopia or sandyx.

The Greeks say they first found minium <note>Red lead or cinnabar</note> in the soil of the Ephesians. Spain abounds in this pigment more than other regions; hence it even gave its name to the river Minius <note>The Miño river</note>. Its distillation produces "liquid silver" <note>Mercury</note>. Some say that this minium is cinnabar <note>original: "cinnabarin"</note>. Cinnabar is named after the dragon and the "barrus"—that is, the elephant. For they say it is the blood of dragons crushed when they entangle elephants. Both the beasts fall and the dragons are overwhelmed, and their spilled blood stains the earth; thus, the pigment is whatever has dyed the soil. It is a red-colored powder.

*Prasin* <note>original: "Prasin"</note> is green chalk; and though it is produced indiscriminately in some lands, the best is in Cyrenaic Libya. Chrysocolla <note>Gold-glue/Malachite</note> is called "leek-green" in color because its vein is said to contain gold. This is found in Armenia and comes as a reputable product from Macedonia. It is dug from copper mines. Its discovery rendered silver and indigo <note>original: "indicum"</note> useless, for its veins have a natural affinity with them. Cyprian earth comes from the island of Cyprus, where it is found in great quantities. Sandarac <note>original: "Sandaraca"</note> is produced on Topazos, an island in the Red Sea, and is the color of cinnabar with a sulfurous odor. It is found in gold and silver mines; the better and redder it is, the more it smells of poison. Also, white lead <note>original: "cerusa"</note>, if toasted in a furnace, becomes sandarac, whence the color is flame-like. And if it is toasted with an equal part of *rubrica* added, it yields sandyx. Arsenic, which the Latins call *auripigmentum* <note>Orpiment/Gold-pigment</note> because of its gold color, is gathered in Pontus from gold-bearing material, where sandarac is also found. The best is that which shifts into a gold color, pure and easy to split into thin veins. That which is paler or resembles sandarac is judged inferior. There is also a third, scaly kind, where a gold color is mixed in. Their power is like that of sandarac, but sharper. Ochre <note>original: "Ocra"</note> is also produced on Topazos, the island in the Red Sea, where sandarac is found. Ochre is also made from burnt *rubrica* in new pots smeared with mud; the more it burns in the furnace, the better it becomes.

"Venetian" blue <note>original: "Venetum"</note> or cerulean was first tempered in Alexandria. In Italy, they make the same from the dust of sand and the "flower" of nitre. But if you add copper burned in a furnace to this mixture, it will be a likeness of "Vestorian" blue. *Purpurissum* <note>A purple pigment</note> is made from silver-chalk together with purple dyes; it takes the color quickly. It is excellent for wools. However, another kind is that which is first soaked in a vat with raw medicinal ingredients; once that is removed, more chalk is added to the vessel...

<column-break/>

...the same. And every time this is done, the quality increases because of the most precious purple, for it is most deeply dyed with kermes <note>original: "illicino"</note> and becomes red. Indigo <note>original: "Indicum"</note> is found in Indian reeds, as a foam adhering to the mud. It is a cyan color, providing a marvelous mixture of purple and blue. There is another kind found in the foam of purple-dyeing workshops, floating in bronze cauldrons; the dyers skim it off and dry it.

Black pigment <note>original: "Atramentum," also used for ink</note> is so named because it is black <note>original: "atrum"</note>. It is necessary for painting and daily use. This is among the artificial pigments. It is made from soot in several ways, such as by burning resin-covered torches in a small chamber built to retain the smoke. To this, painters add glue mixed with water so that it shines more brightly. To speed up the work, ground coals of old brushwood mixed with glue also provide the appearance of black pigment for coating walls. There are also those who bake dried wine dregs, claiming that if it is made from good wine, the pigment provides the appearance of indigo. Also, black grape brushwood soaked in the best wine, then dried, burned, and ground with glue, yields the luster of indigo. Burnt ochre <note>original: "ustagium"</note> is very necessary and is produced with no trouble. For if you bake a lump of good flint in a fire and extinguish it by pouring on very sharp vinegar, a soaked sponge yields a purple color. When you have ground it, it will be "burnt" pigment. Black pigment perfects itself. All colors are ruined by the mixture of lime.

Melian white <note>original: "Melinum"</note> is so named because it is found in one of the Cyclades islands called Melos. It is white, but painters do not use it because of its excessive greasiness. "Ring-white" <note>original: "Anulare"</note>, as they call it, is what is used to brighten the paintings of women <note>Likely referring to cosmetics or depictions of women</note>. It is made from chalk mixed with glass gems. White lead <note>original: "Cerusa"</note> is made in this way: in a vessel filled with very sharp vinegar, you place *aminean* brushwood, and over the brushwood you put very thin plates of lead. Then you close the vessel very carefully and seal it so that no air escapes. After thirty days, the vessel is opened, and the white lead is found created from the distillation of the plates. What is removed and dried is ground, mixed again with vinegar, divided into small tablets, and dried in the sun. By this same method, if you put copper plates under the brushwood, they create verdigris <note>original: "eruginem"</note>. *Calcantum* <note>Copperas/Blue vitriol</note> is so named because it is the "thyme"—that is, the flower—of lime <note>original: "calcis"</note>; hence among the Latins it is called the "flower of copper."

# On Building Tools Chapter 18

<margin>A red paraph mark (symbol for a new section).</margin>
**T**he construction of walls must be done according to the square <note>original: "norma"</note> and correspond to the plumb line. The "square" is named from a Greek word, without which nothing straight can be made. It is composed of three rulers in such a way that two are two feet long, and the third has two feet and ten inches. These, polished to equal thickness, are joined at their ends to form the shape of a triangle; that is the square. The "ruler" <note>original: "regula"</note> is so named because it is straight <note>original: "recta"</note>, as if it were a "small straight thing" and has no impediment. The "plumb line" <note>original: "perpendiculum"</note> is that which always hangs down <note>original: "appenditur"</note>. In masonry, unless everything is made certain by the plumb line and ruler, everything will necessarily be constructed poorly—some parts crooked, some leaning, some tilted forward, others backward, and despite this, the whole structure will be unsound. The name for the trowel <note>original: "trulle"</note> was created because it "thrusts" <note>original: "trudit"</note> and "pushes down" <note>original: "derrudit"</note>; that is, it encloses stones within lime or mud.
