### Chapter 19: On Woodworkers

**A** woodworker <note>original: "lignarius"</note> is generally called a worker in wood. "Carpenter" <note>original: "carpentarius"</note> is a specific name, for he only makes a wagon <note>original: "carpentum"</note>, just as a shipwright <note>original: "navicularius"</note> is one who builds only ships. The "joiner" <note>original: "sarcitectus"</note> is so named because he "mends" <note>original: "sarciat"</note> or joins together one straight body from many boards gathered from here and there. He is the same as a woodworker because he applies wood paneling <note>original: "tectoria"</note> to structures. Wood <note>original: "lignum"</note> is named by Greek etymology because when burned it turns into light <note>original: "lumen"</note> and flame. From this also the "wick" <note>original: "lychninium"</note> is named because it gives light. "Material" <note>original: "materia"</note> is the name for any wood from which something might be made; whether you refer to a door or a statue, it will be the "matter." For "matter" must always be understood in relation to something else, just as we say the elements are the "matter" of things, because from them we see the things that are made. And *materia* is named as if it were a "mother" <note>original: "mater"</note>. Beams <note>original: "trabes"</note> are so called because they are placed "crosswise" <note>original: "transverso"</note> to hold both walls together. However, joists <note>original: "tigna"</note> are one thing and beams are another; for joined joists make a beam. Beams are specifically those that have been hewn <note>squared with an ax</note>. A *tholus* <note>boss or cupola</note> is properly like a short shield in the middle of a roof where the beams meet. "Couplers" <note>original: "copulae"</note> are named because they couple together those that are "wrestling" <note>original: "luctantes"</note>. Those that stand upright holding each other in the manner of wrestlers are called "wrestlers" <note>referring to rafters</note>. *Agrantes*... <note>The text here is likely corrupted in the OCR</note>. Boards <note>original: "asseres"</note> are named from "unity" <note>original: "asse"</note> because they are placed alone and not joined. Shingles <note>original: "scandulae"</note> are named because they are "split" <note>original: "scindantur"</note>, that is, divided. Pegs <note>original: "epigri"</note> and nails <note>original: "clavi"</note> are the things by which wood adheres to wood. Nails are called *clavi* as if they were "steely" <note>original: "chalybi"</note>, because they are made of steel <note>original: "chalybe"</note>, which is iron. Boards <note>original: "tabulae"</note> were called *tagulae* by the ancients, specifically from "covering" <note>original: "tegendo"</note>, from which also "rules" <note>original: "regulae"</note> or slats are named. A "joint" <note>original: "commissura"</note> is the joining together of boards. A "section" <note>original: "sectio"</note> is named from "following" <note>original: "sequendo"</note> what it has begun. For "to cut" <note>original: "secare"</note> is "to pursue" <note>original: "sectari"</note> and "to follow." The name of the "saw" <note>original: "serra"</note> is made from its sound, that is, from its screeching. A certain youth named Perdix invented the use of the saw and the compass <note>original: "circinus"</note>; his uncle Daedalus <note>The mythical architect of the Labyrinth</note> had taken him as a boy to be taught in studies. The boy's genius is said to have been so great that while seeking a shortcut for dividing material, he imitated a fish's spine by sharpening an iron blade and arming it with a biting row of teeth; this the craftsmen call a "saw." Out of envy for this invention, his master Daedalus threw the boy headlong from a citadel. Afterward, Daedalus went into exile in Crete and remained there for a while until, as the myths say, he flew from Crete on wings and came to Cilicia. The compass is named because by turning <note>original: "vergendo"</note> it makes a circle <note>original: "circulum"</note>. Its method involves a doubled line, which had been a simple one extended in width. The point <note>original: "punctus"</note> in the middle of the compass is called the "center" <note>original: "centrum"</note> by the Greeks, in the middle of which all things converge. An ax <note>original: "securis"</note> is named because with it they "cut down" <note>original: "succidant"</note> trees, as if it were a *succuris*. Likewise, *securis* is like "half-curis" <note>original: "semicuris"</note>. For it is sharp on one side and a digging tool on the other. This was called a "wing" <note>original: "penna"</note> by the ancients; one having a sharp edge on both sides is a "double-wing" <note>original: "bipennis"</note>. For it is called *bipennis* because it has a sharp edge on both sides, 

<column-break/>

as if it had two wings. The ancients used to call something sharp *pennum*, from which even the "wings" <note>original: "pennae"</note> of birds are named because they are sharp. And behold, this is a name that has preserved antiquity, for the ancients said *pennas*, not *pinnas*. These are also "mattocks" <note>original: "dolabrae"</note> because they have "two lips" <note>original: "duo labra"</note>; for a standard ax is simple. A "hand-ax" <note>original: "dextralis"</note> is one manageable for the right hand <note>original: "dexterae"</note>. An "adze" <note>original: "ascia"</note> is named from the "chips" <note>original: "astulis"</note> which it removes from the wood; its diminutive is *asciola*. It has a short handle and on the opposite side resembles either a simple mallet, a hollowed one, or a two-pronged rake. A "chisel" <note>original: "scalprus"</note> is named because it is fit for "carving" <note>original: "sculpturi"</note> holes, as if it were a *scalphus*; its diminutive is *scalpellus*. An "auger" <note>original: "terebra"</note> is named after a wood-worm called a *terebra*, which the Greeks call *teredon*. Hence the tool is called a *terebra* because it bores by "rubbing" <note>original: "terendo"</note> like the worm; as if it were "bore-bearing" or "boring through." A "gimlet" <note>original: "taratrum"</note> is as if it were a "borer." A "rasp" <note>original: "scophina"</note> is named because by clinging it makes "shavings" <note>original: "scophae"</note>. A lantern <note>original: "lanterium"</note>. Gallic words: *buvia* <note>These appear to be obscure regional terms for tools</note>.

### Chapter 20: On the Invention of Woolworking

**T**he pagans praise a certain Minerva for many talents; they say she first showed the use of woolworking. They claim she also began the loom and taught how to dye wool. They also say she was the inventor of the olive tree and of craftsmanship, and the discoverer of many arts. Therefore, craftsmen commonly pray to her. But this is a poetic fiction. Minerva is not truly the author of these arts. Rather, because wisdom is said to be in the head of a human, and Minerva is fabled to have been born from the head of Jove, this represents "genius" <note>intellect</note>; and so the sense of the wise man who invented all these things is in the head. Thus Minerva is called the goddess of arts, because nothing is more excellent than the genius by which all things are governed.

### Chapter 21: On Priestly Vestments

**T**here are eight kinds of priestly garments in the Law <note>The Old Testament/Torah</note>. The *poderis* is a linen priestly tunic, fitted to the body and descending to the feet <note>original: "pedes"</note>, from which it takes its name; for the Greeks call feet *podes*. This is commonly called a *camisia* <note>A shirt or chemise</note>. The *abanet* is a round priestly girdle <note>sash</note> woven with many-colored art from scarlet, purple, and hyacinth, so that flowers and gems seem to be distinguished within it. The *pilleum* is a round cap of fine linen like a half-sphere, covering the priest's head and bound at the back with a ribbon. The Greeks and our people call this a "tiara" or helmet. The *machil* <note>The me'il or robe</note> is a tunic reaching the ankles, entirely of hyacinth-color <note>violet/blue</note>, having seventy-two bells at the feet, with pomegranates interspersed and hanging down. The *ephod* is interpreted in Latin as an "over-garment." It was a shoulder-cape woven from four colors and gold, having on each shoulder two emerald stones set in gold, in which were engraved the names of the patriarchs. The *logium* <note>The breastplate</note>, which in Latin is called the "rational" <note>original: "rationale"</note>, is a double cloth of gold and four woven colors, the size of a palm's breadth square, into which were inserted twelve most precious stones. This cloth was fastened against the priest's chest over the ephod. The *petalum* <note>plate</note> is a golden plate on the priest's forehead, which had the ineffable name of God, the "tetragrammaton," written in Hebrew letters. The *batin*, or "breeches," are linen drawers reaching to the knees, by which the nakedness of the priest was veiled. For in Hebrew, *bat* <note>Hebrew: "bad"</note> means linen.

## On the Names of Clothing and Others, Chapter 22

**T**he diversity of garments includes the covering <note>original: "tegmen"</note>, the mantle, the clothing, the vestment, and the rest. A "covering" is so called because it covers the members; thus, a "roof" <note>original: "tegumē"</note> or "coverings" <note>original: "tecta"</note> are things that cover the body. An "under-garment" <note>original: "indumentum"</note> is so called because it is put on <note>original: "induitur"</note> inside, next to the body, as if it were an "inner-body" <note>original: "intumentum"</note>. A "cloak" <note>original: "amictus"</note>. A "vestment" <note>original: "vestimentum"</note> is truly that which reaches down to the footprint <note>original: "vestigium"</note>, as if it were a "footprint-garment" <note>original: "vestigimentum"</note>, such as an ankle-length tunic. But this custom of speech is widely used by authors. "Attire" <note>original: "vestitutus"</note>, however, is distinguished from "finery" <note>original: "cultu"</note>, for the elegant are understood to have finery. Likewise, finery is distinguished from "habit" <note>original: "habitu"</note>, for habit pertains to nature, while finery pertains to men. Moreover, most garments are named either from the time when they are most in use, or from the places where they were first made or are most claimed, or from the type of color, or from the name of their inventors. The most ancient garment of men was the *perizoma* <note>original: "picomatum"</note>, that is, a loincloth, which covers only the genitals. The first mortals made this for themselves from the leaves of trees, when, blushing because of their transgression, they covered their shameful parts. Some barbarian nations, though they are otherwise naked, maintain the use of this even today. These are also called "field-garments" <note>original: "campestria"</note>, for the reason that young men, who exercise naked in the field <note>original: "campo"</note>, cover their genitals with them. The "tunic" <note>original: "tunica"</note>, a very ancient garment, is named because in the motion of one walking it makes a sound; for a "tone" <note>original: "tonus"</note> is a sound. But first there were "skin tunics" <note>original: "pelliceę"</note>, with which Adam and Eve were clothed after their offense and expulsion from Paradise. An "ankle-length tunic" <note>original: "talaris"</note> is named because it descends all the way to the ankles <note>original: "talos"</note> and flows down to the feet. There is the "breast-cloth" <note>original: "pectoralis"</note>, which among the ancients was short so that it covered only the chest, though now it is more flowing. A "sleeved tunic" <note>original: "manicleata"</note> is one with sleeves, because it has sleeves <note>original: "manicas"</note>, which the Greeks call *chirodyta* <note>Greek: "hand-covering"</note>. The "Dalmatic" <note>original: "dalmatica"</note> garment was first woven in Dalmatia, a province of Greece. The "priestly tunic" is white with purple stripes. The "russet-red" <note>original: "russata"</note> garment, which the Greeks call "phoenician," and we call "scarlet," was invented by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> to hide the appearance of the color of blood whenever someone was wounded in the battle line, lest the heart of the adversary should be emboldened by the sight. The Romans used this under the consuls, which is why they were called "the russet-red ones." For they were accustomed to display it before the headquarters on the day before they were to fight, as a reminder and sign of the coming battle. A "checkered garment" <note>original: "laculata"</note> is one that has certain square "pools" <note>original: "lacus"</note> with pictures woven into them, or added with a needle. A "hyacinthine garment" <note>original: "hyacyntina"</note> is one shining with an airy <note>sky-blue</note> color. "Mallow-cloth" <note>original: "holocinia"</note> is that which is made from the fiber of mallows; some call it "honey-colored," others "mallow-thread." "Silkworm-cloth" <note>original: "bombycina"</note> is that which is produced from the silkworm <note>original: "bombyce"</note>, a small worm which generates very long threads from itself, the weaving of which is called *bombycinum*; it is produced on the island of Cos. Silk <note>original: "serica"</note> is named from the "Seres" <note>The Chinese</note>, or because the Seres first traded it. "All-silk" <note>original: "holoserica"</note> is entirely silk, for *holo* means "total." "Silk-warp" <note>original: "tramoserica"</note> has a linen warp and a silk woof. "All-purple" <note>original: "holoporpyra"</note> is entirely of purple. "Byssine" <note>original: "byssina"</note> is a white cloth made from a certain type of thick flax; there are those who think that *byssus* is a type of silk. "Beaver-cloth" <note>original: "fabrina"</note> has a woof from the wool of the beaver <note>original: "fibri"</note>. "Hare-cloth" <note>original: "lapina"</note>. "Black-cloth" <note>original: "melena"</note> because it is black in color; for the Greeks call black *melan*. "Mastic-colored" <note>original: "masticina"</note> because it has the color of mastic. "Linen" <note>original: "linea"</note> is that which is made from flax <note>original: "lino"</note> alone. "Linostema" is a garment woven from wool and flax together; and it is called *linostema* because it has flax in the warp and wool in the woof. A garment is called "upright" <note>original: "recta"</note> which they weave while standing and looking upward. "Segmented" <note>original: "segmen-

<column-break/>

tata"</note> garments are those adorned with certain fringes or trimmings, as if they were "cut-offs." For they call small particles of any material cut away "pre-segments." "Lightly-woven" <note>original: "leuidentis"</note> because it is lightly densified with thin thread. "Beaten-cloth" <note>original: "pauitensis"</note> is the opposite of the lightly-woven; it is so called because it has been heavily pressed and trodden. "Citron-like" <note>original: "citrosa"</note> as if curled like the grain of citron wood. "Snow-white" <note>original: "neuus"</note>. "A beautiful garment of gold and a citron-like cloth." The "Velenensian" tunic is one that is brought from the islands. An "exotic garment" <note>original: "exotica"</note> is a foreign one coming from outside, as in Spain from the Greeks. "Multi-threaded" <note>original: "polymita"</note> is of many colors, for the weave of *polymitum* is of many colors. "Needle-painted" <note>original: "acupicta"</note> is a garment woven with a needle or adorned with a needle. This is the same as "Phrygian," for those skilled in this art are called "Phrygians," either because it was invented in Phrygia or because the craftsmen who do it are called Phrygians. Virgil says: "And a Phrygian cloak." "Three-ply" <note>original: "trilicis"</note> from three threads, which is simple and double. "Thin-cloth" <note>original: "ralla"</note> which is commonly called "shorn." An "interpolated" <note>original: "interpola"</note> garment is that which, while it is old, is returned to a new appearance. "Patched" <note>original: "panutia"</note> is named because it is covered with various rags <note>original: "pannis"</note>. A "colobium" is so called because it is long and without sleeves; for the ancients used this more often. A "libitoniarium" is a *colobium* without sleeves, such as the Egyptian monks use. A "loincloth" <note>original: "lumbare"</note> is so called because it is tied to the loins <note>original: "lumbis"</note>, or because it clings to the loins. In Egypt and Syria, not only women but also men use this. Hence Jeremiah took his loincloth across the Euphrates and hid it there in a hole in a rock, and later found it torn. This is also called a "kidney-wrap" <note>original: "renale"</note> by some because it is tied to the kidneys. A "limus" is a garment that is drawn from the navel down to the feet. This garment has at its edge a purple "lima" <note>border</note>, that is, a wavy one, from which it took its name; for we call *limum* something oblique. A "licinum" is so called because its weave is tied in a twist, as if one were to say "liginum," with the 'c' substituted for the letter 'g'. A "shoulder-cloak" <note>original: "armelausa"</note> is commonly so called because it is divided and open in front and behind, and closed only at the shoulders <note>original: "armos"</note>, as if it were "armiclausa," with the letter 'c' removed. We call them "shirts" <note>original: "camisas"</note> because we sleep in them in "beds" <note>original: "camis"</note>, that is, in our bedding. "Breeches" <note>original: "femoralia"</note> are named because they cover the thighs <note>original: "femora"</note>. These are also "trousers" <note>original: "brachę"</note> because they are short and cover the shameful parts of the body with them. They say they are called "leg-covers" <note>original: "lubrucos"</note> because they rule the shins and the trousers. "Pipe-trousers" <note>original: "tubraci"</note> because they reach from the breeches all the way to the shins.

## On the Clothing of Certain Nations, Chapter 23

**T**o certain nations, however, there is a specific garment proper to each: as the *sarabarae* to the Parthians, the *linneae* to the Gauls, the *rhenones* to the Germans, the *stringes* to the Spaniards, and the *mastruce* to the Sardinians. *Sarabarae* are flowing and billowing garments, of which we read in Daniel: "And their trousers <note>original: "sarabarae"</note> were not changed." And Publius: "As if the Parthians hung trousers <note>original: "sarabara"</note> in your belly." Among some, however, *sarabara* are named as certain head coverings, such as we see painted on the heads of the Magi. *Linneae* are square and soft cloaks, of which Plautus says: "The Gallic weaver is covered with a *linna*." *Rhenones* are coverings for the shoulders and chest reaching to the navel, and are so shaggy with twisted tufts that they repel rain; they are commonly called "creepers" <note>original: "repros"</note> because the length of the tufts seems to creep along. Of which Sallust says: "The Germans cover their naked bodies with *rhenones*." Moreover, they are called *rhenones* from the Rhine, the river of Germany, where these are frequently used. The *mastruca* is a Germanic garment made from the skins of wild beasts. Of which...

# XIX

**mastruca, pallium, chlamys, toga, trabea, paludamentum, sagum, penula, lacerna, mantum, praetexta, cuculla, melotes, stola, ricinium** <note>These terms represent the diverse types of cloaks and ethnic garments discussed in the following chapters.</note>

Cicero, in his speech *For Scaurus*, says: "Whom the royal purple did not move, the Sardinian *mastruca* <note>original: "mastruca"</note> changed." The *mastruca* is so named because it is "monstrous" <note>original: "monstruosa"</note>, for those who wear it are transformed as if into the appearance of wild beasts. Nations are distinguished by their dress just as they are by their differing languages. The Persians rule their arms and legs with linen wraps and their heads with a tiara. The Alans are distinguished by their high-pointed caps. The Scots are covered with tattoos on their jaws, as if with barking tongues. The Alemanni are cloaked in the *sagum*. The Indians wear linen. Most of the Chinese <note>original: "Seres"</note> wear silk decorated with gems. The Armenians carry quivers. Some nations claim certain marks on their bodies as their own unique insignias, not just in their clothing: for example, we see the curls <note>original: "cirros"</note> of the Germans, the braids and cinnabar dye of the Goths, and the tattoos of the Britons. The Jews circumcise their foreskins; the Arabs pierce their ears. The Getae have yellow hair on their heads; the Albani shine with white hair. The land of the Moors produces black bodies; the Gauls have white skin. The Alans wander uncertainly without horses <note>original: "sine equis"; usually "without homes" (sine sedibus) in other manuscripts</note>. Nor is the nation of the Picts absent, whose name comes from their bodies, because a skilled craftsman pricks them with tiny needle points and includes the expressed juice of a native plant, so that the body bears scars to represent its character, a spotted nobility with painted limbs. Even slaves have an established appearance in their dress: for men, the hair is shorn; for women, there is an abundance of hair, which is especially a sign for virgins, whose very adornment is such that the hair is gathered on the crown to cover the circumference of the head itself.

->## XXIV. On the Cloaks of Men<-

A "mantle" <note>original: "pallium"</note> is that in which the shoulders of those serving are covered, so that they may run about unhindered while they serve. Plautus says: "If you are going to do anything, hang your mantle on your shoulders and proceed with as much speed as your feet can muster." It is called a *pallium* from "skins" <note>original: "pellibus"</note>, because the ancients previously wore skin undergarments, as if they were "skin-like" <note>original: "pellea"</note>; or it is derived from *palla*. The *chlamys* <note>original: "chlamys"</note> is a cloak put on from one side and not sewn, but fastened with a buckle <note>original: "fibula"</note>; it takes its name from the Greek. The "toga" <note>original: "toga"</note> is so called because it rules and covers the body with its veil. It is a plain mantle with a round shape, and a fuller, flowing fold <note>original: "sinu"</note>; coming under the right arm, it is placed over the left shoulder. We see its likeness in the coverings of statues or paintings, and we call these "toga-wearing" <note>original: "togatas"</note> statues. The Romans wore the toga in times of peace, but in times of war they wore the *paludamentum*. The measure of a proper toga is six cubits. The *toga palmata* was so called because it was earned by those who brought back the palms of victory from the enemy. It was also called the *toga picta* ("painted toga") because it featured the victors with embroidered palms. The *toga candida* was the same as the *toga cretata* ("chalked toga"), in which the candidates—those seeking the power of the magistracies—canvassed, having added chalk so they would be whiter and more distinguished. Cicero wrote of this in the speech he gave against his competitors "in the white toga" <note>original: "in toga candida"</note>. The "Gabine cinch" <note>original: "Cinctus Gabinus"</note> is when the toga is put on such that a flap of the toga, which is thrown back over the shoulder, is drawn back to the chest so that pictures hang from the shoulders on both sides, as the priests of the heathens used to do, or as leaders would gird themselves. The *trabea* was a type of toga made of purple and scarlet, which the best kings of the Romans originally wore. Romulus is said to have first introduced this to distinguish the royal dress. It was called *trabea* because it "carried the man across" <note>original: "transveherer"</note> into greater glory, and made him blessed <note>original: "beatum"</note> with a further and more ample dignity of honor. The *paludamen-*

<column-break/>

*-tum* was the distinguished cloak of emperors, marked by scarlet, purple, and gold. Of this, Sallust says: "He exchanged the toga for the *paludamentum*." For it was a warlike cloak, so named (as it seemed to some) because the one dressed in it made "plain" <note>original: "palam faceret"</note> that he would be the commander of a future war. The "bordered cloak" <note>original: "circumtextum"</note> is what is called a *cyclas* in Greek. Of this, Virgil says: "And a veil bordered <note>original: "circumtextum"</note> with yellow acanthus." It is called *circumtextum* because it is a round mantle. *Diplois* is a Greek name, from the fact that it is a "double" <note>original: "duplex"</note> wrap. Horace says: "Against which patience is veiled with a double cloth." The *sagum* <note>original: "sagum"</note> is a military garment, the use of which first began in the Gallic expeditions from enemy spoils. Concerning this is that voice to the Senate: "The citizens, having set aside their togas, turned to their *saga*." *Sagum* is a Gallic name. It is called *sagum quadrum* ("square sagum") because among them it was originally square or fourfold. The *penula* is a mantle with long fringes. The *lacerna* is a fringed mantle that once only soldiers used; hence, in distinguishing the camp crowd from the city crowd, they called the latter "toga-wearers" and the former "lacerna-wearers." They are called *lacernae* because the ends of the fringes are cut off <note>original: "amputatis"</note>, nor are they as wide as the *penulae*. The Spanish call a *mantum* that which "wipes the hands" <note>original: "manus tergat"</note> only, for it is a short wrap. The *praetexta* is a boy’s mantle, which noble boys wore under the care of discipline until they were sixteen years old; hence they were called *praetextati* boys. It is called *praetexta* because a wider purple border "bordered" <note>original: "praeterebant"</note> it. The *casula* <note>the ancestor of the modern chasuble</note> is a hooded garment, named as a diminutive from "house" <note>original: "casa"</note>, because it covers the whole man, like a "little house." From this comes the "cowl" <note>original: "cuculla"</note>, as if it were a "little cell" <note>original: "cella"</note>; the Greeks say the same. They wish them to be called *planetae* ("planets") because they wander with straying borders; hence the "planet" stars, that is, wanderers, because they run about wandering in their own error and motion. The *birrus* derives its name from the Greek, for they call it a *birrum bibron*. The *melotes*, which is also called a *pera* ("pouch"), is a goat skin hanging from the neck and girded down to the loins. It is a garment properly necessary for the exercise of work. Some believe they were previously made from the skins of badgers <note>original: "melonum"</note>, from which they were called *melotes*. Fringes <note>original: "fimbriae"</note> are called the edges of garments—that is, the "ends" <note>original: "fines"</note>—and they derive the word from the Greek, for they call these the "extremities of the borders."

->## XXV. On the Cloaks of Women<-

The *regillum* is the distinguished little mantle of queens, from which it is named. The *peplum* is a matron’s mantle, marked with purple, whose fringes shine at the top with golden threads. The *palla* is a square woman's garment drawn down to the feet, with gems set in order. It is called *palla* from the Greek word *pellein*, that is, from the "mobility" <note>original: "mobilitate"</note> which is around the end of this kind of clothing, or because it is crimped into vibrating folds. The *stola* is a matronly covering which, with the head covered, is cast from the right side over to the left shoulder. It is called *stola* in Greek because it is "placed over" <note>original: "superimmittatur"</note>. The same is called a *ricinium* in its Latin name, because half of it is "thrown back" <note>original: "retro eijcitur"</note>; it is commonly called a *maforte*. They say it is called a *maforte* as if "Mars-like" <note>original: "martem"</note>. For the sign of marital dignity and power is in it; for the "head of the woman is the man," therefore it is over the woman's head. The *amiculum* is the linen mantle of prostitutes. Among the ancients, those caught in adultery were made to wear this, so that they might pollute their modesty in such a "little cloak" rather than in a *stola*. For it was...

This, among the ancients, was a sign of a prostitute’s garment; now in Spain, it is a sign of respectability. The **theristrum** <note>original: "Theristrum"</note> is a woman's cloak, so named because it protects the bodies of women in *theri*—that is, in heat and scorching sun <note>original: "in theri·id ē in ęstu"; the name is derived from the Greek "theros" meaning summer</note>—which women in Arabia and Mesopotamia use even today to veil themselves, finding it the safest protection against the heat. Of this garment, we read in Isaiah. The **anaboladium** <note>original: "Anaboladiū"</note> is a linen wrap for women that covers the shoulders, which the Greeks and Latins call *syndon* <note>original: "syndonē"; fine linen</note>.

### Chapter XXVI: On bedding and other garments in use

The **stragulum** <note>original: "Stragulū"</note> is a multi-colored garment distinguished by various patterns from the hand of a craftsman. It is so named because it is suitable for both bedding <note>original: "stratu"</note> and clothing. Of this, Solomon says: "She made herself a tapestry garment." Some believe **lodices** <note>shrouds or blankets</note> are named after *ludi*—that is, theaters. For when young men came out of a brothel or theater, they would cover their heads and faces with this veil, as those who had entered a house of ill-repute were accustomed to blush with shame. **Fulcra** <note>original: "Fulcra"</note> are the ornaments of beds, so called because we are "supported" <note>original: "fulcimur"</note> by them—that is, sustained—or because they support the cushions or the head; the common people call these "recliners." **Cervicalia** <note>pillows</note> are so named because they are placed under the *cervix* <note>the neck</note> or the elbow. The **puluillus** <note>cushion</note> is named after the *puluinari* <note>a cushioned seat for the gods</note>, which is a bed for the wealthy. **Culcitrae** <note>mattresses</note> are so called because they are "trodden"—that is, stuffed with feathers or wool <note>original: "tomento"</note>—to make them softer and warmer. **Tapeta** <note>tapestries or carpets</note> are named because they were first spread at the feet, as if they were *tapedia* <note>ground-footings</note>. Tapestries are either simple or **amphitapa**. Simple tapestries are shaggy on one side; **amphitapa** are shaggy on both sides. Lucilius says: "And soft *amphitapa* with huge tufts." **Mantelia** <note>tablecloths</note> are now used for covering tables; as the name itself indicates, they were once provided for wiping the hands <note>original: "manus"</note>; alternatively, *mantelia* comes from *mandendo* <note>eating</note>. The **mappe** <note>napkins</note> for guests and feasts are like *manupę* <note>hand-guides</note>, and are named for that reason; the diminutive is *mappella*. **Toralia** <note>original: "Tozalia"</note> are long and wide napkins named after the *torus* <note>bed or couch</note>. **Sabanum** is a Greek name <note>a towel or linen cloth</note>. The **facitergium** <note>face-wiper</note> and **manutergiū** <note>hand-wiper</note> are named for wiping the face or hands. **Vela** <note>curtains or veils</note> are so called because by their presence they "veil" <note>original: "velent"</note> the interiors of houses. **Aulea** <note>original: "Aulea"</note> are large, painted curtains; they are called *aulea* because they were first found in the royal court <note>original: "aula"</note> of the King of Asia <note>referring to Attalus III of Pergamum</note>, whom the Roman people succeeded. **Cortinae** <note>curtains</note> are *aulea*—that is, curtains made of hides—such as are read of in Exodus, with which the Tabernacle was covered on the outside. They are called *cortinae* from *coriis* <note>hides/skins</note>, because they were originally made from skins. Hence, in the same Tabernacle of the Law, it is commanded that curtains be made of red ram skins and violet-colored skins. The Arabs call **cilicia** <note>haircloth</note> coverings woven from goat hair, from which they make their tents.

### Chapter XXVII: On wools

**Lana** <note>wool</note> is named from *laniando*—that is, from plucking or tearing. From this also comes **vellus** <note>fleece</note>, because formerly wool was plucked <note>original: "vellereť"</note>, not shorn. **Linum** <note>linen</note> arises from the earth with a shining appearance; its name is derived from the Greek. For the Greeks call linen *linarin* <note>original: "linarin"; likely a corruption of "linon"</note>, perhaps because it is soft and smooth <note>original: "lene"</note>. **Stuppa** <note>tow or oakum</note> comes from hemp or linen. According to ancient orthography, it is called *stuppa* because the cracks of ships are "stuffed" <note>original: "stipentur"</note> with it. From this, those who pack it into bundles are called "stowaways" <note>original: "stipatozes"</note>.

<column-break/>

**Tomentum** <note>original: "Lomētū"; stuffing</note> is so called because it swells <note>original: "tumeat"</note> either in the thread or in the weaving, and lacks fineness. **Cannabum** <note>original: "Lanabum"; hemp</note> is named from its similarity to a reed <note>original: "canne"</note>, or from Greek etymology, for they call hemp *cannabin*. **Byssus** <note>fine linen</note> is a type of linen that is exceedingly white and soft, which the Greeks call *papatē*. **Fibrinum** <note>beaver wool</note> is the wool of the animals they call *fibros* <note>beavers</note>; they are also thought to be the same as *castores* <note>castors</note>, who, when pursued by hunters, castrate themselves. **Aranea** <note>spider silk/cobweb</note> is so named because it is nourished by the infusion of air in the foliage. **Sericum** <note>silk</note> is so called because the Chinese <note>original: "Seres"</note> first sent it. Small worms are said to be born there, by which these threads are drawn around trees. These worms are called *bombyces* <note>silkworms</note> in Greek. **Plucium** is tow and something like the coarseness of silk; it is a Greek name.

### Chapter XXVIII: On the colors of clothing

It is called **tinctura** <note>dyeing</note> because it is "tinged" <note>original: "tingitur"</note> and colored into another deceptive appearance for the sake of brightness. The Greeks call it **coccum** <note>scarlet</note>; we call it red or *vermiculus* <note>little worm; the origin of the word "vermilion"</note>. It is indeed a "little worm" from wild foliage. **Conchylium** <note>purple</note> is so named because its color is gathered from marine shells <note>original: "conculis"</note>. This is also called **ostrum**. *Ostrum* is found as a purple color in many places, but the best is produced on the island of Cyprus, or in those places which the path of the sun specifically illuminates. *Conchylia* are sea creatures which, when cut with iron, emit tears of a purple color. Once collected, the purple color is tempered from these. It is said to be called *ostrum* because the liquid is drawn out from the shell <note>original: "ex teste"</note>. Among the Latins, **purpura** <note>purple</note> is named from the purity of light. Among the Greeks, it is called *purphyra* with an aspiration; among us, it is *purpura* without the aspiration. **Ferrugo** <note>iron-rust color</note> is the color of dark purple which is made in Spain, like the "shining Iberian *ferrugo*." It is called *ferrugo* because every first dyeing of purple results in a color of this sort. **Glaucus** <note>bluish-gray</note> is a color somewhat dark with *ferrugo*. **Elbidum** is named from the color *elbus*. *Elbus* is a middle color between black and white, derived from *albus* <note>white</note>. **Luteus** is a reddish color which is saffron-like. For saffron is of a yellow <note>original: "lutei"</note> color, as in: "the fleeces changed by saffron *luto*." **Melinum** is that which is of a black color, for the Greeks call black *melan*. **Masticinum** is that which has the color of mastic <note>a resin</note>. **Blatteum** is purple-red. **Ostirium** <note>sooty/burnt color</note> is so called because it is from "burnt" <note>original: "vsto"</note>. For it is made from the soot that hangs over and is cast out by constant fires. Hence the color of that dye is flame-like.

### Chapter XXIX: On the tools of clothing

**Tela** <note>the loom or the web</note> is named for the length of the warp-threads <note>original: "staminū"</note>; its derivative is *telaria*. **Insubuli** <note>yarn beams</note> are so named because they are below and above <note>original: "infra ꝛ supꝛa"</note>, or because the thread is wound upon them. **Radii** <note>shuttles</note> are named because they are made by scraping <note>original: "radendo"</note>. **Pectines** <note>reeds or combs</note> are so called because they separate the threads and press them together. The **colus** <note>distaff</note> is so named because it is in length and roundness like a small column <note>original: "quasicolūna"</note>. The **fusus** <note>spindle</note> is named because through it that which is spun <note>original: "netum"</note> is "poured out" <note>original: "fundať"</note>. The **alabrum** <note>original: "Alibum"; a reel</note> is where the threads are "liberated"—that is, loosened. The **calathus** <note>basket</note> is a light vessel made of wood, reed, or rush, in which either weighed allotments of wool are placed or flowers are gathered. For in Greek, *cala* is wood, from which *calathus* is derived. In Latin, it is called a *quassillus* <note>a small basket</note>. Cicero says in the *Philippics*: "Or let this man weigh out gold among the wool-baskets." The **pensum** <note>the daily allotment of wool</note> for women is named from "weighing" <note>original: "pendendo"</note>. Hence *pensa* and *impensa* <note>expenses</note>. **Nerum** <note>original: "Nerum"; likely "netum" or "nervum"</note> are called threads, either because they are made from the hair of animals, or because the craft of wool consists of thin threads...

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s Book XIX of the Etymologies. It concludes the technical vocabulary of weaving and textile production before transitioning into a comprehensive survey of personal ornaments, jewelry, and headgear used by various ranks, genders, and cultures of the ancient world.</meta>

...in the manner of hairs, that is, as if they were threads. **Matara** <note>original: "Matara"</note> is so called from the "circuit" or massing together of threads. For a *meta* <note>a turning post or boundary</note> is named for a circuit, or because it is transferred. **Bubellum** <note>a ball of thread</note> is a corrupted form of *globellum*, a diminutive of *globus* <note>a sphere or ball</note>. **Panulae** or **panuclae** <note>bobbins or spindles</note> are those from which cloths are woven; for they run back and forth through the loom. The **stamen** <note>original: "Stamen"; the warp</note> is so named because it "stands" <note>original: "stat"</note> upright. The **trama** <note>original: "Trama"; the weft or woof</note> is so called because it "transmits" <note>original: "transmittat"</note> its path straight through the web; for it is the thread running between the warp. **Licia** <note>heddles or leashes</note> are those by which the warp threads are bound, as if the word were *ligia* <note>from "ligare," to bind</note>. To *dedere* <note>original: "D:dire"</note> is to rub or wear away.

### Chapter XXX: On Ornaments

Thus far we have spoken of clothing; from here let us come to other forms of grooming. **Ornaments** <note>original: "Ornamenta"</note> are so named because the "faces" <note>original: "ora"</note> and countenances are "decorated" <note>original: "decorentz"</note> by their care. The first ornament is the **corona** <note>crown</note>, a badge of victory or a royal sign of honor. These are placed on the heads of kings to signify that they are surrounded by the world <note>original: "circūsūsos in orbe"</note>, as if their own head were crowned by the circle that girds them. This was called a *corolla* by Lucilius and a *stephane* by Homer <note>original: "stephane"; Greek for crown</note>. The pagans believe the origin of this comes from Liber <note>the god Bacchus</note>, because he instituted the practice of binding the head with ribbons to delay the effects of wine while drinking; therefore, in ancient times, crowns were made of linen or wool, as was the custom among pagan priests. The name "crown" was given for this reason: because in the beginning, people would "run around" <note>original: "circū aras curreret"</note> the altars, and the crown was formed and named after the image of a "circle" <note>original: "circūn'"</note> or a "choir" <note>original: "chori"</note>. Roman emperors and certain kings of nations use gold crowns. The Persians wear **tiaras**; of these, the kings wear them upright, and the satraps <note>provincial governors</note> wear them curved. The tiara was invented by Semiramis, the queen of the Assyrians. That nation retains this type of ornament to this day. The Athenians used to wear gold **cyclades** <note>circular ornaments</note>, some on the crown of the head and some on the forehead. For the insignia of all kingdoms are not the same. The prophets of the pagans used the **infula**, the **apex**, the **pilleus**, or the **gallerius**. The *infula* is a white priestly head-band in the manner of a **diadema**, from which **vittae** <note>ribbons</note> hang down from both sides, which bind the *infula*; hence they are called *vittae* because they "bind" <note>original: "vinciant"</note>. The *infula* was often wide, and often twisted from white and scarlet. The *apex* is a slender cap used by pagan priests, named from *apiendo*, that is, "by binding." For the small rod that was on the cap was connected by a thread made from the wool of a sacrificial victim. The *galerius* <note>original: "Galeriū"</note> was a cap made from the skin of a slaughtered victim. The *pilleus* <note>original: "Pilleū"</note> was named from the "skin" <note>original: "pelle"</note> of the victim from which it was made. The **cydaris** <note>original: "Cydarim"</note> was also a priestly item, which is called a **mitra** <note>mitre</note> by many. The ornaments for women's heads are the *diadema*, the *nimbus*, the *capitulum*, and the *mitra*. The **diadema** is an ornament for the heads of matrons woven from gold and gems, which is fastened at the back with its ends brought around; it is so named in Greek because it "binds around" <note>original: "pęliget̃"</note>. The **nimbus** is a transverse band of gold sewn onto linen that is worn on the foreheads of women. Plautus says: "The more I look at her, the more *nimbated* <note>crowned with a nimbus</note> she is." For the light painted around the heads of angels is also called a *nimbus*, though a *nimbus* can also be the density of a cloud. The **capitulum** is what the common people call a *capitulare*. It is the same as a **cappa**, either because it has two points like the letter 'p' <note>referring to the shape of the letter in certain scripts</note> or because it is an ornament of the "head" <note>original: "capitis"</note>. The **mitra** is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as the head ornament of devoted women. But the *pilleus* belongs to men, while *mitrae* belong to women. **Redimicula** are those ribbons

<column-break/>

with which mitres are tied. The *pilleus*, as we said before, was made of skin, but the *mitra* is made of wool. The **rigula** is a mitre for a maiden's head. **Vittae** <note>ribbons</note> are those which are woven into the hair, by which flowing locks are bound; they are called *vittae* because they "bind" <note>original: "vinciāt"</note>. The **taenia** <note>original: "Tenia"</note> is the hanging end of the ribbons, often of various colors. Also, a *vitta* is that which binds a crown, while the *taenia* is the extreme part of the ribbon from which the crowns hang. The **reticulum** <note>hairnet</note> is that which collects the hair; it is named because it "retains" <note>original: "retinet"</note> the hair so it does not spill out. **Discriminalia** <note>hair-pins or dividers</note> of women's heads are so called because they "distinguish" <note>original: "discernant"</note> the head with gold. For to *discriminare* means to divide. **Anciae** are curls hanging down near the ears, named from the Greek word for "ears" <note>original: "ab auribus"</note>. **Acus** <note>needles or pins</note> are those by which the arrangement of hair is held in place for women's grooming, so the hair does not flow too loosely or scatter and dissipate. **Inaures** <note>earrings</note> are named from the "holes in the ears" <note>original: "aurium foraminib'"</note>, from which precious beads of stone hang. In Greece, girls used these in both ears, but boys wore them only in the right ear. **Torques** <note>torcs</note> are gold circles hanging from the neck down to the chest. *Torques* and **bullae** <note>charms or lockets</note> are worn by men; but by women, **monilia** <note>necklaces</note> and **catellae** <note>little chains</note> are worn. They are called *torques* because they are "twisted" <note>original: "tortę"</note>, and *bullae* because they resemble the roundness of "bubbles" <note>original: "bullis"</note> inflated by wind in water. A **monile** <note>necklace</note> is an ornament of gems that usually hangs from a woman's neck, named from the word for "gift" <note>original: "munere"</note>. This is also said of serpents, as it consists of certain gold jars and various gems in the shape of a serpent's form. Some call this a **segmentum** or long robes, though we also speak of *segmentated* garments, as in "she had slept as a little girl in segmentated cradles." Generally, however, all ornaments of matrons are signified by the term *monile*, whatever is given to them as a gift. It is commonly called a **murena** <note>lamprey</note> because, with the gold metal becoming flexible in small rods, a certain chain of winding order is woven in the likeness of the *murena* serpent <note>the moray eel</note>, which is fitted to adorn the neck. This is sometimes rubbed with rods of gold and silver. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: "We will make you gold *murenulas* <note>little lamprey-chains</note> inlaid with silver." **Catellae** are little neck chains catching one another in the manner of a chain, from which they are named. **Dextras** <note>bracelets</note> are common to both men and women, so named because they are on the "right hands" <note>original: "dextrę"</note> of both sexes; they are large and worn before the sleeve, and can be joined there by a single pin. **Armillae** <note>armlets</note>, however, specifically belong to men, given to soldiers for victory because of their "courage in arms" <note>original: "armoȝ virtutē"</note>. Hence they were once commonly called *virilia* <note>manly things</note>. But the name *armilla* differs from the understanding of a "circle" <note>original: "circuli"</note> because a circle constricts whatever it is placed on by surrounding it, while an *armilla* extends more widely, whereas a circle is made round. **Fibulae** <note>brooches or clasps</note> are those by which the breasts of women are adorned, or by which a cloak is held by men on the shoulders, or a belt on the loins. **Lunulae** <note>little moons</note> are ornaments for women in the likeness of the moon, hanging as little gold bubbles. **Specula** <note>mirrors</note> are so called because women gaze at their faces in them. It is called a *speculum* either because it reflects from its "splendor" or because women, gazing there, consider the "appearance" <note>original: "specie"</note> of their own face and add whatever ornament they see is missing. **Periscelides** are ornaments for women’s legs or "armlets for the feet," with which their steps are adorned. **Olfactoriola** are small vessels for women in which perfumes are carried.

<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s Book XIX of the *Etymologies*. It transitions from general ornaments to specific categories of personal attire: rings, belts, and footwear. The translator maintains continuity with the previous section’s focus on the social and linguistic origins of Roman dress.</meta>

### On Rings, Chapter 31.

**P**rometheus is said to have been the first to encircle his finger with an iron ring containing a stone. By this custom, men began to have rings. Now, **rings** <note>original: "Anuli"</note> are named as a diminutive from "circles" <note>original: "circulis"</note> or from *ani* <note>meaning "circular" or "rings"</note>, which are found around the arms and around the legs. From this, their small signs are called **seal-rings** <note>original: "sigilla"</note> as a diminutive. For *signa* <note>signs or seals</note> are larger, while *sigilla* are, as it were, smaller signs. Men first began to wear rings on the fourth finger from the thumb, because a certain vein reaches from there all the way to the heart; the ancients thought this finger should be noted and adorned with some sign. Among the Romans, rings were given from the public treasury, and not without distinction. For rings with gems were given to men of the highest dignity, while solid rings were given to the rest. Neither a slave nor a freedman wore a **gold ring** <note>original: "anulo aureo"</note> in public; free men used a gold ring, freedmen a silver one, and slaves an iron one. Among the ancients, it was considered shameful for a man to wear more than one ring. Gracchus said in an oration: "Consider, citizens, the left hand of him whose authority you follow, who for the sake of a woman's desire is adorned like a woman." Crassus, who perished among the Parthians, had two rings in his old age, offering as a reason that his immense wealth had grown. Many Romans also abstained from wearing a ring on the finger for the sake of gravity. Women did not use rings, except for those which a fiancé had sent to his bride; nor were they accustomed to having more than two gold rings on their fingers. But now, because of gold, no part of a woman's body is light or free from it. Among the types of rings are the **fingernail-ring** <note>original: "vngulus"</note>, the **Samothracian**, and the **Thynian**. The *ungulus* is gemmed, and called by this name because, just as a fingernail is set in the flesh, so the gem of the ring is surrounded by gold. The *Samothracian* is indeed gold, but with an iron head; it is named after the place. The *Thynian* is pure, first manufactured in Bithynia, which they once called Thyna. Flaccus says: "While my life grieves, I seek neither emerald nor beryl for myself, Flaccilla, nor shining pearls of bright white; I seek neither the little rings that the Thynian file polishes, nor jasper stones."

### On Belts, Chapter 32.

**A** **belt-cloth** <note>original: "Cinctus"</note> is a wide girdle, the **thigh-band** <note>original: "femicinctium"</note> is less wide, and the smallest of both is the **belt** <note>original: "cingulum"</note>. For *cingulum* is named as a diminutive from *cinctus*. Young men used to cover themselves with a *cinctus* out of modesty during exercises in the field; hence it was also called a **field-cloth** <note>original: "campestris"</note>. The **baldric** <note>original: "Balteus"</note> is called a military belt, because from it the "signs" or badges hang to demonstrate the total number of the military legion—that is, six thousand six hundred—from which number they themselves consist. From this, the *balteus* is named not only for that which girds, but also that from which weapons hang. **Girdle** <note>original: "Zona"</note> is a Greek term, which they call *zonarium* and we call a *cingulum*. The **breast-band** <note>original: "Strophium"</note> is a gold belt with gems. Concerning which Cinna says: "Girdled with a *strophium* on her milky breasts." And Prudentius: "This name of the gem is bound in the *strophium*." The **limus** <note>original: "Limus"</note> is a belt which slaves wear publicly. And it is called *limus* because it has transverse purple stripes, which are called *limae*. The **caltulum** is a type of belt named from "gathered" <note>original: "coacto"</note> or "twisted." **Clasp** <note>original: "Fibula"</note> is a Greek term, which they call *fiblin* because it binds. The **under-clasp** <note>original: "Subfibula"</note> is a loincloth. The **head-band** <note>original: "Redimiculum"</note> is what we call a "girdle-band" or **arm-band** <note>original: "bracile"</note>, which, descending

<column-break/>

over the neck and divided from the sides of the neck, encircles the hollow of both armpits and girds them here and there, so that by constraining the width it clothes the body and arranges it by joining. This is commonly called a *bracile*, as if it were a "brachial" <note>from *brachium*, arm</note>, although now it is a belt for the kidneys and not the arm. It is called a **succinctorium**, however, because, as has been said, it is drawn under the arms, encircles the hollow of the armpits, and girds them on both sides. The **bandage** <note>original: "Fascia"</note> is that by which the chest is ruled and the breasts are compressed, and the chest is narrowed more tightly by the curling belt. And it is called *fascia* because it binds the body in the manner of a little bundle <note>original: "fasciculi"</note>. From this also come the "bandages" with which wounds are bound. The **ribbon** <note>original: "Vitta"</note> is so called because it binds the chest like a "vine" <note>original: "vitis"</note> binding things. The **border** <note>original: "Limbus"</note>, which we call an "edge," is a small bandage that encircles the extremity of garments, woven either from threads or from gold, and sewn on the outside at the furthest part of a garment, such as a cloak. Concerning which Virgil says: "Surrounded by a Sidonian cloak with a painted border."

### On Footwear, Chapter 34.

**S**andals <note>original: "Soleae"</note> are so named because they are sewn together by inserting the bristles <note>original: "setis"</note> of pigs into a thread, that is, they sew them as if they were "bristle-sewn." A **boot-maker** <note>original: "Caligarius"</note>, however, is not named from the "callus" of the feet, but from *calus*, that is, from wood; hence those shoes that cannot be sewn together are called by the Greeks *calopodion* <note>a wooden last</note>. They were formerly made only from willow. From this, footwear is also called *calciamenta* because they are made on a *calus*, that is, on wood, or because they are "trampled" <note>original: "calcentur"</note>. The Greeks used **slippers** <note>original: "Crepidae"</note> or *anreptas*. It is a type of singular form, and the same is fit for either foot, whether the right or the left. They are called *crepidae* because they tighten with a sound, or from the "creaking" <note>original: "crepitu"</note> of the feet in walking. Kings and Caesars used **shoes** <note>original: "Calceis"</note in their own form. Romulus discovered **patrician shoes** <note>original: "Patricios calceos"</note> with four straps and a sewn-on moon <note>original: "luna"</note>. Only patricians used these. The "moon" in them did not signify the form of the star, but the mark of the number one hundred, because in the beginning the patrician senators were one hundred. **Greaves** <note>original: "Ocreae"</note> are called tibial footwear because they cover the shins <note>original: "crura"</note>. **Buskins** <note>original: "Coturni"</note> are what tragic actors wore, because they were to perform in the theater and sing songs in a high and thundering voice. It is indeed a footwear in the manner of a slipper which heroes used; but it is such that it fits the right or the left foot. The **barca** <note>a clog</note> was the footwear of comic actors, just as buskins were for tragic ones. Some also call these *calones* because they were made from willow. For the Greeks, as we have said, called wood *calo*. **Ankle-shoes** <note>original: "Talares"</note> are **slippers** <note>original: "socci"</note>, which seem to be named because they are of such a figure that they touch the ankle <note>original: "talum"</note>, just as "sub-ankles" are under the ankle. **Stitched-shoes** <note>original: "Obstrigilli"</note> are those sewn from the soles, and they draw the laces from the upper part so that they might constrain the foot, from which they are named. I think **hose** <note>original: "Osas"</note> were first made from bone <note>original: "oso"</note>, and although they are now made from another kind, they still retain the ancient name. **Mullet-shoes** <note>original: "Mullei"</note> are similar to buskins with a high sole, but in the upper part they have bone or bronze little hammers <note>original: "malleolis"</note> to which the laces were tied. They are named from their red color, such as that of the mullet fish. **Sole-sandals** <note>original: "Soleae"</note> are those by which only the soles of the feet are covered, named from the "sole" of the feet. Likewise, "material" sandals are woven from leather material. **Slippers** <note>original: "Socci"</note>, the diminutive of which is called *soccelli*, are named from the fact that they have a "socket" <note>original: "soccum"</note> into which the part of the sole is cast. **Little boots** <note>original: "Caligulae"</note> or **boots** <note>original: "caligae"</note> are named either from the "callus" of the feet or because they "bind" <note>original: "ligent"</note>. For slippers do not bind, but are only stepped into. **Lernian slippers** are without a separate sole, which we call "leafy" <note>original: "foliaros"</note>. **Hobnailed** <note>original: "Clauati"</note>, because

# Book Twenty Begins.
## On Tables, Chapter 1.

**Daedalus was the first**
**to make tables and chairs.**
**A certain Apicius** <note>A famous Roman gourmet and lover of luxury</note>
**first composed a treatise on**
**the apparatus of the kitchen;**
**he died by a voluntary death**
**after consuming his wealth**
**in it, and deservedly so, because**
he who serves gluttony and voracity kills both soul and body. The word **table** <note>original: "mensa"</note> is said to be sacred from "eating" <note>original: "esu"</note> and "dining" <note>original: "comesu"</note>. For it has no other use. A **couch** <note>original: "torus"</note> is named from the "twisted" <note>original: "toris"</note> herbs which are placed under the shoulders of those reclining. A **semicircular couch** <note>original: "stibadium"</note> is named from "posts" <note>original: "stipitibus"</note>, as if it were a *stipadium*; for it was first constructed in this way. A **place for reclining** <note>original: "accubitus"</note> is named from "food" <note>original: "cibo"</note>, as if it were the "receiving" <note>original: "accibitum"</note> of banquets. A **banquet** <note>original: "convivium"</note> among the Greeks is named from "drinking together" <gloss>drinking together <note>original: "συµποσιον"</note></gloss>. Among us Romans, however, it is more correctly named from "living together" <note>original: "convictu"</note>, or because it involves the conversation of life. Likewise, a banquet is named from the multitude of those "eating together" <note>original: "convencentium"</note>. For a private table is "sustenance" <note>original: "victus"</note>; it is not a banquet. A banquet has a triple mode: reclining, eating, and drinking. Reclining, as in: "ordered to recline on embroidered couches" <note>Quoting Vergil's *Aeneid*</note>. Eating and drinking, as in: "after the first quiet of the feast and the tables were removed, they set out great bowls and crown the wine."

## On Foods, Chapter 2.

**FOOD** <note>original: "cibus"</note> **is so called because it is taken by the**
**mouth** <note>original: "capitur ore"</note>**, just like a morsel** <note>original: "esca"</note>**, because the**
**mouth takes it. Sustenance** <note>original: "victus"</note> **is properly so called**
**because it retains life** <note>original: "vitam"</note>**; hence to invite**
**to food is called "to invite to sustenance."**
**Nourishment** <note>original: "alimonia"</note> is so called because the body is nourished <note>original: "alatur"</note> by the taking of it. Young people receive this for growth; old people for preservation. For flesh cannot subsist unless it is strengthened by nutrients. For **nutrient** <note>original: "alimentum"</note> is that by which we are nourished; **nourishment** <note>original: "alimonia"</note> is the care of nourishing. **Abundance** <note>original: "affluentia"</note> is named as if it were the effusion of a thing overflowing <note>original: "eruberantis"</note> too much beyond what is enough; and there is no limit. **Opulence** <note>original: "opulentia"</note> is named from "resource" <note>original: "ope"</note>; if you examine it, you will find it keeps a limit. For how can that which is excessive be "resourceful," since too much is often as inconvenient as too little. **Feasts** <note>original: "epulae"</note> are named from the opulence of things. Simple feasts, however, are divided into two necessary things: bread and wine; and into two superfluous things which are sought from land and sea for the sake of eating. **Banquets** <note>original: "dapes"</note>, however, belong to kings; **feasts** <note>original: "epulae"</note> to private citizens. **Delicacies** <note>original: "delitiae"</note> are so named because men are "delighted" <note>original: "delectentur"</note> by them and seek them sweetly. **Relish** <note>original: "pulmentum"</note> is named from "porridge" <note>original: "pulte"</note>; for whether it is porridge alone or something else mixed with it, it is properly called *pulmentum*. **Satiety** <note>original: "satietas"</note> and **fullness** <note>original: "saturitas"</note> differ from each other. For satiety can be said of a single food, because it is "enough" <note>original: "satis"</note>. But fullness takes its name from "full" <note>original: "saturo"</note>, which is composed of a varied preparation of foods. **Indigestion** <note>original: "crapula"</note> is immoderate voracity, as if it were a "raw feast" <note>original: "cruda epula"</note>, from whose rawness the body and stomach, being burdened, suffer from indigestion. For immoderate voracity is a vice; there is only as much health as suffices for the support of nature. **Breakfast** <note>original: "jentaculum"</note> is the first food by which a fast is broken, whence it is named. Nigidius says:

<column-break/>

"We ourselves break fasts with light breakfasts" <note>original: "jentaculis"</note>. **Lunch** <note>original: "prandium"</note> is named from the preparation of eating. Properly, however, the ancients called the food of all soldiers before a battle *prandium*, whence comes that address of a leader: "Let us lunch as if we are to dine in the underworld." **Afternoon snack** <note>original: "merenda"</note> is food taken as the day declines, as if "to be eaten after midday" <note>original: "post meridiem edenda"</note> and at the start of dinner. Whence they are also called "before-dinners" <note>original: "antecenia"</note> by some. Likewise, "to snack" <note>original: "merendare"</note> is as if to eat at midday. **Provisions** <note>original: "annona"</note> is derived from the time that the ancient Romans called for food; thus the poet Martial says: "The Emperor commands the breaking of the high couches at the ninth [hour]" <note>original: "nona"</note>, which the common people do even today. **Dinner** <note>original: "cena"</note> is named from the "communion" <note>original: "communione"</note> of those eating. For the Greeks call "common" *koinon*. Whence also "communicants," because they come together "commonly," that is, together. Among the ancients it was customary to eat in a small space and feast together lest solitude breed luxury. Dinner is evening food, which the ancients called the "evening meal." For lunches were not in use. **Bread** <note>original: "panis"</note> is so called because it is served with all food, or because every animal seeks it. For "all" <note>original: "pan"</note> in Greek means "everything." **Libum** <note>original: "libarum"</note> is what is given to servants for food, and is not delicate. **Leavened** bread is made with leaven. **Unleavened** <note>original: "azymum"</note> is not leavened. For *azymus* is without leaven, pure. **Acricium** is lightly leavened, as if "sharp-unleavened." **Siligineous** bread is named from a type of grain. For *siligo* is a kind of wheat. **Reddish** bread is twice-baked and made red. **Baked-under-ashes** <note>original: "subcineritius"</note> is cooked in ash and turned over. This is also **hearth-bread** <note>original: "focatius"</note>. **Libanitius** is cooked in an earthen vessel. **Sponge-bread** <note>original: "spungia"</note> is bread washed for a long time in water; it takes a little fine flour and a little leaven and has more moisture than any bread, whence it took the name of sponge. **Cakes** <note>original: "placentae"</note> are those made from spelt, which others call *liba* because they "please" <note>original: "libeant"</note> and "satisfy" <note>original: "placeant"</note>. **Laganum** is a broad and thin bread which is first cooked in water, then fried in oil. **Sweets** <note>original: "dulcia"</note> are types of baker’s work named from their flavor. For they are taken sprinkled with honey <note>original: "mel"</note>. **Cookies** <note>original: "crustula"</note> is a diminutive of "crust"; bread sprinkled with oil, concave in the middle and toasted. These are also called "toasted bread." **Crust** <note>original: "crusta"</note>, however, is the surface of the bread. The same are "fragments," because they are divided as "broken" <note>original: "fracta"</note> pieces. **Fine flour** <note>original: "simila"</note> is the most subtle flour. **Starch** <note>original: "amylum"</note> is the thinnest flower of flour, which can be carried away by a light breeze from the mill <note>original: "mola"</note>; whence it is named as if "from the mill." **Flour** <note>original: "farina"</note> and **bran** <note>original: "furfures"</note> are named from "spelt" <note>original: "far"</note> when they are the sweepings. **Fine dust** <note>original: "pollen"</note> is a kind of very white flour. **Leaven** <note>original: "fermentum"</note> is named from "boiling" <note>original: "fervore"</note>, because it cannot be contained for more than one hour. For by growing it overflows. **Meats** <note>original: "carnes"</note> are so called because they lack [strength?] or from "creating" <note>original: "creando"</note>, whence they are called *kreas* by the Greeks. **Raw** <note>original: "crudum"</note> is that which is bloody, for it is cooked with blood. But something cooked for a long time is also called [undigested?]. **Roasted** <note>original: "assum"</note> because it "burns," as if "burned" <note>original: "arsum"</note>. **Boiled** <note>original: "elixum"</note> because it is cooked down in water alone. For *lura* <note>original transcribed as "lira"</note> means water, from being "loose"; whence the loosening of lust and moved limbs are called *lura*. **Fried** <note>original: "frixum"</note> is named from the sound when it burns in oil. **Salted** <note>original: "salsum"</note> as if sprinkled with salt, with three syllables removed from the middle. **Rancid** <note>original: "rancidum"</note> is named from a fault because it makes one hoarse. **Preserved meats** <note>original: "succidia"</note> are meats put aside for use, named from "cutting from below." **Lard** <note>original: "lardus"</note> is so called because it is preserved and kept in the home. For the ancients called houses "lares." *Larca* is the word for lard in the Gallic tongue. Whence it is said: "I ate lard in a rose." A **fattened cock** is a larea fed on fat. **Grease** <note>original: "arungia"</note> is named from "anointing." **Suet** <note>original: "sebum"</note> is named from a "sow" <note>original: "sue"</note>, as if it were *suebum*, because it has more fat...
