<meta>This page continues Book XX of Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*. Following the initial discussion of tables and seating, Isidore moves into the etymologies of various foods (meats, dairy, and honey) and drinks (water and wine), explaining their names through historical anecdotes, linguistic roots, and medical theories of the time.</meta>

<header>Book</header>

this animal has. **Bones** <note>original: "Ossa"</note> are the very "fruit of the teeth." The diminutive is **little bone** <note>original: "osella"</note>. From this also come **bone-cooks** <note>original: "ossarii coci"</note>, because they cook meat piece by piece, or rather, "bone by bone" <note>original: "ossatim"</note>. Now, a **bone** <note>original: "ossa"</note> is for barking dogs; for if it is thrown into a dog's mouth, it is immediately satisfied, restrained, and becomes silent. **Fruit** <note>original: "fructum"</note> is so called because it is received by the **throat** <note>original: "frumine"</note>. For the *frumen* is the upper part of the gullet. **Pulp** <note>original: "pulpa"</note> is so named because it was once eaten mixed with **pottage** <note>original: "pulte"</note>. From this also come the words **relish** <note>original: "pulmentum"</note> and **side-dish** <note>original: "pulmentarium"</note>. Pulp, however, is meat without fat, named because it "palpitates" <note>original: "palpitet"</note>; for it often springs back. Most call it **flesh** <note>original: "viscum"</note> because it is sticky <note>Isidore relates "viscus" to "viscous" or "gluey."</note>. **Lucanian sausages** <note>original: "lucanicae"</note> are named because they were first made in Lucania <note>A region in Southern Italy.</note>. **Stuffing** <note>original: "farcimen"</note> is meat cut into tiny pieces, named because the intestine is "stuffed" <note>original: "farciatur"</note>; that is, filled with a mixture of other things. **Minced meat** <note>original: "minutal"</note> is so called because it is made from fish, forcemeat, and vegetables cut into "tiny" <note>original: "minutatim"</note> pieces. **Foamy dish** <note>original: "afratum"</note> is what is called "foam" <note>original: "spumam"</note> in Latin; for in Greek, foam is called *aphros* <note>original: "aphro"</note>. **Mortar-dishes** <note>original: "martia"</note>, that is, made from fish in a **mortar** <note>original: "mortario"</note>, from which they are named. They say the **isox** <note>likely a salmon or large pike</note> is a certain fish from which **stuffed-bits** <note>original: "isicia"</note> were first made; and although they are now made from other kinds of fish, the original fish gave the name to the dish. **Galatic dishes** are named from their "milky" <note>original: "lacteo"</note> color; for the Greeks call milk *gala*. **Spheres** <note>original: "sphaeras"</note> are named from their roundness by a Greek word; for whatever is formed into a round shape is called a *sphaera* by the Greeks. The masters of the kitchen named **broth** <note>original: "jus"</note> from **law** <note>original: "jure"</note>, because it is the "law" or rule of its seasoning. The Greeks call this *zema*. **Cheese** <note>original: "caseus"</note> is so named because it "lacks whey" <note>original: "careat sero"</note>, as if it were *careum*; for all the whey is drawn out from it so that it may be tested by its weight. **Beestings** <note>original: "colostrum"</note> is new milk, which is of the neuter gender. **Milk** <note>original: "lac"</note> is derived from the Greek language and from its brightness <note>original: "candore"</note>. For the Greeks call white *gleucon*. Milk and blood are related because they both nourish. For we are nourished by milk and we live by blood. **Curds** <note>original: "quactum"</note> are as if "driven together" <note>original: "coactum"</note> and as if "coagulated." For once it has accepted another substance into itself, it coagulates. **Honey** <note>original: "mel"</note> is of Greek naming, which is proven to have its name from bees; for in Greek, a bee is called *melissa*. But formerly, honey came from dew and was found on the leaves of reeds. Whence Virgil says: "Thus far the celestial gifts of aerial honey" <note>original: "hactenus aerii mellis caelestia dona"</note>. Indeed, even now it is found collected in India and Arabia, clinging to branches in the likeness of salt. But all honey is said to be sweet. **Sardinian honey** is bitter because of the wormwood, of which there is a great abundance that the bees of that region feed upon. A **honeycomb** is called *favus* because it is "eaten" rather than drunk; for the Greeks call "to eat" *phagein*. Physicians, and those who have written about the nature of human bodies—especially Galen in his books whose title is <unclear>title missing</unclear>—say that the bodies of children, youths, and men of mature age, as well as women, boil with innate heat, and that for these ages, hot foods are harmful because they increase the heat. They say it is conducive to health to take cold things for food; just as, on the contrary, for the elderly, because they suffer from phlegm and cold, hot foods and old wines are beneficial.

### On Drink, Chapter 3.

**Drink** <note>original: "potio"</note> is named from a Greek derivation. For they call it *potos*. **Water** <note>original: "aqua"</note> is generally named because its "appearance" <note>original: "suspicies"</note> is as if it were equal <note>Isidore links *aqua* to *aequalis*</note>; hence also the word for "level surfaces of the sea" <note>original: "aequora"</note>. Some call it "fresh" <note>original: "recentem"</note> because it is "thrown back" <note>original: "rejicitur"</note> as new from a spring or a river. For old water putrefies; it is not useful when old like wine, but is best when immediately taken from a river, spring, or well; for it grows stale when old. **Wine** <note>original: "vinum"</note> is named from this:

<column-break/>

because its passage quickly refills the "veins" <note>original: "venas"</note> with blood. Others call it *Liaeum* <note>A name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note> because it releases us from "care" <note>original: "cura"</note>. The ancients used to call wine "poison" <note>original: "venenum"</note>. But after the juice of a deadly "virus" <note>original: "virus"</note> was found, this was called "wine" <note>original: "vinum"</note> and that was called "poison" <note>original: "venenum"</note>. Whence also Jerome, in the book he wrote on preserving virginity, said: "young girls should flee wine as if it were poison," lest they drink it with the boiling heat of their age and perish. For this reason, among the ancient Romans, women did not use wine except for the sake of sacrifices on certain days. We say **pure wine** <note>original: "merum"</note> when the wine is unmixed and sincere; likewise "pure water," where nothing is mixed into either thing. From this also comes **afternoon snack** <note>original: "merenda"</note>, because in antiquity it was the time given to boys in the fields when "pure bread" <note>original: "panis merus"</note> was given, or because they ate "at midday" <note>original: "meridie"</note> at that same time—that is, alone and separately, not as at lunch or dinner at a single table. From this we also believe that the time which is after the middle of the day is called **midday** <note>original: "meridiem"</note>, because it is "pure" <note>Isidore associates the clarity of the noon sun with the "purity" of unmixed wine.</note>. **Must** <note>original: "mustum"</note> is wine immediately taken from the vat. It is believed to be called *mustum* because it has "mud" <note>original: "limum"</note> and "earth" <note>original: "terram"</note> mixed in it. For *mus* means earth, whence also comes the word for "soil" <note>original: "humus"</note>. Its force of fermentation is so great that it will immediately burst even large vessels if they are full of it and kept without a vent. **Rosy wine** is that with redness; for a rose is red. **Aminnean wine** <note>original: "Aminuum"</note> is so called as if "without red-lead" <note>original: "sine minio"</note>, that is, without redness; for it is white. **Amber wine** <note>original: "sucinatum"</note> is similar to the amber gem, that is, of a tawny color. **Limpid wine** is clear wine, named from the appearance of water, as if it were "watery" <note>original: "lymphidum"</note>. For *lympha* is water. **Turbid wine** is as if "earthy" <note>original: "terbidum"</note>, that is, mixed with earth, which is the dregs. **Falernian wine** is named from the Falernian region of Campania where the best wines are produced. He named a **strained wine** <note>original: "colatum"</note> from the specific vessel in which it is carried. **Gazan wine** <note>original: "sagerum"?</note> is named from the region from which it is brought; for Gaza is a town in Palestine. **Offered wine** <note>original: "infertum"</note> is said to be that which is poured as a libation and offered at the altar. **Filthy wine** <note>original: "spurcum"</note> is that which it is not permitted to offer, or that to which water has been added, as if "spurious" <note>original: "spurium"</note>; that is, unclean. **Honorary wine** is that which is offered to kings and powerful people for the sake of honor. Cato says regarding his own innocence: "When I was an ambassador in the province, many gave 'honorary wine' to the praetors and consuls; I never accepted it, not even as a private citizen." **Raw wine** <note>original: "crudum"</note> is the unpleasant kind that slaves drink. **Sour wine** <note>original: "acidum"</note> is so called either because it is "sharp" <note>original: "acutum"</note> or because it is mixed with "water" <note>original: "aqua"</note>. For wine mixed with water is quickly reduced to this flavor. Whence also "acid" is as if "watery" <note>original: "aquidum"</note>, because the grapes are washed with water in the press after the wine has been squeezed out. It is a cheap drink suitable for slaves. **Spiced wine** <note>original: "conditum"</note> is so called because it is not simple but composed of a mixture of "pigments" <note>original: "pigmentorum"</note> or spices. **Milk-drink** <note>original: "lactatum"</note> is a potion made from milk. **Mead** <note>original: "mulsum"</note> is mixed from honey. For it is a potion of water and honey, which the Greeks call *melicraton*. **Honey-must** <note>original: "inomellum"</note> is must mixed with honey, violently shaken and stirred. **Honey-water** <note>original: "hydromellum"</note> is made from water and Martian apples. **Sack-wine** <note>original: "saccatum"</note> is a liquid of water mixed with wine dregs; it is made by being pressed through a "sack" <note>original: "sacco"</note> and mixed with other material, from which it retains both sweetness and sourness. **Rose-honey** <note>original: "rodomellus"</note> is so called because honey is mixed into the juice of a rose. **Honeyed wine** <note>original: "mellicratum"</note> is wine mixed with honey. **Mead** <note>original: "medus"</note> is as if "honey-like" <note>original: "melus"</note>, because it is made from honey; just as *calamitas* is used for *cadamitas*. **Wine-syrup** <note>original: "fecula"</note> is rich grape juice boiled down to the thickness of honey and cooled; it is useful for the stomach.

--- Page 211 ---
<meta>This page continues Isidore of Seville’s encyclopedic survey of human life. Having just finished a list of meats and seasonings, he now turns to various types of beverages—from raisin wine and beer to fish sauce—before transitioning into a detailed catalog of household vessels used for eating and drinking.</meta>

**Raisin wine** <note>original: *passum*</note> is whatever flows out from a compressed dried grape. It is called *passum* from "suffering" <note>original: *patiendo*</note>; for the grape undergoes a period of dryness and is boiled down, and from this raisin wine is made. **Reduced wine** <note>original: *defrutum*</note> is so named because it is "cheated" <note>original: *defraudetur*</note>, in that it suffers a "fraud" <note>original: *fraude*</note> in its volume through boiling. **Carenon** <note>original: *carenum*</note> <note>The OCR reads *Larenū*, but Isidore refers to *carenon*.</note> is so called because through boiling it "lacks" <note>original: *careat*</note> a part. For when a third part of the must is lost, what remains is *carenon*. The opposite of this is **sapa**, which, through boiling, is reduced until only a third remains. **Strong drink** <note>original: *sicera*</note> is any beverage that can intoxicate besides wine. Although its name is Hebrew, it sounds Latin because it is prepared from the juice of grain or fruits, or the fruit of palms is pressed into liquid, or when grains are boiled, the water becomes thicker—like a juice—and is strained; this drink itself is called *sicera*. **Beer** <note>original: *cervisia*</note> is named after Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>, that is, after grain. It is a drink made from the seeds of grain in various ways. **Celia** <note>A traditional Spanish wheat beer.</note> is named from "heating" <note>original: *calefaciendo*</note>. It is a drink made from the juice of part of a wheat crop. The power of the germ in the moistened grain is "awakened" <note>original: *suscitatur*</note> by fire, then dried, and after being reduced to flour, it is mixed with a mild juice. Once fermented, it gains a sour flavor and the heat of intoxication. This is made in those parts of Spain where the land is not fertile for wine. **Dregs** <note>original: *fex* (OCR: *Fer*)</note> are so called because they settle and "attach" <note>original: *affigat*</note> themselves to the bottom of the vessel. **Fish sauce** <note>original: *barum* or *garum*</note> is a salty liquid from fish, which was once made from a fish that the Greeks called *garon*; although it is now made from an infinite variety of fish, it retains its original name from its origin. It is called **liquamen** because the little fish, dissolved in the pickling, "melt" <note>original: *liquant*</note> into that same moisture. This liquid is also called **brine** <note>original: *salsugo*</note> or **pickle-water** <note>original: *muria*</note>. Indeed, *muria* is water mixed with salt, made to taste like the sea. **Juice** <note>original: *sucus*</note> is named because it is "pressed out" <note>original: *sacca*</note>, as is the case with **barley water** <note>original: *tisana*</note>. *Tisane*, *zema*, and *apocima* are all Greek terms.

### Chapter IV: On Eating Vessels

**Vessel** <note>original: *vas*</note> is named from "eating" <note>original: *vescendo*</note>, because food is placed in it. Its diminutive is **little vessel** <note>original: *vasculum*</note>. **Earthenware** <note>original: *fictilia*</note> is so called because it is fashioned and "molded" <note>original: *fingantur*</note> from earth. For "to fashion" <note>original: *fingere*</note> is to make, to form, and to mold; hence they are also called **potters** <note>original: *figuli*</note>. And an "earthen vessel" <note>original: *vas fictile*</note> is not called "false" <note>original: *fictum*</note> in the sense of a lie, but because it is formed so that it exists and has some shape. Thus the Apostle says: "Does the molded object <note>original: *figmentum*</note> say to the one who molded it, 'Why have you made me thus?'" Earthen vessels are said to have been first invented on the island of Samos, made from clay and hardened by fire; hence they are called **Samian vessels**. Later, it was discovered how to add red ochre and mold them from red clay. They say the use of earthenware vessels is older than the casting of bronze or silver. Among the ancients, they had neither gold nor silver, but only earthenware vessels. Thus they devised **vats** <note>original: *dolia*</note> for wine, **amphorae** for water, **water-jars** <note>original: *hydria*</note> for baths, and other things used by humans that are either made on a wheel or shaped by hand. **Clay** <note>original: *argilla*</note> that has been baked is called **pottery** <note>original: *testa*</note>, because while it was soft, it became a hard shell; it does not share its name with its former state, for what it was, it is no longer. **Arretine vessels** are named after Arretium, a town in Italy where they are made; they are red. Concerning these, Sedulius says: "The red pottery serves the greens placed within it." Some think **Samian vessels** take their name from the Greek town of Samos. Others say there is a type of clay in Italy, found not far from Rome, which is called Samian. **Chased vessels** <note>original: *celata vasa*</note> are made of silver or gold with figures

<column-break/>

standing out prominently, embossed either inside or out. They are named from "chasing" <note>original: *celo*</note>, which is a type of iron tool that the common people call a *ciliodem*. **Chrysen** vessels are gilded; this is a Greek term. **Bas-relief** <note>original: *anaglypha*</note> vessels are so called because they are carved on the upper surface; for in Greek *ana* means "up" and *glyphe* means "carving"—that is, "up-carved." A **dish** <note>original: *discus*</note> was formerly called a "shield" <note>original: *scutum*</note> from its appearance; hence also **saucer** <note>original: *scutella*</note> as a diminutive. It is indeed similar to a shield. Later it was called a *discus* because it "gives" <note>original: *det*</note> food, that is, presents it. From this, those who recline at the table are called *discumbentes*. Or it may be from the Greek *tou dikein*, meaning "to throw." A **serving platter** <note>original: *missorium*</note> is named by derivation from "table," as if it were a "measurer" <note>original: *mensorum*</note>. A **side-dish** <note>original: *parapsis*</note> is a four-cornered and four-sided vessel, named for its "equal sides" <note>original: *paribus absidis*</note>. A **plate** <note>original: *patena*</note> is so named because its edges are spread out and "open" <note>original: *patens*</note>. **Platters** <note>original: *lances*</note>. A **bowl** <note>original: *gavata*</note> is as if it were "hollowed out" <note>original: *cavata*</note>, with the letter *g* placed for *c*. From this also comes the **shell** <note>original: *concha*</note>; but the former is "hollowed," while the latter is "concave." The Greeks name these similarly. An **apophore** <note>original: *apophoreta*</note> is named by the Greeks from "carrying" fruit or something else, for it is flat. A **salt-cellar** <note>original: *salinum*</note> is a vessel suitable for salt. The same is also called a **sauce-boat** <note>original: *salcicam*</note>, as if it were for "salty things." A **vinegar-cruet** <note>original: *acetabulum*</note> is as if it were "vinegar-bearing" <note>original: *acetiferum*</note>. A **spoon** <note>original: *cochlear*</note> was first named for its use with **snails** <note>original: *cochleis*</note>. From this comes that verse: "I am handy for snails, yet no less useful for eggs. Do you not know why I am rather called a *cochleare*?" **Tripods** <note>original: *trisceles*</note> are Greek; in Latin they are *tripedes*. Those that stand on four feet are named improperly. In vessels, three things are sought to please: the hand of the craftsman, the weight of the silver, and the brightness of the metal.

### Chapter V: On Drinking Vessels

A **cup** <note>original: *poculum*</note> is named from "drinking" <note>original: *potando*</note>. Indeed, it is any vessel from which it is customary to drink. **Phials** <note>original: *phialae*</note> are so called because they are made of glass. For in Greek glass is called *hyalin*. **Pateras** <note>libation bowls</note> are called phials either because we are accustomed to drink from them or because they are "open" <note>original: *patentes*</note> with spreading lips. A **mixing bowl** <note>original: *cratera*</note> is a cup having two handles, and it is a Greek name. Among them it is declined as "this crater." In Latin, it is "this cratera," as Persius says: "If silver craters for you," and Virgil: "They set out large craters and crown the wines." They were first made by joining together twigs. From this they are called *craterae*, from the Greek *apo tou kratein*, meaning they "hold each other" together. **Cyathi**, **cyphi**, and **cymbia** are also types of cups. Among them, *cymbia* are cups shaped like a "skiff" <note>original: *cymba*</note> or boat. **Emittes** are a type of cup from which one drinks "continuously" <note>original: *ductim*</note>, that is, in one breath. **Bacchia** were first named from Bacchus, which is wine; later they came into use for water. **Chalice**, **calari**, and **scalae** are types of cups formerly made from wood, and named from it. For the Greeks called all wood *kala*. A **flask** <note>original: *ampulla*</note> is like a "large bubble" <note>original: *ampla bulla*</note>; for it is similar in its roundness to the bubbles that form from the spray of water when they are inflated by the wind.

### Chapter VI: On Wine and Water Vessels

A **wine-carrier** <note>original: *oenophorum*</note> is a vessel for carrying wine; for *oinos* is wine. From this comes the line: "The bottom of the wine-carrier changes our opinion." **Flasks** <note>original: *flascae*</note> are named from a Greek word. These were first made for carrying and storing phials, and were named accordingly. Later they passed into use for wine, while keeping the Greek name from which they began. **Flagon** <note>original: *lagena*</note> and **bucket** <note>original: *situla*</note> are Greek names, modified in part to become Latin. For they say *laginos*, we say *lagena*; they say *sitile*, we say *situla*. A **water-jar** <note>original: *hydria*</note> is a type of vessel for water...

<meta>This page continues Isidore’s discussion of household containers. In the previous section, he began describing vessels for drinking and wine. Here, he moves through various specialized containers for water, oil, cooking, storage, and lighting, explaining the linguistic origins of their names, often linking Latin terms to Greek or even Persian roots.</meta>

### Liber Z

...called by derivation. For the Greeks call water *hydor* <note>original: "Ydo"</note>.
The **bucket** <note>original: *situla*</note> is so named because it is suited for those who are thirsty <note>original: *sitientibus*</note> to drink. This is the vessel which the Greeks call a *kados*. The **earthenware vessel** <note>original: *vas fictile*</note> in Latin is better spoken of in the neuter gender than the masculine. Just as a **salt-cellar** <note>original: *salinum*</note> is called a vessel suited for salt. The **pitcher** <note>original: *urceus*</note> is a type of amphora, whose smaller name is the diminutive *urceolus*, and the even smaller *urcelolus*. The **basin** <note>original: *lyphus*</note> is where we wash our hands. The **small jar** <note>original: *seriola*</note> is a small *orca* <note>a large jar</note> arranged in a row, or an earthenware vessel for wine; it was first devised in Syria, just as **Cilician vessels** <note>original: *cilicises*</note> are named after Cilicia, from where they were first imported. **Casks** <note>original: *dolium*</note>, **vats** <note>original: *cupas*</note> are so called from "taking" <note>original: *capiendo*</note>, that is, because they are named for receiving water or wine; from which we also get "innkeepers" <note>original: *caupones*</note>. **Skins** <note>original: *utres*</note> are named from the "womb" <note>original: *utero*</note>. The **milking-pail** <note>original: *mulagarium*</note> is a vessel in which livestock are milked. The same is also called a *mulctrum*, from the fact that milk is milked into it. The **tub** <note>original: *labrum*</note> is so called because it is customary for the washing <note>original: *lauationem*</note> of infants to take place in it; its diminutive is *labellum*. The same is also called a **trough** <note>original: *alueum*</note>, because washing used to be done in it. **Basins** <note>original: *pelues*</note> are so named because feet <note>original: *pedes*</note> are washed there. The **siphon** <note>original: *siphon*</note> is a vessel named because it pours out water by blowing. For the Easterners use this; when they perceive a house is burning, they run with siphons full of water and extinguish the fires; but they also clean the upper parts of altars by squeezing out water with them.

->### Chapter VII. On Oil Vessels<-

The **omicadium** <note>an oil-press vessel</note> is an oil vessel. The **scortia** is an oil vessel named because it is made of hide <note>original: *corio*</note>. The **alabaster flask** <note>original: *alabastrum*</note> is a vessel for ointment, named after a stone of its own kind, which they call *alabastrites*, because it keeps ointments incorrupt. **Pyxides** <note>original: *pirides*</note> are small ointment vessels made of boxwood. For what we call boxwood, the Greeks call *pyxos*. The **lenticula** is a modest bronze or silver vessel, four-sided on its wide side, which is also called a *lekythos* <note>original: *lechitū*</note>. For it is a vessel for oil with which kings and priests were anointed; it is named from "soothing" <note>original: *lenitendo*</note>.

->### Chapter VIII. On Kitchen Vessels<-

All vessels prepared for the sake of cooking are called **cook-pots** <note>original: *cocula*</note>. Plautus says: "All my substance is cooked away in bronze pots." The **pot** <note>original: *olla*</note> is named because water bubbles <note>original: *ebulliat*</note> in it when fire is placed beneath, so that the steam is emitted higher up. From which also the "bubble" <note>original: *bulla*</note> is named, which is sustained by the breath of wind inside the water. The **small pan** <note>original: *patella*</note> is as if it were "open" <note>original: *patula*</note>. For an *olla* has its mouth narrowed. The **kettle** <note>original: *lacabus*</note> and the **cooking-pot** <note>original: *cucuma*</note> are named from the sound of boiling. These names are common to both Greeks and Latins. But whether the Latins borrowed these words from the Greeks, or the Greeks from the Latins, is uncertain. **Cauldrons** <note>original: *lebetes*</note> are bronze vessels named in the Greek language; for they are smaller pots prepared for use in cooking. The **frying-pan** <note>original: *sartago*</note> is named from the rattling sound when oil burns in it. **Tripods** <note>original: *tripedes*</note> are named because they stand on three feet; the Greeks call these *tripodas*. The **amula** <note>a small vessel</note> is named from its roundness, like the fruit of apple trees <note>original: *mala pomorum*</note>; so also the Greeks. The **threshing-vessel** <note>original: *tribulum*</note> is named because grain runs there, as if "grain-runner" <note>original: *currifrugum*</note>. The **poker** <note>original: *rutabulum*</note> is named from "driving forward" <note>original: *pruehendo*</note> dung or fire, for the sake of baking bread.

->### Chapter IX. On Storage Vessels<-

The **treasury** <note>original: *gazophylacium*</note> is a chest where those things sent for the needs of the poor are collected in the temple. The name is composed from the Persian and Greek languages. For in the Persian tongue *gaza* means "treasure," and in Greek *phylakion* is interpreted as "custody." The **chest** <note>original: *arca*</note> is so named because it "shuts out" <note>original: *arceat*</note> sight and prevents it. From this also comes "secret" <note>original: *arcanum*</note>; from here

<column-break/>

and "secret" <note>original: *arcanum*</note>, that is, a hidden thing from which others are "shut out" <note>original: *arcentur*</note>. *Liburum* is a Greek name for what we call a chest. The **compartment** <note>original: *loculus*</note> is a place <note>original: *locus*</note> made for putting something in the earth, or for guarding clothes or money. Whence it is also called as a diminutive. *Monocicia* is as if "small" <note>original: *modicia*</note>; whence also "modicum" <note>a little bit</note>, just as Italians are accustomed to say *ocie* for *hodie* <note>meaning "today"</note>. **Cases** <note>original: *scrinia*</note>. The **sack** <note>original: *saccus*</note> is named from *sagus* <note>a coarse cloak</note>, because it is made by being sewn together like a cloak. The **purse** <note>original: *marsupium*</note> is a small bag for coins, which the Greeks call *marsypos*. For certain Greek names are slightly inflected into Latin for the sake of Roman speech. **Provisions-bags** <note>original: *sitarcia*</note> belong to sailors, from the fact that they are "sewn" <note>original: *sutae*</note>. The **wrapper** <note>original: *inuolucrum*</note> is so named because it holds something "wrapped up" <note>original: *inuolutu*</note> within itself. The **fiscus** <note>the state treasury</note> is a public bag; from which both "little baskets" <note>original: *fiscellae*</note> and "wicker baskets" <note>original: *fiscinae*</note> are named. The tax collectors have this, and into it they put the public debt which is rendered to kings. But *fiscus* belongs to the primary authority; the derivative is *fiscina*, the diminutive is *fiscella*. The **basket** <note>original: *canistrum*</note> is woven from "reeds" <note>original: *cannis*</note>, from which it is named; others assert it is Greek. The **little casket** <note>original: *cistella*</note> is named from the "ribs" <note>original: *costis*</note> of reed or wood from which it is woven. The **hamper** <note>original: *cophinus*</note> is a vessel suited for clearing out dung and transporting it, from woven twigs; about which the Psalmist says for Israel: "His hands served in the hamper." However, the *cophinus* is named as if it were "curved" <note>original: *couuus*</note> or "hollow" <note>original: *cauus*</note>. **Wicker-baskets** <note>original: *corbes*</note> are so called because they are woven from "curved" <note>original: *curuatis*</note> twigs. The **small basket** <note>original: *sportula*</note> is a diminutive from *sporta*. A **basket** <note>original: *sporta*</note> is so called because it "carries out" <note>original: *exportet*</note> something, or because it is made of Spanish broom <note>original: *sparto*</note>. For *spartum* is a twiggy shrub without leaves, named for its "roughness" <note>original: *asperitate*</note>, similar to sedge-grass, and ropes are fashioned from it.

->### Chapter X. On Lighting Vessels<-

From "tending" <note>original: *colendo*</note> fire and wood, the ancients called it the **hearth** <note>original: *focus*</note>. For *phos* in Greek is "fire" in Latin. Whence also, according to certain philosophers, all things are created. And indeed, without heat nothing is born—to the point that it is said of self-production: "nothing is produced in sterile cold." Varro, however, says they are called *foci* because they "foster" <note>original: *foueant*</note> fires. For the fire itself is the flame, but whatever fosters the fire is called a *focus*, whether it be an altar or anything else in which fire is fostered. The **lamp** <note>original: *lucerna*</note> is named from *lychnus* <note>a Greek lamp</note>; from which the "lu" syllable is short, as Persius says: "The lamps being arranged vomited a thick cloud." For if it were named from "light" <note>original: *luce*</note>, the meter would not stand. However, *lychnus* is as if "lucinus." For it is the wick of the lamp. The **candelabrum** is named from "candles" <note>original: *candela*</note>, as if it were a "candle-bearer" <note>original: *candeliferum*</note> because it carries a candle. **Wax tapers** <note>original: *cerei*</note> have their name by derivation from the "wax" <note>original: *cera*</note> from which they are formed; of which someone said: "Here I, a wax light, will provide for you nocturnal fires. When the light is withdrawn, I shall be another light for you." The **candle** <note>original: *candela*</note> is named from "shining white" <note>original: *candendo*</note>, because it shines with white light. **Hanging lights** <note>original: *lacunaria*</note> are as if "light-holders" <note>original: *lucanaria*</note>, that is, shining in the air. **Torches** <note>original: *funalia*</note> are those which are within the wax, named from the "ropes" <note>original: *funibus*</note> which our ancestors had surrounded with wax before the use of papyrus; from which also "funerals" <note>original: *funera*</note> are named. However, the Greeks call torches *scholakes* because they are "twisted" <note>original: *scolices*</note>, that is, winding. These the Romans named ropes and torches. Torch-bearing candelabra among the ancients had protruding hooked points on which the small ropes smeared with wax or similar light-nourishment were fixed. And so these very sharp points were called *funalia*. A **lamp** <note>original: *lampas*</note> is a flame shining at the top, named because it seems to show the motion of a "licking" <note>original: *lambentis*</note> tongue. A **torch** <note>original: *fax*</note> is so called because it "makes hearths" <note>original: *focos faciat*</note>; its diminutive is *facula*. A **lantern** <note>original: *laterna*</note> is so called because it has the "light" <note>original: *lucem*</note> enclosed "within" <note>original: *interius*</note>. For it is made from...

...enclosed in glass and sealed with plaster, so that the blasts of the wind cannot reach it, and it can easily be carried everywhere to provide light. It is called a **night-light** <note>original: *lucubrum*</note> because it shines in the shadows <note>original: *in umbra*</note>. For it is a small fire usually formed from thin hemp and wax. A **pyre** <note>original: *pyra*</note> is that which is usually built in the manner of a tower out of wood so that it may burn. For in Greek, *pyr* <note>original: *pyro*</note> means fire; thus a *pyra* is the heap of wood itself when it is not yet burning. It is called a **funeral pile** <note>original: *rogus*</note> when it has begun to burn, and it is called a **burnt-offering** <note>original: *bustum*</note> when it is already burnt up. The **Pharos** <note>original: *Pharus*</note> is a sea tower, which both Greeks and Latins commonly call *pharos* based on its use. This is because its flame is seen from far away by sailors, as we said above, such as the one Ptolemy is said to have built near Alexandria for eight hundred talents. Its use is to show fires to ships on their nocturnal course to announce shallows and the entrances to ports, so that sailors, deceived by the darkness, do not fall upon the rocks. For Alexandria has dangerous approaches due to deceptive shallows. Hence, the machines built in porticoes for the service of providing light are called *pharos*. For in Greek, *phos* means light, and *oros* means vision. Hence, the "morning star" is called *phosphorus* in Greek <note>literally "light-bearer"</note>.

### On litters and chairs Chapter 11.

**Litters** <note>original: *lectice*</note> are named from "plucked herbs" <note>original: *lectis herbis*</note> <note>Isidore suggests the first beds were made of gathered plants</note>. **Bedding** <note>original: *stratus*</note> is named from "strewing" <note>original: *sternendo*</note>, as if it were a mat. In these alone the ancients used to recline for sleep, before woolen coverings were discovered. A **mat** <note>original: *storia*</note> is that which is spread on the ground. A **cot** <note>original: *cama*</note> is low and near the ground; for the Greeks call "low" *chamai*. A **resting place** <note>original: *cubile*</note> is a place for lying down. A **pallet** <note>original: *grabatum*</note> is a Greek term. A **portable bed** <note>original: *baionula*</note> is a bed which is carried on a journey, from "carrying" <note>original: *baiulando*</note>, that is, conveying. A **cushioned seat** <note>original: *pulvinar*</note> is the bed of the wealthy; from this also comes the "small pillow" <note>original: *pulvillus*</note>. **Sphinxes** <note>original: *sfinge*</note> are litters on which there are carved figures of sphinxes, which we call griffins. **Punic beds** <note>original: *punicani lecti*</note> are small and low, first brought from Carthage and named from there. **Litters without backboards** <note>original: *lectice sine plutei*</note>; regarding these, the satirist <note>Juvenal</note> speaking of his own life says that, against the Emperor's decree, he used litters instead of beds. The **side-board** <note>original: *sponda*</note> is the outer part of the bed; the **back-board** <note>original: *pluteus*</note> is the inner part. **Marriage beds** <note>original: *geniales lecti*</note> are properly those which are prepared for girls getting married, named for "begetting children" <note>original: *generandis liberis*</note>. **Cradles** <note>original: *cunabula*</note> are the little beds in which infants are accustomed to lie; they are named because they are used for the small ones, as if they were "new-born beds" <note>original: *cinabula*</note>. For in Greek, *kyein* <note>original: *cine*</note> means to give birth. A **bier** <note>original: *pheretrum*</note> is so called because the dead are carried in it; it is a Greek name. For it is called *pheretron* from *pherein*, that is, from "carrying." In Latin it is called a *capulus* because it is carried "above the heads" <note>original: *supra capita*</note> of men; thus Plautus says: "A man near the *capulus*," meaning an old man close to the grave. **Benches** <note>original: *scamna*</note> are those things placed by higher beds, named from "climbing" <note>original: *scandendo*</note>, that is, ascending. From this, a **footstool** <note>original: *scabellum*</note> is placed by small beds or chairs for the ascent. A footstool is also called a *suppedaneum*. For what the Greeks call a *hypopodion*, the Latins called a *scabellum*, and others called a *suppedaneum*, because it is "under the feet" <note>original: *sub pedibus*</note>. **Steps** <note>original: *scansilia*</note> are the levels where honored people have their seats. **Seats** <note>original: *sedes*</note> are so named because among the ancient Romans there was no custom of reclining; hence they were said to "sit together." Later, as Varro says in *On the Life of the Roman People*, the men began to recline and the women to sit, because reclining was seen as unseemly in a woman. A **seat** <note>original: *sedes*</note> in the singular number is properly for a kingdom, which in Greek is called a **throne** <note>original: *thronus*</note>. Likewise, what the Greeks call a throne, we call a **royal seat** <note>original: *solium*</note>.

<column-break/>

**Low benches** <note>original: *subsellia*</note> are the chairs of others, such as teachers. A **royal seat** <note>original: *solium*</note> is where kings sit for the protection of their person; according to some, it is named for its "solidity" <note>original: *soliditate*</note>, as if it were solid. According to others, by a change of letters, it is as if it were a *sedium* from "sitting." Whence also a **chair** <note>original: *sella*</note> is named as if it were a *sedda*, and **benches** <note>original: *subsellia*</note> as if they were *subsedia*. **Curule chairs** <note>original: *selle curules*</note> were those in which magistrates sat to deliver judgments. They were called "curule" because among the ancient praetors and consuls, on account of the distance of their travels, they were carried to the forum in a **chariot** <note>original: *curru*</note>; the chairs which were carried behind them, in which they used to sit to declare the laws, were named "curule chairs" from the chariot. **Tripods** are stools having three feet; so also **tripod candelabras** are those which similarly have three feet.

### On vehicles Chapter 12.

A **wagon** <note>original: *carrum*</note> is named from the "axis" <note>original: *cardine*</note> of the wheels. Hence also **chariots** <note>original: *currus*</note> are named because they are seen to have wheels. A **wheel** <note>original: *rota*</note> is so called because it "rushes" <note>original: *ruat*</note>, and "round" <note>original: *rotundum*</note> is named from the wheel. A **carriage** <note>original: *reda*</note> is a type of vehicle with four wheels; the ancients called these *retas* because they had wheels. A **ceremonial carriage** <note>original: *carpentum*</note> is a type of pompous vehicle, as if it were a "pompous wagon." A **heavy wagon** <note>original: *plaustrum*</note> is a vehicle of two wheels by which burdens are carried. It is called a *plaustrum* because it rolls, as if it were called a *pilastrum*. A **high-wheeled cart** <note>original: *caracutium*</note> is a vehicle of very high wheels, as if it were a "sharp wagon." A **carriage-body** <note>original: *capsus*</note> or **coach** <note>original: *carruca*</note> is enclosed on all sides, like a chest <note>original: *capsa*</note>. A **traveling carriage** <note>original: *pilentrum*</note> or **praetorium** is an enclosed vehicle of four wheels, which matrons once used.
> Virgil: *Matrons in soft carriages.*
Horace:
> *More grooms and horses must be fed, and carriages led.*
Formerly, these carriages were of a saffron color, not rosy as they are now; none but chaste matrons could use them, just as they could not use certain headbands. A **litter** <note>original: *basterna*</note> is a vehicle for a journey, as if it were a "soft vessel" <note>original: *vasterna*</note> composed of soft bedding, carried by two animals.

### On the remaining things which are in use Chapter 13.

A **staff** <note>original: *baculus*</note> is said to have been invented by Bacchus, the discoverer of the vine, upon which men moved by wine might lean; just as *baculus* comes from Bacchus, so **stick** <note>original: *bacillus*</note> is its diminutive. **Clubs** <note>original: *fustes*</note> are named because they "stand fixed" in the earth, which peasants call stakes; with these, young men are struck for crimes. **Levers** <note>original: *vectes*</note> are so named because they are "carried" <note>original: *vectentur*</note> by the hands, by which doors and bolts are pried out. **Scissors** <note>original: *forfices*</note>, according to etymology, are spelled with an *f* if they are for "thread" <note>original: *filo*</note>, which are for tailors. If for "hair" <note>original: *pilo*</note>, they are spelled with a *p* <note>original: *forpices*</note>, which are for barbers. If from "taking" <note>original: *accipiendo*</note>, they are spelled with a *c* <note>original: *forcipes*</note>, because they take hold of "hot" things <note>original: *formum*</note>, which are for blacksmiths. For the ancients called "hot" *formum*; hence "beautiful" <note>original: *formosus*</note>. A **razor** <note>original: *novacula*</note> is a thin and quite sharp iron tool. It is called *novacula* because it "renews" <note>original: *inovet*</note> the face. A **comb** <note>original: *pecten*</note> is so called because it makes the hair "combed" <note>original: *pexos*</note> and orderly. A **curling iron** <note>original: *calamistrum*</note> is a needle which, when heated and applied, warms and twists the hair. Whence also those who twist their hair are called *calamistrati*. A **key** <note>original: *clavis*</note> is so called because it "closes" <note>original: *claudat*</note> and opens. A **chain** <note>original: *catenatum*</note> because it "holds by catching" <note>original: *capiendo teneat*</note>. A **sundial** <note>original: *horologium*</note> because there we "read" <note>original: *legamus*</note> the hours, that is, we collect them. For it is placed in a sunny spot, where the shadow runs from a pin along lines to show whatever hour of the day it is.

### On rustic instruments Chapter 14.

A **plowshare** <note>original: *vomer*</note> is named as if it "digs out the ground" <note>original: *vi humum eruat*</note> or from "vomiting" the earth. Concerning which Lucretius says:
> *The hooked plow, the iron plowshare wears away hidden in the fields.*

...he who sins has. For the pile of transgressions grows according to the rank of their merits <note>original: "ordine meritorum"; in a medieval context, this suggests that the higher a person's spiritual or social standing, the more weight their actions carry</note>, and often what is forgiven in lesser people is held against those in higher positions.

### On More Serious Sins, Chapter 19.

Through the experience or the contempt of small sins, greater sins are committed. Thus, people are struck more harshly for great crimes because they refused to be corrected regarding small ones. By divine judgment, they fall into a more wicked state of guilt because they despise the restraint of their minor faults. Many fall from one crime into another because, while having knowledge of God, they neglect the fear of Him; though they know Him through knowledge, they do not honor the covenant. Therefore, they are blinded by divine judgment to commit things that must be punished, and as a penalty for a crime already committed, they add a new crime upon the old. Often one sin is the cause of another; it is committed when one thing arises from another as if it were its own offspring, just as lust is usually born from the excessive gluttony of the belly. 

Indeed, sin is permitted as a punishment for sin when, by the merit of each person's sin, God abandons them and they go into another, worse sin, by which the one who committed it is further defiled. Therefore, the preceding sin is the cause of the following sin, and the following sin is the punishment for the preceding transgression. Thus, preceding sins are the cause of subsequent crimes so that those which follow are the punishment for those which came before. The punishment for preceding sins is itself called "hardening" <note>original: "induratio"; a theological concept where a person becomes spiritually insensitive</note>, coming from divine justice. This is why it says through the prophet: *You have hardened our heart so that we would not fear you* <note>original: "Indurasti cor nostrum ne timeremus te"; quoting Isaiah 63:17</note>. For God does not push anyone who is righteous to become evil; but while they are already evil, they are hardened so that they become worse. As the Apostle also says: *Because they did not receive the truth of God so that they might be saved, God sent upon them a spirit of error* <note>original: "misit illis deus spiritum erroris"; referencing 2 Thessalonians 2:10-11</note>. Therefore, He causes some to sin—those in whom such sins have already preceded—so that by His just judgment they deserve to go toward the worse. Indeed, some sins, when others have preceded them, fall into the punishment which the sins deserve. Some sins come from the wrath of God, which are weighed out according to the merit of other sins. Whence also through the prophet it says: *Behold, you are angry and we have sinned; we have always been in them* <note>original: "ecce tu iratus es et nos peccavimus; in ipsis fuimus semper"; quoting Isaiah 64:5</note>. It is as if he were saying: "Because we have always been in sins, you are angry so that we might sin more grievously." For what it means to deserve the wrath of God, and what it is to provoke God, the wise reader ought to know. For the wrath that is provoked is more serious than that which is merely deserved. For we deserve it when we sin through ignorance; we provoke it when we know how to do good and refuse to do it. Now, while we are alive, we can avoid the wrath of God. Let us fear it, lest when that terror of judgment comes, it might be felt, but cannot be avoided.

### On Manifest and Hidden Sins, Chapter 20.

It is a greater fault to sin openly than secretly. For one is doubly guilty when they offend openly, because they both perform the act and teach it to others. Of such people, Isaiah says: *And they proclaimed their sins like Sodom, and did not hide them* <note>original: "Et peccata sua quasi sodoma praedicauerunt"; quoting Isaiah 3:9</note>. For many who offend publicly proclaim their disgraceful acts without any weight of conscience, nor do they feel any shame for their crime. For it is already a portion of justice to hide one's iniquity from others and to blush within oneself for one's own sins. To commit a sin is a crime; to boast of a sin is a "cry" <note>original: "clamor"; often used in the Bible to describe sins that "cry out" for justice, like those of Sodom</note>. Concerning this, 

<column-break/>

the Apostle also says: *And let outcry be taken away from you, along with all malice* <note>original: "Et clamor: auferatur a vobis cum omni malitia"; quoting Ephesians 4:31</note>—that is, along with the sins themselves. From the very fact that someone does not hide the sin they commit, it is already an indication of judgment, for they do not blush except for the guilt of their conscience. Therefore, by the very fact that someone blushes for their deed, they become their own judge.

### On the Love of Sin, Chapter 21.

It is one thing not to sin out of the love of God, and another out of the fear of punishment. For he who does not sin out of the love of God's charity shrinks from all evil by embracing the good of justice; sin does not delight him even if impunity for the crime were permitted. But he who restrains his vices only by the penalty of punishment—though he may not complete the work of sin, the will to sin still lives within him. He grieves that the forbidden thing is denied to him by the law. He who receives the reward of a good work is the one who acts out of a love for justice, not the one who remains righteous only out of fear of punishments. Some both love sin and do it; some love it and do not do it; many, however, do it and do not love it; some do not do the sin and yet hate justice. But he who not only loves sin but also does it sins more gravely than he who does not do it but loves it. Sometimes he who does not do it receives a greater punishment than he who does it and hates it. It is most serious not only to do sin but also to love it. For there are some who are immediately confused once a disgraceful act is committed, and there are those who not only do not grieve for having done evil, but even boast of the evil work itself. Thus, in the comparison of evil, it becomes worse when, rejoicing in their vices, they are extolled toward the worse. Of such people Solomon says: *Who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things* <note>original: "Qui laetantur cum male fecerint et exultant in rebus pessimis"; quoting Proverbs 2:14</note>.

### On the Necessity of Sinning, Chapter 22.

Sometimes we are also evil by necessity rather than by will, as we might think. However, the necessity of evil must be turned into the will for good. Many sin not by will but by necessity alone, fearing temporal poverty. And while they flee from the necessity of the present world, they are deprived of future goods. Likewise, some commit sin by will and not by necessity; they become wicked though forced by no poverty; in these, the mind alone desires to be evil. For they do not even love the thing they seek; they are delighted only by the malice of the sin itself.

### On the Habit of Sinning, Chapter 23.

It is better to beware of sin than to correct it. For we more easily resist an enemy by whom we have not yet been conquered than one by whom we know we have already been overcome and defeated. Every sin is feared more before it is committed. But however heavy it may be, once it becomes a habit, it is thought of as light and is committed without any fear. In these people, every sin grows as if by certain steps. For a wicked thought gives birth to delight; delight to consent; consent to action; action to habit; habit to necessity. Thus, a person entangled in these bonds is held bound by a certain chain of vices, so that they can in no way be torn away from it unless divine grace takes hold of the hand of the one lying there. To commit a sin is to fall into a pit; but to make a habit of sinning is to narrow the mouth of the pit, so that the one who fell cannot get out.

<summary>This passage explores the progression of sin from minor faults to inescapable habits, emphasizing that sin can be a punishment for previous sins and distinguishing between those who avoid sin out of love for God versus fear of punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book II of Isidore of Seville's Sententiae, following a discussion on how the severity of a sin is magnified by the status of the sinner. This section transitions into the psychological and spiritual mechanics of habit, repentance, and the internal battle of thoughts.</meta>

II
B 2

But sometimes God delivers even such people, provided He changes their despair into the conversion of freedom. For by His mercy sins are forgiven, and by His guidance, one is prevented from going into worse sins. It is most wicked to sin, but it is worse to make a habit of sinning. One rises easily from the former, but from the latter only with great labor, as one must fight against a bad habit. The prophet <note>likely referring to the imagery in the Psalms or Lamentations regarding the "deep pit"</note> asserts that a habit of evil-doing is a descent into the deep, by the use of which a person is held bound as if by a certain law, so that they commit sin even when they do not wish to. However, to rise quickly from a fall is not to go into the deep. The Apostle <note>St. Paul, specifically referencing Romans 7:23</note> says that the law of sin is in his members, which "law" is actually the habit we conceive by sinning; we do not depart from it when we wish because we are already held by the bond of necessity through habit. Truly, love <note>original: "amor"; here meaning the desire for God or virtue</note> works much in a person, but the flesh resists by the law of bad habit. Yet he who prevails in repressing what insolently assails him exults boldly because of a good conscience. Frequent sinning must be avoided; for the very fact that God works our salvation out of our many evils—as wonderful as it is—is also a sign of how depraved we are. Therefore, we must fear trusting that we will be saved in such a way, lest perhaps while we expect to be healed from vices, we instead multiply those vices and do not attain salvation. Therefore, let us strive either not to fall, or, having fallen, to rise up quickly through conversion. Sinning is to be avoided entirely. And if by human frailty a sin should creep in, that which is felt to have been committed wickedly must be corrected immediately. For a fault that is recognized quickly is corrected quickly, but a wound that is applied to rotting limbs only after a long time is healed more slowly by treatments. The repetition of sin is more grievous, just as it is if a disease comes upon a disease, or if rain falls upon rain. Delaying repentance creates a monstrosity of crime. Hence the prophet says: "Woe to you who draw iniquity with the cords of vanity, and sin as if with a cart-rope" <note>original: "Ue inquit qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis"; Isaiah 5:18</note>. For he draws iniquity with cords who delays being converted to God. To draw iniquity is to make a delay in one's sins. Hence the Psalm also says: "They have prolonged their iniquities; the righteous Lord will cut the necks of sinners" <note>Psalm 129:3-4</note>.

# On the Remembrance of Sin, Chapter 24.

It is good for a man to always keep his past sins before his eyes, according to the sentence of the Psalm: "And my sin is always before me" <note>Psalm 51:3</note>. For just as one ought not to remember sin with a sense of pleasure, so it is always necessary for each person to commemorate their sin in weeping. In the just man, the remembrance of sin creates a stretching <note>original: "tensio"; a spiritual striving or tension</note> of the soul. But those who are subject to luxury and greed even glory in the very work of sin with contumacious pride. In a servant of God, the remembrance of sin should be so great that they always confess what they have done with tears. Hence the Psalm also says: "I was turned in my misery while the thorn is fastened... I have made my sin known to you; I will pronounce my injustices against myself to the Lord" <note>Psalm 32:4-5</note>. For he had said above: "Because I was silent"—that is, I did not confess—"all my bones grew old while I cried out all day long." Why does he repent having been silent, if not for the lack of confession of sins? Why does he grieve for having cried out, if not for the defense of his evils? For he who becomes a defender of his own sins

<column-break/>

must necessarily accuse himself through penance for what he perversely admitted through pride.

# On Thought, Chapter 25.

The cause of sinning is two-fold: that is, of deed and of thought. One of these is called iniquity, which is carried out by deed; the other is called injustice, which is admitted by thought. First, however, the action must be cut away, and afterward the thought. First the depraved works, and subsequently the desires. Conversely, however, works proceed from thought, and thought is born from work; for even if someone is vacant from evil deeds, they will not be innocent because of the malice of depraved thought alone. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: "Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes" <note>Isaiah 1:16</note>. For we do not only fail in deeds, but also in thoughts, if we take delight in them when they occur unlawfully. Just as the viper dies when torn apart by the young in her womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us; and once the internal viperous poison is conceived, they consume us and destroy our soul with a cruel wound. It is not within our power to prevent thoughts of evil suggestion from occurring, but it belongs to our will whether we let our thoughts lie in the soul. Therefore, the former is not reduced to guilt, but the latter is imputed as actual fault. For illicit thoughts to occur is the work of demons; but to be delighted by perverse thoughts is our own. It often happens that impure images of bodily things which we have learned are set before our minds and we think of them unwillingly; and the more we strive to turn the sharp edge of the mind away from them, the more they thrust themselves into the soul and creep into us with obscene habits. This happens by the mortal condition which the first man <note>Adam</note> earned as a punishment for his sin. While each person is reached by divine illumination, they are immediately struck by the annoyance of foul thoughts. But the servant of God, by the judgment of the fear of God, rejects carnal temptations from himself and repels the foul ones by placing good thoughts against them. Great observance must be applied to the guarding of the heart, because the origin of either a good or an evil thing consists there. For as it is written: "Out of the heart come evil thoughts" <note>Matthew 15:19</note>. Therefore, if we first resist the depraved thought, we do not fall into the lapse of the deed. It is not to be feared if good and evil things come into thought; rather, one should glory if the evil mind is discerned from the good by the understanding of reason. Likewise, it does no good that we discern between good and evil with a prudent sense unless we either avoid evil thoughts in practice or do the good things we have understood.

# On Conscience, Chapter 26.

The human condition disturbs the mind with various vices; even before the pains of hell, the soul already suffers the pains of conscience through disordered appetite. A man will be able to flee anywhere except from his own heart. For no one can recede from themselves. Wherever he goes, the conscience of his own guilt does not leave him. Though every man who acts wickedly may escape human judgments, he cannot escape the judgment of his own conscience. For even if he hides what he does from others, he cannot hide it from himself, for he fully knows that what he has done is evil. Therefore, a double judgment occurs in him...

<summary>This page explores the internal battle against sin, emphasizing that while deeds are the visible result, the struggle begins in the thoughts and is cemented by habit. It highlights the role of conscience as an inescapable internal judge and the necessity of immediate repentance to prevent minor faults from becoming ingrained "laws" of behavior.</summary>
